ideas.name: Managed recovery tier (15% drafted-for-you, 20% with escalation)
ideas.mechanism: Only for the existing withheld_customer_payment category (BUILD_PLAN §14.7). When the builder opens a recovery case they choose a service tier, recorded on the case before any pursuit: Self-serve 10% (builder drafts from templates); Managed 15% (a JobGuard recovery-desk credit controller drafts every reminder, statement of account and letter-before-claim from the cited case facts, monitors replies, and queues each send for the builder's exact approval under D10, so the builder stays the sender); Escalated 20% (adds a partner solicitor's fixed-fee letter of claim, a Pre-Action Protocol compliant bundle and a filled MCOL/N1 pack the builder files themselves; court fees passed through at cost). The fee is charged exactly as today: only on cash settled after case opening, allocated per §14.8, posted through the v3 routine, which already keys cumulative Q by job AND rate (§14.9), so a 15%/20% rate is a parameter, not a new formula. Delivered by an in-house recovery desk (one credit controller per ~150 open cases) plus a panel solicitor on fixed fees.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of recovered cash, per case; court and solicitor disbursements passed through at cost with builder approval.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 1 genuinely withheld case/yr, £1,500 recovered, 50% choose Managed: 0.5 x 1,500 x 15% = £112. Small firm 2 cases x £4,000 = £8,000 recovered, 60% managed at blended 16%: 0.6 x 8,000 x 0.16 = £768. Firm 4 cases x £6,000 = £24,000, 70% managed at blended 17.5%: 0.7 x 24,000 x 0.175 = £2,940. Case counts are guesses; the research found no UK data on withheld payments for domestic builders (report, 'Builders' willingness to pay'). Ordinary late payment and routine reminders stay fee-free per §14.7.
ideas.trust_note: Builder opts in per case and sees the rate before JobGuard lifts a finger; 15-20% sits inside the 8-15% fresh-debt collector band and well under claims firms (report, benchmark table), and JobGuard visibly does the work, which is the fairness condition the research identifies (Xia et al.). Borderline element: if the desk ever contacts the homeowner in JobGuard's own name it stops being 'builder sends' and needs a new D10 version and legal review; keep the builder as sender. Homeowner customers give no Late Payment Act interest to offset the fee, so say so on the case-open screen.
ideas.regulatory: D10 (builder sends; no autonomous collection), D03 v2 case-opening conditions, D01 rate table needs a versioned 10/15/20 entry, D05 for the statement approval. FCA Art 39F 'debt collecting' does not appear to cover recovering services invoices (SRA guidance, needs legal sign-off). Consumer-facing chasing must satisfy DMCC Act 2024 unfair-practice rules and Administration of Justice Act 1970 s.40 (harassment of debtors); the escalated tier must follow the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims when the customer is an individual. Solicitor on fixed fee avoids DBA Regulations 2013. JobGuard never receives the money (AGENTS §3).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-2 (billability), M4-5 (pursuit templates, builder-approved sends), M4-9/M4-10 (v3 derivation and statements), behind G4 with D01/D03/D10 approved. New work: a service_tier field on recovery_case fixed at open, a rate parameter in the D01 policy version, a 'drafter' membership role with no send authority. Roughly one task on top of the M4 chain; the real cost is hiring the desk.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder opens a Managed case to get free chasing labour then settles privately and reports nothing (same residual risk as §14.10); mitigate with case-open terms, a cap on open managed cases per plan tier, and the existing D11 'recovery discussed then no in-app landing' signal. Builder relabels ordinary late payment as withheld to get the desk; the D03 overdue threshold and 'customer refused/disputed/ignored' precondition already gate this.
ideas.precedent: UK debt collectors 8-15% on fresh debt, 20-35% aged; hybrid £25-75 file fee + 6-10% (Cosmo DCA 2026, in success_fee_benchmarks.md §3). Chaser pairs credit-control software with a commission-based collections service (commission not published; chaserhq.com/debt-collections).

ideas.name: Credit-control desk add-on (flat monthly, ordinary late payment)
ideas.mechanism: A flat add-on to the subscription, not a percentage: a JobGuard credit controller reviews the builder's aged-debtor list weekly, drafts the routine reminders, statements and 'payment due Friday' messages from invoice facts, and queues each for one-tap builder approval and send (D10: builder remains sender). Covers exactly the ordinary late payment that §14.7 says can never carry a success fee, so it monetises the government-measured pain (£11bn/yr, £26bn owed) with a predictable fee. Priced £39/month (Solo), £49/month (Builder plan), £99/month (Firm), ex VAT. Delivered by the same in-house recovery desk as the managed tier; one controller handles ~80 add-on accounts.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, monthly, alongside the subscription.
ideas.assumptions: Take-up assumptions: Solo 10% x £39 x 12 = £47; Small firm 35% x £49 x 12 = £206; Firm 50% x £99 x 12 = £594. Take-up is a guess anchored on LSBS 2024 (51% of no-employee businesses giving credit hit late-payment problems) and Satago/Chaser existing at £45-£199/month.
ideas.trust_note: Plain labour-for-money; nothing hidden, no percentage, and it addresses the loss the builder already knows about. The only care point is keeping it separate from the 10%/15% case path so a builder never feels a routine reminder was 'converted' into a fee case: the add-on must never open a recovery case; only the builder can.
ideas.regulatory: D10 and M4-16 communication control (builder approves exact text and recipient); DMCC Act 2024 unfair-practice rules for consumer-facing reminders; not FCA debt collecting on the SRA reading (legal sign-off required). D09 add-on entitlement; D05 for the recurring charge.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-5 (templates and approved sends) and M4-16 (dunning and communication control), plus a 'drafter' role and an add-on entitlement on subscription_terms (M4-13). About one task; behind G4 for real sends to real customers.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Builders may try to use it for disputed invoices (dispute work is out of scope and must route to the dispute pack); the desk must refuse to draft anything that alleges more than the invoice facts show (M4-5 'each factual amount has evidence').
ideas.precedent: Chaser £199/month under £4m turnover; Satago £45/£80/£200 fixed tiers (success_fee_benchmarks.md §6, vendor comparison not fetched). Bookkeepers charging £100-£200/month for sole traders show builders already buy admin labour monthly (wearegro.co.uk 2026 guide).

ideas.name: Dispute and evidence-pack preparation (fixed fee, human-reviewed)
ideas.mechanism: The M4-3 deterministic evidence bundle (already built synthetically in #92) becomes a sellable product in three grades, ordered by the builder for a named dispute: (a) Automated narrative pack £49: bundle plus a generated, cited chronology (accepted quote, approved variations, proof photos, messages, invoices, receipts) with the verifier report; (b) Reviewed pack £395 under £10k / £750 £10k-£50k: a panel QS or claims consultant (contracted at £350-£800/day, ~2-5 hours) checks the chronology, writes a factual summary of what was agreed, done and paid, flags evidence gaps, and formats it for FMB conciliation, mediation or a small-claims filing; (c) Adjudication-grade £1,500+: for commercial disputes, a referral-ready bundle structured to the CIC Low Value Disputes procedure. Packs contain facts and citations only; anything the builder must assert is marked 'builder to complete'. Paid by hosted Stripe checkout; a platform service invoice is issued through M4-10.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, one-off per pack; can be recovered as costs in some forums but JobGuard makes no promise of that.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 0.3 disputes/yr, half buy the reviewed pack (£395) and half the automated one (£49): 0.3 x (0.5 x 395 + 0.5 x 49) = £67. Small firm 1 dispute/yr, 60% reviewed at £600 blend, 40% automated: 0.6 x 600 + 0.4 x 49 = £380. Firm 2.5 disputes/yr, 70% reviewed at £900 blend, 30% automated: 2.5 x (0.7 x 900 + 0.3 x 49) = £1,612. Dispute frequency is a guess; Payapps (n=127, subcontractors) reports 73% see routine payment-application disputes, which is not the domestic market.
ideas.trust_note: The evidence is the builder's own; the pack is why they captured proof all job. It is the visible-effort service the research says makes fees feel fair (Buell & Norton). One rule: pack preparers work only from builder-visible data; no pre-lock shadow signal may ever appear in or inform a pack, or the pack becomes a disclosure route (§14.3) and a trust breach.
ideas.regulatory: Legal Services Act 2007: preparing documents for a litigant in person is fine, but JobGuard must not conduct litigation or hold itself out as giving legal advice; label packs as factual assemblies. D12: packs carry homeowner personal data, so minimal disclosure and redaction (M4-3) and a named lawful basis (legitimate interests / legal claims). Claims-management regulation does not cover construction payment (FCA sector list). D06 for any invoice content.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 packs (synthetic exists; live packs need G4 evidence controls), M4-10 platform service invoices, M4-11 hosted checkout for one-off purchases, plus a review-order workflow and a scoped external-reviewer role. One to two tasks plus panel contracts.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low for JobGuard's money. Risk that packs are used to pressure homeowners over favours the builder chose to do free; keep packs factual, require the builder to state the claimed amount themselves, and never generate threats (M4-5 rules apply).
ideas.precedent: Construction claims consultants £400-£1,200/day (RKA Associates FAQ); building mediation £75-£300 per party (buildingdisputesmediation.co.uk); RICS low-value adjudication application fee £425 inc VAT (rics.org); HMCTS small-claims issue fees £35-£455 up to £10k (justclaim.co.uk fee table, 2026).

ideas.name: Adjudication and claims-consultant panel referral
ideas.mechanism: For commercial or subcontract disputes above roughly £10k (mostly the Firm archetype), JobGuard maintains a vetted panel of adjudication specialists, claims consultants and construction solicitors. With the builder's explicit consent the adjudication-grade pack is handed to a panel member, who quotes the builder directly. JobGuard earns a disclosed introducer fee of 12.5% of the panel member's fees on referred matters (or, alternative that avoids the conflict entirely, a flat £250 'referral-ready handoff' charged to the builder and credited against the pack). Fee agreements are between builder and consultant; JobGuard never takes a share of the sum recovered.
ideas.who_pays: The panel consultant (introducer fee, disclosed to the builder in writing), or the builder if the flat-fee variant is chosen.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo ~0 (homeowner customers; residential-occupier contracts generally fall outside statutory adjudication, unverified). Small firm 0.3 referrals/yr x £3,500 consultant fee x 12.5% = £131. Firm 1.5 referrals/yr x £7,000 x 12.5% = £1,312. Consultant fee sizes derived from £400-£1,200/day x 5-8 days.
ideas.trust_note: Uncomfortable: JobGuard is paid by the adviser it recommends, which is the same structure builders distrust in R&D-credit boutiques. It does not touch the invoice watchdog (consultants are not suppliers), but it is a conflict and must be disclosed on the referral screen in plain words with the amount. The flat builder-paid handoff is cleaner and should be the default; the introducer fee is the 'borderline' variant listed for completeness.
ideas.regulatory: SRA rules require solicitors to disclose referral arrangements to the client (referral fees banned only in personal injury). Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 s.106 excludes residential-occupier contracts from statutory adjudication (verify). Not a regulated claims-management sector. Referral agreements need legal review; no debt assignment.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 packs plus a partner directory, consent-to-share record and audited handoff export (D12 disclosure of personal data to a third party). Small build; mostly contracts and legal review.
ideas.gaming_risk: Panel members over-recommend adjudication to earn fees; mitigate with panel vetting, a builder rating loop and no exclusivity. JobGuard staff steering builders toward referrals to earn introducer fees; cap the fee and publish it.
ideas.precedent: Specialist construction firms offer no-win-no-fee final-account recovery, consultants take 'a relatively small percentage' (Helix Law via search summary, unverified); claims consultants quote bespoke after free consultation (RKA). Introducer commissions are standard in UK professional services; no software-platform precedent for construction found (success_fee_benchmarks.md §4 gaps).

ideas.name: Pre-send quote review by a panel QS (prevention sold as a fixed fee)
ideas.mechanism: At 'Send this quote', the builder can add a human review before the quote goes out: a panel quantity surveyor (freelance, contracted at roughly £45-£60/hour) reviews the priced, cited proposal for omissions against the walk-through transcript, rates against the builder's rate book and current merchant prices, missing prelims/skips/scaffold/making-good, contingency and payment-stage sanity, and returns labelled suggestions (AGENTS §5.9: human suggestion, never a silent edit) within one working day. Priced £95 (quote under £20k), £195 (£20k-£60k), £345 (over £60k), ex VAT; JobGuard margin about 40-55% after reviewer time. This is the cleanest way to charge for prevention value: the builder pays a known fee for a known piece of work, no counterfactual needed.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, per reviewed quote, at checkout before send.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: quotes sent exceed jobs won. Solo 30 quotes/yr, 10% reviewed at £95 = £285. Small firm 40 quotes/yr, 15% at £195 = £1,170. Firm 50 quotes/yr, 15% at £345 = £2,587. Take-up is a guess; the research reports 34% of tradespeople get nothing for extras (Simply Business, weak) but nothing on quote omissions.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and disclosed at once; anything found at quote stage becomes baseline scope, which is fee-free forever, so this service reduces JobGuard's shadow-bill base rather than feeding it. That is a selling point worth stating. Reviewers see the quote and transcript only, never job evidence, so no shadow interplay.
ideas.regulatory: None regulated. Reviewer professional-indemnity cover and JobGuard terms on reliance; suggestions must not invent prices to fill lines (AGENTS §5.9). D04 if any reviewer works outside the UK/EU boundary.
ideas.build_dependency: M1 quote/proposal flow (M1-3 to M1-6), M2-1 rate book for price comparison, a 'review requested' Decision that pauses send, a scoped external-reviewer role with labelled-suggestion writes, hosted checkout (M4-11 rails; before G4 it can run as a manually invoiced pilot service). One to two tasks.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Builder blames the reviewer for a later omission; terms state the review is an aid, not a guarantee, matching the plan's 'counters are aids' language.
ideas.precedent: Freelance QS retainers from £400/month for 8 hours (constructivetalent.co.uk); FairRate audits trade quotes at £0.99 per audit for consumers, the reverse direction (report, 'No rival...'); Qted bundles an AI upsell generator at £59/month.

ideas.name: Final-account desk (done-for-you final account and customer invoice)
ideas.mechanism: For builders who hate the paperwork, a JobGuard desk operator (QS-qualified or trained admin, working as a delegated member of the builder's tenant with the ordinary builder-visible role) assembles the final account from the frozen baseline plus approved variations, chases outstanding proof and customer approvals, prepares the customer invoice draft and walks the builder through the review step. The builder still performs 'Complete final account' and the invoice issue Decision themselves (lock and issue stay builder-authorised). Priced £150 (final account under £15k), £350 (£15k-£50k), £600 (over £50k). Rule that makes it trustworthy: any shadow catch revealed on a desk-prepared account is permanently fee-free (recorded as a D13 ineligibility reason), because JobGuard cannot charge 10% for gaps in a bill its own staff helped build.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, one-off per job, invoiced with the subscription.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 19 jobs/yr (150k/8k), 10% use the desk at £150 = £285. Small firm 24 jobs/yr, 20% at £350 = £1,680. Firm 33 jobs/yr, 20% at £600 = £3,960. Desk cost 3-8 hours per job at ~£35/hour, so the £150 tier is near break-even and exists for adoption.
ideas.trust_note: With the fee-free-catch rule it reads as honest help; without it, it is a 2: 'your staff built my bill, then your machine found the holes and charged me' is exactly the betrayal pattern the research warns about. Desk staff must never hold or see the jobguard_shadow role, and the desk team must be organisationally separate from anyone with break-glass shadow access.
ideas.regulatory: None regulated. D06 (invoice issue remains builder-authorised; pilot invoice scope), D02 VAT presentation, and a D13 amendment adding 'desk_prepared' as a permanent fee-ineligibility reason. VAT on the service fee.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-12 final-account assembly, SV-4 lock, UIWIRE-9 final review UX, a delegated-actor membership role with full audit attribution, and the D13 ineligibility flag on the lock. One task plus policy text; ops hire.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder uses the desk on every job specifically to neutralise the 10% on catches; that is the intended trade (fixed fee instead of contingent fee) and is priced so JobGuard is indifferent. Builder disputes a catch on a non-desk job by claiming desk involvement; the lock records whether a desk actor touched the revision.
ideas.precedent: Outsourced QS retainers explicitly include 'valuations and final account settlement' from £400/month (constructivetalent.co.uk); no trade-app precedent for a done-for-you final account was found (report, 'Final accounts... not marketed by any small-trade tool').

ideas.name: White-glove import of in-flight jobs and onboarding
ideas.mechanism: Self-serve 'adopt a job' (M1-17) stays free. The paid layer is people: a JobGuard onboarding specialist takes the builder's existing quote, emailed variations, POs, WhatsApp photos and messages and builds the attested baseline and variation register with the builder on a call, plus rate-book and customer import from Tradify/ServiceM8/Xero CSVs. Priced £49 per job, £199 for up to five jobs, £750 Firm package (up to 15 jobs, CSV migrations, two-hour remote setup). Imported records carry provenance=imported and the builder attests the accepted value; the specialist works under the builder-visible role only.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, one-off at sign-up.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo has 2 live jobs at sign-up, 50% take the £49/job service: 0.5 x 2 x 49 = £49. Small firm 5 jobs, 60% take the £199 package = £119. Firm 80% take the £750 package = £600. One-off, so steady-state revenue per builder is near zero; it matters for cash at acquisition and for conversion of larger firms.
ideas.trust_note: Helpful and ordinary in this market. Borderline point to state plainly: evidence the builder hands over at import (old messages, photos) is 'evidence' under §14.2 and could later become a paid catch at lock. A builder who paid £49 to have JobGuard read their WhatsApp and then paid 10% on what was in it will feel set up. Recommended rule: anything the onboarding specialist personally handled is treated as disclosed_before_lock (fee-free) for that job; automated imports stay evidence but the onboarding screen says so in one sentence.
ideas.regulatory: M1-17 requires its own decision record (D06/D11 as applicable) before production import; D12 lawful basis and Article 14 route for imported customer messages; D04 for any migration tooling. VAT on the service.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-17 adopt-a-job (planned, medium effort, not needed for the M1-15 trial), CSV import tooling, and the fee-ineligibility flag for specialist-handled evidence. Service layer itself is small.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder attests an inflated or false baseline; under v3 there is no cap so it changes no fee, but it weakens later catches and packs, which is why imported lineage is visibly marked. Builder imports a nearly finished job purely to get a free 'second check' on it; acceptable, the check is the product.
ideas.precedent: Payaca charges a one-off £1,500 onboarding on Growth and Scale (payaca.com/pricing); Buildertrend coaching reportedly $500-$2,000 and about $100/month for month-to-month customers (Projul, competitor blog); simPRO setup reported at $2,000-$10,000 (solve8.com.au, third party). Tradify and Fergus give onboarding free.

ideas.name: Firm Care: premium support and named account management
ideas.mechanism: An add-on for the Builder and Firm plans: a named account manager, priority phone line (same-day), quarterly 30-minute 'profit review' call walking through the firm's own numbers (quote-to-final variance, overcharge findings, readiness warnings acted on, capture discipline by site lead, aged debt), template and rate-book setup, and new-starter walkthroughs. Priced £99/month on Builder, £199/month on Firm, ex VAT; one customer-success manager covers about 60 accounts. The profit review uses only builder-visible data and locked jobs; it never touches pre-lock shadow signals.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, monthly, on the subscription invoice.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Small firm 15% take x £99 x 12 = £178. Firm 40% take x £199 x 12 = £955. Take rates are guesses; larger per-user tools charge firms £370-£880/month for software alone (report), so £199 for a human is within their spend.
ideas.trust_note: Standard and welcome, with one hazard: the account manager is the person a builder will ask 'is there anything else on this job?'. They must be structurally unable to see shadow signals and trained to give the onboarding-terms answer; a single leak makes that signal fee-free and, worse, tells the trade that JobGuard staff know things they are not saying.
ideas.regulatory: None. D09 add-on entitlement, D05 recurring authority.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-13 subscription terms with add-on entitlements and M4-10 invoice lines; the support role must be a distinct membership with no shadow grants (SV-2 role isolation). Trivial build; ops hire.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material.
ideas.precedent: Buildertrend reportedly charges about £2k/year for support in the UK (BuildersAI blog, conflicting with its US pricing); Chaser sells a specialist add-on at £900-£2,099/month (benchmarks note §6); Fergus includes a free one-hour onboarding session.

ideas.name: Site-lead training and JobGuard capture certification
ideas.mechanism: Paid training in capture discipline: how to walk a job for the proposal, when to use Log an extra rather than the diary, proof photos before covering work, readiness checks, and reading the Decision Inbox. Formats: self-paced online course with certificate £49 per person; live remote team session £295 per firm; on-site half-day £750 for up to eight people. Delivered by JobGuard trainers, later by accredited partner trainers who keep 60%. A certificate is recorded against the member profile (optional). The pitch is honest: trained crews log their own extras, which are fee-free, so the course lowers JobGuard's 10% base and raises the builder's billing.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business; the online course can be bought per person.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 20% buy the £49 course = £10. Small firm 30% buy a remote session plus three seats: 0.3 x (295 + 3 x 49) = £133. Firm 40% buy an on-site day plus eight seats: 0.4 x (750 + 8 x 49) = £457. CITB short-course grant eligibility would raise take-up but is unverified.
ideas.trust_note: The strongest trust signal in this list: JobGuard sells the thing that reduces its own contingent income. Say that on the sales page.
ideas.regulatory: None. CITB grant eligibility only if the course is CITB-approved (unverified).
ideas.build_dependency: No code beyond an optional certification record on membership. Content production and trainer time.
ideas.gaming_risk: None.
ideas.precedent: Buildertrend coaching packages ($500-$2,000, Projul); Fergus and Tradify give onboarding free, so paid training has weak trade-app precedent and should be positioned as crew training, not software training.

ideas.name: Books-ready accounting sync plus disclosed bookkeeper partner programme
ideas.mechanism: Two parts. (1) 'Accounts sync' add-on: JobGuard pushes job-costed sales invoices, credit notes, matched supplier bills with three-way-match status, CIS labels and VAT codes to Xero or QuickBooks through an approved SV-7 accounting connector, with a monthly reconciliation pack the bookkeeper can trust; £15/month (Solo and Builder plans), £25/month (Firm). (2) Partner programme: vetted bookkeepers who know JobGuard exports are listed in-app; a builder can hire one at the partner's own price (£100-£200/month typical for a sole trader); JobGuard receives a disclosed 10% introducer fee on first-year fees, or, cleaner, no fee and the listing is free. Bookkeepers are not suppliers whose invoices JobGuard checks, so the watchdog conflict does not arise.
ideas.who_pays: The builder for the sync add-on; the bookkeeping partner for the introducer fee (disclosed to the builder).
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo sync 40% x £15 x 12 = £72, plus introducer 8% take x £1,500 first-year fees x 10% = £12. Small firm 60% x £15 x 12 = £108 plus 8% x £3,000 x 10% = £24. Firm 80% x £25 x 12 = £240, introducer negligible (already has an accountant). MTD ITSA (over £50k income from April 2026) pushes sole traders to buy software and bookkeeping anyway (report).
ideas.trust_note: The sync is plainly useful and competitors bundle Xero sync free at mid tiers, so £15 must buy real reconciliation work, not a link. The introducer fee is the borderline part (JobGuard paid by a party it recommends); disclose the amount or drop it. This is not selling builders' data: the export goes where the builder points it.
ideas.regulatory: D04 residency: Xero and QuickBooks host data outside the UK/EU boundary in at least some regions, so the connector needs a verified route and D12 update before real data. Accountants' professional bodies (ICAEW, AAT) require members to disclose commissions to clients. Not FCA regulated.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-7 approved accounting connector (medium effort, its own D04/D12 review) and M4-13 add-on entitlement. Sync cannot launch before SV-7; the partner listing needs only a directory.
ideas.gaming_risk: None for JobGuard. Partner quality risk handled by vetting and ratings.
ideas.precedent: Tradify, Powered Now and WorkflowMax include Xero/QuickBooks sync in paid tiers; Xero's advisor partner programme and Dext practice pricing (£391/month for 50 clients, third party) show the bookkeeper channel; sole-trader bookkeeping £100-£200/month (wearegro.co.uk, vjmglobal.com 2026 guides).

ideas.name: Seasonal dormant plan (works because the meter is live jobs)
ideas.mechanism: When a builder has zero live jobs (the same fact the live-jobs meter already counts), they can switch to Dormant at £9/month for up to four months a year instead of cancelling: data, quoting and the free quote flow stay on, watchdog and final-check features are off, reactivation is instant when a job goes live. The live-jobs meter makes this clean: Dormant is only offered when the meter reads zero, and any job switched live ends dormancy automatically at the next period boundary. Direct revenue is small; the value is retained accounts and a lower reason to churn in winter.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, monthly at the reduced rate.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 30% go dormant for 2 months: 0.3 x 2 x £9 = £5.40; those months would otherwise be £29 if kept or £0 if cancelled. Retention value: if 12% of solos would otherwise cancel in winter and half never return, losing ~8 months at £29 (£232), avoided loss is 0.12 x 0.5 x 232 = £14. Small firm 10% pause: £1.80 direct, ~£10 retained. Firms rarely reach zero live jobs. All untested (research notes call the winter-pause idea an untested hypothesis).
ideas.trust_note: Feels fair and respects cash-poor sole traders. Only trap: a builder who closes jobs without locking to reach zero and go dormant loses their final check; the D11 'invoice or payment activity with no lock' signal already covers this, and the dormant screen should say 'jobs you close without completing the final account get no final check'.
ideas.regulatory: D09 (pause terms), D05 (reactivation charge authority). Business-to-business, so consumer subscription rules do not apply.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-13 (subscription pauses are already in its Done-when) and M4-14 concurrency metering (zero-live-jobs rule). Small.
ideas.gaming_risk: Toggling dormant while jobs are effectively live but not switched live in JobGuard; that is the same 'keep small jobs off the system' risk the report flags for the live-jobs meter and is mitigated by generous job allowances, not by policing.
ideas.precedent: No trade-app pause plan was found in the research; general SaaS pause plans exist (e.g. Shopify's reduced-price pause plan, recalled from memory, unverified).

ideas.name: Multi-entity group account with pooled live-job allowance
ideas.mechanism: For builders who run more than one trading entity (a Ltd plus a sole-trader CIS entity, a sister company for a second region, a joint venture), a Group links separate tenants under one owner login with consolidated reporting, a shared rate book pushed to each tenant, and a pooled live-job allowance. Each entity remains its own tenant with full RLS (AGENTS §5.1); only an explicitly reviewed, read-only cross-tenant reporting path is added. Priced at the parent plan plus £49/month per additional entity, with the group's pooled allowance priced at least as the sum of the tiers it replaces so splitting entities never undercuts the meter.
ideas.who_pays: The group owner, monthly.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo none. Small firm 10% have a second entity: 0.1 x £49 x 12 = £59. Firm 30% have on average 1.5 extra entities: 0.3 x 1.5 x £49 x 12 = £265.
ideas.trust_note: Straightforward. The only sensitivity is that group reporting is a cross-tenant read, which must be reviewed as an explicit exception rather than a shortcut.
ideas.regulatory: AGENTS §5.1 tenant-isolation review for the cross-tenant read path; D09 pricing terms. None external.
ideas.build_dependency: A new control-plane task (tenant group, owner linkage, reviewed read-only projection), M4-14 pooled metering, M4-13 billing. Medium effort with a mandatory security review.
ideas.gaming_risk: Entity splitting to stay in cheaper live-job tiers; defeated by pooled-allowance pricing that is never below the sum of the component tiers.
ideas.precedent: Payaca's Enterprise tier is described as '100+ or multi-entity' (uk_trade_job_software.md); Procore prices on annual volume with unlimited users; no small-trade group pricing found.

ideas.name: Historic supplier-invoice back-audit (20% of cash refunds, builder-commissioned)
ideas.mechanism: A one-off, builder-commissioned audit of the previous 12 months of supplier invoices from before the builder joined JobGuard: the builder uploads or forwards statements and invoices, JobGuard's existing supplier intake and matching (migrations 0033/0036/0037) plus a human auditor compare them with agreed rates, quotes, delivery notes and duplicate patterns, and JobGuard drafts the refund requests for the builder to send. Priced £295 setup (Builder plan) or £495 (Firm) plus 20% of cash refunds actually received; Solo pays no setup and 25% of refunds. This is a new, separately commissioned category, not the live 10% supplier-overcharge fee, and needs its own D03 version. JobGuard never accepts anything from the supplier.
ideas.who_pays: The builder: setup fee up front, contingent share on refunds after they land.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: materials about 40% of turnover; overcharge/duplicate rate 0.5% (Solo) to 0.75% (firms) of materials spend; 40-50% of what is found comes back as cash rather than credit notes. Solo: £60k x 0.5% = £300 found, 40% cash = £120 x 25% = £30, 20% take-up = £6. Small firm: £240k x 0.75% = £1,800, 50% cash = £900 x 20% = £180 + £295 setup = £475, 30% take-up = £143. Firm: £800k x 0.75% = £6,000, 50% cash = £3,000 x 20% = £600 + £495 = £1,095, 40% take-up = £438. The research found no UK data on supplier-error rates for small builders, so the overcharge rate is the weakest assumption here.
ideas.trust_note: The builder asks for it, the money is clearly found by JobGuard's work, and 20-25% sits below the 20-30% recovery-audit norm. It must stay on the builder's side of the counter: no merchant rebates, no supplier-funded anything, or the invoice watchdog is compromised. Credit notes against future purchases are worth showing but not charging for.
ideas.regulatory: New D03 category version (§14.7 says new categories need one) and D01 rate entry; contract terms with the builder; not FCA regulated. D12 for supplier contact data.
ideas.build_dependency: Existing supplier intake/facts/matching (M2 work, built), M4-2 billability review, M4-8 settlement evidence for cash refunds, statement authorisation. Medium; mostly human audit labour.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder has already claimed or offset the refund and reports nothing; contingent share means JobGuard bears the audit time. Mitigate with the setup fee and refund-evidence requirement (bank-verified under M4-7 once live).
ideas.precedent: Accounts-payable recovery auditors usually charge 20-30%, range 10-40% (apexanalytix, vendor blog); Inspired PLC telecoms cost audits cover six years of bills (success_fee_benchmarks.md §2); no small-builder precedent found.

ideas.name: Contract and payment-schedule pack (reviewed terms, cancellation notice, staged payments)
ideas.mechanism: Every quote can carry a partner-solicitor-reviewed contract pack: plain-English terms, a staged payment schedule aligned to the quote's stages, a variation clause that mirrors Log an extra and customer approval, and the Consumer Contracts Regulations off-premises cancellation notice that many builders omit (omission lets a homeowner cancel up to 12 months later). Sold as £29/month unlimited on Solo/Builder, £49/month on Firm, or £10 per quote; bespoke clause review by the partner solicitor at £295. Prevention value sold as a fixed fee: fewer withheld payments, cleaner variations, fewer disputes.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, monthly add-on or per quote; bespoke review one-off.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 40% take x £29 x 12 = £139. Small firm 50% x £29 x 12 = £174 plus 20% buy a £295 bespoke review = £59; total £233. Firm 60% x £49 x 12 = £353 plus 50% x £295 = £148; total £501.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and reduces JobGuard's own contingent base (clearer variation clauses mean more builder-captured extras). Must not be marketed as legal advice from JobGuard; the solicitor partner owns the templates.
ideas.regulatory: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013; Consumer Rights Act 2015; Legal Services Act 2007 (template supply is not a reserved activity, but advice must come from the partner solicitor). D06 (invoice/contract templates for the pilot) and M4-19 reviewed templates; no universal Construction Act regime assumed.
ideas.build_dependency: D06-approved templates and the M1 quote send path for attaching them; M4-19 for reviewed notice templates and jurisdiction profiles. Small code; the cost is legal drafting and review.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material.
ideas.precedent: JCT sells homeowner contract forms for a small fixed price and FMB gives contracts free to members (recalled, unverified); no trade app found bundling reviewed terms with cancellation compliance.

ideas.name: Annual profit-leak review (fixed-fee human analysis of the firm's own year)
ideas.mechanism: Once a year a JobGuard analyst (QS or commercial manager) works through the firm's builder-visible, locked-job data: quote-versus-final variance by job type, overcharge findings and what was recovered, readiness warnings that cost days, proof gaps, extras captured per site lead, invoice-to-cash days and aged debt, and returns a written report with three to five specific changes to rates, stages or crew habits. Priced £295 (Solo), £750 (Builder plan), £1,500 (Firm), for roughly 3, 6 and 12 analyst hours. The report is labelled an aid built from the firm's own records, not a guarantee, and never quantifies 'money JobGuard saved you' beyond settled figures (forbidden claims in §14.1). It only ever uses locked jobs and builder-visible data.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, one-off per year.
ideas.assumptions: Assumptions: Solo 10% take x £295 = £30. Small firm 25% x £750 = £188. Firm 40% x £1,500 = £600. Take rates are guesses; larger firms already pay £2,500-£8,000 for independent QS cost reviews (constructioncapital.co.uk), so £1,500 is not out of range.
ideas.trust_note: Sells prevention insight for a fixed fee, which is the honest alternative to a success fee on unprovable savings. Hazard: an analyst with any view of pre-lock shadow signals would poison it; restrict to locked jobs and the builder role, and state that restriction in the report.
ideas.regulatory: None. Must respect §14.1 forbidden claims and D11 (advisory signals only). Analyst PI cover.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-16 integrity signals (advisory), VALUE-2 cards and M4-3 packs as data sources; an export for locked jobs. Minimal code; analyst time.
ideas.gaming_risk: None for JobGuard; risk of overclaiming savings in the report, handled by the forbidden-claims rule.
ideas.precedent: Cost-reduction consultancies take 50% of savings for 12-60 months (P3, single vendor) and QS cost reviews run £2,500-£8,000 (constructioncapital.co.uk); JobGuard's fixed fee is the lower-friction version. No trade-app precedent found.

ideas.name: Live-job slot meter with soft overage, lock-frees-a-slot and off-season pause (the honest answer on the meter)
ideas.mechanism: A job occupies one slot from switch-live until the builder completes the final-account lock (§14.4); after lock the job is free and read-only. Tiers are counted on concurrent slots (report recommendation: Solo up to 3 at £29, Builder up to 10 at £59, Firm up to 25 at £119, Contractor on request). Overage is soft: going over the tier for a calendar month adds one pro-rata slot at about £8/slot/month and prompts an upgrade next month, never a block. A 'winter pause' keeps read access at a nominal £5/month with no live slots. Money flows through the Stripe hosted subscription (M4-11 as rewritten) and metering Decisions (M4-14). Because locking frees a slot, the meter pushes builders towards the lock, which is exactly the event that triggers JobGuard's final check.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (monthly or annual, ex VAT).
ideas.assumptions: Report tier prices (£29/£59/£119, ex VAT). Solo 2–3 live jobs sits in the 3-slot tier; Small firm 5–6 in the 10-slot tier; Firm 15 in the 25-slot tier. Overage assumes two months a year over tier by 1–3 slots at £8/slot. Honest assessment of whether the meter works: it does for all three archetypes, it is the same unit ServiceM8 already sells (jobs, unlimited users), and it does not punish adding site staff who feed evidence. Its known weaknesses: (1) it under-captures the top end relative to value-based rivals — Procore's 0.1–0.2% of annual construction volume would be £2,000–£4,000 a year on a £2m firm, versus £1,428 here — so most extra Firm-end revenue has to come from add-ons (ideas below), not the meter; (2) builders may keep small jobs off JobGuard to stay in tier, which shrinks the shadow-bill fee base, so allowances must be generous and overage soft; (3) long jobs consume slot-months, which is fair (the watchdog works longer) but must be explained; (4) building is seasonal, hence the pause. Weighted slots (a £60k job = 2 slots) would re-introduce value metering by the back door and is not recommended.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest: one number to understand, unlimited users, and locking (which they must do anyway to invoice) frees capacity. The only tension is that the meter creates a small incentive to lock early; that helps the builder's cash flow and JobGuard's final check alike.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 (amount, frequency, tiers, overage, pause, price-change notice), D05 (bounded renewal authority), D02 (VAT). Subscription charging is enabled independently of success fees under §14.18.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-11 (Stripe hosted subscription sign-up, rewritten in §14.13) and M4-14 (concurrency metering and explicit tier-upgrade Decisions, currently 'kept, optional' — it becomes required). Slot state derives from existing switch-live (M1-7) and the new lock (SV-4). Effort: medium (2–4 weeks) once SV-4 lands; the metering rule needs property tests around month boundaries.
ideas.gaming_risk: Running several customers as one 'job' to save slots (unrealistic because quotes and invoices are per customer); leaving jobs unswitched to avoid slots (already a D11 signal: won-but-never-live); locking prematurely to free a slot (harmless to JobGuard, and later revisions are allowed after confirmed catches).
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 charges by jobs per month with unlimited users at £25/£59/£119 (https://www.servicem8.com/uk/pricing). Procore charges ~0.1–0.2% of annual construction volume, about $15–30k a year for $10–50M firms (https://www.scanmanifold.com/blog-posts/procore-pricing-2026-contractors; https://costbench.com/software/construction-management/procore/). Buildertrend moved to 11 annual-volume brackets in 2026 (https://projul.com/blog/buildertrend-pricing-analysis-2026/).

ideas.name: Watchdog add-on tier with a Chargeflow-style ROI guarantee (charge for prevention directly)
ideas.mechanism: Split the subscription into a base (quote, Log an extra, final account, invoicing, customer portal) and a 'Watchdog' add-on that unlocks the prevention engine: three-way supplier matching, PO-versus-agreed-price checks, site-readiness warnings, proof-before-cover prompts and the Decision Inbox. Price the add-on per tier (+£15/+£30/+£60 a month), not per user. Back it with a written guarantee modelled on Chargeflow's '4x ROI': if the builder-confirmed prevented findings (corrected supplier invoices, caught quote omissions the builder accepted, etc.) over 12 months total less than 4× the add-on price, JobGuard credits the difference against the next year's add-on. Findings are counted only when the builder confirms them in the Inbox, so no counterfactual claim is made; the guarantee is a refund promise, not a success fee.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, as part of the monthly subscription.

revenue_per_year.solo: £180 (add-on at £15/month) for a builder who takes it

ideas.assumptions: Prices are proposals scaled to the report's tiers; attach rate is unknown and could be 30–70% (Tradify's AI bill reader sits in its £44 Plus plan, £10 above Lite, and Buildertrend put change and purchase orders only in its $799 Advanced tier, so builders already pay for these features as upsells). Figures are per builder who takes the add-on. The guarantee's cost depends on the pilot's measured prevention rate, which §14.17 will produce; until then treat the guarantee as an untested retention device.
ideas.trust_note: This is the most honest route to prevention value: the builder pays for the checking itself, sees every finding, and gets money back if it does not pay off. It also answers the founder's 'we save them thousands but can't claim for it' directly without touching the 10% fee.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 (tier definition and guarantee terms), D02 (VAT on credits). The guarantee wording must avoid 'JobGuard saved you £X' before confirmation (§14.1 forbidden claims).
ideas.build_dependency: The prevention features exist (supplier intake and matching migrations 0033/0036/0037, readiness risks #89, inbox #90). Needed: entitlement gating by tier in the subscription model (M4-11/M4-14) and a 'builder-confirmed finding value' projection for the guarantee (reuse the Inbox decision records). Effort: small to medium (1–3 weeks).
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder could confirm findings loosely to protect the guarantee — irrelevant, because confirming a finding only reduces JobGuard's refund exposure. JobGuard's own incentive to over-flag is bounded because findings must be builder-confirmed and the Inbox already separates mandatory from advisory.
ideas.precedent: Chargeflow: 25% per recovered chargeback plus a '4x ROI Guarantee' (https://www.chargeflow.io/pricing). Tradify Lite £34 vs Plus £44 with SmartRead for bills (https://www.tradifyhq.com/uk/pricing). ApprovalMax gates bill-to-PO matching at Advanced (https://www.approvalmax.com/pricing/approvalmax-for-xero). Coalition bundles active monitoring with the policy and reports ~70% fewer claims (https://www.coalitioninc.com/cyber-insurance).

ideas.name: Flat per-catch fee on confirmed prevented supplier overcharges (Chargeflow's $29 deflection fee, translated)
ideas.mechanism: Chargeflow takes 25% of recovered chargebacks but a flat $29 for each chargeback it deflects before it happens. Translation: when the three-way match flags a supplier invoice line above the PO/agreed price and the supplier then issues a corrected invoice or credit before the builder pays, and the builder marks the finding 'corrected by supplier' in the Inbox with the supplier document attached, JobGuard bills a flat £10 per confirmed prevented overcharge, capped at £40 a month. No percentage, no counterfactual claim: the supplier's own corrected document is the proof the error was real. Billed on the monthly subscription invoice as a labelled line.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, monthly.
ideas.assumptions: Materials ≈ 40% of turnover (Solo £60k, Small £240k, Firm £800k). One confirmed prevented overcharge per £10k of materials spend — an assumption with no UK data behind it (the research found none for small builders; PRGX cites recoveries of ~0.1% of spend for large AP departments, and small-builder error rates are probably higher). Cap chosen so the Firm pays at most £480 a year.
ideas.trust_note: It is provable and small, but it is a running meter on the builder's supplier admin, and builders dislike taxi-meter charges (Prelec & Loewenstein; Lambrecht & Skiera in the report). The founder's brief says prevented spend 'currently earns nothing'; this does not touch the 10% or the meter, but it is a new charge type and will feel like a fee for doing what the subscription promised unless it is bundled as an alternative to idea 2 rather than stacked on it.
ideas.regulatory: Needs a new decision record (or D01 v4) because D03 v2 says prevention never qualifies for the success fee and this is a different charge; D02 for VAT; G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Supplier matching and the terminal `prevention` recovery case type (migration 0034) exist. Needed: a 'supplier corrected' disposition with document evidence, a fee derivation with unique source identity, cap logic, and statement lines (M4-9/M4-10 as rewritten). Effort: medium (2–3 weeks).
ideas.gaming_risk: JobGuard's incentive to over-flag is real; mitigations are builder confirmation, the supplier document requirement and the cap. A builder can decline to record the correction and pay nothing. A supplier could dispute that a 'correction' was an error rather than a pricing update; only the builder's confirmation counts, never the model.
ideas.precedent: Chargeflow Alerts: $29 per deflected chargeback (https://www.chargeflow.io/pricing). AP recovery auditors sell prevention as a separate subscription product alongside contingency audits (PRGX 10-K: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1007330/000100733020000003/a201910kprgx.htm).

ideas.name: Insurance-backed guarantee issued from the locked evidence pack (QANW / FMB translation)
ideas.mechanism: After the final-account lock, the job's evidence pack (scope, approved variations, hashed proof photos, lock record) is offered to a partner IBG insurer as the basis for an insurance-backed guarantee on the work. The builder buys the IBG per job (installers already pay £35–£250 per job for damp/roofing IBGs) and lists it as a quote line, so the customer effectively funds it. JobGuard earns an introducer commission from the insurer per policy and gives the builder a 'guaranteed job' badge on the customer portal. Money: insurer pays JobGuard commission monthly; JobGuard never handles the premium.
ideas.who_pays: The builder (premium, usually passed through in the quote); the insurer pays JobGuard's commission.
ideas.assumptions: Jobs per year = turnover ÷ average job (19 / 24 / 33). Premium ≈ 1% of job value with a £40 floor (QANW damp IBGs are £35–£80 for work up to £5k and £200–£250 for larger jobs). Attach 40% on domestic work, 30% for the Firm's larger and partly commercial jobs. 20% introducer commission is an assumption; broker-level commissions on general insurance are commonly 15–25% but no partner terms exist.
ideas.trust_note: The builder gains a sales tool and the customer gains protection, so it sits in the builder's interest. The commission comes from an insurer, not a supplier, so it does not compromise the invoice watchdog. It must not become a condition of using the final account, and the builder must see the commission.
ideas.regulatory: IBGs are insurance: JobGuard would act as an introducer appointed representative of an FCA-authorised insurer/broker, or hand off entirely at a link. Insurance distribution rules limit JobGuard to introduction, not advice. Commission must be disclosed. New decision record plus D12 (sharing the pack with the insurer needs builder consent and a lawful basis).
ideas.build_dependency: Evidence packs (M4-3, merged #92) and the lock (SV-4). Needed: a consented pack-share export in the insurer's format and a policy-reference record on the job. Effort: small (1–2 weeks) after a commercial partner exists; the partnership itself is the long pole.
ideas.gaming_risk: Fraud against the insurer (staged photos, work not done). JobGuard must state that hashes prove integrity and existence, not authenticity (AGENTS §5.8), and leave underwriting to the insurer.
ideas.precedent: QANW issues IBGs paid by the installer, not the customer (https://qanw.co.uk/insurance-backed-guarantees/); damp IBG cost £35–£80 up to £5k of work, £200–£250 for larger houses (https://www.insituscp.co.uk/what-does-an-insurance-backed-damp-guarantee-cost); FMB Building Work Guarantee (https://www.fmbinsurance.co.uk/insurance-products/fmb-building-work-guarantee/). HomeServe sells cover at £15.55–£32.50 a month, showing homeowner appetite for post-work protection (https://www.homeserve.co.uk/insurance/boiler-and-central-heating-cover-service-xs1).

ideas.name: 'Evidence-verified builder' insurance discount with introducer commission (telematics + Coalition translation)
ideas.mechanism: Fleet insurers give 5–20% premium discounts for telematics and dashcam data because it cuts claims and disputes; Coalition bundles monitoring with cyber cover and reports ~70% fewer claims. Translation: a partner insurer or broker offers builders a discount on public liability, employers' liability and contractors' all-risks when the builder consents to share JobGuard's job-integrity metrics (share of jobs with proof-before-cover photos, signed variations, locked final accounts, dispute-free completions). JobGuard is paid an introducer commission per policy placed, and the builder pays less. The builder's saving is the prevention value made visible in a premium.
ideas.who_pays: The insurer/broker pays JobGuard's commission; the builder pays a lower premium.
ideas.assumptions: Premiums: Simply Business says the average tradesperson pays £200–£300 a year for £1m public liability, builders at the higher end; CAR is quoted at £600–£1,500 per project; a 15-staff firm's PL+EL+CAR is assumed at ~£6,000. Simply Business's affiliate scheme pays 10% capped at £100, which is the floor case; an IAR arrangement at 15% is the upper case. The discount itself is unproven for building work — insurers would need loss data, so expect a pilot with one insurer first.
ideas.trust_note: Clearly in the builder's interest, and the payer is an insurer, not a supplier. The risk is over-claiming what JobGuard's data proves; the pitch must be 'documented jobs' not 'safe builder'.
ideas.regulatory: FCA insurance distribution: JobGuard as introducer appointed representative or pure referrer; no advice. Data sharing needs D12 (consent, lawful basis, insurer as separate controller) and D04 (residency of the insurer's systems).
ideas.build_dependency: Lock (SV-4), proof uploads (0015/0025) and evidence packs (M4-3). Needed: a tenant-level, consented 'integrity summary' export with no customer personal data. Effort: small (1–2 weeks) after a partner; the insurer deal is the long pole (months).
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders could photograph selectively to lift their score; the insurer bears that risk and JobGuard should only report counts of server-verified evidence, never quality judgements.
ideas.precedent: UK fleet telematics discounts of 5–10% for tracking, 10–15% for behaviour monitoring, 15–20% for AI dashcams (https://surecam.com/blog/can-fleet-dashcams-reduce-insurance-surecam; https://www.quotezone.co.uk/fleet-insurance/guides/fleet-telematics-and-insurance). Lytx insurance partner programme (https://www.lytx.com/partners/insurance). Coalition Active Insurance (https://www.coalitioninc.com/cyber-insurance). Simply Business affiliate: 10% of premium, £100 cap (https://www.simplybusiness.co.uk/affiliates/); builders' PL pricing (https://www.simplybusiness.co.uk/business-insurance/builders-insurance/; https://www.mybuilder.com/new-build/price-guides/builders-insurance-cost).

ideas.name: Application fee on customer payments through JobGuard's hosted Stripe/GoCardless surfaces (Buildertrend / Fergus / Stripe Connect translation)
ideas.mechanism: When the customer pays a deposit, stage payment or final invoice through the hosted checkout link on the JobGuard invoice, JobGuard adds a Stripe Connect application fee on top of Stripe's processing (e.g. +0.3% on cards, a flat £1 on pay-by-bank/GoCardless open-banking). Stripe deducts it at settlement and pays it to JobGuard's platform balance; funds never touch JobGuard (AGENTS §3 hosted surfaces only, M4). Because the payment is recorded automatically, it also feeds the §14.8 receipt allocation, which is what makes the success fee provable — so the payment rail is worth subsidising, not just monetising.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, as a visible per-transaction fee; the customer cannot be surcharged for cards under UK rules.
ideas.assumptions: Share of invoiced value paid through the hosted surface: 40% for Solo (deposits and small balances), 25% for Small firm, 10% for the Firm (large sums go by bank transfer). Blended JobGuard margin 0.3% across card and pay-by-bank. Fergus charges 1.6% + 20p all-in and Buildertrend Payments ~2.99% on cards, so a total in that range is market-normal.
ideas.trust_note: Standard and transparent, and it makes recording payments effortless. It must stay optional (bank transfer always allowed) and the JobGuard slice shown separately from Stripe's; a builder who feels JobGuard 'clips every payment' will route around it.
ideas.regulatory: Stripe (and GoCardless) are the regulated payment institutions; JobGuard uses Connect application fees, not its own PI licence. Consumer Rights (Payment Surcharges) Regulations bar passing card fees to consumers. D05 for any standing mandates; D02 VAT on the fee; G4.
ideas.build_dependency: M4 payment tasks (Stripe hosted surfaces, GoCardless in a separate task) and M4-8 receipt allocation; the subscription Stripe integration (M4-11) supplies webhook/idempotency/unknown-outcome patterns. Requires Stripe Connect onboarding of each builder (Stripe runs KYC). Effort: medium to large (4–6 weeks).
ideas.gaming_risk: None material: builders who avoid the rail simply pay nothing; that only weakens payment evidence for the success fee.
ideas.precedent: Buildertrend Payments: cards ~2.99%, ACH small flat fee, priced per transaction (https://buildertrend.com/help-article/buildertrend-payments-faqs/). Fergus UK 1.6% + 20p (report table). Stripe Connect application fees for SaaS platforms (https://docs.stripe.com/connect/saas/tasks/app-fees; https://support.stripe.com/questions/monetizing-payments-with-stripe-connect). Xero monetises payment flow via Stripe/GoCardless partnerships (https://www.electronicpaymentsinternational.com/news/xero-partners-transferwise-stripe/).

ideas.name: Finance referral on JobGuard-verified jobs: homeowner project finance and 'get paid now' on a locked final account (Buildertrend–Nelnet / Payapps Early Payment / iwocaPay translation)
ideas.mechanism: Two triggers. (a) At quote acceptance, the customer portal offers a partner lender's project finance (Buildertrend routes homeowners to Nelnet for $3k–$150k loans; the builder is paid in full on completion). (b) At final-account lock, the builder can offer the customer a pay-later option or take invoice finance on the locked, evidence-backed final account, iwocaPay-style: the lender pays the builder now, the customer pays the lender over 1–12 months. JobGuard passes the immutable lock and evidence pack (with consent) as underwriting evidence and earns a lender-paid referral fee per funded deal. JobGuard never lends, holds or moves money.
ideas.who_pays: The lender pays JobGuard a referral fee; the customer (or builder, for seller-paid pay-later) bears the finance cost.
ideas.assumptions: Attach 10% of domestic jobs (Solo 90% domestic, Small 70%, Firm 50%). Lender referral fee 1% of financed amount for consumer project finance (assumption; no partner terms exist), 0.5% on larger commercial invoice finance. iwocaPay's seller fee is 'a fixed percentage' that it does not publish.
ideas.trust_note: Helpful for cash flow and for winning bigger jobs, but the payer is a lender, the product is debt, and the customer is the builder's, which brushes the 'selling their customers as leads' risk. It must be builder-initiated per job, commission disclosed on screen, and never pushed by the watchdog.
ideas.regulatory: Consumer credit broking is FCA-regulated (permission or appointed-representative status); lending to sole traders under £25k is also regulated. Undisclosed intermediary commissions have been penalised (Expert Tooling v Engie, CA 2025, from the research notes), so disclose. D12 for sharing job data with the lender; D10 route review; G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Customer acceptance page (M1) and the lock (SV-4) plus evidence packs (M4-3). Build is a consented referral hand-off and a 'financed' fact on the job: small (1–2 weeks). Legal setup and partner onboarding: months.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders inflating quotes to fit finance, or pushing credit on customers who cannot afford it — the lender's affordability checks own that; JobGuard must not vary the watchdog or the shadow bill by finance status.
ideas.precedent: Buildertrend Financing powered by Nelnet Bank, $3k–$150k, contractor paid via the platform (https://buildertrend.com/press-releases/homeowner-financing-partner-nelnet/; https://buildertrend.com/financial-tools/client-financing/). Payapps Early Payment: contractors configure discount settings for early payment inside the claim workflow; one builder reported ~AUD 160k of transparent discounts in year one (https://www.prnewswire.com/apac/news-releases/more-than-half-of-subcontractors-add-a-risk-margin-for-slow-payments-as-payapps-launches-early-payment-feature-302737761.html). iwocaPay: seller pays a fixed percentage for interest-free customer terms, or customer pays interest (https://www.iwoca.co.uk/iwocapay-seller-offer-pay-later).

ideas.name: Statutory late-payment interest and compensation finder for business customers (R&D-tax-software translation, 10% within the existing withheld-payment category)
ideas.mechanism: R&D-tax platforms take 5–10% of a statutory entitlement the SME did not know how to claim. Translation: for invoices to business customers (main contractors, landlords, developers), the Late Payment of Commercial Debts Act gives statutory interest at base + 8% plus fixed compensation of £40/£70/£100 per invoice. JobGuard already holds invoice date, terms and the settlement date from the bank feed, so it can compute the exact entitlement, show it, and let the builder add it to a recovery case they explicitly open (the fixed withheld-payment rule). If the interest/compensation is actually paid and allocated, it counts as recovered principal for that case and the ordinary 10% applies. The counterfactual is not needed: the money is new and statutory.
ideas.who_pays: The builder pays 10% of settled statutory interest/compensation; the late-paying business customer funds it.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0–£15 (almost all customers are homeowners, where the Act does not apply)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £50–£100 (≈3 late B2B invoices × ≈£340 each × 10%, at 50–100% take-up)
revenue_per_year.firm: £400–£850 (≈8 late B2B invoices × ≈£1,060 each × 10%, at 50–100% take-up)

ideas.assumptions: B2B share of jobs: Solo 10%, Small 30%, Firm 50%. Share paid late: 40–50%. Average lateness 30–45 days at base + 8% (≈13% used) on £25k / £60k invoices plus the fixed sum. Many builders will waive it to keep the relationship, hence the take-up range. Homeowner customers are excluded by law, which is why Solo is near zero.
ideas.trust_note: Feels like found money because it is: an entitlement the builder never claims. Fits the fixed decision because it only rides on a case the builder opened and only on settled cash. Show it as an option, never as pressure to sour a client relationship.
ideas.regulatory: D03 v3 (interest and compensation are not 'net principal' as drafted; the category text must say whether they count, and how VAT on interest is treated). D10 (communications remain the builder's). No FCA activity on the research found: helping a business collect its own service invoices is not Article 39F debt collecting, but legal sign-off is required.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-7 bank feed and M4-8 allocation (settlement dates), invoice terms on the final account, recovery cases (0034) and the withheld-payment entry test (§14.7). Effort: small to medium (1–2 weeks) plus a D03 revision.
ideas.gaming_risk: Dates are server facts, so lateness cannot be faked; the only leakage is a builder collecting the interest outside JobGuard, which is the accepted D11 residual risk.
ideas.precedent: UK R&D tax software platforms charge 5–10% of the benefit (https://www.myriadassociates.com/resources/news/2025/how-much-should-you-be-paying-your-rd-tax-advisor/). Late Payment Act interest at base + 8% and fixed compensation £40/£70/£100 for business debts (https://www.gov.uk/late-commercial-payments-interest-debt-recovery; Cosmo DCA 2026 guide https://www.cosmodca.com/blog/debt-collection-agency-charges-uk).

ideas.name: Fixed-fee legal escalation ladder inside an opened recovery case (Garfield AI translation)
ideas.mechanism: Garfield, an SRA-authorised AI law firm, charges fixed fees (£2 chaser, £7.50 letter before action, £50 claim filing) and has settled £1.7m of small debts. Translation: once a builder has opened a withheld-payment case and agreed the 10% terms, the case screen offers optional, fixed-price escalation steps delivered by an SRA-regulated partner from JobGuard's evidence pack: formal letter before action, small-claims filing, and (for commercial customers) adjudication referral. JobGuard earns a referral margin or resale margin on each step (say 20–30% of the partner fee) or a flat £25 'court-ready pack' preparation fee. The 10% success fee remains separate and is clearly stated to exclude these costs (the report flags that ambiguity).
ideas.who_pays: The builder pays the partner's fixed fee per step; the partner pays JobGuard a margin, or JobGuard charges its own pack fee.
ideas.assumptions: Cases per year: 1 / 3 / 6 (no data; withheld-payment frequency is the pilot's job to measure). Margin per case £30–£50 assuming one or two paid steps at Garfield-like prices with a 25–30% partner margin, or the flat pack fee.
ideas.trust_note: The builder chooses each step, the price is fixed and small, and it makes the 10% feel earned (JobGuard did the paperwork). The risk is upsell pressure inside a stressful dispute; keep the tone factual (D10) and never let a model recommend escalation.
ideas.regulatory: Reserved legal activities (Legal Services Act 2007): the partner must be SRA-authorised; JobGuard only prepares evidence and refers. D10 (pursuit route), D07 (retention of the pack), and legal review that referral margins from a law firm are permitted (SRA rules on referral fees in non-PI matters allow disclosed arrangements — verify).
ideas.build_dependency: Recovery cases and evidence packs exist (0034, #92); M4-5 recovery pursuit and D10 govern communications. Build: a partner hand-off with pack export and a case-cost ledger line. Effort: small (1–2 weeks) after the partner agreement.
ideas.gaming_risk: None on the builder side. JobGuard must not vary the 10% or the shadow bill by whether escalation was bought.
ideas.precedent: Garfield.Law fixed fees from £2 (chaser) and £7.50 (letter before action) to £50 (filing); £1.7m paid or settled by September 2026; first SRA-approved AI-only firm (https://www.accountingweb.co.uk/tech/tech-pulse/ai-law-firm-targets-small-business-debt-recovery; https://www.lexisnexis.com/en-gb/legal/news/ai-law-firm-debut-sparks-hopes-concerns). UK debt collectors' hybrid model: £25–£75 file fee plus 6–10% (Cosmo DCA).

ideas.name: Court-ready, anchored dispute-defence pack as a paid service (Lytx claims-defence translation)
ideas.mechanism: Fleets pay Lytx partly for analyst-reviewed incident packages that win insurance claims and litigation. Translation: the basic evidence pack stays free and exportable (it is the builder's data), but JobGuard sells a 'defence pack' for a specific dispute: externally timestamp-anchored hashes (M4 anchoring), a chronological narrative of scope, approvals, photos and messages, a variation-by-variation approval proof, and a signed integrity statement describing exactly what the hashes do and do not prove. Priced per pack (£40–£50) or included in the top tier. Sold at the moment of need: a customer dispute, an insurer claim, an adjudication.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, per pack, or via the Firm tier.
ideas.assumptions: Disputes per year 1 / 3 / 6 (no data). Price £40–£50 per pack, comparable to the cost of one hour of a QS at the £350–£800/day rates in the research.
ideas.trust_note: Valuable when needed, but charging to package the builder's own records can read as holding their evidence hostage. Mitigation: raw export always free; the paid product is the anchoring, narrative and integrity statement. Never call it tamper-proof (AGENTS §5.7).
ideas.regulatory: Retention/legal-hold policy (D07) before WORM or Object Lock; D02 VAT; no regulated activity. Anchoring service provider needs D04 residency review.
ideas.build_dependency: Evidence packs (M4-3, merged). Needs M4 Object Lock and external timestamp anchoring (after retention approval) and a narrative renderer. Effort: medium (2–3 weeks) once anchoring exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: None; the pack reports what the immutable record contains and states its limits.
ideas.precedent: Lytx DriveCam's analyst-reviewed event packages are cited as the strongest incident review material for commercial auto insurers and litigation counsel (https://heavyvehicleinspection.com/blog/post/ai-dashcam-roi-netradyne-lytx-samsara-fleet; https://www.lytx.com/partners/insurance). Construction claims consultants charge £400–£1,200 a day (https://rkaassociates.com/construction-claims-faq).

ideas.name: Materials price benchmark add-on built from JobGuard's supplier documents (energy-audit / FairRate translation, flat fee not shared savings)
ideas.mechanism: Cost-reduction firms take 50% of savings for 12–60 months and FairRate charges £0.99 per invoice audit against 'local rates'. Both monetise price information. Translation: JobGuard already extracts supplier line items from invoices and POs; an anonymised, aggregated regional benchmark ('you paid £X per unit; the JobGuard median in your region over the last 90 days is £Y') runs (a) at quote time to catch underpriced materials and (b) at PO time to flag above-market prices before ordering. Sold as a flat monthly add-on. A shared-savings percentage is deliberately not used because the counterfactual for prevention is unprovable; a flat fee is the honest form.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, monthly add-on.
ideas.assumptions: Prices are proposals. Needs enough tenants in a region to make medians meaningful (k-anonymity threshold, e.g. at least 10 tenants and 30 observations per item), so it is a year-two product. Attach rate unknown.
ideas.trust_note: No supplier pays and no data is sold, but it uses pooled builder data and some builders will feel their buying is exposed. It must be opt-in with a plain explanation, contribute-to-benefit, and never identify a merchant's account terms for a named builder. Aggregated purchase-price sharing between competitors also needs a competition-law check.
ideas.regulatory: D12 (lawful basis and terms for aggregated cross-tenant use; supplier prices are mostly not personal data but the extraction pipeline touches counterparties), D04 residency, and a reviewed cross-tenant exception under AGENTS §5.1 (an explicit aggregated projection, not a runtime RLS bypass). Competition-law review of price-information exchange.
ideas.build_dependency: Supplier facts and matching (0033/0036/0037) exist per tenant. Needs an aggregated, anonymised projection built by a separate infrastructure role with catalog tests, plus quote-time and PO-time checks in the watchdog. Effort: medium to large (4–6 weeks).
ideas.gaming_risk: Poisoned inputs (fake invoices) — use only server-verified supplier documents and trim outliers; a merchant could try to learn rivals' prices — publish only medians/ranges above the anonymity threshold.
ideas.precedent: FairRate: £0.99 per line-by-line audit against local market rates, consumer-facing (https://www.fairrate.ai/). P3 Cost Analysts: 50/50 savings share for 12–60 months (https://www.costanalysts.com/). Builders' merchant trade pricing is typically 10–40% off list, so price dispersion is large (https://squote.app/knowledge/general/trade-accounts).

ideas.name: 'JobGuard Verified' public profile and customer-portal reputation page (Checkatrade translation without selling leads)
ideas.mechanism: Checkatrade charges £30–£500+ a month for membership and leads. JobGuard should not sell leads or the builder's customers, but it holds something Checkatrade cannot verify: server-recorded facts about how the builder runs jobs (jobs with locked final accounts, share of variations approved by the customer before the work, proof-before-cover photo rate, invoice-to-payment days). Translation: an opt-in public profile page and a badge on quotes and the customer portal that publishes those counts, generated only from locked jobs, sold as a small add-on or bundled into the middle tier as a hero feature. Builders use it to win work; no lead fees, no marketplace.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, monthly add-on.
ideas.assumptions: Proposed prices; attach unknown. Value depends on JobGuard becoming recognisable to homeowners, which takes time; early on it may work better bundled than sold.
ideas.trust_note: The data is the builder's own and opt-in, and nothing is sold to third parties. The line not to cross is turning the portal into a marketplace or charging for enquiries from the builder's own customers.
ideas.regulatory: D12 (publishing aggregate counts only; no customer data), Consumer law on accurate claims (the badge must state exactly what is counted). None otherwise.
ideas.build_dependency: Lock (SV-4) and existing proof/variation records. Build: a stats projection and a public page. Effort: small to medium (2 weeks).
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders could avoid locking bad jobs; publish 'jobs completed in JobGuard' as the denominator so unlocked jobs are visible as a gap, and count only server-verified evidence.
ideas.precedent: Checkatrade public plans Free/£30/£59, real bills £100–£500+ a month, 12-month contracts, per-lead fees £5–£25 on some plans (https://nobleleads.uk/blog/how-much-does-checkatrade-cost; https://localadder.co.uk/blog/checkatrade-cost/). Checkatrade bundles a free quoting tool with membership (https://www.checkatrade.com/blog/news/checkatrade-quoting-and-invoicing-tool/).

ideas.name: Applied supplier credit notes as qualifying recovery (the D03 extension the plan already anticipates)
ideas.mechanism: Fixed decision: supplier overcharge earns 10% only when refunded in cash after the builder paid; credit notes 'stay excluded until D03 extends'. AP recovery auditors count credit memos taken as recoveries. Translation: when a post-payment overcharge is settled by a supplier credit note and JobGuard can evidence that the credit was applied to a later invoice the builder actually paid (supplier statement plus the settled invoice via bank feed), the applied amount joins Q for that case and the ordinary 10% applies. Unapplied credits never count; a credit later reversed triggers the linked compensation path.
ideas.who_pays: The builder pays 10% of the applied credit value; the supplier funded it.
ideas.assumptions: Materials 40% of turnover; post-payment overcharge rate 0.5% of materials (assumption; PRGX's ~0.1% is for large, well-controlled AP); 60% settled by credit rather than cash; JobGuard catches half. The honest conclusion is that supplier-overcharge fees are small money for JobGuard at any archetype; the value is in prevention (idea 2) and in demonstrating the watchdog works.
ideas.trust_note: Builders will see this as JobGuard finding real money they had already lost; the only friction is proving the credit was actually used, which is why the evidence rule matters.
ideas.regulatory: D03 v3 (extend the supplier-overcharge category to applied credits with an evidentiary standard), D01, D02; G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Supplier document intake (0033), recovery cases (0034), M4-7 bank feed and M4-8 allocation for the 'later invoice paid' fact; supplier statement ingestion via SV-7 connectors. Effort: small to medium (2 weeks) plus the D03 revision.
ideas.gaming_risk: Double counting a credit and a cash refund for the same line — unique derivation identity per case line (AGENTS §5.6); a supplier could reclassify a genuine price cut as a 'credit' — only credits linked to a flagged overcharge count.
ideas.precedent: PRGX contingency fees are a percentage of amounts clients recover from overpayment claims (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1007330/000100733020000003/a201910kprgx.htm); AP recovery audit fees typically 20–30% (https://www.apexanalytix.com/resources/blog/recovery-audit-cost/).

ideas.name: CIS and site-labour compliance add-on (Hammr translation)
ideas.mechanism: Hammr sells construction payroll and prevailing-wage compliance on subscription and markets it as margin protection (case study: $30k saved). The UK analogue for small builders is the Construction Industry Scheme: subcontractor verification, 20%/30% deductions, monthly CIS300 returns and payment-and-deduction statements, plus employment-status checks. JobGuard already knows who worked on which job (site staff feeding evidence) and what was paid on supplier/subcontractor invoices. Translation: a CIS add-on that generates deduction statements and the monthly return from job-linked subcontractor invoices, with penalty-avoidance reminders. Sold at a flat monthly price, like Xero's £5/month CIS module but job-linked.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, monthly add-on.

revenue_per_year.solo: £60 (£5/month, only if the builder uses subcontractors)

ideas.assumptions: Prices sit just above Xero's £5/month CIS add-on because the value is job-linking. Many builders will already do CIS in their accounting package, so attach is uncertain. This is defensive scope; it is included because Hammr was in the lens, not because it is a strong earner.
ideas.trust_note: Pure builder benefit (avoiding HMRC penalties and admin). No trust issues.
ideas.regulatory: HMRC agent/online-filing registration if JobGuard files; otherwise export to the accountant. Employment-status determinations must remain the builder's decision with signposting, not JobGuard's advice.
ideas.build_dependency: Subcontractor invoices via supplier intake (0033) and job linkage exist; needs a CIS module, HMRC filing integration or accounting-connector export (SV-7 accounting connector). Effort: medium to large (4–6 weeks). Low priority.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material.
ideas.precedent: Hammr: construction payroll/HR platform on subscription, marketed on saved hours and dollars (https://www.hammr.com/; https://www.hammr.com/blog/custom-masonry-saves-30000-hammr-case-study). Xero UK charges £5/month for CIS returns (https://www.xero.com/uk/pricing-plans/).

ideas.name: Pooled purchasing rebates from merchants (NMBS / Fortis / IBG translation) — listed because it is the biggest number, and flagged because it poisons the watchdog
ideas.mechanism: NMBS pools 1,000+ merchants' invoices, guarantees supplier payment, and returns an average rebate of about 3.84% on invoices cleared through it. Translation: JobGuard aggregates its builders' materials spend (it already ingests POs and invoices), negotiates rebates with participating merchants, passes most of the rebate to builders and keeps a slice (1% of spend assumed). This is the classic way to monetise purchasing data.
ideas.who_pays: Merchants/suppliers pay JobGuard; builders receive a partial rebate.
ideas.assumptions: Materials 40% of turnover; half of spend at participating merchants; JobGuard retains 1 point of a ~3–4 point rebate. NMBS can earn its rebate partly because it guarantees payment, which JobGuard cannot do (it never holds funds), so JobGuard's negotiating position would be weaker than assumed.
ideas.trust_note: This is the idea the brief warned about: once merchants pay JobGuard, every overcharge flag against a paying merchant is suspect, and every non-flag looks bought. The research notes on energy brokers (hidden per-kWh commissions now under Ofgem regulation and a Court of Appeal fiduciary ruling) show where supplier-paid intermediaries end up. Recommendation: do not build. The safe cousin is builder-side only: JobGuard checks that the builder's own trade discounts and rebates were applied correctly on each invoice, which is prevention and belongs in idea 2.
