ideas.regulatory: No licence, but disclosure duties and fiduciary-style exposure (Expert Tooling v Engie, CA 2025, half-secret commissions), D11 conflict-of-interest rules, and it contradicts the spirit of the supplier watchdog in the build plan.
ideas.build_dependency: Supplier intake exists; would need merchant agreements and a rebate ledger. Effort is not the constraint; trust is.
ideas.gaming_risk: Merchants steering pricing to JobGuard builders while raising list prices elsewhere; JobGuard's own temptation to soften flags on paying merchants. Not mitigable by policy alone.
ideas.precedent: NMBS: average rebate 3.84% on invoices processed, achieved by pooling turnover and guaranteeing member payments; it clears invoices for Fortis, CBA, H&B, PHG, NBG, IBC and IPG (https://www.nmbs.co.uk/faqs/; https://www.nmbs.co.uk/). UK SME energy brokers earn 0.3–2p/kWh in supplier-paid commission, now subject to Ofgem disclosure rules (research notes, section 2).

ideas.name: Value-receipt annual review with a conditional fair-price escalator
ideas.mechanism: On each subscription anniversary a worker builds the builder's 12-month value receipt from posted facts only (the VALUE-2 cards in BUILD_PLAN §14.13): 'Tracked through to your bill' (£ of builder-captured variations invoiced), 'Flagged before you paid' (count and £ of supplier lines above agreed price caught at three-way match — worded 'flagged', never 'saved', per §14.1 forbidden claims), 'Found after your bill was complete' (recovered £ and fee), and median days quote→invoice. Terms pre-agree an annual step of the lesser of 8% or a fixed amount that keeps the left digit (Solo £29→£31, Builder £59→£64, Firm £119→£129). The step is applied only when tracked+recovered £ ≥ 20× the subscription paid that year; otherwise the price is frozen and the receipt says so. 30 days' notice with the receipt attached; cancel without penalty. A new `subscription_terms` version (§14.12) references the receipt hash; the period obligation is charged through the ordinary D09 path.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (subscriber), from year 2 of tenure.

revenue_per_year.solo: +£24 per builder-year of tenure if qualifying (£2 × 12); expected +£18 at 75% qualifying, on a £348 baseline
revenue_per_year.small_firm: +£60 if qualifying (£5 × 12); expected +£45 at 75% qualifying, on a £708 baseline
revenue_per_year.firm: +£120 if qualifying (£10 × 12); expected +£90 at 75% qualifying, on a £1,428 baseline

ideas.assumptions: Baseline = report recommendation £29/£59/£119 monthly → £348/£708/£1,428 a year. Steps chosen to keep the first digit (report §'£29 beats £30'). Threshold 20×: Solo £348×20 = £6,960 of tracked+recovered extras a year (~5% of £150k turnover) — assumed reached by 75% of accounts; no data on extras volume exists (report §'Frame the price against lost money' says the only UK figure is a weak insurer survey). Compounds in later years. Evidence for value-justified rises is weak: dual-entitlement research (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler 1986, report §'The hidden final check') finds cost-justified rises fair and advantage-taking unfair; a rise pegged to the customer's own gain is untested. Operational transparency (Buell & Norton 2011) supports showing the receipt.
ideas.trust_note: Can read as 'you charge me more because I did well'. The visible freeze when value is low is the fairness gesture that makes it tolerable; keep steps small. Never cite JobGuard-found catches as justification for a subscription rise — the fee already pays for those. The 'flagged' line must not be described as money saved (§14.1).
ideas.regulatory: B2B price-variation clause in standard terms — UCTA 1977 reasonableness and clear notice; D09 v2 must define price changes, notice and grandfathering (it lists these as undefined); D02 VAT on the subscription. No FCA implication.
ideas.build_dependency: VALUE-2 value receipt (SV-6) and D09 metering (M4-11 subscription sign-up, M4-13 agreement) must exist; add `subscription_terms` versioning and an anniversary worker. Small once those land (~1 task).
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Inflating tracked extras raises the builder's own price (no incentive). A builder might keep extras off JobGuard to stay under the threshold — a £24–£120 rise is too small to motivate that if the step stays small.
ideas.precedent: Annual uplift clauses of 5–10% are common SaaS practice (general knowledge, not in the research). No precedent found for a value-conditional freeze. Report §'A higher price buys little credibility' on why framing, not level, does the work.

ideas.name: Value-floor guarantee that justifies a higher Builder and Firm price
ideas.mechanism: Raise Builder to £79 and Firm to £149 (Solo stays £29 — raising the entry price fights the free Checkatrade tool and 29% software adoption, report §Recommendation) and attach a guarantee: 'If your 12-month value receipt — extras tracked through to your bill, supplier lines flagged before you paid, and money found after your bill was complete — comes to less than 5× what you paid us, we credit the shortfall against your next year, up to what you paid.' Trigger is computed at anniversary from posted facts; the credit is a subscription credit only, issued as a platform credit note (M4-10) with a linked journal. It never touches success fees (D01/D09 no-offset rule intact).
ideas.who_pays: Builder businesses on Builder and Firm pay the higher list price; JobGuard pays the credits.

revenue_per_year.solo: −£17 expected (no list change; 10% of accounts trigger a credit averaging 50% of £348)

ideas.assumptions: Trigger rate 10% and average credit 50% of subscription are guesses; the 5× threshold is easy for an active builder (a small firm logging ~£36k of extras a year clears 5 × £948 = £4,740 many times over) so the guarantee mostly protects builders who barely use the product. The compromise effect (report §'Three tiers work…') needs the middle plan easy to justify: at £29/£79/£149 the middle is 2.7× Solo rather than the ~2× the report suggested — untested. No quantitative evidence on money-back guarantees in SaaS was found (price_level note §5 gaps). Price-quality signalling is small and weak for familiar buyers (report §'The founder's price-signals-quality hunch').
ideas.trust_note: JobGuard bears the risk, which is the strongest quality signal the research identifies (a fee/guarantee earned only on results). Honest only if 'tracked' is labelled as the builder's own work tracked, not 'found', and 'flagged' is never 'saved'. Do not market it as insurance.
ideas.regulatory: Confirm the credit is a price adjustment on JobGuard's own service, not a contract of insurance (FSMA/RAO); B2B terms; D09 amendment for credits; D02 VAT credit-note treatment; D01 unaffected.
ideas.build_dependency: VALUE-2 receipt (SV-6), M4-10 credit-note document with journal, M4-11 subscription. Small on top of those.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder could under-use the product to trigger the credit, but pays a full year first and the credit is capped at the subscription paid. Disputes over the receipt are resolved from the immutable record.
ideas.precedent: Chargeflow '4x ROI Guarantee' with 25% success fee (success_fee_benchmarks §6); BigChange '£5 saved per £1' ROI claim without a guarantee (construction_platforms note). Report §Recommendation for the £59/£119 spacing.

ideas.name: Peak-live-jobs bands with a published Contractor tier and monthly auto-step
ideas.mechanism: Define 'live' precisely: switched live and final account not yet locked, with a dormancy rule (no activity for 60 days → not counted until it wakes). Meter = peak concurrent live jobs in the billing month. Bands: Solo ≤3 £29; Builder ≤8 £59; Firm ≤15 £119; Contractor ≤30 £199; above → on request. If the month's peak exceeds the band, that month bills at the next band (one-off step, no upgrade lock-in), with an in-app notice when the builder is one job below the band. Never block a switch-live. The period obligation is derived from the metered fact (D09 `metering_execution`).
ideas.who_pays: Builder businesses whose peak month exceeds their band; the Contractor tier captures 16–30-job firms that the report left 'on request'.

revenue_per_year.solo: +£60 (peaks at 4 live jobs in ~2 months a year × £30 step)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 (5–6 live jobs sits inside the Builder band)
revenue_per_year.firm: +£320 (~15 live on average, peaks of 16–18 in ~4 months × £80 step to Contractor)

ideas.assumptions: Peak distributions are guesses. Honest verdict on the meter: it works as a capacity meter — it is the ServiceM8 workload model (report §'UK builders already pay…') and scales roughly with headcount. Three caveats. (1) It is coarse: the band widths and the ceiling tier set the price, not the unit — a 15-person firm at 15 live jobs pays £119 where Tradify would charge it £510–£660 (report §Recommendation), so tightening the top bands is where realised price lives. (2) 'Live' must be defined so it cannot be gamed by early locking or never switching live. (3) It does not track value at all (three £40k jobs cost the same as three £3k jobs), which is exactly why the success fee, not the subscription, must carry value capture.
ideas.trust_note: A monthly step with warning is fairer than a hard cap or a forced annual upgrade, but surprise steps annoy; the at-band notice and 'never block' rule are what keep it acceptable. The known risk is builders keeping small jobs off JobGuard to stay in band, which starves the shadow bill (report §'Charge for live jobs, not people').
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 must define concurrency intervals and billing periods; D05 bounded renewal authorisation needs an explicit amount ceiling (the next band's price); D02.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-14 (optional active-job tiers) plus a metering worker; needs `job.switched_live` (M1-7) and `final_account_lock` (SV-4) for the live definition. Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Locking early or leaving jobs unswitched to reduce the count — self-harming (no tracking, no final check) and already a D11 v2 signal ('invoice or payment activity with no lock'). Keep bands generous and steps monthly.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 £25/£59/£119/£269 by jobs per month, unlimited users (report table). Usage-overage steps are standard SaaS practice.

ideas.name: Winter pause instead of a 'two months free' annual discount
ideas.mechanism: Launch without the standard 17% annual discount. Any monthly subscriber may pause for up to 2 consecutive months a year: data retained, quoting still free, live jobs frozen (no watchdog, no locks, evidence accepted but not analysed — state this plainly). Paused periods create a £0 D09 period obligation with reason `paused`. If an annual plan is offered later, make it one month free (8%), not two.
ideas.who_pays: Nobody extra; JobGuard forgoes less discount than under the market-standard annual deal.

revenue_per_year.solo: +£12 vs an annual-discount baseline (0.4 × £58 discount avoided − 0.2 × £58 pause cost)

ideas.assumptions: Baseline assumes 40% of builders would take annual at two months free (Powered Now, YourTradebase, Joist all use that wording — report table); 20% would use a two-month pause. Both rates are guesses. The research explicitly flags a winter pause as an untested hypothesis that might cut churn more than annual prepay for seasonal trades (price_level note §6). Annual-plan churn claims are confounded by self-selection (report §'Offer annual billing, don't force it').
ideas.trust_note: Matches how building work actually runs. Only risk is confusion about what is off during a pause — say it in one sentence.
ideas.regulatory: D09 must define pause; D05 bounded renewal must permit £0 periods; nothing else.
ideas.build_dependency: A `paused` state in the subscription period machine (M4-11/M4-13). Small.
ideas.gaming_risk: Pausing while a job is still active to dodge two months — capped at 2 months a year and the watchdog is off, so the builder loses protection for the months they pause.
ideas.precedent: Consumer subscription pauses (general practice, not in the research). Two-months-free annual is the trade norm (report table).

ideas.name: Success fee on applied supplier credit notes (D03 v3 extension)
ideas.mechanism: Today a supplier overcharge earns 10% only as a cash refund (§14.7). Extend D03: a credit note raised after the builder paid an overcharged invoice qualifies once it is shown applied — consumed against a later supplier invoice that the builder then paid in full — evidenced by the supplier statement or the later invoice carrying the credit line, matched in supplier intake. Qualifying principal = applied credit net of VAT; fee derived by the same v3 routine with source identity (credit note id, applied invoice id). Unapplied credits and pre-payment invoice reductions (prevention) never qualify. Only for overcharges JobGuard flagged and the builder opened as a case with fee terms approved, as for withheld payments.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, 10% of the applied credit, after their next supplier bill is settled.

revenue_per_year.solo: +£17 (150 supplier invoices × 2% post-payment overcharges = 3 × £80 = £240 × 70% by credit note = £168 × 10%)

ideas.assumptions: Materials ≈ 40% of turnover; average supplier invoice £400–£530; only 2% of invoices produce an overcharge found after payment (most are caught before payment and earn nothing under the fixed rule); 70% of merchant refunds come as credit notes. No UK data on supplier error rates for small builders exists (WTP note §6 gaps).
ideas.trust_note: The builder gets real money back, but 10% of a credit they had to phone the merchant about can feel like '10% for noticing' — the fairness crux is who did the work (Xia, Monroe & Cox, report §'The hidden final check'). Requiring a JobGuard-originated flag and an explicit case with approved terms keeps it honest. Suppliers pay JobGuard nothing, so the invoice watchdog stays uncompromised.
ideas.regulatory: D03 v3 (new category version), D01, D02. No FCA implication.
ideas.build_dependency: Supplier statement intake and credit-note-application matching (extends supplier intake 0033/0036/0037 or SV-7 connectors), D03 review flow, new source type in the v3 derivation. Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Refunds parked as never-applied credits stay fee-free forever — accept it. Require supplier documents (hashed), never builder attestation, for the 'applied' fact.
ideas.precedent: AP recovery auditors (PRGX) charge 20–30% contingency on recovered value including credits (success_fee_benchmarks §1).

ideas.name: Size-banded success fee: 15% on the first £1,000 of each recovery
ideas.mechanism: D01 v4: per coalesced recovery, fee = 15% of the first £1,000 of qualifying net principal plus 10% above £1,000, computed cumulatively and rounded once, with the same reversal mechanics as §14.9. The headline '10%' still applies to everything above £1,000; small catches carry the higher band. The band must bind to the coalesced work item, not to individual receipts.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, on small recoveries.
ideas.assumptions: Base fee case (assumption; no public data on recoverable value per job — WTP note §6): jobs a year 19/24/33; 70% locked; a paid catch on 25% of locked jobs; average catch 2% of job value (£160/£500/£1,200); base fee revenue £55/£210/£700 a year.
ideas.trust_note: The founder fixed 10%; the report says keep the rate identical everywhere so it does not blur the comparison, and that 10% is already the credible floor. Banding mirrors FCA claims-management bands where small claims pay more — the sector JobGuard should not resemble. Included because it is in scope, not because it is recommended.
ideas.regulatory: D01 v4 and D03; the FCA CMC cap does not apply (construction payment is not a regulated CMC sector) but 'claims' language should be avoided (report legal notes).
ideas.build_dependency: Generalise the v3 routine to banded rates (SV-6) with a v4 fixture table replacing §14.9's; small-medium, but it reopens a fixed decision.
ideas.gaming_risk: JobGuard-side incentive to avoid coalescing so more recoveries sit in the 15% band — must be prevented structurally (§14.10 one recovery per work item).
ideas.precedent: FCA CMC fee bands 15–30% by claim size; UK debt collectors 8–15% fresh debt (report benchmark table).

ideas.name: Minimum fee of £25 per confirmed catch
ideas.mechanism: D01 v4: fee = max(10% × Q, £25) per coalesced recovery, applied only once settled cash exists; the floor bites when Q < £250. Shown as an explicit line on the statement.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, on catches under £250.
ideas.assumptions: Same base fee case as the size-banded idea. Catch-size distribution is guessed. The revenue is negligible; the only real argument is cost coverage per evidence pack.
ideas.trust_note: A £25 fee on a £120 catch is 21%, on a £60 catch 42% — it reads as a penalty on small honest recoveries, and JobGuard's per-catch effort is automated so the effort-based fairness argument is weak. Not recommended; listed for completeness.
ideas.build_dependency: Trivial change to the v3 routine plus new fixtures; the cost is in trust, not code.
ideas.gaming_risk: None from the builder.
ideas.precedent: Cosmo DCA file-opening fee £25–£75 plus 6–10% (success_fee_benchmarks §3); Chargeflow $29 per deflected chargeback.

ideas.name: 'Final Check Only' pay-per-use for non-subscribers
ideas.mechanism: A non-subscriber imports their accepted quote, uploads receipts, supplier invoices, photos, customer messages and their draft final bill, pays a flat £29 per check at upload (Stripe hosted), then declares 'this is my complete final account' — which creates the §14.4 lock. A worker runs the §14.5 final check on evidence received before lock; the reveal shows each candidate with its evidence; the builder confirms or dismisses. A confirmed catch is invoiced through JobGuard on its own invoice and paid via JobGuard's hosted payment link (separate invoice → §14.8 rule 2 → verified settlement). Fee 15% (non-member rate, D01 v4) under exact statement approval. Members pay 10% and get the watchdog all job long, so every check ends with a subscribe prompt.
ideas.who_pays: Non-subscribing builders: £29 per check plus 15% of settled catches.

revenue_per_year.solo: £338 if used instead of subscribing (10 checks × £29 = £290, plus 10 × 20% × £160 × 15% = £48); baseline subscription £348

ideas.assumptions: Half of jobs get checked; upload-only evidence is thinner so a paid catch on 20% of checks (vs 25% for subscribers); priced so subscribing wins for anyone with more than ~12 jobs a year. The 15% rate is a second rate (needs D01 v4).
ideas.trust_note: Nothing is held back mid-job because the job is already over, so the hold-back objection is absent. The 10% vs 15% gap must be explained plainly ('members pay less'). Late extra bills to homeowners are B2C and more dispute-prone (report legal notes).
ideas.regulatory: D12 Article 14 route for uploaded customer messages (third-party personal data); D13 lock and disclosure rules; D01 v4 (second rate), D03, D02; Stripe hosted surfaces only (no card data, M4); evidence uploaded after lock can never qualify (§14.6).
ideas.build_dependency: Quote import + upload-only intake (proof uploads 0015/0025 and supplier intake 0033 exist), SV-3/4/5/6, M4-11 hosted payment for catch invoices. Large; after SV-6 and G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Highest residual risk of any idea: with no bank feed, a builder can take the reveal and bill outside JobGuard (§14.10 residual risk). The flat £29 covers the cost; treat the 15% as upside. A bill uploaded with items already invoiced elsewhere produces no fee because settlement never flows through JobGuard.
ideas.precedent: FairRate £0.99 per audit (homeowner direction, report §'No rival sells…'); Chargeflow no-subscription 25%; QuickPrice pay-per-quote.

ideas.name: Prepaid recovery credits
ideas.mechanism: Builder buys £250 of success-fee credit for £200 (20% off), valid 24 months, refundable at face less discount on cancellation. Success fees derived under v3 are settled from the credit balance first, in a fee-prepayment ledger separate from the subscription book (the D09 'subscription never offsets fees' rule is untouched). The statement reads '£1,000 recovered · fee £100 paid from your recovery credit · balance £150'.
ideas.who_pays: Builders who opt in, in advance.

revenue_per_year.solo: −£10 (base fee £55 × −20% ≈ −£11; solos rarely buy; small breakage)

ideas.assumptions: Same base fee case. Breakage 15% is a guess and refundable credits reduce it further. The point is not price: prepayment decouples the pain of paying from the reveal (Prelec & Loewenstein 1998), so the found money feels like a windfall (Arkes et al. 1994) and the fee does not feel like a toll — WTP note §2. That effect is theory, not measured on tradespeople.
ideas.trust_note: Prepaying 'to be told what you missed' is an odd purchase, and expiring credits are a classic trust irritant — must be refundable. Benefits are cash-flow and retention, not realised price.
ideas.regulatory: Prepayment for JobGuard's own services is single-purpose (not e-money, not client money) — confirm; refund terms; D01/D05 for settlement source; D02 VAT tax point on receipt of prepayment.
ideas.build_dependency: Fee-prepayment ledger and settlement order in M4-12 collection; M4-10 statements. Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Minimal; refunds on cancellation bound it.
ideas.precedent: Prepaid credit packs are common SaaS practice (general knowledge); none in the research. Flat-rate bias evidence (Lambrecht & Skiera 2006) suggests some builders overpay for predictability.

ideas.name: Card at switch-live: first live job subscription-free, fee charged normally
ideas.mechanism: Quoting stays free forever (§5.10). The subscription starts at the first switch-live: the switch-live screen is the paywall ('Switch live — JobGuard watches this job. Free on your first job.'), the card is captured on Stripe hosted sign-up (M4-11), the first live job's subscription is waived for up to 90 days, and the 10% success fee applies normally on that job so the builder experiences the real model (report §Recommendation). The subscription period obligation starts when the waiver ends.
ideas.who_pays: Builders who win a job and switch it live; the first job is subscription-free.

revenue_per_year.solo: £290 in year 1 per converted builder (£348 less ~2 months waived); the lever is conversion: at 6% → 15% of free quoters, expected revenue per quoter rises from ~£21 to ~£52
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £590 in year 1 (£708 less £118); expected per quoter ~£42 → ~£106
revenue_per_year.firm: £1,190 in year 1 (£1,428 less £238); expected per quoter ~£86 → ~£214

ideas.assumptions: Conversion figures borrow ChartMogul 2026: card-required trials 25–35% vs no-card 4–6% — B2B SaaS with sophisticated buyers, not tradespeople (report §'Let the trial run until the first job is live' says whether a card at switch-live helps or hurts is untested). Waiver ≈ 2 months average.
ideas.trust_note: Pay when you commit is intuitive and the free first job is a genuine gift. A sceptical builder asked for a card before seeing value may bounce — must be A/B tested (£29 vs £39 Solo, card vs no card, as the report recommends before charging).
ideas.regulatory: D09 (trial/free period), D05 (bounded renewal authorisation from the card), Stripe hosted only; §5.10 preserved because the charge arises at switch-live, an explicit separately authorised boundary, not at quoting.
ideas.build_dependency: Wire M4-11 subscription sign-up to the switch-live command (M1-7); small-medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Leaving the first job live to stretch the free window — capped at 90 days. Quoting in JobGuard and running the job elsewhere is the free layer working as designed.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 free tier of 30 jobs; Qted 3 months free with a card; ChartMogul 2026 conversion benchmarks (report table and price_level note §5).

ideas.name: Fixed-fee court-ready evidence pack for withheld-payment cases
ideas.category: Paid document product alongside the recovery fee
ideas.mechanism: When a builder has opened a `withheld_customer_payment` case (§14.7) and the customer still ignores the builder's own approved reminders, the builder can buy a small-claims evidence pack: the immutable evidence pack (M4-3) rendered as a dated PDF bundle — accepted quote, approved variations with customer approvals, proof photos, invoices, statement of account, reminder history and a factual chronology — for a flat £49 (Solo/Builder) or £99 (Firm), paid by exact approval through the command boundary. The 10% fee on cash settled afterwards is unchanged. JobGuard does not send it, represent the builder or draft argument (D10).
ideas.who_pays: The builder, per case, at the point they decide to escalate.
ideas.assumptions: Withheld-case frequency and 60% attach are guesses; late payment is the one well-measured pain (£26bn owed at any time, 51% of no-employee businesses affected — WTP note §6). The report notes agencies' percentages exclude court and enforcement costs and that JobGuard should say whether escalation is included — this makes it an explicit, cheap line.
ideas.trust_note: A builder owed £5k will gladly pay £49 for a bundle a claims consultant charges £400–£1,200 a day to assemble. Obviously in the builder's interest.
ideas.regulatory: Assembling the builder's own records without legal advice should not be a reserved legal activity or regulated claims management (construction payment is not a CMC sector) — needs legal confirmation; D10 (no representation), D12 (customer personal data in the pack, builder as controller for their own claim), D07 retention; court fees are the builder's.
ideas.build_dependency: Evidence packs exist (M4-3, #92); add PDF rendering, a paid document product on the command boundary and an M4-10 platform document line. Small-medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material.
ideas.precedent: Cosmo DCA £25–£75 file fee plus commission; RKA construction claims consultants £400–£1,200 a day; Chaser's collections add-on (success_fee_benchmarks §3–§6).

ideas.name: Paid finance seat for external bookkeepers and accountants
ideas.mechanism: Site users remain unlimited so evidence capture is never discouraged (report §'Charge for live jobs, not people'). Add a separate 'finance seat' role — read/export of posted facts, invoice and credit-note issue, accounting export, reconciliation view, no site capture needed — for an external bookkeeper or accountant at £15 a month per seat, metered on the subscription (D09 add-on). Firm includes one seat.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, per finance seat.
ideas.assumptions: Attach rates are guesses. Bookkeepers are plausibly the buying channel for solos (49% of no-employee businesses use accountancy software; MTD forces more — WTP note §5), so charging the channel could slow acquisition.
ideas.trust_note: Fair on its face, but Xero gives advisers free access precisely to drive adoption; a paid seat may cost more in lost referrals than it earns for Solo. Consider free for Solo, paid above.
ideas.regulatory: None beyond D09; the role needs its own permission scope and RLS tests (AGENTS §5.1).
ideas.build_dependency: Role/permission model in membership plus seat metering (M4-14-style). Small-medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Sharing the owner login with the bookkeeper — not worth policing.
ideas.precedent: YourTradebase £29 plus £15 per extra user (report table); Xero's free adviser access is the counter-precedent.

ideas.name: Same-screen fee statement with prompt bounded Direct Debit collection
ideas.mechanism: When qualifying settlement is verified (M4-8), show the statement on the same screen as the customer receipt — '£1,000 received · £900 yours · JobGuard fee £100 (10%)' — with the evidence trail one tap away; the builder approves the exact statement (D05 default) and JobGuard collects by Direct Debit (GoCardless, M4-12) within 7 days. Optionally a bounded, revocable standing authority (D05 option: amount ≤ 10% of the verified receipt, re-checked at execution) removes the approval step for builders who choose it. JobGuard still never touches the customer's money; the fee is a separate collection.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, the same fee as today, collected sooner and more reliably.
ideas.assumptions: Collection rate 95% with a same-screen prompt and DD vs 80% for a separate invoice weeks later — both guesses; the direction follows Thaler's integration principle (a small loss inside a larger gain hurts less) and the report's explicit warning that a separate invoice later 'would feel like an isolated loss' (report §'The hidden final check'; WTP note §2). Netting at source is impossible because JobGuard holds no customer funds.
ideas.trust_note: The most builder-friendly way to present a fee the founder has already fixed; the evidence trail on the same screen is what legitimises it (Buell & Norton 2011).
ideas.regulatory: D05 standing authority (bounded, revocable, checked again at execution — AGENTS §5.3), D01, D02 VAT invoice, GoCardless mandate rules; TrueLayer route per D10 for settlement evidence.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-8 settlement evidence, M4-9 derivation, M4-10 statement, M4-12 collection; the same-screen UI sits in SV-6's value receipt. Small on top of those.
ideas.gaming_risk: None; the builder can revoke standing authority and fall back to per-statement approval.
ideas.precedent: Paddle Retain and Chargeflow deduct from recovered flows (they hold the money; JobGuard cannot); Fergus nets its 1.6% + 20p card fee at source (report table).

ideas.name: Stage-payment and retention add-on priced per feature, not job value
ideas.category: Feature add-on (borderline vs the rejected value meter)
ideas.mechanism: An optional per-job add-on, 'Stage-payment watch', at £39 per live month: stage-payment schedule tracking, application and notice reminders, a retention ledger and a customer-facing stage statement. Bought per job by an explicit decision and charged on the subscription invoice per live month. It is bought for the feature; nobody with a simple deposit/final-balance job needs it.
ideas.who_pays: Builders running jobs with stage payments or retention — in practice mostly larger jobs.
ideas.assumptions: Job counts, live months and attach rates are guesses. The feature does not exist and its main buyers are the Firm archetype (average job £60k), which is why it looks like the contract-value meter the founder rejected entering by the back door.
ideas.trust_note: Honest only if it is genuinely a feature purchase and cheap enough that nobody feels forced by job size. Say so plainly on the pricing page.
ideas.regulatory: D06 currently forbids automating Construction Act notices, CIS, domestic reverse charge and retention in the pilot — the feature needs legal/tax review and a D06 revision; the Construction Act excludes residential occupiers so domestic and commercial jobs differ. Heavy.
ideas.build_dependency: Not built: a new stage-payment/retention module plus per-job add-on metering (D09). Large; M4 or later, after D06.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial; the exposure is legal, from automated notices.
ideas.precedent: Site Samurai £99–£699 and Payapps sell payment-application tooling to the subcontract chain (report §'No rival sells…').

ideas.name: Watchdog work allowance inside the live-jobs tiers (and the honest answer on the live-jobs meter)
ideas.mechanism: Keep the founder's live-jobs tiers (research recommendation: Solo up to 3 live jobs £29, Builder up to 10 £59, Firm up to 25 £119 ex VAT, Contractor on request). Add a second included allowance per tier that scales with the checking WORK JobGuard does rather than with turnover: supplier documents processed through intake (M2-2) plus purchase orders checked (M2-1) per billing period, e.g. 40 / 150 / 500 a month. Over the allowance, either £0.40 per extra document metered from immutable intake events aggregated per period (the M4-14 pattern), or a next-period upgrade proposal; never a mid-period block. A job counts as live from switch-live until the final-account lock (quotes stay free per AGENTS §5.10). Statement line reads 'documents checked', never 'money saved'. Honest verdict on the live-jobs meter: it works. It is simple, tracks workload, does not punish adding site staff who feed photos and notes, scales from sole trader to 20 staff, and ServiceM8 shows builders accept a jobs meter. Its three real weaknesses are (a) job-size blindness (a firm running 3 x £400k jobs lands on the Solo tier), (b) definition gaming (jobs kept off JobGuard or closed early), (c) seasonality. This allowance fixes (a) without turnover; generous allowances plus counting until lock and a D11 'invoice activity without lock' signal address (b); a winter pause option addresses (c).
ideas.who_pays: Builder (subscription, standing authority under D05)

revenue_per_year.firm: £1,428 (Firm tier; overage £0 at ~150 documents/month; an outlier with 3 large jobs and 400 documents/month on Solo would pay ~£150/month overage and be steered to Firm)

ideas.assumptions: Prices £29/£59/£119 from the report §'Recommendation'. Document volumes assumed at ~8 supplier documents per £8k job, ~25 per £25k job, ~50 per £60k job → 12 / 50 / 150 per month for Solo / Small / Firm at 2.5 / 5.5 / 15 live jobs. Overage £0.40 ≈ 3x marginal extraction+matching cost (assumption). Incremental revenue over a pure live-jobs tier is ~£0 for the typical archetype; the allowance mainly changes which tier an atypical builder lands in. Context for the other ideas: the credible non-borderline set below (documented supplier corrections, retention, evidence packs, file fee, statutory interest share, payment rails, applications add-on) adds roughly £280 / £1,040 / £3,140 a year on top of these subscriptions, all as assumptions to be tested in the pilot.
ideas.trust_note: Paying for verifiable checking work is the most defensible meter available; it is the one place where a prevention product can charge for effort without claiming an unprovable saving (Buell & Norton 'labour illusion', report §'The hidden final check'). Must never be framed as a share of savings.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (tiers, allowances, overage, pause, notice periods), D05 (bounded standing authority for renewals and tier changes), D02 VAT on the subscription. No FCA or consumer-law issue (B2B).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-14 (concurrency metering, currently 'optional' under rev 2.3 §14.13) becomes required and gains a document-count meter sourced from M2-2 intake events; M4-11 subscription checkout; M4-13 agreement; D09 v3. Effort: low-medium (M4-14 is already specified; one extra meter source plus fixtures).
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders withhold documents to stay under the allowance (self-defeating: no checks, and it feeds the value-guarantee activity condition); jobs closed early to drop a tier (count live until lock; D11 advisory signal). Cached counts must be rebuildable so an inconsistent counter cannot trigger a charge (M4-14 done-when).
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 charges by jobs per month with unlimited users at £25/£59/£119 (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'); Xero Ignite caps bills and invoices per month; Dext prices by document volume (raw note construction_platforms_and_ai.md §1).

ideas.name: Documented supplier correction fee (prevented overcharge proved by the supplier's own reissued invoice or credit note)
ideas.mechanism: New D03 v3 category `supplier_overcharge_corrected_pre_payment`. Trigger chain: (1) M2-5 raises a cited discrepancy Decision on an UNPAID supplier invoice line (price above agreed rate, quantity above GRN, duplicate line, pack-unit error); (2) the builder resolves it as 'disputing with supplier'; (3) a later supplier document — credit note, reissued invoice or corrected statement — arrives through intake (M2-2), is extracted and human-confirmed (M2-3) and matches the same supplier + invoice reference + line (M2-4); (4) the documented reduction = original confirmed line net minus corrected line net (exact pence) and is ≥ £25 net (the M2-5 recall threshold). Fee = greater of 5% of the documented reduction and £10, capped at £250 per catch, derived under the same locking/unique-derivation rules as §14.9, posted as a 'supplier correction' line on the monthly platform statement, approved per statement (D05 default) and collected via the M4-11/M4-12 rail. If the builder had already paid and the supplier refunds cash, the existing 10% `supplier_overcharge` category applies instead — never both (unique derivation identity on the coalesced discrepancy). The permitted wording is factual: 'Invoice 1234 line 3 was £180 above your agreed rate; Supplier X issued credit note C567 for £180 on 12 May' — no 'saved you' claim. The lower rate is the honest price of a weaker counterfactual: some builders would have caught it themselves.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: Materials spend 35% / 38% / 40% of turnover = £52.5k / £228k / £800k. Documented corrections = 0.75% of materials spend (assumption; the research found NO UK data on supplier invoicing errors for small builders — raw note success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp.md §6; large-firm AP audits recover ~0.1% after controls, small builders with no check assumed higher) → £394 / £1,710 / £6,000 corrected a year. Average catch £65 / £95 / £133 → 6 / 18 / 45 catches; the £10 floor applies to most, 5% only on the few larger ones; 30% of corrections never get re-uploaded so earn nothing. Solo: 6 x £10 x 0.7 ≈ £42. Small: 18 x £10 x 0.7 ≈ £126 plus a few larger at 5% ≈ £150. Firm: 45 x £10 x 0.7 ≈ £315 plus ~5 catches of £500 at 5% ≈ £420. Adoption (does the builder upload supplier documents at all) is the real driver.
ideas.trust_note: 'JobGuard spotted it, showed the arithmetic, the merchant's own paperwork proves the correction' is the strongest fairness position in the lens: JobGuard visibly did work the builder could not easily do (Xia/Monroe/Cox fairness finding, report §'The hidden final check'). Risk is nickel-and-diming on £10 catches; consider rolling floors into one monthly line. Honest limit: the fee is on the documented correction JobGuard flagged first, not on a proven saving.
ideas.regulatory: D03 v3 (new category, evidence sufficiency: both documents received via intake with hashes and object versions), D01 v4 (rate, floor, cap), D02 (VAT on the fee). No consumer-facing element; no FCA issue.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-2 → M2-5 must be live and passing the M2-5 held-out gate (FDP ≤ 5%, recall ≥ 90% at £25); D03 v3 + D01 v4 records; M4-9/M4-10 derivation and statement extended with a `documented_correction` source; SV-6 value receipt gains a 'Corrected before you paid' card. Effort: medium (a pure-domain predicate leaf plus a derivation/statement leaf).
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder negotiates an unrelated discount and the reissued invoice looks like a correction → require the JobGuard Decision to precede the correction, the correction to match the flagged line, and a builder confirmation 'corrected as flagged' (D11 advisory signal when corrections consistently exceed flagged deltas). Builder avoids uploading the corrected document to dodge the fee → the invoice stays 'disputed' in their own records; accepted residual, D11 signal. Supplier reissues for another reason (VAT fix) → only the flagged line's net delta counts.
ideas.precedent: AP recovery auditors (PRGX, apexanalytix) charge 20–30% contingency on recovered overpayments — post-payment only (report benchmark table; raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §1). ApprovalMax, Planyard and Tradify Plus sell bill-to-PO matching as a tier feature, not a fee; FairRate charges £0.99 per audit (report §'No rival sells a final check'). No product found charging on a pre-payment correction.

ideas.name: Statutory late-payment interest and compensation share (business customers only)
ideas.category: D03 extension — money on top of principal
ideas.mechanism: For a withheld-payment or retention case where the builder's customer is a business, JobGuard computes statutory interest (Bank of England base + 8%) and fixed compensation (£40 / £70 / £100 by debt size) under the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 from the immutable invoice issue and due dates (M1-12), includes them as separate lines in the builder-approved demand (M4-5), and takes 50% of the interest and compensation ACTUALLY paid — verified landing (M4-7/M4-8) explicitly allocated to those lines. The fixed 10% stays on principal only; this is a separate D03 category so the two never blend. Most small builders never claim these sums, so the counterfactual is unusually strong: the money exists because JobGuard computed and included it.
ideas.who_pays: Builder, out of sums the debtor paid on top of the principal
ideas.assumptions: Business-customer share 10% / 30% / 50%; B2B cases opened per year 0.5 / 2 / 5; average overdue invoice £8k / £10k / £25k, 60 days late at ~13% (assumed base 5% + 8%) → interest £171 / £214 / £534 plus compensation £70 / £70 / £100; only 50% of claimed statutory sums actually get paid (debtors often refuse); JobGuard share 50% → £60 / £71 / £159 per case → £30 / £142 / £793.
ideas.trust_note: The builder keeps every pound of principal beyond the fixed 10% and receives money they would not have asked for. Builders may waive interest to protect a relationship; the share applies only if paid, and the builder decides whether to include the lines at all.
ideas.regulatory: Late Payment Act applies to business debtors only (report §'No rival sells…', raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §3); D03 v3 new category; D10 pursuit scope (builder sends, JobGuard drafts); the interest calculation must be a versioned pure function with the base rate as a dated fact, never model-derived; not FCA debt collecting for the builder's own service invoices per SRA guidance — confirm with a lawyer.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-1/M4-2 case model and eligibility review; M4-5 templates with interest and compensation lines (professionally reviewed via M4-19); M4-8 allocation of receipts to interest lines; D03 v3. Effort: low-medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Customer pays principal and refuses interest → no fee. Builder cannot inflate lateness because invoice dates are immutable from issue. A builder could open a case only to add interest to a debt already about to be paid → the existing withheld-payment entry test (overdue beyond threshold, own reminder ignored) applies.
ideas.precedent: Some UK B2B agencies run a 'debtor-pays' model keeping the statutory compensation and recovery costs as their fee (industry practice recalled from memory, not looked up — verify). Collection-agency file-fee-plus-percentage hybrids in raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md summary table.

ideas.name: Retention release tracking and chase (5% of overdue retention released after a JobGuard-dated demand)
ideas.mechanism: For jobs with a contractual retention (commercial/subcontract work modelled in M4-18), JobGuard records the retention sum and release dates at switch-live or application stage and raises a Decision when a release date passes unpaid. If the builder explicitly opens a retention case with fee terms (mirroring the `withheld_customer_payment` entry test: past due, own reminder ignored) and approves and sends JobGuard's drafted release application (M4-5), then 5% of retention CASH settled after case opening and allocated to the case (M4-8, bank-verified via M4-7 or verified remittance) is the fee. 5% rather than 10% because the money is a contractual entitlement that usually needs only a timely, correctly worded demand.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: Commercial/subcontract share of turnover 5% / 25% / 40%; retention 5% of that value → £375 / £7,500 / £40,000 held a year; 25% of it overdue at the release date (assumption — the 2017 BEIS retentions consultation reported large sums of retention unpaid or lost to insolvency; verify figures before quoting); JobGuard chases and it settles → £94 / £1,875 / £10,000 x 5%. Almost entirely a Firm-tier revenue line.
ideas.trust_note: Builders widely forget retention; the chase is visible, dated work and the fee is on cash that arrived after it. Must not touch retention paid on time (the fixed 'ordinary late payment does not count' rule).
ideas.regulatory: D03 v3 category; D10 (builder is sender); Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 payment/pay-less notice rules shape the demand text (M4-19 reviewed templates); residential occupiers are outside the Act (raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §4, unverified); not FCA debt collecting — confirm.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-18 (interim applications and retention schedule), M4-19 (reviewed notices), M4-5, M4-7/M4-8 landing and allocation, D03 v3. Effort: medium; late in M4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Case opened on retention that would have been paid on the due date anyway → entry test requires the date to have passed and a builder reminder ignored. Retention paid outside the app → landing must be bank-verified or it stays non-billable.
ideas.precedent: Payapps and Site Samurai track retention and applications as flat-fee features (raw note construction_platforms_and_ai.md §2); UK collectors take 8–15% on fresh B2B debt (report benchmark table). No product charges on retention release.

ideas.name: Certified evidence pack sold per pack
ideas.mechanism: In-app viewing and plain PDF export of the builder's evidence stay free. The hash-verified, timestamp-anchored bundle (M4-3 manifest + M4-4 RFC-3161 anchoring + standalone verifier, with redaction and recipient-bound authority) is a paid artefact: £49 standard pack (dispute, insurer, handover) and £149 anchored pack with verifier report. Triggered by an explicit builder command 'Export certified pack' that creates and approves the Decision atomically (AGENTS §5.3); charged to the platform statement. This is the prevention value — proof before covering, three-way-matched supplier records, approved variations — turned into a document a third party will accept.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (may recharge to their customer or insurer)
ideas.assumptions: Packs per year 1 / 3 / 8 (assumption: roughly one dispute or insurer/warranty query per ~19 jobs for a solo builder, more on commercial work). Mix: 1 x £49; 2 x £49 + 1 x £149; 5 x £49 + 3 x £149.
ideas.trust_note: Pay-per-use for a tangible artefact is fair; the failure mode is builders feeling their own evidence is held hostage. Keep in-app access and plain export free and charge only for the anchoring and verification service.
ideas.regulatory: D07 retention (pack contents and holds), D12 (third-party personal data in packs, redaction), D04 (timestamp provider residency). Claims wording limited to integrity and existence, never proof of workmanship (AGENTS §5.8).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 evidence packs (merged as #92), M4-4 Object Lock and timestamp anchoring, a small commerce leaf on M4-10 statements. Effort: low once M4-4 exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Minimal; a builder reusing one pack across disputes is fine.
ideas.precedent: Construction claims consultants charge £350–£1,200 a day to assemble bundles (report benchmark table); FairRate charges per audit; no small-trade software sells certified packs.

ideas.name: Payment-rail margin on hosted 'pay now' (card and pay-by-bank)
ideas.mechanism: From M4, customer invoices carry a hosted Stripe pay-now link (card) and a pay-by-bank option (GoCardless Instant Bank Pay / Open Banking). JobGuard's Stripe Connect application fee: 0.4% on card payments; pay-by-bank: £0.30 margin per payment. Funds settle directly to the builder's connected account via direct charges; JobGuard never holds them. Disclosed on the pricing page and shown gross and net on every statement per M4-17 reconciliation rules. Faster invoicing (a prevention value JobGuard creates through final-account assembly) is what makes the rail get used.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (deducted by the processor from the payout, shown transparently)
ideas.assumptions: Card share of receipts 15% / 8% / 3% (homeowner deposits and small jobs by card; large sums by transfer); pay-by-bank used for 30% of ~3 / 4 / 5 payments per job. Solo: £150k x 15% x 0.4% = £90 + 19 jobs x 3 x 30% x £0.30 ≈ £5. Small: £600k x 8% x 0.4% = £192 + 24 x 4 x 30% x £0.30 ≈ £9. Firm: £2m x 3% x 0.4% = £240 + 33 x 5 x 30% x £0.30 ≈ £15.
ideas.trust_note: Standard in the category and transparent; only a trust problem if buried inside 'processing fees'.
ideas.regulatory: Stripe Connect Standard/direct charges are intended to keep the platform outside the Payment Services Regulations 2017 — confirm with a lawyer and Stripe; the UK consumer card-surcharge ban means the builder cannot pass card fees to homeowners; D05, D02; D04 provider residency; AGENTS §3 permits hosted Stripe/GoCardless only in M4 and never holding funds.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-11/M4-12 (Stripe hosted surfaces and webhooks), M4-15 (GoCardless as a separate rail), M1-12 customer invoice send. Effort: low incremental once the rails exist.
ideas.gaming_risk: None; builders choose the rail per invoice.
ideas.precedent: Fergus 1.6% + 20p, Jobber 2.9% + 30¢, Tradify and ServiceM8 Stripe pass-through (raw note uk_trade_job_software.md §5).

ideas.name: Applications-for-payment and construction-notices add-on (£39/month)
ideas.mechanism: The M4-18/M4-19 capability — interim applications, cumulative valuations, reviewed Construction Act payment and pay-less notices, deadline calculator with source and version, service evidence — sold as a monthly add-on to builders doing commercial or subcontract work, and included in the Contractor tier. It monetises the prevention of pay-less disputes and missed application deadlines, which cannot carry a success fee, as a feature with a clear buyer.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: £39/month ex VAT (£468/year); adoption 5% / 30% / 70%, tied to the assumed commercial-work share of each archetype.
ideas.trust_note: Plain feature pricing; nothing withheld, nothing contingent.
ideas.regulatory: D06 (jurisdiction and contract templates), M4-19 professional review of notice templates; no universal 'UK Construction Act deadline' hardcoded; the Act's residential-occupier exclusion (raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §4, unverified).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-18 and M4-19 (late M4, after M4-17); D09 add-on terms. Effort: high for the features, low for the commerce.
ideas.gaming_risk: None.
ideas.precedent: Site Samurai £99–£699 flat, Payapps priced on request, Construction AI £130+ (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45').

ideas.name: Documented-value guarantee ('catches or your subscription back')
ideas.mechanism: On Builder and Firm tiers: if in any rolling 12 months the builder's value receipt (SV-6) shows documented events — supplier corrections (idea above), confirmed final-check extras, recovered cash — totalling less than 3x the subscription paid, the builder can claim a subscription credit for the shortfall up to 100% of that year's subscription. Conditions: the account processed at least N supplier documents a month and locked at least M final accounts, so JobGuard had the chance to work. The credit applies to the subscription only and never offsets a success fee (fixed decision). It turns prevention into a marketing promise that licenses market-rate pricing, and it is cheap because the guarantee is measured on documented events, not on claimed savings.
ideas.who_pays: Nobody directly; JobGuard bears the refund risk

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 (excluded: low document volume makes the guarantee too often claimable)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: +£67 net (assumed +£120 price uplift minus £53 expected credits)
revenue_per_year.firm: +£133 net (assumed +£240 price uplift minus £107 expected credits)

ideas.assumptions: The guarantee lets JobGuard hold £59 / £119 instead of discounting to £49 / £99 (assumed −£10 / −£20 a month without it) = +£120 / +£240 a year; expected claim rate 15% x average 50% credit of £708 / £1,428 = −£53 / −£107. Conversion uplift not modelled: the research found no quantitative SaaS evidence on money-back guarantees (raw note price_level_and_tier_psychology.md §5).
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and consistent with the report's 'let results signal quality' stance. It also gives the value receipt a job beyond reassurance.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (terms, conditions, claim window), D02 (platform credit-note VAT). B2B, so consumer law is not engaged.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-6 value receipt as a documented-value ledger; M4-10 platform credit notes; D09 v3 wording. Effort: low.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder withholds documents to trigger the refund → activity conditions. Builder dismisses catches after the fact → only confirmed and settled events count; dismissals never reduce the ledger retroactively.
ideas.precedent: Chargeflow's '4x ROI guarantee' (raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §6); BigChange's '£5 for every £1' marketing claim (raw note construction_platforms_and_ai.md §4).

ideas.name: Withheld-payment case file fee (£35 at opening) alongside the existing 10%
ideas.mechanism: When the builder explicitly opens a `withheld_customer_payment` case (already gated by D03 v2: overdue beyond threshold, customer refused or ignored the builder's own reminder, fee terms approved), JobGuard charges a flat £35 file fee at opening for assembling the case pack, drafting the reviewed letters and tracking. Non-refundable and not credited against the 10%. Posted to the platform statement; the approval is the same Decision that opens the case. Builder or Firm tiers could include two cases a year rather than waiving the fee on success.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: Cases opened per year 1 / 2 / 4 (assumption: 5–12% of jobs go seriously overdue and only a fraction become cases).
ideas.trust_note: Paying to chase your own money stings when the chase fails; the research notes collectors' percentages exclude court and enforcement costs and that a builder chasing a homeowner bears the whole fee (report §'No rival sells…'). Acceptable because the builder opts in per case and sees the work.
ideas.regulatory: D01/D03 amendment; not FCA debt collecting for the builder's own service invoices per SRA guidance (report legal notes) — confirm; Late Payment Act interest only for B2B debtors; DMCC drip-pricing rules bite the builder's homeowner bill, not JobGuard's fee.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-1 case workbench, M4-5 templates, M4-10 statements. Effort: low.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder opens a case to get the letters and settles outside the app → file fee is still earned; no fee-side gaming.
ideas.precedent: UK collection 'fixed-fee hybrid: £25–75 file fee + 6–10%' (raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md summary table); Chaser subscription plus a separate collections service (report §'No rival sells…').

ideas.name: Value-indexed tier step at renewal (outcome-linked tier move)
ideas.mechanism: At each renewal (annual, or quarterly on monthly plans), if the trailing-12-month documented value on the SV-6 ledger exceeds 8x the subscription paid, JobGuard proposes the next tier (Solo→Builder, Builder→Firm, Firm→Contractor), showing the numbers and what the tier adds (allowances, included packs, applications add-on). The builder accepts through an explicit Decision creating a new bounded standing authority; declining changes nothing. With the guarantee above it forms a symmetric 'pay in proportion to documented results' band without putting a percentage on prevention.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: Acceptance 20% / 30% / 20%; step values +£30/month (Solo→Builder), +£60/month (Builder→Firm), +£80/month (Firm→Contractor at ~£199). Small firm: 30% x £720 = £216.
ideas.trust_note: Reads as 'you did well so we charge more' unless the step carries real extra capacity and is opt-in; fairness research says exploiting an advantage is judged unfair even where passing on costs is accepted (Kahneman/Knetsch/Thaler, report §'The hidden final check'). Never automatic.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3; D05 (a tier change is a new bounded authority, not something JobGuard may apply alone).
ideas.build_dependency: SV-6 ledger; M4-14 already specifies upgrade proposals with exact commercial impact; D09 v3. Effort: low.
ideas.gaming_risk: JobGuard-side temptation to inflate 'documented value' → only confirmed and settled events count, and the same figures sit on the builder's value receipt all year.
ideas.precedent: Usage-cap upgrade prompts (ServiceM8 job caps, Xero plan limits); no outcome-indexed tier precedent found.

ideas.name: Agreed-rate benchmark add-on (£15/month) — data-trust flag
ideas.mechanism: With opt-in, JobGuard aggregates human-confirmed supplier invoice lines across tenants (M2-3 confirmed data) into anonymised SKU price bands by region and month (k-anonymity of at least 10 tenants per cell) and shows a builder 'your agreed rate vs the band' in the M2-1 pre-commit check and at rate renewal. Sold as an add-on to builders only; never shown or sold to merchants; symmetric (you contribute to see); no tenant-identifiable row leaves the tenant. Better rates are prevention value with no provable counterfactual, so it is priced as a feature.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: £15/month; adoption 20% / 40% / 60%. Needs several hundred contributing tenants before cells populate, so this is year-2+ revenue.
ideas.trust_note: This is the 'selling builders' data' risk named in the brief, in its mildest form: aggregated, opt-in, builder-only. Survivable only with an absolute, tested rule that merchants never see anything and that the aggregation runs in an isolated role like `jobguard_shadow`.
ideas.regulatory: New decision record (D12 v3 / D04) on aggregate processing, lawful basis and ICO anonymisation standard; competition-law sensitivity is low for buyers pooling merchant prices but should be checked.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 and M2-3 confirmed data at scale; an aggregation worker under a separate database role with catalog tests; decision record. Effort: medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Merchants seeding false invoices to skew bands (weak); builders opting in with too few documents (cell thresholds).
ideas.precedent: Prolo (AI procurement for SME construction, revenue model undisclosed) and FairRate's 'local market rates' (raw note construction_platforms_and_ai.md §4).

ideas.name: Dispute and legal-expenses cover introduction commission — regulated flag
ideas.mechanism: Partner with one UK insurer or broker offering contract-dispute or legal-expenses cover to builders. JobGuard's proof discipline (proof gates before covering, three-way matching, certified packs) lowers the insurer's claims risk; JobGuard introduces consenting builders and earns an introducer commission. No advice and no arranging beyond passing details unless JobGuard is set up as an appointed representative.
ideas.who_pays: Insurer (commission); the builder indirectly through the premium
ideas.assumptions: Premium £250/year, commission 20% = £50; take-up 20% / 30% / 40%. Small money; included because guarantees and insurance were in the brief.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest if the product is good, but it edges toward 'selling builders as leads' and a partner paying JobGuard, both flagged in the brief. Opt-in, single-partner, disclosed commission.
ideas.regulatory: FCA insurance distribution: introducing for remuneration is generally regulated unless within the introducer exclusion (RAO art. 72C) or via IAR status — needs legal review; D12 for data transfer.
ideas.build_dependency: Consent capture and a referral link only; commercial work, not engineering. Effort: very low technically.
ideas.gaming_risk: None.
ideas.precedent: Trade-body affinity insurance schemes (FMB, Checkatrade member cover) — not looked up.

ideas.name: Quote-stage catch fee (site-visit omission proposed by JobGuard, accepted by builder and customer) — borderline
ideas.mechanism: When JobGuard's site-visit review proposes a scope line the builder did not mention (scope item provenance `model_suggestion`, cited to the walkthrough or photos per AGENTS §5.9), the builder accepts it into the quote, and the customer accepts that quote version with the line priced at £100 or more, charge a flat £5 per such line capped at £25 per accepted quote, recorded from the immutable scope-item identity (§5.2) and the accepted quote snapshot, and charged at switch-live (not at quote) to respect 'free quoting never bills'. Measurement is exact; the counterfactual is not: the builder priced and did the work.
ideas.who_pays: Builder
ideas.assumptions: Jobs quoted per year 19 / 24 / 33 at a 60% win rate; 1.5 / 2 / 3 accepted JobGuard-proposed lines per won job x £5. The acceptance rate of proposals is unknown.
ideas.trust_note: Charges on the builder's own work; the report's fairness evidence says builders reject fees where the extra 'was already in their head'. It also creates a JobGuard incentive to over-propose, and strains AGENTS §5.10 unless charged at switch-live. Recommended only as a counted item in the value receipt and guarantee, not as a charge.
ideas.regulatory: Would require amending §5.10 wording (charge at switch-live), D01; D02 VAT.
ideas.build_dependency: M1 provenance already separates model suggestions from human edits; needs a fee leaf on M4-9/M4-10. Effort: low; policy cost high.
ideas.gaming_risk: JobGuard over-proposes; builders retype lines to strip provenance (which also loses the citation) — both damage the product.
ideas.precedent: Qted includes an 'AI upsell generator' in its £59 plan rather than charging per line; Buildbite is per-user with a self-reported 30% change-order lift (raw note construction_platforms_and_ai.md §4).

ideas.name: Merchant-paid e-invoicing connector — supplier-side, flagged
ideas.mechanism: Builders' merchants pay JobGuard a flat connector fee to deliver invoices, delivery notes and credit notes directly by API through the SV-7 canonical evidence-observation contract instead of email and PDF, cutting their query volume. Flat per merchant, never per invoice, never contingent on match outcomes; detection code paths must be provably merchant-blind (architecture tests), and every discrepancy screen would disclose the relationship.
ideas.who_pays: Merchant
ideas.assumptions: £500/month per merchant per 1,000 connected builder accounts, spread across builders; only meaningful at scale.
ideas.trust_note: The brief says suppliers paying JobGuard compromises the invoice watchdog, and it does: even a flat fee creates the perception that JobGuard is 'in with the merchants', which is fatal for a product whose flagship prevention feature is checking merchants' invoices. Listed so it can be explicitly rejected or ring-fenced, not recommended.
ideas.regulatory: D04/D12 for the connector; the energy-broker experience (supplier-paid commission → Ofgem disclosure rules and Expert Tooling v Engie fiduciary finding) shows the transparency exposure (raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §2).
ideas.build_dependency: M2-2 intake plus the SV-7 connector pattern. Effort: medium per merchant.
ideas.gaming_risk: Merchant pressure to soften checks; structural independence required.
ideas.precedent: Supplier-network platforms (Coupa, Tradex) charge suppliers; UK energy brokers' supplier-paid commission model and its backlash (raw note success_fee_benchmarks.md §2).

ideas.name: Live-jobs ladder: Solo / Builder / Firm / Contractor (the meter itself)
ideas.mechanism: Tenant-level subscription metered on PEAK concurrent live jobs in the billing period, derived from immutable switch-live and close events (M4-14). 'Close' = final-account lock or an explicit 'close without final account' command; inactivity alone never closes a job. Tiers (research recommendation, not yet D09 values): Solo £29/mo up to 3 live; Builder £59/mo up to 10; Firm £119/mo up to 25; Contractor priced on request above 25. Unlimited users on every tier; quoting free on every tier. Exceeding the allowance never blocks switch-live: it raises an upgrade Decision, and the first over-limit period is a free grace. Charged monthly in advance via hosted Stripe subscription (M4-11) or GoCardless DD (M4-15) under bounded standing authority (D05). The platform invoice prints the period, tier, peak live count and the source events so the number is auditable.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (tenant), monthly, ex VAT. Never per job, never per user.
ideas.assumptions: Archetype live counts (2–3 / 5–6 / 15) sit inside the Solo/Builder/Firm allowances; monthly billing; prices are the research report's recommendation (§'Recommendation'), D09 v2 has not adopted them. DOES THE JOBS METER WORK? Yes for these archetypes, with three honest caveats: (1) it under-captures at the top — a Firm with ~£900k of work under watch pays £1,428/yr, so the ladder cannot do the value capture there; the success fee and the add-ons below must; (2) Solo sits on its allowance edge (3 of 3), so a fourth job is a 100% price jump unless idea 2 or a 4-job Solo allowance softens it; (3) the meter penalises exactly the behaviour JobGuard wants (more jobs on the platform feed the shadow bill), so allowances must stay generous and over-limit must never block. If a builder took every add-on listed below, the stack roughly reaches ~£1,000/yr (Solo, including a Builder upgrade), ~£2,400/yr (Small firm) and ~£3,800/yr (Firm).
ideas.trust_note: Simple, predictable, matches how builders think about workload. Unlimited users means the site lead and labourers who feed evidence are never a cost. The only trust risk is indirect: a tight allowance tempts builders to keep small jobs off JobGuard.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 (prices, allowances, cancellation, price-change notice, grandfathering), D05 (bounded renewal authority), D02 (VAT on platform invoices — a non-VAT-registered sole trader pays £34.80 for a £29 plan; state ex-VAT plainly). B2B, so DMCC drip-pricing rules do not bite. No FCA permission. Production charging gated by G4.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-13 (subscription terms + bounded standing authorization), M4-14 (concurrency metering — currently marked 'optional; only if D09 v2 adopts active-job tiers'; this ladder makes it mandatory), M4-11 (Stripe hosted subscription sign-up), M4-16 (dunning/suspension). Medium effort; M4-14 is already specified.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders under-declare by not switching small jobs live or delaying switch-live until near completion (D11 v1 'won-but-not-live' signal already exists). Peak-concurrency counting on immutable activation events resists close-and-reopen tricks. Do not add hard blocks: a blocked switch-live loses the fee base.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 £25/£59/£119 by job volume with unlimited users (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'); TradeFlow £36 flat; the report's own recommendation table.

ideas.name: Per-live-job overage ('extra job slot') instead of a forced upgrade
ideas.category: Packaging tweak inside the meter — usage line on the tier
ideas.mechanism: When peak live jobs exceed the tier allowance, each extra job in that period is billed as a flat slot on the next platform invoice (illustrative: £9 per job-month on Solo, £7 on Builder, £5 on Firm) rather than forcing a tier change. Slot prices are set so persistent overage costs about the same as upgrading (Solo +3 jobs × £9 = £27 ≈ the £30 step to Builder), so the upgrade nudge is arithmetic, not a block. Metered from the same M4-14 events; the invoice line cites the peak count and the jobs. The builder pre-approves overage in the subscription terms as a bounded standing authority (cap: no more than one tier step per period); without pre-approval an over-limit raises a Decision and the job still goes live.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, monthly in arrears on the platform invoice.
ideas.assumptions: Generous allowances from idea 1; overage frequency guessed, not measured; slot prices illustrative. Under tight allowances (Solo 2 / Builder 6 / Firm 15) the same archetypes would pay roughly £54–£81 / £0–£42 / £0–£60, but the research warns against tight allowances because they starve detection. This is a fairness device, not a revenue line.
ideas.trust_note: A soft meter is fairer than a hard cliff and is opt-in; but builders prefer flat prices to running meters (Prelec & Loewenstein, Lambrecht & Skiera, cited in the report), so overage must be rare and always shown as 'cheaper than upgrading this month'.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 must define slot price and cap; D05 must bound the standing authority (max overage per period) or each overage needs its own approved Decision; D02 VAT.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-14 (metering), M4-13 (terms with bounded overage authority), M4-10 (platform invoice lines). Low incremental effort once M4-14 exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Same as idea 1, plus the reverse risk: a stale 'live' job must never generate an overage charge, so the builder needs a visible live-jobs list with one-tap close (with recorded reason) before any overage is billed.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 charges 15p per extra job on Premium Plus; YourTradebase £15 per extra user; Jobber $29 per extra user (raw notes, uk_trade_job_software.md).

ideas.name: Weighted job slots: small-job allowance and large-job weighting
ideas.category: Packaging tweak inside the meter — keeps jobs as the unit
ideas.mechanism: At switch-live the already-frozen accepted_net_value_pence (M1-7, reused by §14.6) sets a fixed slot weight: ≤£2,500 net = 0.5 slot ('small jobs count half'), £2,500–£75,000 = 1 slot, £75,000–£200,000 = 2 slots, >£200,000 = 3 slots. The meter compares the weighted peak against the tier allowance. Weight is fixed at switch-live and never changes with variations or catches, so nothing JobGuard finds can move the meter. One pricing-page sentence: 'Small jobs count half; very large jobs count double.'
ideas.who_pays: The builder, through the tier/overage mechanics of ideas 1–2.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 (all ~£8k jobs = 1 slot; the half-weight lets two £2k jobs share a slot, slightly reducing upgrades)
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 within the archetype (15 jobs, say 3 above £75k → 18 weighted slots ≤ 25); revenue appears only in the tail — a firm running ten £150k jobs reaches Contractor pricing (illustrative £249/mo → £2,988/yr) instead of sitting on £119

ideas.assumptions: Firm job-value distribution guessed; thresholds and Contractor price illustrative. The purpose is to protect the top of the ladder and to pull small jobs (which feed the shadow bill) onto JobGuard, not to earn from the mid-market.
ideas.trust_note: The small-job half-weight is plainly in the builder's interest. The large-job weight is a mild value tilt that stays a job count rather than a turnover meter; state it plainly and never re-weight mid-job.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 (weights and thresholds). No other permission; it uses a field the plan already freezes, so no new data.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-14 (add weight to the activation concurrency event), M1-7 (accepted net value frozen at switch-live — built). Low effort.
ideas.gaming_risk: Splitting one large contract into several 'jobs' to dodge weight creates more slots, so it is self-limiting; under-quoting to sit below a threshold is implausible because the accepted quote is the customer's contract.
ideas.precedent: None known for weighted job slots in trade software. Procore/Buildertrend price on construction volume (report, 'Above the trade band') — that is the turnover meter the founder rejected; this is the job-count-preserving version.

ideas.name: Annual upfront plan ('two months free') with an optional winter pause on monthly plans
ideas.mechanism: Annual prepayment at 10× monthly (Solo £290, Builder £590, Firm £1,190) through one Stripe hosted checkout (M4-11) and one platform invoice for the year; mid-year tier changes are pro-rated upgrades only, downgrades apply at renewal. Monthly plans get the alternative of one 30-day pause per calendar year (read-only access and existing watchdog preserved, no new switch-live) for the quiet winter. Annual is offered, never forced, and never discounted beyond two months free — no Fergus-style '75% off' introductory deals.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, once a year in advance.

revenue_per_year.solo: £290 (10 × £29; £58 less than monthly, but paid on day one)

ideas.assumptions: Take-up unknown; 15–20% is the market norm and the popular '40–60% lower churn' claims are untraceable and confounded by self-selection (report §'Offer annual billing, don't force it'). Value to JobGuard is cash timing and a selection effect toward committed builders, not margin.
ideas.trust_note: Standard, transparent, the builder chooses. The pause is a goodwill device for seasonal trades; test it before promising it.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 (annual terms, refund/cancellation), D05 (auto-renew authority needs clear advance notice), D02 (VAT point at invoice date for the full year). B2B, so consumer cancellation rights do not apply, but sole traders expect a clear cancellation route.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-13 (terms and billing-cycle basis), M4-11 (hosted checkout), M4-10 (platform invoice). The pause needs a small M4-14 extension (paused period counts zero and blocks new activations). Low–medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: Buying annual Solo then running 8 live jobs — handled by ideas 2/3 (pro-rated upgrade Decision or overage).
ideas.precedent: YourTradebase, Powered Now and Joist all use 'two months free' (report table); Site Samurai gives 17% annual (raw notes).

ideas.name: Accounting sync (Xero/QuickBooks via Codat or direct) and MTD-ready bookkeeping export
ideas.category: Add-on on Solo; included in Builder and Firm
ideas.mechanism: Human-confirmed, idempotent push of customer invoices, credit notes, receipts and confirmed supplier bills (with the three-way-match result attached as a note) into the builder's Xero/QuickBooks (M5-1/2/3); an export Decision binds target company and exact source revisions. For sole traders inside MTD for Income Tax (over £50k from April 2026, £30k in 2027, £20k in 2028), JobGuard produces the categorised income/expense records their HMRC-recognised software needs for quarterly updates. JobGuard does not file and must not call itself MTD-compatible. Why the split: at £59+ sync is table stakes (Tradify includes it on all plans), so it belongs in Builder/Firm; on Solo it is the feature MTD makes compulsory, so it carries a £9/month add-on (free on annual Solo as the annual incentive).
ideas.who_pays: The builder: £9/month on Solo; in tier on Builder/Firm. The builder pays Xero/QuickBooks separately.

revenue_per_year.solo: £108 (12 × £9, if taken — likely, since a £150k sole trader is already inside MTD ITSA)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 (in tier; it makes JobGuard the system of record and protects the £708)

ideas.assumptions: Solo take-up assumed high because of MTD; accounting software costs the builder £18–£70/month separately (report §'Accounting software'). Value is removed double entry and cleaner year-end, not a measurable saving.
ideas.trust_note: Pure builder benefit. Only risk is data leaving the EU/UK boundary through Codat — verify the actual route under D04.
ideas.regulatory: D04 (Codat/Xero/QuickBooks destinations and residency), D12 (customer personal data on invoices flows to a third party; the builder is controller of their books), D02 (adviser-approved tax-code mappings), G5. HMRC recognition is required before any 'MTD-compatible' claim — do not claim it; feed recognised software.
ideas.build_dependency: M5-1 (Codat + canonical export contract), M5-2 (Xero), M5-3 (QuickBooks); M5-1 depends on M4-23 and G5. High effort, but the highest-demand integration in the market.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial. Operational rule already in M5-1: a 'paid' label imported from Xero never counts as settlement evidence for the 10%.
ideas.precedent: Tradify syncs Xero/Sage/QuickBooks on all plans; Powered Now puts Xero/QuickBooks in its Professional tier; Xero sells CIS returns as a £5/month add-on (raw notes construction_platforms_and_ai.md, uk_trade_job_software.md).

ideas.name: CIS module: verification records, deduction statements and payment reconciliation
ideas.mechanism: M4-22: subcontractor verification/status records, deduction bases (labour vs materials), monthly deduction statements, and reconciliation of net amounts paid against gross subcontractor invoices. Mirror view for builders who are themselves subcontractors: 'CIS suffered' tracking on their own invoices to contractors, reconciled against contractor payment statements so the year-end offset is complete. JobGuard does not submit the CIS300 return; it feeds the accountant/software. Priced £15/month add-on with unlimited subcontractors, on any tier, because most domestic-only builders never need it and bundling it into Firm would make them pay for it.
ideas.who_pays: The builder.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 (assume a domestic sole trader neither pays subbies under CIS nor is deducted; £180 if they subcontract to contractors)

ideas.assumptions: Firms with 5–15 staff typically pay subcontractors under CIS; headline assumes 100% take-up for Small firm/Firm, realistic take-up nearer 50%. Value is fewer HMRC penalties and clean offsets — not quantified.
ideas.trust_note: Unambiguously in the builder's interest. No conflict with the fee: M4-22 already says a correctly evidenced deduction is never a recovery.
ideas.regulatory: D06 excludes CIS from the M1 pilot; D02; adviser-approved fixtures are mandatory (M4-22); never claim HMRC filing or a verification without its evidence. Getting a deduction base wrong exposes the builder to penalties, so professional review gates release.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-22, which sits at the end of the chain M4-18 → M4-19 → M4-20 → M4-21 → M4-22. High effort because of the reviewed-rules dependencies.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial.
ideas.precedent: Xero CIS returns £5/month add-on; BuildersAI explicitly excludes CIS; Procore has no native CIS (raw notes). No small-trade tool found bundling CIS reconciliation with job records.

ideas.name: Stage payments (domestic) and applications for payment with Construction Act notices (commercial)
ideas.category: Domestic stage payments in Builder/Firm tier; applications & notices as a £29/month add-on
ideas.mechanism: Two layers. (a) Domestic stage payments — Builder and Firm: a payment schedule attached to the accepted quote (deposit, first fix, second fix, completion), stage invoices issued from the same baseline plus approved variations, with the existing proof-photo gate as the trigger ('second-fix stage invoice ready: 12 of 12 proof items verified'). (b) Applications & notices add-on, £29/month on any tier: interim applications/valuations against a contract schedule with cumulative reconciliation (M4-18), professionally reviewed payment/pay-less/payee notice templates and a deadline calculator (M4-19). Every issue is an exact Decision; nothing auto-sends. Why add-on: JCT/NEC subcontract work is a discrete regime most domestic builders never touch.
ideas.who_pays: The builder.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 (domestic; stage invoices need Builder tier, so a Solo who wants them upgrades — counted under idea 1)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £348 (12 × £29 if they subcontract to main contractors; assume half do)
revenue_per_year.firm: £348 (12 × £29; most 15-person firms do some commercial work)

ideas.assumptions: Value is cash weeks earlier and fewer disputed applications (Payapps survey: 79% of subcontractors 'almost always paid late', n=127, vendor source — weak). Take-up guessed.
