ideas.trust_note: Directly serves cash flow. One care point: notices and reminders are subscription features; they must never blur into the 10% withheld-payment category, which requires a separate, explicit, builder-opened case (§14.7).
ideas.regulatory: D06 (reviewed contract/jurisdiction templates; M4-19 forbids a hard-coded universal Construction Act deadline; residential-occupier exclusion handled by templates), D02 (VAT and DRC on applications — M4-21). §14.3: a stage invoice before lock must not vary with shadow signals.
ideas.build_dependency: (a) M1-12 (customer invoices — built) plus a small new task for a schedule on the accepted quote: medium. (b) M4-18, M4-19, M4-21: high.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial. Operational: a notice served late is the failure mode — M4-19 already requires queued / provider-accepted / served to be separate states.
ideas.precedent: Site Samurai £99–£699/month flat for payment applications and notices; Payapps (price on request); Construction AI from £130 (report §'No rival sells a final check'). Tradify Pro adds progress invoicing at £37/user.

ideas.name: Retention tracking and release reminders
ideas.category: Add-on on Solo/Builder (£9/month); included in Firm
ideas.mechanism: M4-20: record retention percentage and terms per contract at acceptance, hold the retained balance as a separate receivable on the job, run durable timers for practical completion and end of the defects period, raise a release-review Decision, and issue the release invoice from the same final-account lineage. Dashboard line: 'retention outstanding across live and closed jobs: £X'. The feature page prints the rule that retention release is never a 10% recovery (M4-20).
ideas.who_pays: The builder.

revenue_per_year.firm: £0 (in tier; part of the case for £119)

ideas.assumptions: Retention is typically 3–5% held 6–12 months; if a third of a Small firm's £600k is commercial at 5%, ~£10k is retained per year, some of which is commonly forgotten — no UK statistic for the forgotten share was found; do not quote one.
ideas.trust_note: This is the builder's own money; a percentage of released retention would feel like a tax on it (do not). A flat charge for the reminder and invoice is fair.
ideas.regulatory: D06 (contract terms), D02 (VAT on release invoices), D03 (release is not a qualifying recovery). If retention is withheld beyond terms and the builder opens a withheld-payment case, §14.7 applies separately.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-20 (depends on M4-19, M4-18). Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: None.
ideas.precedent: Payapps tracks retentions; Site Samurai tracks retention valuation (raw notes). No small-trade app found with retention timers.

ideas.name: Estimating and drawing takeoff with site-walk coverage diff
ideas.category: Add-on module, £19/month, any tier (quote stays free)
ideas.mechanism: Upload architect's drawings/PDF plans; the AI gateway proposes measured quantities (areas, lengths, counts) with citations to drawing regions — proposals only, never an invented quantity (§5.9) — the builder confirms, and confirmed quantities price against the builder's own rate book (M1-4 observations) into the free quote. The distinctive part is the coverage diff between the site walk-through and the drawing: 'the drawing shows a soil-stack move you did not mention on site'. That is prevention of site-visit omissions, JobGuard's largest but unfeeable value, captured as a flat add-on. Unlimited users; the paid part is the measuring, not the quote.
ideas.who_pays: The builder.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 (bathrooms/kitchens from a site walk; assume no take-up)

ideas.assumptions: Take-up guessed. Kreo charges £25–£125 per user for takeoff alone, so £19 per business is under market; the price can rise once the coverage diff proves itself in pilot.
ideas.trust_note: Fully in the builder's interest. Watch two things: 'quoting is free' must not become 'free unless you have drawings', and the model must never fill a line to look complete.
ideas.regulatory: D04 (drawings through the approved EU/UK AI route), D12 (drawings carry the homeowner's address), D09 (add-on price). No other permission.
ideas.build_dependency: New task, not in the plan: extend M1-3/M1-4 (walk-through capture and quote editor) with a drawing-extraction prompt suite in packages/ai and a golden set (pnpm eval) scoring omission, unsupported additions and citation validity; depends on M1-4 rate book and M0-6 evidence storage. High effort — a new model capability with its own eval gate.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial.
ideas.precedent: Kreo takeoff £25/£50/£125 per user; Buildertrend puts takeoff in its Advanced tier; Handoff (US) $149–$899 for voice-to-estimate (raw notes construction_platforms_and_ai.md).

ideas.name: 'Are you underpricing?' regional rate benchmark (give-to-get)
ideas.category: Add-on module, £15/month; free for contributors on annual plans
ideas.mechanism: Opted-in builders contribute their human-confirmed rate observations (M1-4 rate_book_observation, already written since M1) to an aggregated pool. At quote review JobGuard shows where each rate sits against the anonymised band for the same trade/unit/region over 12 months: 'your plastering rate £X/m² is below the 25th percentile of 140 confirmed rates in the South West'. Only bands and counts are shown, never another tenant's rate; a band appears only when n ≥ 20 from ≥ 10 tenants. Until the pool is large enough, seed with a licensed published price book and label it as such.
ideas.who_pays: The builder.

revenue_per_year.solo: £180 (12 × £15; the archetype most likely to underprice — assume taken)

ideas.assumptions: One under-priced £8k job corrected by 5% is £400, so the add-on pays for itself on one job; cold start needs hundreds of contributing tenants per region; price-book licence cost not estimated.
ideas.trust_note: Borderline. Rates are competitively sensitive; a builder must never see JobGuard as a channel that leaks their prices to rivals or to homeowners (FairRate does the homeowner direction, the opposite of what builders want). Give-to-get, aggregation thresholds and a written promise never to sell rate data to merchants, insurers, lead platforms or homeowners make it acceptable; selling it outward would be a 1.
ideas.regulatory: M5-6 explicitly disables cross-tenant learning without a separate privacy/commercial decision — a new decision record (D14 candidate: data pooling and benchmarking) is required. UK competition law: exchange of price information between competitors needs care; aggregated, historical, anonymised benchmarks with minimum group sizes are generally acceptable under CMA information-exchange guidance, but this needs legal review before launch. D12 for any personal data in observations (none by design).
ideas.build_dependency: M5-6 (rate-book learning) currently sits behind M5-5 merchant adapters; the dependency can be re-cut so benchmarking needs only M1-4 observations plus a new pooling task. Medium once the decision exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders contributing junk rates to pollute the pool — mitigated by using only rates confirmed on accepted quotes; gaming your own view gains nothing.
ideas.precedent: FairRate (£0.99 per audit, homeowner-facing) shows demand for rate comparison exists; no builder-facing aggregate benchmark found in UK trade software (report §'No rival sells a final check').

ideas.name: Supplier price benchmark ('you paid 12% over median')
ideas.category: Add-on module, £15/month (tierable £15/£29/£49); free for contributors on annual plans
ideas.mechanism: From confirmed merchant invoice line facts (M2-3/M2-4), pool SKU/alias-normalised net unit prices across opted-in tenants; show at PO pre-commit (M2-1) and at invoice match: 'your price £9.40/bag; JobGuard median £8.20 (n=312, 90 days, your region); best quartile £7.60'. A finding only — no order changes, no merchant is contacted. Adds a periodic per-tenant 'materials price position' report. Funded only by builders: merchants never pay JobGuard for placement, data, rebates or referrals, in writing.
ideas.who_pays: The builder.
ideas.assumptions: If materials are ~35% of turnover, Solo buys ~£52k/yr (3% better prices ≈ £1,500) and Firm ~£700k (3% ≈ £21k), so a flat £15 under-prices Firm — tier it if the founder wants to lean on it. Materials share, price dispersion and cold start are guesses.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and feels like JobGuard doing work they cannot do. The hard line is funding: any payment from a merchant compromises the invoice watchdog and must be excluded in writing. Pooled purchase-price data is less sensitive than selling-price data, but the same aggregation rules apply.
ideas.regulatory: Same new pooling decision as idea 10; competition-law review (purchase-price benchmarks are lower risk than selling-price exchange but still need aggregation); merchant trade-account terms may restrict sharing negotiated prices — check before pooling them; D04/D12 not engaged (no personal data).
ideas.build_dependency: M2-3/M2-4 (confirmed invoice line facts — built), M5-4 (supplier identity resolution and alias hardening), plus the pooling task shared with idea 10. Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: None for the builder. JobGuard-side risk of a wrong 'median' from mis-normalised units — M2-4's unit/pack conversion and confidence rules must gate what enters the pool.
ideas.precedent: None known in UK trade software; AP recovery auditors sell this as a service at 20–30% of findings (report table) — a flat add-on is far cheaper for the builder.

ideas.name: Verifiable Job Record: independently timestamped evidence pack per job
ideas.category: Included per closed job on Builder/Firm; £15 per pack on Solo; £49 'dispute pack' on any tier
ideas.mechanism: At final-account lock (and after the final check), assemble the M4-3 deterministic bundle — accepted quote, every variation with its customer approval record, proof photos with server-verified hashes and receive times, supplier documents, final account and invoices — anchor the manifest hash with an RFC-3161 timestamp (M4-4) and sign the export (M5-9). A 'dispute pack' re-issue adds a standalone verifier and a plain-English cover sheet ('what this proves and what it does not') for a specific dispute, small-claims filing, insurer or trade-body complaint. Packs generated before lock never include shadow content — an export that varied with signals would be a disclosure (§14.3).
ideas.who_pays: The builder, per pack (standard packs via tier on Builder/Firm).

revenue_per_year.solo: £98 (2 dispute packs × £49; buying the £15 pack on all ~19 jobs would be £285, unlikely)

ideas.assumptions: Dispute frequency guessed (Simply Business: 34% of tradespeople receive no payment for some extra work — a survey figure, not a dispute rate). Pack prices illustrative.
ideas.trust_note: The builder's own record, and the 'show the work' that the fairness research (Buell & Norton, in the report) says makes the fee feel earned. Two cautions: per-pack pricing must not read as a per-job platform fee (AGENTS §5.10 forbids a per-job base charge; a per-artifact purchase is different — say so in D09); and the pack must state only integrity and existence relative to a trusted timestamp, never 'court-ready' or proof of work quality.
ideas.regulatory: D07 (retention/WORM approval before Object Lock — M4-4), D12 (packs contain the customer's personal data; disclosure to third parties is the builder's decision as controller; minimal-disclosure/redaction from M4-3), D09 (pack pricing). Producing a record is not legal advice — no legal-services permission.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 (built, #92), M4-4 (Object Lock + RFC-3161, needs D07), M5-9 (signed exports). Medium; most of the pipeline exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial.
ideas.precedent: Site Samurai subcontractor portal with evidence attachments; Payapps audit trail (raw notes). No consumer-side precedent for a timestamped job record found.

ideas.name: API access and webhooks
ideas.category: Add-on £49/month on Firm; included in Contractor
ideas.mechanism: Scoped, tenant-bound read API (jobs, scope, variations, invoices, receipts, evidence manifests) plus webhooks for job events (switched live, variation approved, invoice issued, payment recorded) for the firm's own reporting, their bookkeeper's tooling or a BI dashboard. Write endpoints only for non-commercial fields; every commercial action stays behind the command boundary and exact Decisions, so a token cannot send, issue or charge. Responses are byte-identical with and without shadow signals before lock (§14.3) and run under the same RLS context.
ideas.who_pays: The builder (Firm/Contractor).

revenue_per_year.firm: £588 (12 × £49) if taken; realistically one in four 15-person firms has someone to use it, so expected ~£147

ideas.assumptions: Demand comes from firms with a bookkeeper/ops person; not a Solo product. A free read-only 'accountant seat' should exist regardless (Xero gives accountants free access), so the API is for systems, not people.
ideas.trust_note: The builder's own data leaving on the builder's instruction. No conflict, provided tokens cannot reach shadow tables or commercial commands.
ideas.regulatory: D04/D12 (the builder becomes responsible for onward destinations; JobGuard documents it), D09 (price). Token scopes and rate limits are security, not regulatory.
ideas.build_dependency: M0 already generates OpenAPI (NestJS); needs scoped API tokens and a principal contract (M5-7 policy-based permissions) plus an outbox-driven webhook adapter (M0 outbox exists). Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial. Security: M5-7's conformance suite must prove API tokens cannot broaden finance/order/export authority.
ideas.precedent: Standard SaaS add-on; Tradify sells an Instant Website add-on at £10/month and SMS at 10p (raw notes) — add-ons are normal here, though no UK trade tool was found charging for API access specifically.

ideas.name: Watchdog depth as the tier differentiator: supplier-invoice checking on Builder and above
ideas.mechanism: Keep the whole live-job spine on every tier (quote, switch-live, Log an extra, proof, final account, invoice, final check). Make the merchant-document watchdog a Builder+ feature: Solo gets PO price checks against the builder's own agreed rates; Builder and Firm get inbound-email intake of supplier invoices/delivery notes, extraction, three-way matching, overcharge and short-delivery findings (M2-2 to M2-5). Structurally, no intake on Solo means no detection on Solo — it is not a suppressed finding. The upgrade prompt is evidence-based: 'You uploaded 14 supplier invoices this month; on Builder, JobGuard checks each one against your order and price.'
ideas.who_pays: Solo builders with material spend who upgrade to Builder.

revenue_per_year.solo: +£360 (12 × the £30 Solo→Builder step) for each Solo who upgrades; assume 40% do → expected +£144

ideas.assumptions: Solo material spend ~£50k/yr makes overcharge checking worth well over £30/month; the upgrade fraction is a guess. Note the fee-side cost: no intake on Solo means no supplier-overcharge cash refunds and no supplier-document shadow signals from Solo tenants.
ideas.trust_note: Uncomfortable because it withholds prevention from the cheapest customers, and an uncaught overcharge on Solo is close to the 'JobGuard knew but did not say' story — acceptable only because JobGuard genuinely does not hold the document. It must be true structurally (no intake, no detection), never a hidden finding; otherwise it breaks the spirit of 'never degrade the builder's own billing to create fees' even if not the letter. Standard market practice (bill capture sits in top tiers at Tradify and Powered Now), which is why it is listed.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v2 (tier feature matrix). D11/D13: a tier gate can never suppress a must-surface finding on anything JobGuard actually holds.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 to M2-5 are built or in flight; needs a per-tier entitlement check in the intake path (small M4-13/M4-14 extension). Low.
ideas.gaming_risk: Solo builders uploading supplier invoices as 'proof photos' to get checks free — make it a non-issue: photos on Solo are evidence only and the supplier-document detector does not run on Solo.
ideas.precedent: Tradify Plus (£44) for AI bill reading; Powered Now Premium for the receipt scanner; ApprovalMax Advanced for bill-to-PO matching; Planyard Professional (report §'No rival sells a final check').

ideas.name: Customer payments through JobGuard: hosted pay-by-bank and card on customer invoices (no funds held)
ideas.category: Transactional module at the edge of this lens — new M4 rail, after G4
ideas.mechanism: Every customer invoice or stage invoice JobGuard issues carries a hosted payment link: Open Banking pay-by-bank (TrueLayer Payments — D10 already contemplates TrueLayer) for large sums, hosted Stripe card checkout for deposits. Funds settle directly to the builder's bank or connected account (Stripe Connect direct charges with an application fee, or TrueLayer settlement to the builder with JobGuard's fee billed monthly); JobGuard never touches the money. The provider settlement event becomes a verified receipt on the job — stronger evidence for §14.8 allocation than a builder's 'mark paid', after the existing verification checks. Pricing: pay-by-bank 0.25% + 20p capped at £10 per payment; card at provider cost + 0.4% JobGuard margin. Separate platform revenue line, never a success fee, never offset against fees.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, per payment (deducted at settlement or billed monthly per the provider model). Never surcharge consumers on cards.

revenue_per_year.solo: ~£300 (19 jobs × 2 payments × 60% via link ≈ 23 pay-by-bank at ~£8 avg ≈ £184, plus ~11 card deposits of ~£2,400 × 0.4% ≈ £106)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: ~£430 (24 jobs × 3 payments × 60% ≈ 43 payments at the £10 cap)
revenue_per_year.firm: ~£530 (33 jobs × 4 payments × 40% ≈ 53 payments at the £10 cap; big invoices still go by plain bank transfer)

ideas.assumptions: Payment mix, link usage and the cap are guesses; provider costs unverified; the value captured is 'faster invoicing → faster cash', which the report says is the one robustly measured pain (late payment costs the UK economy ~£11bn/yr, Small Business Commissioner).
ideas.trust_note: Builders like being paid faster and customers like a link; the fee is per payment and visible. It sits at the edge of the lens — a rail, not a module — and AGENTS bans extra payment rails before their tasks, so this is a proposal for a new M4 task, not something to slip in. A card margin is the one place JobGuard earns from the customer's payment; keep it small and shown.
ideas.regulatory: FCA: taking an application fee via Stripe Connect or a TrueLayer settlement to the builder without ever holding funds is generally outside PSR 2017 authorisation, but needs a legal opinion (commercial-agent / limited-network analysis) before launch. D04 (provider destinations), D05 (no standing authority over the customer's money — the customer initiates each payment), D06/D02 (receipt and VAT point), D10 (TrueLayer route). Consumer card surcharges are banned in the UK (general knowledge, confirm) — never offer them. AGENTS §3 'never handle raw card data or hold builders' customer funds' is satisfied only by hosted surfaces.
ideas.build_dependency: New M4 task (proposal) building on M4-7 (TrueLayer consent route), M4-11 (Stripe adapter, signed webhooks, unknown-outcome handling) and M1-12 (customer invoices, record customer payment). Medium–high; after G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: None commercial. The settlement webhook is evidence of settlement for §14.8 only after the existing verification checks — never an automatic qualifying recovery.
ideas.precedent: Fergus 1.6% + 20p on card payments; Jobber 2.9% + 30c card and 1% ACH; ServiceM8, Joist and Tradify all take card-processing margins (report table and raw notes). Pay-by-bank pricing was not in the research — unverified.

ideas.name: Trade-body endorsed plan (FMB / NFB) with referral fee to the body
ideas.mechanism: JobGuard joins the FMB Associate directory / NFB Strategic Partners and is listed as a member benefit alongside the existing software, warranty and TradePoint offers. Members redeem a verified membership number at Stripe subscription sign-up (M4-11 replacement) and get 'two months free' on the annual plan; JobGuard pays the body a referral fee per converted paying member (assume 15% of first-year subscription, paid quarterly on a self-billed statement) plus a flat associate/listing fee. Optional co-branded output: the locked final account and evidence pack carry a 'Master Builder / NFB member' mark on the customer-facing PDF. Success fee unchanged and never shared with the body. The charge to the builder is still the subscription; the body is paid by JobGuard, not the builder.
ideas.who_pays: Builder pays the (discounted) subscription; JobGuard pays the trade body a referral fee and listing fee.

revenue_per_year.solo: £247 net year 1 (£348 base subscription × 10/12 months × 0.85); £348 from year 2 — no incremental revenue per builder, this is a CAC/trust channel

ideas.assumptions: Report-recommended (unapproved) prices £29/£59/£119 ex VAT = £348/£708/£1,428 a year. Two months free on annual = 10/12 of list. 15% first-year referral fee is an assumption (FMB/NFB do not publish partner terms; Simply Business pays affiliates 10% capped at £100, Xero pays 30% refer-a-friend). FMB members mostly run a few long domestic jobs, so the founder's live-jobs meter fits this channel better than ServiceM8-style jobs-per-month would; state that at sign-up. Incremental revenue per builder is zero; the value is lower acquisition cost and the endorsement halo in a word-of-mouth trade.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest: a discount via a body they already trust, and a mark that helps them win work. Only risk is if the body later demands a share of success fees or visibility of findings — refuse both contractually.
ideas.regulatory: None specific. Trade-body endorsement rules and ASA/CAP code for the co-branded claims; the co-branded mark must not imply the body verified the work.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-11 (rewritten: Stripe hosted subscription sign-up) and M4-13 subscription terms must exist; add a partner-attribution table, membership-number validation, and partner payout statements via M4-10 platform documents. D09 v2 must define promo/annual terms. Effort: 1–2 weeks after M4-11.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Shared membership numbers or lapsed members claiming the discount — validate against the body's member API or list at sign-up and annually; cap one redemption per membership number.
ideas.precedent: FMB member benefits: partner discounts (10% off TradePoint), software offers, warranty discounts (https://www.fmb.org.uk/become-a-master-builder/membership-benefits.html; https://www.fmb.org.uk/supplier-directory.html). NFB Strategic Partners and buying-power deals (https://builders.org.uk/the-nfb/partners). Checkatrade bundling QuickBooks at 75% off for members (https://construction-update.co.uk/2024/07/24/checkatrade-partners-with-intuit-quickbooks-and-wickes-to-expand-member-benefits/).

ideas.name: Insurance introducer: in-app cover check at switch-live with commission from a partner broker
ideas.mechanism: At switch-live JobGuard already knows job value and type. A non-blocking 'cover check' card compares the frozen accepted value against the builder's declared public liability / contractors' all-risks limits and expiry (builder-entered, optional). If cover is missing, thin or expiring, the builder can tap through to a partner broker/insurer (Simply Business, Superscript, an FMB Insurance-type broker) with pre-filled trade, turnover band and job mix — only with an explicit consent tap. The broker pays JobGuard a commission per policy bound and per renewal. JobGuard never advises, compares or recommends a specific policy: it passes contact details and consented facts (introducer role).
ideas.who_pays: The broker/insurer pays JobGuard commission out of its own remuneration; the builder pays the premium to the insurer as normal.

revenue_per_year.solo: £8/yr (25% of Solos buy via JobGuard × £300 PL premium × 10% commission = £7.50)
revenue_per_year.firm: £200/yr (25% × £8,000 premium × 10%); could be 2–3× if JobGuard became an authorised broker itself (15–25% commercial-lines commission), which is a different business

ideas.assumptions: Premiums are assumptions: sole-trader PL £150–£500, 5-staff builder £1,500–£3,500 with EL and CAR, 15-staff firm £5k–£12k. 10% commission uncapped is negotiated partner terms; the public Simply Business affiliate deal is 10% capped at £100 with a 7-day cookie, which would make the Firm figure £100. 25% take rate in any year is a guess (annual renewal cycle; most builders already have cover). This is small money per builder; its real value is completeness of the 'protect the job' story and a second reason to switch live in JobGuard.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest when cover is genuinely thin; becomes an irritant if the card nags or if any feature or proof gate is tied to buying insurance. Never gate. Never share job evidence with the insurer under this idea (see the separate evidence-pack idea).
ideas.regulatory: FCA: insurance distribution. JobGuard must stay within the introducer exemption (passing contact details/consented facts, no advising or arranging) or become an Introducer Appointed Representative of the broker; anything more needs authorisation. Financial-promotion rules for the card wording. D12 for the consented data transfer; D04 residency for the broker's systems. Needs a new commercial/legal decision record — none of D01–D13 covers partner commissions.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-7 switch-live (frozen accepted value) exists; needs a builder 'cover details' field set, a partner handoff with consent record and audit event, and a commission reconciliation import. Effort: 1–2 weeks plus broker agreement and FCA structuring.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Builders cannot game it; risk is JobGuard drifting into 'advice' wording to lift conversion — fix the copy in the eval/copy audit.
ideas.precedent: Procore Risk Advisors (Procore's own brokerage with Allianz and Swiss Re programmes, using platform data for terms) (https://www.procore.com/press/procore-launches-construction-insurance-brokerage-to-empower-builders). Buildertrend + Assurely in-app insurance marketplace (https://buildertrend.com/press-releases/assurely-partnership/). Checkatrade + Superscript member offer (https://gosuperscript.com/news-and-resources/superscript-partners-with-checkatrade/). Simply Business affiliate: 10% commission, £100 cap (https://affi.io/m/simplybusiness-co-uk-cpa; https://www.simplybusiness.co.uk/partner/).

ideas.name: Insurer-paid claim-time evidence pack (and the flagged per-policyholder data variant)
ideas.mechanism: Variant A (clean): when a builder faces a liability, damage or customer-dispute claim, they tap 'Send evidence to my insurer'. JobGuard assembles the signed, recipient-bound evidence bundle already specified in M4-3/M5-9 (accepted scope, approved variations, timestamped proof photos with server-verified hashes, customer messages, readiness warnings acknowledged) and delivers it to the insurer's claims team. The insurer pays JobGuard a per-pack fee (assume £75) because verified contemporaneous evidence shortens handling and cuts disputed liability; the builder pays nothing. Variant B (flagged): the insurer pays JobGuard a per-policyholder-year fee or funds a premium discount for builders who consent to 'JobGuard-verified proof gates' status (a Zego-telematics style data-for-discount deal). B requires ongoing data flow about the builder to the insurer.
ideas.who_pays: A: insurer pays per pack delivered, builder-initiated. B: insurer pays per consenting policyholder-year.

revenue_per_year.solo: A: £4/yr (5% claim frequency × £75). B: £10/yr (assumed £10 per policyholder-year)

ideas.assumptions: Claim frequency per business-year is a guess (5% Solo, 15% Small, 40% Firm, scaling with staff and jobs). £75 per pack is an assumption — no UK insurer publishes what it pays for evidence bundles. B's £10–£20 per policyholder-year is a guess anchored on telematics-style discounts. Honest reading: neither variant is a revenue line; A is a trust and marketing line ('insurers accept JobGuard packs') and a retention hook.
ideas.trust_note: Variant A scores 5: the builder chooses to send their own evidence to their own insurer and pays nothing. Variant B scores 2: it is selling a builder-level data feed to an insurer, which is on the founder's list of trust risks, and a builder who loses a discount because their proof compliance dropped will feel surveilled. List B only as a flagged option; do not build it without a founder decision.
ideas.regulatory: D12: the pack contains the builder's customer's personal data (a third party) — lawful basis and Article 14 route needed; the insurer is a separate controller. D07 retention and export receipts. No FCA issue for evidence transfer (JobGuard is not handling the claim). Variant B needs its own data-protection decision and a fairness review.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 evidence packs are merged (#92) with recipient-bound authority; M5-9 signed export manifests for external verification; a per-insurer delivery adapter and invoice line for per-pack fees via M4-10. Effort: 2–3 weeks per insurer after M5-9.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. A builder cannot fabricate server-received hashes or receive times; the pack states what it does and does not prove (integrity/existence, not authenticity of every assertion).
ideas.precedent: Procore leveraging platform data for insurance terms (https://www.ironpros.com/project-management-software/article/22908076/procore-leverages-data-to-help-contractor-customers-with-insurance). Zego app-based telematics rewards for tradespeople's vans as a UK data-for-discount pattern (https://www.zego.com/business-van-insurance/). LABC Warranty requires photographic evidence per plot, showing insurers already value structured site photos (https://www.labcwarranty.co.uk/about-labc-warranty/site-inspection-process). No UK insurer paying a job-app per evidence pack was found.

ideas.name: Per-job insurance-backed guarantee or warranty offered at final account, with introducer commission
ideas.mechanism: After the final-account lock (SV-4) and before invoice issue (M1-12), the builder can add an optional, clearly priced 'insurance-backed guarantee' line to the customer invoice from a partner IBG/warranty provider (QANW, HIES, CWG, FMB Insurance's member warranties; LABC Warranty / Build-Zone / Protek for structural work). JobGuard's locked scope, approved variations and hash-verified stage photos are the 'documentation quality' the provider prices on, so partner premiums can be lower than walk-in. The customer pays the premium as a pass-through line on the builder's invoice; the provider issues the policy to the homeowner; the provider pays JobGuard an introducer commission (assume 15% of premium). Structural-warranty variant: proof photos are mapped to the provider's stage checklist (foundations, superstructure, pre-plaster, drains, pre-handover) and delivered as a signed pack per plot, earning a per-plot referral fee.
ideas.who_pays: The homeowner pays the premium via the builder's invoice; the IBG provider pays JobGuard commission from that premium.

revenue_per_year.firm: £891/yr (33 × 30% = 9.9 jobs × £600 premium (1% of £60k) = £5,940 × 15%); structural-warranty plots would add a per-plot fee on top

ideas.assumptions: Jobs per year = turnover ÷ average job (19 / 24 / 33). Premium at 1% of job value is an assumption: IBG providers price on property risk, job complexity and documentation quality and publish no per-job figures; small damp jobs are cheapest, basements and listed buildings 20–40% more. 30% customer take-up is a guess (higher on bigger jobs where lender acceptance matters). 15% commission is assumed; scheme-member contractors normally sell IBGs directly, so JobGuard's cut has to come from provider margin, not a mark-up to the homeowner.
ideas.trust_note: Builder wins jobs with a guarantee, homeowner gets protection, JobGuard's proof gates become worth more to the builder. The one thing that would poison it: making the watchdog's proof gates or the final check depend on selling the IBG. Keep it an optional line the builder adds, never a default-on add-on.
ideas.regulatory: FCA insurance distribution: the IBG scheme is the authorised entity and the builder typically sells as a scheme member; JobGuard must be an introducer/IAR only. Consumer Duty applies to the provider. The invoice line is a consumer sale by the builder — DMCC drip-pricing rules mean it must be optional and shown with its price up front, never pre-ticked. D02 VAT treatment of the pass-through line (insurance premium tax vs VAT) needs the accounting reviewer. New decision record for partner commissions.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-4 final-account lock and M1-12 invoice issue; an 'optional third-party line' invoice line type that is excluded from the builder's net principal (so it never inflates Q in §14.9); provider API/CSV handoff; commission reconciliation. Structural variant needs the proof-stage mapping on M1-10. Effort: 3–4 weeks after SV-4 plus provider agreements.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low for builders. Guard against the caught-item logic: an IBG line must never count as a 'catch' or as recovered principal; make it a distinct line kind that §14.8 allocation ignores.
ideas.precedent: QANW: IBG cost driven by documentation quality and job risk (https://qanw.co.uk/insurance-backed-guarantees/; https://www.insituscp.co.uk/what-does-an-insurance-backed-damp-guarantee-cost). HIES IBGs (https://www.hiesscheme.org.uk/what-we-do/insurance-backed-guarantees/). FMB members get warranty discounts via FMB Insurance (https://www.fmb.org.uk/become-a-master-builder/membership-benefits.html). LABC Warranty stage inspections with mandatory photo evidence (https://www.labcwarranty.co.uk/about-labc-warranty/site-inspection-process).

ideas.name: Merchant rebate passed 100% to the builder with a disclosed JobGuard admin fee (watchdog conflict, structured)
ideas.category: Partnerships & channels — merchants and buying groups
ideas.mechanism: JobGuard negotiates a 'JobGuard Trade' arrangement with one or more merchants on an open panel (any merchant can join on the same published terms): a point-of-sale trade discount or a quarterly volume rebate for JobGuard builders. Hard structure: (1) every penny of merchant discount/rebate goes to the builder — a rebate is paid by the merchant straight into the builder's own bank account, never through JobGuard's books (JobGuard must not hold builders' money); (2) JobGuard takes no money from any merchant — no marketing fees, no per-order payments, no data sales; (3) JobGuard charges the builder a disclosed admin fee (assume 10% of rebate received, or a flat £5/month) shown on the platform statement; (4) the watchdog is unchanged and merchant-blind: PO pre-commit checks and three-way matching run against the builder's own agreed rates (M2-1) whoever the merchant is; (5) JobGuard publishes per-merchant overcharge and delivery-discrepancy rates to its builders, so partner merchants are visibly held to the same test.
ideas.who_pays: Merchant pays the rebate to the builder; the builder pays JobGuard a disclosed admin fee. Merchants pay JobGuard nothing.

revenue_per_year.solo: £54/yr (materials 40% of £150k = £60k; 30% via partner merchants = £18k; 3% rebate = £540; 10% admin fee)

ideas.assumptions: Materials at 40% of turnover, 30% of materials routed through partner merchants, and a 3% builder-side rebate are all assumptions. Published precedents are point-of-sale discounts (10% TradePoint for FMB members, 10% Wickes TradePro for Checkatrade members) rather than rebates; NMBS's 3.84% average rebate is merchant-side (merchants buying from suppliers), not builder-side, so it is only an indication of the margin that exists in the chain. With a POS discount instead of a rebate, JobGuard's fee would have to be flat (say £60/yr) because there is no rebate to meter.
ideas.trust_note: Flagged plainly: any merchant relationship will be read by some builders as 'JobGuard is in bed with Travis', and that reading damages the supplier-invoice watchdog even if the money flows are clean. The pass-through-plus-disclosed-fee structure, open panel, merchant-blind checks and published merchant scorecards are the minimum to make it defensible; the founder should still weigh whether £54–£720 per builder is worth the perception risk. Do not do the simpler version (merchant pays JobGuard) at all.
ideas.regulatory: Bribery Act 2010 concerns disappear with full disclosure and pass-through. VAT on the admin fee. If JobGuard ever routed rebate cash it would be holding builders' money (AGENTS §3, never) — hence merchant-to-builder direct only. Competition law: no exclusivity, no resale-price terms. Needs a new commercial decision record and an integrity review under D11.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 agreed rates/PO pre-commit, M2-2 merchant intake, M2-4 three-way matching (M2). Add: partner-merchant registry, rebate statement import and reconciliation to the builder's own POs, admin-fee line on M4-10 platform documents, merchant scorecard report. Effort: 3–4 weeks after M2-4 plus merchant negotiation.
ideas.gaming_risk: Medium. Merchants could try to influence what the watchdog flags — structurally impossible if checks use builder rates only, but pressure will come through commercial channels; write the merchant-blind rule into the contract. Builders could route non-JobGuard purchases through the panel to earn rebates — harmless to JobGuard.
ideas.precedent: FMB members get 10% off at TradePoint (https://www.fmb.org.uk/resource/the-inside-scoop-five-ways-fmb-membership-can-benefit-you.html). Checkatrade members get 10% via Wickes TradePro (https://construction-update.co.uk/2024/07/24/checkatrade-partners-with-intuit-quickbooks-and-wickes-to-expand-member-benefits/). NMBS merchant buying society: average 3.84% rebate on invoices, £8bn sales (https://www.nmbs.co.uk/faqs/). Fortis independent merchant buying group (https://www.fortismerchants.co.uk/). No UK job app found that runs a builder-side rebate pass-through.

ideas.name: Main contractor / housebuilder / property-manager pays per project; subcontractors get JobGuard free (Payapps model)
ideas.category: Partnerships & channels — main contractors and housebuilders
ideas.mechanism: A main contractor, regional housebuilder, housing association or property manager buys a 'Project' licence (assume £25 per active subcontractor per month, or £150 per project per month) and onboards its subcontractor panel onto JobGuard for that project. Subs capture variations through Log an extra, upload proof photos, submit interim applications (M4-18), receive/issue Construction Act notices (M4-19), track retention (M4-20) and CIS (M4-22). The paying client gets evidenced applications, fewer disputes and a live proof record; it never gets shadow data or anything the sub has not submitted. The sub keeps their own tenant and the normal success-fee terms: 10% only on a withheld-payment case the sub explicitly opens against that client, or a missed variation revealed after the sub's own final-account lock. Subs convert to their own paid subscription for non-project work (channel effect).
ideas.who_pays: The main contractor / client pays the project licence; the subcontractor pays nothing for licensed projects.

revenue_per_year.solo: £15/yr of client-paid licence attributable to a Solo sub (10% of Solos work under an MC × 1 project × 6 months × £25) plus later own-subscription conversion
revenue_per_year.firm: £360/yr (60% × 3 projects × 8 months × £25); plus success fees on withheld-payment cases the firm chooses to open

ideas.assumptions: Per-sub-per-month price and share of each archetype working under main contractors are assumptions; Payapps prices main contractors by projects and claims assessed per month with a fixed annual fee and does not publish figures. Long subcontract jobs are where the founder's live-jobs meter is weakest: a sub on a 12-month project occupies a 'live job' slot all year for one job, so licensed projects should not count toward the sub's own live-job tier, and the meter should be sampled monthly with generous allowances.
ideas.trust_note: The sub must be told plainly who is paying. If the MC pays JobGuard while JobGuard's final check finds variations the sub never billed the MC, the MC will resent it and the sub will wonder whose side JobGuard is on. Make it explicit in both contracts: on variations and applications JobGuard works for the sub; the MC is buying clean evidence and fewer disputes. Payapps-type surveys say 79% of subs are almost always paid late and 73% see routine application disputes, so subs have real value here — but keep the MC out of the sub's tenant.
ideas.regulatory: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 payment/notice provisions (already M4-19); CIS (M4-22); no licence required. D12: the MC is a separate controller; sole-trader subs are data subjects. D10: JobGuard never pursues debt itself.
ideas.build_dependency: Needs M4-18 interim applications, M4-19 construction notices, M4-20 retention, M4-22 CIS, plus a multi-party job model where the customer is another JobGuard tenant with scoped, read-only visibility of submitted artifacts. This is post-M4 work: 6–10 weeks. Do not build enterprise hierarchy early (AGENTS §1).
ideas.gaming_risk: Medium. An MC could try to use JobGuard's timestamps against a sub (e.g. late notices) — acceptable, it cuts both ways and is what the Act intends. Subs could open withheld-payment cases prematurely to get JobGuard's templates — the §14.7 entry test (overdue beyond threshold, reminder ignored, terms approved) already gates that.
ideas.precedent: Payapps: main contractors pay a fixed annual fee by projects/claims, subs get their first application free each month (https://www.payapps.com/uk/pricing-main-contractors/; https://www.payapps.com/uk/pricing-subcontractors/). Buildbite: free for clients and subcontractors, paid by the contractor (https://buildbite.com/insights/ai-construction-tools). Prequalification schemes show subs already pay £219–£909/yr to be onboardable (https://www.tradecomply.co.uk/guides/chas-cost; https://www.tradecomply.co.uk/guides/constructionline-cost).

ideas.name: Accountant and bookkeeper referral channel with recurring revenue share and a free practice view
ideas.mechanism: Practices enrol as JobGuard Advisers. They get a free read-only practice seat over consenting builder clients showing per-job WIP (accepted baseline + approved variations − invoiced), unbilled approved variations, retentions, CIS deductions and DRC VAT flags, plus the locked final accounts as year-end evidence. JobGuard pays the practice 20% of referred subscription revenue for 24 months on a quarterly self-billed statement. Success fees are never shared. Making Tax Digital for Income Tax (from April 2026 for sole traders over £50k, dropping to £30k in 2027 and £20k in 2028) is pushing practices to put builder clients onto software now, which is the opening.
ideas.who_pays: Builder pays the subscription; JobGuard pays the practice a share of it.

revenue_per_year.solo: £278/yr net (£348 × 0.80) for two years, then £348 — no incremental revenue per builder; this is acquisition

ideas.assumptions: 20% for 24 months is an assumption between Xero's 30% refer-a-friend and its £50 flat referral; practice seats cost JobGuard nothing because plans are unlimited-user. Effective CAC per builder: £70 (Solo) to £286 (Firm) a year for two years. Builder consent per practice link; the practice sees only what the builder shares. Report notes the Small Business Survey: only 29% of no-employee construction businesses use software, so the accountant is often the person who chooses it.
ideas.trust_note: Builders trust their accountant more than any app vendor; a referral from them is the strongest endorsement available. Professional-body rules (ICAEW/ACCA) require the accountant to disclose commissions to the client — make the share visible in the builder's terms so it is never a surprise.
ideas.regulatory: None for JobGuard beyond D12 (practice as recipient of client data with consent; likely independent controller). Accountants' own professional rules on commission disclosure. Partner payouts need a self-billing VAT arrangement.
ideas.build_dependency: M0-6 membership/permissions for a scoped 'adviser' role; partner attribution and payout statements (shared with the trade-body idea); the practice view is a reporting layer over M1-11 final accounts, M1-9 variations, M4-20 retention and M4-22 CIS. M5-2/M5-3 Xero/QuickBooks adapters make it stickier but are not required. Effort: 2–3 weeks for attribution and a basic view; more as M4 finance tasks land.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. A practice could enrol clients who never use JobGuard — pay share only on collected subscription revenue, and stop share on cancellation.
ideas.precedent: Xero partner programme: free, subscription discounts, 30% refer-a-friend commission or £50 per referral (https://www.xero.com/uk/partner-programme/; https://www.xero.com/uk/campaign/refer-a-friend/). Dext partner programme per-client practice pricing (https://help.dext.com/en/articles/273220-dext-plans-for-accountants-and-bookkeepers). MTD ITSA timeline (https://gocardless.com/blog/mtd-itsa-sole-traders-landlords-2026-guide).

ideas.name: Practice-paid 'year-end job pack' per builder client (Dext-style wholesale add-on)
ideas.mechanism: Separate from referral share: the practice buys a per-client add-on (assume £4 per builder client per month, 10-client minimum, billed to the practice annually) that gives them, for each consenting builder client: year-end WIP and revenue-recognition schedule built from immutable accepted quotes, approved variations and issued invoices; unbilled-approved-variations list (fee-free, all builder capture); retention and CIS reconciliations; DRC VAT flags; a signed export of every locked final account for the year as audit evidence. The builder pays nothing extra; the practice pays because it replaces hours of chasing job-costing from builders at year-end.
ideas.who_pays: The accounting practice pays per builder client per month; the builder pays nothing extra.
ideas.assumptions: Price is an assumption anchored below Dext's per-client practice pricing (reported around $17.70/client/month, quote-only since 2024). Assumes the practice values structured job costing more than a raw export, and that the builder consents. Revenue is per builder client with an enrolled practice, so multiply by the share of builders whose accountant enrols (unknown; assume 20–30% at maturity).
ideas.trust_note: The builder gets a cheaper year-end and a happier accountant; nothing is hidden and no data leaves without consent. Keep the free data-portability export intact so this is a convenience for practices, not a toll on the builder's own data.
ideas.regulatory: None beyond D12 consent/controller roles and D02 for how VAT figures are labelled in the pack. Any 'revenue recognition' schedule must be labelled as a projection of recorded facts, not accounting advice.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-11 final accounts, M1-9 variations, M5-1 canonical accounting export model, M5-9 signed exports, M4-20/M4-22 for retention and CIS. Effort: 3–4 weeks after M5-1.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material.
ideas.precedent: Dext practice plans priced per client per month with a 10-client minimum (https://costbench.com/software/accounting/dext/; https://dext.com/en/partner/pricing). Xero job costing only on its £70 Ultimate plan, showing job-costing data is priced at a premium (https://www.xero.com/uk/pricing-plans/).

ideas.name: White-label / OEM 'watchdog module' for a lead-gen platform or trade-body app, wholesale per live job
ideas.mechanism: Checkatrade (50,000 members, free quoting tool, free TradeMore AI job app), MyBuilder, Rated People or a trade body's own app embeds JobGuard's supplier-overcharge check, proof gates, final-account assembly and post-lock final check as a co-branded module behind their login (SSO via the M0-6 principal contract, tenant provisioning API). The platform pays JobGuard wholesale per live job per month (assume £4) or a flat per-member rate; the platform sets the retail price and keeps the margin. The 10% success fee stays entirely with JobGuard under the builder's direct terms — do not share it with the platform, because a partner with an interest in reveals is exactly the conflict D13 exists to avoid. All D13 rules (no pre-lock disclosure, shadow tables invisible, must-surface rules) bind the partner contractually and are structurally enforced anyway.
ideas.who_pays: The platform pays JobGuard wholesale; the builder pays the platform (or gets it inside their membership).
ideas.assumptions: £4 per live job per month wholesale is an assumption (about a third of direct list). The live-jobs meter works cleanly as a wholesale meter because switch-live and lock are explicit commands, so 'live' is auditable; the honest weakness is that builders (and platforms) can keep small jobs off the module to stay cheap, which cuts evidence and fee base — generous allowances and 'suggest upgrade next month, never block' are the mitigations already in the report. Success fees are additional and unchanged.
ideas.trust_note: Trust rides on the partner's brand. Checkatrade's standing with trades is mixed (12-month contracts, real bills of £80–£500 a month reported), and a builder who feels the platform 'took a cut of the find' will blame both. Keep the success fee a direct JobGuard-builder relationship, keep the plain one-sentence explanation of the final check on the partner's screens, and reserve the right to surface the fee explanation unedited.
ideas.regulatory: D12: controller/processor roles shift (the platform may be the account controller); D04 residency of the platform's infrastructure and support tooling must be verified; D13 onboarding disclosure must appear in the partner's flow before the first job. Competition: avoid exclusivity that blocks the direct channel.
ideas.build_dependency: Watchdog features must exist first (M2-1..M2-7), plus multi-brand theming, partner SSO/provisioning API, per-partner wholesale metering (M4-14 concurrency metering, optional under D09) and partner invoicing via M4-10. Effort: 6–8 weeks after M2, plus the commercial deal.
ideas.gaming_risk: Medium. A platform could under-report live jobs — meter server-side from switch-live/lock events, never from partner-supplied counts. A platform could pressure for early hints of findings to drive its own retention — refuse; structurally the builder runtime role cannot read shadow tables.
ideas.precedent: Checkatrade partner offers (QuickBooks 75% off, Wickes TradePro, Superscript) and its free TradeMore app (https://construction-update.co.uk/2024/07/24/checkatrade-partners-with-intuit-quickbooks-and-wickes-to-expand-member-benefits/; https://www.checkatrade.com/partnerships). Simply Business offers white-label and direct-integration partnerships (https://www.simplybusiness.co.uk/partner/). ServiceM8's jobs-based tiers as the closest workload-metered precedent (https://www.servicem8.com/uk/pricing).

ideas.name: Franchise / network licence for home-improvement franchisors with an aggregate network dashboard
ideas.mechanism: Home-improvement franchisors (Dream Doors with about 100 showrooms under Neighbourly; kitchen, bathroom, loft and driveway networks) sign a network agreement: JobGuard is the recommended or mandated quote-to-final-account tool; the franchisor pays a network fee (assume £2,000/yr) and franchisees are billed at a wholesale network rate (assume £39/month for the Builder tier). The franchisor gets an aggregate dashboard — variation rate, proof-gate compliance, dispute rate, final-account cycle time — built only from data each franchisee consents to share under the franchise agreement, and never anything from shadow tables. Success fees remain between JobGuard and each franchisee; the franchisor gets no share and no visibility of catches.
ideas.who_pays: Franchisee pays the wholesale subscription (or the franchisor bills it within the management fee); franchisor pays the network fee.

revenue_per_year.solo: £468/yr (£39 × 12 at network Builder tier; franchisees are typically Solo/Small-sized)
revenue_per_year.firm: £1,188/yr (£99 × 12 network Firm rate — rare in franchise networks)

ideas.assumptions: Network wholesale rates and the £2,000 network fee are assumptions; no franchisor's mandatory-software terms were found. Franchisees run few concurrent installs, so the live-jobs meter suits them. Assumes the franchisor's interest in fewer customer disputes outweighs franchisee resistance to central oversight.
ideas.trust_note: Franchisees may resent head office seeing operational data, and a mandated tool is a captive audience — that is a trust cost. Mitigate by making the dashboard aggregate-only, publishing exactly which fields the franchisor sees, and keeping shadow findings and success-fee statements strictly between JobGuard and the franchisee.
ideas.regulatory: None specific. D12: franchisor as a separate controller for the aggregate data; franchise-agreement consent must be genuine. No enterprise isolation before its task (AGENTS §1).
ideas.build_dependency: Requires an organisation hierarchy with read-only aggregate views — deferred M5-era work by AGENTS §1 ('do not add enterprise isolation before its task'); partner billing via M4-10. Effort: 4–6 weeks once the hierarchy task exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Franchisees could keep jobs off JobGuard to avoid oversight — a franchisor-side compliance issue, and also a D11-style 'activity inconsistent with being run in JobGuard' signal, advisory only.
ideas.precedent: Dream Doors: about 100 showrooms, part of Neighbourly, with a 13-week induction and in-territory support (https://www.franchiseinfo.co.uk/franchise/dream-doors/; https://www.dreamdoorsfranchise.co.uk/). Home-improvement franchise directory (https://www.totalfranchise.co.uk/Category/54-Home-Improvement). No precedent found of a UK franchisor mandating a job-management tool with a network dashboard.

ideas.name: ADR-ready 'dispute evidence pack' with FMB conciliation / TrustMark Ombudsman / mediation partner referral
ideas.mechanism: When a customer dispute is recorded (the D13 must-surface dispute rule already fires and any related signal becomes fee-free), the builder can generate a signed, chronological dispute pack: accepted quote, scope items, every variation with approval provenance, hash-verified timestamped photos, messages, invoices and receipts, in the format FMB conciliation, TrustMark's Dispute Resolution Ombudsman or Money Claim Online expects. The raw export stays free (data portability); the formatted, signed ADR pack is charged at a flat £79 ex VAT per pack (or one free per year on Builder, three on Firm). A partner mediation provider (Fair Way Resolution-type firms already handle Master Builder disputes) pays a referral fee (assume £50) when the builder books mediation through JobGuard.
ideas.who_pays: Builder pays per pack (or it is included in tier); mediation provider pays a referral fee.
ideas.assumptions: Domestic dispute rates of 4–6% of jobs are guesses; the only hard number found is subcontract-side (73% of subs see routine application disputes). £79 per pack and £50 referral are assumptions. FMB conciliation is free to the consumer and mediation is at 'nominal cost to both parties', so the pack must be priced as time saved, not as access to justice.
ideas.trust_note: It is the builder's own evidence, in their own interest, at the moment they most need it — but charging at the moment of distress reads badly if the free export is hidden or the must-surface dispute warning is ever gated. Keep the free export one tap away and the paid pack clearly a convenience. Never use claims-management language.
ideas.regulatory: Not legal advice and must not be presented as such; not regulated claims management (construction is outside the FCA sectors, per the report's legal note). D12 for the customer's personal data in the pack; D07 retention. A one-off charge needs D09/D02 coverage for platform documents and VAT.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 evidence packs are merged (#92); needs the ADR formatting templates, M5-9 signed manifest, and a one-off hosted payment via the M4-11 Stripe surface with an M4-10 platform invoice. Effort: 2–3 weeks after M5-9 and M4-11.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material. A builder could omit unfavourable evidence — the pack is a signed manifest of what the builder chose to include and says so.
ideas.precedent: FMB dispute resolution: free conciliation, referral to independent mediation at nominal cost (https://www.fmb.org.uk/find-a-builder/dispute-resolution.html; https://www.fairwayresolution.com/help-for-you/building-and-construction/master-builder-disputes). TrustMark Dispute Resolution Ombudsman access and £6-per-party escrow (https://www.trustmark.org.uk/business/benefits/). Chaser pairs credit-control software with a separate collections service as a 'software plus service' precedent (https://www.chaserhq.com/blog/debt-collection-software).

ideas.name: Invoice-finance / credit-control partner referral on issued final accounts (flagged: FCA and watchdog conflict)
ideas.mechanism: When a final account or interim application (M1-12 / M4-18) is issued and still unpaid past a builder-chosen day count, an opt-in settings page (never the Decision Inbox, never a watchdog Finding) offers a referral to an invoice-finance or credit-control partner (Satago, Kriya, iwoca-type). The partner pays JobGuard a referral commission (assume £150 per funded facility or 1% of first advance). JobGuard shares only what the builder consents to; the invoice itself is already the builder's document.
ideas.who_pays: The finance partner pays JobGuard a referral commission; the builder pays the partner's finance charges.

revenue_per_year.small_firm: £25/yr (10% × £250 average of £150 flat / 1% of a £25k advance)

ideas.assumptions: Take rates and commission are assumptions; Satago's own product is £45–£200/month and Chaser prices by revenue, so partners exist but publish no referral terms. Late payment costs UK business £11bn a year and 14,000 closures (Small Business Commissioner), so demand is real; the question is whether JobGuard should be the one selling debt.
ideas.trust_note: Borderline. A 'profit watchdog' that nudges builders toward borrowing looks like the opposite of its purpose, and it collides with the withheld-payment success fee: JobGuard would earn either from finance or from a recovery case on the same invoice, which a builder could read as JobGuard steering. If built at all, keep it off the inbox, behind an explicit opt-in, and never offered on an invoice with an open recovery case.
ideas.regulatory: FCA credit broking (RAO art. 36A): introducing sole traders and small partnerships to lenders for regulated credit (agreements up to £25,000 for business purposes) requires authorisation or an exemption; limited-company borrowing is unregulated but many builders are sole traders. Financial-promotion rules (FSMA s.21). D10 (no autonomous pursuit), D12. Needs legal review and a decision record before any build.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-12 invoices and M4-16 dunning/cancellation controls; a consented handoff and commission reconciliation. Effort: 1–2 weeks; the legal gating dominates.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low for builders. The risk is internal: revenue pressure to promote finance over recovery — forbid the referral where a recovery case is open, and audit the offer as a commercial send under §5.3.
ideas.precedent: Satago credit control plus invoice finance at £45–£200 a month; Chaser subscription plus collections service (https://www.chaserhq.com/blog/debt-collection-software). Late-payment scale from the Small Business Commissioner (https://www.smallbusinesscommissioner.gov.uk/late-payments-research-2/). No UK trade job app found earning finance referral commissions.

ideas.name: Subcontractor-invite growth channel: free 'sub' access on invited jobs, converting to paid tenants, with a subscription credit for the inviter
ideas.mechanism: A builder invites the subcontractors on a job (electrician, plumber, roofer) into that job with a scoped role: they upload their proof photos to the builder's stage gates, attach their invoices (which become evidence and feed three-way matching), and see only their own items. The sub gets a free 'Sub' tenant limited to invited jobs — no own quoting, no final account. When the sub starts their own jobs they subscribe. The inviting builder earns one month's subscription credit per converted sub (a subscription credit under D09, which is permitted: it never offsets a success fee). Subs' invoices and photos enrich the inviter's evidence, so the watchdog gets better for free.
ideas.who_pays: Converted subs pay their own subscription; JobGuard funds the inviter's credit from that revenue.

revenue_per_year.solo: £95/yr net (invites 2 subs × 15% conversion = 0.3 × £348 Solo-sized sub subscription = £104, less £9 inviter credit)

ideas.assumptions: Invites per year and a 15% twelve-month conversion are assumptions; converted subs are assumed Solo-sized. The credit is one month of the inviter's own plan per conversion (£29/£59/£119). Downstream revenue is attributed to the inviter for this estimate but is really new-tenant revenue.
ideas.trust_note: Builders already coordinate subs by WhatsApp; a scoped invite is a convenience and the credit is a plain thank-you. Make clear to subs what the inviter can and cannot see, and that a sub's own future jobs are their own tenant with the same fee-free capture rules.
ideas.regulatory: D12: sole-trader subs are data subjects (Article 13/14 notices at invite); D08 offline/permission conflicts once M3 exists. Credits need D09 terms.
ideas.build_dependency: M0-6 membership/permissions extended with a per-job scoped external role; M1-10 proof capture by an external principal; M2-2 intake of sub invoices as evidence; D09 credit rules; conversion attribution. Effort: 3–5 weeks after M2-2. Not enterprise hierarchy — scoped job membership only.
ideas.gaming_risk: Medium. Fake sub accounts to farm credits — pay the credit only after the converted sub has had a live job for 30 days and paid one period; cap credits per year; the same idempotent, unique conversion identity rules as fee derivations.
ideas.precedent: Buildbite is free for clients and subcontractors, paid by the contractor (https://buildbite.com/insights/ai-construction-tools). Xero's £50 referral and 30% refer-a-friend as software-referral norms (https://www.xero.com/uk/campaign/refer-a-friend/). Dext rewards partner referrals with a free month (https://help.dext.com/en/articles/273220-dext-plans-for-accountants-and-bookkeepers).

ideas.name: Pay-now links on every JobGuard invoice (card + pay by bank) with a small capped platform fee
ideas.mechanism: Every deposit request, stage request and final invoice JobGuard issues carries a hosted Stripe payment link on the builder's own Stripe Connect Standard account (Stripe is the regulated institution and settles to the builder; JobGuard never touches the money). The customer chooses Pay by Bank (Stripe list price 0.5% + 20p, capped £5) or card (1.5% + 20p; a credit card also gives the homeowner Section 75 cover on £100–£30,000). JobGuard adds a Stripe application fee of 0.3% capped at £6 per successful payment, itemised on the builder's platform statement as 'JobGuard payment fee'. Measurement: charge.succeeded / application_fee webhooks reconciled to the customer-receipt fact in M4-8. Because each link is minted for one invoice (or a caught line's separate invoice), a rail payment is an explicit allocation under §14.8 rule 1 by construction, and the payer pays a JobGuard-verified account rather than bank details copied from an email (invoice-redirection fraud is a real loss for builders and homeowners). Money: Stripe pays the builder; the application fee lands in JobGuard's platform balance and is booked as payment-service revenue, never as a success fee.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (UK law bans surcharging consumers for card/consumer-instrument payments; commercial cards may be surcharged at cost only). Bank transfer stays free.
ideas.assumptions: Archetype jobs/yr: Solo 19 (£150k/£8k), Small 24, Firm 33. Payments per job: Solo 2, Small 3, Firm 5; average payment £4k / £8.3k / £12k. Share of invoiced value paid through JobGuard links (assumed): Solo 40%, Small 30%, Firm 15% (commercial customers pay by BACS). Solo: 15 rail payments × £6 cap = £90 (uncapped 0.3% × £60k = £180). Small: 22 × £6 = £130 (0.3% × £180k = £540). Firm: 25 × £6 = £150 (0.3% × £300k = £900). Stripe Connect Standard has no per-account fee, so margin ≈ gross. Note for every idea in this list: adoption figures overlap; the per-idea figures must not simply be summed.
ideas.trust_note: Builders already pay Fergus 1.6% + 20p; the fee is visible per payment and capped, bank transfer remains free, and the builder gets explicit allocation plus fraud-safe payment details. The line not to cross is nudging customers toward the paid rail to pump fees; the link must be one option beside the builder's bank details.
ideas.regulatory: No FCA permission needed while JobGuard never holds funds and Stripe is the regulated payment institution (Connect Standard; Stripe performs KYB). Consumer Rights (Payment Surcharges) Regulations 2012 as amended 2018: no surcharge to consumers. D02 (VAT on JobGuard's fee), D04 (verify Stripe's UK/EU processing route), D06 (invoice templates). G4 for real money.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-12 customer invoice and M4-11 Stripe adapter (rewritten for subscriptions; needs a sibling 'customer payment links' task reusing its webhook/idempotency/unknown-outcome acceptance), then M4-8 receipt-to-line allocation and M4-17 reconciliation. Roughly 2–3 sprints after M4-11; production behind G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. A builder routing payments outside to avoid £6 is fine. JobGuard-side risk: treating a provider-cleared charge as 'settled' before payout/dispute windows; keep 'provider cleared' distinct from 'settled' (M4-11/M4-17 already require this).
ideas.precedent: Fergus UK 1.6% + 20p (research report, competitor table); Tradify/ServiceM8 Stripe pass-through (research notes); Stripe UK pricing pages https://stripe.com/gb/pricing and https://stripe.com/gb/pricing/local-payment-methods.

ideas.name: Deposit at acceptance plus a stage-payment schedule collected by Direct Debit or variable recurring payment
ideas.mechanism: At quote acceptance JobGuard raises the deposit request from a D06-reviewed template (e.g. 10–25%). At switch-live the customer signs one GoCardless Bacs mandate (1% + 20p capped £4) or, when commercial VRP is available, a bank-on-file consent. Each stage in the approved schedule (M4-18) becomes a Decision when the builder marks the stage complete with proof; on approval the collection is submitted with the Bacs advance notice and the customer can cancel any single collection. JobGuard charges a 'Get paid on schedule' add-on of £9/month (or bundles it into the Firm tier) plus £1 per collection above provider cost, billed on the platform subscription invoice (D09), never deducted from the customer's payment.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (add-on and per-collection fee). The customer pays nothing extra.
ideas.assumptions: Adoption: Solo 15%, Small 40%, Firm 60%. Solo: 0.15 × £108 = £16 + 6 collections × £1 = £22. Small: 0.4 × £108 = £43 + 29 collections × £1 = £72. Firm: 0.6 × £108 = £65 + 99 collections × £1 = £164. Collections = jobs × payments per job × adoption.
ideas.trust_note: Predictable cash is what small builders want, and the fee is a flat, stated add-on. Two honest warnings for onboarding: the Direct Debit Guarantee lets a homeowner reclaim a collection through an indemnity claim even after the work is done, and a timer must never collect without the builder's proof-gated approval.
ideas.regulatory: GoCardless/TrueLayer are the regulated institutions. Bacs advance-notice rules apply. Commercial VRP for one-off ecommerce use is still being rolled out under the UK Payments Initiative (2026), so availability is a risk. D05 bounds only JobGuard's own subscription authority; customer mandates are between builder and customer via the provider. D06 governs deposit templates.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-15 GoCardless rail and M4-18 staged customer invoicing must exist; then metering of the add-on under D09 (M4-14 pattern). Medium; late M4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Risk is on the builder's side: collections raised for stages not actually complete invite indemnity claims and disputes; the proof gate and the customer's cancel right are the controls.
ideas.precedent: GoCardless UK pricing https://gocardless.com/pricing; Qted offers Stripe deposits (research notes); Buildertrend/Jobber stage payments.

ideas.name: Opt-in instant payout on rail receipts
ideas.mechanism: Card and pay-by-bank receipts through idea 1 normally reach the builder in T+2 to T+7. Stripe Instant Payouts cost 1% (minimum 40p). JobGuard offers a per-payout 'Get it now' toggle at 1.5% (minimum £1) and keeps the 0.5% difference as a platform fee. Trigger: the builder taps the toggle for a specific payout; measured from Stripe payout objects with method=instant, reconciled in M4-17. Off by default; never applied to subscription or fee collections.
ideas.who_pays: Builder, per payout, only when chosen.
ideas.assumptions: Value through JobGuard rails as in idea 1 (£60k / £180k / £300k). Opt-in share of that volume: Solo 25%, Small 25%, Firm 15%. Solo £60k × 25% × 0.5% = £75; Small £180k × 25% × 0.5% = £225; Firm £300k × 15% × 0.5% = £225.
ideas.trust_note: An honest per-use price for speed, which cash-tight sole traders value. It only stays honest if it is never default-on and the price is shown before the tap.
ideas.regulatory: None beyond Stripe's terms; D02 for VAT on the fee.
ideas.build_dependency: After the customer payment-links task (idea 1); small.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material.
ideas.precedent: Jobber charges +1% for instant payouts (research notes, uk_trade_job_software.md); Stripe Instant Payouts 1% https://stripe.com/gb/pricing.

ideas.name: Statutory late-payment interest and compensation on business customers, claimed inside a withheld-payment case
ideas.mechanism: For invoices to business customers only, the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 entitles the builder to 8% over Bank of England base rate plus fixed compensation of £40 / £70 / £100 per invoice (under £1,000 / £1,000–£9,999 / £10,000+) from the day after the due date. JobGuard computes the exact entitlement daily from immutable invoice facts (exact arithmetic, half-even). When the builder opens a withheld_customer_payment case under the §14.7 entry test (overdue beyond threshold, own reminder ignored, fee terms approved), the statutory sums are added to the builder-approved claim letter (M4-5). Cash received after case opening and allocated under M4-8 (principal, interest and compensation) is qualifying recovered value at 10%. Needs a D03 v3 clause stating that statutory interest and compensation collected in an open case count as recovered value (they are not 'net principal' in today's wording).
ideas.who_pays: Builder, only out of cash actually received; the business customer pays the statutory sums.
ideas.assumptions: Incremental over principal recovered in the same cases (already the fixed 10%). Business-customer invoiced value: Solo £15k (10%), Small £180k (30%), Firm £1m (50%). Share that becomes an open case: 10%. Interest ≈12% p.a. (base ≈4% + 8%) for an average 60 days ≈ 2% of the overdue value, plus £70–£100 per invoice. Solo: £1.5k × 2% = £30 + £70 = £100 → £10. Small: £18k × 2% = £360 + 3 × £100 = £660 → £66. Firm: £100k × 2% = £2,000 + 8 × £100 = £2,800 → £280.
ideas.trust_note: Money the builder is legally owed and almost never claims; JobGuard visibly does the calculation and drafting, and the builder approves every send. Nothing is withheld and nothing is charged unless cash arrives.
ideas.regulatory: The Act applies to business-to-business debts only; claims against consumers are excluded and must be hard-blocked (counterparty type declared by the builder). Not FCA-regulated debt collecting: the builder collects its own debt and sends the letters (D10). Not legal advice; templates need the M4-5/M4-19 professional review. D03 v3 amendment for the interest/compensation line.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-1/M4-2 case types, M4-5 reviewed templates, M4-8 allocation; small extension once withheld-payment cases exist. Production behind G4 and D03.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder could mark a consumer as a business to add interest: treat counterparty type as a D06/D11 review signal, never auto-add sums, and exclude ambiguous counterparties.
ideas.precedent: GOV.UK late commercial payments guidance (cited in the research report); Small Business Commissioner late-payment figures (£11bn/yr cost) in the report; Chaser adds statutory interest in its credit-control product.

ideas.name: Retention ledger and release watchdog on subcontract work (10% only on retention released after a case is opened)
ideas.category: Recovery (existing withheld-payment category applied to retention)
ideas.mechanism: At switch-live the builder declares the contract's retention terms (percentage, first/second moiety, defects period). JobGuard keeps an append-only retention balance per application (M4-20): certified, retained, released, overdue, with release-due dates and reminders as a subscription feature. When a release date passes and the builder's own reminder is ignored (§14.7 withheld test), the builder can open a withheld_customer_payment case; JobGuard drafts the release request (M4-5), tracks the receipt through the bank feed (M4-7/M4-8) and only cash released after the case opened and allocated to the retention line qualifies at 10%. On-time releases attract nothing.
ideas.who_pays: Builder, 10% of retention that would otherwise have sat unclaimed; nothing on retention released without a case.
ideas.assumptions: Work under retention: Solo 10% commercial × 30% with retention = £4.5k; Small £600k × 30% × 40% = £72k; Firm £2m × 50% × 60% = £600k. Retention 5%: £225 / £3.6k / £30k per year. Share that ends up overdue and chased through a case: 25% (BEIS-commissioned research: 44% of contractors had unrecovered retention; ≈£240m/yr lost to insolvency). Fee: 10% × 25% × retained = £6 / £90 / £750.
ideas.trust_note: Retention loss is the industry's most resented leak, and the fee attaches only to money JobGuard visibly chased after the builder's own reminder failed. The objection 'I'd have chased it anyway' is real; the case-opening consent and ignored-reminder test are the answer, and JobGuard must never delay a reminder to let a case ripen.
ideas.regulatory: The builder's own contractual debt; no FCA permission. Construction Act notice and adjudication mechanics are legal work (M4-19 templates need professional review; D06, D10). Runway caveat: the Commercial Payments Bill (published May 2026) bans retention clauses with a two-year transition after commencement and applies prospectively to new contracts, so retention releases continue for roughly 3–4 years, after which the product becomes a ban-compliance check (penalty: the higher of £40 or 50% of the retention debt).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-18 interim applications → M4-19 notices → M4-20 retention balances; i.e. late M4, large. Production behind G4/D03/D06.
ideas.gaming_risk: None against JobGuard. Builder-side residual: settling outside JobGuard after opening a case (D11 signal, not a penalty). Do not let retention released on schedule be logged as a case.
ideas.precedent: Payapps and Site Samurai retention tracking (research report, 'No rival' section); BEIS/Pye Tait figures via https://www.retentiondepositscheme.org/insights/the-impact-of-retentions-on-construction-firms; Commercial Payments Bill summary https://www.hilldickinson.com/our-view/articles/the-reshaping-of-retentions-what-s-next-for-retentions-in-construction-contracts/.

ideas.name: Early-pay referral on issued business invoices (selective invoice finance)
ideas.mechanism: On any issued invoice to a business customer with terms of 14+ days, a builder-initiated 'Get this invoice paid early' button sends the invoice, its evidence pack (M4-3: approved variations, proof photos, customer approvals) and the customer's payment history to an FCA-authorised invoice-finance partner. The lender advances 70–85% within 1–2 days for 1.5–4% per 30 days (construction applications for payment 1–3%). JobGuard receives an introducer commission from the lender (Apollo publishes up to 25% of the upfront minimum plus up to 25% of the monthly service fee), roughly 0.4–0.75% of financed value, paid into the platform book and disclosed on the button. No data leaves JobGuard until the builder taps.
ideas.who_pays: The lender, out of the fee it charges the builder.
ideas.assumptions: Business-customer invoiced value: Solo £15k, Small £180k, Firm £1m. Share financed: Solo 5%, Small 10%, Firm 15%. JobGuard share 0.6% of financed value. Solo £750 × 0.6% = £5; Small £18k × 0.6% = £108; Firm £150k × 0.6% = £900.
ideas.trust_note: Acceptable while builder-initiated, off by default and commission-disclosed; the evidence pack genuinely lowers the lender's dispute risk, which is value JobGuard created. A finance nudge on every unpaid invoice would read as JobGuard profiting from builders' cash-flow pain, and the M4-3 verifier language must make clear JobGuard does not certify the debt.
ideas.regulatory: Receivables finance to a limited company is outside consumer-credit regulation. For sole traders and partnerships of up to three, agreements of £25,000 or less can be regulated credit, making JobGuard's introduction credit broking (RAO art 36A): either exclude those borrowers, become an IAR/AR of the authorised partner (weeks to ~3 months), or seek limited permission (6–12 months). D12 lawful basis for sharing customer data with a lender; D04 residency; a new decision record for third-party referrals.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-12 invoices and M4-3 evidence packs exist; needs a partner API or manual-referral task with consent capture. Medium. Pilot builders may be referred only if no JobGuard charge arises, and a referral decision record is approved first.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. A builder could finance an invoice they know is disputed; that is the lender's underwriting risk, provided JobGuard never labels a pack as proof of an undisputed debt.
ideas.precedent: Apollo introducer terms https://www.apollofinance.biz/introducers/; construction invoice finance rates https://marketinvoice.co.uk/construction-finance/ and https://www.expertsure.com/uk/business-finance/invoice-finance-rates/; Chaser + Satago pairing (research report).

ideas.name: Homeowner finance at quote through an FCA-authorised principal (JobGuard as AR/IAR or referral)
ideas.mechanism: On a free quote for a domestic job the builder can switch on 'spread the cost'; the homeowner sees an interest-bearing option (typically 7.9–14.9% APR) or a 0% option for 12–24 months that the builder subsidises.
