The application runs in the lender's or broker's hosted journey; on payout the lender pays the builder directly (JobGuard never holds funds) and pays commission down the broker chain; JobGuard's share is assumed at 1–2% of the loan. Trigger: loan paid out; measured from the principal's payout report reconciled to the invoice receipt (M4-8 explicit allocation). The quote total is identical with or without finance.
ideas.who_pays: The lender (interest-bearing) or the builder (0% subsidy, assumed 8–12% of the loan). The homeowner pays interest on interest-bearing loans.
ideas.assumptions: Domestic jobs: Solo 17, Small 17, Firm 16. Share financed: 10% (Firm 8%). Average loan: £8k / £25k / capped at £25k. JobGuard share 1.5%. Solo 1.7 × £8k = £13.7k × 1.5% = £205; Small 1.7 × £25k = £42k × 1.5% = £630; Firm 1.3 × £25k = £33k × 1.5% = £495. Commission levels are assumptions: UK home-improvement broker commissions are not published; Ideal4Finance states it receives lender commission and discloses it on request.
ideas.trust_note: Builders win bigger jobs, a real value, but JobGuard would now earn from a lender on the builder's customer, commission must be disclosed to the homeowner, and 0% subsidies tempt builders to inflate quotes, which the quote watchdog cannot police. Kanda, the tradesperson-finance broker with ~700 tradesperson IARs, was restricted by the FCA in February 2026 and entered liquidation in May 2026; that is the reputational blast radius.
ideas.regulatory: Credit broking is regulated (RAO art 36A). FCA guidance: limited permission is unavailable where the sale takes place in the customer's home, so direct authorisation means full permission (6–12 months, Consumer Duty, CONC, financial-promotion rules for '0% finance' adverts). The faster route is AR or IAR status under an authorised principal (1–3 months; the FCA has tightened principal oversight since 2022 and after Kanda). Each builder who introduces customers must also be covered (as the principal's IAR) or the introduction must happen only on JobGuard's regulated surface. Commission disclosure under CONC 4.5, sharpened by Johnson v FirstRand (UKSC 2025). New decision record for credit broking plus D12 for customer data.
ideas.build_dependency: After M1-12 quote acceptance and the payment-links task; needs a principal agreement, hosted journey and payout reconciliation. Large; legal work first; production behind G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Quote inflation to fund 0% subsidies; builders steering customers to finance for commission. Controls: JobGuard pays the builder nothing, shows one quote total, and logs finance uptake as a D11 review signal.
ideas.precedent: Novuna Retail Finance (retailer-subsidised 0%, 7.9–14.9% APR interest-bearing) https://www.novuna.co.uk/consumer-finance/our-specialist-retail-sectors/home-improvement/; Ideal4Finance commission disclosure https://windowcost.co.uk/guides/window-replacement-finance-uk/; FCA notice on Kanda https://www.fca.org.uk/news/news-stories/kanda-products-services-ltd-enters-liquidation; FCA credit-broker guide https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/authorisation/consumer-credit-brokers.

ideas.name: Insurance-backed guarantee and deposit protection per job, registered from the evidence pack
ideas.mechanism: At switch-live the builder can attach an insurance-backed guarantee (IBG: the workmanship guarantee is insured for 10 years if the builder ceases trading) and deposit-protection cover to the job. JobGuard's confirmed scope, proof photos and completion record become the registration and underwriting data. Premium is per job (HomePro: about £48 on an £8,000 re-roof, IPT included; assumed ≈0.6% of contract value for general building work). JobGuard earns 10–20% of premium as introducer or AR commission from the intermediary; the builder builds the cost into the quote (insurers require it to be shown as included cover, not a separate line). Trigger: policy issued at practical completion; measured from the intermediary's monthly bordereau.
ideas.who_pays: Builder pays the premium through the intermediary; the intermediary pays JobGuard commission.
ideas.assumptions: Uptake: Solo 60% of 19 jobs, Small 50% of 24, Firm 40% of 33. Premium 0.6% of average job: £48 / £150 / £360. JobGuard share 15%. Solo 11.4 × £48 × 15% = £82; Small 12 × £150 × 15% = £270; Firm 13.2 × £360 × 15% = £713.
ideas.trust_note: Homeowners increasingly demand IBGs (TrustMark), it helps builders win, and JobGuard's proof photos are exactly what an underwriter wants, so premiums may fall for JobGuard users. The one trust line: never imply cover is compulsory when it is not.
ideas.regulatory: Insurance distribution (RAO arts 25 and 39A; IDD). A pure introduction may fit the art 72C exclusion (information passed on an incidental basis) if JobGuard neither advises nor assists in concluding; taking commission and embedding the flow makes AR status of an FCA-authorised intermediary the safer route (1–3 months). Insurance Premium Tax 12%. D12 for passing customer details.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 evidence pack and M1-12 exist; partner integration and a per-job attach flow. Medium. Commission requires a referral decision record; the pilot may register policies but JobGuard takes no commission in pilot_no_charge.
ideas.gaming_risk: Minimal. Policies registered for incomplete work are the risk; gate registration on the completion proof pack.
ideas.precedent: HomePro IBG pricing https://www.homepro.com/roofing-ibg-cost/; QANW IBG and Deposit Protection Insurance https://qanw.co.uk/insurance-backed-guarantees/; TrustMark scheme requirements.

ideas.name: Single-use virtual purchasing card per purchase order (interchange share)
ideas.mechanism: When a purchase order is approved at the agreed price, JobGuard issues a virtual commercial card through Stripe Issuing UK on the builder's own connected account, with the limit set to the PO gross, single-use, and locked to builders'-merchant categories. The float is the builder's own money topped up to their Stripe Issuing balance (held by Stripe, not JobGuard). The supplier charges the card; the authorisation returns exact amount, merchant and time, which becomes the 'paid' fact for three-way matching (M2 supplier matching). Because the limit equals the PO, an overcharge is declined at the till, so prevention becomes something the builder feels. JobGuard earns a share of interchange on successful spend (commercial cards sit outside the 0.2%/0.3% consumer caps; merchant-side commercial interchange is roughly 1.0–2.5%; assume JobGuard nets 0.5% after Stripe's share). Stripe charges £3.50 per physical card and 0.2% + 15p per transaction beyond £500k of platform volume.
ideas.who_pays: The merchant's acquirer pays interchange; the builder pays nothing extra.
ideas.assumptions: Materials at 35% of turnover: £52.5k / £210k / £700k. Share put on JobGuard cards: Solo 30%, Small 40%, Firm 40%. Net 0.5%: Solo £15.75k × 0.5% = £79; Small £84k × 0.5% = £420; Firm £280k × 0.5% = £1,400. The 0.5% net share is an assumption; Stripe does not publish UK issuing revenue shares.
ideas.trust_note: JobGuard would earn when the builder spends, which sits awkwardly beside 'we cut your waste', and the builder's own money is on deposit with a provider, a new thing to explain. There is no relationship with any named merchant, so the invoice watchdog's independence survives, but the disclosure must be plain: 'we earn a small card-network fee, not anything from your merchant'.
ideas.regulatory: Stripe is the regulated issuer and holds the funds; JobGuard is a programme manager under Stripe's terms. Verify at implementation whether any FCA registration applies (commercial cards under a BIN sponsor usually need none). D04 residency of Issuing data, D05 (no standing authority: the builder tops up), D12; KYB/AML run by Stripe.
ideas.build_dependency: New rail on top of the M4-11 Stripe adapter; an Issuing task with PO binding and authorisation ingestion into supplier matching (M2-2/M2 three-way match). Medium-large; behind G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: A merchant splitting a charge across two authorisations to beat the PO limit; cards used for personal spend (MCC lock and per-PO cards mitigate). JobGuard never takes a fee on a declined overcharge because interchange arises only on successful spend.
ideas.precedent: Stripe Issuing commercial cards, UK available https://stripe.com/issuing/commercial; UK interchange caps and commercial rates https://www.businessexpert.co.uk/data/payments/uk-interchange-rates/; Ramp/Brex spend cards (US, unverified for UK economics).

ideas.name: Regulated escrow for stage payments on large domestic jobs, released against JobGuard proof
ideas.mechanism: For domestic jobs above about £25,000 the builder can offer 'protected stage payments': the homeowner funds each stage into an FCA-authorised escrow (Transpact charges £2.99 per party up to £10,000; TrustMark's Transpact-backed escrow starts at £6 per party). JobGuard's stage-complete Decision raises the release request with the proof pack attached and the homeowner releases. JobGuard earns a referral or integration fee per stage (assume £10, to be negotiated) and the builder wins jobs against competitors offering no protection. JobGuard never holds funds.
ideas.who_pays: Homeowner and builder pay the escrow provider's fee; JobGuard's share comes from the provider.
ideas.assumptions: Domestic jobs: Solo 17, Small 17, Firm 16. Uptake: 10% / 25% / 40%. Stages per job: 3 / 4 / 5. £10 per stage. Solo 1.7 × 3 × £10 = £51; Small 4.2 × 4 × £10 = £168; Firm 6.6 × 5 × £10 = £330.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously good for homeowners and a selling tool for builders, but builders dislike escrow (cash-flow lag, release disputes), so it must stay opt-in per job. JobGuard's pack must not become the arbiter of release: 'verified' means hashes and existence, not workmanship approval (M4-3 verifier language).
ideas.regulatory: The escrow firm must be FCA-authorised (payment/e-money institution or client-money holder). JobGuard integrating without touching funds is not a payment service. D06 (customer approval, jurisdiction), D12 (customer data to the provider).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-18 staged invoicing and M4-3 packs; partner API. Medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: None against JobGuard; release disputes are the builder's risk.
ideas.precedent: TrustMark escrow https://www.trustmark.org.uk/trustmark-escrow; Transpact prices https://www.transpact.com/Prices.aspx; Dospay construction escrow; BuildWiz guidance on £50k+ jobs.

ideas.name: CIS and reverse-charge VAT handling as a compliance add-on, with a flat-fee refund-partner referral
ideas.mechanism: For subcontractor builders JobGuard reconciles CIS deductions (20% or 30%) on each receipt to the contractor's payment-and-deduction statement, keeps the annual CIS-suffered total and produces the year-end pack; for contractors it verifies subcontractors and prepares monthly CIS return data; on invoices it flags (not automates) the construction VAT domestic reverse charge until D06 review. Priced as a £6–£8/month add-on (Xero charges £5/month for CIS). Optionally refer sole-trader subcontractors to a partner accountant for the CIS refund claim at a flat referral fee (£30–£50 per claim), since refund firms charge 15–30% of the refund.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (add-on); the accountant partner pays the flat referral.
ideas.assumptions: Solo: 30% do subcontract work × (£8 × 12 = £96 + £40 referral) ≈ £41 + non-CIS DRC use 30% × £96 = £29 → ≈£70–£75. Small: 60% × £96 = £58. Firm: 80% × £96 = £77.
ideas.trust_note: Keeps money in the builder's pocket. The refund referral must be flat, disclosed and optional; a percentage of the refund would look like the refund-firm model builders resent.
ideas.regulatory: No FCA. Filing returns or making refund claims is tax-agent activity needing HMRC agent registration and AML supervision; JobGuard stays at records and handoff. D06 explicitly defers CIS and DRC automation to review; D02 for VAT rounding.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-7/M4-8 bank receipt reconciliation; invoice-side flags need M1-12 and D06 review. Small-medium.
ideas.gaming_risk: None.
ideas.precedent: Xero CIS add-on £5/month (research notes, construction_platforms_and_ai.md); UK CIS refund firms at 15–30% (general market knowledge, unverified).

ideas.name: Working-capital loan referrals from the stage-payment cash-flow view
ideas.mechanism: JobGuard's cash-flow view (deposits due, stages due, supplier bills due) shows a shortfall; a builder-initiated 'borrow against this' button refers the builder to an FCA-authorised business lender or broker, with the stage schedule as supporting data. The lender pays JobGuard an introducer commission, assumed 1–3% of the drawn loan. Off by default; no targeting or prompts.
ideas.who_pays: The lender.
ideas.assumptions: Take-up: Solo 20% × £10k loan × 2% = £40; Small 30% × £30k × 2% = £180; Firm 30% × £75k × 2% = £450. Commission levels are assumptions; UK business-lending introducer rates are not published.
ideas.trust_note: Encouraging debt is the opposite of a profit watchdog, the commission is a conflict, and 'JobGuard sells you loans' is exactly the word-of-mouth line the founder fears. Listed for completeness; if done at all, opt-in only and commission-disclosed.
ideas.regulatory: Limited-company borrowers: unregulated. Sole traders and small partnerships borrowing £25,000 or less: regulated credit, so credit broking permission or AR/IAR status is required. D12 for sharing data; new decision record.
ideas.build_dependency: Cash-flow view (M4-18) plus a partner link; technically small, legal first.
ideas.gaming_risk: None against JobGuard; the lender bears credit risk.
ideas.precedent: iwoca and Funding Circle introducer programmes (commission percentages unverified); bank referral schemes (Tide, Starling).

ideas.name: Commercial applications-for-payment add-on (AfPs, payment and pay-less notice deadlines)
ideas.mechanism: For firms invoicing main contractors under Construction Act contracts: a monthly application-for-payment cycle valued from the frozen baseline plus approved variations, application issue through an exact Decision, payment-notice and pay-less-notice deadline tracking with reminders, and the final-account roll-up. Priced as a 'Commercial' add-on of £39/month or bundled into the Contractor tier as a D09 subscription line, not a fee. Its money value is the notice deadlines builders miss: when a payer misses its payment or pay-less notice, the applied sum becomes the notified sum due.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (add-on).
ideas.trust_note: A plain product with a plain price, and the comparison set (Site Samurai £99–£699) is far above it.
ideas.regulatory: No FCA. Notice templates and deadline rules need professional review (M4-19; D06); no universal 'UK Construction Act deadline' may be hard-coded.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-18 and M4-19; large; late M4.
ideas.gaming_risk: None.
ideas.precedent: Site Samurai £99–£699 and Payapps (research report, 'No rival' section and construction_platforms_and_ai.md); Construction AI payment applications.

ideas.name: Homeowner job portal: approvals, messages and stage sign-off (free; the demand-side engine)
ideas.category: Demand-side foundation, included in the subscription
ideas.mechanism: Builder sends the homeowner a per-job magic link (no password; authenticated customer-link approval as distinct from builder attestation, M1-6/D06). The portal shows the accepted quote, priced variations awaiting approval (Approve = an authenticated customer approval bound to the variation revision hash), a message thread, stage completion with proof photos and 'confirm this stage is done', the final account and invoices. Every message and approval received through JobGuard is evidence under BUILD_PLAN §14.2 and can support a missed_variation_final_account catch after lock; approvals through the portal also make confirmed catches far more collectable. No charge to homeowner or builder. Direct money only through the existing 10% on qualifying settled catches; ideas 2-13 all hang off this surface. Demand-side answer on the live-jobs meter: once the homeowner holds a portal link and expects approvals there, the builder cannot keep the job off JobGuard to sit in a cheaper tier without the customer noticing. The customer becomes the meter's enforcement, which is the honest reason a live-jobs meter can work where turnover would only invite under-reporting. Generous allowances still matter (research report §'Charge for live jobs, not people').
ideas.who_pays: Nobody directly (in the builder's subscription). Indirectly the homeowner pays confirmed catches; JobGuard earns 10% of settled qualifying net principal.
ideas.assumptions: Incremental success fee only. Jobs/yr: Solo 19 (£150k/£8k), Small 24, Firm 33. Portal used on 60% of jobs; 20% of portal jobs yield one qualifying catch that exists only because a customer message/approval came through JobGuard; average catch 3% of net job value (£240/£750/£1,800); 70% of confirmed catches billed and paid; fee 10%. Solo 19×0.6×0.2×£240×0.7×0.10 = £38; Small 24×0.6×0.2×£750×0.7×0.10 = £151; Firm 33×0.6×0.2×£1,800×0.7×0.10 = £499. Uptake and catch rates are guesses; §14.17 pilot measurement must replace them. Context: the research report's £29/£59/£119 tiers give £348/£708/£1,428 a year; the non-conflicted demand-side set here (ideas 2,3,4,5,9,11) adds roughly £630/£1,570/£3,480 at full adoption.
ideas.trust_note: Builders want customer approvals in writing; that is the value. Uncomfortable part: customer messages through JobGuard feed the shadow bill, so JobGuard has a fee interest in routing conversation through its portal. Onboarding must say so plainly (D12 v2 already requires it), and the portal must be the builder's channel ('powered by JobGuard'), never presented to the homeowner as JobGuard checking the builder on their behalf. Any homeowner-facing wording of that kind poisons the watchdog.
ideas.regulatory: D06 (authenticated customer approval); D12 v2 (JobGuard's role for homeowner data; UK GDPR Art. 13/14 notice to the homeowner); Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 (a variation approved remotely can be a distance/off-premises contract with a 14-day cancellation right unless the homeowner expressly requests work to begin, so the approval step should capture that request); D04 residency for notification providers.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-6 authenticated customer-link approval and M1-9 customer approval evidence (D06), M1-10 proof, SV-7 'customer message page' via the evidence-observation contract, M0-6 AuthProvider extended with a customer principal that is not tenant membership. Must pass the SV-2/SV-3 rule that no portal response varies with shadow signals. Effort: medium (3-5 weeks) on the existing web shell; after G1 for real homeowners.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder can keep the homeowner off the portal to avoid creating evidence; that is fee-free and permitted (§14.2 favours the builder). A homeowner could manufacture 'requests' in the thread for work never done: Test E ('not completed') dismisses these, and no fee arises without builder confirmation and settled cash.
ideas.precedent: Client portals bundled in Houzz Pro (£85-£275/month, looked up), Buildertrend Essential client communication, Powered Now Premium and TradeFlow (£36 flat) customer portals (research report §'UK builders already pay £25-£45'; raw notes uk_trade_job_software). None charges the homeowner.

ideas.name: 'Pay now' on the portal: pay-by-bank and card links with a JobGuard application fee
ideas.category: Payment surface (builder is merchant of record; JobGuard never holds funds)
ideas.mechanism: Each issued invoice, stage application or confirmed-catch invoice carries a hosted pay link: pay-by-bank (open banking) via GoCardless 'Pay by Bank' or Stripe, card via Stripe Checkout using Connect direct charges on the builder's own connected account. Funds settle to the builder's bank; the provider deducts a per-payment JobGuard application fee from the builder's balance. Trigger: signed provider settlement event through the M0-9 provider inbox. Measurement: settled gross per payment. Side benefit that may be worth more than the fee: the payment is bound to the exact invoice, so §14.8 rule 1 (explicit allocation) applies to any caught line and M4-7 bank-feed matching becomes trivial for those receipts.
ideas.who_pays: Builder, as a per-payment deduction (surcharging the homeowner is unlawful). Homeowner pays nothing extra.
ideas.assumptions: JobGuard fee 0.3% of gross capped at £15 per payment, on top of provider cost; 30% of payments use the link (bank transfer is free, so uptake is limited). Gross receipts £180k/£720k/£2.4m (all three archetypes are VAT-registered; homeowners pay gross). Payments per job 2/4/5. Solo: 19×2×0.3 = 11.4 payments × avg £4,737 × 0.3% (£14.21) = £162. Small: 24×4×0.3 = 28.8 × (£7,500 × 0.3% = £22.50, capped £15) = £432. Firm: 33×5×0.3 = 49.5 × £15 cap = £743. Uncapped the Firm figure would be about £2,160, but a percentage on £15k transfers when a bank transfer is free would be refused.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest only if optional, cheaper than their current Stripe-per-app pass-through and visibly faster (same-day pay-by-bank). Honest tension: JobGuard benefits twice (the fee and cleaner fee attribution on caught lines), so pay links must appear identically on every invoice and never be pushed harder on invoices that carry catches.
ideas.regulatory: Payment Services Regulations 2017: JobGuard must stay outside the payment chain (provider is the PSP, builder is merchant of record via Connect direct charges); legal review of the technical-service-provider/commercial-agent position. Consumer Rights (Payment Surcharges) Regulations 2012 (no surcharge to the homeowner). AGENTS §3/§5.10: no card data, never hold customer funds. AGENTS §1: no extra payment rails before their tasks; M4-11/12/15 are JobGuard's own billing rails, so this customer-to-builder rail needs a 'Discovered later' entry and its own task. D04 residency for provider data.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-12 invoice issue; M0-9 provider inbox and idempotency; reuse the M4-11 Stripe and M4-15 GoCardless adapter patterns (signed webhooks, unknown-outcome handling); M4-7/M4-8 so provider settlement becomes a verified receipt. Builder onboarding through Stripe's hosted Connect KYC. Effort: medium (4-6 weeks) once M4-11 exists. Not before M4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Builder can always ask for a bank transfer; the cap stops JobGuard chasing big transfers. Refund and chargeback events must flow into §14.9 reversals so a refunded catch reverses its fee.
ideas.precedent: Fergus 1.6% + 20p, Tradify/ServiceM8 Stripe pass-through, Jobber 2.9% + 30¢ (research report benchmark table; raw notes uk_trade_job_software 'success fee' section). GoCardless Pay by Bank 1% + 20p capped at £4 (looked up). Stripe Connect application fees on direct charges, connected account as merchant of record (looked up, Stripe docs). Checkatrade Pay activates its guarantee (looked up).

ideas.name: Homeowner-paid Sealed Job Record (evidence-pack certificate)
ideas.category: Homeowner-paid product built from evidence JobGuard already holds
ideas.mechanism: After final-account lock and final payment the portal offers the homeowner a sealed record: accepted quote, every customer-approved variation with its approval record, proof photos of work later covered (drainage runs, DPC, insulation, first-fix wiring) with server timestamps and SHA-256 hashes, certificates the builder uploaded (Part P, Gas Safe, FENSA etc.), final invoice and payment record, plus an RFC-3161 timestamp anchor (M4-4). A basic PDF summary is free; the paid version adds anchored hashes, 15-year hosted retention, share links for conveyancers/surveyors/insurers and export to an RLBA-style property logbook. Strict subset rule: nothing from shadow tables, watchdog findings, D11 signals, supplier prices or builder margins ever enters the customer pack. Trigger: homeowner checkout on JobGuard's own Stripe hosted surface. Measurement: one-off sale.
ideas.who_pays: Homeowner (£69 + VAT one-off). Builder may gift it at a £39 trade price as a closing gesture. Builder's own copy stays free (M4-3).
ideas.assumptions: Uptake 10%/20%/25% of jobs (rises with job size: extensions and lofts are what people need at resale); price £69 ex VAT. Solo 19×0.10×£69 = £131; Small 24×0.20×£69 = £331; Firm 33×0.25×£69 = £569. No market data on uptake; it is a guess.
ideas.trust_note: Builder gains a customer-facing proof of a job done properly, fewer 'you never showed me' disputes and a reference asset. Risk: builders may feel JobGuard is selling to their customer, so builder opt-in per job, builder-branded delivery and no other upsell at checkout. If watchdog or shadow content ever leaked into the pack it would become evidence against the builder.
ideas.regulatory: JobGuard sells directly to a consumer: Consumer Rights Act 2015 (digital content), Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 (14-day cancellation, waiver on immediate supply), consumer VAT presentation (D02 covers platform invoices; a consumer sale needs its own tax review), UK GDPR controller role for the homeowner account (D12 v2), D07 retention approval before promising multi-year retention, M4-4 anchoring approval. Certificates remain the issuing scheme's documents; the pack must not imply JobGuard verified them.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 evidence packs (merged, #92), SV-4 lock, M1-10 proof, M4-4 anchoring (needs D07), plus a customer-facing pack renderer, homeowner identity (idea 1) and a JobGuard consumer checkout reusing the M4-11 Stripe hosted adapter. Effort: small-medium (2-4 weeks) after idea 1 and M4-4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low for fees. A builder could upload a certificate they are not entitled to issue; label every document 'uploaded by builder, not verified by JobGuard'.
ideas.precedent: Property logbooks (Chimni, RLBA; basic logbooks free; looked up). Buildbite 'invoices with proof of work attached' (raw notes construction_platforms_and_ai). FMB Building Work Guarantee as an adjacent homeowner product (looked up). No UK product found sells a sealed, hash-anchored job record to homeowners.

ideas.name: Protected-job cover: insurance-backed guarantee and deposit protection via an FCA-authorised partner
ideas.mechanism: At quote acceptance (M1-6) the builder can offer, and the homeowner can add, an insurance-backed guarantee (honours the builder's workmanship guarantee if the builder ceases trading) plus deposit/stage-payment protection. JobGuard passes builder-consented policy inputs (contract value, dates, trade, address, builder identity) to an FCA-authorised IBG administrator/insurer, which issues the policy in the builder's name to the homeowner. JobGuard earns an introducer fee per policy or a share of premium. Genuine underwriting value: the locked baseline, customer-approved variations and stage proof photos are exactly what an IBG claims handler needs and could support lower premiums over time. Trigger: policy issued. Measurement: partner's issued-policy report reconciled to job IDs.
ideas.who_pays: Homeowner by default (premium roughly 1-2% of contract value for a multi-year warranty; about £23 for a basic IBG on a £7k job); the builder may absorb it as a sales tool. JobGuard is paid by the insurer/administrator.
ideas.assumptions: Uptake 25%/30%/35% of jobs; premium 1% of net job value (£80/£250/£600); JobGuard share 20% of premium. Solo 19×0.25×£80×0.2 = £76; Small 24×0.30×£250×0.2 = £360; Firm 33×0.35×£600×0.2 = £1,386. Premium share is an assumption; partner terms unknown.
ideas.trust_note: Offering an IBG is normal (FENSA installers must; FMB members sell Build Assure); it helps the builder win the job and protects the homeowner from the builder's insolvency, not from the builder. Line not to cross: no watchdog, D11 or shadow data may ever reach the insurer, and JobGuard must never let an insurer price a builder on JobGuard's private observations. Builder-consented, builder-visible facts only.
ideas.regulatory: Insurance distribution is FCA-regulated (IDD; 'arranging'): JobGuard would be an Appointed Representative of the authorised administrator, or must stay inside the passive-introducer exclusion (RAO Art. 72C: introduce only, never assist in concluding or administering the contract); legal review decides which. Insurance Premium Tax on premiums. New decision record for regulated introductions (AGENTS §1). D12 for homeowner data to the insurer; D04 residency.
ideas.build_dependency: M1-6 acceptance record, idea 1 portal, partner integration through an approved adapter; no core money changes because the insurer collects the premium. Effort: small technically (2-3 weeks); the commercial and regulatory setup is the long pole (months). After G1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. A builder might buy IBGs only for jobs they expect trouble on, which is the insurer's problem. Claims are between homeowner and insurer; JobGuard must not become a claims handler.
ideas.precedent: HomePro IBG from about £22.97 per job incl. IPT for a ~£7k installation; QANW (installer pays, homeowner pays nothing); FMB Build Assure warranty 1-2% of contract value; Checkatrade Guarantee (free, discretionary, up to £1,000, activated by paying through Checkatrade). All looked up.

ideas.name: 'JobGuard-checked' builder profile, verifiable quote stamp and quote-request page (flat add-on, no lead fees)
ideas.mechanism: A public page per builder showing only builder-consented facts computed from JobGuard records: jobs completed with a locked final account, share of variations approved by the customer before the work, proof photos per job, IBG offered, ADR scheme membership, time on JobGuard. Each quote PDF (M1-5 immutable artifact) carries a QR/hash link so the homeowner can confirm it is the exact version issued. The page includes a 'Request a quote' form capturing a structured brief (photos, access, existing services, must-haves) that lands in Walk it, attacking site-visit omissions, the biggest prevention loss. Trigger: monthly add-on billed with the subscription. Measurement: none per job.
ideas.who_pays: Builder, flat (£9/£15/£25 per month by tier) or included in the top tier.
ideas.assumptions: Per adopting builder: £9×12 = £108; £15×12 = £180; £25×12 = £300. Adoption guess 40-50%. Benchmarks: Checkatrade Approved £30/month, Which? Trusted Traders from £48/month + VAT; JobGuard's is cheaper because it sells no leads and needs no vetting staff.
ideas.trust_note: Builder-controlled, positive, verifiable facts are in the builder's interest. It drops to a 2 the moment the profile shows anything JobGuard learned as watchdog (catches, overcharges, D11 signals, dispute counts without consent), because then JobGuard publicly rates its own customer from data collected for them. No score, no ranking, every metric switchable off, no leads sold from the page.
ideas.regulatory: DMCC Act 2024 and CPUT: 'checked' must be defined, true and not imply endorsement of workmanship; ASA CAP Code for claims; UK GDPR: aggregate facts only, no customer data; PECR not engaged (homeowner initiates contact).
ideas.build_dependency: M1-5 quote hash, SV-4 lock, M1-10 proof, M4-3 packs, plus a public read-only route with tenant opt-in and a Walk-it intake adapter (M1-2). Effort: small-medium (3-4 weeks). Only meaningful after the M1 pilot produces real locked jobs.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builders could lock trivial jobs to inflate counts; show values and dates, not just counts, and locked facts cannot be edited. Quote-stamp verification must not leak prices to anyone without the quote in hand.
ideas.precedent: Checkatrade Approved £30/month and Growth from £59/month; Which? Trusted Traders from £48/month + VAT (looked up); TrustMark scheme-provider fees (looked up); Powered Now certificates (raw notes). Research report notes real Checkatrade bills of £80-£500/month on 12-month contracts.

ideas.name: Verified-builder marketplace: homeowner job requests matched to JobGuard builders, paid per won job (borderline)
ideas.mechanism: Homeowners post a job on JobGuard's public site; JobGuard matches builders with profiles (idea 5) in range; builders quote through Walk it. Success-only charge: 2% of accepted net quote value, charged only when acceptance is recorded (M1-6) and the job is switched live (M1-7) in JobGuard, both existing immutable facts, so the trigger is measurable. Alternative: per-shortlist £15-£50 like MyBuilder. Trigger: switch-live of a marketplace-sourced job. Measurement: accepted net value frozen at switch-live.
ideas.who_pays: Builder.
ideas.assumptions: Marketplace-won jobs per year 2/3/2 (a Firm wins fewer but larger); accepted net £8k/£25k/£60k; 2%. Solo 2×£8,000×2% = £320; Small 3×£25,000×2% = £1,500; Firm 2×£60,000×2% = £2,400. Ignores the homeowner marketing spend needed to create demand, which is large.
ideas.trust_note: Listed because it is the biggest demand-side number, and flagged plainly. (1) JobGuard would be the builder's watchdog and its lead seller, the most resented model in the trade (Checkatrade bills £80-£500/month, 12-month contracts, lead fees regardless of outcome). (2) Conflict: JobGuard gains from routing homeowners to builders who run more live jobs and produce more catches, and from calling builders 'checked' while paid by them. (3) It must never use one builder's homeowners (portal, aftercare) as demand for other builders; that is selling the builder's customers. (4) Keeping 'checked' credible with homeowners means policing builders, which puts JobGuard against its own customers. Recommendation: do the free directory (idea 5) and leave lead fees to Checkatrade.
ideas.regulatory: Not a regulated activity (construction is not a claims-management sector, so lead generation is unregulated here; raw notes success_fee_benchmarks §7). DMCC Act 2024: paid placement/ranking must be disclosed; fake-review rules. UK GDPR/PECR for homeowner marketing; JobGuard becomes controller for homeowner leads (D12 extension). Consumer law governs JobGuard's promises to homeowners about 'checked' builders.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 5 profiles, homeowner accounts and job-posting UX, matching, marketplace attribution bound to acceptance and switch-live records, a billing line in M4-10. Large effort (2-3 months) plus marketing spend. M5 at the earliest.
ideas.gaming_risk: High: builders take the homeowner off-platform to avoid the 2% (Checkatrade's classic leakage); the temptation to police that with D11-style activity signals would turn the watchdog on the builder. A homeowner can take a quote and hire elsewhere; under the success-only model the builder pays nothing, which is the only fair version.
ideas.precedent: Checkatrade (£30-£59+/month plus lead pricing; per-lead equivalents £5-£40) and MyBuilder shortlist fees £5-£35, £50+ on large jobs, non-refundable (looked up); research report and raw notes uk_trade_job_software 'Checkatrade / MyBuilder / Rated People'.

ideas.name: Homeowner finance introductions: 'spread the cost' through an FCA-authorised lender or broker (flagged)
ideas.mechanism: The quote/portal shows an approved 'Spread the cost' option; the homeowner applies on the lender's own site; on completion (portal stage sign-off can serve as the satisfaction note) the lender pays the builder directly, a genuine cash-flow win with no chasing. JobGuard earns an introducer commission from the broker/lender per funded loan; the builder pays a subsidy only on promotional 0% offers. Trigger: lender's funded-loan confirmation matched to the job. Measurement: funded principal.
ideas.who_pays: Lender/broker (commission), builder (optional subsidy on promotional rates), homeowner (interest).
ideas.assumptions: Jobs financed 8%/10%/10%; loan = 60% of gross job value (£5,760/£18,000/£43,200; unsecured lenders cap around £25k-£50k, so Firm loans are partly out of range); JobGuard keeps 1% of funded principal after the broker's share. Solo 19×0.08×£5,760×1% = £88; Small 24×0.10×£18,000×1% = £432; Firm 33×0.10×£43,200×1% = £1,426.
ideas.trust_note: Helps builders win larger jobs and get paid on completion, so not against the builder. But the obvious partner model, Kanda (about 700 tradesperson introducer appointed representatives), entered liquidation in May 2026 after the FCA restricted it, so the regulator is actively hostile to loosely supervised trade-introduced credit; a mis-sold loan complaint lands on JobGuard's brand; and 0% subsidies feel like a hidden charge to builders. Not a watchdog conflict, but a real reputational and regulatory hazard.
ideas.regulatory: Credit broking (RAO Art. 36A) is a regulated activity and 'effecting an introduction' is caught: JobGuard needs FCA authorisation or AR/IAR status under an authorised principal; CONC 3 financial promotions (any 'from £X/month' line on a quote must be approved by an authorised firm); CONC 4.5 commission disclosure; Consumer Duty; s75 CCA liability sits with the lender. Builders displaying the option may themselves need IAR status. Raw notes success_fee_benchmarks §7 already flag that instalment offers move JobGuard toward consumer credit. New decision record required (AGENTS §1). D12 for homeowner data.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 portal; partner hand-off with approved promotions; funded-loan reconciliation to job IDs. Technically small (2-3 weeks); regulatory setup 6-12 months. M5.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low for JobGuard; the lender bears credit risk. Finance-driven jobs could inflate accepted values that later shrink; D11 v1 variance signals already cover that.
ideas.precedent: Kanda: FCA-authorised credit broker with a network of ~700 IARs, mainly tradespeople; liquidators appointed 6 May 2026 after a February 2026 voluntary requirement (looked up, FCA notice). Retail point-of-sale home-improvement finance (Novuna, Propensio type). CONC handbook rules (looked up).

ideas.name: ADR-ready dispute bundle: JobGuard supplies the immutable evidence pack to a CTSI-approved ADR body for a fixed fee
ideas.mechanism: When the homeowner disputes the final account in the portal and direct resolution fails, the builder can invoke the ADR route. JobGuard assembles a homeowner-safe subset of the M4-3 pack (quote, approved variations and approvals, proof photos with hashes and server times, messages, invoice) and transmits it to an approved ADR provider; both parties receive the identical bundle. JobGuard charges the builder a fixed bundle fee (or includes it in the top tier); the ADR provider's own case fee applies and the scheme is free to the consumer. JobGuard never adjudicates and never presents itself to the homeowner as neutral. Trigger: builder invokes ADR. Measurement: per bundle.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (£79 per bundle, or included in the Firm tier). Homeowner free.
ideas.assumptions: Dispute rates reaching ADR 3%/4%/5% of jobs; £79 per bundle. Solo 19×0.03×£79 = £45; Small 24×0.04×£79 = £76; Firm 33×0.05×£79 = £130. Small money; the value is retention and fewer withheld payments.
ideas.trust_note: Builders in the right will welcome it. Tension: JobGuard earns 10% on withheld_customer_payment recovery cases, so it must not steer disputes toward fee-bearing cases; a dispute resolved through ADR is fee-free unless the builder had already opened a D03-compliant case before any JobGuard pursuit. Also honest to say: resolving disputes early shrinks JobGuard's withheld-payment fee base, and that is the right trade.
ideas.regulatory: ADR Regulations 2015 (traders must point consumers to a certified ADR body when a complaint fails; participation voluntary unless scheme-mandated). Construction Act adjudication does not apply to residential occupiers (raw notes success_fee_benchmarks §4). Consumer Rights Act 2015 rights unaffected. Not FCA. D12 for sending homeowner data to the ADR body.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-3 evidence packs (merged, #92), idea 1 portal, homeowner-safe pack subset renderer (shared with idea 3), partner agreement with an ADR provider. Effort: small (about 2 weeks) after idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Neither party can edit the pack. A builder could use ADR as a threat; the bundle is neutral by construction.
ideas.precedent: Dispute Resolution Ombudsman and CEDR home-improvement schemes: free to consumers, trader/member pays case fees (looked up). Checkatrade Guarantee's case-review process with independent expert assessment (looked up). RICS/CEDR fee-on-acceptance model.

ideas.name: Homeowner aftercare record with exclusive repeat-work and referral routing to the same builder
ideas.mechanism: After completion the homeowner keeps a free JobGuard home account: job records, guarantee expiry dates, certificates, 'what's behind the wall' photos and reminders. 'Book [Builder] again' and 'Recommend [Builder]' create a new enquiry that lands in that builder's Walk it and nobody else's; JobGuard never routes the homeowner elsewhere. The builder pays a flat monthly add-on; no per-lead fee on their own customers. Trigger: add-on billing. Measurement: none per lead.
ideas.who_pays: Builder (£8/£12/£20 per month by tier). Homeowner free.
ideas.assumptions: Per adopting builder: £8×12 = £96; £12×12 = £144; £20×12 = £240. One referral that becomes an £8k job is worth far more than the fee, which is the sales argument. Adoption guess 50-60%.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest while the exclusivity rule is absolute. It flips to a 1 if JobGuard ever markets other builders, insurers, energy or solar to these homeowners or 'opens up' the homeowner base; that is selling the builder's customers, the trust risk the founder named. Make exclusivity a contractual promise to builders, not a setting.
ideas.regulatory: UK GDPR controller role for homeowner accounts (D12 v2); PECR: reminders and referral prompts need homeowner consent (account opt-in); the builder remains controller of their own customer list.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 portal, a consumer identity path in the AuthProvider (M0-6) that is not tenant membership, Walk-it intake adapter (M1-2), D07 retention for homeowner records. Effort: medium (4-6 weeks). After G1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. The only abuse is JobGuard's own temptation to monetise the homeowner base.
ideas.precedent: Houzz Pro client portal bundled at £85-£275/month and Buildertrend Complete warranty module (looked up; raw notes construction_platforms_and_ai); property logbooks (Chimni, looked up). No UK trade app found sells exclusive own-customer referral routing.

ideas.name: Independent completion inspection booked through the portal (homeowner-paid, referral fee)
ideas.mechanism: At practical completion the builder can enable an 'independent completion check': the homeowner books a snagging inspector from a JobGuard-vetted panel; the inspector receives the proof-photo record and agreed scope so the check is against what was agreed, not a wish-list; the report goes to both parties and, if clean, the homeowner signs off the final stage in the portal, triggering the final invoice. JobGuard takes a referral fee from the inspector. Trigger: inspection booked and paid. Measurement: per booking.
ideas.who_pays: Homeowner pays the inspector (about £300-£400 for a domestic job); the inspector pays JobGuard a 15% referral fee.
ideas.assumptions: Uptake 5%/8%/10% (larger jobs only); inspection £350; JobGuard 15% = £52.50. Solo 19×0.05×£52.50 = £50; Small 24×0.08×£52.50 = £101; Firm 33×0.10×£52.50 = £173. Referral rate is an assumption.
ideas.trust_note: Feels adversarial (an inspector booked through the builder's own tool to find fault with the builder), so it must be builder-enabled per job and never offered by JobGuard to the homeowner unprompted. Builder-side value is real: an independent clean report closes the job, releases the final payment and pre-empts withheld-payment disputes, and giving the inspector the agreed scope protects the builder from scope creep in the snag list.
ideas.regulatory: Snagging inspectors are unregulated (RICS/RPSA membership as a panel criterion). JobGuard's referral fee must be disclosed to the homeowner (DMCC/CPUT hidden-commission concerns). D12 for sharing job data with the inspector.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 portal, M1-10 proof and stage gates, a panel/referral adapter. Effort: small (about 2 weeks) plus panel recruitment. After G1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Inspector independence must be protected; JobGuard must not favour inspectors who produce clean reports.
ideas.precedent: UK snagging-inspection market (new-build, roughly £300-£600; general knowledge, not looked up this session). Checkatrade Guarantee's independent third-party expert assessment step (looked up). No trade app found offers it.

ideas.name: Customer messaging bundle: SMS/WhatsApp delivery of portal messages, approvals and reminders (usage add-on)
ideas.mechanism: Portal messages, approval requests, stage sign-off requests, invoice and payment reminders are delivered to the homeowner by SMS or WhatsApp Business through an approved UK/EU-resident provider; replies flow back into the job thread and are therefore evidence under §14.2. The builder buys a monthly message allowance sized by tier; overage at cost plus margin. Trigger: monthly billing; overage metered per delivered message. Measurement: provider delivery receipts.
ideas.who_pays: Builder.
ideas.assumptions: Allowance £5/£10/£20 per month = £60/£120/£240 per adopting builder; adoption guess 50%/70%/80%; margin about 60% after provider costs.
ideas.trust_note: Transparent and standard in the category. Honest wrinkle: replies through JobGuard become shadow-bill evidence, so JobGuard has a fee interest in conversations happening in-thread. Disclose it in the D12 v2 onboarding wording and never nudge a builder to move a specific conversation into JobGuard.
ideas.regulatory: PECR (service messages about an existing contract are fine; marketing needs consent); WhatsApp Business platform terms; D04 residency for the messaging provider; AGENTS §5.3: invoice sends already require a Decision, and reminders must stay non-commercial infrastructure messages or go through the command boundary.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 portal thread, SV-7 evidence-observation contract, M0-9 outbox for delivery, provider adapter with D04 review. Effort: small (2-3 weeks).
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. Overage metering must be exact and visible.
ideas.precedent: Incumbents monetise SMS bundles and add-ons: Powered Now AI receptionist £29-£39/month, Jobber/Joist $29-$49 add-ons (raw notes uk_trade_job_software 'Inferences').

ideas.name: Homeowner-paid 'check my builder's final account' (the reverse watchdog): listed to reject
ideas.mechanism: For completeness: the homeowner pays JobGuard a small fee for an independent read of the builder's final account against the agreed quote, approved variations and proof, the FairRate direction (£0.99 per audit) but with JobGuard's own records. Trigger: homeowner purchase. Measurement: per check.
ideas.who_pays: Homeowner (£9.99).
ideas.trust_note: This poisons the watchdog. JobGuard would be paid by the homeowner to audit the builder using data the builder gave it for their own protection; every builder would read it as JobGuard working for the other side, and it collides head-on with the shadow bill (finding unbilled work for the builder while checking overcharges for the homeowner). The homeowner already gets a transparent account and approvals free through the portal; that is the right amount of homeowner-facing transparency. Recommendation: never.
ideas.regulatory: Consumer sale (CRA 2015, CCRs 2013) and a serious UK GDPR purpose-limitation problem: builder data collected for the builder's service repurposed against them (D12).
ideas.build_dependency: Trivial technically (M1-11 final account plus M4-3 pack), which is exactly why it needs an explicit 'no' in BUILD_PLAN §11 'Out of scope unless separately approved'.
ideas.gaming_risk: Not applicable; the risk is to the business, not from users.
ideas.precedent: FairRate £0.99 per trade-invoice audit for homeowners (research report §'No rival sells a final check'), the opposite direction to JobGuard.

ideas.name: Stage-payment escrow with release on proof, held by a regulated third party (borderline)
ideas.mechanism: For larger jobs the homeowner pays each stage into an FCA-authorised escrow or payment-institution account; release triggers when the homeowner confirms the stage in the portal against the proof photos, or after a fixed period without a specific evidenced objection; the provider pays the builder. JobGuard never holds funds and never initiates payments; it passes the stage-confirmation fact to the provider. JobGuard earns a platform/referral share of the escrow fee. Trigger: stage release. Measurement: released principal.
ideas.who_pays: Homeowner and/or builder share the escrow fee (about 1% of escrowed sums); JobGuard's share is a slice of that.
ideas.trust_note: Homeowners love escrow; most builders hate it (cash-flow delay, a third party deciding release, an implication the builder needs policing). Only defensible when the builder chooses it to win a nervous customer and release rules are mechanical and builder-favourable (auto-release after N days unless a specific evidenced objection). Tying release to JobGuard's own proof gates also turns JobGuard's proof rules into a payment gate over the builder, a very different power relationship from 'watchdog'.
ideas.regulatory: The escrow provider must be an authorised payment institution or EMI or hold client money under FCA rules; JobGuard's role must not amount to payment initiation or safeguarding (PSRs 2017/EMRs 2011), legal review required. AGENTS §3 'never hold builders' customer funds' is satisfied only if the provider holds them. CRA 2015/CCRs for the homeowner; D04 residency; new decision record for regulated introductions.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 portal stage sign-off, M1-10 proof gates, M4-18 interim applications, provider adapter with signed events on the M0-9 pattern. Effort: medium (4-6 weeks) plus provider contract. M5.
ideas.gaming_risk: A homeowner could withhold release vexatiously (needs auto-release rules); a builder could pressure early release (provider's rules apply). JobGuard must never earn more when release is delayed.
ideas.precedent: Checkatrade Pay (paying through the platform activates its guarantee; looked up). UK escrow/payment providers for building work (Transpact-style; not looked up this session). FMB deposit protection as the insurance alternative (looked up). No trade app found bundles proof-gated escrow.

result.live_job_definition: A live job is one JobGuard job record that (a) has exactly one paying customer and exactly one accepted quote frozen as its baseline (the M1-7 switch-live snapshot, which already stores accepted_net_value), (b) has been switched live by an explicit builder command, and (c) has not yet reached the earliest of: its final-account lock ('Complete final account'), an explicit close with a recorded reason (lost / abandoned / completed elsewhere), or an automatic dormancy pause. It occupies plan capacity from the switch-live command until that event, and occupies it again in any billing month in which it is resumed from pause. It never occupies capacity before switch-live (quoting, quote acceptance and the accepted-but-not-live state are free, AGENTS §5.10) and never after lock (the final check, confirming catches, later final-account revisions, invoices, payments, receipt allocation and retention release are post-lock activity and consume nothing). Capacity is measured in slots, not raw jobs, while the headline stays 'jobs live at once': a live job takes 1 slot if its frozen accepted net value (ex VAT) is £25,000 or less, 2 slots if it is over £25,000 up to £100,000, and 3 slots if it is over £100,000. Jobs under £1,000 are micro-jobs and take no slot for the first 10 held live at once. The value used is the greater of the accepted and the quoted net value (the D11 option), so a discounted acceptance cannot drop a band. Several accepted quotes for the same customer at the same site with contiguous or overlapping dates are phases of one job and are banded on their combined value, whatever they are called in the app. Slots and overage are metering of one tenant-level subscription (D09): billed as period lines, never attached to a job's commercial record, never a per-job base fee, cap or credit, and never offset against the success fee (§14.1).
counting_rules: Start/stop: a job counts from the switch-live command until the earliest of final-account lock, explicit close with a recorded reason, or dormancy pause. Nothing before switch-live counts; nothing after lock counts.

Slot weight: accepted net value (ex VAT) of £25,000 or less = 1 slot; over £25,000 up to £100,000 = 2 slots; over £100,000 = 3 slots. The band uses the greater of accepted and quoted net value frozen at switch-live. Three bands only, printed on the pricing page as one sentence: 'jobs over £25k take two places, over £100k three'.

Micro-jobs: accepted net value under £1,000 takes no slot, up to 10 live at once on every tier; the 11th and beyond take one slot each. The watchdog and final check still run on them in full, so detections and fee base are not lost.

Re-banding: if approved variations push a job's cumulative accepted-plus-approved net value over the next band threshold, the job moves up one band from the next billing month, once, and the builder is told on the variation-approval screen. A job never moves down. Draft, rejected or withdrawn extras never re-band, so the fee-free capture rule is untouched.

One job = one paying customer + one accepted quote + one final account. Several customers can never share a job (the final account and lock are per customer). Several accepted quotes for the same customer at the same site with contiguous or overlapping dates are phases of one job for counting and are banded on their combined value; different sites for the same customer are separate jobs.

Enforcement moment: capacity is checked only at switch-live. If the tier is full the builder chooses on that screen: upgrade tier, add this job on overage, or leave it accepted-but-not-live. No silent block, no retroactive charge, no billing-date snapshot.

Overage: £9 per extra slot per billing month on every tier, computed from the append-only metering events (switch-live, lock, close, pause, resume, re-band) as the peak concurrent slots above the tier in that month. It stops automatically when the peak falls back inside the tier.

Overage ceiling: a month's subscription plus overage can never exceed the next tier's price; if it would, that month is billed at the next tier's price and the builder is offered the upgrade. This ceiling is the D05 bounded amount the builder pre-authorises when accepting subscription terms.

Upgrade prompt: after two consecutive months in which overage equals or exceeds the step-up difference to the next tier, JobGuard prompts an upgrade. It never auto-upgrades without an approved decision (§5.3, D05).

Dormancy: 45 days without commercial activity (PO, supplier document, proof upload, variation, diary or customer message, invoice, payment) triggers a 'finish or pause?' prompt; at 60 days the job auto-pauses and stops counting. A paused job accepts no new commercial records; any such record resumes it and it counts for that month. Shadow signals, evidence receive times and the lock rules are unaffected by pause.

Post-lock: a locked job never re-counts. New site work after lock is a new, linked job. Documents attached to a locked job are stored, labelled 'received after lock' and are never fee-eligible (§14.6).

Imports: in-flight jobs imported at onboarding count from the 31st day after import (30-day onboarding grace); their baselines are labelled 'baseline as imported' in the evidence pack. The first job any tenant switches live is free for up to 90 days (the trial), with the success fee applying to it as normal so the builder experiences the real model.

Seasonality: monthly plans may step down any month with effect from the next period. Annual plans (two months free) fix the slot count for 12 months and use overage above it. An account with no live jobs can be held at £0 for up to 3 months a year with quoting still free; live jobs cannot be held on a £0 account.
Transparency: every bill lists each job that counted, its band, its slot-months and which rule applied. Metering events are append-only and audited in the same chain as commercial events (§5.7).

Separation: slots and overage are metering of one tenant-level subscription (D09), billed as period lines, never attached to a job's commercial record, never a per-job base fee, cap or credit, and never offset against or refunded because of the success fee (AGENTS §5.10, §14.1). D09 v3 must record the bands, thresholds, overage price and ceiling before any charge.

options.name: Option 1 — Flat live-job count (founder's candidate ladder £29 / £69 / £179 / £349 / custom)
options.structure: Every live job counts as 1 regardless of value. Tier limits were not stated in the candidate; assumed here as 3 / 8 / 20 / 40 live jobs. Unlimited users, quoting free, identical 10% success fee on every tier, annual at two months free. Over the limit: upgrade next month (per the research recommendation) rather than a hard block.
options.per_job_economics: Solo: £9.67 per slot-month, about £18 per job over ~19 jobs a year, 0.23% of turnover. Small firm: £8.63 per slot-month, £34.50 per job over ~24 jobs, 0.14%. Firm: £8.95 per slot-month, £65 per job over ~33 jobs, 0.11%. Per pound of turnover the £2m firm pays half what the sole trader pays, and a £600k firm running 15 kitchens pays exactly what a £2m firm running 15 extensions pays.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £29/month = £348/year (£290 on annual). Plus an illustrative success fee of about £90/year if 20% of jobs yield a qualifying catch worth 3% of job value — an assumption; no UK data exists (research report §'Frame the price against lost money').
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £69/month = £828/year (6 live jobs sits in the 8-job band). Illustrative fee about £360/year on the same assumption.
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £179/month = £2,148/year (15 live jobs sits in the 20-job band). Illustrative fee about £1,190/year. Total ~£3,300 from a £2m business; 15 Tradify Plus seats would cost £7,920.

options.pros: Simplest possible story; matches the ServiceM8 precedent of jobs-not-people (research §'Charge for live jobs, not people'); nothing to argue about at switch-live; the compromise effect works because the comparison is one number; no new data capture; a long job pays for its watch-time month by month, which is proportionate.
options.cons: A £5k bathroom and a £500k extension cost the same slot while cost-to-serve (documents, PO lines, photos, AI calls, final-check depth) and the risk watched scale with value. Leaves money on the table from big firms and over-charges sole traders with many tiny jobs. Invites phase-splitting the wrong way (over-counting phases the builder legitimately invoices separately) and site-bundling (one 'job' for a block of flats). No answer to seasonality other than manual tier changes, no answer to dormant jobs the builder forgets to lock, and no answer to a 15-job firm with big jobs versus a 15-job firm with small ones.

options.name: Option 2 — Weighted slots inside the job count (recommended core)
options.structure: Same headline 'jobs live at once' and the founder's prices, but each live job takes 1 / 2 / 3 slots by frozen accepted net value (≤£25k / £25k–£100k / >£100k), micro-jobs under £1,000 free up to 10, same-customer-same-site phases merged, once-only upward re-band on approved variations. Tier limits in slots: Solo 3 (£29), Builder 10 (£69), Firm 20 (£179), Contractor 40 (£349), custom above. Overage £9 per slot-month, capped at the next tier's price.
options.per_job_economics: Solo: unchanged at £9.67 per slot-month and £18 per job (all jobs ≤£25k). Small firm (assumed 3 jobs ≤£25k + 3 jobs £25k–£100k = 9 slots): £7.67 per slot used, £34.50 per job, 0.14% of turnover. Firm (assumed 4 ≤£25k, 9 at £25k–£100k, 2 >£100k = 28 slots): £8.96 per slot-month, £91 per job, 0.15% of turnover. A £500k extension takes 3 slots (£27/month) against £9 for a £5k bathroom: still under-priced relative to value, never over-priced.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £29/month = £348/year. Unchanged from Option 1. Illustrative fee ~£90.
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £69/month = £828/year (9 slots fits the 10-slot Builder plan). Unchanged from Option 1. Illustrative fee ~£360.
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £179 + 8 overage slots × £9 = £251/month = £3,012/year on Firm; £349/month = £4,188/year if the firm prefers a flat Contractor bill. That is 40–95% more than the flat count, at 0.15–0.21% of turnover, still about half the cost of 15 per-user seats. Illustrative fee ~£1,190. Total ~£4,200–£5,400.

options.pros: Keeps jobs as the headline and the founder's four price points. Uses a value that is already frozen and immutable at switch-live (M1-7), so no new capture and no arguing. Scales with cost-to-serve and with the risk JobGuard watches. Distinguishes a £2m firm with 15 big jobs from a £600k firm with 15 small ones, which no flat count can. Generous micro-job allowance keeps small work on the system, protecting detections and fee base (research warns builders will otherwise keep small jobs off). Overage instead of blocking handles seasonal peaks.
options.cons: Needs one extra sentence on the pricing page and a 'why 2 places?' explanation at switch-live. Band thresholds invite under-declared acceptance values; the greater-of-accepted-and-quoted rule and the D11 variance signal mitigate but do not eliminate this. The £25k/£100k lines are guesses until pilot data show the real job-size distribution per archetype. The slot mixes behind the archetype revenue are assumptions, not measurements.

options.name: Option 3 — Job count with a duration floor and a throughput fair-use ceiling
options.structure: Flat count as Option 1, plus: every job counts for a minimum of one full billing month even if it starts and locks inside a month, and each tier carries an annual 'jobs started' fair-use ceiling (e.g. Solo 40, Builder 120, Firm 300) that triggers an upgrade conversation, not a block. Aimed at the reverse of the long-job problem: a concurrency meter charges a 12-month extension 12 slot-months but charges 26 back-to-back two-week jobs the same one slot.
options.per_job_economics: For the three archetypes (jobs lasting 2–14 months) identical to Option 1: £18 / £34.50 / £65 per job. For a high-throughput user (3 concurrent two-week jobs, ~78 a year) the floor turns 3 slots into ~6.5 job-months a month, moving them from Solo £29 to Builder £69: £10.60 per job instead of £4.46.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £348/year (unchanged; jobs last longer than a month).
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £828/year (unchanged).
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £2,148/year on a flat count; £3,012 if combined with Option 2's weighting. The duration floor changes nothing for firms doing extensions and refurbishments.

options.pros: Fair on cost-to-serve, which is per job (AI proposal, evidence pipeline, final check), not per month. Closes the high-throughput loophole without touching the headline. Cheap to implement from the metering events.
options.cons: Does nothing for size disparity, which is the bigger leak. High-throughput reactive work (call-outs, maintenance) is ServiceM8's market, not JobGuard's; a floor adds rules for a customer JobGuard should not chase. Two counters ('live at once' and 'started this year') dilute the one-number comparison the compromise effect needs.

options.name: Option 4 — Job count plus tier-gated workflow depth (gate workflow, never detections)
options.structure: Flat or weighted count with a feature ladder on top. Every tier keeps every detection (supplier price checks, three-way matching, readiness warnings, proof gates, shadow bill, final check) so the fee base and the trust story are intact. Tiers gate what larger firms need to run the workflow: Builder adds multi-user approvals and accounting sync; Firm adds multi-approver PO/variation sign-off, Construction Act payment and pay-less notices for B2B customers, retention tracking, an office dashboard, evidence-pack export on demand and priority support; Contractor adds multi-entity and custom terms.
options.per_job_economics: If the workflow features pull each archetype up one tier: Solo £43 per job (Builder), Small firm £90 per job (Firm), Firm £127 per job (Contractor). If they do not, identical to the underlying count option.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £348–£828/year depending on whether accounting sync and multi-user approvals pull them to Builder. Assumption: most stay at £29.
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £828–£2,148/year. A 5-staff firm with an office person and B2B customers plausibly wants multi-approver and Construction Act notices; assumption: half move to Firm.
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £2,148–£4,188/year on a flat count; £3,012–£4,188 with weighting. A 15-staff firm working for main contractors almost certainly needs notices, retention tracking and evidence packs, so Contractor £349 is realistic.

options.pros: Captures prevention value through features that only matter when the value is large (a retention or a pay-less notice is worth nothing to a bathroom fitter and thousands to a subcontractor). Every tier remains a real plan somebody would buy (the research's condition for good-better-best). Does not reduce detections or the fee base on lower tiers.
options.cons: A feature grid weakens the one-number comparison and the compromise effect (research: 'the comparison should rest on one or two numbers'). Gating the wrong thing is a trust risk: if any detection is ever gated, lower tiers will feel the watchdog is 'switched off' and the fee looks like the reason. Construction Act and retention features are M4+ work that does not exist yet; this option can only lift revenue when they ship.

options.name: Option 5 — Floating monthly tier with capped overage (seasonality-first)
options.structure: The builder picks a tier as a ceiling; each month's charge is the tier price plus £9 per slot above it at the month's peak concurrency, never more than the next tier's price. Step down any month. Annual plans fix slots and use overage above them. This is Option 2's overage rule promoted to the headline: 'pay for your busiest week, drop back when it's quiet'.
options.per_job_economics: Same per-slot cost as Option 2; the difference is that summer peaks are paid for and winter troughs are not. Solo peaking at 4–5 jobs for three summer months pays about £9–£18 extra in those months; a firm peaking at 34 slots for four months pays £54 extra in those months.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: About £32 average = ~£390/year (assumes a 3-month summer peak of 1–2 extra slots).
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: About £78 average = ~£936/year (assumes a 4-month peak to 12 slots).
revenue_by_archetype.firm: About £269 average = ~£3,228/year with weighting (28 slots baseline, 34 at peak for four months).

options.pros: No winter over-payment and therefore fewer winter cancellations, which the research flags as a real risk for sole traders wary of lock-in. No block at switch-live. Captures peak-season value that a fixed tier gives away. Bounded, so D05 can authorise it.
options.cons: Variable bills; people prefer flat charges to a running meter (Prelec & Loewenstein; Lambrecht & Skiera, cited in the research). Requires D05 bounded standing authority for a variable amount and the ceiling rule to make that honest. Harder to explain than a fixed tier; should be the fine print under Option 2, not the headline.

options.name: Option 6 — Weighted slots plus observable-value add-ons (the 'extract more' bundle)
options.structure: Option 2 as the base, plus revenue lines that charge for something observable rather than for an unprovable counterfactual: (a) a platform margin of about 0.3% on customer payments taken through the M4 hosted Stripe/GoCardless surfaces (JobGuard never holds funds; the processor's own rate is passed through; needs its own decision record and M4-11/12); (b) evidence-pack assembly for disputes at £49 per pack on Solo/Builder, included on Firm+, with raw data export always free; (c) onboarding/import service at £199–£499 one-off for Firm/Contractor migrations from other tools; (d) an accountant/bookkeeper practice plan later (Dext-style per-client pricing); (e) a monthly 'flagged before you paid' statement used as the upgrade and retention lever, labelled 'flagged for your decision', never 'saved' (§14.1 forbids 'JobGuard saved you £X' before settled cash). Listed but flagged: (f) a D03 v3 candidate charging a small flat amount per documented pre-payment supplier correction over £100 — the supplier's corrected invoice makes the counterfactual stronger than generic prevention, but it charges on prevented spend, which the founder said currently earns nothing, and builders may simply stop recording corrections; recommend measuring in the pilot only. Rejected on trust grounds and named plainly: merchant or supplier commissions and preferred-supplier placement (would compromise the invoice watchdog), selling builders' data or their customers as leads (D12 and word-of-mouth risk), and a homeowner-side bill-checking product (JobGuard would be paid by both sides of the same invoice). Insurance or invoice-finance referrals are a milder conflict: disclose fully or leave them out.
options.per_job_economics: Base as Option 2. Add-ons per job are small: the payments margin is worth about £3 per Solo job and £18 per Firm job on the assumed share of payments taken through JobGuard; a dispute pack is a rare £49; import is a one-off.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £348 subscription + ~£180 payments margin (assumes 40% of £150k taken by card/DD through JobGuard at 0.3%) + ~£49 (one dispute pack a year) = ~£577/year. Illustrative fee ~£90.
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £828 + ~£450 (25% of £600k through JobGuard at 0.3%) + ~£98 (two packs) = ~£1,376/year. Illustrative fee ~£360.
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £3,012 + ~£600 (10% of £2m through JobGuard; large sums go by bank transfer) + £299 import in year one = ~£3,900/year. Illustrative fee ~£1,190 plus any withheld-payment cases. Total ~£5,100 from a £2m firm.

options.pros: Monetises prevention through deliverables the builder can see (a payment collected, a pack assembled, a migration done) instead of a counterfactual nobody can prove. The payments margin grows with the faster-invoicing benefit JobGuard actually delivers and is a standard category revenue line (Fergus 1.6% + 20p, Tradify Stripe pass-through per the competitor research). Nothing here touches the fee rules or the shadow bill.
options.cons: Each line needs its own decision record, and the payments margin needs M4 rails that do not exist yet. The amounts are modest: even all together they add roughly 30–65% to the subscription, not multiples. Charging for evidence packs risks 'paying for my own data' unless raw export stays free and the charge is clearly for assembly and attestation. Item (f) reopens the prevented-spend question and should not ship without D03 v3, pilot measurement of whether builders keep recording corrections, and a fairness check against the 'we only earn when you're paid' message.

gaming.vector: Under-declaring the accepted value (a discounted or partial acceptance, or a quote deliberately kept under £25k / £100k / £1,000) to stay in a lower band or inside the micro-job allowance.
gaming.mitigation: Band on the greater of accepted and quoted net value frozen at switch-live (the D11 option; both values are already stored). Re-band once upward when approved variations cross the next threshold. Accepted-versus-final variance stays a D11 advisory signal, never an automatic charge. Residual: a builder who under-quotes and under-invoices the customer to save £9 a month loses far more than they save, so the incentive is weak.

gaming.vector: Splitting one project into several 'jobs' (phases, rooms, trades) so each stays under a band threshold.
gaming.mitigation: Same customer + same site + contiguous or overlapping dates = one job for counting, banded on the combined value; applied at switch-live of the second job with an on-screen explanation. Phases are a sub-structure of one job (separate invoices allowed), so splitting gains nothing. Residual: different sites for the same customer are legitimately separate jobs.

gaming.vector: Bundling many customers into one 'job' (a block of flats, an estate, a landlord's tenants, a maintenance contract) to pay for one slot.
gaming.mitigation: Structural, not a rule: a job has one customer, one accepted quote and one final account, and the lock and final invoice are per customer, so ten leaseholders cannot be invoiced or locked on one account. Multi-site single-customer jobs are legitimately one job and are banded on their total value.

gaming.vector: Pausing jobs to free slots while still working them.
gaming.mitigation: A paused job accepts no PO, supplier document, proof upload, variation, message or invoice; any such record auto-resumes it and it counts for that month. Pause/resume events are audited; 'more than three resumes in a quarter' is a D11 advisory signal for review, never an automatic penalty.

gaming.vector: Locking early (at half completion) to free the slot, then finishing the work on a locked job.
gaming.mitigation: Post-lock evidence never qualifies (§14.6), so the builder forfeits the final check on the rest of the work: it is the fee, not the slot, that leaks. New site work must be a new linked job; 'material evidence after lock' and 'lock with low proof of completion' are D11 advisory signals; final invoice issue still requires the lock, and only one attribution lock exists per job.

gaming.vector: Timing games: locking or pausing on the last day of the month so a billing-date snapshot shows fewer jobs.
gaming.mitigation: There is no snapshot. Capacity is enforced at switch-live and overage is derived from peak concurrent slots across the month, computed from append-only metering events. Nothing done on the last day changes the peak.

gaming.vector: Splitting one business across several tenants (three Solo accounts instead of one Firm plan).
gaming.mitigation: One company registration number, VAT number or UTR per tenant, checked at sign-up; duplicates are a D11 signal for human review, not an automatic action. The natural cost does most of the work: no shared customers, suppliers, rate book, evidence or reporting across tenants, and the shadow bill and final check cannot see across the split.

gaming.vector: Using JobGuard as a free voice-quoting tool and never switching a job live.
gaming.mitigation: They get no watchdog, no final account and no final check, and 'won but never switched live' is already a D11 signal. A fair-use ceiling on AI proposal generation for accounts with no paid plan is capacity control, not billing, so §5.10 (free quoting never bills) stays intact. Quotes themselves remain free forever.

gaming.vector: Closing a job without a lock and billing the customer outside JobGuard to avoid both the slot and any catch fee.
gaming.mitigation: The close-with-reason action must exist because builders cannot be forced to lock; the job stops counting. 'Invoice or payment activity with no lock' remains a D11 signal, and the JobGuard final invoice requires the lock. The real incentive to lock is the final check itself. Accept the residual plainly (§14.10): no metering rule fixes this.

gaming.vector: Growing a small live job through Log an extra so a £20k job becomes £60k while staying in band 1.
gaming.mitigation: The once-only upward re-band on approved variations, disclosed on the approval screen. Draft, rejected and withdrawn extras never re-band, so nothing about the fee-free capture rule changes and there is no incentive to stop logging extras.

gaming.vector: Running large work as many sub-£1,000 'jobs' to live inside the micro-job allowance.
gaming.mitigation: The same-customer-same-site merge rule applies; more than 10 micro-jobs live at once take full slots; a micro-job whose approved variations push it over £1,000 re-bands to a full slot. Genuine handyman-style work stays cheap, which is the intent.

gaming.vector: Importing in-flight or finished jobs in bulk and locking them immediately to run final checks on paper-era work.
gaming.mitigation: Harmless to the meter (imports count from day 31) and harmless to the builder (the fee is theirs to trigger by confirming a catch and getting paid). Imported baselines are labelled 'baseline as imported' in the evidence pack so the lock is honest about what the check could compare.

gaming.vector: Sitting on overage indefinitely instead of upgrading, or a tier so cheap per slot that overage is punitive.
gaming.mitigation: Overage at £9 sits at roughly the average slot cost of every tier (£9.67 / £6.90 / £8.95 / £8.73), so staying on overage is fair to both sides. The ceiling (never more than the next tier's price) and the two-consecutive-month prompt cover the rest. No auto-upgrade without an approved decision (D05).

result.size_disparity_fix: Keep 'jobs live at once' as the headline and put the size inside the job: a live job takes 1, 2 or 3 places according to the accepted net value already frozen at switch-live (£25,000 or less / over £25,000 to £100,000 / over £100,000), stated on the pricing page in one sentence: 'jobs over £25k take two places, over £100k three'. Why three bands and these lines: three is explainable on a site; £25k separates bathrooms, kitchens and small refurbishments from extensions; £100k separates extensions from whole-house, new-build plot and small commercial work; and the value is immutable and already stored by M1-7, so nothing new is captured and nothing is argued at switch-live. Why it is fair: cost-to-serve (supplier lines, POs, photos, AI calls, final-check depth) and the money JobGuard watches both scale with job value more than with job count, yet a £500k extension still pays only three times a £5k bathroom, so weighting under-charges big jobs relative to value and never over-charges them. Guards: band on the greater of accepted and quoted value; re-band once upward when approved variations cross a threshold; merge same-customer-same-site phases; micro-jobs under £1,000 free up to 10 so small work stays on the system and detections are not lost. Effect on the archetypes: Solo unchanged (3 slots, £29); small firm 9 slots (£69, unchanged); the £2m firm 28 slots, so £251 a month with capped overage or £349 on a flat Contractor plan instead of £179. The firm with 15 × £60k jobs now pays more than a firm with 15 × £10k kitchens, which a flat count could never do. Sole traders with many tiny jobs get the opposite relief through the micro-job allowance. The £25k and £100k lines are working assumptions: measure the accepted-value distribution per archetype in the pilot before D09 v3 fixes them. Fallback if the founder wants no weighting at all: keep 1 job = 1 slot, tighten the limits to 3 / 8 / 15 / 30, and gate Construction Act notices, retention tracking, multi-approver POs and evidence-pack export at Firm and above; that reaches £179–£349 for the £2m firm by features rather than by size, at the cost of a longer feature grid and a weaker one-number comparison.
result.recommendation:
