ideas.mechanism: A main contractor, regional housebuilder, housing association or property manager buys a Project licence (~£25 per active subcontractor per month or £150 per project per month) and onboards its subcontractor panel for that project; subs capture variations, upload proof, submit interim applications (M4-18), handle notices (M4-19), retention (M4-20) and CIS (M4-22); the paying client gets evidenced applications, fewer disputes and a live proof record, never shadow data or anything the sub has not submitted. Subs keep their own tenant and the normal success-fee terms (10% only on a withheld-payment case the sub opens against that client, or a missed variation after the sub's own lock) and convert to their own subscription for non-project work. Licensed projects should not count toward the sub's own live-job tier.
ideas.who_pays: The main contractor/client; the sub pays nothing for licensed projects

revenue_per_year.firm: £360 plus success fees on cases the firm opens

ideas.assumptions: Per-sub pricing and share of each archetype working under MCs are assumptions; Payapps prices MCs by projects and claims with an unpublished fixed annual fee. Long subcontract jobs are where the live-jobs meter is weakest (one 12-month project occupies a slot all year), hence exclusion from the sub's own tier.
ideas.trust_note: The sub must be told plainly who is paying; if the MC pays JobGuard while the final check finds variations the sub never billed the MC, the MC resents it and the sub wonders whose side JobGuard is on — both contracts must say JobGuard works for the sub on variations and applications, the MC buys clean evidence; keep the MC out of the sub's tenant.
ideas.regulatory: HGCRA 1996 payment/notice provisions (M4-19); CIS (M4-22); D12 (MC as separate controller; sole-trader subs as data subjects); D10.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-18, M4-19, M4-20, M4-22 plus a multi-party job model where the customer is another tenant with scoped read-only visibility of submitted artifacts. Post-M4, 6–10 weeks; no enterprise hierarchy early (AGENTS §1).
ideas.gaming_risk: An MC using JobGuard's timestamps against a sub — it cuts both ways as the Act intends; premature case-opening for templates — §14.7 entry test.
ideas.precedent: Payapps MC pricing with free first application per month for subs; Buildbite free for clients and subs; CHAS/Constructionline show subs already pay £219–£909/yr to be onboardable.
ideas.merged_from: Main contractor pays per project; subcontractors free (b2b2b lens)

ideas.name: Network licence: white-label / OEM watchdog module for a lead-gen platform or trade-body app, and franchise-network agreements with an aggregate dashboard
ideas.mechanism: Variant A (OEM): Checkatrade, MyBuilder, Rated People or a trade body's app embeds JobGuard's supplier-overcharge check, proof gates, final-account assembly and post-lock final check as a co-branded module behind their login (SSO via the M0-6 principal contract, tenant provisioning API); the platform pays wholesale ~£4 per live job per month (metered server-side from switch-live/lock events, never partner counts) and sets its own retail price. Variant B (franchise): home-improvement franchisors (e.g. Dream Doors, ~100 showrooms) mandate or recommend JobGuard, pay a ~£2,000/yr network fee, franchisees are billed at wholesale (~£39/month Builder, £99 Firm), and the franchisor gets an aggregate-only dashboard (variation rate, proof-gate compliance, dispute rate, cycle time) from consented fields. In both, the 10% success fee stays a direct JobGuard–builder relationship, never shared, and all D13 rules bind the partner contractually and structurally.
ideas.who_pays: The platform or franchisor wholesale; builders pay the partner or get it inside membership
ideas.assumptions: £4 wholesale ≈ a third of direct list; network fees and rates are assumptions; no franchisor mandatory-software terms found. Franchisees run few concurrent installs, so the jobs meter suits them; platforms and builders can keep small jobs off the module — generous allowances, suggest-never-block.
ideas.trust_note: Trust rides on the partner's brand — Checkatrade's standing is mixed (12-month contracts, £80–£500/month bills) — and a builder who feels the platform 'took a cut of the find' blames both; franchisees resent head office seeing operational data. Keep the success fee direct, the one-sentence final-check explanation unedited on partner screens, the dashboard aggregate-only with published fields, and shadow findings and fee statements strictly between JobGuard and the builder.
ideas.regulatory: D12 controller/processor shifts (platform or franchisor as account/aggregate controller; genuine consent in franchise agreements); D04 partner infrastructure; D13 onboarding disclosure in the partner flow before the first job; competition: no exclusivity blocking the direct channel; no enterprise isolation before its task (AGENTS §1).
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1..M2-7 watchdog, multi-brand theming, partner SSO/provisioning, per-partner wholesale metering (M4-14), partner invoicing via M4-10; franchise variant needs the deferred organisation-hierarchy task with read-only aggregate views. 6–8 weeks after M2 plus the deal; franchise 4–6 weeks once hierarchy exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Under-reporting live jobs — server-side metering; partner pressure for early hints of findings to drive retention — refuse, the builder role cannot read shadow tables; franchisees keeping jobs off JobGuard — a franchisor compliance matter and an advisory D11 signal.
ideas.precedent: Checkatrade partner offers and free TradeMore app; Simply Business white-label partnerships; ServiceM8 jobs-based tiers; Dream Doors/Neighbourly; no UK franchisor mandating a job tool with a network dashboard found.
ideas.merged_from: White-label / OEM 'watchdog module' (b2b2b); Franchise / network licence (b2b2b)

ideas.name: Subcontractor-invite growth channel: free scoped 'sub' access on invited jobs, converting to paid tenants, with a subscription credit for the inviter
ideas.mechanism: A builder invites the subs on a job into a scoped role: they upload proof photos to the builder's stage gates and attach their invoices (which become evidence and feed three-way matching), seeing only their own items. The sub gets a free 'Sub' tenant limited to invited jobs (no own quoting or final account) and subscribes when they start their own jobs. The inviter earns one month's subscription credit per converted sub (a D09 subscription credit, never offsetting a success fee), paid only after the sub has had a live job for 30 days and paid one period, capped per year, with the same unique conversion identity rules as fee derivations.
ideas.who_pays: Converted subs pay their own subscription; JobGuard funds the credit from it
ideas.assumptions: 2/6/15 invites a year, 15% twelve-month conversion, converts Solo-sized; downstream revenue is really new-tenant revenue attributed here.
ideas.trust_note: Builders already coordinate subs on WhatsApp; a scoped invite is a convenience and the credit a plain thank-you. Make clear to subs what the inviter can and cannot see, and that their own future jobs are their own tenant with the same fee-free capture rules.
ideas.regulatory: D12 (sole-trader subs as data subjects, Art 13/14 at invite); D08 once M3 exists; D09 credit terms.
ideas.build_dependency: M0-6 per-job scoped external role, M1-10 proof capture by an external principal, M2-2 intake of sub invoices, conversion attribution. 3–5 weeks after M2-2; scoped job membership, not enterprise hierarchy.
ideas.gaming_risk: Fake sub accounts to farm credits — 30-day live-job and paid-period conditions, caps.
ideas.precedent: Buildbite free for subs, paid by the contractor; Xero £50 / 30% referral; Dext free month for partner referrals.
ideas.merged_from: Subcontractor-invite growth channel (b2b2b lens)

ideas.name: Merchant pays JobGuard: e-invoicing connector fees or a slice of pooled purchasing rebates (flagged — poisons the watchdog)
ideas.mechanism: Variant A: merchants pay a flat connector fee (~£500/month per merchant per 1,000 connected builders) to deliver invoices, delivery notes and credit notes by API through the SV-7 evidence-observation contract instead of email and PDF, cutting their query volume; flat, never per invoice, never contingent on match outcomes, with merchant-blind detection proven by architecture tests and the relationship disclosed on every discrepancy screen. Variant B (NMBS translation): JobGuard aggregates builders' materials spend from the POs and invoices it already ingests, negotiates rebates with participating merchants, passes most to builders and keeps ~1 point of a 3–4 point rebate.
ideas.who_pays: Merchants/suppliers pay JobGuard; builders receive a partial rebate under B
ideas.assumptions: A only meaningful at scale; B assumes materials 40% of turnover, half at participating merchants, 1% retained — NMBS earns its 3.84% partly by guaranteeing supplier payment, which JobGuard cannot do (never holds funds), so its position would be weaker.
ideas.trust_note: The idea the brief warned about, and it does compromise the watchdog: once merchants pay JobGuard, every overcharge flag against a paying merchant is suspect and every non-flag looks bought; even a flat fee creates the perception JobGuard is 'in with the merchants', fatal for a product whose flagship prevention feature is checking merchants' invoices. The UK energy-broker experience (hidden supplier-paid commissions → Ofgem disclosure rules, Expert Tooling v Engie fiduciary finding) shows where supplier-paid intermediaries end up. Listed so it can be explicitly rejected; the safe cousin is builder-side only — checking the builder's own trade discounts and rebates were applied correctly on each invoice, which belongs in I12.
ideas.regulatory: D04/D12 for the connector; disclosure duties and fiduciary-style exposure (half-secret commissions); D11 conflict-of-interest; contradicts the supplier-watchdog spirit in the build plan.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-2 intake plus SV-7 connector pattern; merchant agreements and a rebate ledger. Effort is not the constraint; trust is.
ideas.gaming_risk: Merchant pressure to soften checks; merchants steering pricing to JobGuard builders while raising list prices elsewhere; JobGuard's own temptation on paying merchants — not mitigable by policy alone.
ideas.precedent: Coupa/Tradex supplier-network fees; NMBS 3.84% average rebate across 1,000+ merchants; UK SME energy brokers' 0.3–2p/kWh supplier-paid commission and its backlash.
ideas.merged_from: Merchant-paid e-invoicing connector (prevention); Pooled purchasing rebates from merchants (analogues)

ideas.name: Merchant rebate passed 100% to the builder with a disclosed JobGuard admin fee (watchdog conflict, structured)
ideas.mechanism: JobGuard negotiates a 'JobGuard Trade' arrangement on an open panel (any merchant joins on the same published terms) for a point-of-sale discount or quarterly volume rebate. Hard structure: every penny of merchant discount/rebate goes to the builder, paid by the merchant straight to the builder's own bank (JobGuard never holds it); JobGuard takes no money from any merchant (no marketing fees, per-order payments or data sales); JobGuard charges the builder a disclosed admin fee (10% of rebate received, or flat £5/month) on the platform statement; the watchdog stays merchant-blind, checking against the builder's own agreed rates (M2-1) whoever the merchant is; JobGuard publishes per-merchant overcharge and delivery-discrepancy rates so partner merchants are visibly held to the same test.
ideas.who_pays: Merchant pays the rebate to the builder; the builder pays JobGuard a disclosed admin fee; merchants pay JobGuard nothing
ideas.assumptions: Materials 40% of turnover, 30% via partner merchants, 3% builder-side rebate, 10% admin fee — all assumptions; published precedents are POS discounts (FMB 10% at TradePoint, Checkatrade 10% Wickes TradePro), under which the fee would have to be flat (~£60/yr).
ideas.trust_note: Flagged plainly: any merchant relationship will be read by some builders as 'JobGuard is in bed with Travis', damaging the supplier-invoice watchdog even with clean money flows. Pass-through, disclosed fee, open panel, merchant-blind checks and published scorecards are the minimum to make it defensible; weigh whether £54–£720 per builder is worth the perception risk. Never do the simpler version where the merchant pays JobGuard (I65).
ideas.regulatory: Bribery Act 2010 concerns disappear with full disclosure and pass-through; VAT on the admin fee; routing rebate cash would be holding builders' money (AGENTS §3) — merchant-to-builder direct only; competition law (no exclusivity or resale-price terms); new commercial decision record and a D11 integrity review.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 agreed rates, M2-2 intake, M2-4 matching; partner registry, rebate statement import reconciled to the builder's own POs, admin-fee line on M4-10, merchant scorecard report. 3–4 weeks after M2-4 plus negotiation.
ideas.gaming_risk: Merchants trying to influence flags — structurally impossible with builder-rate checks, but commercial pressure will come; write merchant-blindness into the contract. Builders routing non-JobGuard purchases through the panel — harmless.
ideas.precedent: FMB 10% TradePoint; Checkatrade Wickes TradePro; NMBS 3.84% merchant-side rebate; Fortis buying group; no UK job app runs a builder-side rebate pass-through.
ideas.merged_from: Merchant rebate passed 100% to the builder with disclosed admin fee (b2b2b lens)

result.live_job_definition:
A live job is a JobGuard job in the `live` state of the §3.1 job spine (draft → quoting → accepted → live → invoiced → paid). It occupies one place of plan capacity from the server-committed `switch_live` command that freezes `baseline_quote_version_id` and `accepted_net_value_pence` (M1-7) until the earliest of: (a) the server-committed `final_account_lock` (§14.4); (b) an explicit `CloseJob` command with a recorded reason (lost, abandoned, completed elsewhere, cancelled after activation: an audited closure with financial adjustment, never deletion or baseline mutation, §3.1); or (c) automatic dormancy pause after 60 consecutive days with no metered activity (prompt at 45). An explicit `PauseJob` suspends counting from the next calendar day; any metered activity on a paused, dormant or closed job resumes it (audited) and it counts from that day.

Nothing counts before switch-live: draft, quoting, accepted-but-not-live and lost are free (AGENTS §5.10; won-but-not-live is only a D11 advisory signal). Nothing counts after lock (decided for Design B over Design A): the final check, confirming catches, later final-account revisions, invoice issue, receipts, allocation, snagging after lock and retention release are post-lock work and consume nothing; new site work after lock is a new, linked job; documents attached after lock are stored, labelled 'received after lock' and are never fee-eligible (§14.6). Snagging before lock counts, because the builder is still on site capturing proof. A retention balance outstanding after lock is a payment-side fact and never re-enters the meter.

It is a capacity unit, not a value unit: one job = one tenant + one accepting customer party + one site address + one accepted quote baseline. Two customer parties can never share a job because acceptance, the final account, the lock and the final invoice bind one party (a management company or landlord accepting one quote for many units is legitimately one customer). Several phases under one accepted quote are one job; separate accepted quotes are separate jobs; different sites for the same customer are separate jobs. Every live job takes exactly one place, with two rules decided here: (1) small-job allowance: accepted net value under £2,000 ex VAT at switch-live (builder-attested value for imports; the greater of accepted and quoted where both exist) takes no place, fair use 10 at once, and takes a place only from the day approved variations lift its net value above £4,000, once and never back; (2) a reserved, switched-off big-job weighting (over £50,000 accepted net = 2 places, over £150,000 = 3), pre-specified in D09 v3 but dormant until a D09 v3.1 backed by pilot data (§14.17) turns it on. Imported in-flight jobs (M1-17, `lifecyclePoint: live`) count from the 31st day after the import commit; imports at `lifecyclePoint: invoiced` never count. The first job a business switches live is the trial and is excluded until it locks or for 90 days, whichever is first; `pilot_no_charge` jobs are excluded by the explicit D09 inclusion rule (M4-14), never by default.

Every boundary is a server commit timestamp on an immutable metering event (switch-live, lock, close, pause, resume, dormancy, import, allowance trip), appended to the same per-tenant audit chain as commercial events (AGENTS §5.7), so the meter is replayable from the chain and a cached counter can never trigger a charge (M4-14; AGENTS §5.4). Client or offline capture times never move a boundary (AGENTS §5.12). Places and overage are metering of one tenant-level subscription (D09): billed as period lines, never attached to a job's commercial record, never a per-job base fee, cap or credit, and never offset against or refunded because of the success fee (§14.1; AGENTS §5.10).
counting_rules: Unit is job-days (Design A's rule, chosen over Design B's monthly peak). For each calendar day D (Europe/London) in the billing period, places(D) = the number of the tenant's jobs occupying a place at any instant of D: live, not locked, not closed, not paused, not dormant, not trial- or pilot-exempt, not inside the small-job allowance, not inside the 30-day import grace. Boundaries use server commit timestamps only. Why job-days: a one-day overlap between an ending and a starting job costs pence, so there is no grace period, no last-day-of-the-month game and nothing to argue about; a peak rule would bill a whole month's overage for one day of overlap.

Tier fit is checked once, at switch-live, on the instantaneous place count; overage money uses job-days. Both derive from the same immutable event log and must reconcile in the M4-14 replay fixtures (simultaneous activations, late events, time-zone boundaries, reopen).
Each tier includes S places: Solo 3, Builder 6, Firm 12, Contractor 24 (custom above 40). over(D) = max(0, places(D) − S). Overage job-days for the period = Σ over(D).

Overage charge = roundHalfEven(overage_job_days × 2,000 ÷ days_in_period) pence, computed once per period as an exact rational with a single rounding (AGENTS §5.5): £20 per extra job per month, about 66p per job-day in a 30-day month. Decided for A's £20 over B's £9: the ceiling rule below only works if the next plan is never dearer than continuing on overage, which £9 cannot deliver without 12+ extra places per tier; £20 against £9.67–£14.92 per included place is an ordinary bolt-on premium, and it is what makes the upgrade tap the cheaper choice.

Auto-overage ceiling per tier, in extra jobs: Solo 2, Builder 5, Firm 8, Contractor 16. The monetary bound per period is plan + ceiling × £20 = £69 / £169 / £339 / £669, chosen so it never exceeds the next plan's price (Solo+2 = £69 = Builder; Builder+5 = £169 < £179; Firm+8 = £339 < £349). That bound is the D05 bounded standing authority the builder accepts with the subscription terms (M4-13). Up to it, extra jobs run automatically with a plain line at switch-live: 'This job takes an extra place: £20 a month, about 66p a day.'

At the ceiling, the next switch-live presents a one-tap upgrade Decision showing the exact new price and the pro-rata amount for the rest of the period (AGENTS §5.3: the button creates and approves the Decision; M4-14: the over-limit event raises the required Decision), or the builder leaves the job accepted-but-not-live. Already-live jobs are never blocked, throttled or hidden; a worker cannot upgrade a tenant. In addition (from B), after two consecutive periods in which overage equals or exceeds the step-up to the next plan, JobGuard prompts an upgrade; it never auto-upgrades.
Downgrades take effect at the next period boundary and only if the current place count is within the new plan's places + ceiling. No mid-period tier change except a builder-approved upgrade.

Post-lock never re-counts (B over A). Confirming catches, new final-account revisions, invoice issue, receipts, allocation and retention release are the normal post-lock flow and must never put the job back on the meter; charging a builder for the day JobGuard reveals its own catches would be a trust failure. Early-lock gaming is handled structurally instead (see gaming).

Pause: explicit `PauseJob` stops counting from the next calendar day; any metered activity resumes the job and it counts from that day. More than three resumes in a quarter is a D11 advisory signal, never a penalty. D13 must-surface and safety findings still fire on a paused job; shadow signals, evidence receive times and lock rules are unaffected by pause.

Dormancy: 45 consecutive days without metered activity raises a 'finish, pause or close this job?' prompt; at 60 days the job auto-pauses and stops counting from day 61 (job-days, not from the next period). Activity revives it. A closed job that receives activity is reopened by an audited command and counts from that day; 'closed without lock, then activity' is a D11 advisory signal.

Metered activity (drives pause/resume and dormancy only; it never re-counts a locked job): purchase order created or changed; supplier invoice, delivery note or credit received; proof or progress photo uploaded; variation logged, priced or approved; diary or voice note; customer message sent or received through JobGuard; final-account revision before lock. Not metered: recording a customer payment or retention release, reveal dispositions, viewing or exporting, fee statements, D11 signal review, evidence-pack generation.

Small-job allowance: accepted net value under £2,000 ex VAT at switch-live takes no place (attested value for imports; the greater of accepted and quoted net value where both exist, the D11 option, so a discounted acceptance cannot buy the allowance). Fair use 10 at once; the 11th takes a place. A small job takes a place from the day approved variations lift its cumulative net value above £4,000, once, shown on the variation-approval screen, never back; draft, rejected and withdrawn extras never trip it, so the fee-free capture rule is untouched. Sub-£2,000 jobs for the same customer party and site whose dates overlap or fall within 90 days of each other are tested on their combined value (deterministic, shown on the job, D11 advisory). Decided for A's £2,000/£4,000 with hysteresis over B's £1,000: solos' repairs and day jobs sit at £500–£2,000, and a trip-point twice the threshold stops a job flipping on one small extra.

Reserved big-job weighting, recorded in D09 v3 as switched off: over £50,000 accepted net = 2 places, over £150,000 = 3 (greater of accepted and quoted; same-customer-same-site quotes with overlapping or contiguous dates banded on their combined value; once-only upward re-band on approved variations; imports on attested value). It may be switched on only by a D09 v3.1 after pilot measurement of the accepted-value distribution and cost-to-serve per archetype, and switching it on is a price change under the D09 notice rule. Thresholds must never sit on a hero archetype's median, which is why £50,000 (Design A) beats £25,000 (Design B): the small-firm archetype averages £25,000.

Trial: the business's first switch-live starts the trial; that job is excluded until it locks or 90 days, whichever first; the card is taken at that switch-live; the 10% success fee applies normally on it so the builder experiences the real model. One trial per business identity (company number / VAT number / UTR, phone, payment method). Pilot jobs follow the explicit D09 inclusion rule; exemption is never a default.

Imports (M1-17): `lifecyclePoint: live` counts from day 31 after the import commit (B's 30-day onboarding grace, so a firm migrating 15 in-flight jobs is not metered while it learns the product); `lifecyclePoint: invoiced` never counts (A); the attested value serves the small-job test; baselines are labelled 'baseline as imported' in the evidence pack.

Annual plans prepay the plan at 'two months free' (£290 / £690 / £1,790 / £3,490) and fix the places for 12 months; overage is billed monthly in arrears at the same £20, never discounted; the ceiling is unchanged. Annual is offered, never the default (research report §'Offer annual billing, don't force it').

Subscription pause (not a job pause): a monthly plan with zero live jobs for a whole period may pause at £0 for up to 3 periods in any 12; quoting stays free while paused; switching any job live ends the pause; live jobs cannot be held on a £0 account. Untested (research seasonality note): a D09 v3 pilot experiment, not a promise.

Late or replayed events (offline sync, reopen, replay) re-derive the affected period and post a linked compensating subscription line in the next period; posted period lines are never edited (AGENTS §5.5, §5.7).

Transparency: the job list always shows 'N of S places in use; next place £20/month (or free until [date])', rebuilt from events, never a cached counter; every bill lists each job that counted, its place-days and the rule applied (allowance, trial, import grace, pause, overage). No count, page or response may vary with shadow-signal existence (§14.3).

Separation and gating: metering lines are tenant-level D09 subscription facts, never per-job base fees, caps or credits, never offset against or refunded because of the success fee. D09 v3 must record every number here before any charge; missing prices or limits keep paid metering disabled rather than inventing defaults (M4-14). Metering runs only in production_billing after G4; the pilot is no-charge and cannot be billed retroactively (AGENTS §5.10).

options.name: Option 1 — Pure per-live-job price with a monthly minimum (Design A option 1) — rejected
options.structure: £12 per live job per month (job-days, pro rata), minimum £29/month; unlimited users, no tiers; optional volume steps.
options.per_job_economics: Constant £12 per job-month (40p per job-day). Lifetime subscription per job at archetype durations (1.6 / 2.75 / 5.4 months): Solo ~£19, Small ~£33, Firm ~£65; 0.24% / 0.13% / 0.11% of turnover.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £30/month at 2.5 live jobs (the £29 minimum applies at 2) → £360/yr
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £66/month at 5.5 live → £792/yr
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £180/month at 15 live → £2,160/yr

options.pros: Fairest, simplest meter: bill = usage, no cliffs, no tier gaming, no upgrade Decisions; explained in one sentence.
options.cons: A running meter is exactly what builders dislike (Prelec & Loewenstein 1998; Lambrecht & Skiera 2006, research notes): no flat number to compare, no hero plan for the compromise effect, and a variable bill needs a D05 bounded standing authority, which forces tiers back in. Undercharges firms against the per-user comparator (£480–£660/month for 15 staff on Tradify or Powered Now). Rejected.

options.name: Option 2 — Flat tiers by live jobs with forced upgrade at the limit (founder's candidate ladder; Design A option 2 / Design B option 1) — rejected as the shape, kept as the price points
options.structure: £29 ≤3 / £69 ≤5 / £179 ≤10 / £349 ≤20 / custom. Every live job counts 1. Switching a job live beyond the limit requires an upgrade first (M4-14 'enforces the agreed limit').
options.per_job_economics: Per place at the limit: £9.67 / £13.80 / £17.90 / £17.45. Below the limit the marginal job is free; the job that crosses it costs the whole gap: the 6th job costs £110/month, the 11th £170/month.

revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £69 at 5 live, £179 at 6 live → £828 or £2,148/yr; the archetype sits exactly on the cliff
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £349 (15 live on the ≤20 tier) → £4,188/yr; 0.21% of turnover; the highest honest number of any option

options.pros: One number per tier; flat and predictable; simplest D05 mandate; highest firm revenue; matches the ServiceM8 precedent of pricing by jobs, not people.
options.cons: The 5→6 cliff lands on the small-firm archetype (2.6× the price) and the 10→11 cliff on growing firms; forced upgrade at the moment of switch-live is the worst friction (the builder is on site with a won job); the research report §'Charge for live jobs, not people' says suggest an upgrade, never block. A firm at 11 jobs pays £349 for 20 places it does not use. Both designs rejected the cliffs; the price points survive.

options.name: Option 3 — Tiers plus £20 job-day overage with per-tier ceilings (Design A option 3) — adopted as the core
options.structure: Solo £29 (3 places) / Builder £69 (6) / Firm £179 (12) / Contractor £349 (24) / on request above 40. £20 per extra job per month pro rata by job-days, automatic up to 2 / 5 / 8 / 16 extra jobs; at the ceiling the next switch-live is a one-tap upgrade Decision, never a block. Ceilings tuned so plan + overage ≤ next plan.
options.per_job_economics: Per place at the limit: £9.67 / £11.50 / £14.92 / £14.54; extra job £20 (≈66p/day). Effective monthly price is monotone in live jobs: 3→£29, 4→£49, 5→£69, 6→£69, 8→£109, 10→£149, 11→£169, 12→£179, 15→£239, 18→£299, 20→£339, 21–24→£349, 30→£469, 40→£669. Lifetime subscription per job: Solo ~£18, Small ~£35, Firm ~£87 (0.23% / 0.14% / 0.14% of turnover).

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £29 → £348/yr (a month peaking at 4 jobs costs £49)
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £69 → £828/yr (5.5 average inside 6 places; a 7th job for a fortnight ≈ +£9)
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £239 → £2,868/yr on Firm + 3 extra jobs; £349 Contractor if they run 21+ or prefer a flat bill

options.pros: No cliffs, so no reason to keep the 6th job off JobGuard; flat-rate feel with a bounded variable part, which is exactly what D05 'bounded standing authority' needs; the upgrade tap is always the cheaper choice at the ceiling, so it never feels punitive; three real plans with a hero in the middle; per-place price rises mildly with tier without a second number on the page.
options.cons: Two numbers to explain (plan and £20 extra). M4-14 moves from optional to required (job-day aggregation, ceilings, upgrade Decisions, exact per-period arithmetic). The 15-job firm lands at £239, £110 under the founder's £349, unless the reserved weighting (option 5) is switched on.

options.name: Option 4 — Option 3 plus the small-job allowance (Design A option 4a merged with Design B's micro-jobs) — adopted; this is the recommendation
options.structure: As option 3. Jobs under £2,000 accepted net at switch-live take no place (fair use 10 at once); a small job takes a place from the day approved variations lift it above £4,000 (once, never back); sub-£2,000 jobs for the same customer party and site within 90 days are tested on their combined value. Threshold £2,000 (A) chosen over £1,000 (B); B's once-only, never-down move and greater-of-accepted-and-quoted test adopted.
options.per_job_economics: Same tier and overage prices. Small jobs cost £0 subscription; JobGuard's processing cost on them is low and the watchdog and final check still run in full, so detections and fee base are not lost. Assumed share of live jobs under £2,000: Solo 30%, Small 15%, Firm 5% (assumptions).

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £29 → £348/yr (countable ≈1.75 of 2.5; a 4-job month with one small job stays £29 instead of £49)
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £69 → £828/yr (countable ≈4.7; unchanged)
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £224 → £2,688/yr (countable ≈14.25 → 2.25 extra job-months); £239 → £2,868 if none of its jobs is small; about £15/month less than option 3

options.pros: Removes the 'keep small jobs off JobGuard' vector where it bites hardest (solos doing repairs and day jobs), which the research report names as the one risk of a jobs meter; brings evidence and habit onto the platform at near-zero cost; costs almost nothing on the archetypes; easy to say: 'Jobs under £2k don't count.'
options.cons: New split vector (sub-£2k quotes), mitigated by the combined-value rule and the fair-use cap. One more rule on the pricing page. £2,000 and £4,000 are load-bearing numbers that must go into D09 v3 and be checked against pilot data.

options.name: Option 5 — Value-weighted places inside the job count (Design B option 2 / Design A option 4b) — reserved, not launched
options.structure: A live job takes 2 places above a value threshold and 3 above a higher one. B proposed ≤£25k / £25k–£100k / >£100k with limits 3 / 10 / 20 / 40 and £9 overage; A proposed >£50k = 2, >£150k = 3 as an optional deviation. Merged: pre-specify A's thresholds (>£50,000 = 2 places, >£150,000 = 3) in D09 v3, switched off, with B's guards (greater of accepted and quoted; same-customer-same-site contiguous quotes banded on combined value; once-only upward re-band; imports on attested value).
options.per_job_economics: On the merged ladder a £60k job on Firm costs £29.84/month (2 × £14.92) or £40 on overage: 0.05% of its value per month, still under-priced relative to value and never over-priced. Assumed share of jobs over £50k: Solo 0%, Small 5%, Firm 50% (assumption; average firm job £60k).

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £29 → £348/yr (unchanged)
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £69 → £828/yr (≈5.8 places on 6; one big job uses 2 of 6 places)
revenue_by_archetype.firm: 15 jobs ≈ 22.5 places → Contractor £349 → £4,188/yr (0.21% of turnover); matches the founder's ladder outcome for firms. Under B's own bands and limits: £251 → £3,012 or £349 → £4,188

options.pros: The only lever that lifts the 15-job firm to £349 without a turnover meter; distinguishes a £2m firm running 15 extensions from a £600k firm running 15 kitchens, which no flat count can; defensible on cost-to-serve (POs, deliveries, photos, AI calls, final-check depth scale with value) and against the per-user comparator; the value is already frozen and immutable at switch-live (M1-7), so nothing new is captured.
options.cons: It is contract-value pricing by the back door, and the founder rejected contract value as the meter; both designs concede the thresholds are guesses until the pilot measures the accepted-value distribution; it adds a second number to explain and an under-attestation vector at launch; B's £25k line sits on the small-firm archetype's median, the same cliff problem in a new place. Decision: launch flat, keep the rule pre-specified and dormant, switch on only by D09 v3.1 with pilot evidence (§14.17).

options.name: Option 6 — Tier-gated workflow depth for Firm and Contractor (Design B option 4; Design A lever 4) — adopted as packaging
options.structure: Every tier keeps every detection (supplier price checks, three-way matching, readiness warnings, proof gates, shadow bill, final check). Firm adds, as they ship: interim applications and staged invoicing (M4-18), retention tracking and release chasing, Construction Act payment and pay-less notices for B2B customers, multi-approver PO/variation sign-off, office dashboard, evidence-pack export on demand, accounting-connector sync, subcontractor POs, priority support. Contractor adds multi-entity and custom terms. Two or three headline features per tier, not a grid.
options.per_job_economics: If the workflow features pull an archetype up one tier: Solo £43 per job (Builder), Small firm £90 per job (Firm), Firm £127 per job (Contractor). Otherwise identical to option 4.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £348–£828/yr; assumption: almost all solos stay at £29
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £828–£2,148/yr; assumption: half of 5-staff firms with an office person and B2B customers move to Firm for notices and multi-approver sign-off
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £2,688–£4,188/yr; a 15-staff firm working for main contractors almost certainly wants notices, retention tracking and packs, so Contractor £349 is realistic once those features exist

options.pros: Captures prevention value through features that only matter when the value is large (a retention or a pay-less notice is worth nothing to a bathroom fitter and thousands to a subcontractor); every tier remains a real plan somebody would buy (the research's condition for good-better-best); does not reduce detections or the fee base on lower tiers.
options.cons: A feature list weakens the one-number comparison (research: 'the comparison should rest on one or two numbers'); gating any detection would make lower tiers feel the watchdog is switched off and the fee look like the reason, so the rule 'gate workflow, never a detection' is a hard line; the features are M4+ work that does not exist yet, so this lifts revenue only when they ship.

options.name: Option 7 — Job count with a one-month duration floor and an annual 'jobs started' fair-use ceiling (Design B option 3) — rejected
options.structure: Every job counts for at least one full billing month; each tier carries an annual jobs-started ceiling (e.g. Solo 40, Builder 120, Firm 300) that triggers an upgrade conversation.
options.per_job_economics: Identical to option 4 for the three archetypes (jobs last 1.6–5.4 months). For a high-throughput user (3 concurrent two-week jobs, ~78 a year) the floor moves them from Solo £29 to Builder £69: £10.60 per job instead of £4.46.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £348/yr (unchanged)
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: £828/yr (unchanged)
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £2,688–£2,868/yr (unchanged)

options.pros: Fair on cost-to-serve, which is per job (AI proposal, evidence pipeline, final check), not per month; closes the high-throughput loophole cheaply from the metering events.
options.cons: Does nothing for the size disparity, which is the bigger leak; reactive call-out work is ServiceM8's market, not JobGuard's; two counters dilute the one-number comparison; job-days already charge a short job for the days it is live, so the floor is unnecessary. Rejected; keep 'jobs started per year' as a D11 advisory metric only.

options.name: Option 8 — Floating monthly tier with capped peak overage as the headline (Design B option 5) — subsumed into option 3
options.structure: The builder picks a tier as a ceiling; each month is tier price + overage at the month's peak concurrency, never more than the next tier; step down any month.
options.per_job_economics: Same per-place cost as option 3; the difference is that the running meter becomes the headline.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: ≈£32 average → ≈£390/yr (assumes a 3-month summer peak of 1–2 extra jobs)
revenue_by_archetype.small_firm: ≈£78 average → ≈£936/yr (assumes a 4-month peak to 8 jobs)
revenue_by_archetype.firm: ≈£260 average → ≈£3,100/yr (assumes a 4-month peak to 18 jobs)

options.pros: No winter over-payment and fewer winter cancellations, which the research flags for sole traders wary of lock-in; captures peak-season value a fixed tier gives away.
options.cons: Variable bills as the headline are what flat-rate bias warns against; harder to explain than a fixed tier. Decision: keep the flat tier as the headline and the £20 job-day overage as the fine print (option 3 already delivers the seasonal behaviour, and job-days do it more precisely than a peak).

options.name: Option 9 — Observable-value add-ons on top of the ladder (Design B option 6 merged with Design A's levers) — adopted as follow-ons, each needing its own decision record
options.structure: (a) hosted-payments platform margin at M4 (about +0.3% card, +20p Direct Debit on top of the processor's rate; JobGuard never holds funds; disclosed; the builder cannot surcharge consumers); (b) evidence/dispute pack assembly £49–£149 per pack on Solo/Builder, included on Firm+, raw export always free; (c) onboarding/import service £199–£499 one-off for Firm/Contractor migrations; (d) an accountant/bookkeeper practice plan later; (e) a monthly value receipt (VALUE-2) worded 'flagged for your decision', never 'saved you £X' before settled cash (§14.1); (f) pilot-measure only: a D03 v3 candidate charging a lower rate (e.g. 5%, capped per invoice) on a pre-payment supplier correction documented by the supplier's own credit note or revised invoice. Named and rejected on trust: merchant or supplier commissions and preferred-supplier placement (would compromise the invoice watchdog); selling builders' data or their customers as leads (D12 and word of mouth); a homeowner-side bill checker (paid by both sides of one invoice); a paid quote-check add-on (AGENTS §5.10); insurance, warranty or invoice-finance referrals (regulated or a milder conflict: full disclosure or leave them out).
options.per_job_economics: Base as option 4. Add-ons per job are small: the payments margin is worth about £3 per Solo job and £18 per Firm job on the assumed share of payments taken through JobGuard; a dispute pack is a rare £49; import is a one-off.

revenue_by_archetype.solo: £348 + ≈£180 payments margin (assumes 40% of £150k through JobGuard at 0.3%) + ≈£49 (one pack a year) ≈ £577/yr
revenue_by_archetype.firm: £2,688–£2,868 + ≈£600 (10% of £2m; large sums go by bank transfer) + £299 import in year one ≈ £3,600–£3,800/yr

options.pros: Monetises prevention through deliverables the builder can see (a payment collected, a pack assembled, a migration done) instead of an unprovable counterfactual; the payments margin grows with the faster-invoicing benefit JobGuard actually delivers and is standard for the category (Fergus 1.6% + 20p); nothing touches the fee rules, the no-offset rule or the shadow bill.
options.cons: Each line needs its own decision record and the payments margin needs M4 rails that do not exist; together they add roughly 30–65% to the subscription, not multiples; packs risk 'paying for my own data' unless raw export stays free; item (f) reopens prevented spend, which the founder said earns nothing today, and builders may stop recording corrections, so it must not ship without D03 v3, pilot measurement and a fairness check.

options.name: Comparator — research report ladder (£29 ≤3 / £59 ≤10 / £119 ≤25 / custom) — rejected
options.structure: Three tiers, unlimited users, forced upgrades implied, 'Contractor' on request above 25.
options.per_job_economics: £9.67 / £5.90 / £4.76 per place: a steep volume discount, the opposite of cost and value.
options.pros: Cheapest and safest against gaming and against Checkatrade's free tools; allowances so generous the meter almost never binds.
options.cons: Leaves most of the firm's value on the table (a 15-staff firm pays £119 against £480–£660 on per-user rivals, and 4× cheaper is not a quality signal); 10 places for £59 means the small firm never grows into the next tier; per-place price falls with size. Its £59 hero price is worth testing against £69 in the price conversations, but the limits are wrong.

gaming.vector: Keeping jobs, especially small ones, off JobGuard to stay in a cheaper tier, or using JobGuard as a free voice-quoting tool and never switching live.
gaming.mitigation: Small-job allowance (under £2,000 takes no place); £20 job-day overage instead of a cliff (the 6th job costs £20, not £110); first-live-job trial; the value the builder forgoes on the off-platform job itself (PO price checks, proof gates, final account, final check); D11 'won but not live' advisory signal. A fair-use ceiling on AI proposal generation for accounts with no paid plan is capacity control, not billing, so AGENTS §5.10 (free quoting never bills) stays intact. JobGuard loses catch revenue on off-platform jobs, so allowances stay generous (research report §'Charge for live jobs, not people').

gaming.vector: Merging several customers into one job (a block of flats, an estate, a landlord's tenants, a maintenance contract) to pay for one place.
gaming.mitigation: Structural, not a rule: a job binds one accepting customer party at acceptance (§3.1), one final account, one lock and one invoice recipient; two customers cannot both accept one quote or be invoiced from one job; variation customer-approval goes to that party only. A management company or landlord accepting one quote for many units is legitimately one customer and one job.

gaming.vector: Merging phases or sites of one customer into one accepted quote to take one place.
gaming.mitigation: One site address per job is definitional (different sites are separate jobs). Phases under one accepted quote are one job by design: the meter is capacity and the builder pays with a muddier final account and a weaker shadow-bill match. D11 advisory signal: accepted value above 3× the tenant's median, or several site addresses in the job's evidence. If the reserved weighting is ever switched on, the merged quote is banded on its combined value, so merging gains nothing.

gaming.vector: Splitting work into sub-£2,000 quotes to use the allowance.
gaming.mitigation: Fair-use cap of 10 small jobs at once; sub-£2,000 jobs for the same customer party and site with overlapping dates or within 90 days are tested on their combined value; a small job that grows past £4,000 through approved variations takes a place from that day; D11 advisory signal. Under a flat meter, splitting any larger project costs the builder more places, so the allowance is the only split incentive to defend.

gaming.vector: Growing a small job through Log an extra so a £1,900 job becomes £6,000 while keeping the allowance.
gaming.mitigation: The once-only upward trip at £4,000 cumulative net after approved variations, disclosed on the approval screen. Draft, rejected and withdrawn extras never trip it, so nothing about the fee-free capture rule changes and there is no incentive to stop logging extras.

gaming.vector: Under-declaring the accepted value (discounted or partial acceptance) or under-attesting an imported value to buy the allowance or, later, a lower weighting band.
gaming.mitigation: Test on the greater of accepted and quoted net value frozen at switch-live (the D11 option; both values are already stored). Imported lineage is already 'builder_attested_weaker' and the attested value also bounds recovery evidence quality on that job. D11 advisory signals: accepted value materially below quoted; final-account value above 2× the attested or accepted value. Residual: a builder who under-quotes and under-invoices the customer to save £9.67–£20 a month loses far more than they save.

gaming.vector: Locking early (at half completion) to free the place, then finishing the work on a locked job.
gaming.mitigation: Post-lock evidence never qualifies (§14.6), so the builder forfeits the final check on the rest of the work; final invoice issue still requires the lock and only one attribution lock exists per job; new site work must be a new, linked job; documents attached after lock are labelled 'received after lock'. D11 advisory signals: material evidence after lock; lock with low proof of completion. It is the builder's own final check, not the place, that leaks.

gaming.vector: Never locking; invoicing outside JobGuard to avoid both the place and any catch fee; or closing without a lock.
gaming.mitigation: Dormancy after 60 idle days stops the meter (builder-friendly, so it is not a revenue lever either way) and `CloseJob` with a reason must exist because builders cannot be forced to lock. D11 signals: invoice or payment activity with no lock; closed without lock, then activity. The JobGuard final invoice requires the lock, so the builder also forgoes billing and payment tooling, and the real incentive to lock is the final check itself. This is the fee-side residual risk already accepted in §14.10; accept it plainly.

gaming.vector: Pausing jobs to free places while still working them, or pausing on the 1st and un-pausing when needed.
gaming.mitigation: Any metered activity (PO, supplier document, proof upload, variation, diary note, customer message) resumes the job and it counts from that day; pause and resume are explicit, audited and visible in the job list; the meter is job-days, so a genuinely idle job costs nothing and an active one pays. More than three resumes in a quarter is a D11 advisory signal, never a penalty.

gaming.vector: Timing games around the period boundary: downgrade then overage; switch live at 23:59; lock or pause on the last day to shrink a billing-date snapshot.
gaming.mitigation: There is no snapshot: overage is job-days from append-only events with server timestamps, so a late-night switch-live or a last-day lock changes pence; downgrades only at period end and only within the new plan's places + ceiling; no mid-period tier change except a builder-approved upgrade.

gaming.vector: Sitting on overage indefinitely instead of upgrading.
gaming.mitigation: Acceptable and bounded: the per-tier ceiling caps it at £69 / £169 / £339 / £669, never more than the next plan; £20 overage is above every included-place price, so at the ceiling the one-tap upgrade is always cheaper; after two consecutive periods of overage at or above the step-up, JobGuard prompts an upgrade. No auto-upgrade without an approved Decision (D05).

gaming.vector: Trial abuse: a new business per job.
gaming.mitigation: One trial per business identity (company number / VAT number / UTR, phone, payment method); card taken at the first switch-live; trial ends at first lock or 90 days; duplicates are a D11 signal for human review, never an automatic action.

gaming.vector: Splitting one firm into several tenants (three Solo accounts instead of one Firm plan).
gaming.mitigation: Company registration number, VAT number or UTR per tenant checked at sign-up; D11 advisory signal on shared users, phones, addresses and payment methods across tenants; terms. The natural cost does most of the work: no shared customers, suppliers, rate book, evidence or reporting across tenants, and the shadow bill and final check cannot see across the split. Low priority: per-place prices are close across tiers (£9.67–£14.92), so the gain is small.

gaming.vector: Importing in-flight or finished jobs in bulk and locking them immediately to run final checks on paper-era work.
gaming.mitigation: Harmless to the meter (imports count from day 31; invoiced imports never count) and harmless to the builder (the fee is theirs to trigger by confirming a catch and getting paid). Imported baselines are labelled 'baseline as imported' in the evidence pack so the lock is honest about what the check could compare.

gaming.vector: A firm running many short jobs (high throughput) inside a small tier.
gaming.mitigation: Job-days already charge a two-week job for its 14 days; no duration floor. 'Jobs started per year' is a D11 advisory metric for an upgrade conversation only. Reactive call-out work is not JobGuard's target market.

gaming.vector: A cached or inconsistent live-job counter over- or under-charging (an operational rather than builder vector, but the one that would destroy trust fastest).
gaming.mitigation: The meter is rebuilt from immutable audited events; a cached counter can never trigger a charge (M4-14); every bill names the jobs, place-days and rule; late or replayed events re-derive the period and post a linked compensating line, never an edit (AGENTS §5.4, §5.5, §5.7). All mitigations above are deterministic rules or D11 advisory signals; none changes a price or takes an account action outside a valid standing authorization.

result.size_disparity_fix:
Name the disparity rather than hide it: on the merged ladder a £60k job on Firm costs £14.92 a month and an £8k job on Solo £9.67, so the meter charges the £2m firm about 0.14% of turnover and the sole trader 0.23%, and a flat count cannot tell a £2m firm running 15 extensions from a £600k firm running 15 kitchens. Design A accepts this structurally and lifts firm revenue through tier shape; Design B fixes it with value-weighted places at launch. Decision: launch flat, pull the structural levers first, and hold the weighting in reserve, pre-specified. Six levers, in the order to pull them:

1. Accept it structurally. The subscription is a capacity charge; the 10% success fee is the value charge and already scales with job size (a missed £2,400 extra on a £60k job pays £240; the same 4% miss on an £8k job pays £32), and retention money and withheld payments are proportionally bigger on big jobs. A jobs meter that tries to capture value becomes a second percentage fee alongside the 10%.

2. Let the per-place price rise mildly with tier (£9.67 → £11.50 → £14.92), the founder's own ladder shape, justified by document volume and value and invisible on the page: one number per tier.

3. Small-job allowance at the bottom (under £2,000 free) so a solo is not paying £9.67 for a £900 repair. This is the mirror image of the disparity and is what keeps small work, evidence and habit on the system.

4. Tier-gated workflow depth in Firm and Contractor (option 6): interim applications and staged invoicing (M4-18), retention tracking and release chasing, Construction Act notices for B2B, multi-approver sign-off, office dashboard, evidence packs on demand, accounting-connector sync, subcontractor POs. Gate workflow, never a detection; two or three features per tier, not a grid. This is where a 15-staff firm working for main contractors finds £349 worth buying.

5. The reserved big-job weighting (option 5), recorded in D09 v3 switched off: over £50,000 accepted net = 2 places, over £150,000 = 3, greater of accepted and quoted, same-customer-same-site contiguous quotes banded on combined value, once-only upward re-band, imports on attested value. Switch it on only by D09 v3.1 if pilot data (§14.17) show that firm jobs cost materially more than 2× to serve or that Firm-tier revenue lands well under the per-user comparator. Why A's £50k/£150k rather than B's £25k/£100k: a threshold must never sit on a hero archetype's median, and the small-firm archetype averages £25k; £50k separates extensions from kitchens and refurbishments, £150k separates whole-house, plot and small commercial work. It lifts the firm archetype from £224–£239 to £349 (15 jobs ≈ 22.5 places → Contractor). Labelled plainly as a deviation from the pure jobs meter the founder chose.

6. Never fix it with turnover or contract value as the meter: rejected by the founder, intrusive, and it would push the subscription toward a second percentage fee.

Honest answer on the 15-job firm: the flat meter yields £224–£239 a month (0.13–0.14% of turnover), which is about £110 under the founder's £349 and roughly half of 15 per-user seats (£480–£660). With the reserved weighting or the Firm/Contractor features it reaches £349 (0.21%). If prevention is worth about 1% of turnover (an assumption, in line with Buildbite's self-reported 30% change-order lift but unproven), the subscription captures 15–20% of it and the builder keeps the rest, which is the honest shape of a watchdog product and the story the pricing page should tell. A jobs meter will not go past about £349–£669 for a firm this size without becoming a turnover meter in disguise; do not try. Beyond that the value comes from the success-fee categories and the observable-value add-ons (option 9).
result.recommendation:
VERDICT ON THE METER. Yes, jobs live at once works as the subscription meter, and it is the right call over turnover: it is what ServiceM8 already sells (by jobs, unlimited users; research report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'), it does not punish adding the site lead or labourers who feed JobGuard evidence, the builder controls and understands it, and it produces a 12× spread (£29 → £349+) between a sole trader and a 20-job firm while landing under the per-user comparator at every point (£29 vs Tradify £34 for one user; £69 vs £170–£220 for five; £224–£239 vs £480–£660 for fifteen). Cross-check, not a re-argument: it yields 0.13–0.23% of turnover, the same band a turnover meter would, but measured by something visible and fair. Four conditions: (1) it needs a bounded overage, because cliffs put the gaming incentive exactly where the archetypes sit; (2) it needs the precise definition of 'live' above, or snagging, retention and forgotten jobs make it feel like a tax; (3) it needs a small-job allowance, or solos keep repairs off the platform and JobGuard loses the evidence; (4) it caps out around £350–£670 a month even for the largest target firm, so anything beyond that must come from the success fee, the Firm/Contractor features and the add-ons, not the subscription.

RECOMMENDED LADDER (all ex VAT, per business, unlimited users, quoting free forever, identical 10% success fee on every plan, no offset ever):
- Solo £29/month (£290/yr): 3 places. £9.67 per place.
- Builder £69/month (£690/yr), the hero plan: 6 places. £11.50 per place.
- Firm £179/month (£1,790/yr): 12 places, plus the Firm workflow features as they ship. £14.92 per place.
- Contractor £349/month (£3,490/yr): 24 places, everything in Firm, multi-entity. £14.54 per place. Above 40 places: priced on request.
- Extra jobs: £20 per job per month, pro rata by the day (about 66p a day), automatic up to 2 / 5 / 8 / 16 extra jobs. That ceiling is the D05 bounded amount (£69 / £169 / £339 / £669 a period) and never exceeds the next plan; at the ceiling the next switch-live is a one-tap move to the next plan or the job stays accepted-but-not-live. Existing jobs are never blocked. After two periods of overage at or above the step-up, JobGuard suggests the upgrade; it never auto-upgrades.
- Small jobs: accepted net value under £2,000 takes no place (fair use 10 at once; combined value for the same customer and site within 90 days); a small job that grows past £4,000 through approved variations takes a place from that day, once.
- Trial: the first job a business switches live is free until it locks or 90 days, card taken at that switch-live, success fee applies normally. Imported live jobs count from day 31; invoiced imports never count.
- Annual at 'two months free' on the plan only; overage never discounted. Monthly plans may pause at £0 for up to 3 months in 12 with no job live (pilot experiment).
- Reserved, switched off, recorded in D09 v3: over £50,000 = 2 places, over £150,000 = 3. Only a D09 v3.1 with pilot data can switch it on.
- Counting in one breath: job-days per period, Europe/London, server timestamps only; live from switch-live to lock, close or 60-day dormancy (45-day prompt); explicit pause; post-lock never counts; one customer party + one site + one accepted quote = one job; exact rational arithmetic with one half-even rounding per period; upgrades by Decision, never by a worker; every bill names the jobs that counted and why; places and overage are one tenant-level D09 subscription, never a per-job fee, cap or credit, never offset against the success fee.

Effective monthly price by countable live jobs (monotone, no cliffs): 1–3 → £29; 4 → £49; 5 → £69; 6 → £69; 7 → £89; 8 → £109; 10 → £149; 11 → £169; 12 → £179; 15 → £239; 18 → £299; 20 → £339; 21–24 → £349; 30 → £469; 40 → £669.

WHERE THE TWO DESIGNS DISAGREED, AND WHY EACH WAS DECIDED:
1. Value weighting at launch (B) vs flat with a reserve (A): flat at launch. The founder fixed the meter as jobs live at once; both designs admit the thresholds are guesses; the pilot will measure the accepted-value distribution; weighting adds a second number and an under-attestation vector; and tier shape plus overage plus Firm features close most of the gap. The rule is pre-specified and dormant so switching it on later is a versioned price change, not a redesign.
2. Overage unit, job-days (A) vs monthly peak (B): job-days. A one-day overlap costs pence; a peak rule bills a month for a day and reopens timing games; M4-14 already demands deterministic period aggregation with replay.
3. Overage price, £20 (A) vs £9 (B): £20. Ceilings only work if the next plan is never dearer than continuing on overage; at £9 a builder sits on Builder + overage for ever and Firm never sells.
4. Post-lock activity re-counts the job for that day (A) vs never (B): never. Confirming catches, revisions, invoice and payment are the normal post-lock flow; charging for the day JobGuard reveals its own catches would be a trust failure. Early-lock gaming is covered structurally (post-lock evidence never qualifies, invoice needs the lock, new work is a new linked job, D11 signals).
5. Builder limit, 6 (A) vs 10 (B) vs 5 (founder): 6. The hero archetype (5–6 live) must sit flat inside the hero plan; 10 without weighting makes Builder £6.90 a place and the small firm never grows into Firm; 5 puts the archetype on the meter every other month.
6. Firm/Contractor limits, 12/24 (A) vs 20/40 (B) vs 10/20 (founder): 12/24. They make the effective price monotone with the ceilings (Solo 3+2 → Builder 6; Builder 6+5 → Firm 12; Firm 12+8 → Contractor 24); B's limits only make sense with weighting; the founder's 10/20 produce a £50 step at 11→12 jobs.
7. Small-job threshold, £2,000/£4,000 (A) vs £1,000 (B): £2,000 with the £4,000 trip and B's once-only, never-down move and greater-of-accepted-and-quoted test.
8. Phase merging for counting (B): applied only to the small-job allowance (and to the reserve weighting if adopted). Under a flat meter, splitting costs the builder more places, so there is nothing else to defend.
9. Imports from import (A) vs day 31 (B): day 31, plus A's rule that invoiced imports never count. A firm migrating 15 in-flight jobs is exactly the customer to welcome.
10. Dormancy: both 60 days, plus B's 45-day prompt; counting stops from day 61, not the next period.
11. Enforcement at switch-live: A's one-tap upgrade Decision at the ceiling merged with B's three choices (upgrade, add on overage within the ceiling, leave accepted-but-not-live) and B's two-period upgrade prompt.

REVENUE BY ARCHETYPE (assumptions, labelled: Solo 2.5 live on average, 19 jobs/yr at £8k, 1.6 months each, 30% under £2k; Small firm 5.5 live, 24 jobs/yr at £25k, 2.75 months, 15% under £2k; Firm 15 live, 33 jobs/yr at £60k, 5.4 months, 5% under £2k; overage on average concurrency, peaks slightly higher):
- Solo: £29 → £348/yr (£290 annual). About £18 per job, 0.23% of turnover. Founder's ladder £348; research ladder £348.
- Small firm: £69 → £828/yr. About £35 per job, 0.14%. Founder's ladder £828 at 5 jobs but £2,148 at 6 (the cliff); research £708.
- Firm: £224–£239 → £2,690–£2,870/yr on Firm + 2–3 extra jobs. About £81–£87 per job, 0.13–0.14%. £349 → £4,188 if the reserved weighting is switched on, if they run 21+ jobs, or if the Firm/Contractor features pull them up. Founder's ladder £4,188; research £1,428.
- Illustrative success fee on top, everywhere, and only illustrative because no UK data exist on unbilled extras (research report confidence table): if 20% of jobs yield a qualifying catch worth 3% of job value, roughly £90 / £360 / £1,190 a year before any cash supplier refunds or withheld-payment cases.
- Illustrative mix of 1,000 paying builders (60/30/10): about £735k/yr subscription, about £61/month ARPA, before any success fee.
- Against the founder's ladder: same Solo price; same £69 at five jobs; removes the 5→6 and 10→11 cliffs; keeps the rising per-place shape; costs about £110/month on the firm archetype unless the reserve rule or Firm features apply. Against the research ladder: same Solo; £10 more for the small firm in exchange for places it actually needs; roughly double for firms, which the per-user comparator supports.

OTHER WAYS TO CAPTURE PREVENTION VALUE (union of both designs, ranked, each with its trust flag; none touches the 10%, the no-offset rule or the shadow bill):
1. Firm/Contractor workflow depth (option 6): interim applications and staged invoicing (M4-18), retention tracking and release chasing, Construction Act payment and pay-less notices for B2B customers, multi-approver PO/variation sign-off, office dashboard, evidence packs on demand, accounting sync, subcontractor POs, priority support. Gate workflow, never a detection.
2. Hosted-payments platform margin at M4 (about +0.3% card, +20p Direct Debit on top of the processor's rate; JobGuard never holds funds; needs its own decision record and M4-11/12; disclosed; the builder cannot surcharge consumers). Roughly £135–£180 / £450 / £600–£1,200 a year on assumed shares. Trust risk low.
3. Retention money: track due dates, prompt the release request; if withheld beyond the D03 threshold the builder may open a recovery case at 10% under the existing `withheld_customer_payment` category. Firm-tier value; no new policy beyond the threshold.
4. Statutory late-payment interest and fixed compensation (B2B only; the Late Payment Act does not cover homeowners): compute and add to reminders; interest recovered inside a case is new money; extending 'net principal' to interest needs a D03 revision. Late payment is the one well-measured pain (£26bn owed; 14,000 closures a year), so make case-opening prominent.
5. Evidence/dispute pack assembly: £49–£149 per pack on Solo/Builder, included on Firm+, raw export always free (the packs already exist: M4-3-S, #92).
6. Onboarding/import service £199–£499 one-off for Firm/Contractor migrations.
7. Accountant/bookkeeper practice plan later (per-client pricing).
8. Monthly value receipt (VALUE-2): 'caught before you paid £X; proof captured on N items; extras tracked £Y', worded 'flagged for your decision', never 'saved you £X' before settled cash (§14.1). Not a charge; the only honest way to make prevention felt so the subscription renews (Soman & Gourville: bundled subscriptions dull attention).
9. Pilot-measure only, a D03 v3 candidate: a lower rate (e.g. 5%, capped per invoice) on a pre-payment supplier correction proved by the supplier's own credit note or revised invoice referencing the flagged line. The supplier's document makes the counterfactual stronger than generic prevention, but it charges on prevented spend, which today earns nothing; builders may stop recording corrections; trust risk low-to-moderate ('I'd have spotted it'), mitigated by the rate and by showing the three-way-match work (Buell & Norton). Do not ship without D03 v3, a D01 revision, pilot measurement and a fairness check.
Named and rejected on trust: merchant or supplier commissions and preferred-supplier placement (would compromise the invoice watchdog); selling builders' data or their customers as leads (D12 and word of mouth); a homeowner-side bill checker (paid by both sides of one invoice); a paid quote-check add-on (AGENTS §5.10: quoting never bills); a success fee on prevented spend without a supplier document (unprovable counterfactual); insurance, warranty or invoice-finance referrals (regulated or a milder conflict: full disclosure or leave them out).

WHAT THIS NEEDS. This is analysis, not approval: D09 stays `proposed`. To act on it: D09 v3 records the ladder, places, £20 job-day overage, ceilings, the £2,000/£4,000 allowance, the reserved weighting (off), trial, import grace, annual, subscription pause, the metering events and bill transparency; M4-14 moves from optional to required (job-day aggregation, ceilings, upgrade Decisions, replay fixtures reconciling the effective-price table above); M4-13/D05 record the per-tier monetary ceiling as the bounded standing authority; D11 v3 adds the metering advisory signals; `PauseJob`, `CloseJob` with reason, dormancy and the allowance trip go into the build plan under 'Discovered later'; D03 v3 and D01 revisions only if levers 4 or 9 are pursued. Before any charging (G4): the 10–20 structured price conversations and the £29-vs-£39 Solo and card-at-switch-live tests the research report asks for, plus pilot measurement (§14.17) of live-job counts by month, job durations, small-job share and the accepted-value distribution per archetype, and recovered money per job, because every archetype number here is an assumption. The first real-user pilot is no-charge and cannot be billed after the fact.

gaps.area: Paid real-time disclosure plan: prevention sold as a flat tier, fee-free by construction ("Tell me now")
gaps.why_it_matters: Every idea treats the hidden-until-lock check as the only way JobGuard's own findings earn money; I08 only gates the merchant-document watchdog. Nothing lets a builder pay a higher flat price to have JobGuard's shadow signals surfaced live as advisory cards. D13 and §14.3 already make any pre-lock surfacing permanently fee-free (surfaced_early / disclosed_before_lock), so the mechanism exists structurally. This converts the largest unfeeable value (prevention) into subscription revenue, gives a market price for how much builders value the hold-back, and is the natural hedge against the report's stated central risk (report §'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk': betrayal aversion, 'disclosure does not fix a conflict of interest', the 'knew on day 12' reading). Offering a choice is a stronger fairness lever than a sentence in the terms. Plainly: this touches the founder's shadow-bill decision, so it must be framed as an opt-in alternative at a higher price with hidden-until-lock remaining the default.
gaps.generation_prompt: Design a 'Tell me now' plan variant for JobGuard, presented as an opt-in alternative alongside the founder's default hidden-until-lock model, never replacing it. Specify: (1) placement and price — a per-tier uplift (e.g. +£X on Solo/Builder/Firm over the report's £29/£59/£119, §'Recommendation') or a dedicated tier; justify the delta against expected foregone success fees. (2) Mechanism — each shadow_commercial_signal reaching held_for_final_check is surfaced as an advisory 'possible extra' Decision Inbox card via the existing surfaced_early path, setting disclosed_before_lock=true so no missed_variation_final_account fee can ever arise on that tenant's jobs (§14.3, §14.6, D13); the builder still uses Log an extra to bill it. (3) Scope and switching rules — per-tenant, applying only to jobs switched live after the change, so a builder cannot switch to hidden mid-job to create a fee or to live after lock to dodge one; state what the post-lock final check still does on this plan (reconcile only, nothing to reveal). (4) Honest statement of what each side gives up, and the one-sentence pricing-page explanation for both plans. (5) Optional bounded service warranty on the paid plan: if a supplier document JobGuard ingested contained a duplicate or above-agreed-rate line that JobGuard failed to flag and the builder paid it, JobGuard issues a subscription credit for the difference up to £N per period (I07-style credit note via M4-10, never cash, never against a success fee); flag whether this is a contractual service promise or insurance and that it needs legal review. (6) Revenue model per archetype (Solo ~£150k/2–3 live jobs; Small firm ~£600k/5–6; Firm ~£2m/~15): state assumptions for uptake, catches per job (0–2) and recoverable value per catch (£200–£800; research §'How much revenue small builders lose' says the pool is unmeasured), and compare monthly uplift revenue with foregone 10% fees. (7) The D09/D13 record changes required and the §14.17 pilot measurements that would price it (share of builders choosing each plan, perceived fairness, catches surfaced early vs at lock).

gaps.area: Recovery and prevention categories with a documented counterfactual that D03 does not list: supplier rate renegotiation savings, input VAT recovered on missing VAT invoices, CIS suffered reclaimed
gaps.why_it_matters: I12–I15 extend D03 to pre-payment supplier corrections, applied credit notes, statutory interest and retention. But three outcomes have a provable baseline JobGuard already holds immutably, so the founder's 'counterfactual unprovable' objection to prevention fees does not apply: (a) renegotiated supplier rates — the prior agreed rate is frozen in the M2-1 rate book, the new rate is on ingested invoices, and savings = difference × quantity actually bought; this is exactly how cost-reduction consultancies charge 50% of savings for 12–60 months (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §2, P3 Cost Analysts), the most expensive familiar benchmark; (b) input VAT lost when a builder pays a pro-forma or invalid invoice and never obtains a VAT invoice — three-way matching already sees this, and the reclaim on the VAT return is cash; (c) CIS suffered reclaims, where I25 only offers a £30–£50 referral although refund firms charge 15–30%. None of these takes money from merchants or sells data.
gaps.generation_prompt: For each of three candidate categories — supplier_rate_renegotiation_savings, input_vat_recovered_after_missing_invoice_flag, cis_suffered_reclaimed — write a §14.7-style row (qualifies when / never qualifies), the immutable evidence chain (frozen prior agreed rate from M2-1, new rate on human-confirmed intake lines, quantities from matched invoices; VAT invoice obtained after a JobGuard discrepancy Decision plus the reclaim fact; CIS statements and HMRC repayment), fee basis and rate with one-rounding cumulative §14.9 mechanics and reversal handling (e.g. renegotiation: 20–25% of documented savings for 12 months measured monthly from invoices, capped by quantity actually purchased and by a fairness ceiling expressed in £; VAT: 10% of input tax reclaimed; CIS: flat £X or 10% of refund), and which need a D03 v3 version plus D01. State the trust rule explicitly: JobGuard never contacts, negotiates with, or receives anything from a merchant; the builder negotiates using a JobGuard-drafted 'rate review letter' built from their own purchase history and, where opted in, I28 benchmark bands; the watchdog checks the new rate exactly as it checked the old (M2-1). Label HMRC-related outputs as aids, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file (I25/I26 precedent). Estimate revenue per archetype with stated assumptions (materials 35–45% of turnover; achievable renegotiation 2–5% on the top ten SKUs; missing VAT invoices 1–3% of supplier spend for VAT-registered firms; Solo may be below the VAT threshold and outside CIS). Say which of the three is cleanest and which should be a flat add-on instead of a percentage.

gaps.area: Pre-contract counterparty due diligence: credit, insolvency, CCJ and property-ownership checks before the builder commits
gaps.why_it_matters: Late payment is the only government-measured loss (about £11bn a year, 14,000 closures; report §'Frame the price against lost money'), yet every idea monetises it after it happens (I14–I18, I47–I48). Nothing sells prevention at the moment the builder decides whether to take the job or on what deposit terms: a company credit report, CCJ and insolvency history, director history, Land Registry title check (is this person the owner; is there a charge or lease), listed-building or planning status. This is the Satago/Chaser/Creditsafe pattern (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6) using third-party data, per-check cost pass-through plus margin, and it is clean of all three known trust risks. It also produces the identity and terms evidence a later D03 withheld-payment case and the I33 contract pack need.
gaps.generation_prompt: Design a 'Check this customer' step available at quote-send or acceptance (never blocking; findings only, never a recommendation to refuse work, consistent with §5.9/§5.3 that JobGuard does not advise or decide). Specify: data sources and wholesale cost per check (assume Creditsafe/Experian company report £5–£15, Land Registry title register £7, CCJ register lookups; state as assumptions); pricing options — per check £X, a monthly allowance by tier (e.g. 2/10/30) with £X overage, or included on Firm; what the card shows ('this limited company has 2 CCJs in 12 months; last accounts overdue' / 'title held by a different name to the quote') and how it links to actions already in the list (deposit and stage schedule I40, contract pack I33, escrow I42); how the check record later supports the D03 withheld-payment entry test and the I34 evidence pack; UK GDPR and consumer-credit constraints for homeowners (lawful basis, likely limit consumer checks to property ownership and a consented soft search; business customers unrestricted) and the D12 Article 14 route; per-archetype revenue (quotes per month × attach rate × price, stated assumptions). Add a variant: trade-credit-insurance introduction for firms with business customers, paid by the insurer as commission — say plainly this is a regulated introduction like I43/I46 and off by default.

gaps.area: Fee shape at the large-recovery end and per-job fairness floor: annual ceiling, declining bands, deductible, Contractor buy-out
gaps.why_it_matters: I16 explores the small end only (15% band, £25 minimum). The reference policy is an uncapped 10% and no idea examines what happens when recoveries get large: a Firm recovering £40k in a year pays £4,000 plus £1,428 subscription. research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6 shows flat-fee rivals attacking percentage models once recoveries grow (Paddle Retain), and the report notes critics draw the 'too much' line at contingency on top of an engagement fee (§'The hidden final check'). Variants such as an annual ceiling, declining marginal bands, a per-job fee-free deductible (a visible goodwill gesture that answers the 'they take a cut of favours' objection) or a Contractor-tier flat buy-out are D01 versions, not a re-argument of the 10% headline or of the no-offset rule, but the list never evaluates them.
gaps.generation_prompt: Enumerate fee-shape variants that keep 10% as the headline rate and the subscription/fee separation intact: (a) annual per-tenant ceiling expressed in £ (never in subscription multiples, which would read as an offset), (b) declining marginal bands on cumulative annual qualifying principal (e.g. 10% to £10k, 7.5% to £50k, 5% above), (c) per-job deductible (first £100–£250 of qualifying principal per job fee-free, shown as a statement line), (d) Contractor-tier buy-out (higher flat subscription, success fee reduced to 5% or 0 — flag that D01 currently says 'no subscription offset' and that the report §'Three tiers work' advises an identical rate on every tier for the compromise effect). For each: rewrite the §14.9 formula (cumulative exact Q with bands, rounding once, band recomputation on negative delta and reversals across a year boundary), give the D01 v4 / D09 / D05 record implications and the M4-9/M4-10 statement wording, and compute revenue against uncapped 10% for the three archetypes under stated assumptions (catches per job and value; withheld-payment cases per year; supplier cash refunds). Address gaming (splitting a job to reset a deductible; timing recoveries across years) with D11-style advisory signals only. Recommend one variant and state why the others are rejected.

gaps.area: Contractor tier definition: firm-grade controls, evidence retention and archive tiers, and a lapsed-customer vault
gaps.why_it_matters: 'Contractor >25 on request' is empty in I01, and the only bigger-firm levers listed are I11 (entities), I30 (API), I31 (finance seats) and I52 (support). Bigger firms differ from small ones in control needs (who may raise a PO, approve a variation or issue an invoice; spend limits per site lead; director sign-off above £X; SSO/SCIM; audit export) and in evidence mass (hundreds of locked jobs; six-year limitation, twelve-year deeds, fifteen-year retention already assumed in I36; legal hold; Object Lock after D07). These are the classic non-turnover levers for charging more inside a jobs meter, and a read-only vault for lapsed subscribers monetises retention after churn while raw export stays free (I34).
