gaps.generation_prompt: Specify the Contractor tier and Firm add-ons using only non-turnover levers: (1) delegated authority — per-member PO, variation and invoice-issue limits, two-person approval above £X, enforced at the command boundary (§5.3) and recorded as Decisions, with an approval-routing view in the Decision Inbox; (2) SSO/SCIM via the M0-6 principal contract, audit-chain export, sandbox tenant; (3) evidence retention tiers — e.g. 2 years included on Solo, 6 on Builder, 12 on Firm, 15 on Contractor, legal hold and Object Lock (M4, after D07 approval), priced per locked-job-year or as flat archive bands; (4) a 'Vault' plan for lapsed subscribers (£5–£9/month read-only access to locked jobs, evidence and packs; export always free), stating the D07 retention/deletion policy it depends on and how a Vault tenant re-activates; (5) price points and per-archetype revenue (Firm at ~15 live and ~40 locked jobs a year; Contractor at 30+ live; state assumptions), marking each item included vs add-on so live jobs remain the single comparison number (report §'Three tiers work'). Constraints: none of it may vary with shadow signals before lock (§14.3); retention pricing must never create an incentive to delete evidence before lock; approval limits are authorization, never a basis for a charge.

gaps.area: Partner-side money not covered: contract administrators (architects, designers, PMs), retrofit and grant schemes, building control evidence, and builder-to-builder referral
gaps.why_it_matters: Channel ideas cover accountants (I61), trade bodies (I60), main contractors (I62), platforms (I63), subs (I64) and insurers (I37/I45/I46). Missing are the professionals who run larger domestic jobs and originate variations — architects, interior designers and project managers acting as contract administrator on £40k+ jobs, who issue instructions, value stages and certify payment; retrofit and grant schemes whose compliance rests on exactly the timestamped proof photos JobGuard already captures (PAS 2030/2035, TrustMark lodgement, MCS, Boiler Upgrade Scheme, ECO4/GBIS — Payaca charges clean-tech installers £299–£3,199 a month, report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'); building-control and notifiable-work evidence (Part P, Gas Safe, stage notifications); and the plain builder-to-builder referral credit that a word-of-mouth trade runs on. All are partner-side, none pays JobGuard from the merchant side, and none sells builder data.
gaps.generation_prompt: Produce four partner-side mechanisms with pricing and per-archetype estimates (stated assumptions): (a) Contract Administrator seat — an architect/designer/PM practice pays £X/month, or the homeowner pays per job, for a scoped role that issues written instructions, certifies stage completion against proof photos and values applications (M4-18); decide and justify against §14.2 whether a CA instruction received through JobGuard is customer-side evidence (a possible shadow source) or must be treated as capture-equivalent for fairness, and give the practice a referral share modelled on I61; (b) Retrofit/grant compliance pack — per-measure evidence pack mapped to PAS 2035 and TrustMark data-warehouse fields, MCS certificate and BUS voucher evidence, priced per lodgement (£X) or as a £Y/month installer add-on, with the scheme manager or retrofit coordinator as an optional payer; state D12/D04 constraints on sending homeowner data to a scheme; (c) Building-control evidence — stage-notification photo pack and certificate register the local authority or approved inspector can view by recipient-bound link (per pack or included on Firm), reusing M4-3/M5-9; (d) Builder-to-builder referral credit — one month's subscription per converted referral, paid only after the referred tenant has had a live job for 30 days and paid one period, capped per year, unique conversion identity rules as I64, a D09 credit that never offsets a success fee. For each give D-record dependencies (D06, D07, D12), and a one-line check against the three known trust risks.

ideas.name: Check this customer — business counterparty report, pay per check
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — paid third-party data, per check (business customers)
ideas.mechanism: Trigger: a 'Check this customer' button on the quote screen before send (M1-5), on the acceptance record (M1-6) and on the job page. Never blocking: send and acceptance proceed whether or not a check is running or has returned. Flow: builder types the customer name/company number; JobGuard resolves candidates from the Companies House API and the builder confirms the match (human confirmation, AGENTS §5.9). The sheet shows the price ('£19 ex VAT, added to your JobGuard statement') and the builder taps 'Run check', which creates and approves a Decision atomically (the 'Send this quote' pattern, AGENTS §5.3) bound to tenant, job/quote, counterparty entity ID, price and check-policy version. After commit a worker runs the adapters through the outbox (M0-9), never inside a transaction: Companies House (free: status, incorporation date, SIC, accounts and confirmation-statement due/overdue, registered charges, officers and PSCs, strike-off proposals, insolvency filings), The Gazette notices (free: winding-up petitions, administrations), a wholesale CRA company report (Creditsafe or Experian, assumed £5–£15, budget £8; usually includes company CCJs and a suggested credit limit) and, only if the CRA report lacks CCJ detail, a Registry Trust search (£6–£10). Raw provider responses are stored as verified evidence objects (SHA-256, object version ID, server receive time, provider and product version — AGENTS §5.8) of a new evidence type `counterparty_check`, tenant/job/quote-qualified. Results that arrive after the quote is sent post to the Decision Inbox advisory lane (M2-7) as a Finding. The card is headed 'Findings, not a recommendation' and every line names its source and retrieval date, e.g. 'Acme Interiors Ltd, 08123456, incorporated 2014, active'; 'Registered office differs from the site address'; 'Accounts overdue since 31 Mar 2026 (Companies House, 25 Sep 2026)'; '2 CCJs in the last 12 months totalling £4,300, 1 unsatisfied (Registry Trust)'; 'Creditsafe score 34/100 on their scale; suggested credit limit £5,000'; 'Director J Smith was a director of 2 companies that entered liquidation in the last 5 years'; 'Winding-up petitions: none found (Gazette)'. No traffic-light verdict, no 'do not proceed'. Action row, all existing ideas: 'Set a deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Attach the contract pack' (I33), 'Use stage escrow' (I42, when available), 'Ask the customer to confirm who is paying' (portal declaration), 'Noted, carry on'. Money: £19 per completed check charged to the tenant; a failed or `outcome_unknown` provider call is reconciled and not charged (AGENTS §5.4); charges appear as separate 'data checks' lines on the monthly platform statement (M4-10), never mixed with the subscription or the success fee. Measurement: checks run per quote, quote-to-live conversion on checked vs unchecked quotes, and later withheld-payment cases on checked vs unchecked customers (a pilot metric under §14.17).
ideas.who_pays: The builder (tenant), per completed check, on the platform statement. The customer never pays and never sees the report.

revenue_per_year.firm: £532 gross (about £308 margin) if on pay-per-check; see idea 2 for the allowance alternative

ideas.assumptions: Quotes per year from turnover ÷ average job ÷ win rate: Solo 19 jobs won ÷ 40% = 47 quotes; Small firm 24 ÷ 40% = 60; Firm 33 ÷ 35% = 95. Business-customer share of quotes: Solo 10% (5), Small 25% (15), Firm 50% (47). Attach rate on business quotes: 50% / 60% / 60%. Price £19 ex VAT; wholesale cost per check assumed £8–£10 (Companies House and Gazette free; CRA report £8; occasional Registry Trust £6–£10). Solo 5 × 0.5 × £19 = £48; Small 15 × 0.6 × £19 = £171; Firm 47 × 0.6 × £19 = £532. Sole-trader business customers are individuals and route to ideas 3–4, not this one. All figures ex VAT and unvalidated by any pilot.
ideas.trust_note: Builder pays, builder benefits, before they commit. No supplier or merchant money, no data sale, no lead generation, nothing withheld. Report is shown as attributed facts with the retrieved document openable, so the builder can see the work (the report's 'showing the work' finding). The one care point: the copy must never read as JobGuard advising refusal or vetting the builder's customers for its own fee purposes.
ideas.regulatory: UK GDPR for officer/PSC personal data: legitimate interests (Art 6(1)(f)); D12 v2 does not cover counterparty checks, so a D12 v3 must name the controller/processor split (builder as controller instructing the check is the candidate) and the Article 14 route — the quote email and portal page carry the privacy notice at first communication (Art 14(3)(b)), with a documented Art 14(5)(b) position for directors who are not the contact. Companies House and Gazette open-data terms. A CRA reseller agreement: reports are viewable in-app by the tenant only, not exportable or forwarded to the customer. No FCA permission is needed for company credit information (it is not consumer credit). D04: every provider is a UK destination and must be enumerated in the provider register. D07: CRA contracts may cap retention, which conflicts with keeping the check as recovery evidence — needs an explicit retention class. Charging for checks is a new platform charge: a new decision record (D14 'paid data services'), D02 VAT, D09 statement mechanics, real charging behind G4. In pilot_no_charge JobGuard absorbs check costs and labels the charge as hypothetical. Equality Act 2010: findings only, no recommendation, so the builder's decision remains theirs.
ideas.build_dependency: Needs M1-5 and M1-6 surfaces, M0-8 Decisions, M0-9 outbox and adapter contract tests with deterministic fakes, M0-11 versioned evidence, M0-12 provider register (D04), M2-7 advisory inbox lane, M4-10 statement lines for the charge. Suggested new tasks under 'Discovered later': CP-1 entity resolution plus Companies House/Gazette adapters and the card on free data (about 2 weeks, can ship in M2 with no charge); CP-2 CRA adapter and evidence type (2–3 weeks, needs the commercial contract); CP-3 check charging (after M4-10/M4-11, behind G4 and D14).
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder running checks on people who are not customers (competitors, ex-partners, neighbours): bind every check to a quote or job and a named counterparty on it, cap checks per quote, rate-limit per tenant, state the purpose in terms and audit every run. Forwarding the CRA report to the customer breaches the reseller contract: in-app view only, watermarked, no export of the raw report (the finding text can go in the builder's own evidence pack). Builders reading a score as JobGuard's advice: card wording and no colour verdicts.
ideas.precedent: Satago bundles credit reports and risk insights into credit-control software at £45–£200/month (https://www.satago.com/solutions/credit-control/; research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6). Chaser offers Creditsafe checks inside chasing (https://www.chaserhq.com/blog/best-credit-management-software). Creditsafe pay-per-report is reported at £5–£15 (https://www.businessdataguide.com/blog/comparisons/creditsafe-uk-vs-experian-uk). Registry Trust TrustOnline £6–£10 per search (https://www.registry-trust.org.uk/services/trustonline). No UK trade job app reviewed in the report offers a customer check (report §'No rival sells a final check…').

ideas.name: Check allowance inside the live-jobs tiers, with overage, included on Firm
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — subscription packaging of checks (not a change to the meter)
ideas.mechanism: The same checks as ideas 1, 3, 5 and 6 sold as a monthly allowance rather than per use, layered on the existing live-jobs ladder without touching the meter: a 'Checks' add-on of £12/month for 3 checks on Solo, £35/month for 12 checks on Builder, and 30 checks/month included in Firm's £119 (one of the reasons Firm is £119 rather than £99, per the report's Firm-price argument). Overage £15 per check beyond the allowance, never a block; unused checks do not roll over. Each check still needs the per-run Decision (idea 1) so the builder always sees 'this uses 1 of your 12 checks this month' or 'this is £15 overage'. Money: the add-on is a subscription obligation under D09 terms (M4-13) billed with the subscription; overage posts as statement lines (M4-10). Measurement: allowance utilisation per tier, overage frequency, and whether attach on quotes rises when the marginal check is 'free' (the reason to prefer an allowance: the report notes people prefer flat charges to a running meter).
ideas.who_pays: The builder, as a monthly add-on or inside the Firm price; overage per check.

revenue_per_year.solo: £29 (add-on) — do not add to idea 1; it is an alternative for the same checks
revenue_per_year.firm: £96 attributed from the Firm price plus £0 overage at expected volume

ideas.assumptions: Add-on attach: Solo 20% × £12 × 12 = £29; Small firm 35% × £35 × 12 = £147. Firm: £8/month of the £119 price is attributed to the included allowance (a labelled attribution, not new cash) = £96; expected Firm check volume (about 28 business checks plus 17 property checks a year, ideas 1 and 3) is far below 360, so overage is £0. Wholesale cost per check as in ideas 1 and 3 (£7–£10), so the add-on margin is thin at full utilisation and healthy at typical utilisation; the pack is priced assuming 40–60% utilisation.
ideas.trust_note: Flat, predictable and builder-paid. The only trap is unused allowances feeling like waste; keep the per-check option (idea 1) alongside so nobody is forced onto a pack.
ideas.regulatory: Same data-protection and CRA terms as ideas 1 and 3. The add-on is subscription pricing, so it is a D09 v3 item (tier inclusions and overage terms, price-change notice, cancellation) plus D05 for renewal authority and D02 VAT; production charging behind G4.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-13 subscription terms and M4-14 metering (allowance counters are a second meter alongside live jobs), M4-10 overage lines; depends on the check adapters in ideas 1 and 3. About 1–2 weeks once the checks exist.
ideas.gaming_risk: Sharing one Firm account's allowance across unrelated businesses: allowance is per tenant and every check is bound to a quote or job in that tenant. Burst-checking prospects at month end to use up the pack: harmless to JobGuard's margin at these volumes; cap checks per quote.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 sells workload allowances with unlimited users (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). Satago's fixed tiers bundle credit reports (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6). The report's 'two months free' and flat-fee preference findings support a pack over a running meter.

ideas.name: Homeowner property and public-record check (title register, CCJ and insolvency registers, no credit data)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — paid public-register data for domestic customers
ideas.mechanism: Trigger as idea 1 but for a customer who is an individual (homeowner, landlord, sole trader). Two separately priced parts, each its own Decision. Part A, 'Property check' £12: JobGuard orders the HM Land Registry official copy of the title register for the site address (£7 digital fee) through HMLR Business e-services, stores it as `counterparty_check` evidence and extracts: registered proprietor names, tenure (freehold/leasehold, lease term remaining), registered charges (lender), restrictions (e.g. a Form A restriction, a bankruptcy restriction, a management-company consent requirement), and the date of the last transfer. Part B, 'Named-person public-record check' £10: a Registry Trust search of the Register of Judgments, Orders and Fines against the name and address the builder quoted (£6–£10 wholesale) plus the free Insolvency Service Individual Insolvency Register (bankruptcy, IVA, DRO). No consumer credit file is touched. Card lines (findings only): 'Title held by J Smith and K Smith; your quote is addressed to Mr P Jones — different name to the quote'; 'Leasehold, 62 years remaining; a restriction requires the freeholder's consent to certain dealings'; 'Charge registered to Barclays Bank'; 'CCJs against P Jones at this address: 1 in the last 6 years, £1,850, unsatisfied (Registry Trust, 25 Sep 2026)'; 'Insolvency register: no entry'. Action row: 'Ask the customer to confirm the paying party and their authority to instruct the work' (portal declaration, feeds I33), 'Set a deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Use stage escrow' (I42), 'Noted, carry on'. Free alternative shown first: the customer can confirm ownership themselves in the portal by giving their title number or uploading their own £7 copy, at no charge, which JobGuard records as customer-provided evidence. Money: per-part charges on the platform statement as in idea 1. Measurement: name-mismatch rate on quotes, share of checks where the customer self-verified instead.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per part (£12 property, £10 named-person). Never the homeowner.
ideas.assumptions: Homeowner quotes: Solo 42, Small 45, Firm 48 (from idea 1's quote counts and mix). Share of those at £5k+ where a check is plausible: 60% / 80% / 90%. Property-check attach on those: 30% / 35% / 40% → Solo 7.5, Small 12.6, Firm 17.3 checks × £12 = £90 / £151 / £207. Named-person add-on taken on half of those × £10 = £38 / £63 / £86. Wholesale: HMLR £7 (confirmed current digital fee), Registry Trust £6–£8 assumed at volume, IIR free; margins £5 and £2–£4 per part. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Builder-paid and in the builder's interest, and it uses public registers only. Slight awkwardness: a homeowner who later learns (for example via a data-subject access request) that their builder ran a CCJ search may feel judged; the notice route below and the free self-verification path soften that. The mismatch finding is genuinely protective for both sides (work instructed by a non-owner is a classic non-payment and dispute pattern).
ideas.regulatory: Title register data and CCJ register data are public but proprietor and defendant names are personal data: legitimate interests (Art 6(1)(f)) with a recorded balancing test; Article 14 notice through the quote email/portal privacy notice at first communication, naming that ownership and public-register checks may be run for jobs above a value (D12 v3). No consumer credit file, so no CRA consumer permissible-purpose issue and no Consumer Credit Act s.157–160 file-access issue. HMLR Business e-services terms (use for the stated purpose; re-use restrictions on official copies). Registry Trust terms. Equality Act: findings only. D04 register entries (HMLR, Registry Trust, Insolvency Service are UK). D07 retention class for the copies. Charging: D14 plus D02, behind G4; pilot absorbs.
ideas.build_dependency: Same foundations as idea 1 plus an HMLR Business e-services adapter (OC1 official copy ordering and a title-register extraction parser with a golden set under M0-12's eval harness), a Registry Trust adapter and an IIR lookup; the customer self-verification step needs the homeowner portal. About 3 weeks after CP-1; the extraction parser is the risky part (register text is semi-structured).
ideas.gaming_risk: Checking a property the builder has no quote for (nosiness, disputes with neighbours): bind to a quote address and cap per quote. Name-matching false positives on common names: show the search terms used and the register's own address match; never assert identity, only 'an entry matching the searched name and address'. Builders using a CCJ finding to demand unreasonable deposits: outside JobGuard's control; card wording stays factual.
ideas.precedent: Tenant referencing services run consented public-record and ownership checks on individuals for landlords at roughly £15–£30 per reference (assumption; no UK trade-app precedent for customer checks found in the report). HMLR £7 official copy fee confirmed (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/changes-to-fees-for-hm-land-registrys-information-services). Registry Trust £6–£10 per search (https://www.registry-trust.org.uk/services/trustonline).

ideas.name: Consented homeowner soft search ('Verify me') for large domestic jobs
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — consumer credit data with the customer's consent (borderline)
ideas.mechanism: Available only for domestic quotes above a threshold (assume £10k) and only after the builder asks for it at quote-send or acceptance. JobGuard sends nothing itself to a credit file on the builder's say-so; instead the customer's portal page (the quote view or acceptance page) shows a 'Verify me' step: the customer reads the CRA's own notice, ticks consent, and JobGuard runs a soft (quotation-type) search through one UK CRA that leaves no lender-visible footprint. The builder sees a narrow, factual card: 'Customer completed verification on 26 Sep 2026: identity and address confirmed against the credit file; CRA affordability indicator: [CRA's own band and wording]; adverse public data: none on file' — never the file itself and never a score presented as JobGuard's view. Declining is a normal outcome shown as 'Customer did not verify' with no further comment. Money: £15 per completed consented search charged to the builder (assumed wholesale £2–£4 per search plus a CRA minimum annual contract, assumed £10k, carried by JobGuard); consent-declined runs cost nothing. Links: on completion the portal offers the customer the stage schedule for approval (I40) and the contract pack (I33); the verification record goes into the job's evidence. Measurement: request rate, consent rate, drop-off in acceptance after a verify request (the key risk metric), later non-payment on verified vs unverified jobs.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per completed search; the homeowner pays nothing and controls consent.
ideas.assumptions: Homeowner quotes at £10k+: Solo 42 × 30% = 12.6; Small 45 × 50% = 22.5; Firm 48 × 70% = 33.6. Builder requests verification on 40% / 50% / 50%; customer consents 50%. Completed searches: 2.5 / 5.6 / 8.4 × £15 = £38 / £84 / £126. Platform-level: at £3 wholesale and a £10k CRA minimum, JobGuard needs roughly 800 completed searches a year across all tenants to break even, which is about 150 active builders at these rates — a fixed cost, not a per-unit one. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Borderline. Asking a homeowner to submit to a credit search to get a kitchen fitted can cost the builder the job, and it is the first place JobGuard touches a consumer's credit file, which changes what JobGuard is. It is in the builder's interest on big jobs, and consent sits with the customer, but the report's fairness research suggests the customer may resent it. Off by default; a builder must switch it on and it never applies below the threshold.
ideas.regulatory: Consent as lawful basis (Art 6(1)(a)) captured by the CRA-approved wording, with UK GDPR Art 13 notice served directly to the customer at the point of consent (no Art 14 issue for this part). CRA commercial agreement with a permitted purpose (quotation/verification), which typically includes CRA vetting of the end-user population and restrictions on what can be shown to the builder; Consumer Credit Act 1974 s.157–160 obligations sit with the CRA but JobGuard must handle disputes and corrections routing. SCOR reciprocity rules do not apply to a soft search but JobGuard must confirm the product does not require data contribution. ICO guidance on credit referencing; Equality Act (no adverse decision advice). D12 v3 (new consumer data category), D04 (CRA UK route), D07 (CRA-mandated deletion windows), D14 plus D02 for the charge; G1 before any real consumer file is touched, charging behind G4. Legal review required before build; this is not an agent inference.
ideas.build_dependency: Homeowner portal quote/acceptance page, M0-8 Decision for the builder's request, M0-9 adapter with deterministic fake, M0-11 evidence, M0-12 provider register; a CRA contract and its end-user vetting are the long pole (months), so this is an M4-era item at the earliest. Engineering about 3 weeks once the contract exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low on JobGuard's side because the customer consents and the CRA controls the data. Builder-side: using the request to pressure customers or to discriminate; JobGuard can only keep the copy neutral and the threshold high. Fake consent via the builder filling the portal on the customer's device: the consent event is bound to the customer's authenticated portal session, not the builder's.
ideas.precedent: Tenant referencing (Goodlord, HomeLet and similar) performs consented consumer checks for landlords per reference; Paddle Retain/ Satago style verification is not comparable. No UK trade software precedent found in the report. Broker commission and IDD disclosure norms are irrelevant here; CRA commercial terms are the binding precedent.

ideas.name: Property constraints check: listed building, conservation area, Article 4, planning history and flood risk at the site address
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — site and consent facts from open data (low price, near-zero data cost)
ideas.mechanism: Trigger at quote creation or send: 'Check this address' (£5) or included in the checks allowance (idea 2). JobGuard resolves the site address to a UPRN and queries open datasets: Historic England's National Heritage List (listed status and grade), the government planning data platform (conservation areas, Article 4 directions, tree preservation orders, listed-building outlines where published), local authority planning application records via an aggregator where available, and the Environment Agency flood-risk data. Card lines, facts with sources and dates: 'Grade II listed (NHLE 1234567). Internal and external alterations may need listed building consent; carrying out works without consent is an offence for the person who executes them'; 'In the Old Town conservation area; an Article 4 direction removes permitted development for front elevations'; 'Planning history: application 24/01234/HSE (rear extension) approved 12 Mar 2026 with 4 conditions'; 'Coverage note: this council's planning records are not in the national dataset; treat as unchecked'. No legal conclusion is drawn; the card links to the source pages. Actions: 'Add a consent condition to the quote' (quote condition text, builder-authored), 'Attach the contract pack' (I33), 'Flag to site readiness' (M2-6 readiness model so the readiness check asks for the consent document before start), 'Noted'. Money: £5 per address on the statement or allowance; data licences are open (OGL) so the cost is engineering and aggregator fees where used. Measurement: share of quotes with a constraint hit, and how often a readiness check later blocks for missing consent.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, £5 per address or from the allowance; could be included in Builder and above as a differentiator if the founder prefers.
ideas.assumptions: Domestic quotes (42 / 45 / 48) × attach 40% / 45% / 50% × £5 = £84 / £101 / £120. Data cost about £0 (Historic England, planning.data.gov.uk and Environment Agency are open data); an aggregator for council planning records assumed at up to £100/month platform-wide. Margin is almost entirely gross revenue. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Pure prevention in the builder's interest, no third party pays, no customer data beyond an address. Strongest fit in the lens. The only honesty point is coverage: national datasets are incomplete, so the card must say 'not checked' rather than 'none found' where data is absent.
ideas.regulatory: Address-level open data is not personal data in itself; planning application records contain applicant names, so show application references and decisions, not applicant names (data minimisation). Open Government Licence terms for the datasets; aggregator terms. The listed-building offence statement is a fact of the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990 but the wording must be reviewed so it is not legal advice (a D06-style reviewed-wording decision). D04 entries for any aggregator. No charge-specific regulation beyond D14/D02 for the £5.
ideas.build_dependency: UPRN resolution (OS Places or the free OS Open UPRN plus address matching), open-data adapters with contract tests, the M2-6 site-readiness factual adapters as the natural home. About 2 weeks; can ship in M2 free, priced later behind G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Minimal. Builders may quote it to customers as JobGuard's legal view: the card carries the source link and a 'facts, not advice' label. Stale data: show dataset publication dates.
ideas.precedent: Conveyancing search providers sell environmental and planning searches to solicitors for tens of pounds; no small-trade app reviewed in the report offers a constraints check. Buildertrend/Procore-type suites do not either (report §'No rival sells a final check…').

ideas.name: 'Who actually pays?' payer-chain check for subcontract, landlord, managing-agent and insurer-funded jobs
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — paid data on the paying party where it differs from the site customer
ideas.mechanism: At quote-send or acceptance JobGuard asks one question: 'Who will pay this invoice?' with options 'the customer named on the quote', 'a main contractor', 'a landlord or managing agent', 'a housing association or council', 'an insurer's contractor network', 'other'. When the payer differs, the builder names the payer entity and the check runs on that entity (idea 1's business data plus Companies House registered charges, group parent and recent filings, plus the Gazette) and records the site customer separately. The card adds payer-specific facts: 'Payer: BuildCo Main Contractors Ltd; 3 CCJs in 12 months; accounts overdue; parent company registered in Jersey'; 'Payer's payment practices report (gov.uk Payment Practices and Performance data, if the payer is large enough to file): average 52 days to pay, 31% of invoices paid late'; 'Your quote names the homeowner but the payer is the managing agent — the contract pack should name the payer'. Includes a 90-day watch (idea 8's monitoring) in the price so the builder is told if a winding-up petition or strike-off notice appears during the job. Actions: 'Name the payer in the contract pack' (I33), 'Applications for payment schedule' (the existing commercial add-on), 'Deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Noted'. Money: £29 per payer check (assumed wholesale £8 report plus £2–£4 for the watch). Measurement: share of jobs with a distinct payer, later withheld-payment cases by payer type. The payer identity is the single most useful fact for a later D03 case: the Late Payment Act interest and compensation only apply to business debtors (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §3), and a recovery case needs the right legal entity.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per payer check. Off-quote payers are common at Firm scale.
ideas.assumptions: Jobs per year where the payer differs from the site customer: Solo 2, Small firm 6, Firm 15 (assumed from the business-customer mix). Attach 30% / 40% / 60% × £29 = £17 / £70 / £261. Wholesale £10–£12 including the watch, margin about £17 per check. Payment Practices reporting data exists only for large companies (turnover above £36m etc.), so that line appears for a minority of payers. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Clean: the builder pays to learn about the entity that controls their cash flow. It also quietly teaches the builder to contract with the right party, which is the biggest single cause of unrecoverable construction debt. No conflict with any known trust risk.
ideas.regulatory: As idea 1 (company data, officers under legitimate interests, Article 14 route through the first communication with the payer — which for a main contractor may be the order acknowledgement rather than the quote, so the notice must also sit in the contract pack). Payment Practices and Performance data is open government data. D12 v3 category, D04 entries, D14 plus D02 for the charge, G4 for real charging.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1's CP-1/CP-2 adapters plus a payer-party field on the quote/job (M0-7 job spine: a `paying_party` reference distinct from the customer, tenant-qualified) and the I33 contract-pack hook. Monitoring from idea 8. About 2 weeks on top of idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Naming a payer who has not agreed to pay does not make them liable: the card states that the check does not create a contract and offers the contract-pack step. Checks on unrelated companies: bound to a quote or job and rate-limited as in idea 1.
ideas.precedent: Satago and Chaser risk insights on debtors (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6). Payapps-style main-contractor tools (report §'No rival sells…') sit on the other side of the chain and do not check the payer for the subcontractor. Payment Practices reporting is a UK statutory dataset (assumed usable under OGL).

ideas.name: Block-works check: RMC/RTM company and Section 20 consultation status for flats and managed blocks
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — niche statutory-risk check for leasehold block work
ideas.mechanism: Trigger when the customer is a residents' management company, RTM company, freeholder or managing agent, or the site is a block of flats. Two parts in one £39 check. Part 1: the company data of idea 1 on the RMC/RTM/freeholder, with the accounts read for the reserve fund and service-charge arrears figures where filed. Part 2: a structured, builder-completed questionnaire with dated document uploads: was a Notice of Intention served; a Notice of Estimates; were leaseholder observations answered; is there a Tribunal dispensation. JobGuard's card then states facts only: 'Reserve fund shown in the last filed accounts: £14,200; your quote is £48,000'; 'No Notice of Estimates recorded. For qualifying works, without consultation or a dispensation the landlord's recovery from each leaseholder is limited to £250 (Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.20; Service Charges (Consultation Requirements) (England) Regulations 2003)'; '38 leaseholders × £250 = £9,500 recoverable without consultation against a £48,000 quote'. No advice to refuse, no legal conclusion about this contract. Actions: 'Ask the managing agent to upload the s.20 notices' (portal request, stored as evidence), 'Set a deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Applications for payment schedule' (existing commercial add-on), 'Noted'. Money: £39 per block check on the statement (wholesale about £8 for the company report). Measurement: share of block jobs with incomplete consultation at quote; later withheld-payment cases on block jobs.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per block check. Relevant mainly to Small firms and Firms doing external works, roofs and communal areas.
ideas.assumptions: Block/managed-flat jobs per year: Solo 0.3, Small firm 1.5, Firm 4. Attach 30% / 40% / 50% × £39 = £4 / £23 / £78. Wholesale £8; margin about £31 per check. The £250 threshold and consultation stages are as the 2003 Regulations state; the block's leaseholder count comes from the title/lease data or the agent. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Builder-paid prevention of a specific, well-known way block work goes unpaid. No trust conflict. Care point: the statutory wording must be reviewed so a builder does not treat JobGuard as their solicitor.
ideas.regulatory: Company data as idea 1. The s.20 statement is a reviewed fixed text (D06-style legal wording review) and must be presented as a statutory fact, not as advice on the builder's contract. Leaseholder names must never be collected; only counts. D12 v3, D14 plus D02 for the charge; G4 for real charging.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 adapters, a questionnaire form with dated evidence uploads (M0-11), the reviewed statutory text as a versioned fixture. About 1–2 weeks on top of idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: A managing agent uploading forged notices: JobGuard stores what it was given with receive times and hashes; it does not verify authenticity (AGENTS §5.8 limits) and the card says so. Builders misquoting the £250 figure to agents: the text is fixed and sourced.
ideas.precedent: None known as a product; the s.20 cap is a standard leasehold-practice risk described by property law firms. Site Samurai and Payapps (report §'No rival sells…') cover payment applications but not consultation status.

ideas.name: 'Watch this customer': live counterparty monitoring through the job (business customers and payers only)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence extended through the job — recurring data subscription per monitored counterparty
ideas.mechanism: After switch-live, a business customer or named payer that has been checked can be watched until the final invoice is paid. Sources: Companies House streaming API (free: new charges, officer resignations, strike-off proposals, accounts overdue, insolvency events), The Gazette (free: petitions, administrations), a CRA monitoring product for new CCJs and score changes (assumed wholesale £0.50–£1 per entity per month), and Registry Trust monitoring where offered. Each event becomes a Finding in the Decision Inbox advisory lane (M2-7) with the source and date: 'A winding-up petition against BuildCo Main Contractors Ltd was advertised in the Gazette on 3 Oct 2026'; 'New CCJ £6,200 registered 14 Oct 2026'. Watchdog checks stay pure functions producing Findings; nothing is sent, charged or decided. Actions: 'Bring forward the next application for payment' (existing commercial add-on), 'Open a withheld-payment case' (only if the D03 entry test is already met; otherwise the action is hidden), 'Noted'. Homeowners are not monitored (disproportionate under UK GDPR and unwelcome); for domestic jobs the only re-check offered is a fresh £7 title-register copy before a large stage invoice, at pass-through price plus £2, to catch a mid-job sale or new charge. Money: £3 per monitored counterparty per month, pro rata, from switch-live to final payment recorded; stops automatically when the job closes. Measurement: events per monitored entity, time from event to builder action, withheld-payment outcomes on watched vs unwatched jobs.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per monitored business counterparty per month; domestic title re-checks at pass-through plus £2.
ideas.assumptions: Business jobs won per year: Solo 1.9, Small firm 6, Firm 16.5; average live duration 2 / 3 / 4 months; attach 50% / 60% / 70%; £3/month. Solo 1.9 × 2 × 0.5 × £3 = £6; Small 6 × 3 × 0.6 × £3 = £32; Firm 16.5 × 4 × 0.7 × £3 = £139. Wholesale £0.50–£1 per entity-month, so margin about two thirds. Domestic title re-checks are excluded from the figures (assumed rare). Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and builder-paid. Slight discomfort if a builder feels JobGuard is nudging them toward opening a 10% withheld-payment case; mitigate by only showing the case action when the D03 entry test is independently met and by the fee terms being approved per case (§14.7). Homeowner monitoring is excluded on purpose.
ideas.regulatory: Ongoing processing of officer/PSC personal data under legitimate interests with a documented balancing test and a defined stop point (job closed); D12 v3 must cover monitoring as a purpose and the Article 14 route; D07 retention for event records; D04 entries for the streaming and monitoring providers; CRA monitoring contract terms. The D03 entry test remains unchanged: monitoring events never satisfy it. D14 plus D02 for the charge; G4 for real charging.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 adapters, a scheduled/streaming worker under Graphile Worker (M0-9) with idempotent event identities, M2-6 scheduled-check pattern, M2-7 inbox lanes. About 2 weeks after idea 1. A domestic re-check reuses idea 3's HMLR adapter.
ideas.gaming_risk: Duplicate or out-of-order provider events: unique source-event IDs (AGENTS §5.4). A builder keeping a job 'live' to keep watching a company they have no contract with: monitoring stops when the job closes and is bound to a job with an accepted quote.
ideas.precedent: Satago 'real-time alerts of changes' and Creditsafe/Experian monitoring products (https://www.satago.com/solutions/credit-control/; research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6). HMLR Property Alert is owner-only, hence the title re-check design.

ideas.name: Exposure-vs-limit finding on the stage schedule (Builder tier and above)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — subscription feature that turns check data into a factual exposure curve
ideas.mechanism: When a check (idea 1 or 6) returns a CRA suggested credit limit and the quote has a deposit and stage schedule (I40) or the default 'pay on completion' terms, a pure function in packages/core computes the builder's peak unpaid exposure over time from the schedule: cumulative value of work done (by stage) minus cumulative payments due before that point, exact money arithmetic. The card shows a small chart and the numbers: 'Peak unpaid exposure under these terms: £12,400 after stage 3 (week 6). The credit report's suggested limit for this company is £5,000 (Creditsafe, 25 Sep 2026)'. It is a comparison of two facts, not a recommendation; the copy does not say 'reduce exposure'. Actions: 'Edit the deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Use stage escrow' (I42), 'Noted'. On editing, the curve updates live so the builder sees the effect of their own choice. Money: no per-use charge; it is a Builder-and-above feature, part of the Watchdog tier's value story. Measurement: share of checked business quotes where the builder edits the schedule after seeing the curve; later exposure at the point a withheld-payment case opens.
ideas.who_pays: Included in Builder and Firm subscriptions; no separate charge. Solo sees the check but not the curve (or sees it with an upgrade prompt).
ideas.assumptions: No direct revenue; £2/month of the Builder/Firm price is attributed to the feature as a retention/upsell justification, labelled as attribution. Requires the stage schedule (I40) to exist; without it the curve uses the quote's payment terms. Exact arithmetic on Money pence, half-even where rounding is needed. Unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and it makes the third-party limit useful without JobGuard advising. Edge: a chart comparing exposure to a limit is close to advice; the wording must stay descriptive and the limit must be attributed to the CRA, never to JobGuard.
ideas.regulatory: None beyond the check's own terms (idea 1) and CRA display rules for suggested limits (some CRAs restrict on-screen display of derived figures; confirm in the reseller contract). Not financial advice as long as no recommendation is made; legal wording review of the card copy.
ideas.build_dependency: I40 deposit/stage schedule model, idea 1's check evidence, a pure exposure-curve function with property tests in packages/core, a small chart in the web client. About 1 week after I40 and idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material; the curve is derived from the builder's own schedule and a third-party figure. Stale limits: show the retrieval date and offer a re-check.
ideas.precedent: Credit-control tools show recommended credit limits against outstanding balances (Satago risk insights; research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6). No trade app shows exposure against a schedule.

ideas.name: Check record as recovery evidence: identity and terms proof for the D03 withheld-payment entry test and the I34 evidence pack
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — no separate charge; strengthens the existing 10% withheld-payment category
ideas.mechanism: Every check (ideas 1, 3, 6, 7) and every customer portal declaration ('I am the owner / I am authorised to instruct this work / the payer is X') is stored as tenant/job-qualified verified evidence with hashes, object version IDs and receive times (AGENTS §5.8). Later, if the builder opens a withheld-payment case (§14.7: overdue beyond the D03 threshold, customer refused/disputed/ignored the builder's own reminder, builder explicitly opens and approves the fee terms), the case workbench (M4-1) pre-fills from that evidence: the debtor's exact legal identity and registered/service address, the fact that the invoice names the same party that accepted the quote, the deposit and stage terms the customer approved in the portal, and the owner/authority declaration. The M4-5 reviewed pursuit templates then address the right entity first time, and the I34 evidence pack gains a 'Counterparty and terms' section containing the check findings, the declarations and the acceptance record. Checks are never a precondition for the fee and never change the 10%; they only make cases easier to open correctly and to settle. Money: none directly; revenue is the incremental success fee from cases that settle because the identity and terms evidence exists. Measurement: settlement rate and days-to-settle on cases with and without a pre-contract check; pursuit letters returned or re-addressed.
ideas.who_pays: Nobody extra. The existing 10% success fee on cash settled after case opening is the only money; the check itself was paid for under ideas 1/3/6/7.
ideas.assumptions: Withheld-payment cases opened per year: Solo 1 at £2,000; Small firm 2 at £5,000; Firm 4 at £12,000 (assumptions). Having verified identity and approved terms lifts the settled-cash rate by 10 percentage points. Incremental fee = cases × value × 0.10 uplift × 10% fee: Solo £20, Small £100, Firm £480. Only cash settled after case opening counts (§14.7) and ordinary late payment never qualifies. Highly uncertain; the uplift is a guess to be measured in the pilot (§14.17).
ideas.trust_note: Genuinely in the builder's interest (they keep 90% of money they were not going to get), and it makes JobGuard's own recovery work cheaper. The risk is optics: if checks are ever marketed as 'so JobGuard can chase for you', a builder may feel the check was upsold to feed JobGuard's fee. Keep checks framed as prevention, keep the raw export free, and never make a check a condition of the fee.
ideas.regulatory: Reuse of check data for pursuit is a new purpose for the officer/proprietor personal data: D12 v3 must name it and the Article 14 notice must mention it; CRA reseller terms often prohibit using a report in litigation or debt collection without their permission, so the pack may include JobGuard's finding text and public-register copies but not the CRA report itself; D03 v2 entry test unchanged; regulated-activity position as in research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §7 (helping a builder collect its own invoice is not FCA debt collecting on the sources found; legal sign-off required).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-1 case workbench, M4-2 attribution review, M4-3 evidence packs (add a section type), M4-5 pursuit templates; evidence links from ideas 1/3/6/7. About 1 week of integration once those exist; no new providers.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder opening a case on a customer who is merely late to get JobGuard's templates: the D03 entry test and per-case fee approval already gate this; the check record does not weaken it. Contradictory evidence (declaration says owner, title says otherwise): both are shown with dates; JobGuard asserts neither.
ideas.precedent: Debt collectors and solicitors require debtor identity and terms evidence before instruction (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §3 and §7). Chaser pairs risk data with its collections service (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6).

ideas.name: JobGuard network payment-experience signal on business customers (give-to-get, flagged)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — pooled builder-contributed data (trust risk: builders' data reused)
ideas.mechanism: Only for limited companies and LLPs, never individuals or sole traders. A tenant may opt in to contribute facts JobGuard already holds about its own invoices to business customers: invoice date, due date, date the payment was recorded, disputed yes/no. In return, the 'Check this customer' card gains one line built from other opted-in tenants' facts, aggregated and thresholded (minimum 3 contributing tenants, no tenant identities, no free text): 'Across JobGuard builders who have invoiced this company in the last 24 months: 7 invoices, paid on average 41 days after the due date; 2 disputed'. Below the threshold the line says 'Not enough JobGuard data'. Contribution and display are symmetric: no contribution, no line. Money: £5/month add-on for business-heavy tenants who want the line without contributing, or free with contribution; the honest version is free-with-contribution and the add-on is the fallback. Measurement: contribution opt-in rate, coverage of business customers, predictive value against later withheld-payment cases.
ideas.who_pays: The builder: contribution in kind (their own invoice facts) or £5/month.
ideas.assumptions: Solo has too few business customers to buy it (£0). Small firm 20% × £5 × 12 = £12; Firm 70% × £5 × 12 = £42, assuming most buyers choose contribution over cash, so cash revenue is small by design. Value depends on network density: below several hundred business-invoicing tenants the line rarely reaches threshold. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Flagged. This is builders' data reused across tenants, one of the named trust risks, and a company that finds itself described as a slow payer may complain to the builder who invoiced it. It is the established CRA trade-payment-data pattern, and restricting it to companies, to facts JobGuard itself recorded, to aggregates and to opt-in contributors keeps it defensible, but it should be off by default and possibly never built.
ideas.regulatory: Company payment behaviour is not personal data, but a sole trader's is, hence the exclusion; officer names are not shown. Contributing tenants' terms must permit the reuse (a D09/terms change) and each builder's customer contract or notice should mention it (D12 v3). Accuracy duties: facts only, from JobGuard's own invoice and payment records, with a correction route for the customer company (Article 16 style even where not strictly personal data). Defamation risk is low for factual aggregates but the wording must be reviewed. D07 retention window (24 months assumed).
ideas.build_dependency: Cross-tenant aggregation is a deliberate exception to tenant isolation and needs its own reviewed read model with a separate role and RLS exemption tests (AGENTS §5.1), plus M1-12 invoice and payment records as the fact source. About 3 weeks; a D-record and legal review before any real data.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder recording fake late payments to smear a customer: facts come only from issued invoices and recorded receipts within JobGuard, disputes are counted not narrated, thresholds hide single contributors, and D11-style advisory signals flag tenants whose contributions are outliers. A customer company pressuring a builder to withdraw its contribution: contributions are anonymous and aggregated.
ideas.precedent: Creditsafe and Experian trade-payment-data programmes aggregate contributed ledger data; the UK Payment Practices reporting regime publishes large companies' payment performance. No trade-app precedent (report §'No rival sells…').

ideas.name: Trade credit insurance introduction for firms with business customers (insurer-paid commission; regulated; off by default)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — regulated insurance introduction (variant, like I43/I46)
ideas.mechanism: For tenants whose checked business-customer exposure (idea 9) exceeds a threshold (assume £25k peak exposure or £250k annual business invoicing), the check card can show one neutral line: 'Some firms insure business invoices against non-payment. Learn about trade credit insurance' linking to an FCA-authorised broker or insurer partner. JobGuard does nothing beyond the introduction: no advice, no comparison, no quote handling, no policy administration. If the tenant buys cover, the partner pays JobGuard an introducer commission from its own commission on the premium. Disclosure appears on the line itself ('JobGuard may be paid by the partner if you take out cover'). The cover, if bought, can be recorded as evidence on jobs so that the readiness and withheld-payment flows know a policy exists (the insurer's claim conditions often require timely notification). Money: commission per policy paid by the partner to JobGuard; nothing from the builder. Measurement: click-through, policies bound, and whether insured builders open fewer withheld-payment cases (an honest conflict: an insured builder claims from the insurer instead of paying JobGuard 10%).
ideas.who_pays: The insurer or broker, via introducer commission. The builder pays the insurer a premium, not JobGuard.
ideas.assumptions: Take-up among eligible tenants: Solo 0% (no business book); Small firm 10% at an assumed £2,000 annual premium; Firm 25% at £5,000. Broker commission on premium assumed 12.5–25% (source below); JobGuard's introducer share assumed 7.5% of premium. Small 0.10 × £2,000 × 0.075 = £15; Firm 0.25 × £5,000 × 0.075 = £94. Trade credit insurance is usually whole-turnover and often has minimum premiums above what a small firm will pay, so take-up may be lower. Unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Insurer money flowing to JobGuard for pointing builders at a product is a mild conflict, and it competes with JobGuard's own withheld-payment fee (a fully insured builder has less reason to open a case). It does not touch the supplier-invoice watchdog and does not use the builder's customers as leads, so it is cleaner than merchant money. Still: regulated, disclosed, off by default, one partner, no ranking.
ideas.regulatory: Introducing insurance business is an insurance distribution activity unless an exclusion applies (RAO art. 72C 'provision of information on an incidental basis' and PERG 5.6 introducer guidance); taking commission and providing exposure figures may take JobGuard outside the exclusion, so treat it as needing either FCA authorisation, appointed-representative/introducer-appointed-representative status with the partner, or a confirmed exclusion by counsel. ICOBS/IDD remuneration disclosure. Data sharing with the partner needs D12 v3 and D04 entries; the builder's consent to be introduced. A new decision record (like I43/I46) and G4-equivalent gate before any live introduction.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 9's exposure figures and a partner agreement; the technical build is a link, a consent record and an evidence type for the policy (about 1 week). The regulatory route is the dependency, not the code.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. The partner could pressure for placement or ranking: contractually one partner, one neutral line, no performance-based placement. JobGuard steering builders toward cover to earn commission: the line only appears above the threshold and the copy is fixed and reviewed.
ideas.precedent: Chaser and Satago sit near invoice finance and credit insurance offers (research_notes success_fee_benchmarks §6); broker commission 12.5–25% of premium is reported for commercial lines (https://apexinsurancebrokers.co.uk/pi-broker-fees-and-commissions-explained-uk-2026/); FCA PERG 5.6 introducer guidance (https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/perg5). Allianz Trade, Atradius and Coface are the UK trade-credit insurers, reached through brokers.

ideas.name: Supplier rate renegotiation savings share (`supplier_rate_renegotiation_savings`, D03 v3 category)
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (new D03 v3 row; new D01 rate and ceiling)
ideas.mechanism: §14.7-style row. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) a prior agreed rate for (merchant, SKU alias, unit/pack) exists as an M2-1 agreed-rate revision AND is evidenced by at least two matched, settled invoice lines at that rate in the 6 months before the letter (a rate-book entry with no invoice evidence never counts); (2) the builder approved and sent, through the command boundary with an approved Decision, a JobGuard-drafted 'rate review letter' naming the SKUs, built only from their own purchase history and, where opted in, I28 benchmark bands — the letter's send record is the case-opening event, exactly as case-opening is for withheld payments; the builder accepts the rate-review fee terms at that moment; (3) a new, lower agreed-rate revision for a named SKU is human-confirmed from intake lines (M2-3) within 90 days of the letter, with effective date on or after the letter date; (4) savings are measured monthly from invoices: Q = Σ over matched (M2-4), human-confirmed, SETTLED (M4-7 bank feed) invoice lines dated within 12 months of the new revision's effective date of (prior_rate − invoiced_rate)⁺ × quantity, unit-normalised, net of VAT, kept as an exact rational — so the fee is capped by quantity actually bought and by cash actually paid; (5) F = roundHalfEven(min(Q × 20/100, ceiling)) with a fairness ceiling of £1,000 per (merchant, letter) in the reference policy; J = prior posted; posting_delta = F − J on each monthly statement, one rounding on the cumulative value (§14.9). NEVER QUALIFIES: SKUs not named in the letter; a rate revision confirmed before the letter or more than 90 days after; savings the builder attests were a merchant-wide list-price cut or a market fall (builder-favourable: the attestation stops accrual, fee-free, no proof demanded); switching merchant (see the separate flagged idea); backdated refunds of already-paid invoices (those are cash refunds and fall under the ordinary 10% `supplier_overcharge` mechanics, never the 20% share); unsettled invoice lines; invoices where new delivery/surcharge lines appear that offset the unit-rate cut (held for review, not accrued); any credit-note-only outcome. REVERSALS: credit notes on counted lines reduce Q; a later rate rise simply stops accrual; Q never negative; a negative delta creates a linked compensating journal and a refund if collected; history is never edited. TRUST RULE (explicit): JobGuard never contacts, negotiates with, or receives anything from a merchant; the builder negotiates; the watchdog then checks every invoice against the new agreed rate exactly as it checked the old one (M2-1 pre-commit and M2-4/M2-5 discrepancy Decisions). Money flow: JobGuard invoices the builder the monthly delta as a success-fee line (M4-10), shown on the same screen as 'Saved £X this month against your old rate; JobGuard's share £Y', collected under bounded D05 authority (M4-12). Verdict on the three brief categories: this one has the cleanest MEASUREMENT (exact arithmetic on records JobGuard already freezes) but the weakest ATTRIBUTION (market moves, the builder did the negotiating), so it must stay letter-anchored, 12-month bounded and £-capped; input VAT (next idea) is the cleanest category overall; CIS should be a flat add-on.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of the reduced invoices they actually paid; nothing from the merchant, ever.

revenue_per_year.solo: £95 blended (£54–£270 for a Solo who runs one rate review; £48 blended at a 10% share)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £336 blended (£384–£960 for a firm that runs a review; £168 at 10%)
revenue_per_year.firm: £980 blended (£1,120–£2,800 for a firm that runs reviews; the £1,000-per-merchant ceiling binds at the top of that range; £490 at 10%)

ideas.assumptions: Materials = 40% of turnover (brief range 35–45%): Solo £60k, Small £240k, Firm £800k. Top-ten SKUs = 45% / 40% / 35% of materials spend: £27k / £96k / £280k. Achievable renegotiation 2–5%, midpoint 3.5%: savings £945 / £3,360 / £9,800 a year. Share 20%: £189 / £672 / £1,960. Half of builders in each archetype actually send a letter in a year: £95 / £336 / £980. Firm ceiling assumed not to bind at 3.5% because savings spread over ~3 merchants (£1,000 each). At 5% a Firm with two merchants hits the ceiling (£2,800 > £2,000). All figures ex VAT, before any churn effect. A JobGuard-consistent 10% rate halves every figure and is the safer pilot default if the 20% 'P3-lite' framing tests badly.
ideas.trust_note: Borderline. The builder does the phone call, so a 20% share can read as 'a cut of my own negotiation' — the research finding that people accept fees where the provider visibly did work they could not do themselves (matching across a job) and resent them where the value felt like their own (report §'The hidden final check'). Mitigations: the letter is visibly JobGuard's work (purchase-history evidence, drafted, dated); the builder-favourable 'general price cut' attestation; the 12-month stop; the £ ceiling; and the plain statement that JobGuard has no relationship with the merchant. The P3 benchmark (50% for 12–60 months, success_fee_benchmarks §2) makes 20% for 12 months look modest, but P3 is the most resented model in that table, and builders do not know it. Test perceived fairness in the pilot before committing; if it tests badly, use the flat rate-review pack instead.
ideas.regulatory: None regulated: B2B letter sent by the builder in their own name; JobGuard is not a buying group, agent or introducer and takes nothing from merchants (D11/D04 watchdog independence). Needs D03 v3 (new category with its own qualifying test), D01 v3.1 (a 20% rate and a £ ceiling are a different fee basis from '10% of recovered net principal'), D02 (savings net of VAT), D05 (collection authority extended to rate-review fees), and the M4-13 agreement must add rate-review terms accepted at letter send.
ideas.build_dependency: After M2-1 (agreed-rate revisions with validity), M2-3 (human-confirmed intake lines), M2-4 (matched lines with unit/pack normalisation) and M4-7/M4-8 (settled payment facts). New: `rate_review_letter` artifact + approved send command through the outbox (§5.3), a tenant-scoped derivation identity `(tenant, category, merchant, letter_id)` — §14.9 is written per job/rate and M4-9 must be generalised to non-job scopes — a Graphile monthly accrual job, ceiling logic, and the attestation command. Rough effort: 3–4 reviewable tasks, synthetic first (SV-6 pattern), live behind G4. Not before M2-5 lands.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder-side: entering a fake high 'prior rate' before the letter — blocked by the two-settled-lines evidence rule; negotiating outside JobGuard and never recording a letter — no fee, an accepted residual risk exactly as §14.10 accepts billing outside JobGuard. JobGuard-side: claiming market deflation as savings — blocked by the builder-favourable attestation and the 90-day/letter anchoring. Merchant-side: cutting the unit rate and adding delivery or surcharge lines — the offset rule holds those invoices for review rather than accruing.
ideas.precedent: P3 Cost Analysts: 50% of savings shared for 12–60 months (success_fee_benchmarks §2, single vendor); UK utility/telecom cost auditors quote-only. The letter-as-case-opening mirrors JobGuard's own §14.7 withheld-payment entry test. No precedent found for a savings share sold to builders on their own merchant accounts.

ideas.name: Rate review pack — flat per merchant round (alternative form for renegotiation)
ideas.category: flat add-on (D09 add-on SKU), no success fee
ideas.mechanism: The same JobGuard-drafted rate review letter and 12-month savings tracker as the previous idea, sold as a one-off per merchant round rather than a share of savings: £49 ex VAT per round (letter built from the builder's purchase history and rate book, top-ten SKU table with quantities and current agreed rates, optional I28 band if opted in, then a 'what you saved against your old rate' tracker for 12 months). Trigger: builder opens 'Review my prices with [merchant]'; charge is an approved Decision at that moment; the letter itself is still a builder-authorised send. No savings share, no ceiling, no attestation — savings display is a labelled illustration. Alternative packaging: a £15/month 'Buying watch' add-on covering unlimited rounds. Everything the watchdog does with the new rate is unchanged. This is the recommended fallback if the pilot shows builders resent a savings share.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, a flat charge at the moment they start the round; nothing from merchants.

revenue_per_year.solo: £25 (0.5 rounds × £49); or £54 on the £15/month add-on at 30% uptake

ideas.assumptions: Rounds per year: Solo 0.5, Small 2, Firm 5 (one per major merchant). £49 per round chosen to sit under the value of even a 2% cut on £10k of SKU spend (£200). Add-on variant: £15 × 12 × uptake 30% / 40% / 50%. Not additive with the savings-share idea — pick one.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and easy to explain: a fixed price for a letter and a tracker, and the builder keeps 100% of what they negotiate. Lower revenue than the share but no 'cut of my negotiation' story to spread by word of mouth. Still requires the explicit rule that JobGuard has no merchant relationship, otherwise a 'price review' feature could be mistaken for a buying-group tie-in.
ideas.regulatory: None. D09 v2 needs an add-on SKU definition (amount, per-round vs monthly, VAT). No D01/D03 change because no success fee arises.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 rate book + M2-4 matched lines for the letter's evidence table; a letter template and approved send command; a per-round charge as a subscription add-on obligation (D09 `period_obligation` extension). Rough effort: 1–2 tasks, most of it shared with the savings-share idea.
ideas.gaming_risk: Negligible: the charge is fixed and pre-approved. Only risk is the builder expecting JobGuard to 'get' the saving — copy must say the builder negotiates.
ideas.precedent: None known as a standalone flat product for small builders; buying groups offer merchant-funded rate reviews (which is precisely the conflict JobGuard avoids). Tradify sells an Instant Website add-on at £10/month (uk_trade_job_software), showing small flat add-ons are normal in this market.

ideas.name: Input VAT recovered after a missing-VAT-invoice flag (`input_vat_recovered_after_missing_invoice_flag`, D03 v3 category)
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (new D03 v3 row; D01 base wording; D02)
ideas.mechanism: §14.7-style row. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) the tenant is VAT-registered on standard or cash accounting (flat-rate-scheme traders excluded except capital goods ≥ £2,000 incl VAT); (2) a payment to a supplier settled (M4-7 bank feed, matched under M4-8) against a document that is not a valid VAT invoice — pro-forma, quotation, statement, delivery note, invoice missing VAT number/date/VAT amount, or addressed to the wrong entity — and 30 days after settlement no valid VAT invoice (or less-detailed invoice ≤ £250) for that supply was held in intake; (3) JobGuard raised a cited `missing_vat_invoice` Decision (M2-5 discrepancy family) naming the payment, the document held and the input tax at stake; (4) a valid VAT invoice for the same supply was received through intake AFTER the Decision (server receive time and issue date both after it), verified under M2-3 and matched to the settled payment; (5) the input tax was included in a filed VAT return, evidenced by an approved accounting connector (SV-7) or MTD return evidence — builder attestation alone never qualifies in production (§5.6 'mark paid' rule applied to tax); (6) not later credited, disallowed on assessment or repaid. Q = cumulative input tax so evidenced per (tenant, VAT period), exact rational; F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100); posting_delta = F − J once per VAT period. NEVER QUALIFIES: a valid or less-detailed invoice already held at Decision time; an invoice obtained before the Decision; the builder or bookkeeper had already asked the supplier (builder-favourable attestation ends it); flat-rate scheme; partial exemption; supplies where the payment itself is later refunded. REVERSALS: credit note, disallowance or repaid input tax → negative delta, compensating journal, refund if collected. Output labelling: the Decision and the period statement are 'an aid to your VAT records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file returns' (I25/I26 precedent). This is the CLEANEST of the three brief categories: the sequence Decision → invoice received → return is provable from JobGuard's own immutable timestamps, the amount is on the document, and no market counterfactual is involved — but the money is small (see revenue).
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of VAT they would otherwise have paid to HMRC; nothing from suppliers or HMRC.

revenue_per_year.solo: £5 blended (£12 for an eligible Solo; range £3–£8)

ideas.assumptions: Missing/invalid VAT invoices = 2% of supplier spend (brief range 1–3%): Solo £1,200, Small £4,800, Firm £16,000; VAT at 20%: £240 / £960 / £3,200. Half of flagged items yield a VAT invoice after the Decision AND are evidenced as reclaimed via a connector: £120 / £480 / £1,600. Fee 10%: £12 / £48 / £160. Eligibility: Solo 42% (60% VAT-registered × 70% not on flat-rate), Small 90%, Firm 95%: £5 / £43 / £152. Bookkeepers already chase many of these, which is why only half is credited to JobGuard.
ideas.trust_note: JobGuard visibly did the work (matched a payment to a non-invoice and chased it), the builder gets cash they would have lost on inspection, and the builder-favourable 'I had already asked' rule protects the relationship. The honest problem is scale: £5–£20 per item makes the fee look petty on a statement. Options: run it at 10% under the ordinary cumulative machinery (no extra cost once built) or make it a fee-free goodwill feature of the watchdog and count it as subscription value. Never charge on a Solo who is on the flat-rate scheme — the reclaim does not exist there.
ideas.regulatory: HMRC evidence rules for input tax (VAT Regulations 1995 reg. 29; less-detailed invoices ≤ £250; flat-rate scheme rules) — JobGuard applies them as deterministic checks, labelled as aids, never as advice; no filing, no agent authority. Accounting-connector evidence needs D04 (residency) and D12 (third-party data). Needs D03 v3 (new category), D01 (base is 'input tax reclaimed', not recovered net principal — wording change at the same 10%), D02 (tax figures and rounding).
ideas.build_dependency: After M2-3 (document class and VAT-field extraction with citations), M2-4/M2-5 (payment-to-document matching and a `missing_vat_invoice` Decision type), M4-7/M4-8 (settled payments), SV-7 approved accounting connector (return-inclusion evidence). Add tenant VAT-status facts (registered / scheme / partial exemption) as versioned inputs. Derivation identity `(tenant, vat_period)`; M4-9 generalised beyond job scope. Rough effort: 2 tasks plus the connector, which is itself a listed separate idea.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder claiming a reclaim that was never filed — blocked by connector-evidence requirement. JobGuard over-claiming where a valid invoice existed elsewhere (in the builder's email) — the builder-favourable attestation and the Decision's requirement that nothing valid was held in intake keep this fee-free on doubt. Supplier reissuing an invoice with a later date for an invoice the builder already had — attestation resolves in the builder's favour.
ideas.precedent: No product found charges a success fee on input VAT for small firms; Dext/Hubdoc flag missing receipts on flat plans (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). AP recovery auditors include VAT recovery in 20–30% contingency scopes (success_fee_benchmarks §1); no sourced UK VAT-reclaim contingency percentages were found (§5 gaps).

ideas.name: CIS suffered reclaim (`cis_suffered_reclaimed`) — recommended as a flat year-end pack, percentage variant shown for comparison
ideas.category: flat add-on recommended; success-fee category variant needs D03 v3 + D01 + a tax-aid decision
ideas.mechanism: §14.7-style row for the PERCENTAGE variant (narrow, evidence-increment only): QUALIFIES WHEN (1) the tenant is a CIS subcontractor on net payment status with contractor payments and deduction statements tracked (the CIS module is a prerequisite, not part of this idea); (2) JobGuard matched a contractor payment to the sub's invoice and found a deduction suffered with NO deduction statement held, and raised a cited `missing_cis_statement` Decision; (3) the statement (or the contractor's written confirmation of the deduction) was then received through intake after the Decision; (4) the deduction was set off or repaid by HMRC — repayment evidenced on the M4-7 bank feed, set-off evidenced via an approved payroll/accounting connector; (5) only the increment JobGuard evidenced counts. Q = cumulative evidenced-increment deductions repaid/set off per (tenant, tax year); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100), delta per statement. NEVER QUALIFIES: deductions the builder already held a statement for; the routine year-end reclaim of properly evidenced deductions; gross-payment-status subs; amounts not actually repaid or set off; anything HMRC later amends. REVERSAL: HMRC amendment → negative delta and compensation. RECOMMENDED FORM INSTEAD: a flat 'CIS suffered year-end pack' at £59 ex VAT per tax year (Firm £99): reconciled schedule of every deduction suffered against statements and bank receipts, gaps chased with a JobGuard-drafted statement request the builder sends, export for the builder's accountant or their own SA/EPS entry. All outputs labelled 'an aid to your CIS records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file, hold agent (64-8) authority or claim on your behalf' (I25/I26 precedent). Why flat: the money is unarguably the builder's tax and any accountant reclaims it; a percentage of the refund is the refund-firm model the research warns carries the same reputational stain as R&D boutiques (success_fee_benchmarks §5), and the increment JobGuard genuinely causes is too uncertain to measure honestly.
ideas.who_pays: The builder: a flat pack fee at year end (recommended), or 10% of the evidenced-increment HMRC repayment (variant).

revenue_per_year.solo: £18 flat (£59 × 30% in CIS) / £22 percentage variant / £90 if charged refund-firm style on the whole refund (not recommended)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £30 flat (£59 × 50%) / £108 percentage variant / £250 on the whole refund (not recommended)
revenue_per_year.firm: £59 flat (£99 × 60%) / £432 percentage variant / £900 on the whole refund (not recommended)

ideas.assumptions: Share of archetype doing CIS-deducted work: Solo 30% (mostly domestic, outside CIS), Small 50%, Firm 60%. Contractor work as share of turnover 40% / 30% / 30%: £60k / £180k / £600k; labour element 60% → deductions at 20%: £7,200 / £21,600 / £72,000 suffered. Deductions with no statement in the builder's own records: 10% → £720 / £2,160 / £7,200; fee 10% → £72 / £216 / £720; × CIS share → £22 / £108 / £432. Whole-refund figures assume year-end refunds of ~£3,000 / £5,000 / £15,000 × 10% × CIS share. Flat: £59 (Firm £99) × CIS share. Sole traders reclaim through self-assessment; companies set off monthly via EPS and claim any excess after year end — the repayment event JobGuard can see on a bank feed is therefore often a year-end lump.
ideas.trust_note: Flat form scores 4: a reconciled schedule is plainly useful and JobGuard keeps nothing of the refund. Percentage form scores 2: 'you took 10% of my tax refund' is exactly the refund-firm story, the counterfactual (would the accountant have found it?) is weak, and refund firms at 15–30% (brief figure; not independently verified in the research) are a reputational neighbour to avoid. Do not market either as 'we get your tax back'.
ideas.regulatory: CIS rules (FA 2004 and the CIS Regulations 2005: contractor deductions, statements, sub set-off/repayment) applied as deterministic checks only; JobGuard is not a tax agent and files nothing. HMRC repayment evidence via bank feed needs D10/D12; set-off evidence via payroll connector needs D04/D12. Flat form needs only D09 (add-on SKU). Percentage form needs D03 v3, D01 (base = HMRC repayment), D02 and a new decision record covering HMRC-related aids (positioning, disclaimers, no agent authority).
ideas.build_dependency: Requires the CIS module (already a listed idea: verification records, deduction statements, CIS-suffered tracking) plus contractor-payment matching against sub invoices, a statement-request letter/send command, M4-7 bank feed for repayments, and a year-end pack export. Rough effort: pack 1–2 tasks on top of the module; percentage variant 2 more (Decision type, derivation identity `(tenant, tax_year)`, connector evidence).
ideas.gaming_risk: Percentage form: JobGuard over-claiming that it 'evidenced' a deduction the builder already had on paper — builder-favourable attestation makes it fee-free; contractor confirmation letters could be solicited after the fact — anchor to the Decision date. Flat form: none.
ideas.precedent: CIS/tax refund firms charge 15–30% (brief figure); R&D software platforms 5–10% (success_fee_benchmarks §5); Xero sells CIS returns as a £5/month add-on (construction_platforms_and_ai). The flat add-on matches how the market already prices CIS features.

ideas.name: CIS over-deduction on materials or at 30% recovered from the contractor (`cis_over_deduction_recovered`)
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% on contractor cash corrections only)
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual: CIS deductions must exclude the materials element of a sub's invoice, and a verified sub is deducted at 20% not 30%. JobGuard holds the sub-builder's outgoing invoice with a materials split (M1 invoices), the supplier invoices proving those materials (M2-2/M2-4), the contractor's payment (M4-7) and the deduction statement (CIS module). QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) a deduction statement or payment shows deduction applied to the materials element or at 30% despite a verification record; (2) JobGuard raised a cited `cis_over_deduction` Decision with the arithmetic; (3) the builder sent a JobGuard-drafted correction request; (4) the contractor paid the difference in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed and allocated to the case. Q = cumulative cash corrections per (tenant, contractor, tax year); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100); delta per statement. NEVER QUALIFIES: corrections the contractor makes by adjusting a later payment that JobGuard cannot tie to the case (hold for review), any amount recovered from HMRC instead (that route folds into the CIS-suffered idea and, if flat, is fee-free), 30% deductions where the sub was genuinely unverified, disputes the builder settles outside JobGuard. REVERSAL: contractor claws back or HMRC re-determines → negative delta. Labelled as an aid, not tax advice; JobGuard does not contact the contractor.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from cash the contractor paid over after the correction; nothing from contractors or HMRC.

revenue_per_year.solo: £11 blended (£36 for a Solo sub who hits it)

ideas.assumptions: CIS share as in the CIS-suffered idea (30% / 50% / 60%). Contractor work £60k / £180k / £600k; materials element 30% → £18k / £54k / £180k; wrongly deducted at 20% if every invoice were wrong: £3,600 / £10,800 / £36,000; assume 20% of invoices affected: £720 / £2,160 / £7,200; contractor corrects in cash (rather than via HMRC or a later adjustment) 50%: £360 / £1,080 / £3,600; fee 10%: £36 / £108 / £360; × CIS share: £11 / £54 / £216. Frequency of materials over-deduction is a judgement (it is a well-known contractor error) and is not sourced.
ideas.trust_note: The contractor made the error, JobGuard spotted it with arithmetic the builder can inspect, and the builder gets cash they were not going to get. Small sums, but the same 'found money' shape as a supplier overcharge.
