Keep the correction request in the builder's name and make it optional — some subs will not want to press a contractor they depend on, and 'chose not to chase' must be respected as fee-free.
ideas.regulatory: CIS Regulations 2005 (materials exclusion; 20%/30% rates; verification) applied deterministically; no advice, no filing, no agent role. Needs D03 v3 (new category), D01 (10% on contractor cash corrections), D12 (contractor as third-party data subject, Article 14 route) — contractors are businesses but named individuals appear on statements.
ideas.build_dependency: CIS module (listed separately) + invoice materials split on the sub-builder's outgoing invoices + M4-7/M4-8 settlement allocation + a correction-request send command. Derivation identity `(tenant, contractor, tax_year)`. Rough effort: 1–2 tasks after the module and the bank feed.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low: the builder has no incentive to inflate a contractor's error, and a contractor's cash payment is externally evidenced. Risk is JobGuard counting a routine top-up payment as a 'correction' — require the correction request to precede the payment and the amount to match the Decision arithmetic within tolerance.
ideas.precedent: None known. Closest is AP recovery audit's 'pricing and tax errors' class at 20–30% contingency (success_fee_benchmarks §1).

ideas.name: Duplicate supplier payment refunded in cash (`duplicate_supplier_payment_recovered`)
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% on cash refunds)
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual with no market element: M2-2 already assigns a duplicate-intake identity to the same underlying invoice, and M4-7/M4-8 will show two settled bank payments against one invoice identity (or one payment against an invoice already settled on a supplier statement). QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) two settled payments match one confirmed invoice identity, or a payment matches an invoice already marked settled by a matched prior payment; (2) JobGuard raised a cited `duplicate_payment` Decision; (3) the builder sent a JobGuard-drafted refund request; (4) the supplier refunded in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed and allocated to the case. Q = cumulative cash refunds per (tenant, supplier); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100); delta per statement. NEVER QUALIFIES: a credit to the merchant account or a credit note against future purchases (excluded under D03 v2 until the separate listed credit-note extension); refunds the supplier made before the Decision; payments the builder already reversed with the bank; genuine part payments. REVERSAL: refund bounced or re-invoiced → negative delta. This is the cleanest evidence chain of any idea in this list and the classic recovery-audit category.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the supplier's cash refund; nothing from the supplier.
ideas.assumptions: Duplicate/erroneous payments = 0.3% of supplier spend (large-firm recovery audits find ~0.1% of spend; small firms without AP controls assumed higher): Solo £180, Small £720, Firm £2,400. Supplier refunds in cash rather than as an account credit 50%: £90 / £360 / £1,200. Fee 10%: £9 / £36 / £120. Needs the bank feed, so zero before M4-7.
ideas.trust_note: Pure found money: the builder paid twice, JobGuard noticed, cash came back. No one feels short-changed by 10% of that. The only care point is that most merchants will offer a credit, not cash — the builder should see plainly that a credit is fee-free and that JobGuard is not steering them to demand cash for its own benefit (copy: 'a credit on your account is fine; no fee either way unless cash is refunded').
ideas.regulatory: None. Bank data via the TrueLayer route (D10, D04, D12). Needs D03 v3 wording: D03 v2's supplier category is 'overcharge'; a duplicate payment is not an overcharge and needs its own row.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-2 duplicate identity + M4-7 bank feed + M4-8 payment-to-invoice allocation + a refund-request send command. Derivation identity `(tenant, supplier, case)`. Rough effort: 1 task once M4-8 exists; mostly a new Decision type and a case type.
ideas.gaming_risk: None meaningful: paying twice on purpose costs the builder cash flow to earn JobGuard a fee it does not want. JobGuard-side: mis-matching two legitimate invoices with the same number from one merchant — M2-2 explicitly does not treat invoice number as globally unique, and the Decision must cite both documents.
ideas.precedent: PRGX / apexanalytix AP recovery audit, duplicate payments as a core class at 20–30% contingency, 10–40% outer range (success_fee_benchmarks §1).

ideas.name: VAT wrongly charged by a subcontractor or supplier and refunded in cash (`vat_wrongly_charged_refunded`) — DRC and zero-rating errors
ideas.category: D03 v3 clarification of `supplier_overcharge` (tax wrongly charged counts as overcharge); 10% on cash refunds
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual from deterministic rules JobGuard can hold as tenant/job facts: under the construction domestic reverse charge a VAT- and CIS-registered sub must not charge VAT to a builder who is not the end user; work on a qualifying new build is zero-rated; some conversions and energy-saving installs are reduced-rated. If the sub charges 20% and the builder pays it, HMRC can refuse the input tax, so the money is lost unless the sub credits and refunds. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) the job carries confirmed facts (builder's VAT/CIS status, end-user status for the job, build type) entered by the builder as versioned inputs; (2) an M2-3 confirmed sub/supplier invoice shows VAT charged where the rule says none or a lower rate; (3) JobGuard raised a cited `vat_rate_check` Decision (labelled 'check with your accountant'); (4) the builder had already PAID the invoice; (5) the sub issued a credit note and refunded the VAT in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed. Q = cumulative VAT cash refunds per (tenant, supplier); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100). NEVER QUALIFIES: prevention (the invoice was corrected before payment — no fee, consistent with the founder's prevented-spend rule), credit-only corrections, cases where the builder's own facts were wrong, amounts recovered from HMRC rather than the supplier. REVERSAL: refund reversed → negative delta.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the sub's or supplier's cash refund.
ideas.assumptions: Sub spend as share of turnover 10% / 20% / 25%: £15k / £120k / £500k; VAT-registered subs 30% / 50% / 60%: £4.5k / £60k / £300k; invoices wrongly charging VAT 5% of that: £225 / £3,000 / £15,000; VAT at 20%: £45 / £600 / £3,000; paid before correction and then refunded in cash 50%: £22 / £300 / £1,500; fee 10%: £2 / £30 / £150; Solo × 60% VAT-registered → £1. The 5% error rate is a judgement; DRC confusion among small subs is widely reported but unquantified.
ideas.trust_note: JobGuard spotted a tax error the builder would have paid for twice; the sub, not the builder, made the mistake. The care points are (a) never presenting the rule check as tax advice — the Decision must say 'this looks like a reverse-charge supply; confirm with your accountant before asking for a credit', and (b) the end-user/build-type facts come from the builder, so a wrong fact is the builder's and never produces a fee against them.
ideas.regulatory: VAT Act 1994 s.55A domestic reverse charge (construction, from 2021), zero/reduced-rate building rules — applied as deterministic checks, labelled aids, not advice; JobGuard does not file. Needs a D03 v3 clarification that wrongly charged tax refunded in cash is within `supplier_overcharge`, D02 (tax rounding and presentation), D12 (sub as third-party data subject).
ideas.build_dependency: M2-3 (VAT rate/amount extraction with citations) + tenant/job VAT facts as versioned inputs + a deterministic rate-rule check in M2-5 + M4-7/M4-8 for the cash refund. Rough effort: 1–2 tasks. The DRC rule table must be versioned and reviewed by a qualified tax reviewer before any real Decision is raised (D02 owner).
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. JobGuard-side risk is a wrong rule version raising false Decisions that damage sub relationships — versioned rules, held-out fixtures and 'check with your accountant' wording. Builder-side: none (they cannot earn from a false correction).
ideas.precedent: None known. Construction AI and Site Samurai list CIS/VAT handling as flat features (construction_platforms_and_ai); no success-fee precedent.

ideas.name: Builder's own agreed merchant rebate or retrospective discount, unpaid or underpaid, recovered in cash (`unpaid_agreed_rebate_recovered`)
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% on cash rebates) — flagged for its neighbourhood
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual: the M2-1 rate book gains a 'rebate/retro term' revision (threshold spend, percentage, period, payment method) entered by the builder from their own merchant agreement; matched invoices (M2-4) give cumulative spend; at period end JobGuard computes the rebate due and compares it with any rebate received (bank feed) or credit note. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) a versioned rebate term exists with the agreement document held as evidence; (2) matched, settled spend crossed the threshold; (3) no rebate, or a smaller one, was received within the term's payment window; (4) JobGuard raised a cited `rebate_due` Decision with the arithmetic; (5) the builder sent a JobGuard-drafted claim; (6) the merchant paid the rebate in CASH after the Decision, matched and allocated. Q = cumulative cash rebates per (tenant, merchant, period); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100). NEVER QUALIFIES: rebates paid as account credit or credit note (excluded); rebates paid on time without a Decision; rebate terms JobGuard cannot see the document for; any arrangement where JobGuard itself introduced or negotiated the rebate (structurally forbidden). REVERSAL: rebate clawed back → negative delta.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the merchant's rebate cash; JobGuard is never party to the rebate.

revenue_per_year.solo: £1 blended (rebate terms rare below ~£50k merchant spend)

ideas.assumptions: Share of archetype holding a rebate term: 5% / 30% / 70%. Rate-book merchant spend covered by the term: £20k / £150k / £500k at 2.5% rebate: £500 / £3,750 / £12,500; unpaid or underpaid in a year 20%: £100 / £750 / £2,500; paid in cash rather than credit 50%: £50 / £375 / £1,250; fee 10%: £5 / £37 / £125; × term share: £0.25 / £11 / £88 (Solo shown as £1).
ideas.trust_note: The rebate is the builder's own contractual entitlement and the merchant simply did not pay it — found money. Flagged because it sits next to the listed 'merchant rebate with JobGuard admin fee' idea that poisons the watchdog: the difference must be structural and visible — JobGuard never arranges, pools, negotiates or receives rebates, only reads the builder's existing agreement and their invoices. Any drift toward JobGuard-negotiated terms must be refused by policy (D11).
ideas.regulatory: None regulated (B2B contract terms). D03 v3 new row; D01 10%; D11 statement that JobGuard has no merchant income of any kind. Bank feed via D10/D12.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 rate book extended with rebate-term revisions and agreement-document evidence + M2-4 matched spend + a period-end Graphile job + M4-7/M4-8 cash matching + a claim-letter send command. Derivation identity `(tenant, merchant, rebate_period)`. Rough effort: 2 tasks.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder entering a rebate term that does not exist — no benefit to them (the merchant will not pay). JobGuard-side: miscounting spend (returns, credits) — use settled net spend after credits, and cite every invoice in the Decision. Merchant-side: paying as credit to avoid a JobGuard fee — that is fine for the builder and fee-free.
ideas.precedent: Enterprise rebate-management software (flat subscription) exists for distributors; nothing for small builders. AP recovery auditors treat unclaimed rebates as a standard recovery class at 20–30% (success_fee_benchmarks §1).

ideas.name: VAT bad-debt relief reclaimed on written-off customer invoices (`vat_bad_debt_relief_reclaimed`) — borderline
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% of relief) — borderline, flagged
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual: a JobGuard-issued customer invoice, no settlement recorded (bank feed) for six months after the due date, and an explicit builder write-off command; the output VAT already paid to HMRC on that invoice becomes reclaimable as bad-debt relief. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) the invoice was issued through JobGuard and its VAT accounted for; (2) six months have passed since the later of due date and supply; (3) the builder recorded a write-off through the command boundary; (4) JobGuard raised a cited `bad_debt_relief_available` Decision with the exact VAT; (5) the relief was included in a filed return, evidenced by the accounting connector (never attestation); (6) no later recovery. Q = cumulative relief per (tenant, VAT period); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100). NEVER QUALIFIES: invoices under an open withheld-payment case (the two categories must not stack); cash accounting traders (no output VAT paid, no relief); partial payments already accounted; anything the builder's accountant had already scheduled (builder-favourable attestation). REVERSAL: if the customer later pays (including through a withheld-payment case), the relief is repayable to HMRC and Q falls — negative delta and compensation, and the withheld-payment fee then applies instead on the settled cash. Labelled an aid, not advice; JobGuard does not file.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of VAT reclaimed from HMRC on a debt they wrote off.
ideas.assumptions: Write-offs = 0.75% of turnover: £1,125 / £4,500 / £15,000 gross; VAT element (20/120): £188 / £750 / £2,500; portion not already handled by the builder's accountant and evidenced via a connector 40%: £75 / £300 / £1,000; fee 10%: £8 / £30 / £100; Solo × 60% VAT-registered → £5. Most small builders on cash accounting for VAT get no relief at all, which would push Solo and Small lower.
ideas.trust_note: Uncomfortable: it charges a fee on the tax side of a customer who never paid, so the builder is already hurting; 'JobGuard took 10% of my bad-debt relief' is a bad sentence in a trade that runs on word of mouth, and any decent accountant does this routinely so the counterfactual is thin. Listed because the chain is fully documented and exact; recommend it be a fee-free feature of the watchdog (an aid the subscription pays for), not a category.
ideas.regulatory: VAT Act 1994 s.36 and VAT Regulations 1995 regs 165–172 (six-month rule, write-off in accounts, later-payment repayment) as deterministic checks; not advice; no filing. Needs D03 v3, D01 (base = tax relief), D02, and the accounting connector under D04/D12. Interaction with the withheld-payment category must be written into D03 so the two never stack.
ideas.build_dependency: M1 customer invoices + M4-7 receipt matching + a write-off command with audit + a six-month Graphile clock + SV-7 accounting connector evidence. Rough effort: 1–2 tasks. Cheap to build, expensive in trust.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder writing off a debt to trigger relief and then collecting outside JobGuard — an HMRC matter, not JobGuard's; JobGuard would reverse on any visible receipt. JobGuard-side: none.
ideas.precedent: None known as a charged service; accountants include it in ordinary fees.

ideas.name: Insurance payout on a JobGuard-evidenced site loss (theft of delivered materials, storm damage) — listed to reject
ideas.category: success-fee category with a documented counterfactual — likely regulated claims management; listed to reject
ideas.mechanism: The counterfactual is documented (GRN shows delivery, photos and diary show the loss, supplier invoices give value, the evidence pack proves it) and the cash is an insurer's payout on the bank feed, so it superficially fits a 10% category: Decision 'this loss looks claimable', builder claims, payout matched, Q cumulative, F at 10%. It is listed only to be rejected: taking a percentage of an insurance claim is claims-management activity in the FCA's 'financial services or financial product' sector unless done by an authorised firm, and it would put JobGuard in the same bucket as the claims firms whose fees were capped at 15–30% — the exact association the research says to avoid. The already-listed insurer-paid evidence pack is the safe form of this value.
ideas.who_pays: Would be the builder, from the insurer's payout — rejected.
ideas.assumptions: Annual probability of a claimable site loss 5% / 10% / 15%; average claim £1,000 / £2,500 / £5,000; fee 10%. Shown only to size what is being refused.
ideas.trust_note: Feels like a claims firm, and a builder who has just been robbed does not want a platform taking a slice of the insurance money. Reject; keep the evidence-pack route.
ideas.regulatory: FCA claims-management regulation (RAO arts 89G–89M; 'financial services or financial product' claims include insurance claims) — regulated activity unless exempt or authorised; FCA fee caps 15–30% by claim size (report benchmark table). Requires legal sign-off that it is not viable without authorisation; recommend recording the rejection in D03 v3 so no agent revives it.
ideas.build_dependency: None to build. Record the rejection.
ideas.gaming_risk: Not applicable.
ideas.precedent: Claims-management companies 15–30% under the FCA cap (report §'No rival sells…' table; success_fee_benchmarks §7).

ideas.name: Supplier-switch savings measured against the frozen prior rate (`supplier_switch_savings`) — flagged, recommend reject
ideas.category: success-fee category on a documented counterfactual — flagged: attribution weak and watchdog-conflict risk; recommend reject
ideas.mechanism: Variant of the renegotiation share for the case where, after a JobGuard rate review letter, the builder moves the named SKUs to a different merchant. Measurement is available: the prior merchant's frozen agreed rate (M2-1) versus the new merchant's confirmed invoice rate on the same SKU alias, × settled quantity, for 12 months, 20% share, £ ceiling, same reversal rules. It is listed because it is the largest 'savings' pool in the lens, and recommended for rejection because (a) attribution is the weakest of any idea here — a new merchant's price says nothing about what JobGuard caused, and alias matching across merchants introduces quality/spec differences the builder will dispute; (b) a platform that earns when builders switch merchant is one step from steering them, which is the watchdog conflict the founder has ruled out even in its structured form. If the founder still wants it, it must be attestation-driven ('I moved because of the review') and fee-free on any doubt.
ideas.who_pays: Would be the builder from lower invoices at the new merchant — recommend not offering.
ideas.assumptions: Top-ten SKU spend as in the renegotiation idea (£27k / £96k / £280k); switching after a review saves 5%; share 20%; 20% of builders switch a merchant in a year: £27k × 5% × 20% × 20% = £54; £96k → £192; £280k → £560 (ceiling would bind for Firms with few merchants).
ideas.trust_note: Reads as JobGuard profiting from where the builder shops, which is the story that would end the watchdog's credibility with merchants and builders alike. The renegotiation idea explicitly lists switching under 'never qualifies' for this reason.
ideas.regulatory: None regulated, but D11 (commercial integrity) should record that fees never depend on which merchant the builder uses.
ideas.build_dependency: Would reuse the renegotiation build plus cross-merchant alias matching. Recommend recording the rejection instead.
ideas.gaming_risk: High on the JobGuard side (spec mismatches counted as savings) and unsolvable without adjudicating quality, which the watchdog must not do.
ideas.precedent: Cost-reduction consultancies share savings from supplier switches (P3, success_fee_benchmarks §2) — but they are the client's agent and negotiate directly, which JobGuard must not be.

ideas.name: Backdated rate refund after a rate review — treated as ordinary supplier cash refund at 10% (clarification inside D03 v3)
ideas.category: D03 v3 clarification (no new category): cash refunds arising from a rate review use the existing 10% supplier mechanics, never the savings share
ideas.mechanism: When a merchant responds to the builder's rate review letter by backdating the new rate and refunding the difference on invoices already paid, the outcome is settled cash from the supplier, not prospective savings. QUALIFIES WHEN: a cash refund lands on the bank feed after the letter, matched to specific paid invoice lines for the named SKUs, allocated to the rate-review case. Q = cumulative cash refunded, F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100), delta per statement, standard reversal. NEVER QUALIFIES: the same lines counted again under the 20% prospective share (unique derivation identity per invoice line prevents double counting); account credits or credit notes. Listing this separately stops the two fee bases from overlapping and gives the builder the cheaper rate on cash-back, which is the builder-favourable choice §14.8 demands ('never choose the rule that pays JobGuard most').
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the merchant's cash refund.
ideas.assumptions: Assume one in ten rate reviews produces a backdated cash refund covering three months of the saving: Solo 0.5 reviews × 10% × (£945 × 3/12) × 10% fee = £1; Small 2 × 10% × £840 × 10% = £17 → shown as £10 after halving for credit-not-cash; Firm 5 × 10% × £2,450 × 10% = £122 → £30 after assuming most Firms take it as credit. Small money; the point is the rule, not the revenue.
ideas.trust_note: Choosing the lower fee basis when both could apply is exactly the kind of visible fairness the research says builds acceptance; make the rule explicit on the statement.
ideas.regulatory: D03 v3 wording only; D01 unchanged (10% on recovered cash).
ideas.build_dependency: Falls out of the renegotiation build plus M4-8 allocation; one uniqueness constraint on `(tenant, invoice_line_id)` across both fee bases. Effort: trivial once the parent exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: None; the constraint prevents double counting in JobGuard's favour.
ideas.precedent: JobGuard's own §14.8 'first rule that fits, never the one that pays JobGuard most'.

ideas.name: "Tell me now" plan toggle: per-tier uplift (£49 / £99 / £179)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — core plan variant (opt-in; hidden-until-lock stays the default)
ideas.mechanism: PLACEMENT AND PRICE. A per-tenant switch on every tier, not a fourth tier: Solo £29 → £49 (+£20), Builder £59 → £99 (+£40), Firm £119 → £179 (+£60; £199 is defensible if pilot catches sit at the high end). Contractor (on request) quotes both. The delta is set at roughly the central expected missed-variation success fee per builder-year on that tier (£228 / £360 / £594, see assumptions), rounded to a nine-ending monthly step and slightly above it (1.05× / 1.33× / 1.21×) to cover the flat-rate premium builders pay for certainty (research note §2, Lambrecht & Skiera), adverse selection (choosers expect more extras) and the extra cost of serving live cards. Solo is deliberately near break-even because that segment is anchored at £25–£45 (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). MECHANISM. D09 term `disclosure_mode ∈ {hidden_until_lock, tell_me_now}` with `effective_at`. Switch-live copies the tenant's mode into an immutable `job.disclosure_mode`, bound in the switch-live audit event; detectors (SV-3) read the job value, never the tenant's live value. On a `tell_me_now` job, the shadow worker inserts each `shadow_commercial_signal` and, in the same transaction, a `shadow_disclosure_event(kind='tenant_plan_live')`, sets `disclosed_before_lock=true` (monotonic), `first_builder_visible_at=now`, attribution state `surfaced_early`, and writes an advisory-lane Finding of new kind `possible_extra` through the existing inbox path (M2-7-S), the same route D13 must-surface uses (must-surface cards stay mandatory lane on every plan). Disclosure is set at creation, not at display, so the daily advisory budget in `applyInitialSuppression` can never hide a card that later earns a fee. The card shows description, labelled estimate, each evidence item with date/source, and four actions: 'Log this as an extra' (opens Log an extra prefilled — AI structuring of the builder's own entry is builder capture under §14.2), 'Already in my quote/extras' (must pick the scope item or variation → reconciled), 'Not an extra / goodwill' (dismissed, recorded), 'Wrong job or evidence'. The card never creates a variation, debt or fee. Belt and braces: the §14.6 predicate gains `AND job.disclosure_mode = hidden_until_lock`, so a signal created late on a live-mode job cannot qualify even if it somehow escaped disclosure. Delivery setting inside the plan, same price: 'cards as you go' or 'cards when I build the final account' (§14.4 step 1) — foregone fee is identical either way, so the price cannot differ. SCOPE AND SWITCHING. Per tenant. A change applies only to jobs switched live at/after `effective_at` (upgrade: immediate, pro-rata; downgrade: next billing period). In-flight jobs keep the mode bound at switch-live in both directions, so a builder cannot go hidden mid-job to create a fee or live after lock to dodge one, and JobGuard cannot either. No switching rule may depend on signal existence ('switch this job if nothing found yet' would leak §14.3); date-based only. A hidden-plan builder who wants an in-flight job across uses the per-job reveal (idea 4). POST-LOCK ON THIS PLAN. The same worker runs the same 'Running JobGuard's final check' screen, classifies every signal (all already `surfaced_early`), records the run; the reveal list is empty by construction: 'Everything JobGuard found on this job was shown to you during it. Nothing new.' Late-arriving evidence is listed as information only and never qualifies (§14.6). WHAT EACH SIDE GIVES UP. Builder on hidden: mid-job sight of JobGuard's own extra findings (overcharge, readiness and proof checks stay live on both plans), a 10% fee on catches, and late post-account billing to homeowners that is more dispute-prone (research §4, consumer-law inference). Builder on Tell me now: £20–£60 a month whether or not anything is found, more interruptions and the work of logging, and no 'second pair of eyes' surprise. JobGuard on Tell me now: every missed-variation fee on that tenant's live-mode jobs, permanently and structurally, plus adverse selection; it gains predictable revenue and a market price for the hold-back. JobGuard on hidden: keeps fee upside, carries the trust risk, and now has a public price on the hold-back that can be quoted back. ONE-SENTENCE PRICING-PAGE COPY. Standard: 'JobGuard tracks everything you log for free, then runs an independent second check after you complete your final account and takes 10% only of extra money it finds that you then get paid — like a proofread you only pay for if it catches something.' Tell me now: 'For £20 more a month JobGuard shows you every possible extra the moment it spots one, so you bill it yourself the normal way — nothing is held for the final check and there is never a success fee on it.'
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (tenant-level subscription uplift, ex VAT, monthly or annual).

revenue_per_year.solo: £240/yr per builder on the plan (£49 − £29 = £20 × 12); uptake-weighted across the Solo base at 25% = £60; net of the foregone missed-variation fee: +£12 central (£240 − £228), −£1,280 high case, +£211 low case.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £480/yr per taker (£99 − £59 = £40 × 12); uptake-weighted at 35% = £168; net of foregone fee +£120 central (£480 − £360), −£1,440 high case.
revenue_per_year.firm: £720/yr per taker (£179 − £119 = £60 × 12); uptake-weighted at 50% = £360; net +£126 central (£720 − £594), −£1,920 high case; at £199 (+£80) £960/yr, net +£366 central.

ideas.assumptions: All figures ex VAT and labelled assumptions. Tier mapping: Solo→Solo, Small firm→Builder, Firm→Firm at the report's £29/£59/£119 (§'Recommendation'). Jobs per year: 150/8 ≈ 19, 600/25 = 24, 2,000/60 ≈ 33. Foregone-fee model (the pool is unmeasured — research §6): revealed candidates per locked job 0.75 (task range 0–2) × 40% reach confirmed-billed-paid = 0.3 paid catches per job; net value per paid catch £400 / £500 / £600 (task range £200–£800, scaled to job size). Central foregone fee = jobs × 0.3 × value × 10% = £228 / £360 / £594 per builder-year. High case: 2 revealed × 50% paid × £800 = £80 per job → £1,520 / £1,920 / £2,640. Low case: 0.25 × 30% × £200 → £29 / £36 / £50. Uptake 25% / 35% / 50% (firms have office staff to act on cards and more fee at stake; solos are price-anchored). Choosers self-select toward the high case, so the central net is optimistic; the pilot choice share (idea 10) is what corrects the price.
ideas.trust_note: Offering a priced choice is a stronger fairness lever than a sentence in the terms (research §4: disclosure alone does not neutralise a conflict; autonomy does more). Double-edged: it also lets a critic write 'JobGuard charges £20 a month not to withhold things from you', and it publishes a price for the hold-back. Copy must never describe the standard plan as 'we hold back' — only as 'a second check after your bill' — and the paid plan as 'tell me as you go'. Per-card or per-catch charges on surfaced cards are ruled out by D11 v2 ('may not reveal before lock and later charge'); only a flat plan price is compatible with the founder's decisions.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (new term, price, switching, no offset), D13 v2 (paid tenant disclosure route), D05 (plan change is an explicit Decision), D02 (VAT on the uplift), D12 v2 (onboarding wording for both plans). B2B, so largely outside DMCC drip-pricing, but the displayed headline must include the uplift once chosen. Charging behind G4; pilot_no_charge shows the mode with hypothetical prices only.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-0 (D09 v3 / D13 v2 text), SV-1 (mode on the §14.6 predicate; `possible_extra` finding type), SV-2 (`subscription_terms.disclosure_mode`, immutable `job.disclosure_mode`, new disclosure-event kind), SV-3 (detector emits disclosure on live-mode jobs), M2-7-S inbox card, SV-4/SV-5 (reconcile-only path and screen text), M4-13 agreement wording, M4-14 plan-change metering, M4-11 sign-up selection. Effort: medium — mostly plumbing on tables that §14.12 already plans, plus one card and one screen; roughly 3 PRs.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder: toggle hidden before an expected-simple job and live before an expected-complex one — legitimate adverse selection, blunted by per-tenant scope and next-period downgrade; add a D11 v2 advisory signal 'mode changed within N days of a switch-live' (flag only). JobGuard: cannot delay signal creation to earn a fee because the predicate clause on job mode fails regardless of timing. Leak: any rule conditioned on signal existence would breach §14.3 — forbidden by design.
ideas.precedent: Chargeflow sells flat prevention ($29 per deflected chargeback, 'Alerts') beside 25% recovery on the same page; Paddle Retain offers flat fees for small customers and a percentage for larger ones (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). No known precedent for a paid 'disclose now' option against a delayed-disclosure default.

ideas.name: Dedicated "Builder Live" tier (£99, up to 10 live jobs, Tell me now built in)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — placement alternative (listed to compare; recommended against)
ideas.mechanism: A single fourth SKU instead of a per-tier switch: 'Builder Live' at £99/month, unlimited users, up to 10 live jobs, disclosure mode fixed to `tell_me_now`, service credits (idea 7) included. Same job-binding, switching and reconcile-only rules as idea 1. Pros: one price to explain, sits as the 'honest premium' choice, no toggle UI. Cons: a fourth visible price muddles the live-jobs ladder (report §'Three tiers work…': every tier must be a plan someone would buy, and comparison should rest on one number); a Solo who wants live mode pays £70 more (3.7× the central foregone fee), which reads as punitive; a Firm at 15 live jobs cannot use it at all, forcing a 'Firm Live' SKU, at which point it is idea 1 with worse naming.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business.

revenue_per_year.solo: £840/yr per taker (£99 − £29 = £70 × 12); uptake 8% → £67 weighted; net +£612 central, but the ratio to the £228 foregone fee is what makes it look like a penalty.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £480/yr per taker (£99 − £59 = £40 × 12); uptake 35% → £168; net +£120 central (identical to idea 1).
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 — 15 live jobs exceed the SKU's 10-job allowance; adding a 'Firm Live' SKU collapses this into idea 1.

ideas.assumptions: Same foregone-fee model as idea 1. Solo uptake 8% (a £70 jump from the entry plan is out of the £25–£45 anchor band). Small-firm uptake unchanged at 35% because the price equals idea 1's Builder+uplift.
ideas.trust_note: Cleaner to advertise, but the Solo price gap invites the 'pay £70 to be told the truth' reading, which is the exact betrayal framing the report warns about. Keep only if the founder prefers one SKU over a toggle and accepts losing Solo and Firm coverage.
ideas.regulatory: As idea 1 (D09 v3, D13 v2, D05, D02, D12). Nothing additional.
ideas.build_dependency: Same as idea 1 minus the toggle UI; plus M4-14 tier definition. Effort: low once idea 1 exists — it is a pricing-table entry.
ideas.gaming_risk: Same as idea 1. Fewer switching paths because the mode is tied to the tier.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8's feature-gated tiers (report table) — a feature that only exists in an upper plan. None known for disclosure timing as the gated feature.

ideas.name: Per-job Tell me now chosen at switch-live (£19 per job)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — pay-per-job variant (borderline: adverse selection)
ideas.mechanism: Instead of a tenant term, the switch-live command carries `disclosure_mode` for that job, chosen by the builder on the same screen ('Tell me as I go on this job — £19'), bound immutably in the switch-live audit event before any signal exists. Everything else follows idea 1: disclosure at signal creation, predicate clause on job mode, reconcile-only check at lock. The £19 is a one-off per job, charged with the next subscription invoice (or at lock, same figure, no extra decision). A variant selector that is not gameable and does not leak is a job attribute fixed at switch-live, such as customer type: 'live on homeowner jobs, hidden on business jobs', which tracks the consumer-law risk of late bills (research §4).
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, per job.

revenue_per_year.solo: £144/yr (19 jobs × 40% opted × £19); foregone fee on opted jobs £91 central → net +£53; with 2× adverse selection (£182) net −£38.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £182/yr (24 × 40% × £19); foregone £144 central → net +£38; adverse selection (£288) → net −£106.
revenue_per_year.firm: £251/yr (33 × 40% × £19); foregone £238 central → net +£13; adverse selection (£476) → net −£225.

ideas.assumptions: Central per-job fee £12 / £15 / £18 (from idea 1's model). 40% of jobs opted in. Adverse selection: the builder chooses live mode on jobs where extras are likely, so opted jobs carry 2× the central catches. £19 flat for simplicity; tiered £15/£19/£25 changes little.
ideas.trust_note: Transparent, but it adds a paid tick-box at the one moment (switch-live) where the report says friction must be zero, and it invites 'did I tick it on that job?' disputes. Two disclosure regimes inside one tenant are hard to explain in a sentence. Honest flag: the builder has better information than JobGuard at switch-live, so this is structurally a losing trade for JobGuard on complex jobs and a pointless one on simple jobs.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (per-job charge is still a subscription-book item, never a success fee), D13 v2, D02, D05 (the tick is an authorized command). G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1's SV-1/SV-2/SV-3 work plus a switch-live UI option (M1-7) and a per-job subscription line on M4-10 documents. Effort: low-medium on top of idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Adverse selection is the main risk and is not gaming, it is rational. No leak: the choice precedes any signal. Builder cannot flip mode after switch-live; JobGuard cannot either.
ideas.precedent: None known for per-job disclosure choice. FairRate's £0.99 per audit is a per-job flat price for a single check, on the homeowner side (report §'No rival sells…').

ideas.name: "Show me first": paid pre-lock reveal at final review (£39 / £69 / £99 per job)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — pay-per-use, chosen at the point of maximum information (borderline: the 'ransom' reading)
ideas.mechanism: On the standard (hidden) plan, at §14.4 step 2 ('Anything else to add before you finish?') the builder can buy a reveal for this job before declaring. The command records a `shadow_disclosure_event(kind='paid_pre_lock_reveal')`, runs the same reconciliation worker against the current draft revision, marks every signal on the job `disclosed_before_lock=true` / `surfaced_early`, and shows the surviving candidates as 'Things to check before you complete' with evidence, exactly like the post-lock reveal screen. The builder adds what is genuine as final-review lines (builder capture, fee-free). The job is then in a 'revealed' state: any signal created later on that job is disclosed at creation too, so JobGuard cannot earn a fee on evidence that arrives five minutes after the peek. Re-running after adding lines is free (no new information). The eventual lock and final check run as reconcile-only. This is also the bridge for in-flight jobs when a tenant upgrades to idea 1. Presentation rule: the price is on the pricing page from day one as a listed feature of the standard plan, never introduced as a pop-up at lock.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, per job, flat.

revenue_per_year.solo: £111/yr (19 jobs × 15% peeked × £39); foregone fee on peeked jobs with 3× adverse selection: 2.85 jobs × £36 = £103 → net +£8.

ideas.assumptions: A builder peeks when they suspect missed work worth more than 10× the peek price (£390 / £690 / £990 net), so 15% of jobs and 3× the central catch rate on those jobs (0.9 paid catches per peeked job × £400/£500/£600 × 10%). Prices set near the fee JobGuard would expect on a job the builder already suspects.
ideas.trust_note: It is the most honest market price of the hold-back and gives every builder an exit before they sign — but a button reading 'Show me what JobGuard found (£69)' at the review step puts a price tag on withheld information at the moment of maximum leverage, which is the 'held to ransom' reading made literal (report §'The hidden final check…'). Uncomfortable by design; wording and placement decide whether it reads as a fair option or a toll. Do not ship without pilot fairness data (idea 10).
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (a subscription-book service line, not a success fee), D13 v2 (new paid disclosure route), D02 (standard-rated supply), D05 (explicit command). B2B. Avoid any 'claims' language. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-4 review step, SV-5 reconciliation worker reused against a draft revision, SV-2 disclosure-event kind, M4-10 per-job service line. Effort: low-medium — the reveal screen and worker exist by SV-5; this adds a trigger, a state and a price line.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder: none beyond rational selection; peeking then adding lines is the intended outcome. JobGuard: the 'revealed state discloses all later signals' rule removes the incentive to time signal creation. A second job cannot be peeked by reference — the reveal is per job and per lock.
ideas.precedent: None known for a paid pre-commitment reveal against a contingency default. Closest: FairRate per-audit pricing (report) and Chargeflow's flat 'Alerts' beside a percentage product (research §6).

ideas.name: Source-scoped live packs: "Materials live" and "Customer requests live"
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — partial disclosure by evidence source at a lower uplift
ideas.mechanism: Two smaller add-ons on the standard plan, each a tenant term bound per job at switch-live like idea 1, but keyed on `signal_type`. Materials live (+£10 / +£20 / +£40): supplier invoice, delivery note and PO items with no matching baseline or captured scope (the SV-3 deterministic detector) are disclosed at creation as 'Possible extra or ordering mistake: not in your quote or extras'. This is prevention money: an out-of-scope PO line is either an extra to log or a mistake to stop before payment, and the hidden design currently withholds that until lock. Customer requests live (+£5 / +£10 / +£15): every customer request received through JobGuard is surfaced immediately regardless of value (D13's must-surface rule already covers significant requests above its threshold; this lowers the threshold to zero for the tenant). Signals of other types (diary, voice notes, photos) stay hidden and fee-eligible. All disclosed signals set `disclosed_before_lock=true`; the §14.6 predicate additionally checks `signal_type NOT IN tenant.live_sources` for the job's bound set. Rejected variant: a builder-set value floor ('tell me about anything over £X') — disclosure would hinge on a labelled estimate, so a low estimate that kept a big item hidden would look like JobGuard estimating low to earn a fee.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (tenant-level add-on).

revenue_per_year.solo: Materials live £120/yr per taker (+£10 × 12) and Customer requests live £60 (+£5 × 12); uptake 30% / 20% → £36 + £12 = £48 weighted; foregone fee per taker: materials £91 (40% of £228), customer £57 (25%) → net +£29 / +£3.

ideas.assumptions: Share of catches by source (unmeasured; §14.17 will measure 'which sources produce real catches'): supplier documents 40%, customer requests 25%, builder's own diary/voice/photos 35%. Pack prices sum with idea 6 to +£25 / +£50 / +£75, above the full Tell me now uplift so the bundle stays the better deal.
ideas.trust_note: Partial hiding is harder to say in one sentence and invites 'you told me about the invoice line but kept quiet about my diary note' — the answer ('you chose materials live') is true but thin. The Materials pack is squarely in the builder's interest and strengthens the watchdog's prevention story; it also exposes an uncomfortable fact for the founder: the standard plan hides some ordering mistakes until lock. That is worth a D13 must-surface question on its own.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (add-on terms), D13 v2 (source-scoped disclosure and its interaction with the must-surface threshold), D12 v2 (customer-message processing basis unchanged), D02, D05. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1's plumbing plus a `live_sources` set on `subscription_terms` and on the job binding, and a predicate clause in SV-1. SV-3 must tag `signal_type` reliably. Effort: low on top of idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: Coalescing across sources: one extra evidenced by a live source and a hidden source must reconcile as disclosed (builder-favourable), never as a hidden fee-eligible signal — SV-3 coalescing must treat any disclosed member as disclosing the whole coalesced signal. Otherwise none beyond idea 1.
ideas.precedent: Feature-scoped add-ons are standard in the category (Tradify's AI bill reader in Plus; Powered Now's receipt scanner in Premium — report table). None known for disclosure timing by source.

ideas.name: "My own records" live pack: the builder's diary, voice notes and photos surfaced now (+£10 / +£20 / +£20)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — the trust-critical partial pack
ideas.mechanism: The single most resented fee case is Test O in §14.15: a diary note 'fitted outside tap', never logged, omitted at lock, billed by JobGuard at 10% — the builder's own words used against them (report §'The hidden final check…': builders reject the fee where the extra 'was already in their head or their notes'). This pack lifts §14.2's 'no per-note prompt' rule for the tenant, for signals whose evidence is the builder's own diary entries, voice notes and uploaded photos only: at creation the signal is disclosed as a gentle card, 'You noted this — log it as an extra?', with the note or photo cited. Same binding, predicate and reconcile-only rules as idea 5. Third-party evidence (supplier documents, customer messages) stays hidden. Priced above idea 5's customer pack because it forgoes the largest single catch source after supplier documents and because it removes the single worst trust outcome.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business.

revenue_per_year.solo: £120/yr per taker (+£10 × 12); uptake 40% → £48 weighted; foregone (own diary, voice and photo signals ≈ 35% of catches = £80) → net +£40.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £240/yr per taker (+£20 × 12); uptake 40% → £96 weighted; foregone £126 → net +£114.
revenue_per_year.firm: £240/yr per taker (+£20 × 12); uptake 40% → £96 weighted; foregone £208 → net +£32.

ideas.assumptions: Own-record signals = 35% of catches (diary/voice 20%, photos 15%; unmeasured). Uptake 40% across tiers because the trigger is emotional, not scale-driven. Resulting prices £39 / £79 / £139.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and it neutralises the 'you used my own notes against me' story. Plainly: if pilot fairness data (idea 10) shows this case drives most resentment, the right move may be to make own-record signals fee-free by rule (a D13 change), and a paid pack meanwhile gives a market price for that decision rather than pre-empting it.
ideas.regulatory: D13 v2 (an explicit exception to the no-per-note-prompt rule for paying tenants), D09 v3, D12 v2, D02, D05. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Same as idea 5 with `live_sources = {diary, voice_note, builder_photo}`; the diary/voice-note surfaces (SV-7 'job diary if absent') must exist. Effort: low on top of idea 5.
ideas.gaming_risk: Coalescing rule from idea 5 applies (a diary note plus a supplier line for one extra → disclosed as a whole). A builder cannot 'launder' a supplier-evidenced extra into a fee-free one by writing a diary note after the fact — that already reconciles builder-favourably under §14.2's tie-break, which is the founder's intended outcome.
ideas.precedent: None known.

ideas.name: Bounded service credits on Tell me now: missed supplier line and wrong card
ideas.category: Service warranty on the paid plan (contractual service credit; legal review required)
ideas.mechanism: Two narrowly defined credits, both paid only as a subscription credit note issued through M4-10 against the next period's subscription invoice — never cash, never against a success fee, never on the hidden plan's fee book. (a) Missed-line credit: the builder paid a supplier invoice that JobGuard had ingested as verified evidence at least two working days before the payment was recorded; the invoice contained a duplicate of an already-ingested invoice/line, or a line priced above a PO or price agreement held in JobGuard; the deterministic three-way match (M2 supplier matching) produced no finding for it; the builder reports it within 60 days; JobGuard verifies from immutable records (evidence hashes, matching-run log). Credit = the overpaid difference, capped at one month's plan price per period (£49 / £99 / £179). If the builder later recovers the same money from the supplier, no success fee can apply to it (JobGuard missed it; it cannot then charge to recover it). (b) Wrong-card credit: on a live-mode job, a `possible_extra` card dismissed as 'wrong job or evidence' where the immutable evidence link provably belongs to another job/tenant, or the detector version is later marked defective — £5 per verified card, capped at one month's uplift per quarter. Not covered: judgement dismissals ('not an extra', 'goodwill'), AI-proposal misses, documents JobGuard never received, and anything the builder could not evidence. Classification, honestly: a remedy for JobGuard's own service failure capped at fees paid looks like a SaaS service credit (a contractual remedy), but paying the builder's third-party loss (the overpayment) rather than refunding service fees edges towards indemnity, and an arrangement where a provider assumes the risk of an uncertain event and pays money on it is the shape the insurance perimeter tests look for. Keep the cap tied to fees paid, describe it as a service-failure credit, and get legal review before any wording ships. Standalone variant on the hidden plan at +£5 / +£10 / +£15 (credit (a) only) — sells reassurance on the watchdog independent of the hold-back.
ideas.who_pays: JobGuard bears the cost (credit); the builder pays nothing extra on Tell me now, or a small add-on on the hidden plan.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ −£2 (supplier spend £52.5k × 0.5% overcharge/duplicate incidence × 60% ingested × 3% matcher miss × 50% claimed) − £7 wrong-card (19 jobs × 1.5 cards × 5% verifiable detector errors × £5) ≈ −£9/yr; standalone hidden-plan add-on £60/yr per taker, 10% uptake → £6.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ −£9 (£210k × 0.5% × 60% × 3% × 50%) − £9 ≈ −£18/yr; standalone add-on £120/yr per taker, 10% → £12.
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ −£32 (£700k × 0.5% × 60% × 3% × 50%) − £12 ≈ −£44/yr; standalone add-on £180/yr per taker, 10% → £18.

ideas.assumptions: Supplier spend 35% of turnover. Overcharge/duplicate incidence 0.5% of spend (research §6: no UK data for small builders — pure assumption). 60% of supplier spend reaches JobGuard as documents; deterministic matcher miss rate 3% on ingested duplicates/above-rate lines; half of misses are noticed and claimed. Wrong-card rate 5% of live cards, 1.5 cards per job. Its value is what it does for the uplift's credibility, not its cost.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and it makes the paid plan a promise rather than a mode. The fine print (what is not covered) is where the trust risk sits; if the exclusions read like an insurer's, the credit does harm. Never market it as insurance or a guarantee of savings.
ideas.regulatory: Legal review of the insurance perimeter (whether a capped loss-based credit is a contract of insurance rather than a contractual service credit); D02 (credit-note VAT treatment); D09 v3 (credit terms); M4-10 credit-note mechanics; D01 (explicit rule that credits never touch the success-fee book). G4.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-10 credit notes, M2 supplier matching run logs (M2-2/M2-3 matching provenance), SV-2 evidence links, a claim record with an approved Decision. Effort: medium — the money path exists; the claim workflow and verification view are new.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder marks judgement dismissals as 'wrong evidence' to farm credits — mitigated by verifiability from immutable links and the small cap. Builder pays a supplier late so the invoice is 'ingested two days before payment' — irrelevant, JobGuard should have flagged it either way. Colluding supplier duplicates — capped and evidenced, low value.
ideas.precedent: SaaS SLA service credits are general practice (not looked up). Chargeflow advertises a '4x ROI guarantee' beside its percentage fee (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). No known trade-software precedent for a missed-line credit.

ideas.name: Post-fee "switch to Tell me now" offer on the fee statement
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — conversion trigger (uncomfortable; flagged)
ideas.mechanism: Trigger: a success-fee statement is approved on the hidden plan (M4-10-S/M4-12 path). The same screen that shows '£800 found, JobGuard's fee £80, yours £720' also shows, in plain words, 'JobGuard first held this on 14 May; you completed your account on 2 July. On Tell me now (£99 a month) you would have seen it on 14 May and billed it yourself with no fee.' with a 'Switch for future jobs' button that creates the D05 plan-change Decision. No discount, no first-month-free (report §'Where premium should show': avoid introductory offers). The dates are the §14.1 permitted claim, already required. Symmetry required: the same statement logic on the live plan tells a builder whose cards produced nothing all year that the standard plan would have cost them less (see idea 10), so the offer is advice, not pressure.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, via higher uptake of idea 1.

revenue_per_year.solo: ≈ +£22/yr gross across the Solo base (60% of Solos pay at least one fee a year × 15% accept = +9 points uptake × £240); net of foregone fee on switchers (9% × £228 = £21) ≈ +£1.

ideas.assumptions: Share of builders experiencing at least one fee per year 60% / 80% / 95% (from the central catch rate and job counts); 15% of those switch after seeing the dates. The money is roughly neutral; the purpose is giving the builder the exit at the moment of the sting.
ideas.trust_note: Plainly uncomfortable: shown only after a fee it reads as 'pay us to stop doing this to you', the protection-racket framing the report's betrayal research predicts. It is only defensible if the plan choice was visible at sign-up, the dates are shown on every statement regardless of the offer, and the symmetrical downgrade advice exists. If any of those three is missing, do not ship it.
ideas.regulatory: D05 (plan change Decision), D09 v3, D12 v2 (statement wording). B2B, so no consumer pressure-selling rules bite, but the fairness point stands. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1, M4-10 statement rendering, VALUE-2 value receipt. Effort: low.
ideas.gaming_risk: None on money. Reputational: a screenshot of this screen is the most quotable artefact JobGuard will ever produce; review the copy as a public statement.
ideas.precedent: None known. Loosely, 'upgrade to remove ads' patterns, which are widely disliked.

ideas.name: Live-mode trial job: the first live job runs Tell me now, then the builder chooses
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — trial design (touches the trial recommendation, not a fixed decision)
ideas.mechanism: The report's trial is 'watchdog and final account free on the first live job, card at switch-live, success fee charged normally' (§'Recommendation'). This variant runs that first job in `tell_me_now` mode: every possible-extra card is shown as it arises, labelled 'On the standard plan you would see this after you complete your final account', with the fee that would have applied shown as an illustration. At the trial job's lock the builder sees the choice screen (idea 10) with both plans priced and their own job's numbers beside each: 'Cards shown to you during this job: 3 (est. £1,150); you logged 2 (£900). On the standard plan JobGuard's fee on what you logged after seeing the cards would have been £0 — because you logged it; anything you had missed at lock would have cost 10%.' The trial job carries no success fee (all signals surfaced early), which departs from the report's advice to charge the fee normally on the trial job; the trade is one job's fee for a demonstrated engine (operational transparency and reciprocity, research §4) and a revealed-preference price signal. Hidden remains the default for the second job onward unless the builder chooses otherwise.
ideas.who_pays: JobGuard forgoes one job's fee; the builder pays nothing extra.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 direct; forgoes £12 (one job's central fee, £228 ÷ 19); if a live trial lifts trial-to-paid conversion by 5 points, +£17/yr of base subscription per trial starter (5% × £348) plus higher Tell me now uptake.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 direct; forgoes £15; +£35/yr per trial starter at 5 points (5% × £708).
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 direct; forgoes £18; +£71/yr per trial starter at 5 points (5% × £1,428).

ideas.assumptions: Conversion lift of 5 points on a no-card-trial base in the 4–6% to 25–35% range (report §'Let the trial run…'; untested for trades). The report's 90-day trial ceiling applies. Only jobs switched live after the choice take the chosen mode (idea 1's rule).
ideas.trust_note: The builder sees what the engine does before deciding whether to pay for it live or accept the second-check model, which is the fairest possible introduction. It does mean the builder never experiences the hidden model on the trial job, so the 'surprise catch' the report says is the product's strongest quality signal is not demonstrated; the choice screen has to carry that. Flag: this changes a report recommendation (charge the fee on the trial job), not a founder decision.
ideas.regulatory: D13 v2 (trial disclosure route), D09 v3 (trial terms), D12 v2 (onboarding wording). Pilot use needs G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval (§14.11).
ideas.build_dependency: Idea 1 plumbing, M4-11 sign-up/trial state, idea 10's choice screen. Effort: low on top of idea 1.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder could run one large job as the free live trial and cancel — the same risk the report's trial already carries; the 90-day ceiling and card-at-switch-live bound it.
ideas.precedent: Reverse trial (full features then drop back to the free layer) — report §'Let the trial run…' citing Growth Unhinged; no quantitative evidence on uplift.

ideas.name: Plan-choice screen, two-way running comparison and pilot arms: the instrument that prices the hold-back (D09/D13 changes, §14.17 additions)
ideas.category: Pricing instrument and decision-record changes for the whole lens
ideas.mechanism: CHOICE SCREEN. At sign-up and on the plan page: two cards side by side with the one-sentence copy from idea 1, the price of each, and one line under Tell me now stating what it removes ('never a success fee on JobGuard's own finds') and one under Standard stating what it keeps ('10% only on extras JobGuard finds after your bill'). TWO-WAY COMPARISON. Every period, the value receipt (VALUE-2) shows the builder the other plan's arithmetic from their own immutable records: on Standard, 'fees this year £X; Tell me now would have cost £Y'; on Tell me now, 'cards shown £N; you logged M; uplift paid £Y; on Standard your fee on items you had missed at lock would have been £Z (illustration)'. Recommending the cheaper plan when the numbers say so is what makes idea 8 advice instead of pressure. PILOT ARMS (pilot_no_charge, hypothetical fees, after G1 + D12/D13 pilot approval). Randomise each pilot tenant's first live job to hidden or live (fairness and outcome data need randomisation), then let tenants choose per idea 1's rules at displayed hypothetical prices (choice data needs revealed preference), with price variants across cohorts: Solo £49 vs £39 vs £59; Builder £99 vs £79; Firm £179 vs £199. §14.17 ADDITIONS. (1) share choosing each plan by tier and price; (2) perceived fairness after lock in both arms and after any hypothetical fee statement; (3) catches surfaced early — count, estimated £, share converted to Log an extra within 7 days, billed, paid, disputed — versus catches revealed at lock — count, £, confirmed, billed, paid, disputed; (4) false-positive rate by arm and builder minutes per card; (5) share of early cards answered 'goodwill — not charging'; (6) hypothetical would-have-been fee per live-arm builder-year against the uplift — the direct test of the delta (if it exceeds £240 for Solo the uplift is under-priced); (7) plan switches after first lock or first fee, with stated reasons; (8) D11 v2 signals and churn intent by arm; (9) which evidence sources produce real catches (already listed; needed to price ideas 5 and 6). RECORD CHANGES. D09 → `subscription_pricing_policy_v3`: add `disclosure_mode` as a tenant term with price per tier, `effective_at`, job binding at switch-live, upgrade immediate/downgrade next period, no offset or credit against success fees, and the service-credit terms of idea 7. D13 → `shadow_attribution_policy_v2`: recognise `tenant_plan_live`, `paid_pre_lock_reveal` and source-scoped disclosure as pre-lock disclosure routes that set `disclosed_before_lock` at signal creation; add the immutable job binding and the rule that a live-mode job's final check runs reconcile-only and is recorded; keep must-surface rules unchanged on every plan. D11 v2: add the advisory signal 'disclosure mode changed within N days of a switch-live'. D12 v2: onboarding text for both plans. D05: plan change as an explicit Decision. D01: state that plan uplifts and credits never touch the success-fee book. Each is a new version; none rewrites accepted terms.
ideas.who_pays: Nobody directly; it determines what ideas 1–6 charge.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 direct. Output: the measured share choosing Tell me now at £49/£39/£59 and the live arm's hypothetical fee per builder-year; if that fee exceeds £240 the Solo uplift is under-priced, if choice share at £49 is under 10% it is over-priced.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 direct. Same test against £480/yr and a 35% expected choice share at £99.
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 direct. Same test against £720/yr (or £960 at £199) and a 50% expected share at £179.

ideas.assumptions: Pilot size is small (10–20 builders per the report), so price-variant cohorts will be thin; treat the results as directional and repeat with the priced sign-up page test the report recommends before G4. Both arms run hypothetical fees only.
ideas.trust_note: Measuring fairness and publishing the other plan's arithmetic to each builder is itself the strongest trust move in this lens. One caution: the running comparison on the standard plan necessarily prints 'JobGuard first held this on [date]', which is the 'knew on day 12' fact the research says a terms sentence cannot neutralise — it must be printed anyway (§14.1 permitted claim), so the product has to be able to stand behind the timing rationale.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3, D13 v2, D11 v2, D12 v2, D05, D01 wording; G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval before any shadow processing of real pilot data; G4 before any charge. An agent cannot mark any of these approved.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-0 for the record text (proposed status only); VALUE-2 for the comparison cards; M4-11 sign-up choice; pilot instrumentation under M1's measurement tasks. Effort: low for the records and screen; the pilot design is a founder/legal task, not code.
ideas.gaming_risk: Instrument risk only: builders choosing at hypothetical prices overstate willingness to pay; the randomised first job and the later real priced page test are the corrections.
ideas.precedent: Priced sign-up page test and structured price conversations recommended in the report §'Recommendation'; randomised trial-design field experiments cited there (Yoganarasimhan et al.; Zhang & Duan).

ideas.name: 'Tell me now' plan toggle: per-tier uplift (£49 / £99 / £179), with the single-SKU 'Builder Live' placement as a rejected alternative
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — core plan variant (opt-in tenant term; hidden-until-lock stays the default)
ideas.mechanism: A per-tenant switch on every tier rather than a fourth tier: Solo £29 → £49 (+£20), Builder £59 → £99 (+£40), Firm £119 → £179 (+£60; £199 defensible if pilot catches sit high); Contractor quotes both. The delta is set at roughly the central expected missed-variation success fee per builder-year on that tier (£228 / £360 / £594), rounded to a nine-ending step and slightly above it (1.05× / 1.33× / 1.21×) to cover the flat-rate premium people pay for certainty (research note price_level_and_tier_psychology, Lambrecht & Skiera), adverse selection and the cost of serving live cards; Solo sits near break-even because that segment is anchored at £25–£45 (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). Data model: D09 term `disclosure_mode ∈ {hidden_until_lock, tell_me_now}` with `effective_at`; switch-live copies the tenant mode into an immutable `job.disclosure_mode` bound in the switch-live audit event, and detectors (SV-3) read the job value only. On a `tell_me_now` job the shadow worker inserts each `shadow_commercial_signal` and, in the same transaction, a `shadow_disclosure_event(kind='tenant_plan_live')`, sets `disclosed_before_lock=true` (monotonic), `first_builder_visible_at=now`, state `surfaced_early`, and writes an advisory-lane Finding of new kind `possible_extra` through the M2-7-S inbox path (the same route D13 must-surface uses; must-surface cards stay mandatory lane on every plan). Disclosure is set at creation, not display, so the daily advisory budget can never hide a card that later earns a fee. Card: description, labelled estimate, each evidence item with date/source, four actions — 'Log this as an extra' (prefilled Log an extra; AI structuring of the builder's own entry is builder capture under §14.2), 'Already in my quote/extras' (must pick the item → reconciled), 'Not an extra / goodwill', 'Wrong job or evidence'. The card never creates a variation, debt or fee. Belt and braces: the §14.6 predicate gains `AND job.disclosure_mode = hidden_until_lock`. Delivery setting ('cards as you go' vs 'cards when I build the final account') is same price because foregone fee is identical. Switching: per tenant; a change applies only to jobs switched live at/after `effective_at` (upgrade immediate pro-rata; downgrade next period); in-flight jobs keep the bound mode both ways; no switching rule may depend on signal existence (§14.3 leak); date-based only. Post-lock on this plan the same 'Running JobGuard's final check' screen runs, classifies every signal (all `surfaced_early`), records the run and shows an empty reveal: 'Everything JobGuard found on this job was shown to you during it. Nothing new.' Late-arriving evidence is information only. Pricing-page copy — Standard: 'JobGuard tracks everything you log for free, then runs an independent second check after you complete your final account and takes 10% only of extra money it finds that you then get paid.' Tell me now: 'For £20 more a month JobGuard shows you every possible extra the moment it spots one, so you bill it yourself the normal way — nothing is held for the final check and there is never a success fee on it.' REJECTED PLACEMENT (merged): a single fourth SKU 'Builder Live' at £99, up to 10 live jobs, mode fixed to `tell_me_now`, service credits (I72) included. Pros: one price to explain, no toggle UI. Cons: a fourth visible price muddles the live-jobs ladder (report §'Three tiers work…'); a Solo pays £70 more (3.7× the central foregone fee, reads as punitive); a Firm at 15 live jobs cannot use it, forcing a 'Firm Live' SKU, at which point it is the toggle with worse naming.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (tenant-level subscription uplift, ex VAT, monthly or annual).

revenue_per_year.solo: £240/yr per builder on the plan (£20 × 12); uptake-weighted at 25% = £60; net of foregone missed-variation fee +£12 central (£240 − £228), −£1,280 high case, +£211 low case. Single-SKU variant disagrees: £840/yr per taker (£70 × 12) at only 8% uptake = £67 weighted, net +£612 central — the ratio to the £228 foregone fee is what makes it read as a penalty.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £480/yr per taker (£40 × 12); uptake-weighted at 35% = £168; net +£120 central, −£1,440 high case. Single-SKU variant identical.
revenue_per_year.firm: £720/yr per taker (£60 × 12); uptake-weighted at 50% = £360; net +£126 central, −£1,920 high case; at £199 (+£80) £960/yr, net +£366 central. Single-SKU variant: £0 (15 live jobs exceed its 10-job allowance).

ideas.assumptions: All ex VAT and labelled assumptions. Tier mapping Solo→Solo, Small firm→Builder, Firm→Firm at the report's £29/£59/£119 (§'Recommendation'). Jobs per year 19 / 24 / 33. Foregone-fee model (pool unmeasured, §14.17): 0.75 revealed candidates per locked job × 40% reach confirmed-billed-paid = 0.3 paid catches per job; net value per paid catch £400 / £500 / £600 → central foregone fee £228 / £360 / £594 per builder-year. High case 2 × 50% × £800 = £80 per job → £1,520 / £1,920 / £2,640. Low case 0.25 × 30% × £200 → £29 / £36 / £50. Uptake 25% / 35% / 50% (toggle) versus 8% / 35% / n.a. (single SKU). Choosers self-select toward the high case, so central net is optimistic; the pilot choice share (I75) corrects the price.
ideas.trust_note: Offering a priced choice is a stronger fairness lever than a sentence in the terms (research note success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp: disclosure alone does not neutralise a conflict; autonomy does more). Double-edged: it lets a critic write 'JobGuard charges £20 a month not to withhold things from you' and publishes a price for the hold-back. Copy must never describe the standard plan as 'we hold back' — only 'a second check after your bill'. Per-card or per-catch charges on surfaced cards are ruled out by D11 v2 ('may not reveal before lock and later charge'); only a flat plan price is compatible with the founder's decisions. The single-SKU placement scores 3: cleaner to advertise but the Solo gap invites the 'pay £70 to be told the truth' reading, the betrayal framing the report warns about.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (new term, price, switching, no offset), D13 v2 (paid tenant disclosure route), D05 (plan change is an explicit Decision), D02 (VAT on the uplift), D12 v3 (onboarding wording for both plans). B2B, so largely outside DMCC drip-pricing, but the displayed headline must include the uplift once chosen. Charging behind G4; pilot_no_charge shows the mode with hypothetical prices only.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-0 (D09 v3 / D13 v2 text), SV-1 (mode clause on the §14.6 predicate; `possible_extra` finding type), SV-2 (`subscription_terms.disclosure_mode`, immutable `job.disclosure_mode`, new disclosure-event kind), SV-3 (detector emits disclosure on live-mode jobs), M2-7-S inbox card, SV-4/SV-5 (reconcile-only path and screen text), M4-13 agreement wording, M4-14 plan-change metering, M4-11 sign-up selection. Effort: medium — mostly plumbing on tables §14.12 already plans, one card and one screen; roughly 3 PRs. Single-SKU placement would be a pricing-table entry on top.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder: toggle hidden before an expected-simple job and live before an expected-complex one — legitimate adverse selection, blunted by per-tenant scope and next-period downgrade; add a D11 advisory signal 'mode changed within N days of a switch-live' (flag only). JobGuard: cannot delay signal creation to earn a fee because the predicate clause on job mode fails regardless of timing. Leak: any rule conditioned on signal existence would breach §14.3 — forbidden by design.
ideas.precedent: Chargeflow sells flat prevention ('Alerts', $29 per deflected chargeback) beside 25% recovery on the same page; Paddle Retain offers flat fees for small customers and a percentage for larger ones (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). ServiceM8 feature-gated tiers for the single-SKU form (report table). No known precedent for a paid 'disclose now' option against a delayed-disclosure default.
ideas.merged_from: "Tell me now" plan toggle: per-tier uplift (£49 / £99 / £179); Dedicated "Builder Live" tier (£99, up to 10 live jobs, Tell me now built in)

ideas.name: Per-job 'Tell me now' chosen at switch-live (£19 per job)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — pay-per-job variant (borderline: adverse selection)
ideas.mechanism: Instead of a tenant term, the switch-live command carries `disclosure_mode` for that job, chosen by the builder on the same screen ('Tell me as I go on this job — £19'), bound immutably in the switch-live audit event before any signal exists. Everything else follows I67: disclosure at signal creation, predicate clause on job mode, reconcile-only check at lock. The £19 is a one-off per job, charged with the next subscription invoice (or at lock, same figure, no extra decision). A non-gameable, non-leaking selector variant is a job attribute fixed at switch-live such as customer type — 'live on homeowner jobs, hidden on business jobs' — which tracks the consumer-law risk of late bills (research note success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp).
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, per job.

revenue_per_year.solo: £144/yr (19 jobs × 40% opted × £19); foregone fee on opted jobs £91 central → net +£53; with 2× adverse selection (£182) net −£38.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £182/yr (24 × 40% × £19); foregone £144 central → net +£38; adverse selection (£288) → net −£106.
revenue_per_year.firm: £251/yr (33 × 40% × £19); foregone £238 central → net +£13; adverse selection (£476) → net −£225.

ideas.assumptions: Central per-job fee £12 / £15 / £18 (from I67's model). 40% of jobs opted in. Adverse selection: the builder chooses live mode on jobs where extras are likely, so opted jobs carry 2× the central catches. £19 flat for simplicity; tiered £15/£19/£25 changes little.
ideas.trust_note: Transparent, but it adds a paid tick-box at the one moment (switch-live) where the report says friction must be zero, and invites 'did I tick it on that job?' disputes. Two disclosure regimes inside one tenant are hard to explain in a sentence. Honest flag: the builder has better information than JobGuard at switch-live, so this is structurally a losing trade for JobGuard on complex jobs and a pointless one on simple jobs.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (per-job charge is a subscription-book item, never a success fee), D13 v2, D02, D05 (the tick is an authorized command). G4.
ideas.build_dependency: I67's SV-1/SV-2/SV-3 work plus a switch-live UI option (M1-7) and a per-job subscription line on M4-10 documents. Effort: low-medium on top of I67.
ideas.gaming_risk: Adverse selection is the main risk and is rational, not gaming. No leak: the choice precedes any signal. Neither party can flip the mode after switch-live.
ideas.precedent: None known for per-job disclosure choice. FairRate's £0.99 per audit is a per-job flat price for a single check, on the homeowner side (report §'No rival sells…').
ideas.merged_from: Per-job Tell me now chosen at switch-live (£19 per job)

ideas.name: 'Show me first': paid pre-lock reveal at final review (£39 / £69 / £99 per job)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — pay-per-use, chosen at the point of maximum information (borderline: the 'ransom' reading)
ideas.mechanism: On the standard (hidden) plan, at §14.4 step 2 ('Anything else to add before you finish?') the builder can buy a reveal for this job before declaring. The command records `shadow_disclosure_event(kind='paid_pre_lock_reveal')`, runs the same reconciliation worker against the current draft revision, marks every signal on the job `disclosed_before_lock=true` / `surfaced_early`, and shows surviving candidates as 'Things to check before you complete' with evidence, exactly like the post-lock reveal screen. The builder adds what is genuine as final-review lines (builder capture, fee-free). The job then enters a 'revealed' state: any signal created later on that job is disclosed at creation, so JobGuard cannot earn a fee on evidence arriving five minutes after the peek. Re-running after adding lines is free. The eventual lock and final check run reconcile-only. Also the bridge for in-flight jobs when a tenant upgrades to I67. Presentation rule: the price is on the pricing page from day one as a listed feature of the standard plan, never introduced as a pop-up at lock. Distinct from I20 ('Final Check Only' pay-per-use for non-subscribers): this is a subscriber's pre-commitment peek.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, per job, flat.

revenue_per_year.solo: £111/yr (19 jobs × 15% peeked × £39); foregone fee on peeked jobs with 3× adverse selection 2.85 jobs × £36 = £103 → net +£8.

ideas.assumptions: A builder peeks when they suspect missed work worth more than 10× the peek price, so 15% of jobs and 3× the central catch rate on those jobs (0.9 paid catches per peeked job × £400/£500/£600 × 10%). Prices set near the fee JobGuard would expect on a job the builder already suspects.
ideas.trust_note: The most honest market price of the hold-back and an exit for every builder before they sign — but a button reading 'Show me what JobGuard found (£69)' at the review step puts a price tag on withheld information at the moment of maximum leverage, the 'held to ransom' reading made literal (report §'The hidden final check…'). Uncomfortable by design; wording and placement decide whether it reads as a fair option or a toll. Do not ship without pilot fairness data (I75).
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (a subscription-book service line, not a success fee), D13 v2 (new paid disclosure route), D02 (standard-rated supply), D05 (explicit command). B2B. Avoid any 'claims' language. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-4 review step, SV-5 reconciliation worker reused against a draft revision, SV-2 disclosure-event kind, M4-10 per-job service line. Effort: low-medium — reveal screen and worker exist by SV-5; this adds a trigger, a state and a price line.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder: none beyond rational selection; peeking then adding lines is the intended outcome. JobGuard: the 'revealed state discloses all later signals' rule removes any incentive to time signal creation. The reveal is per job and per lock; a second job cannot be peeked by reference.
ideas.precedent: None known for a paid pre-commitment reveal against a contingency default. Closest: FairRate per-audit pricing (report) and Chargeflow's flat 'Alerts' beside a percentage product (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6).
ideas.merged_from: "Show me first": paid pre-lock reveal at final review (£39 / £69 / £99 per job)

ideas.name: Source-scoped live packs: 'Materials live' and 'Customer requests live'
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — partial disclosure by evidence source at a lower uplift
ideas.mechanism: Two smaller add-ons on the standard plan, each a tenant term bound per job at switch-live like I67, but keyed on `signal_type`. Materials live (+£10 / +£20 / +£40): supplier invoice, delivery note and PO items with no matching baseline or captured scope (the SV-3 deterministic detector) are disclosed at creation as 'Possible extra or ordering mistake: not in your quote or extras' — prevention money, since an out-of-scope PO line is either an extra to log or a mistake to stop before payment, and the hidden design currently withholds it until lock. Customer requests live (+£5 / +£10 / +£15): every customer request received through JobGuard is surfaced immediately regardless of value (D13's must-surface rule already covers significant requests above its threshold; this lowers the threshold to zero for the tenant). Other signal types (diary, voice notes, photos) stay hidden and fee-eligible. All disclosed signals set `disclosed_before_lock=true`; the §14.6 predicate additionally checks `signal_type NOT IN tenant.live_sources` for the job's bound set. Rejected variant: a builder-set value floor ('tell me about anything over £X') — disclosure would hinge on a labelled estimate, so a low estimate that kept a big item hidden would look like JobGuard estimating low to earn a fee.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business (tenant-level add-on).

revenue_per_year.solo: Materials live £120/yr per taker and Customer requests live £60; uptake 30% / 20% → £36 + £12 = £48 weighted; foregone fee per taker: materials £91 (40% of £228), customer £57 (25%) → net +£29 / +£3.

ideas.assumptions: Share of catches by source (unmeasured; §14.17 'which sources produce real catches' will measure it): supplier documents 40%, customer requests 25%, builder's own diary/voice/photos 35%. Pack prices sum with I71 to +£25 / +£50 / +£75, above the full Tell me now uplift so the I67 bundle stays the better deal.
ideas.trust_note: Partial hiding is harder to say in one sentence and invites 'you told me about the invoice line but kept quiet about my diary note' — the answer ('you chose materials live') is true but thin.
