The Materials pack is squarely in the builder's interest and strengthens the watchdog's prevention story; it also exposes an uncomfortable fact for the founder: the standard plan hides some ordering mistakes until lock. That is worth a D13 must-surface question on its own.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3 (add-on terms), D13 v2 (source-scoped disclosure and its interaction with the must-surface threshold), D12 v3 (customer-message processing basis unchanged), D02, D05. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: I67's plumbing plus a `live_sources` set on `subscription_terms` and on the job binding, and a predicate clause in SV-1. SV-3 must tag `signal_type` reliably. Effort: low on top of I67.
ideas.gaming_risk: Coalescing across sources: one extra evidenced by a live source and a hidden source must reconcile as disclosed (builder-favourable), never as a hidden fee-eligible signal — SV-3 coalescing must treat any disclosed member as disclosing the whole coalesced signal. Otherwise as I67.
ideas.precedent: Feature-scoped add-ons are standard in the category (Tradify's AI bill reader in Plus; Powered Now's receipt scanner in Premium — report table). None known for disclosure timing by source.
ideas.merged_from: Source-scoped live packs: "Materials live" and "Customer requests live"

ideas.name: 'My own records' live pack: the builder's diary, voice notes and photos surfaced now (+£10 / +£20 / +£20)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — the trust-critical partial pack
ideas.mechanism: The single most resented fee case is Test O in §14.15: a diary note 'fitted outside tap', never logged, omitted at lock, billed by JobGuard at 10% — the builder's own words used against them (report §'The hidden final check…': builders reject the fee where the extra 'was already in their head or their notes'). This pack lifts §14.2's 'no per-note prompt' rule for the tenant, for signals whose evidence is the builder's own diary entries, voice notes and uploaded photos only: at creation the signal is disclosed as a gentle card, 'You noted this — log it as an extra?', with the note or photo cited. Same binding, predicate and reconcile-only rules as I70 with `live_sources = {diary, voice_note, builder_photo}`. Third-party evidence (supplier documents, customer messages) stays hidden. Priced above I70's customer pack because it forgoes the largest single catch source after supplier documents and removes the single worst trust outcome.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business.

revenue_per_year.solo: £120/yr per taker (+£10 × 12); uptake 40% → £48 weighted; foregone (own-record signals ≈ 35% of catches = £80) → net +£40.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £240/yr per taker (+£20 × 12); uptake 40% → £96 weighted; foregone £126 → net +£114.
revenue_per_year.firm: £240/yr per taker (+£20 × 12); uptake 40% → £96 weighted; foregone £208 → net +£32.

ideas.assumptions: Own-record signals = 35% of catches (diary/voice 20%, photos 15%; unmeasured). Uptake 40% across tiers because the trigger is emotional, not scale-driven. Resulting prices £39 / £79 / £139.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and it neutralises the 'you used my own notes against me' story. Plainly: if pilot fairness data (I75) shows this case drives most resentment, the right move may be to make own-record signals fee-free by rule (a D13 change); a paid pack meanwhile gives a market price for that decision rather than pre-empting it.
ideas.regulatory: D13 v2 (an explicit exception to the no-per-note-prompt rule for paying tenants), D09 v3, D12 v3, D02, D05. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: Same as I70 with the own-record source set; the diary/voice-note surfaces (SV-7 'job diary if absent') must exist. Effort: low on top of I70.
ideas.gaming_risk: I70's coalescing rule applies (a diary note plus a supplier line for one extra → disclosed as a whole). A builder cannot 'launder' a supplier-evidenced extra into a fee-free one by writing a diary note after the fact — that already reconciles builder-favourably under §14.2's tie-break, which is the founder's intended outcome.
ideas.precedent: None known.
ideas.merged_from: "My own records" live pack: the builder's diary, voice notes and photos surfaced now (+£10 / +£20 / +£20)

ideas.name: Bounded service credits on 'Tell me now': missed supplier line and wrong card
ideas.category: Service warranty on the paid plan (contractual service credit; legal review required)
ideas.mechanism: Two narrowly defined credits, paid only as a subscription credit note issued through M4-10 against the next period's subscription invoice — never cash, never against a success fee, never on the hidden plan's fee book. (a) Missed-line credit: the builder paid a supplier invoice that JobGuard had ingested as verified evidence at least two working days before the payment was recorded; the invoice contained a duplicate of an already-ingested invoice/line, or a line priced above a PO or price agreement held in JobGuard; the deterministic three-way match (M2 supplier matching) produced no finding; the builder reports within 60 days; JobGuard verifies from immutable records (evidence hashes, matching-run log). Credit = the overpaid difference, capped at one month's plan price per period (£49 / £99 / £179). If the builder later recovers the same money from the supplier, no success fee can apply (JobGuard missed it; it cannot then charge to recover it). (b) Wrong-card credit: on a live-mode job, a `possible_extra` card dismissed as 'wrong job or evidence' where the immutable evidence link provably belongs to another job/tenant, or the detector version is later marked defective — £5 per verified card, capped at one month's uplift per quarter. Not covered: judgement dismissals, AI-proposal misses, documents JobGuard never received, anything the builder cannot evidence. Classification, honestly: a capped remedy for JobGuard's own service failure looks like a SaaS service credit, but paying the builder's third-party loss rather than refunding service fees edges toward indemnity, and 'provider assumes the risk of an uncertain event and pays money on it' is the shape the insurance perimeter tests look for — keep the cap tied to fees paid, call it a service-failure credit, get legal review before wording ships. Standalone variant on the hidden plan at +£5 / +£10 / +£15 (credit (a) only) sells reassurance on the watchdog independent of the hold-back. Distinct from I07 (value-floor 'subscription back' guarantee): this is a specific-incident credit, not a value floor.
ideas.who_pays: JobGuard bears the cost (credit); the builder pays nothing extra on Tell me now, or a small add-on on the hidden plan.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ −£2 missed-line (£52.5k supplier spend × 0.5% incidence × 60% ingested × 3% matcher miss × 50% claimed) − £7 wrong-card (19 jobs × 1.5 cards × 5% verifiable errors × £5) ≈ −£9/yr; standalone hidden-plan add-on £60/yr per taker, 10% uptake → £6.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ −£9 − £9 ≈ −£18/yr; standalone add-on £120/yr per taker, 10% → £12.
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ −£32 − £12 ≈ −£44/yr; standalone add-on £180/yr per taker, 10% → £18.

ideas.assumptions: Supplier spend 35% of turnover. Overcharge/duplicate incidence 0.5% of spend (no UK data for small builders — pure assumption; research note success_fee_benchmarks §1 gaps). 60% of supplier spend reaches JobGuard as documents; deterministic matcher miss rate 3% on ingested duplicates/above-rate lines; half of misses noticed and claimed. Wrong-card rate 5% of live cards, 1.5 cards per job. Its value is what it does for the uplift's credibility, not its cost.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and makes the paid plan a promise rather than a mode. The fine print (what is not covered) is where the trust risk sits; if the exclusions read like an insurer's, the credit does harm. Never market it as insurance or a guarantee of savings.
ideas.regulatory: Legal review of the insurance perimeter (whether a capped loss-based credit is a contract of insurance rather than a contractual service credit); D02 (credit-note VAT treatment); D09 v3 (credit terms); M4-10 credit-note mechanics; D01 (explicit rule that credits never touch the success-fee book). G4.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-10 credit notes, M2 supplier matching run logs (M2-2/M2-3 matching provenance), SV-2 evidence links, a claim record with an approved Decision. Effort: medium — the money path exists; the claim workflow and verification view are new.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder marks judgement dismissals as 'wrong evidence' to farm credits — mitigated by verifiability from immutable links and the small cap. Builder pays a supplier late so the invoice is 'ingested two days before payment' — irrelevant, JobGuard should have flagged it either way. Colluding supplier duplicates — capped and evidenced, low value.
ideas.precedent: SaaS SLA service credits are general practice (not looked up). Chargeflow advertises a '4x ROI guarantee' beside its percentage fee (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). No known trade-software precedent for a missed-line credit.
ideas.merged_from: Bounded service credits on Tell me now: missed supplier line and wrong card

ideas.name: Post-fee 'switch to Tell me now' offer on the fee statement
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — conversion trigger (uncomfortable; flagged)
ideas.mechanism: Trigger: a success-fee statement is approved on the hidden plan (M4-10-S/M4-12 path). The same screen that shows '£800 found, JobGuard's fee £80, yours £720' also shows, in plain words, 'JobGuard first held this on 14 May; you completed your account on 2 July. On Tell me now (£99 a month) you would have seen it on 14 May and billed it yourself with no fee.' with a 'Switch for future jobs' button that creates the D05 plan-change Decision. No discount, no first-month-free (report §'Where premium should show': avoid introductory offers). The dates are the §14.1 permitted claim, already required. Symmetry required: the same statement logic on the live plan tells a builder whose cards produced nothing all year that the standard plan would have cost them less (I75), so the offer is advice, not pressure.
ideas.who_pays: The builder business, via higher uptake of I67.

revenue_per_year.solo: ≈ +£22/yr gross across the Solo base (60% pay at least one fee a year × 15% accept = +9 points uptake × £240); net of foregone fee on switchers (9% × £228 = £21) ≈ +£1.

ideas.assumptions: Share of builders experiencing at least one fee per year 60% / 80% / 95% (from the central catch rate and job counts); 15% of those switch after seeing the dates. Roughly money-neutral; the purpose is giving the builder the exit at the moment of the sting.
ideas.trust_note: Plainly uncomfortable: shown only after a fee it reads as 'pay us to stop doing this to you', the protection-racket framing the report's betrayal research predicts. Only defensible if the plan choice was visible at sign-up, the dates are shown on every statement regardless of the offer, and the symmetrical downgrade advice exists. If any of those three is missing, do not ship it.
ideas.regulatory: D05 (plan change Decision), D09 v3, D12 v3 (statement wording). B2B, so no consumer pressure-selling rules bite, but the fairness point stands. G4.
ideas.build_dependency: I67, M4-10 statement rendering, VALUE-2 value receipt. Effort: low.
ideas.gaming_risk: None on money. Reputational: a screenshot of this screen is the most quotable artefact JobGuard will ever produce; review the copy as a public statement.
ideas.precedent: None known. Loosely, 'upgrade to remove ads' patterns, which are widely disliked.
ideas.merged_from: Post-fee "switch to Tell me now" offer on the fee statement

ideas.name: Live-mode trial job: the first live job runs 'Tell me now', then the builder chooses (variant of I10)
ideas.category: Paid real-time disclosure — trial design (touches the report's trial recommendation, not a fixed founder decision)
ideas.mechanism: I10 is 'watchdog and final account free on the first live job, card at switch-live, success fee charged normally' (report §'Recommendation'). This variant runs that first job in `tell_me_now` mode: every possible-extra card is shown as it arises, labelled 'On the standard plan you would see this after you complete your final account', with the fee that would have applied shown as an illustration. At the trial job's lock the builder sees the choice screen (I75) with both plans priced and their own job's numbers beside each: 'Cards shown to you during this job: 3 (est. £1,150); you logged 2 (£900). On the standard plan JobGuard's fee on what you logged after seeing the cards would have been £0 — because you logged it; anything you had missed at lock would have cost 10%.' The trial job carries no success fee (all signals surfaced early), departing from the report's advice to charge the fee normally on the trial job; the trade is one job's fee for a demonstrated engine (operational transparency and reciprocity, research note success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp) and a revealed-preference price signal. Hidden remains the default from the second job onward unless the builder chooses otherwise.
ideas.who_pays: JobGuard forgoes one job's fee; the builder pays nothing extra.

ideas.trust_note: The builder sees what the engine does before deciding whether to pay for it live or accept the second-check model — the fairest possible introduction. It does mean the builder never experiences the hidden model on the trial job, so the 'surprise catch' the report calls the product's strongest quality signal is not demonstrated; the choice screen has to carry that. Flag: this changes a report recommendation (charge the fee on the trial job), not a founder decision.
ideas.regulatory: D13 v2 (trial disclosure route), D09 v3 (trial terms), D12 v3 (onboarding wording). Pilot use needs G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval (§14.11).

ideas.name: Plan-choice screen, two-way running comparison and pilot arms: the instrument that prices the hold-back (D09/D13 changes, §14.17 additions)
ideas.category: Pricing instrument and decision-record changes for the paid-disclosure lens (no direct revenue)
ideas.mechanism: CHOICE SCREEN. At sign-up and on the plan page: two cards side by side with I67's one-sentence copy, the price of each, one line under Tell me now stating what it removes ('never a success fee on JobGuard's own finds') and one under Standard stating what it keeps ('10% only on extras JobGuard finds after your bill'). TWO-WAY COMPARISON. Every period the value receipt (VALUE-2) shows the other plan's arithmetic from the builder's own immutable records: on Standard, 'fees this year £X; Tell me now would have cost £Y'; on Tell me now, 'cards shown £N; you logged M; uplift paid £Y; on Standard your fee on items you had missed at lock would have been £Z (illustration)'. Recommending the cheaper plan when the numbers say so is what makes I73 advice instead of pressure. PILOT ARMS (pilot_no_charge, hypothetical fees, after G1 + D12/D13 pilot approval): randomise each pilot tenant's first live job to hidden or live, then let tenants choose per I67's rules at displayed hypothetical prices, with price variants across cohorts: Solo £49 vs £39 vs £59; Builder £99 vs £79; Firm £179 vs £199. §14.17 ADDITIONS: (1) share choosing each plan by tier and price; (2) perceived fairness after lock in both arms and after any hypothetical fee statement; (3) catches surfaced early — count, estimated £, share converted to Log an extra within 7 days, billed, paid, disputed — versus catches revealed at lock; (4) false-positive rate by arm and builder minutes per card; (5) share of early cards answered 'goodwill — not charging'; (6) hypothetical would-have-been fee per live-arm builder-year against the uplift (if it exceeds £240 for Solo the uplift is under-priced); (7) plan switches after first lock or first fee, with reasons; (8) D11 signals and churn intent by arm; (9) which evidence sources produce real catches (already listed; needed to price I70 and I71). RECORD CHANGES. D09 → `subscription_pricing_policy_v3`: `disclosure_mode` as a tenant term with price per tier, `effective_at`, job binding at switch-live, upgrade immediate/downgrade next period, no offset or credit against success fees, I72's credit terms. D13 → `shadow_attribution_policy_v2`: recognise `tenant_plan_live`, `paid_pre_lock_reveal` and source-scoped disclosure as pre-lock disclosure routes that set `disclosed_before_lock` at signal creation; add the immutable job binding and the rule that a live-mode job's final check runs reconcile-only and is recorded; keep must-surface rules unchanged on every plan. D11 next version: advisory signal 'disclosure mode changed within N days of a switch-live'. D12 v3: onboarding text for both plans. D05: plan change as an explicit Decision. D01: plan uplifts and credits never touch the success-fee book. Each is a new version; none rewrites accepted terms.
ideas.who_pays: Nobody directly; it determines what I67–I71 charge.

revenue_per_year.solo: £0 direct. Output: measured share choosing Tell me now at £49/£39/£59 and the live arm's hypothetical fee per builder-year; if that fee exceeds £240 the Solo uplift is under-priced, if choice share at £49 is under 10% it is over-priced.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £0 direct. Same test against £480/yr and a 35% expected choice share at £99.
revenue_per_year.firm: £0 direct. Same test against £720/yr (or £960 at £199) and a 50% expected share at £179.

ideas.assumptions: Pilot size is small (10–20 builders per the report), so price-variant cohorts will be thin; treat results as directional and repeat with the priced sign-up page test the report recommends before G4. Both arms run hypothetical fees only.
ideas.trust_note: Measuring fairness and publishing the other plan's arithmetic to each builder is itself the strongest trust move in this lens. One caution: the running comparison on the standard plan necessarily prints 'JobGuard first held this on [date]', the 'knew on day 12' fact the research says a terms sentence cannot neutralise — it must be printed anyway (§14.1 permitted claim), so the product has to stand behind the timing rationale.
ideas.regulatory: D09 v3, D13 v2, D11 next version, D12 v3, D05, D01 wording; G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval before any shadow processing of real pilot data; G4 before any charge. An agent cannot mark any of these approved.
ideas.build_dependency: SV-0 for the record text (proposed status only); VALUE-2 for the comparison cards; M4-11 sign-up choice; pilot instrumentation under M1's measurement tasks. Effort: low for the records and screen; the pilot design is a founder/legal task, not code.
ideas.gaming_risk: Instrument risk only: builders choosing at hypothetical prices overstate willingness to pay; the randomised first job and the later real priced page test are the corrections.
ideas.precedent: Priced sign-up page test and structured price conversations recommended in the report §'Recommendation'; randomised trial-design field experiments cited there (Yoganarasimhan et al.; Zhang & Duan).

ideas.name: Supplier rate renegotiation savings share (`supplier_rate_renegotiation_savings`, D03 v3 category) — with backdated cash refunds routed to the ordinary 10%
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (new D03 v3 row; new D01 rate and ceiling)
ideas.mechanism: §14.7-style row. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) a prior agreed rate for (merchant, SKU alias, unit/pack) exists as an M2-1 agreed-rate revision AND is evidenced by at least two matched, settled invoice lines at that rate in the 6 months before the letter (a rate-book entry with no invoice evidence never counts); (2) the builder approved and sent, through the command boundary with an approved Decision, a JobGuard-drafted 'rate review letter' naming the SKUs, built only from their own purchase history and, where opted in, I28 benchmark bands — the send record is the case-opening event, exactly as case-opening is for withheld payments, and the builder accepts rate-review fee terms at that moment; (3) a new, lower agreed-rate revision for a named SKU is human-confirmed from intake lines (M2-3) within 90 days of the letter, effective on or after the letter date; (4) savings are measured monthly from invoices: Q = Σ over matched (M2-4), human-confirmed, SETTLED (M4-7 bank feed) invoice lines dated within 12 months of the new revision's effective date of (prior_rate − invoiced_rate)⁺ × quantity, unit-normalised, net of VAT, exact rational — so the fee is capped by quantity actually bought and cash actually paid; (5) F = roundHalfEven(min(Q × 20/100, ceiling)) with a fairness ceiling of £1,000 per (merchant, letter); J = prior posted; posting_delta = F − J per monthly statement, one rounding on the cumulative value (§14.9). NEVER QUALIFIES: SKUs not named in the letter; a rate revision confirmed before the letter or more than 90 days after; savings the builder attests were a merchant-wide list-price cut or market fall (builder-favourable: the attestation stops accrual, fee-free, no proof demanded); switching merchant (I86); unsettled lines; invoices where new delivery/surcharge lines offset the unit-rate cut (held for review); any credit-note-only outcome. BACKDATED CASH REFUNDS (merged clarification): when the merchant backdates the new rate and refunds the difference on invoices already paid, that is settled cash from the supplier, not prospective savings — it uses the ordinary 10% `supplier_overcharge` mechanics (Q = cumulative cash refunded matched to specific paid lines for the named SKUs, allocated to the rate-review case), never the 20% share; a unique derivation identity per `(tenant, invoice_line_id)` across both fee bases prevents double counting, and account credits or credit notes never qualify. This gives the builder the cheaper basis on cash-back, the builder-favourable choice §14.8 demands ('never choose the rule that pays JobGuard most'), and the rule is stated on the statement. REVERSALS: credit notes on counted lines reduce Q; a later rate rise stops accrual; Q never negative; a negative delta creates a linked compensating journal and a refund if collected; history is never edited. TRUST RULE: JobGuard never contacts, negotiates with, or receives anything from a merchant; the builder negotiates; the watchdog then checks every invoice against the new agreed rate exactly as it checked the old one (M2-1 pre-commit and M2-4/M2-5 discrepancy Decisions). Money flow: JobGuard invoices the builder the monthly delta as a success-fee line (M4-10), shown as 'Saved £X this month against your old rate; JobGuard's share £Y', collected under bounded D05 authority (M4-12). Verdict across the three brief categories: cleanest MEASUREMENT (exact arithmetic on records JobGuard already freezes) but weakest ATTRIBUTION (market moves, the builder did the negotiating), so it must stay letter-anchored, 12-month bounded and £-capped; input VAT (I78) is the cleanest category overall; CIS (I79) should be a flat add-on.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of the reduced invoices they actually paid (or the merchant's cash refund); nothing from the merchant, ever.

revenue_per_year.solo: £95 blended (£54–£270 for a Solo who runs one rate review; £48 blended at a 10% share); plus ≈ £2 from backdated cash refunds at 10%.
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £336 blended (£384–£960 for a firm that runs a review; £168 at 10%); plus ≈ £10 from backdated cash refunds.
revenue_per_year.firm: £980 blended (£1,120–£2,800 for a firm that runs reviews; the £1,000-per-merchant ceiling binds at the top of that range; £490 at 10%); plus ≈ £30 from backdated cash refunds.

ideas.assumptions: Materials = 40% of turnover (brief range 35–45%): Solo £60k, Small £240k, Firm £800k. Top-ten SKUs = 45% / 40% / 35% of materials spend: £27k / £96k / £280k. Achievable renegotiation 2–5%, midpoint 3.5%: savings £945 / £3,360 / £9,800 a year. Share 20%: £189 / £672 / £1,960. Half of builders in each archetype send a letter in a year: £95 / £336 / £980. Firm ceiling assumed not to bind at 3.5% because savings spread over ~3 merchants; at 5% a Firm with two merchants hits it. Backdated-refund clarification assumes one in ten reviews produces a backdated cash refund covering three months of saving, halved for credit-not-cash. All ex VAT, before churn effect. A JobGuard-consistent 10% rate halves every figure and is the safer pilot default if the 20% 'P3-lite' framing tests badly.
ideas.trust_note: Borderline. The builder does the phone call, so a 20% share can read as 'a cut of my own negotiation' — people accept fees where the provider visibly did work they could not do themselves and resent them where the value felt like their own (report §'The hidden final check'). Mitigations: the letter is visibly JobGuard's work (purchase-history evidence, drafted, dated); the builder-favourable 'general price cut' attestation; the 12-month stop; the £ ceiling; the plain statement that JobGuard has no merchant relationship; and choosing the lower 10% basis on any cash-back. The P3 benchmark (50% for 12–60 months, research note success_fee_benchmarks §2) makes 20% for 12 months look modest, but P3 is the most resented model in that table. Test perceived fairness in the pilot before committing; if it tests badly, use I77 instead.
ideas.regulatory: None regulated: B2B letter sent by the builder in their own name; JobGuard is not a buying group, agent or introducer and takes nothing from merchants (D11/D04 watchdog independence). Needs D03 v3 (new category with its own qualifying test plus the backdated-refund clarification), D01 next version (a 20% rate and a £ ceiling are a different fee basis from '10% of recovered net principal'), D02 (savings net of VAT), D05 (collection authority extended to rate-review fees), and M4-13 agreement terms accepted at letter send.
ideas.build_dependency: After M2-1 (agreed-rate revisions with validity), M2-3 (human-confirmed intake lines), M2-4 (matched lines with unit/pack normalisation) and M4-7/M4-8 (settled payment facts and allocation). New: `rate_review_letter` artifact + approved send command through the outbox (§5.3), a tenant-scoped derivation identity `(tenant, category, merchant, letter_id)` — §14.9 is written per job/rate and M4-9 must be generalised to non-job scopes — a Graphile monthly accrual job, ceiling logic, the attestation command, and one uniqueness constraint on `(tenant, invoice_line_id)` across both fee bases. Rough effort: 3–4 reviewable tasks, synthetic first (SV-6 pattern), live behind G4. Not before M2-5 lands.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder-side: entering a fake high 'prior rate' before the letter — blocked by the two-settled-lines rule; negotiating outside JobGuard and never recording a letter — no fee, an accepted residual risk exactly as §14.10 accepts billing outside JobGuard. JobGuard-side: claiming market deflation as savings — blocked by the builder-favourable attestation and the 90-day/letter anchoring; counting a backdated refund under both bases — blocked by the uniqueness constraint. Merchant-side: cutting the unit rate and adding delivery or surcharge lines — the offset rule holds those invoices for review rather than accruing.
ideas.precedent: P3 Cost Analysts: 50% of savings shared for 12–60 months (research note success_fee_benchmarks §2, single vendor); UK utility/telecom cost auditors quote-only. The letter-as-case-opening mirrors JobGuard's own §14.7 withheld-payment entry test; the lower-basis rule mirrors §14.8. No precedent found for a savings share sold to builders on their own merchant accounts.
ideas.merged_from: Supplier rate renegotiation savings share (`supplier_rate_renegotiation_savings`, D03 v3 category); Backdated rate refund after a rate review — treated as ordinary supplier cash refund at 10% (clarification inside D03 v3)

ideas.name: Rate review pack: flat per merchant round (£49) or 'Buying watch' add-on (£15/month)
ideas.category: Flat add-on (D09 add-on SKU), no success fee — alternative form of I76
ideas.mechanism: The same JobGuard-drafted rate review letter and 12-month savings tracker as I76, sold as a one-off per merchant round rather than a share of savings: £49 ex VAT per round (letter built from the builder's purchase history and rate book, top-ten SKU table with quantities and current agreed rates, optional I28 band if opted in, then a 'what you saved against your old rate' tracker for 12 months). Trigger: builder opens 'Review my prices with [merchant]'; the charge is an approved Decision at that moment; the letter is still a builder-authorised send. No savings share, no ceiling, no attestation — the savings display is a labelled illustration. Alternative packaging: a £15/month 'Buying watch' add-on covering unlimited rounds. Everything the watchdog does with the new rate is unchanged. Recommended fallback if the pilot shows builders resent a savings share. Not additive with I76 — pick one.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, a flat charge at the moment they start the round; nothing from merchants.

revenue_per_year.solo: £25 (0.5 rounds × £49); or £54 on the £15/month add-on at 30% uptake

ideas.assumptions: Rounds per year: Solo 0.5, Small 2, Firm 5 (one per major merchant). £49 per round chosen to sit under the value of even a 2% cut on £10k of SKU spend (£200). Add-on variant: £15 × 12 × uptake 30% / 40% / 50%.
ideas.trust_note: Obviously in the builder's interest and easy to explain: a fixed price for a letter and a tracker, and the builder keeps 100% of what they negotiate. Lower revenue than I76 but no 'cut of my negotiation' story to spread by word of mouth. Still requires the explicit rule that JobGuard has no merchant relationship, otherwise a 'price review' feature could be mistaken for a buying-group tie-in.
ideas.regulatory: None. D09 v3 needs an add-on SKU definition (amount, per-round vs monthly, VAT). No D01/D03 change because no success fee arises.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 rate book + M2-4 matched lines for the letter's evidence table; a letter template and approved send command; a per-round charge as a subscription add-on obligation (D09 `period_obligation` extension). Rough effort: 1–2 tasks, most of it shared with I76.
ideas.gaming_risk: Negligible: the charge is fixed and pre-approved. Only risk is the builder expecting JobGuard to 'get' the saving — copy must say the builder negotiates.
ideas.precedent: None known as a standalone flat product for small builders; buying groups offer merchant-funded rate reviews (precisely the conflict JobGuard avoids). Tradify sells an Instant Website add-on at £10/month (research note uk_trade_job_software), showing small flat add-ons are normal in this market.
ideas.merged_from: Rate review pack — flat per merchant round (alternative form for renegotiation)

ideas.name: Input VAT recovered after a missing-VAT-invoice flag (`input_vat_recovered_after_missing_invoice_flag`, D03 v3 category)
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (new D03 v3 row; D01 base wording; D02) — cleanest chain, smallest money
ideas.mechanism: §14.7-style row. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) the tenant is VAT-registered on standard or cash accounting (flat-rate-scheme traders excluded except capital goods ≥ £2,000 incl VAT); (2) a payment to a supplier settled (M4-7 bank feed, matched under M4-8) against a document that is not a valid VAT invoice — pro-forma, quotation, statement, delivery note, invoice missing VAT number/date/VAT amount, or addressed to the wrong entity — and 30 days after settlement no valid VAT invoice (or less-detailed invoice ≤ £250) for that supply was held in intake; (3) JobGuard raised a cited `missing_vat_invoice` Decision (M2-5 discrepancy family) naming the payment, the document held and the input tax at stake; (4) a valid VAT invoice for the same supply was received through intake AFTER the Decision (server receive time and issue date both after it), verified under M2-3 and matched to the settled payment; (5) the input tax was included in a filed VAT return, evidenced by an approved accounting connector (SV-7 / I26) or MTD return evidence — builder attestation alone never qualifies in production (§5.6 'mark paid' rule applied to tax); (6) not later credited, disallowed on assessment or repaid. Q = cumulative input tax so evidenced per (tenant, VAT period), exact rational; F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100); posting_delta = F − J once per VAT period. NEVER QUALIFIES: a valid or less-detailed invoice already held at Decision time; an invoice obtained before the Decision; the builder or bookkeeper had already asked the supplier (builder-favourable attestation ends it); flat-rate scheme; partial exemption; supplies where the payment itself is later refunded. REVERSALS: credit note, disallowance or repaid input tax → negative delta, compensating journal, refund if collected. Output labelling: the Decision and the period statement are 'an aid to your VAT records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file returns' (I25/I26 precedent). The sequence Decision → invoice received → return is provable from JobGuard's own immutable timestamps, the amount is on the document, and no market counterfactual is involved.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of VAT they would otherwise have paid to HMRC; nothing from suppliers or HMRC.

revenue_per_year.solo: £5 blended (£12 for an eligible Solo; range £3–£8)

ideas.assumptions: Missing/invalid VAT invoices = 2% of supplier spend (brief range 1–3%): Solo £1,200, Small £4,800, Firm £16,000; VAT at 20%: £240 / £960 / £3,200. Half of flagged items yield a VAT invoice after the Decision AND are evidenced as reclaimed via a connector: £120 / £480 / £1,600. Fee 10%: £12 / £48 / £160. Eligibility: Solo 42% (60% VAT-registered × 70% not on flat-rate), Small 90%, Firm 95%: £5 / £43 / £152. Bookkeepers already chase many of these, which is why only half is credited to JobGuard.
ideas.trust_note: JobGuard visibly did the work (matched a payment to a non-invoice and chased it), the builder gets cash they would have lost on inspection, and the builder-favourable 'I had already asked' rule protects the relationship. The honest problem is scale: £5–£20 per item makes the fee look petty on a statement. Options: run it at 10% under the ordinary cumulative machinery (no extra cost once built) or make it a fee-free goodwill feature of the watchdog and count it as subscription value. Never charge a Solo on the flat-rate scheme — the reclaim does not exist there.
ideas.regulatory: HMRC evidence rules for input tax (VAT Regulations 1995 reg. 29; less-detailed invoices ≤ £250; flat-rate scheme rules) applied as deterministic checks, labelled as aids, never advice; no filing, no agent authority. Accounting-connector evidence needs D04 (residency) and D12 (third-party data). Needs D03 v3 (new category), D01 (base is 'input tax reclaimed', not recovered net principal — wording change at the same 10%), D02 (tax figures and rounding).
ideas.build_dependency: After M2-3 (document class and VAT-field extraction with citations), M2-4/M2-5 (payment-to-document matching and a `missing_vat_invoice` Decision type), M4-7/M4-8 (settled payments), SV-7 approved accounting connector (return-inclusion evidence; I26). Add tenant VAT-status facts (registered / scheme / partial exemption) as versioned inputs. Derivation identity `(tenant, vat_period)`; M4-9 generalised beyond job scope. Rough effort: 2 tasks plus the connector.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder claiming a reclaim never filed — blocked by the connector-evidence requirement. JobGuard over-claiming where a valid invoice existed elsewhere (in the builder's email) — the builder-favourable attestation and the Decision's requirement that nothing valid was held in intake keep this fee-free on doubt. Supplier reissuing an invoice with a later date for one the builder already had — attestation resolves in the builder's favour.
ideas.precedent: No product found charges a success fee on input VAT for small firms; Dext/Hubdoc flag missing receipts on flat plans (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). AP recovery auditors include VAT recovery in 20–30% contingency scopes (research note success_fee_benchmarks §1); no sourced UK VAT-reclaim contingency percentages were found (§5 gaps).
ideas.merged_from: Input VAT recovered after a missing-VAT-invoice flag (`input_vat_recovered_after_missing_invoice_flag`, D03 v3 category)

ideas.name: CIS suffered reclaim: flat year-end pack (recommended) with a 10% evidence-increment variant (`cis_suffered_reclaimed`) shown for comparison
ideas.category: Flat add-on recommended (on top of the I25 CIS module); success-fee variant needs D03 v3 + D01 + a tax-aid decision
ideas.mechanism: RECOMMENDED FORM: a flat 'CIS suffered year-end pack' at £59 ex VAT per tax year (Firm £99): reconciled schedule of every deduction suffered against statements and bank receipts, gaps chased with a JobGuard-drafted statement request the builder sends, export for the builder's accountant or their own SA/EPS entry. All outputs labelled 'an aid to your CIS records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file, hold agent (64-8) authority or claim on your behalf' (I25/I26 precedent). The I25 CIS module (verification records, deduction statements, CIS-suffered tracking) is a prerequisite, not part of this idea; the pack is the charged year-end deliverable on top of it. PERCENTAGE VARIANT (narrow, evidence-increment only), §14.7-style row: QUALIFIES WHEN (1) the tenant is a CIS subcontractor on net payment status with contractor payments and deduction statements tracked; (2) JobGuard matched a contractor payment to the sub's invoice and found a deduction suffered with NO deduction statement held, and raised a cited `missing_cis_statement` Decision; (3) the statement (or the contractor's written confirmation) was then received through intake after the Decision; (4) the deduction was set off or repaid by HMRC — repayment evidenced on the M4-7 bank feed, set-off via an approved payroll/accounting connector; (5) only the increment JobGuard evidenced counts. Q = cumulative evidenced-increment deductions repaid/set off per (tenant, tax year); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100), delta per statement. NEVER QUALIFIES: deductions the builder already held a statement for; the routine year-end reclaim of properly evidenced deductions; gross-payment-status subs; amounts not actually repaid or set off; anything HMRC later amends. REVERSAL: HMRC amendment → negative delta and compensation. Why flat: the money is unarguably the builder's tax and any accountant reclaims it; a percentage of the refund is the refund-firm model the research warns carries the same reputational stain as R&D boutiques (research note success_fee_benchmarks §5), and the increment JobGuard genuinely causes is too uncertain to measure honestly.
ideas.who_pays: The builder: a flat pack fee at year end (recommended), or 10% of the evidenced-increment HMRC repayment (variant).

revenue_per_year.solo: £18 flat (£59 × 30% in CIS) / £22 percentage variant / £90 if charged refund-firm style on the whole refund (not recommended)
revenue_per_year.small_firm: £30 flat (£59 × 50%) / £108 percentage variant / £250 on the whole refund (not recommended)
revenue_per_year.firm: £59 flat (£99 × 60%) / £432 percentage variant / £900 on the whole refund (not recommended)

ideas.assumptions: Share of archetype doing CIS-deducted work: Solo 30% (mostly domestic, outside CIS), Small 50%, Firm 60%. Contractor work as share of turnover 40% / 30% / 30%: £60k / £180k / £600k; labour element 60% → deductions at 20%: £7,200 / £21,600 / £72,000 suffered. Deductions with no statement in the builder's own records: 10% → £720 / £2,160 / £7,200; fee 10% → £72 / £216 / £720; × CIS share → £22 / £108 / £432. Whole-refund figures assume year-end refunds of ~£3,000 / £5,000 / £15,000 × 10% × CIS share. Flat: £59 (Firm £99) × CIS share. Sole traders reclaim through self-assessment; companies set off monthly via EPS and claim any excess after year end — the repayment event JobGuard can see on a bank feed is often a year-end lump.
ideas.trust_note: Flat form scores 4: a reconciled schedule is plainly useful and JobGuard keeps nothing of the refund. Percentage form scores 2: 'you took 10% of my tax refund' is exactly the refund-firm story, the counterfactual (would the accountant have found it?) is weak, and refund firms at 15–30% (brief figure; not independently verified in the research) are a reputational neighbour to avoid. Do not market either as 'we get your tax back'.
ideas.regulatory: CIS rules (FA 2004 and the CIS Regulations 2005: contractor deductions, statements, sub set-off/repayment) applied as deterministic checks only; JobGuard is not a tax agent and files nothing. HMRC repayment evidence via bank feed needs D10/D12; set-off evidence via payroll connector needs D04/D12. Flat form needs only D09 (add-on SKU). Percentage form needs D03 v3, D01 (base = HMRC repayment), D02 and a new decision record covering HMRC-related aids (positioning, disclaimers, no agent authority).
ideas.build_dependency: Requires the I25 CIS module plus contractor-payment matching against sub invoices, a statement-request letter/send command, M4-7 bank feed for repayments, and a year-end pack export. Rough effort: pack 1–2 tasks on top of the module; percentage variant 2 more (Decision type, derivation identity `(tenant, tax_year)`, connector evidence).
ideas.gaming_risk: Percentage form: JobGuard over-claiming that it 'evidenced' a deduction the builder already had on paper — builder-favourable attestation makes it fee-free; contractor confirmation letters could be solicited after the fact — anchor to the Decision date. Flat form: none.
ideas.precedent: CIS/tax refund firms charge 15–30% (brief figure); R&D software platforms 5–10% (research note success_fee_benchmarks §5); Xero sells CIS returns as a £5/month add-on (research note construction_platforms_and_ai). The flat add-on matches how the market already prices CIS features.
ideas.merged_from: CIS suffered reclaim (`cis_suffered_reclaimed`) — recommended as a flat year-end pack, percentage variant shown for comparison

ideas.name: CIS over-deduction on materials or at 30% recovered from the contractor (`cis_over_deduction_recovered`)
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% on contractor cash corrections only)
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual: CIS deductions must exclude the materials element of a sub's invoice, and a verified sub is deducted at 20% not 30%. JobGuard holds the sub-builder's outgoing invoice with a materials split (M1 invoices), the supplier invoices proving those materials (M2-2/M2-4), the contractor's payment (M4-7) and the deduction statement (I25 CIS module). QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) a deduction statement or payment shows deduction applied to the materials element or at 30% despite a verification record; (2) JobGuard raised a cited `cis_over_deduction` Decision with the arithmetic; (3) the builder sent a JobGuard-drafted correction request; (4) the contractor paid the difference in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed and allocated to the case. Q = cumulative cash corrections per (tenant, contractor, tax year); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100); delta per statement. NEVER QUALIFIES: corrections the contractor makes by adjusting a later payment that JobGuard cannot tie to the case (hold for review), any amount recovered from HMRC instead (folds into I79 and, if flat, is fee-free), 30% deductions where the sub was genuinely unverified, disputes settled outside JobGuard. REVERSAL: contractor claws back or HMRC re-determines → negative delta. Labelled as an aid, not tax advice; JobGuard does not contact the contractor.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from cash the contractor paid over after the correction; nothing from contractors or HMRC.

revenue_per_year.solo: £11 blended (£36 for a Solo sub who hits it)

ideas.assumptions: CIS share as I79 (30% / 50% / 60%). Contractor work £60k / £180k / £600k; materials element 30% → £18k / £54k / £180k; wrongly deducted at 20% if every invoice were wrong: £3,600 / £10,800 / £36,000; 20% of invoices affected: £720 / £2,160 / £7,200; contractor corrects in cash (rather than via HMRC or a later adjustment) 50%: £360 / £1,080 / £3,600; fee 10%: £36 / £108 / £360; × CIS share: £11 / £54 / £216. Frequency of materials over-deduction is a judgement (a well-known contractor error) and is not sourced.
ideas.trust_note: The contractor made the error, JobGuard spotted it with arithmetic the builder can inspect, and the builder gets cash they were not going to get. Small sums, but the same 'found money' shape as a supplier overcharge. Keep the correction request in the builder's name and optional — some subs will not want to press a contractor they depend on, and 'chose not to chase' must be respected as fee-free.
ideas.regulatory: CIS Regulations 2005 (materials exclusion; 20%/30% rates; verification) applied deterministically; no advice, no filing, no agent role. Needs D03 v3 (new category), D01 (10% on contractor cash corrections), D12 (contractor as third-party data subject, Article 14 route) — contractors are businesses but named individuals appear on statements.
ideas.build_dependency: I25 CIS module + invoice materials split on the sub-builder's outgoing invoices + M4-7/M4-8 settlement allocation + a correction-request send command. Derivation identity `(tenant, contractor, tax_year)`. Rough effort: 1–2 tasks after the module and the bank feed.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low: the builder has no incentive to inflate a contractor's error, and a contractor's cash payment is externally evidenced. Risk is JobGuard counting a routine top-up payment as a 'correction' — require the correction request to precede the payment and the amount to match the Decision arithmetic within tolerance.
ideas.precedent: None known. Closest is AP recovery audit's 'pricing and tax errors' class at 20–30% contingency (research note success_fee_benchmarks §1).
ideas.merged_from: CIS over-deduction on materials or at 30% recovered from the contractor (`cis_over_deduction_recovered`)

ideas.name: Duplicate supplier payment refunded in cash (`duplicate_supplier_payment_recovered`)
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% on cash refunds)
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual with no market element: M2-2 already assigns a duplicate-intake identity to the same underlying invoice, and M4-7/M4-8 will show two settled bank payments against one invoice identity (or one payment against an invoice already settled on a supplier statement). QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) two settled payments match one confirmed invoice identity, or a payment matches an invoice already marked settled by a matched prior payment; (2) JobGuard raised a cited `duplicate_payment` Decision; (3) the builder sent a JobGuard-drafted refund request; (4) the supplier refunded in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed and allocated to the case. Q = cumulative cash refunds per (tenant, supplier); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100); delta per statement. NEVER QUALIFIES: a credit to the merchant account or a credit note against future purchases (excluded under D03 v2 until the I13 credit-note extension); refunds the supplier made before the Decision; payments the builder already reversed with the bank; genuine part payments. REVERSAL: refund bounced or re-invoiced → negative delta. The cleanest evidence chain of any idea in this list and the classic recovery-audit category.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the supplier's cash refund; nothing from the supplier.
ideas.assumptions: Duplicate/erroneous payments = 0.3% of supplier spend (large-firm recovery audits find ~0.1% of spend; small firms without AP controls assumed higher): Solo £180, Small £720, Firm £2,400. Supplier refunds in cash rather than as an account credit 50%: £90 / £360 / £1,200. Fee 10%: £9 / £36 / £120. Needs the bank feed, so zero before M4-7.
ideas.trust_note: Pure found money: the builder paid twice, JobGuard noticed, cash came back. No one feels short-changed by 10% of that. The only care point is that most merchants will offer a credit, not cash — the builder should see plainly that a credit is fee-free and that JobGuard is not steering them to demand cash for its own benefit (copy: 'a credit on your account is fine; no fee either way unless cash is refunded').
ideas.regulatory: None. Bank data via the TrueLayer route (D10, D04, D12). Needs D03 v3 wording: D03 v2's supplier category is 'overcharge'; a duplicate payment is not an overcharge and needs its own row.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-2 duplicate identity + M4-7 bank feed + M4-8 payment-to-invoice allocation + a refund-request send command. Derivation identity `(tenant, supplier, case)`. Rough effort: 1 task once M4-8 exists; mostly a new Decision type and a case type.
ideas.gaming_risk: None meaningful: paying twice on purpose costs the builder cash flow to earn JobGuard a fee it does not want. JobGuard-side: mis-matching two legitimate invoices with the same number from one merchant — M2-2 explicitly does not treat invoice number as globally unique, and the Decision must cite both documents.
ideas.precedent: PRGX / apexanalytix AP recovery audit, duplicate payments as a core class at 20–30% contingency, 10–40% outer range (research note success_fee_benchmarks §1).
ideas.merged_from: Duplicate supplier payment refunded in cash (`duplicate_supplier_payment_recovered`)

ideas.name: VAT wrongly charged by a subcontractor or supplier and refunded in cash (`vat_wrongly_charged_refunded`): DRC and zero-rating errors
ideas.category: D03 v3 clarification of `supplier_overcharge` (tax wrongly charged counts as overcharge); 10% on cash refunds
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual from deterministic rules JobGuard can hold as tenant/job facts: under the construction domestic reverse charge a VAT- and CIS-registered sub must not charge VAT to a builder who is not the end user; work on a qualifying new build is zero-rated; some conversions and energy-saving installs are reduced-rated. If the sub charges 20% and the builder pays it, HMRC can refuse the input tax, so the money is lost unless the sub credits and refunds. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) the job carries confirmed facts (builder's VAT/CIS status, end-user status for the job, build type) entered by the builder as versioned inputs; (2) an M2-3 confirmed sub/supplier invoice shows VAT charged where the rule says none or a lower rate; (3) JobGuard raised a cited `vat_rate_check` Decision (labelled 'check with your accountant'); (4) the builder had already PAID the invoice; (5) the sub issued a credit note and refunded the VAT in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed. Q = cumulative VAT cash refunds per (tenant, supplier); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100). NEVER QUALIFIES: prevention (invoice corrected before payment — no fee, consistent with the founder's prevented-spend rule), credit-only corrections, cases where the builder's own facts were wrong, amounts recovered from HMRC rather than the supplier. REVERSAL: refund reversed → negative delta.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the sub's or supplier's cash refund.
ideas.assumptions: Sub spend as share of turnover 10% / 20% / 25%: £15k / £120k / £500k; VAT-registered subs 30% / 50% / 60%: £4.5k / £60k / £300k; invoices wrongly charging VAT 5% of that: £225 / £3,000 / £15,000; VAT at 20%: £45 / £600 / £3,000; paid before correction and then refunded in cash 50%: £22 / £300 / £1,500; fee 10%: £2 / £30 / £150; Solo × 60% VAT-registered → £1. The 5% error rate is a judgement; DRC confusion among small subs is widely reported but unquantified.
ideas.trust_note: JobGuard spotted a tax error the builder would have paid for twice; the sub, not the builder, made the mistake. Care points: (a) never present the rule check as tax advice — the Decision must say 'this looks like a reverse-charge supply; confirm with your accountant before asking for a credit'; (b) the end-user/build-type facts come from the builder, so a wrong fact is the builder's and never produces a fee against them.
ideas.regulatory: VAT Act 1994 s.55A domestic reverse charge (construction, from 2021), zero/reduced-rate building rules — applied as deterministic checks, labelled aids, not advice; JobGuard does not file. Needs a D03 v3 clarification that wrongly charged tax refunded in cash is within `supplier_overcharge`, D02 (tax rounding and presentation), D12 (sub as third-party data subject).
ideas.build_dependency: M2-3 (VAT rate/amount extraction with citations) + tenant/job VAT facts as versioned inputs + a deterministic rate-rule check in M2-5 + M4-7/M4-8 for the cash refund. Rough effort: 1–2 tasks. The DRC rule table must be versioned and reviewed by a qualified tax reviewer before any real Decision is raised (D02 owner).
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. JobGuard-side risk is a wrong rule version raising false Decisions that damage sub relationships — versioned rules, held-out fixtures and 'check with your accountant' wording. Builder-side: none (they cannot earn from a false correction).
ideas.precedent: None known. Construction AI and Site Samurai list CIS/VAT handling as flat features (research note construction_platforms_and_ai); no success-fee precedent.
ideas.merged_from: VAT wrongly charged by a subcontractor or supplier and refunded in cash (`vat_wrongly_charged_refunded`) — DRC and zero-rating errors

ideas.name: Builder's own agreed merchant rebate or retrospective discount, unpaid or underpaid, recovered in cash (`unpaid_agreed_rebate_recovered`)
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% on cash rebates) — flagged for its neighbourhood to I65/I66
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual: the M2-1 rate book gains a 'rebate/retro term' revision (threshold spend, percentage, period, payment method) entered by the builder from their own merchant agreement; matched invoices (M2-4) give cumulative spend; at period end JobGuard computes the rebate due and compares it with any rebate received (bank feed) or credit note. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) a versioned rebate term exists with the agreement document held as evidence; (2) matched, settled spend crossed the threshold; (3) no rebate, or a smaller one, was received within the term's payment window; (4) JobGuard raised a cited `rebate_due` Decision with the arithmetic; (5) the builder sent a JobGuard-drafted claim; (6) the merchant paid the rebate in CASH after the Decision, matched and allocated. Q = cumulative cash rebates per (tenant, merchant, period); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100). NEVER QUALIFIES: rebates paid as account credit or credit note; rebates paid on time without a Decision; rebate terms JobGuard cannot see the document for; any arrangement where JobGuard itself introduced or negotiated the rebate (structurally forbidden). REVERSAL: rebate clawed back → negative delta.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, from the merchant's rebate cash; JobGuard is never party to the rebate.

revenue_per_year.solo: £1 blended (rebate terms rare below ~£50k merchant spend)

ideas.assumptions: Share of archetype holding a rebate term: 5% / 30% / 70%. Rate-book merchant spend covered by the term: £20k / £150k / £500k at 2.5% rebate: £500 / £3,750 / £12,500; unpaid or underpaid in a year 20%: £100 / £750 / £2,500; paid in cash rather than credit 50%: £50 / £375 / £1,250; fee 10%: £5 / £37 / £125; × term share: £0.25 / £11 / £88 (Solo shown as £1).
ideas.trust_note: The rebate is the builder's own contractual entitlement and the merchant simply did not pay it — found money. Flagged because it sits next to I66 ('merchant rebate with JobGuard admin fee') and I65, which poison the watchdog: the difference must be structural and visible — JobGuard never arranges, pools, negotiates or receives rebates, only reads the builder's existing agreement and their invoices. Any drift toward JobGuard-negotiated terms must be refused by policy (D11).
ideas.regulatory: None regulated (B2B contract terms). D03 v3 new row; D01 10%; D11 statement that JobGuard has no merchant income of any kind. Bank feed via D10/D12.
ideas.build_dependency: M2-1 rate book extended with rebate-term revisions and agreement-document evidence + M2-4 matched spend + a period-end Graphile job + M4-7/M4-8 cash matching + a claim-letter send command. Derivation identity `(tenant, merchant, rebate_period)`. Rough effort: 2 tasks.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder entering a rebate term that does not exist — no benefit to them (the merchant will not pay). JobGuard-side: miscounting spend (returns, credits) — use settled net spend after credits, and cite every invoice in the Decision. Merchant-side: paying as credit to avoid a JobGuard fee — that is fine for the builder and fee-free.
ideas.precedent: Enterprise rebate-management software (flat subscription) exists for distributors; nothing for small builders. AP recovery auditors treat unclaimed rebates as a standard recovery class at 20–30% (research note success_fee_benchmarks §1).
ideas.merged_from: Builder's own agreed merchant rebate or retrospective discount, unpaid or underpaid, recovered in cash (`unpaid_agreed_rebate_recovered`)

ideas.name: VAT bad-debt relief reclaimed on written-off customer invoices (`vat_bad_debt_relief_reclaimed`) — borderline, recommend fee-free
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual (D03 v3 row; 10% of relief) — borderline, flagged
ideas.mechanism: Documented counterfactual: a JobGuard-issued customer invoice, no settlement recorded (bank feed) for six months after the due date, and an explicit builder write-off command; the output VAT already paid to HMRC on that invoice becomes reclaimable as bad-debt relief. QUALIFIES WHEN: (1) the invoice was issued through JobGuard and its VAT accounted for; (2) six months have passed since the later of due date and supply; (3) the builder recorded a write-off through the command boundary; (4) JobGuard raised a cited `bad_debt_relief_available` Decision with the exact VAT; (5) the relief was included in a filed return, evidenced by the accounting connector (never attestation); (6) no later recovery. Q = cumulative relief per (tenant, VAT period); F = roundHalfEven(Q × 10/100). NEVER QUALIFIES: invoices under an open withheld-payment case (the two categories must not stack); cash accounting traders (no output VAT paid, no relief); partial payments already accounted; anything the builder's accountant had already scheduled (builder-favourable attestation). REVERSAL: if the customer later pays (including through a withheld-payment case), the relief is repayable to HMRC and Q falls — negative delta and compensation, and the withheld-payment fee then applies instead on the settled cash. Labelled an aid, not advice; JobGuard does not file.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, out of VAT reclaimed from HMRC on a debt they wrote off.
ideas.assumptions: Write-offs = 0.75% of turnover: £1,125 / £4,500 / £15,000 gross; VAT element (20/120): £188 / £750 / £2,500; portion not already handled by the builder's accountant and evidenced via a connector 40%: £75 / £300 / £1,000; fee 10%: £8 / £30 / £100; Solo × 60% VAT-registered → £5. Most small builders on cash accounting for VAT get no relief at all, which would push Solo and Small lower.
ideas.trust_note: Uncomfortable: it charges a fee on the tax side of a customer who never paid, so the builder is already hurting; 'JobGuard took 10% of my bad-debt relief' is a bad sentence in a trade that runs on word of mouth, and any decent accountant does this routinely so the counterfactual is thin. Listed because the chain is fully documented and exact; recommend it be a fee-free feature of the watchdog (an aid the subscription pays for), not a category.
ideas.regulatory: VAT Act 1994 s.36 and VAT Regulations 1995 regs 165–172 (six-month rule, write-off in accounts, later-payment repayment) as deterministic checks; not advice; no filing. Needs D03 v3, D01 (base = tax relief), D02, and the accounting connector under D04/D12. Interaction with the withheld-payment category must be written into D03 so the two never stack.
ideas.build_dependency: M1 customer invoices + M4-7 receipt matching + a write-off command with audit + a six-month Graphile clock + SV-7 accounting connector evidence (I26). Rough effort: 1–2 tasks. Cheap to build, expensive in trust.
ideas.gaming_risk: Builder writing off a debt to trigger relief and then collecting outside JobGuard — an HMRC matter, not JobGuard's; JobGuard would reverse on any visible receipt. JobGuard-side: none.
ideas.precedent: None known as a charged service; accountants include it in ordinary fees.
ideas.merged_from: VAT bad-debt relief reclaimed on written-off customer invoices (`vat_bad_debt_relief_reclaimed`) — borderline

ideas.name: Insurance payout on a JobGuard-evidenced site loss (theft of delivered materials, storm damage) — listed to reject
ideas.category: Success-fee category with a documented counterfactual — likely regulated claims management; listed to reject
ideas.mechanism: The counterfactual is documented (GRN shows delivery, photos and diary show the loss, supplier invoices give value, the evidence pack proves it) and the cash is an insurer's payout on the bank feed, so it superficially fits a 10% category: Decision 'this loss looks claimable', builder claims, payout matched, Q cumulative, F at 10%. Listed only to be rejected: taking a percentage of an insurance claim is claims-management activity in the FCA's 'financial services or financial product' sector unless done by an authorised firm, and it would put JobGuard in the same bucket as the claims firms whose fees were capped at 15–30% — the exact association the research says to avoid. I37 (insurer-paid claim-time evidence pack) is the safe form of this value.
ideas.who_pays: Would be the builder, from the insurer's payout — rejected.
ideas.assumptions: Annual probability of a claimable site loss 5% / 10% / 15%; average claim £1,000 / £2,500 / £5,000; fee 10%. Shown only to size what is being refused.
ideas.trust_note: Feels like a claims firm, and a builder who has just been robbed does not want a platform taking a slice of the insurance money. Reject; keep the I37 evidence-pack route.
ideas.regulatory: FCA claims-management regulation (RAO arts 89G–89M; 'financial services or financial product' claims include insurance claims) — regulated activity unless exempt or authorised; FCA fee caps 15–30% by claim size (report benchmark table). Requires legal sign-off that it is not viable without authorisation; recommend recording the rejection in D03 v3 so no agent revives it.
ideas.build_dependency: None to build. Record the rejection.
ideas.gaming_risk: Not applicable.
ideas.precedent: Claims-management companies 15–30% under the FCA cap (report §'No rival sells…' table; research note success_fee_benchmarks §7).
ideas.merged_from: Insurance payout on a JobGuard-evidenced site loss (theft of delivered materials, storm damage) — listed to reject

ideas.name: Supplier-switch savings measured against the frozen prior rate (`supplier_switch_savings`) — flagged, recommend reject
ideas.category: Success-fee category on a documented counterfactual — flagged: attribution weak and watchdog-conflict risk; recommend reject
ideas.mechanism: Variant of I76 for the case where, after a JobGuard rate review letter, the builder moves the named SKUs to a different merchant. Measurement is available: the prior merchant's frozen agreed rate (M2-1) versus the new merchant's confirmed invoice rate on the same SKU alias, × settled quantity, for 12 months, 20% share, £ ceiling, same reversal rules. Listed because it is the largest 'savings' pool in the lens, and recommended for rejection because (a) attribution is the weakest of any idea here — a new merchant's price says nothing about what JobGuard caused, and alias matching across merchants introduces quality/spec differences the builder will dispute; (b) a platform that earns when builders switch merchant is one step from steering them, which is the watchdog conflict the founder has ruled out even in its structured form (I65/I66). If the founder still wants it, it must be attestation-driven ('I moved because of the review') and fee-free on any doubt.
ideas.who_pays: Would be the builder from lower invoices at the new merchant — recommend not offering.
ideas.assumptions: Top-ten SKU spend as I76 (£27k / £96k / £280k); switching after a review saves 5%; share 20%; 20% of builders switch a merchant in a year: £27k × 5% × 20% × 20% = £54; £96k → £192; £280k → £560 (ceiling would bind for Firms with few merchants).
ideas.trust_note: Reads as JobGuard profiting from where the builder shops, which is the story that would end the watchdog's credibility with merchants and builders alike. I76 explicitly lists switching under 'never qualifies' for this reason.
ideas.regulatory: None regulated, but D11 (commercial integrity) should record that fees never depend on which merchant the builder uses.
ideas.build_dependency: Would reuse the I76 build plus cross-merchant alias matching. Recommend recording the rejection instead.
ideas.gaming_risk: High on the JobGuard side (spec mismatches counted as savings) and unsolvable without adjudicating quality, which the watchdog must not do.
ideas.precedent: Cost-reduction consultancies share savings from supplier switches (P3, research note success_fee_benchmarks §2) — but they are the client's agent and negotiate directly, which JobGuard must not be.
ideas.merged_from: Supplier-switch savings measured against the frozen prior rate (`supplier_switch_savings`) — flagged, recommend reject

ideas.name: 'Check this customer': business counterparty report, pay per check (£19)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — paid third-party data, per check (business customers)
ideas.mechanism: Trigger: a 'Check this customer' button on the quote screen before send (M1-5), on the acceptance record (M1-6) and on the job page. Never blocking: send and acceptance proceed whether or not a check is running. Flow: builder types the customer name/company number; JobGuard resolves candidates from the Companies House API and the builder confirms the match (human confirmation, AGENTS §5.9). The sheet shows the price ('£19 ex VAT, added to your JobGuard statement') and 'Run check' creates and approves a Decision atomically (the 'Send this quote' pattern, AGENTS §5.3) bound to tenant, job/quote, counterparty entity ID, price and check-policy version. After commit a worker runs the adapters through the outbox (M0-9), never inside a transaction: Companies House (free: status, incorporation date, SIC, accounts and confirmation-statement due/overdue, registered charges, officers and PSCs, strike-off proposals, insolvency filings), The Gazette (free: winding-up petitions, administrations), a wholesale CRA company report (Creditsafe or Experian, assumed £5–£15, budget £8; usually includes company CCJs and a suggested credit limit) and, only if the CRA report lacks CCJ detail, a Registry Trust search (£6–£10). Raw provider responses are stored as verified evidence objects (SHA-256, object version ID, server receive time, provider and product version — AGENTS §5.8) of a new evidence type `counterparty_check`, tenant/job/quote-qualified. Results that arrive after the quote is sent post to the Decision Inbox advisory lane (M2-7) as a Finding. The card is headed 'Findings, not a recommendation' and every line names its source and retrieval date (e.g. 'Accounts overdue since 31 Mar 2026 (Companies House, 25 Sep 2026)'; '2 CCJs in the last 12 months totalling £4,300, 1 unsatisfied (Registry Trust)'; 'Creditsafe score 34/100 on their scale; suggested credit limit £5,000'). No traffic-light verdict, no 'do not proceed'. Action row, all existing ideas: 'Set a deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Attach the contract pack' (I33), 'Use stage escrow' (I42, when available), 'Ask the customer to confirm who is paying' (portal declaration, I55), 'Noted, carry on'. Money: £19 per completed check charged to the tenant; a failed or `outcome_unknown` provider call is reconciled and not charged (AGENTS §5.4); charges appear as separate 'data checks' lines on the monthly platform statement (M4-10), never mixed with the subscription or the success fee. Measurement: checks run per quote, quote-to-live conversion on checked vs unchecked quotes, later withheld-payment cases on checked vs unchecked customers (a §14.17 pilot metric).
ideas.who_pays: The builder (tenant), per completed check, on the platform statement. The customer never pays and never sees the report.

revenue_per_year.firm: £532 gross (about £308 margin) if on pay-per-check; see I88 for the allowance alternative

ideas.assumptions: Quotes per year from turnover ÷ average job ÷ win rate: Solo 19 jobs won ÷ 40% = 47 quotes; Small firm 24 ÷ 40% = 60; Firm 33 ÷ 35% = 95. Business-customer share of quotes: Solo 10% (5), Small 25% (15), Firm 50% (47). Attach rate on business quotes: 50% / 60% / 60%. Price £19 ex VAT; wholesale cost per check assumed £8–£10. Solo 5 × 0.5 × £19 = £48; Small 15 × 0.6 × £19 = £171; Firm 47 × 0.6 × £19 = £532. Sole-trader business customers are individuals and route to I89/I90. All ex VAT and unvalidated by any pilot.
ideas.trust_note: Builder pays, builder benefits, before they commit. No supplier or merchant money, no data sale, no lead generation, nothing withheld. The report is shown as attributed facts with the retrieved document openable, so the builder can see the work. The one care point: copy must never read as JobGuard advising refusal or vetting the builder's customers for its own fee purposes.
ideas.regulatory: UK GDPR for officer/PSC personal data: legitimate interests (Art 6(1)(f)); D12 v2 does not cover counterparty checks, so a D12 v3 must name the controller/processor split (builder as controller instructing the check is the candidate) and the Article 14 route — the quote email and portal page carry the privacy notice at first communication (Art 14(3)(b)), with a documented Art 14(5)(b) position for directors who are not the contact. Companies House and Gazette open-data terms. A CRA reseller agreement: reports viewable in-app by the tenant only, not exportable or forwarded. No FCA permission needed for company credit information (not consumer credit). D04: every provider is a UK destination enumerated in the provider register. D07: CRA contracts may cap retention, conflicting with keeping the check as recovery evidence — needs an explicit retention class. Charging for checks is a new platform charge: a new decision record (D14 'paid data services'), D02 VAT, D09 statement mechanics, real charging behind G4. In pilot_no_charge JobGuard absorbs check costs and labels the charge as hypothetical. Equality Act 2010: findings only, no recommendation.
ideas.build_dependency: Needs M1-5 and M1-6 surfaces, M0-8 Decisions, M0-9 outbox and adapter contract tests with deterministic fakes, M0-11 versioned evidence, M0-12 provider register (D04), M2-7 advisory inbox lane, M4-10 statement lines. Suggested new tasks under 'Discovered later': CP-1 entity resolution plus Companies House/Gazette adapters and the card on free data (about 2 weeks, can ship in M2 with no charge); CP-2 CRA adapter and evidence type (2–3 weeks, needs the commercial contract); CP-3 check charging (after M4-10/M4-11, behind G4 and D14).
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder running checks on people who are not customers (competitors, ex-partners, neighbours): bind every check to a quote or job and a named counterparty on it, cap checks per quote, rate-limit per tenant, state the purpose in terms and audit every run. Forwarding the CRA report to the customer breaches the reseller contract: in-app view only, watermarked, no export of the raw report (the finding text can go in the builder's own evidence pack). Builders reading a score as JobGuard's advice: card wording and no colour verdicts.
ideas.precedent: Satago bundles credit reports and risk insights into credit-control software at £45–£200/month (satago.com; research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). Chaser offers Creditsafe checks inside chasing. Creditsafe pay-per-report reported at £5–£15 (businessdataguide.com comparison). Registry Trust TrustOnline £6–£10 per search (registry-trust.org.uk). No UK trade job app reviewed in the report offers a customer check (report §'No rival sells a final check…').
ideas.merged_from: Check this customer — business counterparty report, pay per check

ideas.name: Checks allowance inside the live-jobs tiers, with overage, included on Firm
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — subscription packaging of checks (a second meter beside live jobs, like I04; not a change to the meter)
ideas.mechanism: The same checks as I87, I89, I91 and I92 sold as a monthly allowance rather than per use, layered on the existing live-jobs ladder without touching the meter: a 'Checks' add-on of £12/month for 3 checks on Solo, £35/month for 12 checks on Builder, and 30 checks/month included in Firm's £119 (one reason Firm is £119 rather than £99, per the report's Firm-price argument). Overage £15 per check beyond the allowance, never a block; unused checks do not roll over. Each check still needs the per-run Decision (I87) so the builder always sees 'this uses 1 of your 12 checks this month' or 'this is £15 overage'. Money: the add-on is a subscription obligation under D09 terms (M4-13) billed with the subscription; overage posts as statement lines (M4-10). Measurement: allowance utilisation per tier, overage frequency, and whether attach on quotes rises when the marginal check is 'free' (the reason to prefer an allowance: people prefer flat charges to a running meter, research note price_level_and_tier_psychology).
ideas.who_pays: The builder, as a monthly add-on or inside the Firm price; overage per check.

revenue_per_year.solo: £29 (add-on) — an alternative to I87 for the same checks, not additive
revenue_per_year.firm: £96 attributed from the Firm price plus £0 overage at expected volume

ideas.assumptions: Add-on attach: Solo 20% × £12 × 12 = £29; Small firm 35% × £35 × 12 = £147. Firm: £8/month of the £119 price attributed to the included allowance (a labelled attribution, not new cash) = £96; expected Firm check volume (about 28 business checks plus 17 property checks a year across I87 and I89) is far below 360, so overage is £0. Wholesale cost per check £7–£10, so add-on margin is thin at full utilisation and healthy at typical utilisation; priced assuming 40–60% utilisation.
ideas.trust_note: Flat, predictable and builder-paid. The only trap is unused allowances feeling like waste; keep the per-check option (I87) alongside so nobody is forced onto a pack.
ideas.regulatory: Same data-protection and CRA terms as I87 and I89. The add-on is subscription pricing, so a D09 v3 item (tier inclusions and overage terms, price-change notice, cancellation) plus D05 for renewal authority and D02 VAT; production charging behind G4.
ideas.build_dependency: M4-13 subscription terms and M4-14 metering (allowance counters are a second meter alongside live jobs), M4-10 overage lines; depends on the check adapters in I87 and I89. About 1–2 weeks once the checks exist.
ideas.gaming_risk: Sharing one Firm account's allowance across unrelated businesses: allowance is per tenant and every check is bound to a quote or job in that tenant. Burst-checking prospects at month end: harmless to margin at these volumes; cap checks per quote.
ideas.precedent: ServiceM8 sells workload allowances with unlimited users (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). Satago's fixed tiers bundle credit reports (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). The report's flat-fee preference findings support a pack over a running meter.
ideas.merged_from: Check allowance inside the live-jobs tiers, with overage, included on Firm

ideas.name: Homeowner property and public-record check (title register, CCJ and insolvency registers, no credit data)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — paid public-register data for domestic customers
ideas.mechanism: Trigger as I87 but for a customer who is an individual (homeowner, landlord, sole trader). Two separately priced parts, each its own Decision. Part A, 'Property check' £12: JobGuard orders the HM Land Registry official copy of the title register for the site address (£7 digital fee) through HMLR Business e-services, stores it as `counterparty_check` evidence and extracts registered proprietor names, tenure (freehold/leasehold, lease term remaining), registered charges (lender), restrictions (Form A, bankruptcy, management-company consent), and the date of the last transfer. Part B, 'Named-person public-record check' £10: a Registry Trust search of the Register of Judgments, Orders and Fines against the name and address the builder quoted (£6–£10 wholesale) plus the free Insolvency Service Individual Insolvency Register. No consumer credit file is touched. Card lines (findings only): 'Title held by J Smith and K Smith; your quote is addressed to Mr P Jones — different name to the quote'; 'Leasehold, 62 years remaining; a restriction requires the freeholder's consent to certain dealings'; 'CCJs against P Jones at this address: 1 in the last 6 years, £1,850, unsatisfied (Registry Trust, 25 Sep 2026)'. Action row: 'Ask the customer to confirm the paying party and their authority to instruct the work' (portal declaration, feeds I33), 'Set a deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Use stage escrow' (I42), 'Noted, carry on'. Free alternative shown first: the customer can confirm ownership themselves in the portal (I55) by giving their title number or uploading their own £7 copy, at no charge, recorded as customer-provided evidence. Money: per-part charges on the platform statement as I87. Measurement: name-mismatch rate on quotes, share of checks where the customer self-verified instead.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per part (£12 property, £10 named-person). Never the homeowner.
ideas.assumptions: Homeowner quotes: Solo 42, Small 45, Firm 48 (from I87's quote counts and mix). Share at £5k+ where a check is plausible: 60% / 80% / 90%. Property-check attach on those: 30% / 35% / 40% → 7.5 / 12.6 / 17.3 checks × £12 = £90 / £151 / £207. Named-person add-on taken on half of those × £10 = £38 / £63 / £86. Wholesale: HMLR £7 (confirmed current digital fee), Registry Trust £6–£8 assumed at volume, IIR free; margins £5 and £2–£4 per part. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Builder-paid and in the builder's interest, using public registers only. Slight awkwardness: a homeowner who later learns (e.g. via a data-subject access request) that their builder ran a CCJ search may feel judged; the notice route and the free self-verification path soften that. The mismatch finding is genuinely protective for both sides (work instructed by a non-owner is a classic non-payment and dispute pattern).
ideas.regulatory: Title register and CCJ register data are public but proprietor and defendant names are personal data: legitimate interests (Art 6(1)(f)) with a recorded balancing test; Article 14 notice through the quote email/portal privacy notice at first communication, naming that ownership and public-register checks may be run for jobs above a value (D12 v3). No consumer credit file, so no CRA consumer permissible-purpose issue and no Consumer Credit Act s.157–160 file-access issue. HMLR Business e-services terms (stated purpose; re-use restrictions on official copies). Registry Trust terms. Equality Act: findings only.
