D04 register entries (HMLR, Registry Trust, Insolvency Service are UK). D07 retention class for the copies. Charging: D14 plus D02, behind G4; pilot absorbs.
ideas.build_dependency: Same foundations as I87 plus an HMLR Business e-services adapter (OC1 official copy ordering and a title-register extraction parser with a golden set under M0-12's eval harness), a Registry Trust adapter and an IIR lookup; the customer self-verification step needs the homeowner portal (I55). About 3 weeks after CP-1; the extraction parser is the risky part (register text is semi-structured).
ideas.gaming_risk: Checking a property the builder has no quote for (nosiness, disputes with neighbours): bind to a quote address and cap per quote. Name-matching false positives on common names: show the search terms used and the register's own address match; never assert identity, only 'an entry matching the searched name and address'. Builders using a CCJ finding to demand unreasonable deposits: outside JobGuard's control; card wording stays factual.
ideas.precedent: Tenant referencing services run consented public-record and ownership checks on individuals for landlords at roughly £15–£30 per reference (assumption; no UK trade-app precedent for customer checks found in the report). HMLR £7 official copy fee confirmed (gov.uk guidance on HMLR information-services fees). Registry Trust £6–£10 per search.
ideas.merged_from: Homeowner property and public-record check (title register, CCJ and insolvency registers, no credit data)

ideas.name: Consented homeowner soft search ('Verify me') for large domestic jobs
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — consumer credit data with the customer's consent (borderline)
ideas.mechanism: Available only for domestic quotes above a threshold (assume £10k) and only after the builder asks for it at quote-send or acceptance. JobGuard sends nothing to a credit file on the builder's say-so; instead the customer's portal page (I55 quote view or acceptance page) shows a 'Verify me' step: the customer reads the CRA's own notice, ticks consent, and JobGuard runs a soft (quotation-type) search through one UK CRA that leaves no lender-visible footprint. The builder sees a narrow, factual card: 'Customer completed verification on 26 Sep 2026: identity and address confirmed against the credit file; CRA affordability indicator: [CRA's own band and wording]; adverse public data: none on file' — never the file itself and never a score presented as JobGuard's view. Declining is a normal outcome shown as 'Customer did not verify' with no further comment. Money: £15 per completed consented search charged to the builder (assumed wholesale £2–£4 plus a CRA minimum annual contract, assumed £10k, carried by JobGuard); consent-declined runs cost nothing. On completion the portal offers the customer the stage schedule for approval (I40) and the contract pack (I33); the verification record goes into the job's evidence. Measurement: request rate, consent rate, drop-off in acceptance after a verify request (the key risk metric), later non-payment on verified vs unverified jobs.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per completed search; the homeowner pays nothing and controls consent.
ideas.assumptions: Homeowner quotes at £10k+: Solo 42 × 30% = 12.6; Small 45 × 50% = 22.5; Firm 48 × 70% = 33.6. Builder requests verification on 40% / 50% / 50%; customer consents 50%. Completed searches: 2.5 / 5.6 / 8.4 × £15 = £38 / £84 / £126. Platform-level: at £3 wholesale and a £10k CRA minimum, JobGuard needs roughly 800 completed searches a year across all tenants to break even, about 150 active builders at these rates — a fixed cost, not a per-unit one. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Borderline. Asking a homeowner to submit to a credit search to get a kitchen fitted can cost the builder the job, and it is the first place JobGuard touches a consumer's credit file, which changes what JobGuard is. It is in the builder's interest on big jobs, and consent sits with the customer, but the report's fairness research suggests the customer may resent it. Off by default; a builder must switch it on and it never applies below the threshold.
ideas.regulatory: Consent as lawful basis (Art 6(1)(a)) captured by the CRA-approved wording, with UK GDPR Art 13 notice served directly to the customer at the point of consent. CRA commercial agreement with a permitted purpose (quotation/verification), typically including CRA vetting of the end-user population and restrictions on what can be shown to the builder; Consumer Credit Act 1974 s.157–160 obligations sit with the CRA but JobGuard must handle disputes and corrections routing. SCOR reciprocity rules do not apply to a soft search but JobGuard must confirm the product does not require data contribution. ICO guidance on credit referencing; Equality Act (no adverse decision advice). D12 v3 (new consumer data category), D04 (CRA UK route), D07 (CRA-mandated deletion windows), D14 plus D02 for the charge; G1 before any real consumer file is touched, charging behind G4. Legal review required before build; this is not an agent inference.
ideas.build_dependency: Homeowner portal quote/acceptance page (I55), M0-8 Decision for the builder's request, M0-9 adapter with deterministic fake, M0-11 evidence, M0-12 provider register; a CRA contract and its end-user vetting are the long pole (months), so this is an M4-era item at the earliest. Engineering about 3 weeks once the contract exists.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low on JobGuard's side because the customer consents and the CRA controls the data. Builder-side: using the request to pressure customers or to discriminate; JobGuard can only keep the copy neutral and the threshold high. Fake consent via the builder filling the portal on the customer's device: the consent event is bound to the customer's authenticated portal session, not the builder's.
ideas.precedent: Tenant referencing (Goodlord, HomeLet and similar) performs consented consumer checks for landlords per reference. No UK trade software precedent found in the report. CRA commercial terms are the binding precedent.
ideas.merged_from: Consented homeowner soft search ('Verify me') for large domestic jobs

ideas.name: Property constraints check: listed building, conservation area, Article 4, planning history and flood risk at the site address (£5)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — site and consent facts from open data (low price, near-zero data cost)
ideas.mechanism: Trigger at quote creation or send: 'Check this address' (£5) or included in the checks allowance (I88). JobGuard resolves the site address to a UPRN and queries open datasets: Historic England's National Heritage List (listed status and grade), the government planning data platform (conservation areas, Article 4 directions, tree preservation orders, listed-building outlines where published), local authority planning application records via an aggregator where available, and Environment Agency flood-risk data. Card lines, facts with sources and dates: 'Grade II listed (NHLE 1234567). Internal and external alterations may need listed building consent; carrying out works without consent is an offence for the person who executes them'; 'In the Old Town conservation area; an Article 4 direction removes permitted development for front elevations'; 'Planning history: application 24/01234/HSE (rear extension) approved 12 Mar 2026 with 4 conditions'; 'Coverage note: this council's planning records are not in the national dataset; treat as unchecked'. No legal conclusion; the card links to source pages. Actions: 'Add a consent condition to the quote' (builder-authored), 'Attach the contract pack' (I33), 'Flag to site readiness' (M2-6 readiness model so the readiness check asks for the consent document before start), 'Noted'. Money: £5 per address on the statement or allowance; data licences are open (OGL) so cost is engineering and aggregator fees where used. Measurement: share of quotes with a constraint hit, and how often a readiness check later blocks for missing consent.
ideas.who_pays: The builder, £5 per address or from the allowance; could be included in Builder and above as a differentiator (I08) if the founder prefers.
ideas.assumptions: Domestic quotes (42 / 45 / 48) × attach 40% / 45% / 50% × £5 = £84 / £101 / £120. Data cost about £0 (Historic England, planning.data.gov.uk and Environment Agency are open data); an aggregator for council planning records assumed at up to £100/month platform-wide. Margin is almost entirely gross revenue. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Pure prevention in the builder's interest, no third party pays, no customer data beyond an address. Strongest fit in the lens. The only honesty point is coverage: national datasets are incomplete, so the card must say 'not checked' rather than 'none found' where data is absent.
ideas.regulatory: Address-level open data is not personal data in itself; planning application records contain applicant names, so show application references and decisions, not applicant names (data minimisation). Open Government Licence terms; aggregator terms. The listed-building offence statement is a fact of the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990 but the wording must be reviewed so it is not legal advice (a D06-style reviewed-wording decision). D04 entries for any aggregator. No charge-specific regulation beyond D14/D02 for the £5.
ideas.build_dependency: UPRN resolution (OS Places or the free OS Open UPRN plus address matching), open-data adapters with contract tests, the M2-6 site-readiness factual adapters as the natural home. About 2 weeks; can ship in M2 free, priced later behind G4.
ideas.gaming_risk: Minimal. Builders may quote it to customers as JobGuard's legal view: the card carries the source link and a 'facts, not advice' label. Stale data: show dataset publication dates.
ideas.precedent: Conveyancing search providers sell environmental and planning searches to solicitors for tens of pounds; no small-trade app reviewed in the report offers a constraints check. Buildertrend/Procore-type suites do not either (report §'No rival sells a final check…').
ideas.merged_from: Property constraints check: listed building, conservation area, Article 4, planning history and flood risk at the site address

ideas.name: 'Who actually pays?' payer-chain check for subcontract, landlord, managing-agent and insurer-funded jobs (£29)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — paid data on the paying party where it differs from the site customer
ideas.mechanism: At quote-send or acceptance JobGuard asks one question: 'Who will pay this invoice?' with options 'the customer named on the quote', 'a main contractor', 'a landlord or managing agent', 'a housing association or council', 'an insurer's contractor network', 'other'. When the payer differs, the builder names the payer entity and the check runs on that entity (I87's business data plus Companies House registered charges, group parent and recent filings, plus the Gazette) and records the site customer separately. The card adds payer-specific facts: 'Payer: BuildCo Main Contractors Ltd; 3 CCJs in 12 months; accounts overdue; parent company registered in Jersey'; 'Payer's payment practices report (gov.uk Payment Practices and Performance data, if the payer is large enough to file): average 52 days to pay, 31% of invoices paid late'; 'Your quote names the homeowner but the payer is the managing agent — the contract pack should name the payer'. Includes a 90-day watch (I94's monitoring) in the price so the builder is told if a winding-up petition or strike-off notice appears during the job. Actions: 'Name the payer in the contract pack' (I33), 'Applications for payment schedule' (I24), 'Deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Noted'. Money: £29 per payer check (assumed wholesale £8 report plus £2–£4 for the watch). Measurement: share of jobs with a distinct payer, later withheld-payment cases by payer type. The payer identity is the single most useful fact for a later D03 case: Late Payment Act interest and compensation (I14) only apply to business debtors (research note success_fee_benchmarks §3), and a recovery case needs the right legal entity.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per payer check. Off-quote payers are common at Firm scale.
ideas.assumptions: Jobs per year where the payer differs from the site customer: Solo 2, Small firm 6, Firm 15 (assumed from the business-customer mix). Attach 30% / 40% / 60% × £29 = £17 / £70 / £261. Wholesale £10–£12 including the watch, margin about £17 per check. Payment Practices reporting data exists only for large companies (turnover above £36m etc.), so that line appears for a minority of payers. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Clean: the builder pays to learn about the entity that controls their cash flow. It also quietly teaches the builder to contract with the right party, the biggest single cause of unrecoverable construction debt. No conflict with any known trust risk.
ideas.regulatory: As I87 (company data, officers under legitimate interests, Article 14 route through the first communication with the payer — which for a main contractor may be the order acknowledgement rather than the quote, so the notice must also sit in the contract pack). Payment Practices and Performance data is open government data. D12 v3 category, D04 entries, D14 plus D02 for the charge, G4 for real charging.
ideas.build_dependency: I87's CP-1/CP-2 adapters plus a payer-party field on the quote/job (M0-7 job spine: a `paying_party` reference distinct from the customer, tenant-qualified) and the I33 contract-pack hook. Monitoring from I94. About 2 weeks on top of I87.
ideas.gaming_risk: Naming a payer who has not agreed to pay does not make them liable: the card states that the check does not create a contract and offers the contract-pack step. Checks on unrelated companies: bound to a quote or job and rate-limited as I87.
ideas.precedent: Satago and Chaser risk insights on debtors (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). Payapps-style main-contractor tools (report §'No rival sells…') sit on the other side of the chain and do not check the payer for the subcontractor. Payment Practices reporting is a UK statutory dataset (assumed usable under OGL).
ideas.merged_from: 'Who actually pays?' payer-chain check for subcontract, landlord, managing-agent and insurer-funded jobs

ideas.name: Block-works check: RMC/RTM company and Section 20 consultation status for flats and managed blocks (£39)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — niche statutory-risk check for leasehold block work
ideas.mechanism: Trigger when the customer is a residents' management company, RTM company, freeholder or managing agent, or the site is a block of flats. Two parts in one £39 check. Part 1: the I87 company data on the RMC/RTM/freeholder, with the accounts read for the reserve fund and service-charge arrears figures where filed. Part 2: a structured, builder-completed questionnaire with dated document uploads: was a Notice of Intention served; a Notice of Estimates; were leaseholder observations answered; is there a Tribunal dispensation. JobGuard's card then states facts only: 'Reserve fund shown in the last filed accounts: £14,200; your quote is £48,000'; 'No Notice of Estimates recorded. For qualifying works, without consultation or a dispensation the landlord's recovery from each leaseholder is limited to £250 (Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.20; Service Charges (Consultation Requirements) (England) Regulations 2003)'; '38 leaseholders × £250 = £9,500 recoverable without consultation against a £48,000 quote'. No advice to refuse, no legal conclusion about this contract. Actions: 'Ask the managing agent to upload the s.20 notices' (portal request, stored as evidence), 'Set a deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Applications for payment schedule' (I24), 'Noted'. Money: £39 per block check on the statement (wholesale about £8 for the company report). Measurement: share of block jobs with incomplete consultation at quote; later withheld-payment cases on block jobs.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per block check. Relevant mainly to Small firms and Firms doing external works, roofs and communal areas.
ideas.assumptions: Block/managed-flat jobs per year: Solo 0.3, Small firm 1.5, Firm 4. Attach 30% / 40% / 50% × £39 = £4 / £23 / £78. Wholesale £8; margin about £31 per check. The £250 threshold and consultation stages are as the 2003 Regulations state; the block's leaseholder count comes from the title/lease data or the agent. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Builder-paid prevention of a specific, well-known way block work goes unpaid. No trust conflict. Care point: the statutory wording must be reviewed so a builder does not treat JobGuard as their solicitor.
ideas.regulatory: Company data as I87. The s.20 statement is a reviewed fixed text (D06-style legal wording review) presented as a statutory fact, not advice on the builder's contract. Leaseholder names must never be collected; only counts. D12 v3, D14 plus D02 for the charge; G4 for real charging.
ideas.build_dependency: I87 adapters, a questionnaire form with dated evidence uploads (M0-11), the reviewed statutory text as a versioned fixture. About 1–2 weeks on top of I87.
ideas.gaming_risk: A managing agent uploading forged notices: JobGuard stores what it was given with receive times and hashes; it does not verify authenticity (AGENTS §5.8 limits) and the card says so. Builders misquoting the £250 figure to agents: the text is fixed and sourced.
ideas.precedent: None known as a product; the s.20 cap is a standard leasehold-practice risk described by property law firms. Site Samurai and Payapps (report §'No rival sells…') cover payment applications but not consultation status.
ideas.merged_from: Block-works check: RMC/RTM company and Section 20 consultation status for flats and managed blocks

ideas.name: 'Watch this customer': live counterparty monitoring through the job (business customers and payers only, £3/month)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence extended through the job — recurring data subscription per monitored counterparty
ideas.mechanism: After switch-live, a business customer or named payer that has been checked can be watched until the final invoice is paid. Sources: Companies House streaming API (free: new charges, officer resignations, strike-off proposals, accounts overdue, insolvency events), The Gazette (free: petitions, administrations), a CRA monitoring product for new CCJs and score changes (assumed wholesale £0.50–£1 per entity per month), and Registry Trust monitoring where offered. Each event becomes a Finding in the Decision Inbox advisory lane (M2-7) with source and date: 'A winding-up petition against BuildCo Main Contractors Ltd was advertised in the Gazette on 3 Oct 2026'; 'New CCJ £6,200 registered 14 Oct 2026'. Watchdog checks stay pure functions producing Findings; nothing is sent, charged or decided. Actions: 'Bring forward the next application for payment' (I24), 'Open a withheld-payment case' (only if the D03 entry test is already met; otherwise hidden), 'Noted'. Homeowners are not monitored (disproportionate under UK GDPR and unwelcome); for domestic jobs the only re-check offered is a fresh £7 title-register copy before a large stage invoice, at pass-through plus £2, to catch a mid-job sale or new charge. Money: £3 per monitored counterparty per month, pro rata, from switch-live to final payment recorded; stops automatically when the job closes. Measurement: events per monitored entity, time from event to builder action, withheld-payment outcomes on watched vs unwatched jobs.
ideas.who_pays: The builder per monitored business counterparty per month; domestic title re-checks at pass-through plus £2.
ideas.assumptions: Business jobs won per year: Solo 1.9, Small firm 6, Firm 16.5; average live duration 2 / 3 / 4 months; attach 50% / 60% / 70%; £3/month. Solo 1.9 × 2 × 0.5 × £3 = £6; Small 6 × 3 × 0.6 × £3 = £32; Firm 16.5 × 4 × 0.7 × £3 = £139. Wholesale £0.50–£1 per entity-month, so margin about two thirds. Domestic title re-checks excluded from the figures (assumed rare). Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and builder-paid. Slight discomfort if a builder feels JobGuard is nudging them toward opening a 10% withheld-payment case; mitigate by only showing the case action when the D03 entry test is independently met and by fee terms being approved per case (§14.7). Homeowner monitoring is excluded on purpose.
ideas.regulatory: Ongoing processing of officer/PSC personal data under legitimate interests with a documented balancing test and a defined stop point (job closed); D12 v3 must cover monitoring as a purpose and the Article 14 route; D07 retention for event records; D04 entries for the streaming and monitoring providers; CRA monitoring contract terms. The D03 entry test remains unchanged: monitoring events never satisfy it. D14 plus D02 for the charge; G4 for real charging.
ideas.build_dependency: I87 adapters, a scheduled/streaming worker under Graphile Worker (M0-9) with idempotent event identities, M2-6 scheduled-check pattern, M2-7 inbox lanes. About 2 weeks after I87. A domestic re-check reuses I89's HMLR adapter.
ideas.gaming_risk: Duplicate or out-of-order provider events: unique source-event IDs (AGENTS §5.4). A builder keeping a job 'live' to keep watching a company they have no contract with: monitoring stops when the job closes and is bound to a job with an accepted quote.
ideas.precedent: Satago 'real-time alerts of changes' and Creditsafe/Experian monitoring products (satago.com; research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). HMLR Property Alert is owner-only, hence the title re-check design.
ideas.merged_from: 'Watch this customer': live counterparty monitoring through the job (business customers and payers only)

ideas.name: Exposure-vs-limit finding on the stage schedule (Builder tier and above)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — subscription feature that turns check data into a factual exposure curve (I08 Watchdog-tier differentiator)
ideas.mechanism: When a check (I87 or I92) returns a CRA suggested credit limit and the quote has a deposit and stage schedule (I40) or the default 'pay on completion' terms, a pure function in packages/core computes the builder's peak unpaid exposure over time from the schedule: cumulative value of work done (by stage) minus cumulative payments due before that point, exact money arithmetic. The card shows a small chart and the numbers: 'Peak unpaid exposure under these terms: £12,400 after stage 3 (week 6). The credit report's suggested limit for this company is £5,000 (Creditsafe, 25 Sep 2026)'. A comparison of two facts, not a recommendation; the copy does not say 'reduce exposure'. Actions: 'Edit the deposit and stage schedule' (I40), 'Use stage escrow' (I42), 'Noted'. On editing, the curve updates live so the builder sees the effect of their own choice. Money: no per-use charge; a Builder-and-above feature, part of the Watchdog tier's value story. Measurement: share of checked business quotes where the builder edits the schedule after seeing the curve; later exposure at the point a withheld-payment case opens.
ideas.who_pays: Included in Builder and Firm subscriptions; no separate charge. Solo sees the check but not the curve (or sees it with an upgrade prompt).
ideas.assumptions: No direct revenue; £2/month of the Builder/Firm price attributed to the feature as a retention/upsell justification, labelled as attribution. Requires the stage schedule (I40); without it the curve uses the quote's payment terms. Exact arithmetic on Money pence, half-even where rounding is needed. Unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: In the builder's interest and it makes the third-party limit useful without JobGuard advising. Edge: a chart comparing exposure to a limit is close to advice; the wording must stay descriptive and the limit must be attributed to the CRA, never to JobGuard.
ideas.regulatory: None beyond the check's own terms (I87) and CRA display rules for suggested limits (some CRAs restrict on-screen display of derived figures; confirm in the reseller contract). Not financial advice as long as no recommendation is made; legal wording review of the card copy.
ideas.build_dependency: I40 deposit/stage schedule model, I87's check evidence, a pure exposure-curve function with property tests in packages/core, a small chart in the web client. About 1 week after I40 and I87.
ideas.gaming_risk: None material; the curve is derived from the builder's own schedule and a third-party figure. Stale limits: show the retrieval date and offer a re-check.
ideas.precedent: Credit-control tools show recommended credit limits against outstanding balances (Satago risk insights; research note success_fee_benchmarks §6). No trade app shows exposure against a schedule.
ideas.merged_from: Exposure-vs-limit finding on the stage schedule (Builder tier and above)

ideas.name: Check record as recovery evidence: identity and terms proof for the D03 withheld-payment entry test and the I34 evidence pack
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — no separate charge; strengthens the existing 10% withheld-payment category
ideas.mechanism: Every check (I87, I89, I92, I93) and every customer portal declaration ('I am the owner / I am authorised to instruct this work / the payer is X') is stored as tenant/job-qualified verified evidence with hashes, object version IDs and receive times (AGENTS §5.8). Later, if the builder opens a withheld-payment case (§14.7: overdue beyond the D03 threshold, customer refused/disputed/ignored the builder's own reminder, builder explicitly opens and approves the fee terms), the case workbench (M4-1) pre-fills from that evidence: the debtor's exact legal identity and registered/service address, the fact that the invoice names the same party that accepted the quote, the deposit and stage terms the customer approved in the portal, and the owner/authority declaration. The M4-5 reviewed pursuit templates then address the right entity first time, and the I34 evidence pack gains a 'Counterparty and terms' section containing the check findings, the declarations and the acceptance record. Checks are never a precondition for the fee and never change the 10%; they only make cases easier to open correctly and to settle. Money: none directly; revenue is the incremental success fee from cases that settle because the identity and terms evidence exists. Measurement: settlement rate and days-to-settle on cases with and without a pre-contract check; pursuit letters returned or re-addressed.
ideas.who_pays: Nobody extra. The existing 10% success fee on cash settled after case opening is the only money; the check itself was paid for under I87/I89/I92/I93.
ideas.assumptions: Withheld-payment cases opened per year: Solo 1 at £2,000; Small firm 2 at £5,000; Firm 4 at £12,000 (assumptions). Having verified identity and approved terms lifts the settled-cash rate by 10 percentage points. Incremental fee = cases × value × 0.10 uplift × 10% fee: Solo £20, Small £100, Firm £480. Only cash settled after case opening counts (§14.7) and ordinary late payment never qualifies. Highly uncertain; the uplift is a guess to be measured in the pilot (§14.17).
ideas.trust_note: Genuinely in the builder's interest (they keep 90% of money they were not going to get), and it makes JobGuard's own recovery work cheaper. The risk is optics: if checks are ever marketed as 'so JobGuard can chase for you', a builder may feel the check was upsold to feed JobGuard's fee. Keep checks framed as prevention, keep the raw export free (I34), and never make a check a condition of the fee.
ideas.regulatory: Reuse of check data for pursuit is a new purpose for the officer/proprietor personal data: D12 v3 must name it and the Article 14 notice must mention it; CRA reseller terms often prohibit using a report in litigation or debt collection without permission, so the pack may include JobGuard's finding text and public-register copies but not the CRA report itself; D03 v2 entry test unchanged; regulated-activity position as research note success_fee_benchmarks §7 (helping a builder collect its own invoice is not FCA debt collecting on the sources found; legal sign-off required).
ideas.build_dependency: M4-1 case workbench, M4-2 attribution review, M4-3 evidence packs (add a section type), M4-5 pursuit templates; evidence links from I87/I89/I92/I93. About 1 week of integration once those exist; no new providers.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder opening a case on a customer who is merely late to get JobGuard's templates: the D03 entry test and per-case fee approval already gate this; the check record does not weaken it. Contradictory evidence (declaration says owner, title says otherwise): both are shown with dates; JobGuard asserts neither.
ideas.precedent: Debt collectors and solicitors require debtor identity and terms evidence before instruction (research note success_fee_benchmarks §3 and §7). Chaser pairs risk data with its collections service (§6).
ideas.merged_from: Check record as recovery evidence: identity and terms proof for the D03 withheld-payment entry test and the I34 evidence pack

ideas.name: JobGuard network payment-experience signal on business customers (give-to-get, flagged)
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — pooled builder-contributed data (trust risk: builders' data reused across tenants)
ideas.mechanism: Only for limited companies and LLPs, never individuals or sole traders. A tenant may opt in to contribute facts JobGuard already holds about its own invoices to business customers: invoice date, due date, date the payment was recorded, disputed yes/no. In return, the I87 'Check this customer' card gains one line built from other opted-in tenants' facts, aggregated and thresholded (minimum 3 contributing tenants, no tenant identities, no free text): 'Across JobGuard builders who have invoiced this company in the last 24 months: 7 invoices, paid on average 41 days after the due date; 2 disputed'. Below the threshold the line says 'Not enough JobGuard data'. Contribution and display are symmetric: no contribution, no line. Money: £5/month add-on for business-heavy tenants who want the line without contributing, or free with contribution; the honest version is free-with-contribution and the add-on is the fallback. Distinct from I29 (regional rate benchmark, give-to-get): different data and a named counterparty. Measurement: contribution opt-in rate, coverage of business customers, predictive value against later withheld-payment cases.
ideas.who_pays: The builder: contribution in kind (their own invoice facts) or £5/month.
ideas.assumptions: Solo has too few business customers to buy it (£0). Small firm 20% × £5 × 12 = £12; Firm 70% × £5 × 12 = £42, assuming most buyers choose contribution over cash, so cash revenue is small by design. Value depends on network density: below several hundred business-invoicing tenants the line rarely reaches threshold. Ex VAT; unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Flagged. This is builders' data reused across tenants, one of the named trust risks, and a company that finds itself described as a slow payer may complain to the builder who invoiced it. It is the established CRA trade-payment-data pattern, and restricting it to companies, to facts JobGuard itself recorded, to aggregates and to opt-in contributors keeps it defensible, but it should be off by default and possibly never built.
ideas.regulatory: Company payment behaviour is not personal data, but a sole trader's is, hence the exclusion; officer names are not shown. Contributing tenants' terms must permit the reuse (a D09/terms change) and each builder's customer contract or notice should mention it (D12 v3). Accuracy duties: facts only, from JobGuard's own invoice and payment records, with a correction route for the customer company. Defamation risk is low for factual aggregates but the wording must be reviewed. D07 retention window (24 months assumed).
ideas.build_dependency: Cross-tenant aggregation is a deliberate exception to tenant isolation and needs its own reviewed read model with a separate role and RLS exemption tests (AGENTS §5.1), plus M1-12 invoice and payment records as the fact source. About 3 weeks; a D-record and legal review before any real data.
ideas.gaming_risk: A builder recording fake late payments to smear a customer: facts come only from issued invoices and recorded receipts within JobGuard, disputes are counted not narrated, thresholds hide single contributors, and D11-style advisory signals flag tenants whose contributions are outliers. A customer company pressuring a builder to withdraw its contribution: contributions are anonymous and aggregated.
ideas.precedent: Creditsafe and Experian trade-payment-data programmes aggregate contributed ledger data; the UK Payment Practices reporting regime publishes large companies' payment performance. No trade-app precedent (report §'No rival sells…').
ideas.merged_from: JobGuard network payment-experience signal on business customers (give-to-get, flagged)

ideas.name: Trade credit insurance introduction for firms with business customers (insurer-paid commission; regulated; off by default) — trade-credit variant of the I46 introduction pattern
ideas.category: Pre-contract due diligence — regulated insurance introduction (variant of I43/I46, distinct product and trigger)
ideas.mechanism: For tenants whose checked business-customer exposure (I95) exceeds a threshold (assume £25k peak exposure or £250k annual business invoicing), the check card can show one neutral line: 'Some firms insure business invoices against non-payment. Learn about trade credit insurance' linking to an FCA-authorised broker or insurer partner. JobGuard does nothing beyond the introduction: no advice, no comparison, no quote handling, no policy administration. If the tenant buys cover, the partner pays JobGuard an introducer commission from its own commission on the premium. Disclosure appears on the line itself ('JobGuard may be paid by the partner if you take out cover'). The cover, if bought, can be recorded as evidence on jobs so that the readiness and withheld-payment flows know a policy exists (insurers' claim conditions often require timely notification). Money: commission per policy paid by the partner; nothing from the builder. Measurement: click-through, policies bound, and whether insured builders open fewer withheld-payment cases (an honest conflict: an insured builder claims from the insurer instead of paying JobGuard 10%). Differs from I46 (builder's own liability/legal-expenses cover checked at switch-live) in product, trigger and its direct interaction with the withheld-payment fee.
ideas.who_pays: The insurer or broker, via introducer commission. The builder pays the insurer a premium, not JobGuard.
ideas.assumptions: Take-up among eligible tenants: Solo 0% (no business book); Small firm 10% at an assumed £2,000 annual premium; Firm 25% at £5,000. Broker commission on premium assumed 12.5–25%; JobGuard's introducer share assumed 7.5% of premium. Small 0.10 × £2,000 × 0.075 = £15; Firm 0.25 × £5,000 × 0.075 = £94. Trade credit insurance is usually whole-turnover and often has minimum premiums above what a small firm will pay, so take-up may be lower. Unvalidated.
ideas.trust_note: Insurer money flowing to JobGuard for pointing builders at a product is a mild conflict, and it competes with JobGuard's own withheld-payment fee (a fully insured builder has less reason to open a case). It does not touch the supplier-invoice watchdog and does not use the builder's customers as leads, so it is cleaner than merchant money. Still: regulated, disclosed, off by default, one partner, no ranking.
ideas.regulatory: Introducing insurance business is an insurance distribution activity unless an exclusion applies (RAO art. 72C 'provision of information on an incidental basis' and PERG 5.6 introducer guidance); taking commission and providing exposure figures may take JobGuard outside the exclusion, so treat it as needing FCA authorisation, appointed-representative/introducer-appointed-representative status with the partner, or a confirmed exclusion by counsel. ICOBS/IDD remuneration disclosure. Data sharing with the partner needs D12 v3 and D04 entries; the builder's consent to be introduced. A new decision record (like I43/I46) and a G4-equivalent gate before any live introduction.
ideas.build_dependency: I95's exposure figures and a partner agreement; the technical build is a link, a consent record and an evidence type for the policy (about 1 week). The regulatory route is the dependency, not the code.
ideas.gaming_risk: Low. The partner could pressure for placement or ranking: contractually one partner, one neutral line, no performance-based placement. JobGuard steering builders toward cover to earn commission: the line only appears above the threshold and the copy is fixed and reviewed.
ideas.precedent: Chaser and Satago sit near invoice finance and credit insurance offers (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6); broker commission 12.5–25% of premium reported for commercial lines (apexinsurancebrokers.co.uk explainer); FCA PERG 5.6 introducer guidance. Allianz Trade, Atradius and Coface are the UK trade-credit insurers, reached through brokers.
ideas.merged_from: Trade credit insurance introduction for firms with business customers (insurer-paid commission; regulated; off by default)

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts fail on every axis but one. Harm to the builder: none inherent — the count is derived only from the builder's own commands (switch-live, lock, explicit close), unlimited users removes the per-seat penalty on the site staff who feed evidence, and job-size blindness cuts in the builder's favour. Independence: builder-paid, no supplier money. Withheld information: nothing JobGuard finds, holds or hides can move the meter, so it cannot be read as profiting from the shadow bill. Fairness (report §'The hidden final check', Xia et al. / Kahneman dual entitlement): a flat, known price for capacity the builder controls, with a jobs-based unit builders already accept from ServiceM8 (§'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). The one genuine trust exposure is the sentence 'locking frees a slot'. The lock is the event that starts JobGuard's own fee-earning check (§14.4–14.5). If allowance pressure makes a builder lock before their own review is finished, catches they would have captured fee-free become 10% fees — the exact 'knew and profited' reading the research says spreads by word of mouth. The meter therefore works only if it is structurally severed from the lock. The idea's reliance on a homeowner portal (I55) as 'the enforcement' for the meter is a customer-relationship risk and is not accepted as part of this verdict.
verdicts.conditions: (1) The count is computed only from immutable switch-live, lock and explicit-close events; no evidence, signal, finding or document count may influence it, and D09 v2 says so in one sentence. (2) Over-limit never blocks or delays switch-live, and no builder-facing surface ever proposes locking or closing a job to free a slot; the final-account flow shows nothing about the meter. (3) Explicit close (recorded reason, no lock) is one tap from the live list and is clearly described as 'no final check on this job'; it is never counted as a lock and never triggers a reveal. (4) Allowances stay at or above the report's 3/10/25 and are only ever raised, never cut, for existing subscribers without renewal-period notice (D09 grandfathering). (5) The platform invoice prints period, tier, peak count and the source events, and the live list shows the running count all month. (6) The builder's customer is never used as an enforcement or verification mechanism for the meter. (7) Show the VAT-inclusive price alongside ex-VAT for tenants that declare they are not VAT-registered (report §'£29 beats £30' open question).
verdicts.key_risk: Allowance pressure inducing a premature lock, which converts the builder's own fee-free captures into JobGuard's 10% catches and reads as profiting from withheld information.

verdicts.reasons: Partly refuted. Three problems: (a) it is a running meter, which the research says builders dislike relative to flat prices (Prelec & Loewenstein; Lambrecht & Skiera flat-rate bias); (b) because inactivity never closes a job, a forgotten live job can bill overage for doing nothing, which a reasonable builder reads as exploiting an advantage; (c) a per-job-month charge sharpens I01's lock-pressure problem — a builder near their limit is nudged every month toward locking (the only path that keeps invoicing inside JobGuard), and every premature lock enlarges the shadow bill. The whole-month auto-step variant is worse: one extra job costs a full tier step, a cliff dressed as a soft limit. The idea survives only as what its own text calls it, a fairness device rather than a revenue line: a small, published, pre-agreed per-slot price with notice and citations is 'passing on a cost', which dual-entitlement research judges fair, and it is plainly better for the builder than a hard block. It must be impossible for the overage to touch a job that is finishing.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Per-slot form only; no whole-month tier auto-step. (2) Slot price published on the pricing page and in D09 v2; total overage in any period capped at the difference to the next tier. (3) Charged only under an explicitly accepted D05 bounded authority that states the slot price and cap; without it, an over-limit raises a Decision, the job still goes live and nothing is charged until approved. (4) Before the first overage in any period, a notice cites the specific jobs and gives at least 7 days with one-tap close (recorded reason); a job closed in that window is never charged. (5) A job never creates overage while a draft final-account revision exists for it or while it has had no builder activity in the period; only genuinely worked jobs count. (6) First over-limit month in any rolling 12 is free and says 'cheaper than upgrading this month'. (7) No mention of overage or the meter anywhere in the final-account or lock flow. (8) The invoice line cites period, job IDs and source events.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£60 (grace month and finishing-stage exemption trim the low end)
revised_revenue.firm: £0–£320 (only if peaks exceed 25 or a tight top band is chosen)

verdicts.key_risk: A per-job-month meter that quietly pushes builders to lock early or bills a forgotten job, both of which read as JobGuard exploiting its position.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted. All of the idea's revenue sits in the upward weights, and those are contract-value pricing by the back door: a builder with one £200k extension is told it counts as three jobs. That contradicts the founder's rejection of turnover/contract value as the meter, and it fails the dual-entitlement test — JobGuard cannot point to a cost the builder can see, because the honest cost driver (documents to check) is priced directly and visibly by I04. Running I03 and I04 together would charge for job size twice. It also breaks I01's main strength, one number builders understand, and requires the builder to trust a multiplier table rather than a count they can verify from their own live list. The analogues source already recommended against it for the same reason. The half-weight for tiny jobs is genuinely pro-builder, but it is an allowance rule, not a weighting scheme, and carries no revenue; it does not rescue the idea. The gaming and shadow-bill interactions are clean (weight fixed at switch-live, nothing JobGuard finds moves it), which is why the score is 2 rather than 1.
verdicts.conditions: None rescue the idea as written. If the founder wants the small-job relief, fold 'jobs with accepted net value under £2,500 do not count toward the allowance' into I01's D09 v2 terms as a plain allowance rule with no multiplier above 1. Retaining any weight above 1 keeps this a reject.

revised_revenue.firm: £0 (the Contractor tail disappears with the upward weights)

verdicts.key_risk: Perceived as turnover pricing under another name, undermining the 'one simple number' meter and the builder's sense that the subscription is a fair capacity charge.

verdicts.reasons: Mostly survives refutation. It is the one prevention charge that passes the fairness tests: the builder pays for verifiable work JobGuard actually performed (a document read and checked, with a visible result), which is 'passing on cost' rather than 'exploiting an advantage', and the labour-illusion evidence (Buell & Norton) says visible effort raises perceived value. It never claims a saving, so §14.1's forbidden claims are respected. Independence and customer relationship are untouched. Three refutations bite and become conditions: (a) a builder near the allowance may withhold supplier documents, which removes their overcharge protection — so the cost of going over must be trivial and never a mid-period block; (b) the 'pays twice' objection (report §'The hidden final check') sharpens if the builder is charged to have a document read and JobGuard then also earns 10% from what it found in that document — every counted document must therefore produce a builder-visible check result, so the builder can see what the 40p bought; (c) connector-ingested items (SV-7 email forwarding, later accounting links) are JobGuard's own evidence gathering and must never count, or the shadow bill would be billed to the builder by the page.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Only builder-submitted supplier documents and POs count; connector-ingested items, photos and diary content never count. (2) Every counted document has a builder-visible check outcome (matched / discrepancy / no PO) at the time it is counted; a document with no visible outcome is not billable. (3) Overage requires an explicitly accepted D05 bounded authority with the per-document price and a period cap equal to the next tier step; without it, documents are still checked and an upgrade proposal is raised at no charge. (4) Never a mid-period block or slowdown; checking behaviour is byte-identical inside and outside the allowance. (5) Statement line reads 'documents checked' with a link to the results, never 'money saved' or 'findings'. (6) Counters are rebuildable from immutable intake events; an inconsistent count cannot charge. (7) Allowances start at or above 40/150/500 and the running count is visible all period.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 overage at ~12 docs/month
revised_revenue.firm: £0 at ~150/month; an outlier (3 large jobs, 400 docs/month on Solo) pays ~£150/month and is steered to Firm

verdicts.key_risk: Builders withholding supplier documents to avoid 40p charges, which removes their own overcharge protection and starves the watchdog.

verdicts.reasons: Could not refute. It respects how building work runs and the cash position of sole traders, costs JobGuard little, and the research (§'Offer annual billing') suggests it may retain better than prepay for this segment. Independence, customer relationship and withheld-information tests are all clean: dormancy is the builder's choice and nothing JobGuard holds changes it. Two small trust edges become conditions. First, if eligibility requires zero live jobs, a builder with one lingering winter job is nudged to lock it early to save £29, and an early lock is JobGuard's gain (§14.4–14.5); pause must therefore be available on request with jobs simply put on hold. Second, 'evidence accepted but not analysed' must mean exactly that: nothing in dormancy may run the builder-facing watchdog off while the shadow engine runs on, or dormancy becomes a period where JobGuard reads and the builder is blind.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Pause available on request regardless of live count; live jobs are marked 'on hold', keep their slot history and resume without loss; a lock is never required to become eligible. (2) During dormancy, no detector of any kind runs on new evidence (builder-facing or shadow); evidence is stored with receive time and analysed only on reactivation, so evidence-before-lock rules still hold. (3) Onboarding and the pause screen say in one sentence that jobs closed without a lock get no final check, and that paused jobs still get it when resumed. (4) Reactivation takes effect from the next period boundary or immediately on switch-live, whichever the builder chooses, with the price shown before confirming. (5) Paused periods appear as £0/nominal D09 obligations with reason 'paused'; no back-billing on reactivation. (6) Annual subscribers who pause have their term extended by the paused months.

revised_revenue.solo: £5 direct, ~£15 retained (or +£12 vs an annual-discount baseline)

verdicts.key_risk: Eligibility rules that nudge a builder to lock a lingering job early, or a dormancy in which JobGuard's shadow engine keeps reading while the builder's own watchdog is off.

verdicts.reasons: Could not refute in substance. It is the market-standard 'two months free' the builder already sees at YourTradebase, Powered Now and Joist, it is opt-in, and it is transparent about what the money buys. Independence, withheld information and customer relationship are untouched. The residual fairness exposure is lock-in for a sole trader whose circumstances change mid-year (injury, folding, winter), and auto-renewal without clear notice; both are exactly where the research says builders are wary. The gaming concern (annual Solo then running eight live jobs) is handled by I02 without any trust cost. Not a revenue idea so much as a cash-timing and selection choice, which the report says is its real value.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Monthly is the default at every checkout; annual is offered, never pre-selected. (2) Renewal notice at least 30 days before the charge with one-tap cancel (D05 bounded renewal authority). (3) A mid-term cancellation converts remaining months to a pause credit or a pro-rata refund net of the discount, stated on the pricing page. (4) Upgrades pro-rated mid-term; downgrades at renewal; no deeper introductory discounts and no 'first year' pricing that jumps later. (5) One Stripe hosted checkout and one platform invoice showing the ex-VAT and VAT amounts and the tax point (D02). (6) Paused months extend the term (I05).

revised_revenue.solo: £290 (£58 less than monthly, paid day one)

verdicts.key_risk: Lock-in and silent auto-renewal for cash-poor sole traders.

verdicts.reasons: Survives, but only after its ledger is narrowed. The strongest point stands: JobGuard bearing refund risk is the clearest quality signal the research identifies, and it is the one honest way to hold a market-rate list price. Three refutations bite. (a) Independence: if 'builder-confirmed prevented findings' count toward the value that voids a refund, the watchdog acquires a financial motive to over-flag and to nudge confirmation, and it counts value the builder cannot verify — a guarantee measured by JobGuard's own unprovable prevention numbers is not a guarantee. (b) Fine print: activity conditions and 'dismissals never reduce the ledger' are where money-back offers are perceived as never paying out; and a lock-count condition ties the guarantee to the event that starts JobGuard's own fee check. (c) Credit-only remedy keeps the builder's money unless they stay. The list-price uplift is defensible only if the guarantee is a standard term on the tier, not a paid feature. It must never be sold as insurance and every counted pound must be visible on the value receipt as it accrues, so the claim outcome is never a surprise.
verdicts.conditions: (1) The ledger counts only externally evidenced or settled value: supplier corrections backed by a corrected invoice, credit note or cash refund; confirmed final-check extras only once customer cash is settled and allocated; recovered cash under an opened case. 'Flagged', 'prevented' and builder-confirmed-but-unevidenced items never count. (2) Builder captures ('tracked') never count and are shown separately as the builder's own work. (3) The running guarantee total is visible on the monthly value receipt with each counted item and its evidence, in the §14.1 permitted wording. (4) Claim is self-service, one tap, decided from posted facts only, with no dispute step required to receive the credit. (5) Activity conditions are at most two, stated in one sentence on the pricing page, shown as progress during the year, and never include confirming or not dismissing a JobGuard finding. (6) Remedy is a credit note against future subscription, converted to a cash refund on cancellation (M4-10 credit note plus refund work). (7) Same multiple on every tier that carries it; the guarantee is a standard term, not an add-on. (8) Legal confirmation before launch that a credit of own fees is not a contract of insurance; D09 v3 records terms and claim window. (9) Guarantee wording may never state or imply an amount saved.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (excluded)
revised_revenue.small_firm: +£0 to +£150 net (assumption: claim rate roughly doubles when only externally evidenced value counts)

verdicts.key_risk: A guarantee measured by JobGuard's own unverifiable prevention numbers gives the watchdog a motive to over-flag and reads as fine print designed never to pay.

verdicts.reasons: Survives narrowly, and only in a specific shape. The core objection is real: a 'profit watchdog' whose cheapest plan does not watch sits next to 'JobGuard knew but did not say'. It is acceptable only because on Solo JobGuard genuinely does not extract the document — and that must be true for every purpose. The decisive refutation is asymmetric extraction: the shadow engine's deterministic detectors (SV-3) include supplier items and POs with no matching scope, so if a Solo tenant's uploaded invoice photo were read for shadow signals while the builder's overcharge check did not run, JobGuard would be reading the document for its own 10% while withholding the finding that stops the builder paying away money. That goes beyond the decided shadow-bill rule (which hides unbilled extras, not overcharges) and would be indefensible. Second refutation: readiness warnings, proof-before-cover prompts and the Decision Inbox are cheap, deterministic, evidence-protecting functions; gating them harms the builder's own dispute position at near-zero marginal cost and starves the photo evidence JobGuard itself wants. Only the merchant-document engine can be gated. The add-on-with-guarantee form is the more honest route because the builder chooses it and sees what it costs; the evidence-based upgrade prompt is acceptable only if it cites counts and never implies a discrepancy exists.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Tier gate applies only to the merchant-document engine (supplier intake, extraction, three-way matching, overcharge and short-delivery findings). Readiness warnings, proof-before-cover prompts, the Decision Inbox and all D13 must-surface rules run on every tier. (2) No asymmetric extraction: on a tier without intake, no supplier document, PO or invoice photo is OCR'd, extracted or read by any detector for any purpose, including shadow signals; SV-3 detectors that consume supplier documents are entitlement-checked at the same point as the builder-facing check, and a test proves a Solo tenant's documents produce zero shadow signals. (3) Anything JobGuard does extract, on any tier, always runs the builder-facing check; a tier gate can never suppress a finding on a document JobGuard has read. (4) The upgrade prompt states only a count ('you uploaded 14 supplier invoices this month; checking is on Builder') and never states or implies a discrepancy or an amount. (5) The add-on is priced flat per tier and shown on the pricing page in one line; if backed by the I07 guarantee, I07's conditions apply. (6) D09 v2 records the feature matrix; §14.1 forbidden claims apply to all guarantee and upgrade wording. (7) No supplier or merchant money in any form funds or influences the watchdog (independence).

revised_revenue.solo: +£144 expected (40% upgrade × £360) or £180 add-on

verdicts.key_risk: Asymmetric extraction: JobGuard reading a Solo builder's supplier documents for shadow signals while withholding the overcharge check on the same document.

verdicts.reasons: This is the one idea in the set where the fee follows work JobGuard visibly does, which is the fairness condition the research isolates (Xia, Monroe & Cox on who does the work; Buell & Norton on visible effort; report §'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk'). A collector or claims firm earns its percentage by chasing; here the desk drafts, tracks and assembles the bundle while the builder stays sender under D10. The builder chooses per case, sees the rate before JobGuard lifts a finger, and only after the customer has already refused, disputed or ignored the builder's own reminder (D03 v2, BUILD_PLAN §14.7), so ordinary late payment is not taxed. 15% sits inside the UK fresh-debt collector band (8-15%), 20% is under claims firms (15-30%) and far under the 50% DBA cap (success_fee_benchmarks §7 and summary table). No supplier money is involved and nothing is withheld: withheld-payment cases are builder-opened. Refutations that partly land and define the safeguards: (a) JobGuard gains an incentive to steer builders to the higher tiers or to let self-serve go thin, which is 'exploiting an advantage' in dual-entitlement terms; (b) a builder whose homeowner pays after one JobGuard-drafted reminder will feel 15% of money they were always owed was a lot for a letter, and consumer debtors carry no Late Payment Act interest to offset it (benchmarks note lines 61-65); (c) Escalated stacks a solicitor's fixed fee and court fees on top of 20%, so a failed claim can leave the builder out of pocket; (d) chasing homeowners is consumer-facing and legally sensitive (Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims, AJA 1970 s.40, DMCC) and any contact in JobGuard's name changes the regulatory analysis. None is fatal because the builder opts in with full information and JobGuard does the work.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Rate chosen and locked at case opening; one rate per case, never 10% plus an uplift; a worked example of total cost including solicitor fixed fee and court fee is shown before the builder confirms. (2) The self-serve 10% tier keeps the full template set, reminders and tracking; Managed adds human drafting and case management and must never be created by degrading self-serve. (3) Neutral tier selection: no default to Managed, no case-value nudges, no 'most builders choose' copy. (4) No approved send, no uplift: if the case settles before at least one builder-approved, JobGuard-drafted send, the fee reverts to 10% for that case. (5) The builder remains the identified sender (D10); the desk and panel solicitor never contact the homeowner in JobGuard's name without a new D10 and legal review. (6) JobGuard takes no referral fee or commission from the panel solicitor; disbursements at cost, itemised and approved in advance. (7) The case screen states that consumer debts carry no statutory interest or compensation, so the builder bears the whole fee. (8) D03 v2 entry test unchanged; amounts paid before opening never count. (9) Fee only on settled, allocated, unreversed cash (§14.8-14.9) under a versioned D01 rate table (10/15/20) with D05 statement approval. (10) The D11 signal 'managed case opened then no landing' is human-reviewed, never auto-penalised. (11) Legal sign-off on Article 39F and claims-management scope, the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims and consumer-chasing rules before any live case. (12) JobGuard cannot change the tier mid-case; the builder may downgrade before the first approved send.

revised_revenue.solo: £100 (incremental ~£30) — neutral presentation and the no-send fallback lower blended take-up to ~40-55%; case counts remain guesses

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard's own incentive to push builders towards the 15-20% tiers on money they were always owed, chased from homeowners with no statutory interest to offset it: if self-serve is thin or the choice is nudged, a reasonable builder reads it as a toll on their distress, and the consumer-chasing legal exposure sits with the builder as sender.

verdicts.reasons: The builder is asked to pay £35, at the moment a customer is withholding their money, for a case pack assembled from evidence the subscription already pays JobGuard to hold, and to pay it whether or not anything is recovered, on top of an unreduced 10%. Every fairness test in the research points the wrong way: the builder bears the cost of failure (Xia et al.), the charge lands at a point of distress (dual entitlement: exploiting an advantage), and it stacks a third charge on one outcome (the R&D-adviser critique of contingency fees on top of an engagement fee, report §'The hidden final check'). The precedent the idea cites refutes it: UK collectors pair a £25-75 file fee with a lower 6-10% commission (success_fee_benchmarks line 58); JobGuard's version keeps the full 10% and adds the fee, so it reads as worse than a debt collector. The idea's own gaming note ('opening a case for the letters then settling outside — fee still earned') is exactly the story a builder will retell: paid £35, chased it themselves, JobGuard kept the money. It also deters case opening, which is the only gate to JobGuard's 10% on withheld payments, so it works against JobGuard's own revenue. The fair variants (credited against the 10%, refunded on failure, or included in Builder/Firm tiers) all yield roughly zero, and £35-£140 a year cannot justify any trust cost. No supplier money or withheld information is involved; this is rejected purely on fairness and alignment.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable (rejected). If a case pack is wanted as a feature, include case opening and pack assembly in the subscription tiers at no charge; any file fee would have to be fully credited against the success fee or refunded when nothing is recovered, at which point it is no longer a revenue idea.
verdicts.key_risk: Charging a builder to chase their own money at their worst moment, with no refund on failure and no reduction in the 10%, against a market norm where the file fee buys a lower commission, is the kind of small unfairness that spreads by word of mouth and deters builders from opening the very cases that earn JobGuard its fee.

verdicts.reasons: The builder commissions it, the money is found by JobGuard's own work (human audit plus matching) on invoices the builder had already paid, the rate sits below the 20-30% AP-recovery norm (success_fee_benchmarks §1) and nothing comes from suppliers, so the watchdog's independence is intact. That passes the 'who did the work' test. Refutations that partly land: (a) AP recovery audit is almost universally pure contingency, 'no recovery, no fee' (PRGX, Westgate Moore, CRA; benchmarks lines 13-17), so a £295/£495 setup fee paid before anything is found is worse than market on structure and makes the builder bear the cost of a fruitless audit; at the idea's own assumptions a small firm nets only about £25-£425 after setup and fee, which a reasonable builder may read as JobGuard being the main beneficiary; (b) a second, higher percentage gives JobGuard an incentive to over-flag historic overcharges and encourage aggressive claims against merchants the builder still trades with, which can cost credit terms and goodwill; (c) builders will ask why old invoices carry 20-25% when the live watchdog charges 10%, answerable only if the human audit labour is visible; (d) historic invoices span other jobs and suppliers' personal data (D12). Revenue is small at any rate; the idea is acceptable to the builder only if it is unambiguously on the builder's side of the counter and the builder cannot end up worse off for commissioning it.
verdicts.conditions: (1) No-find-no-fee: drop the setup fee, or refund/credit it in full where cash refunds received fall below the setup amount; the builder can never end the audit worse off. (2) Every finding is cited to the invoice, PO/quote or delivery note; the builder chooses what to pursue; no pressure metrics or 'you are leaving £X' nudges. (3) The builder sends every refund request (D10); JobGuard never contacts suppliers in its own name. (4) Nothing from suppliers, ever: no referral, rebate or data arrangements, stated in the terms. (5) Supplier credit notes and prevented future overcharges are shown but never charged (D03 v2 already excludes credit notes). (6) Fee only on bank-verified cash refunds (M4-7/M4-8) under a separate D03 category and D01 rate line that never bleeds into the live 10% overcharge category. (7) The audit contract states the rate, setup terms and an honest hit-rate ('most audits find under 1% of spend; some find nothing'). (8) D12 review for historic supplier and job data, with retention and deletion of imported documents. (9) Output labelled human-reviewed versus machine-matched. (10) Not marketed as a claims or cost-cutting consultancy.

revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£105 — assumes ~30% of audits refund the setup because cash refunds fall below it; other assumptions unchanged and weak

verdicts.key_risk: A setup fee the builder pays before anything is found, against a market norm of no-find-no-fee, plus a 20-25% rate that gives JobGuard a motive to over-flag and to push builders into chasing merchants they still depend on.

verdicts.reasons: The trust profile is cleaner than the live shadow bill: the job is finished, the builder brings their own bill and asks for a second look, so there is no 'knew on day 12' problem and nothing is withheld mid-job; the timing is the builder's own choice. £29 for a visible piece of work with evidence shown per candidate fits the operational-transparency finding, and a paid 'nothing found' outcome is fair if stated in advance as a check, not a guarantee. The 15% non-member rate is a price difference with a visible reason (members fund the always-on watchdog) and stays inside every benchmark. Refutations that land: (a) the main builder-harm and customer-relationship risk is timing: if the builder has already issued the final bill, every catch becomes a late supplementary invoice to a homeowner, which the report flags as consumer-law-sensitive and dispute-prone (report §'The hidden final check', DMCC point); the live product avoids this by requiring the lock before the invoice is issued (§14.4) and this product must do the same; (b) two charges (£29 plus 15%) on one event must be on one screen before payment or it reads as drip pricing even though B2B; (c) thinner evidence means more false positives, so the 'already included', 'not chargeable' and 'I chose not to charge' dispositions must be respected, fee-free and never nagged; (d) the 'payment link' must never route the customer's money through JobGuard (AGENTS §3); (e) 15% versus 10% can read as a penalty for not subscribing; stated plainly it is acceptable, and honouring the member rate on that check's catches if the builder subscribes soon after removes the sting. The residual that a non-member takes the reveal and bills outside JobGuard is the builder's right and no trust problem; it only means the 15% line is largely notional without a bank feed.
verdicts.conditions: (1) The check runs before the final invoice is issued: the builder declares the bill unissued (a lock as in §14.4) and confirmed catches go on that invoice; if the bill has already gone out, show a prominent warning that late extra bills to consumers are more disputed and let the builder decide. (2) £29, the 15% rate and the member 10% comparison on one screen before Stripe checkout; no later add-ons. (3) 'Nothing found' described in advance as a normal paid outcome; no 'typically finds £X' claims until pilot data exist. (4) Hosted Stripe only, builder as merchant of record for the customer's payment; JobGuard never holds funds. (5) Every candidate shows its evidence and the 'missing from' proof; dispositions are fee-free and final with no follow-up pressure. (6) 15% needs D01 v4 under the same D03/D02/D13 rules: post-lock evidence never qualifies, disclosed items are never charged, only settled allocated cash counts. (7) D12 Article 14 route for uploaded customer messages and the same onboarding disclosure as members. (8) Recommended: a builder who subscribes within 30 days of a check pays the member 10% on that check's catches. (9) Non-member uploads are used only for that check under a stated retention policy.

revised_revenue.solo: £338 if used instead of subscribing (unchanged; the £29 line is reliable, the 15% line is largely goodwill-dependent without a bank feed)

verdicts.key_risk: Running the check after the builder has already issued the final bill, so catches become late supplementary invoices to homeowners that are dispute-prone under consumer law and damage the builder's relationship, compounded by the 15% non-member rate reading as a penalty if it is not shown plainly beside the member rate.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on the builder's interest, on clarity and on the idea's own arithmetic. A typically cash-poor builder (report §'Builders' willingness to pay') is asked to lend JobGuard £200 for up to 24 months against fees on money that may never be found, for a discount on a fee already at the floor of every benchmark. The 15% breakage that props up the revenue line is revenue from builders who paid and got nothing, which is the expiring-credit resentment the idea itself concedes; if credits are fully refundable and never expire, as fairness requires, breakage is zero and the idea is more revenue-negative than its own −£10/−£30/−£110. It also undermines the clarity the fixed v3 model depends on: a prepaid balance labelled 'recovery credit' beside a subscription invites builders to read it as a subscription credit or offset, muddying the founder's 'subscription never offsets the fee' rule (§14.1, D09). Worse for trust, a prepaid balance gives JobGuard a visible motive to consume it: a builder shown zero catches with £150 outstanding will suspect JobGuard is not trying, or later that it found things to use up the balance. The behavioural rationale (Prelec & Loewenstein decoupling) is theory not measured on tradespeople, and the same benefit is delivered better and free by the same-screen statement in I22. No independence or withheld-information problem, but no reasonable builder would see prepaying to be told what they missed as in their interest.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable (rejected). Achieve the payment-pain decoupling through I22's same-screen statement instead.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected; the fair, refundable, non-expiring version is more negative than the idea's own −£10)

verdicts.key_risk: Breakage revenue from cash-poor builders' unused credit, the perception that JobGuard holds a prepaid balance it is motivated to consume, and blurring of the no-offset rule between subscription and fee.

verdicts.reasons: Not a new charge; the most builder-friendly way to present the fee the founder has already fixed. Integrating a small loss into a larger gain at the moment cash lands (Thaler 1985) and showing the evidence trail on the same screen (Buell & Norton 2011) are the two strongest behavioural findings in the research, and the report warns that a separate invoice weeks later 'would feel like an isolated loss' (report §'The hidden final check'; psychology note §2). The builder keeps 90% in their own account because JobGuard never touches the customer's money, so 'who bears the cost' stays visible and fair. Refutations tried: (a) a large Approve beside a happy receipt can be a dark pattern that turns the statement into rushed consent, cured by equal-weight query/dispute actions and nothing pre-selected; (b) the optional standing Direct Debit authority is where a reasonable builder could feel money left their account before they had checked; if it defaults on, collects during an open attribution dispute, or fires on an unverified receipt, the most builder-friendly idea becomes the most damaging, and AGENTS §5.3 and D05 already require it to be bounded, revocable, re-checked at execution and opt-in with per-statement approval the default; (c) '£900 yours' without the VAT/tax basis is a forbidden claim under §14.1; (d) seven-day collection is fine with per-statement approval but must respect DD advance-notice rules and a reversal path (§14.9 compensation) if the receipt is later refunded. All are cheap, precise safeguards on rules the plan already contains.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Per-statement approval is the default (D05); standing authority is separate, opt-in, explained in plain words, bounded to the derived fee under the versioned policy and ≤10% of the verified receipt, capped per period, revocable in one tap and re-checked at execution. (2) No collection while an attribution dispute or query is open; disputed attributions are fee-free until a human resolves them against the immutable record (D13). (3) Collection only against a bank-verified, cleared receipt (M4-7/M4-8), never a builder 'mark paid'. (4) Statement wording states the basis: '£1,000 received (net of VAT) · JobGuard success fee £100 + VAT · you retain £900 before tax', with the evidence pack and the §14.8 allocation rule one tap away. (5) Approve, Query and Dispute have equal visual weight; nothing pre-selected; no countdown or urgency copy. (6) DD advance notice per GoCardless/Bacs rules; refunds by linked compensation per §14.9 when a receipt reverses. (7) A test that this screen and its timing cannot vary with shadow signals before lock (§14.3), even though it only exists after lock and settlement. (8) JobGuard never nets its fee from, or holds, the customer's payment (AGENTS §3).

revised_revenue.solo: +£8 (unchanged; a collection-rate guess on the same fee base)

verdicts.key_risk: The standing Direct Debit authority: if it becomes a default, collects during a dispute or before funds are verified, the builder's story becomes 'they took it out of my account before I'd checked', the exact betrayal reading the research says spreads fastest.

verdicts.reasons: Fails every test in the lens. It charges the builder for their own work: the builder will do the physical work of the line, price it, quote it, win it and bill it, while JobGuard's contribution is structuring a proposal from the builder's own walk-through; §14.2 already says AI structuring of a builder's own capture is builder capture, so a fee on quote-stage model_suggestion lines contradicts the spirit of the fixed decision that builder capture is fee-free. The fairness research is direct: builders reject fees where the extra 'was already in their head' (report §'The hidden final check'; psychology note §3), and a site-visit proposal is very often exactly that. It collides with two fixed rules: §5.10 ('creating, editing, reviewing, generating, or sending a quote cannot create platform fee obligations'; deferring the charge to switch-live does not change that the obligation is derived from the quote's content) and the founder's decision that the platform charge is a tenant subscription, 'never a per-job base fee', which a £5-per-line, £25-per-quote charge at switch-live plainly is. It compromises independence in a new way: JobGuard is paid to over-propose, degrading the proposal quality the confirmation screen depends on, while builders retype lines to strip provenance, an adversarial loop that damages the product on both sides. Revenue of £86-£297 a year is trivial against that cost. The idea's own recommendation is right: count accepted proposed lines in the value receipt, never charge for them.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable (rejected). Record accepted model_suggestion lines as a counted, labelled item in the builder's value receipt and any guarantee (I07) with no charge; do not amend §5.10.
verdicts.key_risk: A fee on the builder's own scope that rewards JobGuard for over-proposing: the clearest 'who did the work' unfairness in the set, in direct conflict with §5.10 and the no-per-job-fee decision.

verdicts.reasons: A plain feature at a plain price: the builder chooses it, sees what it costs, and gets tools only Site Samurai (£99-£699), Construction AI (£130+) and Payapps (price on request) offer today (construction_platforms_and_ai lines 47-50). Nothing is withheld, no supplier pays, every notice and application is an exact Decision the builder issues, and the price undercuts the alternatives. Refutations tried: (a) the fee boundary: reminders, notices, retention timers and release invoices are subscription features and must never become 'JobGuard pursuit' that turns ordinary late payment or a contractually withheld retention into a 10% withheld-payment case; D03 v2 needs the customer to have refused/disputed/ignored the builder's own reminder and an explicit builder-opened case, so the rule is never auto-open, never nudge; (b) the £39 per live-job-month variant looks like the per-job platform charge the founder ruled out (D09 'never a per-job base fee') and edges towards a value meter; drop it and price flat per business or bundle in Contractor; (c) the real builder-harm vector is a wrong deadline: a mis-calculated pay-less notice date can cost a subcontractor the whole application, so the calculator must be professionally reviewed, jurisdiction- and contract-specific and versioned, never a universal 'Construction Act deadline' (M4-19; D06 currently defers this); (d) an interaction with the fixed shadow-bill rule: on commercial contracts variations are often time-barred if not notified (NEC compensation-event notification, JCT notice provisions), so an extra held hidden until final lock could be lost to the builder outright, making the shadow bill actively harmful; D13's 'legal or contractual duty to tell' and 'written agreement needed before the work proceeds' rules are the right home for a deterministic time-bar trigger that surfaces early and fee-free; (e) interim applications and stage invoices are issued before lock and must not vary with shadow signals (§14.3), and receipts before a catch line exists are never spread onto it (§14.8 rule 3), both already in the plan. With those safeguards a reasonable builder sees this as straightforwardly in their interest.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Flat monthly price per business (£29-£39) or bundled in Contractor; no per-job or per-live-job-month pricing. (2) Explicit boundary in terms and UI: notices, reminders, retention timers and release invoices are subscription features and never a JobGuard pursuit; a withheld-payment case is opened only by the builder after the D03 v2 preconditions; no auto-suggestion of the 10% path from a pay-less notice or a late retention. (3) Retention released on time or after a reminder is fee-free; only a builder-opened case after refusal can qualify. (4) M4-19 professional review of templates and deadline rules per jurisdiction/contract with source and version; residential-occupier exclusion enforced; every deadline shown with its basis; JobGuard never serves a notice itself. (5) Add a deterministic D13 must-surface trigger for contract types with variation-notification time bars so held signals surface early and fee-free before the bar, and state it in the add-on's terms. (6) Stage invoices and interim applications issued before lock are byte-identical with or without shadow signals (§14.3 test); deposits and stage receipts are never allocated to a later catch (§14.8). (7) D02/M4-21 VAT and DRC treatment reviewed before commercial invoicing; D06 amended for notices and retention before live use.
