(8) No 'paid on time, guaranteed' or unverified Payapps-style claims in marketing.

revised_revenue.solo: £0-£35 (flat variant only; per-job variant dropped)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £140-£350 (flat; prefer retention bundled rather than a separate £9 add-on)

verdicts.key_risk: The line between subscription features and the 10% category: if a notice, reminder or retention timer ever slides a builder into a fee, or a hidden extra is lost to a contractual notification time bar because JobGuard held it until lock, the builder will see JobGuard profiting from its own silence.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation succeeds. Variant B is a price rise pegged to the builder's outcomes, not to JobGuard's costs. Dual-entitlement research (report section 'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk'; raw notes success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp, fairness section) finds cost-justified rises fair and advantage-taking unfair, and the idea itself concedes value-pegged rises are untested. Its trigger ('tracked + recovered >= 20x subscription') counts the builder's own fee-free captures (BUILD_PLAN 14.2) and JobGuard-found recoveries that the 10% already paid for, so it charges twice for the same events and contradicts the idea's own rule never to cite catches as justification. It penalises engagement: the builder who logs most pays more, the builder who logs least is told their price is frozen, and it creates a small incentive to log less, which starves the watchdog of the captures it needs. Variant A is opt-in and declining changes nothing, but its only distinctive element is indexing an upgrade pitch to the value receipt. If the builder needs more live-job capacity, the cap prompt already in the plan covers it (report 'Charge for live jobs, not people'; M4-14). If they do not, '£X of value, so upgrade' offers nothing they need and reads as cashing in the reciprocity the value receipt was meant to earn honestly (Buell & Norton, cited in the report). It also turns the SV-6 value receipt from a trust artefact into a sales lever, and the report's premium signal is steady prices with no gimmicks (Recommendation, 'Where premium should show'). Ordinary cost-justified, uniform, notified price changes under D09 v2 remain available and are not this idea.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as specified. What would survive is not this idea and carries no revenue attributable to it: (a) capacity-triggered upgrade prompts only when a builder reaches the live-jobs allowance, with numbers shown and decline changing nothing (already in plan); (b) cost-justified, uniform price changes under D09 v2 with 30 days' notice and grandfathering, never conditioned on any builder's tracked or recovered value; (c) the value receipt is never attached to a price ask.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected; the idea's +£18–£72 is not earned)

verdicts.key_risk: 'You did well, so we charge more' is read as exploiting an information advantage, and it corrodes the credibility of the value receipt JobGuard needs builders to trust.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation fails on the core. The builder gets a genuinely free first live job with the watchdog and final check, quoting stays free forever (AGENTS 5.10), and the card ask lands at the moment they commit a won job to JobGuard. The report recommends exactly this ('Let the trial run until the first job is live'; Recommendation, 'The trial'), and Qted (3 months free with card) and ServiceM8 (30 free jobs) are live precedents. Charging the success fee normally on the free job is fair: under BUILD_PLAN 14.6 a fee arises only from a lock the builder declared, evidence dated before it, a catch the builder confirmed, and cash the customer paid; a fee-free first job would teach that the fee is negotiable, which the report warns against. Nothing is withheld, no supplier money, no effect on the builder's customer. The residual fairness risks are all the subscription-trap pattern, not the fee: a silent conversion when the waiver ends, an ambiguous end-of-waiver rule, a card on file treated as standing authority for fees, or non-payment locking the builder out of their own records. Each is fixable and listed below. The conversion evidence (ChartMogul 25–35% vs 4–6%) is B2B SaaS, not tradespeople, so whether the card ask helps or hurts sign-ups is unknown; that is a JobGuard-side risk, not a builder harm.
verdicts.conditions: 1. The switch-live screen states in one sentence when the free period ends (the first live job is locked or 90 days from first switch-live, whichever comes first; a second live job during the window starts the plan with notice) and the price that then applies. 2. A reminder at least 7 days before the first charge and on the day the waiver ends; one-tap cancel with no penalty and no loss of access to existing job data or the final account. 3. The captured card authorises only the bounded subscription renewal under D05; success-fee statements keep per-statement approval; the screen says so. 4. The fee illustration and the D13 final-check disclosure are shown before card capture, not after. 5. Non-payment after the waiver may pause the watchdog on live jobs with notice but never blocks reading, exporting or invoicing existing jobs. 6. A/B test card-at-switch-live against no-card before adopting it as default (report Recommendation). 7. Only after G4, D09 v2 and D05; pilot_no_charge is unaffected.

revised_revenue.solo: Unchanged: £290 year 1 per convert; ~£21 → ~£52 expected per free quoter if conversion rises 6% → 15% (conversion effect untested for tradespeople)
revised_revenue.small_firm: Unchanged: £590 year 1 per convert; ~£42 → ~£106 per quoter
revised_revenue.firm: Unchanged: £1,190 year 1 per convert; ~£86 → ~£214 per quoter

verdicts.key_risk: A sceptic asked for a card before seeing value bounces, and any silent or ambiguous conversion at the end of the waiver reads as a subscription trap in a word-of-mouth trade.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation fails. This is an opt-in convenience for owners who already run two legitimate entities (Ltd plus sole-trader/CIS entity, a sister company): one login, consolidated view, shared rate book and a pooled live-job allowance at parent plus £49 per extra entity. No supplier money, nothing withheld, no effect on the builder's customers. Pooled pricing never below the sum of the tiers it replaces means the owner pays for convenience rather than saving money, which is fair as long as two separate accounts remain allowed and the pricing page says so. The only trust exposure is data. The cross-tenant read is a deliberate hole in the AGENTS 5.1 isolation every other builder relies on, so the harm to refute is a sister entity, a JV partner or a departed co-owner seeing another entity's rate book, margins or, worst of all, shadow signals. The JV case fails that test: two different controllers with one 'owner login' cannot both be entitled to the other's job data, so JVs should be out of scope. With same-controller linkage and a reviewed, group-scoped projection that carries only what the owner can already see in each entity, a reasonable builder sees this as fair and useful. Revenue is small at every archetype (Payaca 'multi-entity' is the only trade precedent found, raw notes uk_trade_job_software).
verdicts.conditions: 1. Linkage only where the same verified natural person(s) hold owner-level membership in every entity, re-checked on every group read; JVs and third-party partners out of scope. 2. The cross-tenant path is one reviewed control-plane construct (tenant_group) materialised by a worker into group-scoped rows with their own RLS; it never joins shadow tables, in-progress fee derivations, raw evidence or customer personal data; per-entity RLS and FORCE RLS are unchanged; independent adversarial tests under AGENTS 5.1. 3. Success fees, locks, cases and customer invoices stay per entity; only the live-job allowance and reporting are pooled. 4. Any entity can be unlinked by its own owner at any time and drops out of the projection immediately. 5. The pricing page states the group account is optional, that separate accounts remain available, and names the single paying legal entity for the VAT invoice (D02). 6. Mandatory security review before enabling.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (unchanged)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £59 (unchanged; assumes 10% of small firms have a second entity)
revised_revenue.firm: £265 (unchanged; assumes 30% of firms with 1.5 extra entities)

verdicts.key_risk: The cross-tenant projection is a designed exception to the tenant boundary every builder trusts; a JV or ex-partner leak would be a headline trust failure for tiny revenue.

verdicts.reasons: This is the strongest prevention idea under the trust lens and the refutation mostly fails, but only with the safeguards, and it moves the founder's 'prevented spend earns nothing' line at the margin, so it needs an explicit D03 v3 decision rather than being assumed. Why fair: JobGuard visibly does work the builder cannot easily do (three-way matching against agreed rates, GRNs and duplicates, which the report names as the case where builders accept a fee, section 'The hidden final check'); the flag is shown immediately in the Decision Inbox, so nothing is withheld; the reduction is proved by the supplier's own credit note or reissued invoice, not JobGuard's estimate; the builder confirms each catch as 'corrected as flagged' and can decline at no cost; suppliers pay nothing, so the watchdog stays independent. Where the refutation bites: (a) the counterfactual is still unprovable for duplicates and obvious errors the builder would have caught on the statement, so the per-catch confirmation is the valve that lets the builder say 'I had that' and pay nothing; (b) a £10 floor on a £25–£99 correction is a 10–40% rate, the same 'penalty on small honest recoveries' objection as I16 and inconsistent with one rate everywhere; (c) the taxi-meter effect (Prelec & Loewenstein, raw notes) unless rolled into one monthly line and capped; (d) JobGuard now earns from supplier errors, so over-flagging harms the builder's merchant relationship and must be bounded by the M2-5 held-out precision gate and deterministic rule types only; (e) nagging for uploads to realise fees would be a UX harm. A percentage variant tuned for fee income would be the watchdog policing for profit; a small flat fee with a monthly cap keeps it a service charge.
verdicts.conditions: 1. New D03 v3 category supplier_overcharge_corrected_pre_payment approved by the founder as a deliberate, narrow exception to 'prevention earns nothing'; D01 v4 rate; D02; G4. 2. Sequence enforced by immutable records: cited discrepancy Decision from deterministic detector types only (price above agreed rate, quantity above GRN, duplicate, pack-unit) → builder resolves 'disputing with supplier' → supplier credit note or reissued invoice arrives via intake with hash and object version, human-matched to the same supplier, invoice and line → builder confirms 'corrected as flagged'. Any missing step, no fee. 3. Effective fee never exceeds 10% of the documented net reduction: flat £10 only when the reduction is at least £100, or 5% with no floor; one labelled monthly statement line; monthly cap (£40 flat, £250 percentage); per-statement approval under D05. 4. Never stacked with the 10% cash-refund or applied-credit category for the same line: one derivation identity shared across I12, I13 and cash refunds. 5. Wording factual ('line 3 was £180 above your agreed rate; Supplier X issued credit note C567'); never 'saved you'. 6. Detector thresholds are versioned pure functions identical for fee and no-fee tenants; the M2-5 held-out precision gate must pass before enabling; a D11 signal flags corrections that exceed flagged deltas. 7. One factual follow-up on an open Decision, no repeated prompts; a Decision with no correction uploaded closes quietly and is fee-free. 8. Offered as an alternative to I08, never stacked; disclosed in the M4-13 agreement before any catch.

revised_revenue.solo: £20–£40 (assumption: the ≤10%-of-correction rule removes floor income on sub-£100 corrections; deterministic-only flags and per-catch opt-out; 5% variant at the low end)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £80–£160 (same assumptions; materials 37.5% of turnover, ~one correction per £10k spend, 70% uploaded)
revised_revenue.firm: £200–£350 (same assumptions; upload adoption remains the real driver; no UK small-builder error-rate data exists)

verdicts.key_risk: Nickel-and-diming on small catches and a fee-driven incentive to over-flag would turn the invoice watchdog from a service the builder trusts into a meter the builder resents; the rate cap and deterministic-only flags are what prevent it.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation fails. The builder had already paid an overcharge JobGuard flagged, opened a case and approved fee terms; the supplier's credit was consumed against a later invoice the builder paid in full, so the builder is economically in the same position as after a cash refund. Treating the two settlement forms alike is consistent, and a reasonable builder would find the opposite odd. Suppliers pay nothing, nothing is withheld, and D03 already anticipates this extension ('applied credits remain excluded until an approved extension'; BUILD_PLAN 14.7). Where the refutation bites: (a) '10% for noticing' is answered because the flag must be JobGuard-originated and the case builder-opened before pursuit, so the builder chose the fee; (b) the fee can land months after the catch when the credit is finally applied, which feels like an isolated loss (report, 'How the fee is charged matters too'); (c) the applied fact must come from hashed supplier documents, never builder attestation, and the builder must be able to say the credit is unrelated; (d) double counting with cash refunds or with I12 must be structurally impossible. The idea's own conclusion holds: small money at every archetype, so the safeguards cost little.
verdicts.conditions: 1. D03 v3 adds applied credits with evidentiary sufficiency: the credit note and the later paid invoice or supplier statement both via intake with hashes and object versions; the 'later invoice paid' fact from M4-7/M4-8. 2. Only credits linked to a JobGuard-flagged overcharge inside a builder-opened case with approved terms; a credit the builder marks as unrelated or as a negotiated discount is excluded (builder-favourable). 3. Unique derivation identity per (case, credit note, applied invoice) shared with the cash category and I12; unapplied credits and pre-payment reductions never qualify; a reversed credit triggers linked compensation. 4. Fee shown on the same screen as the applied-credit fact ('£X credit applied; JobGuard £Y; yours £Z') and billed on the next statement, not weeks later. 5. Ordinary 10% only; G4; D01/D02.

revised_revenue.solo: £5–£17 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: A credit that was really a negotiated discount or price cut being counted as a JobGuard recovery; the case linkage and builder-favourable exclusion are what keep this honest.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation fails for the 10% variant and succeeds for the 50% variant. Statutory interest (base + 8%) and fixed compensation (£40/£70/£100) are money a business debtor legally owes the builder that most builders never claim (raw notes success_fee_benchmarks, section 3). JobGuard computes it from server-held dates with a versioned pure function, drafts the lines, the builder approves every send (D10), and a fee arises only from sums actually paid and allocated. That is 'found money' in the sense the research says builders accept; nothing is withheld, no supplier money, and the builder keeps 90%. The 50% variant fails fairness: the same case already pays 10% on principal, and taking half of a legal entitlement for a calculation reads as double-dipping at no-win-no-fee levels and breaks 'one rate everywhere'. Real builder harms to guard against: (a) customer relationship, since many builders waive interest to keep main contractors sweet, so any nudge or default-on line pushes the builder into a relational cost JobGuard does not bear; (b) misclassifying a homeowner as a business would put an unlawful demand in the builder's name (the Act is B2B only); (c) adding interest to a debt disputed on substance inflames the dispute; (d) the builder's own contract terms may displace the statutory rate. All fixable by conditions.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Ordinary 10% only; the 50% variant is rejected. D03 v3 defines interest and compensation as a separate qualifying line type (not 'net principal'); VAT treatment per D02 (outside scope); legal sign-off that this is not regulated debt collection. 2. Lines are proposed, never auto-added: the builder sees the arithmetic and can remove them with one tap before approving the demand; declining is never a D11 signal and never triggers 'you're leaving £X' messaging. 3. Counterparty type is a builder-attested fact confirmed at case opening with a plain explanation; consumer and ambiguous counterparties (private landlords, sole-trader customers, mixed use) are hard-blocked; reclassification is a D06/D11 review signal. 4. No interest lines on a debt the customer has disputed on substance unless the builder explicitly overrides. 5. Base rate as a dated fact; issue, due and settlement dates are server facts from immutable invoice and M4-7 records. 6. Where the builder's own terms specify interest, those govern, not the Act. 7. Fee only on interest and compensation cash allocated under M4-8; the 10% on principal is untouched.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£6 (assumptions: 10% variant only; B2B share 10%; 45% paid late; ~60 days at ~12.5%; ~30% of late B2B invoices become an opened case; ~50% of claimed statutory sums paid)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £10–£30 (same assumptions; B2B share 30%; the idea's upper figures assumed the 50% variant)

verdicts.key_risk: Pressure to add interest, or a mis-typed consumer counterparty, puts an unlawful or relationship-damaging demand in the builder's name; opt-in per demand and a hard consumer block are essential.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation fails narrowly. Retention is the trade's most resented leak and this mirrors the founder's fixed withheld-payment test: release date passed, the builder's own application ignored, a case opened with fee terms, only cash after opening counts. The builder chose the fee, JobGuard does visible dated work (ledger, Decision, drafted release application), the counterparty is a business paying nothing to JobGuard, and on-time releases attract nothing. Where the refutation bites: (a) 'I'd have chased it anyway' is true for many, so the ignored-reminder and post-opening-cash tests are load-bearing, not decorative; (b) the shadow-like temptation to delay the reminder so a case can ripen, which the idea itself names, must be structurally impossible, and the ordinary chase must be free; (c) relationship cost with a main contractor who gives repeat work, so JobGuard must not pressure; (d) 5% versus 10%: one rate everywhere means 10%, and at 10% of a £3,000 retention the builder must feel the chase was real, which case consent secures; (e) Construction Act notice mechanics are complex and D06 currently forbids automating retention, so this is late M4 with legally reviewed templates; (f) the runway claim (a retention ban with a two-year transition) and the 44% unrecovered-retention statistic are not in the research notes and must be verified before sizing or marketing.
verdicts.conditions: 1. D03 v3 category applying the withheld-payment entry test to retention: declared release date passed, the builder's own application or reminder sent and ignored beyond an approved threshold, explicit case with fee terms, only bank-verified cash settled after opening (M4-7/M4-8). 2. Release-date Decisions and the free reminder are a versioned pure function of the declared dates, tested to fire on the earliest date; no code path may defer a reminder. 3. Ordinary 10% only; drop the 5% variant. 4. Factual Decision wording; no 'open a case' nudging beyond the Decision; declining is never a D11 signal. 5. Residential occupiers and any counterparty outside the Construction Act excluded; D06 revised and M4-19 templates legally reviewed before any real send; confirm this is not FCA debt collection. 6. Retention paid outside JobGuard or before case opening stays non-billable. 7. Verify the retention-ban runway and the unrecovered-retention statistic before sizing or marketing.

revised_revenue.solo: £5–£10 (10% only; unchanged assumptions)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£750 (10% only; almost entirely Firm tier; runway unverified)

verdicts.key_risk: Any suspicion that JobGuard sat on a release reminder so it could take 10% would repeat the shadow-bill betrayal risk in the segment with the most repeat-work relationships to lose.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation succeeds. The founder fixed 10%, and the report says keep one rate on every plan and that 10% already sits at the floor of the benchmarks; raising it moves JobGuard toward the claims-management sector whose 15–30% bands the FCA capped (report, 'No rival sells a final check...' and Recommendation, 'The 10% fee'). A 15% band on the first £1,000 or a £25 floor hits exactly the small honest recoveries the report says JobGuard uniquely makes economic (£50–£300 on £500–£3,000 catches): £25 on a £60 catch is 42% and reads as a penalty, and it charges the builder more precisely where the sum is too small to argue about, which is textbook advantage-taking under dual entitlement. Structurally it creates a JobGuard-side incentive not to coalesce signals so more recoveries sit in the higher band, in direct conflict with BUILD_PLAN 14.10 (one economic recovery per work item) and 14.2 (builder-favourable matching). It reopens a fixed decision for tiny money (+£13 to +£290 a year) and the idea itself is listed for completeness only.
verdicts.conditions: None; rejected. The fee stays 10% flat, uncapped, with a single derivation per coalesced work item. Small catches are handled by billing them on the same statement as larger ones, not by raising the rate.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected)

verdicts.key_risk: A higher rate on small sums is read as exploiting the builder's indifference threshold and gives JobGuard a fee-driven reason to under-coalesce, the exact conflict of interest the shadow-bill rules exist to exclude.

verdicts.reasons: The meter works as a capacity proxy and the price points are at market: ServiceM8 charges £25/£59/£119 by jobs with unlimited users (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'; §Recommendation). What does not hold is the idea's own £348/£708/£1,428, which assumes a builder's average live count equals the billing-month peak. My simulation (assumptions: Poisson arrivals at 18.75 jobs/yr for the Solo, ~7 weeks live per job ±35%, lock 0–3 weeks after practical completion) has a Solo averaging 2.6 live jobs exceed a peak-of-3 allowance in ~46% of months, rising to ~65% with a 3-week lock lag, because 'live until lock' measures the builder's admin discipline rather than workload. Small firm (avg 6.3, peak 7.4 vs 10) and Firm (avg 15.4, peak 16.7 vs 25) are safe. So Solo ≤3 on peak metering is a £59 plan with a £29 headline, for the cohort with 29% software adoption and a second compulsory MTD subscription (report §'Builders' willingness to pay'), and it is precisely the running-meter feel the report warns against (§'The hidden final check', Prelec & Loewenstein). Job-size blindness is real and no meter rule fixes it (see I03); the success fee has to carry the top end. Honest scale: 100 mixed builders yield roughly £60–70k subscription ARR, a floor not a business, which is consistent with the report's 'the subscription has to pay its own way'. Build reality: M4-14 is marked 'optional; only if D09 v2 adopts active-job tiers', D09 v2 currently says only 'optional active-job or business-size tiers', and as written M4-14 sits behind M4-9→M4-10→M4-11→M4-12→M4-13 (fee derivation, invoices, Stripe sign-up, fee collection, terms). §14.18 lets subscription charging go live independently of fees, so the chain can be re-sequenced, but that is a plan change, not the '2–4 weeks once SV-4 lands' the idea claims. Gaming (delay switch-live, close without lock) is self-harming and already a D11 signal; peak counting on immutable events resists close-and-reopen.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Solo allowance ≥5, or meter on the average daily live count (or a 90th-percentile day) instead of the absolute peak; on my numbers Solo ≤5 with average-daily metering cuts over-limit months to ~20%. (2) D09 v2 must actually adopt live-job tiers with allowances, cancellation, notice and grandfathering before M4-14 is un-optioned; missing prices keep metering disabled per M4-14. (3) A visible live list showing the source switch-live/lock events and a one-tap explicit close with recorded reason, before any tier consequence exists. (4) One published sentence: 'a job counts as live until you complete its final account or close it', plus the note that a closed-without-lock job gets no final check. (5) Re-sequence M4-14 ahead of fee collection under §14.18 if subscriptions are to precede success fees. (6) Contractor is a qualification rule (>25 live, or any single accepted job over ~£250k) handled by a conversation, not a fourth meter.

revised_revenue.solo: £348 only if the Solo allowance is ≥5 or metering is average-daily; under peak-of-3 the realistic outcome is £550–£708 (forced Builder months or overage) with higher churn; first year ~£87 lower for the first-job trial
revised_revenue.small_firm: £708 (peak ~7.4 vs 10 allowance; ~3% lower blended if 15–20% take the annual plan)

verdicts.key_risk: Peak-of-3 metering on 'live until lock' makes the entry plan a coin-flip every month for solos, turning a flat £29 price into a running meter on the most price-anchored cohort.

verdicts.reasons: A fairness device, not a revenue line, and the charging half of it should not be built yet. Given I01's simulation, per-slot overage on a Solo ≤3 plan would bill 5–8 months a year at £8 (£40–£64), and the whole-month-step variant would bill £30 × 5–8 = £150–£240 for a single day's overlap, i.e. a doubled bill. Both are running meters on the cohort that most prefers flat prices (report §'The hidden final check': Prelec & Loewenstein, Lambrecht & Skiera). ServiceM8's 15p extra job is ~0.06% of its Premium Plus price; £8 is 28% of Solo, so the precedent does not transfer. D05 v1 authorises only 'defined renewals' under separately accepted bounded terms; a variable overage needs a D05/D09 addition for a bounded variable amount. M4-14's own acceptance already says an over-limit 'raises the required Decision or enforces the agreed limit; it does not silently change price/tier', so 'never block switch-live + Decision + next-period upgrade proposal' is in the plan at no extra build; the overage charge is the increment, and it is what the report advises against (§'Charge for live jobs, not people': 'suggest upgrading next month rather than blocking'). Gaming risk is nil; the reverse risk (a stale live job billed as overage) is the trust problem.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Ship 'never block, raise a Decision, propose the upgrade next period' first; it is already M4-14 acceptance. (2) No overage charging until at least six months of metering data show how often peaks exceed allowances after I01's allowance fix. (3) If introduced: per-slot only, never whole-month step; capped at the upgrade delta; first overage in any 12 months free; only on jobs visible in the live list with close. (4) D05 v2 bounded variable-amount authority approved before any pre-approved overage; otherwise each overage is its own Decision. (5) A live job with no activity since it became lock-eligible prompts 'close or keep?' rather than a charge.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 in year one (deferred); ≈ £0–£40 if introduced later after the allowance fix

verdicts.key_risk: Charging a metered top-up on a job the builder considers finished, which converts a £29 fairness device into a word-of-mouth complaint.

verdicts.reasons: In-archetype revenue is £0 by the idea's numbers and mine. The tail it targets (a £1.2m firm running three £400k jobs on Solo) moves from £29 to £59 under ×3 weights, £360/yr, still a giveaway, so it does not fix job-size blindness; it only adds a second number to the one the report says the comparison should rest on (§'Three tiers work because people pick the middle'). It is value metering by the back door, which the founder rejected as the primary meter, and builders will read 'my big job counts double' as exactly that. The half-weight for small jobs cuts revenue from many-small-jobs builders and further reduces Solo tier pressure that I01 already needs to relax. Requires D09 v2 to define and defend thresholds and weights with no precedent in trade software (the idea concedes Procore/Buildertrend volume pricing is the rejected model). accepted_net_value excludes variations, so a cost-plus or provisional-sum job with a low base and large variations weights light: normal practice, not gaming, but it makes the weight arbitrary.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a meter rule. If pilot data show firms parking very large jobs on Solo, use a Contractor qualification rule (any single accepted job over ~£250k, or >25 live) handled by a sales conversation, and rely on the success fee for top-end value, as I01 already states.

revised_revenue.firm: £0 (tail: +£360/yr from a firm that belongs on Contractor anyway)

verdicts.key_risk: Reintroduces visible value pricing for zero typical revenue and hands the D09 approver a second metric to define.

verdicts.reasons: Revenue ≈ £0 for every archetype (12/50/150 documents a month against 40/150/500 allowances; my assumptions agree). A document meter runs directly against the fee model: every supplier document a builder rations to stay under allowance is a lost supplier-overcharge signal and a lost shadow-bill source (§14.2 treats supplier documents and purchase orders as evidence). Dext is not a comparable: documents are Dext's product, whereas here they are JobGuard's raw material and the economics improve with volume. It adds a third number to the pricing page (report §'Three tiers work': one or two numbers) and a running meter (§'The hidden final check'). Build cost is a second meter in M4-14 from M2-2 intake events, rebuildable counters, statement lines and D09 v3 terms, for nothing. The labour-illusion benefit the idea cites (Buell & Norton, report §'The hidden final check') is real but needs no charge.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a meter. Keep only the labour-illusion element: an unmetered 'documents checked this month' line on the SV-6 value receipt, labelled as effort and never as savings (§14.1 forbidden claims). If intake cost per tenant ever becomes material, handle it with a fair-use notice, not a price.

revised_revenue.firm: £0 (outliers only, and each withheld document costs fee-side evidence)

verdicts.key_risk: Any document allowance teaches builders to forward less, starving the detectors that carry the 10%.

verdicts.reasons: Direct revenue is ~£0 and the idea says so; the retention estimate stacks three untested assumptions (30% pause × 12% would cancel × 50% never return), and the report labels the winter pause 'not tested' (§'Offer annual billing, don't force it'). Reworked with my own assumptions (20% of solos hit zero live jobs for two months, 40% of those would otherwise cancel, half never return, a pause halves the loss) the retained value is ≈ £10–£15/yr per Solo; Small firm and Firm rarely reach zero live jobs (simulated Small firm average 6.3 live). A priced Dormant tier at £5–£9 is worse than what JobGuard already has: quoting is free forever, so zero live jobs is by definition the free layer, and the reverse-trial design already places the card at switch-live (report §'Let the trial run until the first job is live'). 'Pause on request' while jobs are live switches off the watchdog and the lock path, which starves the final check; reject that variant. Build is genuinely small: M4-13 already lists subscription pauses in its acceptance and D09 v2 already asks for 'any trial or free period'.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Implement as the free layer (£0, data retained, quoting on, no watchdog because no jobs are live), not a £5–£9 SKU. (2) Reactivation only through switch-live under the existing bounded D05 authority; no silent re-billing. (3) No pause while jobs are live; the only way to stop paying with live jobs is to lock or close them, and the screen says jobs closed without a lock get no final check. (4) Instrument pause and return in §14.17 pilot measurement before claiming any churn effect.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct; ~£10–£15/yr retained on stacked, unmeasured assumptions

verdicts.key_risk: Building a paid dormant state that duplicates the free quoting layer, or letting 'pause on request' switch the watchdog off on live jobs.

verdicts.reasons: Standard, expected and cheap: YourTradebase, Powered Now and Joist all show 'two months free' (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45'). But it is not a revenue idea. Per-builder revenue falls £58/£118/£238 for those who take it; at 15–20% take-up the blended effect is about −£10/−£20/−£40 per builder per year, bought with cash timing and a churn effect the report says 'has no traceable data' and is confounded by self-selection (§'Offer annual billing, don't force it'). For JobGuard, job continuity and the free layer do the retention job better than lock-in. Year-one risk: an annual Solo who stops at month four becomes a refund dispute in a word-of-mouth trade (raw notes: 'refund disputes, resentment could be large'). Annual plus a live-jobs meter needs pro-rated mid-year upgrades in M4-13/M4-14 and credit notes in M4-10, small but real; D02 fixes the VAT point at invoice date. Comparable: Site Samurai 17% annual; the market norm is 15–20%.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Monthly first (M4-11 'first-period payment'); add annual only after at least six months of monthly churn data so the discount is not handed to builders who would have paid monthly. (2) Offered, never default; no deeper introductory discounts (report §Recommendation: avoid Fergus-style 75% off). (3) Pro-rata upgrade and no-refund-on-downgrade rules written into D09 v2. (4) A plain early-cancellation refund rule approved with D09 so a dispute has an answer.

revised_revenue.solo: £290 when taken; blended ≈ −£10/yr versus monthly
revised_revenue.firm: £1,190 when taken; blended ≈ −£40/yr; cash arrives ten months earlier for the 15–20% who take it

verdicts.key_risk: Paying a 17% discount for retention JobGuard would mostly have had anyway, plus year-one refund disputes before the product has proved itself.

verdicts.reasons: The strongest positioning idea in the set and the least priceable today. The revenue case rests entirely on an unsupported price uplift ('held £10–£30/month higher than otherwise'); the report finds the price-quality signal small and weakest for services (§'The founder's price-signals-quality hunch is true but small'), and the raw notes record no quantitative SaaS evidence on money-back guarantees. Strip the uplift and the guarantee is a pure cost: on my assumptions (year-one detection immature; 25% of Builder-tier firms below 3 × £708 = £2,124 documented value; half claim; 50% credit) it costs ≈ −£44 per Small firm and −£71 per Firm; with a £10/month uplift that holds, +£76 and +£49. Sign uncertain, expected ≈ £0. The definitional problem is worse than the arithmetic: the report's confidence table rates how much builders lose to unbilled extras and supplier errors as Unknown, so N cannot be set from evidence; and the ledger must count 'flagged', not 'saved' (§14.1 forbidden claims), which blunts the headline. The idea's gaming rule ('dismissals never reduce the ledger') contradicts itself: counting a finding the builder rejected as 'value delivered' is exactly the unfairness Kahneman and Xia predict builders punish (report §'The hidden final check'). Activity conditions (minimum documents, accounts locked) read as small print. Build is late: SV-6 value receipt sits after SV-5 → SV-3/SV-4 → SV-2 → SV-1, plus M4-10 credit notes and a claim workflow. Comparables (Chargeflow 4x ROI, BigChange £5-per-£1) are marketing claims from vendors with years of outcome data.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Not before 12 months of §14.17 pilot measurement of documented value per tier; set N from the observed 10th–20th percentile, not a marketing number. (2) 'Documented' means builder-confirmed only; dismissed findings are excluded, and the under-use gaming is accepted because payout is capped at one year's subscription. (3) No list-price uplift until a priced sign-up test (report §Recommendation: £29 vs £39). (4) One-sentence terms, at most one activity condition (final accounts locked), a 12-month claim window, credit note via M4-10 against subscription only, never against a success fee. (5) Legal confirmation it is a refund warranty, not insurance. (6) Wording passes §14.1: 'documented catches or your subscription back', never 'savings'.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (excluded)
revised_revenue.small_firm: −£45 to +£75 depending on whether a £10/month uplift holds; expected ≈ £0 in year one

verdicts.key_risk: Writing the guarantee before the value ledger has data, so it either pays out widely while detection is immature or carries conditions that read as a trick.

verdicts.reasons: The tier-gate form fails on its own premise: a Solo tier without the watchdog is a £29 quoting app in a market where quoting is free (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45': Checkatrade's free tool, TradeMore, VoxTrade £15, Qted £29), and 'profit watchdog' is the product. Gating readiness warnings, proof-before-cover and the Decision Inbox on tier would also break the M1 core loop (AGENTS.md §6 lists the Inbox and verified proof in the loop), so only merchant-document intake, extraction and matching (M2-2..M2-5) can honestly be gated. Revenue rework: the +£144 figure assumes a £30/month tier step at 40% attach, double Tradify's £10 Lite→Plus delta for SmartRead (§'No rival sells a final check'); at a market-comparable +£15 add-on and 25–35% attach, expected Solo revenue is ≈ £45–£63/yr, and the extraction cost saved on non-buyers is ~£15–£25/yr per Solo (assumption: ~12 documents a month at £0.10–£0.15), so the net is ~£30–£50/yr for a third number on the pricing page. Small firm and Firm: £0 (in tier). Fee-side money cost is small (Solo supplier refunds at 10% of ~£250–£300/yr ≈ £30) but the integrity condition is severe: if Solo supplier documents are accepted as 'evidence' but 'not checked on your plan', SV-3's supplier-item detector must be gated identically, or JobGuard would be analysing documents for its own fee while telling the builder it is not, the trust failure the report predicts (§'The hidden final check', Bohnet & Zeckhauser). The honest variant refuses supplier-document intake on Solo altogether, which also removes those documents from the shadow bill. No attach-rate evidence exists; the raw notes record no data on which tier trades customers choose.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Tier-gate form rejected; add-on form only, +£15 on Solo, deferred until pilot data show Solo supplier-document volume and detection yield. (2) Gate only M2-2..M2-5 merchant-document checking; never readiness, proof prompts, Inbox, variations, final account or the final check. (3) Without the add-on, intake refuses supplier documents with a plain message; no 'held but unchecked' evidence, and SV-3 supplier detectors gated identically. (4) Must-surface rules unaffected for anything JobGuard does hold. (5) Upgrade prompts count refused uploads only, never findings JobGuard withheld. (6) Pair with I07's guarantee only after I07's data condition is met.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈ £45–£63 gross (+£15/month at 25–35% attach), ≈ £30–£50 net of extraction cost saved

verdicts.key_risk: A Solo tier whose defining feature is switched off, one step from 'JobGuard held the document and said nothing' unless intake and shadow detection are gated together.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on three counts. (1) Variant A has nothing to sell: the founder's meter is live jobs, so 'the next tier' adds only job capacity. A Solo builder running 2-3 live jobs will not buy a 10-job plan because a receipt says they had value; the genuine over-limit upgrade prompt already exists as M4-14. The 20-30% acceptance assumption is a B2B-SaaS feature-tier number, not acceptance of capacity a builder does not need; 5% is generous. For Firm there is no next tier below 'Contractor, priced on request'. (2) Variant B earns exactly what a plain, unconditional annual review at the same first-digit steps would earn (+£24 / +£60 / +£120 a year) while adding a value gate, a subscription_terms version bound to a receipt hash, an anniversary worker and D09 v3 price-change/notice/grandfathering rules plus D05 (a tier change is a new authority). After 30-40% of subscribers never reach a second anniversary and only ~50% of Solo tenants clearing 20x subscription (£6,960 of tracked value), the mechanism yields £8-£80 per year-1 subscriber. (3) The fairness research the report relies on (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler dual entitlement and Xia et al., report section 'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk') says cost-justified rises are accepted and advantage-taking is not; a rise pegged to the builder's own tracked extras is the second kind, and 'tracked' value is the builder's own work, the exact attribution crux the report warns about. It also creates a builder-side gaming vector the idea misses: log fewer extras through JobGuard and the price stays frozen, a second reason (after the live-jobs meter, report section 'Charge for live jobs, not people') to keep work off the system, which starves the shadow bill and the detection base. Precedent: 5-10% SaaS uplift clauses exist without any value peg; no outcome-indexed subscription precedent exists, and the report notes value-based-pricing churn claims trace to marketing pages. Build is small, but it is small machinery for a policy that earns nothing a boring clause would not.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a value-indexed mechanism. The substitute is a standard D09 v3 clause: an annual review capped at the lesser of CPI+2% or the first-digit-preserving step, 30 days' notice, cancel without penalty, no value trigger and no 'we froze your price' messaging. Keep M4-14's over-limit upgrade prompt as the only tier move, and never cite JobGuard-found catches or the builder's own tracked extras as justification for any price change.

revised_revenue.solo: +£8-£18/yr per year-1 subscriber (B: £24 step x ~50% clearing 20x x ~65% year-2 retention; A: ~5% x £360 for capacity not needed)
revised_revenue.small_firm: +£36-£40/yr (B: £60 step x ~85% qualifying x ~70% retention; A ~5% x £720)
revised_revenue.firm: +£80/yr (B: £120 step x ~90% x ~75%; A has no next priced tier)

verdicts.key_risk: Reads as 'you did well so we charge more' and gives builders a reason to keep extras off JobGuard, for revenue a plain annual review clause delivers with none of the fairness exposure.

verdicts.reasons: Hard to refute on direction: this is the report's own recommendation (section 'Recommendation: £29, £59 and £119, a first-job trial and an unchanged 10%': watchdog and final account free on the first live job, ~90-day ceiling, card at switch-live, success fee charged normally). AGENTS 5.10 is preserved because nothing is charged until switch-live, which is already the explicit authorized boundary, and ServiceM8 (30 free jobs) and Qted (3 months free, card required) are UK precedents (report section 'UK builders already pay £25-£45 a month'). The refutation is on the number and the timing. ChartMogul's 25-35% card-required vs 4-6% no-card is B2B SaaS at $50-249 ARPA with sophisticated buyers (report section 'Let the trial run until the first job is live'); every mainstream UK trade tool (Tradify, Fergus, ServiceM8, YourTradebase, Powered Now, Jobber, Joist) runs 14-30 days with no card, and only 29% of one-person construction firms use any software, so a card ask is against the category norm for the most sceptical buyer group. The idea's 6%->15% is optimistic; 5%->10% of free quoters is defensible. The real cost is not lost sign-ups but lost switch-lives: the live-jobs meter and the shadow bill both depend on jobs going live, so a card wall at switch-live is a wall in front of the fee engine; a 30% drop in switch-lives would cost more fee base than the card gains in subscription, and the pilot cannot measure this because pilot_no_charge never asks for a card. Year-1 revenue per convert is nine paid months, not twelve. Gaming (keeping the first job live to stretch the waiver) is bounded by a 90-day server-time cap; the unaddressed leak is the builder who quotes free forever and never switches live, which Checkatrade's free quoting tool already normalises and a card does not fix. Build is small (wire M4-11 hosted subscription sign-up to the M1-7 switch-live command, D09 trial terms, D05 bounded renewal authority) but it is gated by G4 and D09/D05 approval, so A/B evidence arrives late.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Do not hard-block switch-live on card capture in the first release: ask at switch-live with 'skip for now' and require the card before the second live job or day 90, whichever comes first, so no live job (and no shadow-bill base) is lost to the card ask. (2) Run the report's priced sign-up test with card-at-switch-live vs deferred card as one arm and read switch-live rate, not only sign-up rate. (3) Waiver = first live job, up to 90 days from switch-live server time, once per tenant, written into D09 v3 trial terms with the D05 bounded renewal authority starting at waiver end; M4-14 metering treats the waived job per the approved inclusion rule. (4) The success fee applying to the free job is stated on the switch-live screen (D13 onboarding disclosure), never only in terms. (5) pilot_no_charge jobs stay exempt and can never be retro-billed; the M4-11 acceptance (verified provider outcome, not a redirect, records payment) applies unchanged.

revised_revenue.solo: £261 year 1 per convert (9 paid months at £29) plus the normal fee on the first job; ~£13 -> ~£26 expected per free quoter if conversion moves 5% -> 10%
revised_revenue.small_firm: £531 year 1 per convert; ~£27 -> ~£53 per free quoter
revised_revenue.firm: £1,071 year 1 per convert; ~£54 -> ~£107 per free quoter; downside: each 10% fall in switch-lives removes 10% of the shadow-bill and fee base

verdicts.key_risk: A card ask at the moment of commitment, against a no-card category norm, may cut switch-lives, and every lost switch-live also loses the 10% fee engine on that job.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on price structure and cost. At £49 per extra entity the add-on costs more than a second Solo account (£29), so a group owner with a small second entity (the typical Ltd plus sole-trader CIS vehicle) simply opens a second account; and 'pooled allowance never priced below the sum of the tiers it replaces' means pooling gives no price benefit at all, so the customer pays a premium purely for consolidated reporting and a shared rate book, which a 5-15 person builder will not value at £20+/month. The incremental revenue over 'two accounts' is therefore near zero; the only new money is from second entities that would not otherwise subscribe, which at Solo-level pricing is ~£35/yr for 10% of small firms and ~£160/yr for 30% of firms, i.e. £4-£50/yr averaged across the base. Against that the build is not medium: AGENTS 5.1 makes any cross-tenant read a change to the trust boundary (RLS, exports, caches, search, later sync projections), needing a control-plane tenant-group model, owner linkage, a separately credentialled read-only projection, M4-14 pooled metering and a mandatory security review; the plan already parks this class of work in M5-7/M5-8 (enterprise SSO, policy permissions, stronger isolation). The precedents (Payaca Enterprise multi-entity at £299-£3,199/mo, Procore volume pricing; report section 'UK builders already pay') are enterprise products, not the £25-£45 trade band, and Payaca's own listing puts multi-entity in its 100+ seat tier. Entity-splitting gaming is moot: per-business flat pricing already gives two Solo accounts (£58) no advantage over one Builder plan (£59).
verdicts.conditions: Rejected for M0-M4. Record as a discovered-later M5 item and revisit after M5-7/M5-8 only if at least 10% of paying Firm-tier tenants ask for it; price the extra entity at or below Solo, and build the cross-tenant projection as a separately credentialled, independently tested exception per AGENTS 5.1, never a shortcut through RLS.

revised_revenue.small_firm: £0-£35/yr (10% x one extra entity that would not otherwise subscribe, at <= £29/mo; ~£0 incremental over two separate accounts)
revised_revenue.firm: £50-£160/yr (30% x 1.5 entities at <= £29/mo; ~£0 incremental over separate accounts)

verdicts.key_risk: Opening a cross-tenant read path for £0-£160 a year per tenant is the wrong trade against the tenant-isolation invariant.

verdicts.reasons: This is the best-argued prevention fee on the list (the supplier's own credit note proves the correction and JobGuard's Decision provably preceded it) but it fails on money, on who controls the evidence, and on shape. Money: with materials at 37.5% of turnover (£56k / £225k / £750k), the idea's 0.75% documented-correction rate is far above the ~0.1% large-firm AP-audit recovery it cites, and it assumes corrections arrive as matched credit notes through intake; trade-counter and phone corrections usually show up only as a statement adjustment. At 0.3% and a £75 average correction the £10 floor dominates (the 'greater of 5% and £10' variant never bites above it), giving ~£20 / £90 / £300 a year before adoption; supplier-document capture is a premium feature elsewhere (Tradify Plus bill reader, Powered Now Premium; report section 'No rival sells a final check...'), so 30/50/70% upload rates cut it to roughly £6 / £45 / £210. Evidence control: the builder must upload the credit note and confirm 'corrected as flagged' in order to charge themselves £10; the rational builder does neither, so the fee self-selects toward zero, the same residual risk BUILD_PLAN 14.10 states for catches but at stakes nobody will contest. Shape: the report's mental-accounting evidence (section 'The hidden final check', Prelec & Loewenstein and Lambrecht & Skiera) says people prefer flat charges to a running meter, and a monthly statement of £10 lines is a meter. Precedent: Chargeflow's $29 per deflected chargeback is the only per-prevention fee found; PRGX/apexanalytix charge 20-30% post-payment only; ApprovalMax and Planyard sell matching as a tier feature. Build: M2-2 through M2-5 live and past the M2-5 held-out gate (FDP <= 5%, recall >= 90%), a D03 v3 category, D01 v4 rate/floor/cap, M4-9/M4-10 source type, an SV-6 card, then G4: 2-3 weeks of code plus three policy revisions for tens of pounds per tenant. The founder's 'prevented spend currently earns nothing' leaves the door open, but the value of pre-payment bill checking is captured the way every comparable product captures it: as the feature that justifies the Builder and Firm tiers.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a fee. Substitute: put supplier invoice/PO/GRN checking in the Builder and Firm tiers and show 'corrected before you paid' on the SV-6 value receipt with no charge and factual wording only. Re-open only if pilot_no_charge data show at least one documented correction per tenant per month at >= 50% supplier-document upload, and then only the flat £10 capped £40/month variant, offered instead of (never stacked on) tier gating, with the Decision required to precede the correction and VAT-only reissues excluded.

revised_revenue.solo: £5-£20/yr (~2 documented corrections x £10 floor x 30% upload rate)
revised_revenue.firm: £150-£300/yr (~30 corrections x £10 x 70%; flat capped variant <= £480)

verdicts.key_risk: The builder controls the evidence and pays for supplying it, so the fee collapses toward zero while the statement line still reads as a taxi meter.

verdicts.reasons: The logic is sound and the money is not. Sound: a credit consumed against a later invoice the builder then paid in full is economically a cash refund, and excluding it leaves a trivial loophole in the already-fixed cash-refund category (accept a credit note instead of cash and pay no fee), which is why BUILD_PLAN 14.7 and D03 v2 say 'excluded until D03 extends' rather than 'never'. Not: materials 37.5% of turnover (£56k / £225k / £750k), post-payment overcharges JobGuard actually flagged at ~0.3% of materials (the idea's 0.5% is above the AP-audit benchmark), ~65% settled by credit rather than cash, 30/50/70% supplier-document upload, and, the step the idea underweights, the builder must open a formal case with fee terms for what is typically a £50-£150 credit, which halves volume again. Qualifying principal is then roughly £20 / £110 / £500 a year, i.e. fees of ~£2 / £11 / £50, and each event needs a credit note, the later invoice, a supplier statement and an M4-7 bank fact matched and human-reviewed under M4-2 for a fee smaller than the review cost. The idea's own line, that supplier-overcharge fees are small money at any archetype, is right. The precedent (PRGX/apexanalytix contingency fees include credit memos taken) is enterprise AP at 20-30% on millions of spend. Trust fit is genuinely good: suppliers pay nothing so the watchdog stays clean, the builder had already lost the money, and a JobGuard-originated flag plus an explicit case answers '10% for noticing'. So the extension costs nothing in goodwill; it just cannot pay for its own pipeline.
verdicts.conditions: Keep only as wording inside the D03 v3 revision that other categories will need anyway: an applied credit qualifies when (a) the overcharge was a JobGuard-flagged Decision, (b) the builder opened the case with fee terms before the credit was issued, (c) the credit is shown applied on a later invoice settled in full per M4-7/M4-8 evidence (hashed supplier documents, never builder attestation), (d) net credit per case is >= £250, below which the case closes fee-free, and (e) a reversed credit triggers linked compensation. No supplier-statement ingestion or SV-7 connector work is justified by this alone; reuse the M4-8 allocation model with a 'credit applied against paid invoice' settlement fact and unique derivation identity per case line to prevent double counting with a cash refund.
verdicts.key_risk: Per-event verification (three matched documents plus a bank fact and human review) costs more than the £5-£15 fee it earns.

verdicts.reasons: The strongest fairness position on the list: sums the builder is legally owed under the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 and almost never claims, computed from server-held invoice and settlement dates, drafted by JobGuard, approved by the builder (D10: the builder sends) and charged only on cash allocated. The direct fee at the fixed 10% is nonetheless tiny. Rework: B2B share 10/30/50% of jobs, ~1.5-2 invoices per B2B job, ~12% of B2B invoices reaching the 14.7 entry test (overdue, builder's reminder ignored, case opened with terms), not the 40-50% 'paid late' figure, which counts every late payment; ~60 days at base+8% (~2% of principal) plus £40-£100 compensation; ~30% of claimed statutory sums actually paid, because main contractors routinely settle principal and ignore interest lines. That gives statutory sums recovered of ~£20 / £120 / £720 a year, so ~£2 / £12 / £72 at 10%. The 50% variant (~£10 / £60 / £360) is where the idea's £280-£850 comes from and should be dropped: two rates on one statement breaks the 'one rate everywhere' rule the report gives (section 'Three tiers work because people pick the middle'), 50% is the no-win-no-fee legal cap and claims-firm territory the report says to avoid (section 'Two legal points'), and taking half of a compensation entitlement reads as advantage-taking under dual entitlement. The real return is indirect: £70-£100 compensation plus interest offsets much of JobGuard's 10% on principal for a £5k-£25k B2B case (the raw benchmark note makes this point), which makes opening a withheld-payment case rational for the builder, and principal cases are the large-ticket category for firms (£2,500 fee on a £25k final balance). That effect is unmeasured, so it argues for a cheap build, not a revenue line. One design flaw must be fixed: under a 14.8-style pro-rata allocation a debtor who pays principal only would have part of the receipt deemed to interest/compensation lines, manufacturing a fee on money never paid as interest. Legal: on the SRA reading in the report, helping a builder collect its own invoices is not FCA debt collecting, but consumer counterparties are outside the Act and must be hard-blocked; VAT on interest and compensation is a D02 question. Precedent: Chaser adds statutory interest as a flat feature; GOV.UK late-payment data (£11bn a year, £26bn owed) is the safest marketing number in the report. Build: M4-1/M4-2 case types, M4-5 templates, M4-7/M4-8 allocation to statutory lines, a versioned pure function with base rate as a dated fact; 1-2 weeks plus D03 v3.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Ordinary 10% only, as two sources (principal; statutory sums); no 50% variant. (2) B2B counterparties only: counterparty type is a recorded fact, consumer or ambiguous cases are hard-blocked, and a change of type is a D06/D11 review signal; the lines are offered, never auto-added. (3) Statutory lines are allocated last: only an explicit remittance or a receipt exceeding principal can settle them, overriding pro-rata for these lines. (4) The builder can strip the lines from the demand with one action and nothing is charged. (5) Base rate is a dated fact per the Act's six-monthly reference dates in a versioned pure function, never model-derived. (6) D03 v3 wording that interest/compensation are a separate qualifying source, D02 treatment, legal sign-off on M4-5/M4-19 templates; no 'claims' language. (7) Build after M4-5 and M4-7/M4-8 land, not before, and measure case-opening rate with and without the lines in the pilot.

revised_revenue.solo: £0-£5/yr (~0.3 B2B cases; homeowners excluded by law)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £10-£15/yr at 10% (~1.3 cases; ~£60 only if a 50% share were adopted, which it should not be)
revised_revenue.firm: £50-£100/yr at 10% (~4 cases); unmeasured indirect upside of ~£1,000-£2,500/yr if compensation offsets lift withheld-payment case-opening by one £10k-£25k case a year

verdicts.key_risk: Direct revenue is tens of pounds; the value lies in making withheld-payment cases worth opening, and a pro-rata allocation bug could charge on interest the debtor never paid.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on segment, dependency and originality. Segment: retention exists only in the subcontract/commercial chain (residential occupiers are outside the Construction Act) and only on the part of commercial work run under a main contractor; assume 60% of commercial turnover (7/27/45% of turnover) at 5% retention, ~25% overdue at release and ~60% of that paid after a case opens: retained ~£300 / £4,900 / £27,000, overdue-and-recovered ~£45 / £730 / £4,000, fee at 10% ~£5 / £73 / £405 (the 5% variant halves it). It is a Firm-tier product for a business built around small builders talking through domestic jobs on site. Dependency: it sits at the end of M4-18 -> M4-19 -> M4-20 (interim applications, professionally reviewed construction notices, retention ledger with durable timers), the deepest late-M4 chain in the plan, and those tasks cannot be justified by a £200-£400/yr fee; if they are built it is because Firm-tier subscribers want what Payapps and Site Samurai already sell as flat features (report section 'No rival sells a final check...'; Site Samurai £99-£699/mo). Originality: a retention balance withheld past its release date after the builder's own reminder is ignored is a withheld customer payment; BUILD_PLAN 14.7 already covers it if the invoice concept extends to the release application, and M4-20 already says retention release goes through D03 attribution separately, so no new category or rate is needed. The 'I'd have chased it anyway' objection is stronger here than for a disputed final balance: the release date is a known contractual date and JobGuard's contribution is a reminder and a drafted application, which under the report's fairness framing (who did the work) invites resentment of a £500 cut on a £5k release. The BEIS/Pye Tait 44% figure and the Commercial Payments Bill runway are not verified in the material read; if the Bill does phase retention out, the category has a 3-4 year life. 10% is inside the 8-15% fresh-B2B-debt agency band (report benchmark table), so the rate itself is not the problem.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a distinct category and rate. When M4-20 exists, treat overdue retention as withheld_customer_payment under the existing 14.7 entry test (release date passed, builder's own reminder ignored, case explicitly opened with terms, cash settled after opening) at the ordinary 10%, with the ledger, timers and reminders free in the Firm tier and a structural rule that JobGuard never delays a reminder to let a case ripen. Verify the retention-loss statistic and the Bill's transition before any marketing claim.

revised_revenue.firm: £200-£400/yr (10% of ~£2,000-£4,000 overdue retention recovered after a case; 5% variant £100-£200)

verdicts.key_risk: Almost all revenue is Firm-tier, behind the longest M4 dependency chain, in a category the law may be phasing out.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted by the idea's own trust note and by the report. A £25 floor on a £60 catch is a 42% fee, above the FCA's 15-30% claims-management cap range; banded rates copy the claims-management fee structure the report says JobGuard must not resemble (section 'Two legal points'); and the report's tier guidance is that the 10% should be identical everywhere so it never blurs a comparison (section 'Three tiers work because people pick the middle'). It reopens a fixed founder decision (D01 v3 -> v4 and new 14.9 fixtures) for at most +£27 / +£105 / +£290 a year on the idea's own base case (3.3 / 4.2 / 5.8 paid catches at 2% of job value, 70% locked), and even that rests on the report's finding that no public data on recoverable value per job exists. It also builds an incentive against JobGuard's own integrity control: BUILD_PLAN 14.10 requires one economic recovery per coalesced work item, and a 15% band on the first £1,000 pays JobGuard to under-coalesce. On the demand side, a late-revealed small extra is billed to a homeowner as a consumer add-on the report flags as more disputed and harder to collect; a £25 floor guarantees builders dismiss £60-£250 catches as 'not chargeable', so the floor's revenue is closer to zero than the +£30 quoted, while the trust cost (10% at the floor of every benchmark is JobGuard's single most-cited fairness asset) is paid on every statement. The precedents (FCA CMC bands, Cosmo DCA £25-£75 file fee, Chargeflow $29) all come from sectors whose fee optics JobGuard is trying to escape. Build is small (generalise the v3 routine to bands and floors), which is the only point in its favour.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected outright. If small catches genuinely cost more to settle than they earn, the honest lever is a builder-facing de-minimis (for example, catches under £100 net are revealed and fee-free), which improves trust rather than penalising small honest recoveries.

revised_revenue.solo: +£0-£27/yr (band); ~£0 (floor, once builders dismiss small catches)
revised_revenue.firm: +£0-£290/yr (band); ~£0 (floor); net negative after any churn attributable to a two-rate statement

verdicts.key_risk: Trades the 'one modest rate' trust asset for a few hundred pounds a year and pays JobGuard to split recoveries.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutation fails; the meter is legally clear. Relationship: JobGuard-to-builder is B2B. A builder buying JobGuard 'for purposes relating to' its trade is a trader under Consumer Rights Act 2015 s.2, so CRA Part 2 unfair-terms control, the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 cooling-off, and both DMCC Act 2024 consumer chapters (unfair practices/drip pricing in force since April 2025; the subscription-contract chapter) do not apply between JobGuard and the builder (report §'The hidden final check'; research note on B2B scope). What does apply: UCTA 1977 s.3 (written standard terms must pass the reasonableness test for any clause limiting liability or letting JobGuard render 'substantially different' performance); Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 reg 3 and the CAP Code for B2B price claims (ex-VAT prices are allowed for business audiences if clearly stated); VAT Act 1994 with VAT Regs 1995 reg 90 (continuous supply of services, tax point per periodic invoice/payment) and reg 14 VAT-invoice particulars on the platform invoice; UK GDPR for staff user accounts (Art 13) and the D12 third-party-data question, which the meter does not change because concurrency events are job data, not personal data. FCA: a software subscription is not a regulated activity; collecting one's own fees via Stripe/GoCardless is not a payment service under PSRs 2017 and triggers no MLR 2017 registration; JobGuard never touches builder-customer money. One correction to the idea's 'B2B; no FCA' line: sole-trader and two-to-three-person partnership builders are 'individuals' under CCA 1974 s.189, and business credit under £25,000 is not exempt by amount (RAO art 60C), so monthly billing in arrears relies on the RAO art 60F trade-credit exemptions (no interest or charges for the deferral). That reliance, and any late-payment interest or admin fee in M4-16 dunning, needs a solicitor's confirmation under D05. The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 does apply to JobGuard's own invoices to builders (B2B), giving JobGuard statutory interest/compensation rights that should be bounded for trust reasons. HGCRA 1996/Scheme, CIS, domestic reverse charge, competition law, AML and claims-management rules are not engaged by a platform subscription. No appointed-representative or partner route is needed because nothing here is a regulated activity. Timeline/cost: one commercial-solicitor review of the subscription terms (meter definition, tier assignment, notice, grandfathering, suspension) alongside D09 v2/D05, roughly £3–8k and 2–4 weeks before G4; no regulatory application. None of this is certain legal advice; the consumer-credit and UCTA points are for a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Hygiene, not blockers: (1) define 'live job' (switch-live until lock or a recorded close) and the peak-per-period rule in the terms verbatim from the meter code; changes to prices, allowances or the meter are price changes requiring the D09 notice period (30 days suggested) and never apply mid-period. (2) Pricing page shows tier prices with '+VAT' visibly (CAP/BPMMRs); the platform invoice carries full VAT-invoice particulars plus period, tier, peak count and source events. (3) Suspension for non-payment preserves data access, export and DSAR handling (UK GDPR; M4-16 already requires this). (4) Solicitor confirms the arrears-billing trade-credit position for sole-trader builders under RAO art 60F and UCTA reasonableness of the standard terms. (5) D02 accounting review confirms per-period revenue recognition. Contractor 'on request' pricing needs a written quote each time so there is no undisclosed price.

revised_revenue.solo: £348 ex VAT (unchanged by the legal lens; a solo below the VAT registration threshold bears £417.60 cash cost, a willingness-to-pay point, not a legal one)

verdicts.key_risk: A sole-trader builder is an 'individual' for consumer-credit purposes, so any drift from clean pay-for-service billing into interest-bearing arrears charges or instalment plans would need FCA analysis; keep the subscription strictly a price for a service and get the art 60F reliance confirmed.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts: (a) Penalty doctrine — fails if drafted correctly. Under Cavendish v Makdessi / ParkingEye v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67 the rule bites only on secondary obligations triggered by breach; an extra-slot fee or a one-month band step is a primary price for additional usage, so it must be worded as a price ('each extra live job is £8 a month'), never as a charge for 'exceeding your limit'. (b) Misleading pricing — B2B, so DMCC drip-pricing is out, but BPMMRs 2008 reg 3 and the CAP Code apply: the tier price must state the allowance and overage rate up front, and 'cheaper than upgrading this month' must be arithmetically true on the screen that says it. (c) Unilateral variation — the auto-step is a pre-agreed formula, not a unilateral price change, so UCTA s.3(2)(b) is unlikely to bite provided the terms define it; a version where JobGuard chooses the shape after the fact is weaker. (d) The real cost is collection mechanics: a varying monthly amount collected by Direct Debit needs Bacs advance notice of the changed amount (GoCardless sends its notice 3 working days ahead), and card-scheme recurring-billing rules require notice of a changed amount (typically at least 7 days). 'Bill it on the next invoice' therefore needs a notice step in M4-13/M4-16, otherwise a valid debt can be reversed by a Direct Debit indemnity claim or card dispute. (e) Consumer credit — overage billed in arrears to a sole-trader 'individual' is trade credit; it stays inside RAO art 60F only with no interest or charge for the deferral (solicitor to confirm with D05). (f) D05 — a bounded standing authority capped at one tier step is the right shape; an over-limit without pre-approval raising a Decision while the job still goes live also protects JobGuard from a UCTA 'no performance' argument. No FCA permission and no AR or partner route needed. Cost: covered by the same terms review as I01 (£3–8k), plus engineering for notice-before-collect. Not certain legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Draft overage as a price for extra usage, never a breach charge; disclose allowance and overage rate on the pricing page and on the invoice line that cites the jobs; build advance notice before collecting a changed amount (Bacs/GoCardless and card-scheme rules); no interest or admin charge on the arrears line; a visible live-job list with one-tap recorded close before any overage bills; a disputed overage line is excluded from dunning (M4-16); choose one shape (per-slot or month-step) and record it in D09 v2 so the terms are deterministic; the standing authority is capped at one tier step and revocable.

revised_revenue.solo: £27–£60 (unchanged; billing may slip one cycle where a notice period is required)

verdicts.key_risk: Collecting a changed amount without the required advance notice: the debt is valid, but Direct Debit indemnity claims and card disputes would reverse it and cost trust; and wording the overage as a 'limit breach' invites a penalty-clause argument that a plain price never faces.

verdicts.reasons: No regulatory hook: weighting by frozen accepted_net_value is a contractual pricing formula between businesses. Refutation attempts: (a) Misleading headline — the only real legal exposure. A page saying 'Solo: up to 3 live jobs' while a £100k job counts double is a material pricing condition; under BPMMRs 2008 reg 3 and the CAP Code (misleading omissions), the weight table must appear beside the tier price, not only in the terms. (b) Unilateral variation — because the weight is fixed at switch-live and never re-weighted, JobGuard cannot be accused of moving the price mid-job (UCTA s.3(2)(b) comfort); later threshold changes are price changes needing D09 notice and must apply only to jobs switched live afterwards. (c) Data — accepted_net_value is the builder's commercial data, ex VAT per D02; not personal data, no DPIA element; it is frozen before any shadow signal exists, so it cannot leak the shadow bill. (d) The founder rejected turnover metering; there is no legal line between job-count and value metering, so the analogues source's objection is a product concern, not a legal one. (e) VAT, CIS, HGCRA, Late Payment Act, FCA, AML, competition law: not engaged. No AR or partner route needed. Cost: one paragraph in the same solicitor terms review; no separate timeline.
verdicts.conditions: Publish the weight table beside every tier price and print it on the invoice line ('2 slots: accepted value £120,000'); freeze the weight at switch-live and record the value used; threshold changes only prospectively with D09 notice; state in one sentence that JobGuard's findings never change the weight. No solicitor input beyond the general terms review.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts: (a) Usage metering as a hidden charge — B2B, so DMCC drip-pricing is out, but BPMMRs reg 3 and the CAP Code require the document allowance and the £0.40 rate on the pricing page and each invoice; 'documents checked' must describe an automated check and never imply human review or 'money saved' (§14.1 forbidden claims also apply). (b) Penalty doctrine — a per-document price is a primary obligation, not a penalty, if worded as a price. (c) UK GDPR — supplier documents contain third-party personal data (sole-trader suppliers' names, addresses, bank details); that processing already exists under M2-2 and needs D12's lawful basis and Article 14 route before real documents are processed at all (a G1 gate). The meter counts intake events and adds no new processing, so no new DPIA element, but the count must never be derived from shadow signals or it becomes a leak path (§5.14). (d) Consumer credit — overage billed in arrears to a sole-trader 'individual' relies on RAO art 60F as in I02: no interest or charges on the line. (e) Collection — variable-amount notice rules as in I02. (f) VAT — a standard-rated usage line on the same invoice, tax point per reg 90. (g) A £150/month overage for a Solo outlier is lawful, but capping overage at the next tier's price removes any penalty flavour and the BPMMR argument that the 'cheaper' plan was not cheaper. No FCA permission, no AR or partner route. Cost: absorbed in the terms review; the rebuildable counter is already an M4-14 requirement. Not certain legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Allowance and overage rate disclosed with the tier price; overage capped at the upgrade step or converted into a next-period upgrade proposal; statement line reads 'documents checked (automated)' with no savings claim; counter rebuildable from immutable intake events and never derived from shadow signals; D12 lawful basis and Article 14 route approved before any real supplier document is processed; no interest or charges on the arrears line; solicitor confirms the art 60F position.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts: (a) 'Knew but did not say' during dormancy is the sharpest legal edge. D13 lists 'any legal or contractual duty to tell' as a must-surface rule; a duty needs knowledge, and with detectors off there is none. But if a builder can pause 'on request' while jobs are live, JobGuard accepts evidence on a job it contracted to watch and does not look at it — the fact pattern for a UCTA 1977 s.3(2)(b) 'substantially different performance' complaint, or a negligent-misstatement claim if the terms or marketing imply continuous watching. Cure: pause only at zero live jobs (or after an explicit recorded close of each job), or keep the deterministic must-surface detectors running on any job still live. (b) The DMCC subscription-contract chapter (reminders, easy cancellation) is consumer-only; not applicable, though mirroring it costs nothing. (c) VAT — a £0 period is no supply for consideration (outside scope); £5–£9 is a standard-rated supply; the D09 period obligation with reason 'paused' is fine under D02. (d) UK GDPR storage limitation — retaining data during a paid or nominal dormancy is justified by the live contract; a lapse to £0 with no contract for months must be covered by D07 retention terms so JobGuard is not holding builder-customer data with no basis. (e) Direct Debit and card-scheme rules — switching amounts (£29 → £5 → £29) needs the same advance notice as I02; reactivation at the period boundary keeps it clean. (f) Late Payment Act, FCA, AML, HGCRA, CIS: not engaged. No AR or partner route. Cost: a terms paragraph in the same solicitor review; engineering for a 'paused' state in M4-13. Not certain legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Dormancy only when the meter reads zero live jobs, or after every live job is closed with a recorded reason; terms and the pause screen state in one sentence that no analysis, watchdog or final check runs while dormant and that jobs closed without a lock get no final check; evidence received while dormant is timestamped on receipt so D13's before-lock rule still works on reactivation; D07 defines retention for dormant and lapsed accounts; amount-change notices before collection; D09 v2 records the pause price, maximum months and reactivation rule.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts: (a) Consumer credit — upfront prepayment is not credit, so the annual plan is outside CCA 1974/FCA scope entirely. The variant 'annual commitment paid monthly' would be fixed-sum credit to a sole-trader 'individual' and must fit RAO art 60F(2) (no more than 12 payments within 12 months, no interest or charges) or need FCA lending permission — no appointed-representative route exists for lending, so avoid it or get advice. (b) Cooling-off and refunds — Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 and the DMCC subscription chapter are consumer-only, so there is no statutory cancellation right; refund terms are contractual, but under UCTA s.3 a 'no refund in any circumstances' clause is exposed if JobGuard terminates, withdraws the tier or materially changes the service mid-term; give a pro-rata refund in those cases. (c) 'Two months free' — CAP Code 'free' rules and BPMMRs reg 3: the monthly price must be a genuine price people actually pay, and the annual price (£290) must be shown as a price, not only as a saving. (d) VAT — VAT Regs 1995 reg 90: tax point is the annual invoice or payment, so 20% VAT on the full annual sum falls in that VAT period; a pro-rata upgrade is a further supply with its own tax point; a mid-term refund needs a reg 38 credit note. (e) Auto-renewal — no statutory reminder duty in B2B, but D05 requires bounded renewal authority, and card-scheme rules require a reminder before infrequent (annual) recurring charges and notice of any price change; Stripe's subscription requirements surface these. (f) Insolvency — prepaid builders are unsecured creditors; no duty to ring-fence, but a plain statement avoids a misrepresentation argument. (g) HGCRA, CIS, Late Payment Act, AML, competition law: not engaged. Cost: absorbed in the terms review; an accountant confirms deferred-revenue treatment under D02. Not certain legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Offer, never default; state the annual price and its monthly equivalent; renewal reminder and price-change notice before the renewal charge (D05); pro-rata refund if JobGuard terminates, withdraws or materially changes the plan; downgrades at renewal only; no instalment variant without consumer-credit advice; VAT invoice at payment; deferred-revenue accounting recorded under D02.
