verdicts.reasons: The one idea where a regulated-activity question is live. (a) Insurance — under the Prudential v IRC test and FCA PERG 6, a contract is insurance where, for a premium, the provider pays money on an uncertain adverse event. A guarantee that refunds up to the price paid when the provider's own service under-delivers is generally a warranty of the provider's own performance, not insurance, and attracts no IPT — but only while the payout is capped at the subscription actually paid and the trigger is JobGuard's own performance metric. Any variant that pays the 'shortfall' beyond the subscription, or pays on an external event ('if you lose money on a job'), becomes a contract of insurance: effecting and carrying out insurance is a regulated activity (RAO art 10) that no appointed-representative route can cover (ARs distribute, they do not underwrite); it would need an insurer partner plus insurance-distribution permissions — a different product, 6–12 months and five-figure cost. Keep the cap and get a short solicitor opinion (about £1–3k, 1–2 weeks). (b) Misleading marketing — BPMMRs 2008 reg 3 and the CAP Code guarantee rules (conditions stated before purchase, valid claims refunded promptly, significant limitations made clear): the metric must be defined in the offer, and 'documented value' may count only posted facts labelled per §14.1 ('tracked' is the builder's own work; 'flagged' is never 'saved'); a guarantee measured on an opaque JobGuard-valued figure is the exposure. (c) UCTA s.3 — activity conditions (minimum documents, accounts locked) are lawful in B2B, but if they make the guarantee practically unclaimable a court can treat the clause as unreasonable; keep them to what JobGuard genuinely needs to have had a chance to work. (d) VAT — the credit is a reduction in consideration for the subscription: VAT Regs 1995 reg 38 credit note reducing output tax (M4-10 already models credit notes). (e) Accounting — variable consideration/refund liability under FRS 102 or IFRS 15: revenue must be recognised net of expected credits; the D02 mapping needs this, and it is the true P&L cost rather than the headline uplift. (f) Consumer credit, claims management, Late Payment Act, HGCRA: not engaged; the 'credit' is a refund, not credit in the CCA sense. (g) Conditioning the guarantee on locking final accounts is lawful, but the lock is also the reveal event; the terms must say so plainly to avoid a misrepresentation argument that the condition was designed to expose the builder to fees. Not certain legal advice; the insurance point is for a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Cap the credit at the subscription actually paid in the guarantee year and never pay a shortfall beyond it; solicitor opinion on insurance characterisation before launch; publish the exact value-receipt definition and the N multiple with the offer; conditions limited to genuine-use minima; a stated claim window and prompt credit-note issue; reg 38 VAT credit note and a refund-liability provision in the D02 accounting mapping; credit applies to subscription only, and D09 v3 must record the guarantee explicitly because D09 v2 says subscriptions are 'not refunded'; never describe it as insurance or as 'we'll make you whole'.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts: (a) 'JobGuard knew but did not say' — there is no general B2B duty to volunteer information, so withholding a feature is lawful, but liability can arise from (i) a contractual promise or marketing implying checking ('JobGuard checks your supplier invoices'): BPMMRs reg 3 misleading advertising and the Misrepresentation Act 1967; and (ii) D13's must-surface duties where JobGuard has actual knowledge. Both are defeated only if JobGuard genuinely has not extracted the document. The condition is therefore structural: on Solo, no supplier-document extraction runs in any pipeline, including the shadow-bill detectors (SV-3 lists supplier items and POs as a shadow source) and including photos that happen to be invoices. If extraction runs and the finding is merely hidden, JobGuard holds a known overcharge it will not tell a paying customer about; overcharge is not a D13 must-surface category, so that is lawful, but it is the exact trust failure the founder named and a misrepresentation exposure if the page implies checking. (b) The upgrade prompt 'you uploaded 14 supplier invoices' requires JobGuard to classify Solo uploads; classification is not knowledge of an overcharge, but it weakens the 'we never looked' position — count by the builder's own chosen evidence type instead. (c) The add-on-with-guarantee form inherits I07's insurance characterisation condition (refund cap only). (d) UCTA s.3 — a tier feature scope defines the service rather than excluding liability; fine if the pricing page and the terms match. (e) UK GDPR — no extra processing; fewer documents processed on Solo reduces D12 exposure. (f) Builder-to-homeowner consumer law, HGCRA, CIS, FCA, AML: not engaged. No AR or partner route needed. Cost: absorbed in the terms review and the I07 opinion; engineering for a per-tier entitlement check at intake (M4-13/M4-14). Not certain legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Structural: supplier-document intake and extraction disabled at tenant-tier level for every pipeline (watchdog and shadow), so nothing is known and nothing is suppressed; pricing page states plainly which tiers include supplier-document checking; upgrade prompts count builder-declared evidence types, not JobGuard classification; must-surface findings on anything JobGuard actually extracted are shown regardless of tier; on upgrade, documents received before the upgrade are checked prospectively only and any signal from them is treated as disclosed/ineligible; the add-on guarantee follows I07's conditions.

verdicts.key_risk: The moment any JobGuard pipeline extracts a Solo supplier invoice for another purpose (the shadow bill) and a tier gate hides the overcharge, the structural defence collapses into 'knew but did not say' — lawful, but a misrepresentation exposure and the trust failure the founder named.

verdicts.reasons: UK B2B position: the builder buys JobGuard for the business, so it is a trader, not a consumer (CRA 2015 s.2; DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 definitions). CRA Part 2 unfair terms, the DMCC subscription-contract chapter and the drip-pricing rules therefore do not apply to the JobGuard-to-builder price, and no statute forbids an annual step or a value-indexed offer (report §'Offer annual billing' and success_fee_psychology §4 both note the B2B carve-out). What actually bites: (1) UCTA 1977 s.3 is not engaged by a price term unless the clause lets JobGuard render substantially different performance, so reasonableness review is unlikely; (2) incorporation: an outcome-indexed escalator is unusual, so under the Interfoto v Stiletto line it must be fairly and prominently brought to the builder's attention at sign-up, not buried in terms; (3) certainty and discretion: if 'documented value' or 'tracked+recovered' is a figure JobGuard computes, Variant B is a contractual discretion subject to the Braganza v BP Shipping [2015] UKSC 17 implied duty (honest, rational, not arbitrary) and an undefined metric risks the step failing for uncertainty; the lesser-of-8%-or-first-digit formula is certain only if 'tracked' and 'recovered' are defined by reference to posted, settled facts and the receipt hash in the versioned subscription_terms; (4) payments: a changed recurring amount needs payer consent under the PSRs 2017 and card-scheme recurring-billing rules (advance notice of an amount change, easy cancellation) enforced through Stripe; Variant A's explicit Decision satisfies this outright, Variant B relies on a pre-agreed determinable formula plus 30 days' notice, which schemes accept; (5) BPMMRs 2008 reg 3: the value receipt used to justify the rise is a representation to a trader and must not mislead (settled/confirmed events only, same figures all year); (6) UK GDPR Art 5(1)(b): using the builder's job outcomes to set the builder's price is a purpose that must appear in the privacy notice (own-tenant data, so no third-party issue). No FCA permission, AML, CIS, VAT (beyond D02) or competition point arises; D09 v2 must set price-change, notice and grandfathering, and D05 treats any tier change as a new bounded authority. Variant A is legally clean; Variant B is lawful but is the one that needs drafting care. Cost: solicitor drafting/review of the variation clause and receipt wording, roughly £1,000–£3,000, 1–2 weeks, folded into the M4-13 terms review; no regulatory timeline. Needs a solicitor: adequacy of incorporation and whether a JobGuard-computed metric passes the Braganza/certainty tests. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Prefer Variant A (opt-in tier proposal accepted by an explicit Decision creating a new D05 authority). Variant B only if: the metric is objectively defined from posted settled/confirmed facts and the receipt hash is referenced in the subscription_terms version; the escalator is prominently disclosed at sign-up (separate bold clause or tick-box); 30 days' notice with penalty-free cancellation before the step applies; Stripe/scheme-compliant amount-change notice; D09 v2 price-change/grandfathering approved; privacy notice names the purpose; never cite JobGuard-found catches as justification; never retrospective.

verdicts.key_risk: An outcome-indexed unilateral price term is unusual and JobGuard-computed: unless prominently incorporated and objectively defined (Interfoto/Braganza/uncertainty) it is unenforceable and card-scheme rules let the builder charge it back; the legal cost is low but a disputed rise reads as 'you did well so we charge more'.

verdicts.reasons: The contract is B2B, so the DMCC Act 2024 subscription-contract chapter (pre-contract information, reminder notices, cooling-off) and the CRA 2015 do not apply, and AGENTS §5.10 is preserved because the obligation arises only from the explicit switch-live command, never from quoting. What binds in practice is scheme and payments law, not statute: (1) Visa and Mastercard free-trial/'negative option' rules, enforced via Stripe's terms: express consent to the recurring mandate at capture, clear display of the amount and the date the first charge falls (the earlier of first-job lock or day 90), a reminder before the first charge (Visa's rule is at least 7 days), and easy in-app cancellation; breach means chargebacks and Stripe account risk rather than a fine; (2) PSRs 2017 / SCA: the card must be captured through an SCA-authenticated off-session setup (Stripe SetupIntent) and the mandate must state how the variable amount (tier by live jobs) is determined — D05's bounded renewal authority is the right container; (3) advertising to traders: BPMMRs 2008 reg 3 and the CAP Code 'free' rules apply to B2B marketing, so 'first live job free' is accurate only if qualified in the same breath — 'subscription-free; the 10% success fee still applies to qualifying recoveries'; (4) the success fee 'charged normally' on the trial job can only be real after G4 with D01/D03/D13 approved; in pilot_no_charge it remains a labelled illustration (§14.1), so this part of the design is legally inert until then; (5) hosted Stripe surfaces mean no raw card data reaches JobGuard (PCI SAQ-A), consistent with AGENTS §3. No FCA permission (a free period is not credit; no regulated activity), no AML (Stripe is the regulated institution), no VAT issue beyond D02 (the waived period is simply no supply for consideration), no third-party GDPR issue. The commercial effect is untested for tradespeople (report §'Let the trial run until the first job is live'; price_level notes §5 warn the ChartMogul card-required figures are B2B SaaS). Cost/timeline: Stripe Billing trial_end plus scheme-compliant reminder emails are configuration; solicitor review of trial/renewal wording sits inside the M4-13 terms review (roughly £500–£1,500). Needs a solicitor: final trial wording and the mandate description of a variable-tier amount. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Show amount, tier and first-charge date at card capture; send a pre-charge reminder at least 7 days before the first charge; one-tap cancellation before and after conversion; SCA-authenticated off-session mandate with a variable-amount description; every 'free' claim qualified with the success fee in the same sentence; 90-day cap and tier recorded in subscription_terms; success fee on the trial job only post-G4 and only under D13-approved shadow processing; A/B test card-at-switch-live against no card before committing (report §Recommendation).

verdicts.reasons: Linking separately registered businesses under one login is lawful; the issues are contractual, data protection, VAT and, for JVs, competition. (1) Contracting party and authority: each legal entity is a separate customer; JobGuard needs a warranty that the group owner has authority to bind and view each entity (director or proprietor), and clear allocation or joint-and-several liability for subscription and success fees. (2) VAT invoicing: a VAT invoice must be addressed to the entity receiving the supply (VAT Notice 700 §16). If the parent pays a pooled subscription that also serves a sister company, either the parent is the sole customer with affiliates as users (one supply to the parent) or each entity is invoiced its share; a success fee on a sister entity's job must go to the entity that earned the recovery unless the terms make the parent the customer for all. Pick one model and record it in D02/D09; a mis-addressed invoice blocks input-tax recovery. (3) UK GDPR: each entity is a controller of its customers' and staff's personal data; consolidated reporting is a controller-to-controller disclosure within common ownership (Art 6(1)(f) legitimate interests is available) needing transparency (Arts 13/14 via D12) and a group data-sharing clause; DSARs from a sister entity's staff or customers must be answerable per entity. (4) CIS/MTD: no CIS effect (JobGuard performs no construction operations); MTD requires digital records per business, so consolidated reporting is fine only if per-entity records stay separate and exportable. (5) VAT disaggregation (VATA 1994 Sch 1 paras 1A/2): a Ltd plus sole-trader entity artificially split below the threshold is the builder's own HMRC risk, but a shared rate book and consolidated reports are evidence HMRC could use, so JobGuard must not market the feature as a way to run two businesses. (6) Competition law: entities under common control are a single economic unit, so no Chapter I CA98 issue; linking two independent builders in a JV with a shared rate book and consolidated pricing is a competitively sensitive information exchange between competitors — restrict linking to common-control groups (>50% ownership or the same proprietors) or to JV-specific data only. (7) Security: AGENTS §5.1 requires the cross-tenant read to be a reviewed exception with independent tests; membership must be verified per tenant, never via a header. No FCA, AML, Construction Act or consumer-law point. Cost: group/affiliate clause, authority warranty and data-sharing clause, roughly £1,000–£2,000 of solicitor time; the security review is engineering. Needs a solicitor: the customer-of-record structure for VAT and the JV information-exchange boundary. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Common-control test for linking (JV linking limited to JV-specific data); per-entity authority warranty and authorised signatory; explicit customer-of-record and VAT invoicing model approved under D02/D09; group data-sharing clause and per-entity privacy notices (D12); per-entity MTD-ready records and exports; no tax-split marketing; AGENTS §5.1 reviewed read-only projection with RLS and catalog tests; severability of the link on sale or insolvency of an entity.

verdicts.reasons: A fee to the builder for a documented pre-payment supplier correction is an ordinary B2B contingent service charge. It is not FCA debt collecting (RAO art 39F covers only debts under consumer credit or hire agreements, and here the builder owes the supplier, not the reverse), not claims management (supplier disputes are not among the RAO arts 89G–89M sectors; success_fee_benchmarks §7), and the DBA Regulations 2013 caps apply to legal representatives only. JobGuard neither contacts the supplier nor moves money, so D10 and AML are untouched; CRA 2015 and DMCC drip-pricing do not apply to a trader customer. What matters: (1) contract certainty — the trigger must be objective (cited Decision precedes the correction; same supplier, invoice and line; ≥£25 net; builder confirmation 'corrected as flagged'), and the 'agreed rate' the discrepancy is measured against must be an evidenced contractual price (the builder's supplier quote, trade-account price list or PO), not a rate-book estimate — otherwise the fee is charged on a goodwill discount and is open to challenge; (2) VAT — the supplier's credit note or reissued invoice adjusts the builder's input tax (VAT Regulations 1995 reg 38); the fee base is the net delta on the flagged line only and JobGuard's fee is a separate standard-rated supply (D02); (3) transparency to traders — BPMMRs 2008 reg 3 and CAP price rules: a £10 floor or 5% rate must be stated wherever the 10% success fee is advertised; a floor yielding 40% on a £25 correction is lawful in B2B but cannot be presented as '5%'; (4) UCTA 1977 is not engaged by a price term and the penalty doctrine (Cavendish v Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67) does not apply because the fee is not payable on breach; (5) UK GDPR — supplier documents carry business contact data only; D12 covers it. The real cost is governance, not law: the founder's fixed decisions say prevented spend currently earns nothing and there is one 10% rate, so I12 needs D03 v3 (new category with evidence sufficiency: both documents via intake with hashes and object versions) and D01 v4 (different rate, floor and cap), each reviewed before G4. Legal cost: clause drafting inside the M4-13 terms review, roughly £500–£1,500; no regulatory timeline. Needs a solicitor: floor/cap wording and the definition of 'agreed rate'. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: 'Agreed rate' must be an evidenced contractual price, never a rate-book estimate; the Decision must precede the correction; line-level match plus builder confirmation; both supplier documents via intake with hashes/object versions; net-delta base on the flagged line only; floor/cap displayed beside the headline rate everywhere; D03 v3 and D01 v4 approved before G4; offered as an alternative to I08, not stacked; one monthly statement line approved per statement (D05).

verdicts.key_risk: Not regulatory: the fee rides on the supplier's paperwork and an 'agreed rate' JobGuard may not hold evidence for; without a contractual-price rule it charges on goodwill discounts, and it needs D01 v4/D03 v3 to depart from the fixed no-prevention, one-rate model.

verdicts.reasons: Same regulatory footing as the existing cash-refund supplier-overcharge category: no FCA permission (no consumer credit agreement, no claims-management sector), no AML (no funds pass through JobGuard), the builder sends under D10, and B2B so CRA/DMCC do not apply. The question is contractual and accounting, not regulatory. (1) 'Recovered' must be redefined in the fee agreement to include a credit note applied and consumed against a later invoice that the builder then paid in full; otherwise a fee on a paper credit is a fee on unrealised money and disputable. The two-document evidence rule (supplier statement or later invoice carrying the credit line, hashed via intake, plus the M4-7/M4-8 'later invoice paid' fact) gives that certainty. (2) VAT: a credit note reduces the builder's input tax (VAT Regulations 1995 reg 38) and the supplier's output tax; qualifying principal net of VAT is correct, and JobGuard's 10% is a separate standard-rated supply (D02). (3) Partial application or partial payment: terms must state that only the applied and paid portion counts, pro-rata in the §14.8 manner. (4) Supplier insolvency before application leaves nothing recovered and no fee, consistent with 'unapplied never qualifies'. (5) A credit later reversed triggers the linked compensating journal (§14.9), which the terms must permit. (6) D03 v2 expressly excludes applied credits 'until an approved extension' (BUILD_PLAN §14.7), so this is a D03 v3 revision with legal and accounting review before G4. (7) Case-based consent (JobGuard-flagged overcharge, builder opened the case and approved terms) satisfies D05's per-statement authority. UK GDPR: supplier statements are business data; SV-7 email or accounting connectors need their own D04/D12 route review. Legal cost: small — a D03 v3 definition and a terms clause, roughly £500–£1,000 within the M4-13 review, plus accounting review of revenue recognition on credit-based recoveries. Honest sizing per the idea and success_fee_benchmarks §1: small money at every archetype. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: D03 v3 defines applied-credit recovery with the two-document evidence rule; only JobGuard-flagged overcharges opened as cases with terms approved; applied-and-paid portion only; unique derivation identity per (credit note id, applied invoice id); reversal triggers compensation; hashed supplier documents, never builder attestation; SV-7 sources pass D04/D12 before use.
verdicts.key_risk: Contract certainty: 'recovered' must be redefined and proven from the supplier's own statement or next invoice; a fee on a credit never fully consumed or later reversed is the dispute case, and the category stays excluded until D03 v3 is approved.

verdicts.reasons: (1) Entitlement: the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 ss.1–2 implies statutory interest into contracts for goods or services where both supplier and purchaser act in the course of a business; homeowners are outside it entirely and ambiguous purchasers (landlords, mixed use) must be excluded as the idea proposes. Rate: base + 8% (Rate of Interest (No.3) Order 2002) with the reference base rate fixed at 30 June or 31 December preceding the due date, so the 'dated base-rate fact' must be the six-monthly reference rate, not the daily rate. Start: s.4 — the day after the agreed payment date, or 30 days after the later of delivery and invoice if none; for business customers on construction contracts the agreed date is the contract's or Scheme's final date for payment (HGCRA 1996 s.110), so JobGuard must take it from the contract record, not invoice+30. Compensation: s.5A fixed £40/£70/£100 per debt plus, under s.5A(2A) (2013 Regulations), reasonable recovery costs above the fixed sum — which arguably lets the builder pass JobGuard's fee to the debtor (solicitor to confirm). Contracting out: ss.8–9 — if the contract provides a 'substantial remedy' (e.g. a main contractor's own interest clause) the statutory rate is displaced, so JobGuard must check the builder's and customer's terms before computing. (2) FCA: computing and drafting a demand the builder sends is not debt collecting (RAO art 39F is confined to debts under consumer credit or hire agreements, per the SRA reading in success_fee_benchmarks §7) and not claims management (arts 89G–89M); no appointed-representative route is needed because no regulated activity is performed. One open point for a solicitor: where the business debtor is a sole trader or small partnership, a deferred-payment invoice is 'credit' for CCA purposes unless exempt under RAO art 60F (≤12 payments within 12 months, no interest or charges) or art 60C (over £25,000, business purpose); statutory interest is imposed by the Act rather than charged for credit and should not disturb the exemption, but confirm before adding any contractual interest clause to JobGuard's quote templates. (3) VAT: statutory interest and s.5A compensation are generally outside the scope of VAT for the builder; JobGuard's fee on them is standard-rated — D02 must record both. (4) Consumer law: the hard block on consumers is mandatory; adding interest to a homeowner's bill would be a misleading or aggressive practice under DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 1 and a CRA 2015 problem, so counterparty type must be a recorded, reviewable fact (D06/D11), never model-inferred. (5) Construction Act: payment and pay-less notices (ss.110A–111) determine whether a sum is due; a demand for interest on a sum covered by a valid pay-less notice is wrong, so M4-19 templates must gate on notice status. (6) UK GDPR: sole-trader debtors are individuals; Art 14 route per D12. No AML (funds go direct to the builder). Cost/timeline: commercial or construction solicitor review of the computation rules and templates, roughly £1,500–£3,000, 2–4 weeks, alongside M4-19; no licence. Revenue is Firm-weighted and thinner than the idea's estimate once displaced-rate contracts, pay-less notices and ambiguous counterparties are excluded. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Business debtors only with recorded counterparty type; ambiguous cases excluded; start date from the contract or Scheme final date for payment; six-monthly reference base rate as a dated fact; check for contractual displacement (ss.8–9) before computing; never add against sums under a valid pay-less notice; D02 records the outside-scope VAT treatment; D03 v3 adds interest/compensation as a separate qualifying class; builder approves every send (D10); solicitor confirms the CCA position for sole-trader debtors and the s.5A(2A) pass-through option; M4-19 template review.

verdicts.reasons: Retention is a contractual mechanism in commercial construction; HGCRA 1996 Part II applies to construction contracts except with residential occupiers (s.106), so this is Firm-tier B2B work. (1) Not FCA regulated: retention withheld by a paying party is a trade debt, not a consumer credit agreement (RAO art 39F), and construction payment is not a claims-management sector; no appointed-representative route needed. (2) Not a reserved legal activity: drafting a payment application or release notice is not litigation or reserved instrument work under the Legal Services Act 2007 s.12, but a wrong template creates negligence exposure, so JobGuard must disclaim legal advice and draft on the builder's instructions. (3) The 'release date' is a legal determination, not a fact: many subcontract retention clauses tie release to the main contract's certificate, which s.110(1A) (inserted by the LDEDC Act 2009) makes ineffective with the Scheme for Construction Contracts substituting, so JobGuard must treat the date as the builder's declared contractual date and never assert entitlement. (4) Notice mechanics: a release 'application' is an application for payment under ss.110A–110B; if the payer serves no payment or pay-less notice (s.111) the applied sum becomes due, so M4-19 templates must follow the Act's timing or they are ineffective; adjudication (s.108) is available at any time but is outside JobGuard's scope. (5) Late Payment Act interest may also run on overdue retention (apply the I14 rules). (6) Fee: a 5% or 10% B2B contingency on retention cash settled after case opening is lawful and uncapped (DBA caps apply to legal representatives only); certainty requires an allocation rule for receipts that mix retention with other sums (M4-8). (7) Legislative sunset: the idea cites a Commercial Payments Bill (May 2026) banning retentions prospectively with a two-year transition; verify against the Bill text (the government consulted on retention reform in 2025), but if enacted the category has roughly a 3–4-year runway. (8) UK GDPR: main-contractor contact data; D12. No AML; VAT only via D02 (retention is part of the contract sum, tax point on release). Cost/timeline: construction solicitor review of the retention-ledger logic and templates, roughly £2,000–£5,000, 3–6 weeks, within M4-19; D03 v3 category plus D05 per-case consent. The BEIS/Pye Tait 44% unrecovered-retention figure in the idea is unverified in the research and should be checked before being quoted. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Builder-declared release terms with JobGuard asserting no entitlement; templates reviewed for ss.110–111 timing and s.110(1A); case opens only after the date passed and the builder's own reminder was ignored; never delay a reminder to ripen a case; allocation rule for mixed receipts; residential-occupier contracts excluded from Act-based templates; verify the retention-ban Bill and set a sunset review date; D03 v3, D10 and M4-19 before any live use.

verdicts.reasons: No statute caps a B2B success fee: FCA CMCOB 5 bands apply only to regulated claims management for consumers, the DBA Regulations 2013 caps only to legal representatives, CRA 2015 does not apply to a trader customer, UCTA 1977 does not police price terms, and a minimum fee is not a penalty (Cavendish v Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67) because it is not payable on breach. So neither a 15% band nor a £25 floor is unlawful. The true cost lies elsewhere: (1) it reopens the founder's fixed 10% and the report's 'one rate everywhere' (report §Recommendation), requiring D01 v4 with its own review; (2) BPMMRs 2008 reg 3 and CAP Code price-claim rules apply to B2B marketing, so a '10%' headline with a floor that yields 42% on a £60 catch is misleading unless the floor is stated with equal prominence everywhere the rate appears; (3) it mirrors the CMC fee-band structure that Parliament and the FCA capped after fees of up to 40% (success_fee_psychology §3; report §'The hidden final check'), inviting exactly the claims-firm comparison the plan says to avoid; (4) the small catches most affected are late extras billed to homeowners after the final account — a consumer transaction where CRA 2015 s.51 limits an unagreed price to a reasonable one and DMCC Part 4 Ch 1 polices surprise or pressured billing — so the uplift rides on the least enforceable, most dispute-prone base (success_fee_psychology §4); (5) the JobGuard-side incentive to avoid coalescing conflicts with §14.10 and must be structurally prevented, adding engineering cost for trivial revenue. Timeline/cost: nil regulatory; D01 v4 review plus marketing-compliance review. Verdict is reject: legally permissible, but it contradicts a fixed decision, creates a misleading-headline-rate exposure, and its revenue is negligible. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended. If ever revisited: D01 v4 approved; floor or band stated wherever the 10% appears (BPMMR/CAP); structural controls against coalescing avoidance (§14.10); no application to consumer-billed catches where the recovered sum is below a reasonable-price threshold.

verdicts.reasons: FCA perimeter is not the problem. Procuring payment of a builder's own services invoice is not 'debt collecting' under RAO 2001 art 39F, which is tied to debts under credit agreements or consumer hire (the SRA guidance the research cites in §7 of the benchmarks note gives a building company as the example), and construction payment recovery is not one of the six regulated claims-management sectors (RAO arts 89G–89M), so no FCA permission or appointed-representative route is needed for a JobGuard desk, provided JobGuard never takes assignment, never collects in its own name (D10 already requires the builder as sender) and the case does not involve an instalment or deferred-payment arrangement with the homeowner that could make the debt one 'under a credit agreement' (CCA 1974 s.189 treats individuals and sole traders as consumers; whether an art 60F-exempt agreement still engages art 39F needs a solicitor). The real legal weight sits elsewhere. (1) Damages-based agreements. A 15–20% fee payable only out of money recovered, in return for drafting reminders, statements and a letter before claim, looks like an agreement with a person providing 'claims management services' under Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 s.58AA, whose definition is imported from FSMA s.419A ('advice or other services in relation to the making of a claim' for 'repayment... or any other remedy... in respect of an obligation') and is NOT limited to the six FCA sectors. If s.58AA applies, the Damages-Based Agreements Regulations 2013 apply: written agreement, prescribed terms (claim, circumstances of payment, reason for the rate), 50% cap including VAT, 'payment' net of costs recovered from the other side; a non-compliant DBA is unenforceable against the builder. The idea's note that a fixed-fee panel solicitor 'avoids the DBA Regulations' is right for the solicitor's fee and wrong for JobGuard's own contingent charge. Zuberi v Lexlaw [2021] EWCA Civ 16 confines the Regs to the payment term, which helps a hybrid design, but this needs a solicitor's opinion and a DBA-compliant tier agreement. The same question technically hangs over the existing self-serve 10% and should go into the D03/D10 review. (2) Consumer debtors. The Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims (England and Wales) applies whenever a business, including a sole trader, claims a debt from an individual: prescribed Letter of Claim with Information Sheet, Reply Form and Financial Statement, and a 30-day standstill before issue. Administration of Justice Act 1970 s.40 (harassment, documents resembling court forms, false claims of authority) and DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 1 (aggressive or misleading practices) bind the builder as sender, so every desk template is a D10-reviewed artefact. Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 interest and fixed compensation are B2B only; on homeowner cases the builder bears the whole 15–20% (research §3). Scotland has no PAP-DC and uses Simple Procedure below £5,000; the desk and panel must be jurisdiction-gated. (3) Reserved activity. Conduct of litigation is reserved under the Legal Services Act 2007 Sch 2 para 4; Ndole Assets v Designer M&E Services [2018] EWCA Civ 2865 held that an unauthorised claims consultant serving a claim form acted unlawfully. The desk may draft; only the panel solicitor (acting for the builder as its client) or the builder personally may issue or serve. (4) Economics the law forces onto the screen. Small-claims track (≤£10,000) costs are not recoverable (CPR 27.14), court issue fees scale with value, and the solicitor's fixed fee is a disbursement the builder pays win or lose; on a £1,500–£6,000 debt the Escalated tier can exceed 30% of the sum in dispute, which the case screen must show before opening. (5) Referral. No LASPO 2012 s.56 ban outside personal injury, but any referral payment from the panel solicitor must be disclosed (SRA Code for Solicitors 5.1); simplest is none. (6) UK GDPR. The desk reads homeowner personal data JobGuard did not obtain from the homeowner: D12 Article 14 route, Art 6(1)(f) balancing, and a processor agreement with the builder (or joint-controller analysis given JobGuard's fee interest). None of this is a blocker; it is a conditions-and-cost picture, and it is not certain until a solicitor has looked at s.58AA.
verdicts.conditions: Solicitor opinion (assumption: £5–12k, 6–10 weeks, alongside the D03/D10 review) on (a) whether the Managed/Escalated contingent fee is a DBA under CLSA 1990 s.58AA/FSMA s.419A, with a DBA Regs 2013-compliant tier agreement if so (or a restructure to fixed per-letter fees, which takes JobGuard outside the DBA regime), and (b) the art 39F position where a homeowner is on an instalment plan; carve such cases out of the desk. Build the Escalated pack on the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims for England and Wales, with a separate Scottish route or exclusion. Desk templates reviewed under D10 against AJA 1970 s.40 and DMCC Act 2024 Part 4; builder remains sender; no JobGuard letterhead. Panel solicitor retained by the builder as client, fixed fee, no referral fee (or SRA-disclosed); JobGuard never issues or serves proceedings (Ndole). Case screen states non-recoverable small-claims costs, court fee, solicitor fee and that homeowner debts carry no statutory interest. D12 processor/joint-controller terms and Article 14 route for the desk's access to homeowner data. Professional indemnity cover for the desk (assumption £1–3k/yr). D01 versioned 10/15/20 rate table, D03 v2 entry test and D05 statement approval unchanged.

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard's own 15–20% contingent fee is held to be a damages-based agreement and, without DBA Regs 2013 drafting, is unenforceable against the builder; second, desk-drafted letters to homeowners breach AJA 1970 s.40 / DMCC 2024 and expose the builder-sender.

verdicts.reasons: A fixed £35 fee for assembling a case pack is an ordinary B2B service charge: no credit is extended so the Consumer Credit Act is not engaged; it is not FCA debt collecting (art 39F not engaged for a services invoice, subject to the same confirmation as I17) and not claims management under RAO Part 3B; standard-rated VAT applies (D02). DMCC Act 2024 drip-pricing does not bite a fee charged to a trader-builder, but the fee must sit in the subscription terms and be shown at the moment the builder opens the case, because misrepresentation and UCTA 1977 s.3 (reasonableness of standard written terms, including any 'non-refundable whatever happens' clause) still apply in B2B. Two live points. First, if the 10% withheld-payment fee is a DBA (I17), a fixed fee alongside it is a 'hybrid'; after Zuberi v Lexlaw the fixed fee for a defined deliverable (the pack) sits outside the DBA 'payment' term, but the drafting must keep it a fee for the pack, not a fee for the claim, and it must not be netted against or credited to the contingent payment (which the idea already says). Second, the pack itself must not resemble a court document or imply authority the builder lacks (AJA 1970 s.40(1)(c)–(d)), and the builder cannot pass the £35 on to a homeowner (no Late Payment Act 1998 rights against consumers; any indemnity term in the builder's own terms faces CRA 2015 s.62). 'Two cases a year included' in Builder/Firm tiers is a D09 term with no separate legal issue. Cost is a paragraph in the I17 opinion, not a separate project; the legal lens has nothing to refute here beyond the trivial revenue.
verdicts.conditions: Include the hybrid-fee point in the I17 DBA opinion and draft the £35 as a fee for the case pack deliverable, never credited against or netted with the contingent fee. Show the fee on the case-open Decision screen and in D01/D03/D09 terms before the builder confirms. Pack documents reviewed under D10 for AJA 1970 s.40 (no court-form styling, no implied authority). VAT-inclusive presentation per D02. Do not build any mechanism for the builder to recharge the fee to a consumer.

verdicts.reasons: Contingent accounts-payable recovery audits are an established UK service (research §2 and §8, 20–30% norm) and no licence is needed: no credit or claims sector (FCA not engaged), no consumer law (trader buyer), no competition-law issue (no buying group, no supplier-side arrangement), and JobGuard is not a 'relevant person' under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 unless invoice auditing is characterised as 'accountancy services' making JobGuard an external accountant or bookkeeper needing HMRC supervision (reg 8/11) — unlikely for a document-matching service, but confirm rather than assume. Legal cost is in the detail. (1) DBA, weak form: FSMA s.419A's 'claim for repayment... by way of voluntary arrangement' is wide enough that a solicitor should confirm the 20–25% contingency needs no s.58AA drafting; UK AP-audit firms do not generally treat it as a DBA, so this is a check, not a rebuild. (2) Limitation Act 1980 s.5 gives six years for overcharge and duplicate-payment restitution (money paid under mistake of fact), but merchant trading terms commonly bar invoice queries after 30–90 days, so refunds on older items rest on goodwill; the contract must promise a review, not a recovery, and marketing of typical yields is B2B advertising under the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008. (3) VAT and MTD: a supplier refund arrives with a credit note; the builder must reduce input tax (VAT Regulations 1995 reg 38) in MTD-compatible records, JobGuard's share must be computed on the net-of-VAT refund, and JobGuard's own fee invoice is standard-rated (D02 tax-adviser item). (4) D03 v2 excludes credit notes against future purchases; showing them without charging is right and must stay. (5) UK GDPR: supplier documents contain business-contact and sole-trader-supplier personal data (D12 Article 14, legitimate interests). (6) D10: the builder sends every refund request; if a JobGuard auditor ever contacts a merchant directly that is a new D10 decision and a representation question, and it also touches the trust rule that JobGuard must stay on the builder's side of the counter. (7) UCTA 1977 s.3 reasonableness on the non-refundable setup fee and on any cap for missed items. (8) Bank-verified refund evidence (M4-7) runs on the TrueLayer AIS route already gated by D10/D12. Nothing here refutes the idea; the law simply makes it a service with modest, provable yield.
verdicts.conditions: Fold into the I17 solicitor opinion (assumption £1–3k): DBA applicability of the contingent share and whether invoice auditing is an MLR 2017 'accountancy service'. Contract promises a review, not recovery; no yield claims in marketing without JobGuard's own data. Fee computed on net-of-VAT cash refunds only, with the reg 38 input-tax adjustment surfaced to the builder; tax adviser sign-off under D02. Credit notes displayed but never charged (D03 v2). Builder sends all refund requests; any direct merchant contact needs a new D10 record. D12 Article 14 route for supplier personal data. UCTA-reasonable setup-fee and liability terms.

verdicts.key_risk: Yield claims outrun what supplier terms and the six-year limitation allow, drawing a misleading-marketing complaint from a builder who paid £295–£495 upfront and recovered little; secondary risk is JobGuard drifting into direct merchant contact without a D10 decision.

verdicts.reasons: This idea carries the most legal weight per pound of revenue. (1) UK GDPR. A non-subscriber uploads customer messages, photos and supplier documents about people who have never heard of JobGuard and were never shown the D12/D13 onboarding notice, and JobGuard analyses them for its own fee interest; that makes JobGuard a controller for the shadow analysis (the D12 candidate position), not a processor. Consequences: an Art 6(1)(f) legitimate-interests assessment, an Art 14 notice to the homeowner within one month (Art 14(3)) unless a documented 'disproportionate effort' reliance under Art 14(5)(b), which is thin when the builder is a live channel to the homeowner; a DPIA under Art 35 for systematic evaluation of individuals' communications; D07 retention rules for a one-off user; and a DSAR path that can disclose a candidate (already handled by §14.11, but here the lock and reveal are minutes apart so the exposure is small). The subscriber flow pushes the notice through onboarding; the pay-per-use flow cannot, so JobGuard must serve it or the builder must contractually undertake to. (2) Money. 'JobGuard's payment link' must be a Stripe Connect direct charge on the builder's own connected account. If JobGuard's account receives the homeowner's money and pays the builder, JobGuard provides a payment service under the Payment Services Regulations 2017; the commercial-agent exclusion (Sch 1 Pt 2 para 2(b)) is read narrowly by the FCA (PERG 15) for platforms acting for both sides, and AGENTS §3/§5.10 forbid holding customer funds in any case. (3) Consumer law downstream. A separate invoice to a homeowner after the final account, for an extra never priced or documented, is the most attackable bill JobGuard can generate. CRA 2015 s.51 allows only a reasonable price where none was agreed and the builder must prove the extra was ordered; under the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 an extra agreed at the consumer's home is an off-premises contract, and if no cancellation information was given the cancellation period runs up to 12 months plus 14 days (reg 31) and the consumer may owe nothing for services performed in it (reg 36(6)); DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 1 governs the builder's chasing. The drip-pricing ban targets the quoted headline price to consumers, not JobGuard's £29, but the late extra bill fails on contract formation rather than drip pricing. All of these land on the builder, and the fee base with them; the research's own note (§7 of the behavioural note) flags this second-order risk. (4) Contract with the non-subscriber: one-off B2B terms must incorporate the D13 disclosure, the two-rate structure (D01 v4), D03 and D02 before the £29 is taken; a sole-trader builder is a trader, so CRA 2015 does not apply to JobGuard's own sale. (5) The 15% contingent fee on money the builder collects for its own work is not a 'claim' under FSMA s.419A in any natural reading, so the DBA point is weaker than in I17, but include it in the same opinion. (6) Post-lock evidence never qualifying (§14.6) is already the rule and is what keeps this fair. No statutory blocker, but the DPIA + Article 14 route + Stripe Connect + one-off contract stack is real cost for revenue that the homeowner-dispute point erodes.
verdicts.conditions: D12 v2 approval covering JobGuard-as-controller for uploaded third-party material, with a written Article 14 mechanism for homeowners not onboarded through a subscriber (JobGuard-served notice or builder undertaking) and a completed DPIA before real data (assumption £4–8k legal, 2–3 months, partly shared with the subscriber D12 work). Stripe Connect direct charges on the builder's connected account only; JobGuard never receives customer money. D01 v4 (15% non-member rate) with the 10% vs 15% gap stated on the paywall; D03, D02 and D13 lock rules apply unchanged; post-lock uploads never qualify. One-off terms shown and accepted before the £29 Stripe checkout, including the final-check disclosure. Reveal UI warns that extras billed after the final account to a homeowner need documented agreement (CRA 2015 s.51, CCRs 2013 cancellation information) and offers the customer-approval flow before the separate invoice is issued. D07 retention schedule for non-subscriber uploads.

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard becomes controller for homeowner messages it obtained from a one-off user with no Article 14 route, and a payment-link design that routes customer money through JobGuard turns it into an unauthorised payment service; both are avoidable but neither is cheap.

verdicts.reasons: No statute forbids a prepaid credit for JobGuard's own services, so this is a rejection on true legal and tax cost against a product the behavioural lens already scores revenue-negative. (1) Not e-money: EMRs 2011 reg 2 requires acceptance by persons other than the issuer; closed-loop credit spent only on JobGuard fees is outside. Not client money (no CASS regime applies to JobGuard). (2) Deposit-taking, RAO 2001 art 5: money repayable on demand is a 'deposit' unless it is an advance payment for services 'repayable only in the event that the... services are not in fact provided' (art 5(3)); a credit that the builder can cash out at will 'on cancellation' looks like repayable-on-demand money, and art 5(1)(b) bites where a firm's other activities are financed 'to a material extent' from such sums, which a small company selling credit packs could satisfy. Fixable by drafting (refund only on termination, limited to services not yet provided), but it needs a solicitor's view before launch. (3) VAT: a prepayment for a standard-rated supply fixes a tax point on receipt (VATA 1994 s.6(4)); if structured as a voucher it is a single-purpose voucher under VATA 1994 Sch 10B with VAT due at issue on the £200; refunds need credit notes (VAT Regs 1995 reg 38); breakage is income with no VAT adjustment. This is a D02 tax-adviser item and it moves VAT cash out earlier, the opposite of the cash-flow benefit claimed. (4) Accounting: a 24-month deferred-revenue liability with a refund obligation; on insolvency the builder is an unsecured creditor with no statutory protection in B2B, which is a trust point the terms would have to state. (5) UCTA 1977 s.3 reasonableness on expiry and forfeiture terms (largely neutralised by refundability, which is what creates the art 5 point in (2)). (6) Consumer law does not apply (trader buyer). The legal structuring, tax treatment and accounting overhead exceed the (negative) contribution; the fee-prepayment ledger in M4-12 would also be a new money surface for G4's penetration review.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended. If revived, re-shape as a non-refundable annual subscription bundle inside D09 (no refund-on-demand, so no art 5 question), take tax-adviser sign-off on the s.6(4)/Sch 10B tax point under D02, and obtain a solicitor's confirmation on deposit-taking before any sale.

verdicts.key_risk: A refundable-on-demand credit financing operations is analysed as accepting deposits under RAO art 5, while the tax point on receipt removes the cash-flow rationale; legal cost with negative revenue.

verdicts.reasons: Legally the cleanest idea in the set. JobGuard collecting its own fee by Direct Debit through GoCardless makes JobGuard the payee/creditor; GoCardless is the FCA-authorised payment institution and Bacs service user, so JobGuard needs no FCA permission, no Payment Services Regulations 2017 registration and no MLR 2017 supervision (the partner route does the regulated work). No credit is extended because the fee is collected after the customer receipt is verified, so the Consumer Credit Act 1974 is not engaged even though sole-trader builders are 'individuals' under s.189. Conditions are procedural rather than substantive. (1) Bacs scheme rules require advance notice to the payer of each collection's amount and date (GoCardless's default is 3 working days, shorter than the scheme default by agreement in the mandate); the 'within 7 days' window must include that notice, and the Direct Debit Guarantee lets a builder claim an indemnity for a disputed collection through their bank, which JobGuard must treat as a reversal through the linked-compensation path, not as a chargeback to contest. (2) D05: the DD mandate is itself a standing authority in Bacs terms; the plan's per-statement approval and the ≤10%-of-verified-receipt bound are contractual overlays that must be in the M4-13 agreement and revocable at any time, which is what AGENTS §5.3 already requires. (3) D02: the on-screen statement must show the VAT basis ('fee £100 + VAT £20, £120 collected') because §14.1 forbids 'you kept £X' without the tax basis; the mock-up in the idea ('£900 yours') breaches the plan's own rule as written. (4) Where the fee arises from a withheld-payment case, the DBA question in I17 attaches to the underlying fee, not to the collection mechanism. (5) Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 applies B2B to JobGuard's own unpaid fee invoices if a mandate is cancelled, a mild lever that should be in the terms. (6) The customer receipt evidence on the same screen is homeowner personal data within D12, already covered by the M4-7/M4-8 route. No external legal cost beyond the M4-13 terms review (assumption).
verdicts.conditions: Bacs advance-notice compliance built into the statement-approval step (notice sent at approval; collection no earlier than the notice period). Direct Debit indemnity claims mapped to the reversal/compensation path in M4-12. D05 approval of the per-statement default and the bounded standing authority (≤10% of the verified receipt, re-checked at execution, revocable). D02: VAT shown on the same screen; no 'yours' figure without the tax basis. M4-13 terms cover mandate cancellation, retry limits and Late Payment Act interest on unpaid fee invoices. GoCardless merchant onboarding and mandate wording reviewed under D05.

revised_revenue.solo: +£7 (was +£8; 1–2% shaved for DD indemnity reversals)

verdicts.key_risk: Collecting inside the Bacs advance-notice window or presenting the fee without VAT, either of which produces indemnity claims and a builder complaint that JobGuard 'took money without warning'.

verdicts.reasons: No statute forbids charging a builder £5 per accepted AI-proposed quote line, and a fee to a trader-builder sits outside DMCC Act 2024 drip-pricing. The rejection is on legal cost and exposure relative to £86–£297 a year, not on a prohibition. (1) It requires amending AGENTS §5.10 ('creating... a quote cannot create platform fee obligations') and D01/D02; charging at switch-live does not change that the obligation is created by quote content, so the plan's own invariant is the first casualty. (2) It gives JobGuard a financial interest in enlarging a consumer's quote. The homeowner is a consumer under CRA 2015 and DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 1; the builder as trader is liable if a proposed line is unnecessary or misleadingly presented, and a third-party fee that rewards added lines is discoverable evidence in any such dispute and in any CMA or Trading Standards look at AI-assisted quoting. JobGuard is not the trader, so direct DMCC liability is unlikely, but the incentive contradicts AGENTS §5.9 (proposals, not facts; never invent to satisfy a count) and would have to be disclosed in JobGuard's terms, which the fairness evidence (research §5) says builders read as a charge on their own work. (3) The fee is unenforceable in practice: provenance can be stripped by retyping and the incentive to over-propose degrades the product the subscription pays for. (4) The lawful, cost-free alternative already proposed elsewhere is to count accepted proposed lines in the value receipt with no charge. If pursued anyway: a §5.10 amendment, D01 v4, and a consumer-law review of quote-generation disclosures (assumption £2–4k) for trivial revenue.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended as a charge. Keep the counted-not-charged version in the value receipt (I07). If the founder insists, the conditions would be: a signed amendment to AGENTS §5.10 and D01 v4, builder-facing disclosure of the per-line incentive in terms, a consumer-law review of the proposal UI so that model_suggestion lines are visibly optional to the builder, and a cap that cannot be gamed by over-proposal (which no legal drafting can provide).

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected)

verdicts.key_risk: An AI incentive to inflate consumer quotes surfaces in a homeowner dispute or regulator inquiry and taints the builder's quote as fee-driven, for a few pounds per job.

verdicts.reasons: Legally sound if built on the plan's existing deferrals (D06, M4-19 professional review, M4-21/22 tax) and the true cost is professional review per jurisdiction plus liability cover. (1) Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 Part II, as amended by the Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009, and the Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/649, amended by SI 2011/2333) govern stage-payment entitlement (s.109, contracts of 45 days or more), payment notices (s.110A, 5 days after the due date), payee default notices (s.110B), pay-less notices (s.111; Scheme default 7 days before the final date), the pay-when-paid ban (s.113) and adjudication (s.108). Section 106 excludes contracts with a residential occupier, so the domestic stage-payment layer is purely contractual: templates must not imply statutory notice rights or statutory adjudication against homeowners (JCT Home Owner contracts carry their own scheme), and the deadline calculator must refuse residential-occupier jobs. (2) Jurisdiction: Scotland has its own Scheme (SI 1998/687 as amended) and Northern Ireland its own Order and Scheme; the plan already forbids a universal 'UK deadline', so launch England and Wales only, one contract profile (JCT, NEC, bespoke) at a time. (3) Liability: a missed pay-less notice can cost the full sum applied for (ISG v Seevic; S&T v Grove [2018] EWCA Civ 2448). Drafting notices is not a reserved legal activity under the Legal Services Act 2007, but negligence exposure is real; standard-term liability caps face UCTA 1977 s.3 reasonableness, so professional indemnity insurance is needed (assumption £1–3k/yr) and the product must be described as a tool, not advice. (4) Tax: an application for payment is not a VAT invoice (the construction stage-payment tax point under VAT Regulations 1995 reg 93 is the earlier of payment or VAT invoice); retention has its own tax-point rule (reg 89); CIS-reportable supplies between VAT-registered businesses fall under the domestic reverse charge (from 1 March 2021) unless end-user status is notified, so DRC wording and a labour/materials split are mandatory and none of it may be inferred from job type (already M4-21/M4-22 and D02). (5) Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 interest and compensation apply to commercial applications, never against residential occupiers. (6) Domestic layer consumer law: CRA 2015 Part 2 fairness of deposit and stage terms (Sch 2 paras 4–5), CCRs 2013 off-premises information and cancellation, and the DMCC total-price rule for the quoted scope; the proof-photo gate as a stage trigger is fine provided the stage sums are in the accepted quote. (7) Retention has no statutory regime (the Construction (Retention Deposit Schemes) Bill lapsed; the Fair Payment Code is voluntary), so it is contract tracking only, and a release reminder must never drift into a fee-eligible recovery, which M4-20 already states. (8) §14.3: stage invoices issued before lock must not vary with shadow signals; that is an engineering invariant, not a legal one, but a stage invoice is a real customer document under D06. (9) Per-live-job-month pricing must not be re-read as the rejected contract-value meter under D09. Cost and timeline assumption: construction-solicitor review of E&W templates and date rules £8–20k over 3–6 months, plus annual refresh and a jurisdiction gate for Scotland and NI.
verdicts.conditions: D06 v2 and M4-19 professional review by a construction solicitor for England and Wales templates, date rules and service methods (assumption £8–20k, 3–6 months), with Scotland and Northern Ireland blocked until separately reviewed. Residential-occupier detection that disables statutory-notice and adjudication language and the deadline calculator for homeowner jobs; domestic stage schedules use contractual wording only. Professional indemnity insurance in place before real notice issue; UCTA-reasonable liability terms; product described as a tool with human approval per Decision. D02/M4-21/M4-22 tax review for reg 93 stage-payment and reg 89 retention tax points, DRC wording and CIS labour/materials split; applications never styled as VAT invoices. Late Payment Act interest templates enabled only for business customers. Retention reminders and notices kept as subscription features, never converted into I14/I15-style fee cases without an explicit builder-opened case. D09 add-on terms; per-job-month pricing labelled as a feature price, not a contract-value meter.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£30 (was £0–£35; England and Wales only at launch, domestic layer contract-only)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £120–£300 (was £140–£350; E&W-only launch and slower adoption while jurisdictions gate)

verdicts.key_risk: A deadline or notice template that is wrong for the contract or jurisdiction, or applied to a residential-occupier job, causes a builder to lose a pay-less or payment-notice argument and JobGuard faces a negligence claim its standard terms cannot fully exclude.

verdicts.reasons: Would builders pay? Some, per case, once a debt is genuinely stuck: UK collectors already charge 8–15% on fresh debt and 20–35% on aged debt (report, benchmark table; benchmarks note §3), so 15/20% opt-in with the rate shown first is inside what a builder already recognises. Refutations: (1) The Managed tier's differentiator is thin. M4-5 already gives the self-serve 10% builder AI-drafted, cited reminders and letters queued for exact approval; 'Managed' adds only a human reviewing those drafts, and the builder still has to send, chase and negotiate. Five extra points for a human proofread is a hard sell on a £1–3k homeowner debt. (2) Most small-builder withheld payments are quality/snagging disputes, not pure non-payment; letters do not resolve those, and the D03 v2 entry test (overdue beyond threshold, customer refused/disputed/ignored the builder's own reminder, case explicitly opened) filters out ordinary late payment, so 1/2/4 qualifying cases a year is high; I assume 0.5/1.5/3 with 55% recovery on claims of £2k/£6k/£10k. (3) Desk economics: one controller per ~150 open cases at ~£40k loaded is ~£50–70 per case if cases turn in 60–90 days; on a solo case (£1.1k expected recovery) the incremental 5 points is ~£55, so Managed is break-even at best and Escalated (if the solicitor's fixed-fee letter, typically £150–250, is absorbed in the 20%) loses money below roughly £3k recovered. Only the Firm archetype, with larger and more often B2B debts (where Late Payment Act interest and £40–£100 compensation partly offset the fee, report §'Withheld payments from homeowners'), pays for the desk. (4) Precedent cuts both ways: the hybrid model in the market is a £25–75 file fee plus a LOWER 6–10% commission, not a higher percentage (benchmarks note §3); Chaser pairs software with a collections service but its commission was not found. (5) Regulatory: helping a builder collect its own services invoice appears outside FCA debt collecting (SRA guidance via report), but consumer debtors bring the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims (prescribed letter-of-claim content, 30-day reply), DMCC 2024 unfair/aggressive-practice rules and AJA 1970 s.40; a fixed-fee solicitor route avoids the DBA regulations for the solicitor, but JobGuard's own 20% share still needs a legal opinion that it is not a claims-management or DBA arrangement. Build: `service_tier` on `recovery_case` and a rate parameter on the v3 routine are one small task, but revenue is impossible before M4-1→M4-5 (pursuit needs D10), M4-7/M4-8 settlement evidence, M4-9/M4-10, G4 and D01 rate table v-next — i.e. the same late-M4 point as the base fee. Gaming: opening a Managed case to harvest drafting labour and settling privately is real and unpaid labour for JobGuard; the fee-on-cash-settled-after-opening rule and D11 'settled outside the app' signal detect but do not prevent it. Top failure reasons: desk becomes a loss-making cost centre on small homeowner debts; builders do not perceive a difference between AI-drafted and human-reviewed letters; scope creep toward JobGuard contacting homeowners in its own name, which D10 forbids and would need new legal review.
verdicts.conditions: Build the rate table and `service_tier` only when M4-9 v3 is implemented (cheap, parameterised, D01 versioned 10/15/20). Do not hire a desk until pilot data (§14.17) shows qualifying withheld cases per builder-year and average claim size. Escalated tier requires a minimum net claim (suggest ≥£3k) and passes the panel solicitor's fixed fee and court fees through as approved disbursements, never absorbed in the 20%. Builder remains the sender under D10 as written; legal sign-off on Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims content, DMCC 2024 and AJA 1970 s.40 for consumer debtors, and on whether JobGuard's 15/20% share is outside DBA/claims-management rules. Cap open Managed cases per tenant, tie every case to the D03 v2 entry test unchanged, and pair with the D11 'recovery discussed then no landing' signal. For B2B debtors show Late Payment Act interest and fixed compensation on the case screen; for homeowners say plainly there is no statutory offset. Fee posts only via the v3 routine on settled, allocated, unreversed cash (§14.8/14.9).

revised_revenue.solo: ≈£75/yr total fee income incl. the 10% base, of which ≈£20 is incremental (0.5 qualifying cases × £1,100 expected recovery [£2k claim × 55%] × 3.5-point blended uplift [40% Managed at +5, 15% Escalated at +10]); net of desk/solicitor cost ≈ £0 or negative
revised_revenue.small_firm: ≈£670/yr total, ≈£170 incremental (1.5 cases × £3,300 expected recovery [£6k × 55%] × 3.5 points); net of desk cost ≈ £100
revised_revenue.firm: ≈£2,200/yr total, ≈£580 incremental (3 cases × £5,500 expected recovery [£10k × 55%] × 3.5 points); net of desk ≈ £400 — the only archetype where Escalated pays for itself

verdicts.key_risk: The desk is a fixed cost sold against small, disputed homeowner debts where 5–10 extra points do not cover a controller or a solicitor letter; any drift toward JobGuard contacting homeowners in its own name to make the tier feel 'managed' breaks D10 and triggers FCA/DMCC/Pre-Action Protocol exposure.

verdicts.reasons: The number is not defensible as revenue: at 0.5/1.5/3 qualifying D03 v2 cases a year, a £35 fee yields £18/£53/£105 gross, and the idea's own suggestion of bundling two cases into Builder/Firm tiers reduces that to ≈£0–£35 for the archetypes that would ever generate it. Builders would pay £35 against a £2k+ stuck invoice, so willingness is not the objection; positioning is. The report's central finding is that JobGuard's strongest quality signal is 'a fee it earns only when the builder is paid' (report §'The founder's price-signals-quality hunch' and Conclusion); a non-refundable, non-credited file fee contradicts that headline exactly at the moment the builder is most anxious, and the failed-chase case ('they charged me £35 and I got nothing') is the kind of small grievance that travels in a word-of-mouth trade. The market precedent does not support the structure as proposed: the UK hybrid is a £25–75 file fee paired with a LOWER 6–10% commission (benchmarks note §3), whereas £35 + an unchanged 10% pushes the effective rate on a £1.5k recovery to ≈12.3%, still inside the 8–15% band but no longer at its floor. Gaming: none — the fee is itself an anti-frivolity device, which is its only genuine merit, and that merit can be had without contradicting the marketing (see conditions). Build cost is low (a fixed platform line posted under the case-opening Decision, D01 amendment, D02 VAT treatment, M4-10 statement), but production posting is behind G4 like everything else, so it delivers nothing early. Top failure reasons: trivial revenue; undermines the 'no win, no fee' signal; adds a third charge type to explain (subscription, file fee, success fee) when the report already warns the builder must see clearly what each payment buys.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable as proposed. What would change the verdict: if the pilot (§14.17) shows frivolous case openings, introduce a refundable case deposit that is credited against the success fee on recovery and refunded on a documented no-recovery close — this keeps 'we only earn when you're paid' true while deterring free-letter harvesting; it would need D01/D03 wording and D02 tax-point treatment, and must never be described as a fee.

revised_revenue.small_firm: ≈£53/yr gross; ≈£0 if two cases a year are bundled into the Builder tier as the idea suggests
revised_revenue.firm: ≈£105/yr gross; ≈£35 if two cases are bundled

verdicts.key_risk: For ≈£20–£50 a year per builder it contradicts the one marketing claim the research says carries JobGuard's credibility — a fee earned only when the builder is paid.

verdicts.reasons: The revenue collapses under its own assumptions and the labour cost exceeds it under every credible one. (1) The cash-refund assumption is wrong for builders' merchants: a trade account customer who still buys from the merchant gets a credit note against future purchases, not cash, and D03 v2 explicitly excludes supplier credit notes until a future extension (§14.7). Realistic cash share is ~10–20%, not 40–50%. (2) Merchant terms usually restrict price queries to 30–90 days; a 12-month look-back finds mostly duplicates and arithmetic errors, and even those are often already credited. (3) 'Existing intake/matching' does not apply: M2 matching compares supplier invoices to JobGuard purchase orders and quoted prices, and pre-JobGuard invoices have neither; trade pricing is negotiated and undocumented, so an auditor cannot establish 'agreed rates' for the historic period. It becomes a manual, rate-less review. (4) Economics: assuming materials at 40% of turnover and a generous 0.5% error rate, a small firm has ≈£1,200 of findable errors, half pursued successfully, 15% as cash = ≈£90 cash, 20% of which is £18; plus a £295 setup at 30% take-up (≈£89) gives ≈£105 one-off against 15–20 auditor hours (2,000+ invoices). Firm: ≈£260 one-off against 40–50 hours. Solo: ≈£6 against ~5 hours. Every archetype is loss-making. (5) Comparable products: AP recovery auditors at 20–30% work for corporates where $1bn of spend yields ~$1m (benchmarks note §1, PRGX claim); Inspired PLC's telecoms audit spans six years of bills — these need scale that a £150k–£2m builder cannot supply. (6) Would builders pay £295–£495 up front, days after signing up for £29–£119 a month, for an audit of last year's invoices? Very few; the Solo version (no setup, 25%) is the only frictionless one and returns ≈£6. Trust is fine (builder commissions it, nothing from suppliers) and gaming is minor (builder nets the refund and reports nothing — which, given the labour already spent, just deepens the loss). Top failure reasons: merchants credit rather than refund; no agreed rates to audit against; human audit cost dwarfs revenue; it diverts the small ops team into low-value labour before the core product is proven.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable as proposed. What would change the verdict: a fully automated, free duplicate/VAT-arithmetic scan of imported historic invoices as an onboarding hook and pilot data source — no setup fee, no auditor, no contingent share; anything it finds is a value-receipt item, not a fee.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈£6 one-off (£60k materials × 0.5% × 50% pursued × 15% cash × 25%); ≈5 auditor hours → net −£100 or worse
revised_revenue.small_firm: ≈£105 one-off (£89 setup at 30% take-up + £18 contingent on ≈£90 cash refunds); ≈15–20 auditor hours → net ≈ −£300
revised_revenue.firm: ≈£260 one-off (£198 setup at 40% take-up + £60 contingent); ≈40–50 auditor hours → net ≈ −£900

verdicts.key_risk: Merchants settle historic overcharges with credit notes, which D03 v2 excludes, so the contingent share is near zero while the human audit labour is real.

verdicts.reasons: As a revenue line it is weak, cannibalising and leaky; as a funnel it is priced wrong. (1) Cannibalisation: all three archetypes run 19–33 jobs a year, so at £29 a check the only rational pay-per-use customers are cherry-pickers; a Solo using it on half their jobs pays ≈£276–£338, roughly the £348 Solo subscription, while JobGuard delivers no watchdog, no retention and thinner catches. (2) Leakage is worst here: the §14.10 residual risk (builder takes the reveal and bills outside JobGuard) is bounded for subscribers by the relationship, the same-invoice rule (§14.4) and later bank verification (M4-7); a non-subscriber has none of those, so the paid-catch rate on which the 15% depends is more like 10% than 20%. (3) Evidence quality: an imported quote lacks JobGuard scope-item identities, photos are untagged, POs are absent, so the §14.6 tests 'absent from accepted scope' and 'absent from builder captures' rest on weaker matching → more false positives → more disputes, and D13 requires unresolved disputes to be fee-free. (4) Consumer-law exposure: for subscribers the catch goes on the same final invoice before issue; a pay-per-use builder has often already sent their own bill, so a confirmed catch becomes a late, separate extra bill to a homeowner — exactly the DMCC-era dispute-prone scenario the report warns about (§'The hidden final check', Linklaters/TLT points). (5) Reworked revenue for a non-subscriber: Solo ≈3 checks × £29 + ≈£5 of catches (25% catch rate × £400 × 10% billed-and-paid via JobGuard × 15%) ≈ £90; Small firm ≈£160; Firm ≈£270 — and each check costs model calls plus dispute handling. (6) Build is large and late: quote import plus upload-only intake, SV-3/4/5/6, non-member tenancy and onboarding, M4-11 hosted payment, D12 Article 14 for uploaded customer messages, and a second D01 rate (v4) that complicates every fee fixture in §14.9. (7) Comparable products: FairRate charges £0.99 per audit and serves homeowners, not builders; QuickPrice gives three free quotes a month; the report's conversion benchmarks show no-card trials converting 4–6% — a £29 paid entry is neither a free funnel nor a subscription. Gaming: the builder pays £29, harvests the reveal, bills elsewhere; the idea concedes the £29 'covers cost' and the 15% is 'upside', which is an admission the upside is not collectible. Top failure reasons: uncollectible 15%; cannibalised subscriptions; disputes on late homeowner bills; a second rate that muddies the plain '10% on every plan' message the report recommends.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable as proposed. What would change the verdict: after SV-6, offer a free one-off 'final check on a finished job' (no £29, no 15%) purely as acquisition and §14.17 measurement, with catches fee-free unless the builder subscribes and bills the catch through JobGuard at the standard 10%; no D01 v4 second rate; D12 Article 14 route for uploaded messages still required.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈£90/yr from a non-subscriber (3 checks × £29 + ≈£5 of 15% catches at a 10% billed-and-paid rate); ≈1:1 cannibalisation of the £348 Solo subscription if a subscriber downgrades
revised_revenue.small_firm: ≈£160/yr (5 checks + ≈£15 catches) against a £708 Builder subscription foregone
revised_revenue.firm: ≈£270/yr (8 checks + ≈£40 catches) against a £1,428 Firm subscription foregone

verdicts.key_risk: A non-subscriber has every incentive and no barrier to take the reveal and bill outside JobGuard, so the 15% is largely uncollectible while the check's thin evidence produces disputed, late extra bills to homeowners.

verdicts.reasons: Revenue-negative by design and behaviourally backwards. (1) The idea's own arithmetic is −£10/−£30/−£110 a year; mine is worse because breakage on a refundable credit is near zero, so the 20% discount is pure fee erosion: an 8% effective rate on a fee the report already places at the floor of every benchmark (report, benchmark table). (2) The behavioural rationale does not transfer: Prelec & Loewenstein and flat-rate bias (psychology note) explain why people prefer prepaying for consumption they anticipate; nobody anticipates 'being told what they missed', and a builder who has never seen a catch has no basis for valuing £250 of credit. (3) It damages the fairness framing the report says is JobGuard's real pricing risk: a catch should feel like found money; a prepaid builder either resents JobGuard when nothing is found ('I paid £200 for nothing', refundable or not) or is nudged to confirm marginal catches to use up credit. (4) Cash-flow benefit is trivial (£200 per builder, 0.01% of a Firm's turnover) against a new liability book: single-purpose prepayment is likely outside e-money and client-money rules, but a refundable, 24-month balance still needs refund ops, D02 tax-point treatment on receipt, and reconciliation in M4-17. (5) It adds a third money pot (subscription, credit, fee) when the report warns the builder must see clearly what each payment buys, and the fee-prepayment ledger and settlement order in M4-12 are a medium build for a negative return. Would builders pay? Sole traders are cash-constrained and wary of lock-in (report §'Offer annual billing'); prepaying a contingent fee is the least attractive prepayment imaginable. Gaming: minimal. Comparable products: prepaid SaaS credit packs sell metered consumption the buyer controls; no recovery-fee vendor sells prepaid contingency. Top failure reasons: negative revenue, no demand, wrong psychology, needless ledger.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable; nothing short of removing the discount (which removes the only incentive to prepay) would make the number positive.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈ −£8 to −£12/yr (8% effective fee on a ≈£55 fee base; ≈0 breakage on a refundable credit) plus refund handling
revised_revenue.firm: ≈ −£140/yr on a ≈£700 fee base; a £200 prepayment is ≈0.01% of turnover, no cash-flow value

verdicts.key_risk: It discounts the only fee that is already at the benchmark floor, in exchange for a refund liability and a worse fairness story.

verdicts.reasons: This is collection hygiene, not new revenue, and it should be judged as such. In its favour: the report explicitly recommends this presentation — show '£1,000 recovered; JobGuard's fee £100; yours £900' on the same screen when cash is recorded, because a separate invoice weeks later 'would feel like an isolated loss' (report §'The hidden final check', Thaler integration; psychology note (a)). JobGuard cannot net at source (it never holds customer money), so prompt, same-moment collection is the closest legal substitute, and at scale JobGuard's own receivables from thousands of small builders — a trade with a well-documented late-payment problem (report, Small Business Commissioner figures) — would otherwise become a dunning and bad-debt cost that swamps the per-builder numbers. Refutations that limit it: (1) The 'same screen as the customer receipt' moment does not exist as described. A builder's 'mark paid' is an unverified manual receipt that D03 v2 says can never qualify; the statement can only fire on settlement verified through M4-7 (TrueLayer) and allocated in M4-8, which may be days later and outside the builder's flow. So the mechanism is 'the screen where verified settlement is confirmed', which weakens the integration effect. (2) 80% vs 95% collection are guesses; direction is right, magnitude unknown, and the fee base itself (≈£55/£210/£700) is a pilot-dependent guess, so the protected amount is ≈£5–£10/£20–£40/£70–£120 a year. (3) 'Collected by Direct Debit' is not final: the DD Guarantee lets the builder claim an indemnity, and card payments can be charged back, so M4-8/M4-12 must treat both as reversal events. (4) Dependency order: GoCardless is M4-15, after M4-11→12→13→14; Stripe per-statement collection (M4-12) arrives first, so the DD version is a later increment. (5) The standing authority (≤10% of verified receipt) is bounded and revocable as AGENTS §5.3 requires, but it is a D05 approval item; the default remains approval of each exact statement. (6) Wording: §14.1 forbids 'you kept £X' without stating the VAT/tax basis, so the screen must say 'before VAT and tax'. Would builders accept it? Yes if the evidence trail is one tap away; the fairness research (Buell & Norton, Xia et al.) says visible work legitimises the charge. Gaming: none; revocation falls back to per-statement approval. Comparable products: Paddle Retain and Chargeflow deduct from flows they hold; Fergus nets card fees at source — JobGuard cannot, which is precisely why this matters. Top failure reasons: settlement verification lags the builder's moment of gain; reversals; D05 not approved so only per-statement approval ships.
verdicts.conditions: Ship in two stages: (1) same-screen statement with per-statement exact approval and Stripe hosted collection on M4-12; (2) GoCardless bounded standing authority on M4-15 only after D05 approval, bound ≤ the fee on the verified receipt, revocable, re-checked at execution (AGENTS §5.3). Trigger only on verified, allocated settlement (M4-7/M4-8), never on a builder 'mark paid'.
