Wording must state 'before VAT and tax' per §14.1 and link the evidence trail (lock, reveal, confirmation, allocation). Treat DD indemnity claims and card chargebacks as reversal/dispute events that suspend collection and create linked compensation (M4-8, M4-12). Report as protected collection, not new revenue, in any forecast.

revised_revenue.solo: +£5–£10/yr protected (not new) on a ≈£55 fee base if collection rises from ≈80% to ≈90–95%
revised_revenue.firm: +£70–£120/yr protected on a ≈£700 fee base; the real value is avoided dunning and bad debt across thousands of small receivables

verdicts.key_risk: The 'same screen' moment only exists once settlement is bank-verified and allocated (M4-7/M4-8), which can lag the builder's receipt by days, and DD/card reversals mean 'collected' is not final.

verdicts.reasons: Small money for a large policy and trust cost, with a perverse incentive at its core. (1) Revenue: 19/24/33 won jobs a year × 1/1.5/2 accepted model-proposed lines ≥£100 × £5 ≈ £95/£180/£330; the £25 cap rarely binds. That is 0.06% of a Solo's turnover. (2) It breaks the spirit of AGENTS §5.10 ('Creating, editing, reviewing, generating, or sending a quote cannot create platform fee obligations'): charging at switch-live for a fee whose cause is quote content is a timing fig leaf; it would need §5.10, D01 and D02 amended and every free-quoting promise re-worded. (3) Fairness: the report's own evidence says builders reject fees where the extra 'was already in their head' (§'The hidden final check', Xia et al.; Kahneman dual entitlement); a line the builder omitted from a site-walk narration but always intended to price is exactly that case, and `model_suggestion` provenance becomes a contested label rather than proof. (4) Incentive corruption: JobGuard would be paid to over-propose, which is in direct tension with §5.9 (cited proposals, never invent lines) and, worse, means JobGuard profits from inflating homeowner quotes — a reputational hazard in a trade where the builder's customer relationship is the asset. (5) Gaming is symmetrical and self-defeating: builders retype lines to strip provenance (cheap, undetectable, damages the scope spine), and JobGuard's detectors drift toward padding. (6) Comparable products: Qted bundles its 'AI upsell generator' in a £59 plan; Buildbite sells capture-at-source per user and merely reports a 30% change-order lift (construction note §4) — nobody charges per suggested line, because the value is captured in the subscription. Would builders pay? A few would tolerate £5, but the resentment cost of a fee on their own quote is out of proportion. Build is low, policy cost is high, and it arrives behind G4 anyway. Top failure reasons: violates free-quoting, pays JobGuard to pad quotes, contested provenance, trivial revenue.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable. The defensible version is the one the idea itself recommends: count model-proposed, accepted, priced lines in the value receipt (VALUE-2 'How JobGuard helps') and use that to justify subscription price and tier upgrades, never as a charge.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈£95/yr (19 won jobs × 1 accepted model-proposed line ≥£100 × £5)
revised_revenue.firm: ≈£330/yr (33 × 2 × £5); cap of £25 per quote almost never binds

verdicts.key_risk: It pays JobGuard to pad homeowner quotes and charges builders for their own work, breaching the free-quoting promise for under £350 a year per builder.

verdicts.reasons: Two different things are bundled, and they earn different verdicts. Domestic stage payments (deposit/first-fix/second-fix/completion on the accepted quote, stage invoices from baseline plus approved variations, proof-photo gate as trigger) are table stakes — Tradify Pro, ServiceM8 and others ship progress invoicing (trade note; construction note §2) — and JobGuard needs them anyway because §14.8 rule 3 must never spread deposits and stage receipts onto a later catch. So layer one is a core Builder-tier feature with £0 incremental revenue; its value is retention and the £59 plan being credible. The commercial layer (interim applications, Construction Act payment/pay-less/payee notices, retention ledger) is where the refutation bites: (1) Applicability. The archetypes are domestic-leaning (£8k–£60k jobs); contracts with a residential occupier are excluded from the Act, so notices and applications only matter for subcontract and commercial work — perhaps 0–10% of Solo jobs, 10–20% of Small firm, 30–50% of Firm. The idea's 30–70% adoption assumes a commercial-work share the archetypes do not have. (2) Cost. M4-18→M4-19→M4-20→M4-21 all sit behind M4-17, need D06 professional review of templates per contract family (JCT/NEC/bespoke), a deadline calculator with sources, jurisdiction profiles, and — for subcontractors in the CIS chain — M4-21 DRC VAT and M4-22 CIS before the layer is usable at all. A missed or late pay-less notice is a direct, quantifiable loss to the builder, so professional-indemnity exposure and liability terms come with it. This is the most expensive build in the list by a wide margin. (3) Price. £29–£39/month is far under Site Samurai's £99–£699 and Construction AI's £130+ (report table), so it would win on price, but reworked revenue is ≈£23/£95/£235–£470 a year per builder — meaningful only at Firm tier, where it is more naturally a reason the Firm/Contractor price is £119+ than a separate add-on. The £39 per live job-month variant reads as the contract-value meter the founder rejected and should be dropped. (4) Vendor data is weak (Payapps' '79% paid late' is a vendor claim). Trust fit is genuinely 5 — a plain feature at a plain price — provided notice reminders never blur into the 10% withheld-payment or retention categories; §14.7 already requires an explicitly opened case and M4-20 states retention release is not a fee-eligible recovery by default. Gaming: none commercially. Top failure reasons: heavy legal/build cost for a layer most archetype jobs are excluded from; liability for a late notice; stage payments mistaken for a paid add-on when they are a baseline expectation.
verdicts.conditions: Split the idea. (1) Build domestic stage payments as a core Builder-tier feature after M1-12 (schedule on the accepted quote, stage invoices from baseline plus approved variations, proof-photo gate, deposits recorded so §14.8 never spreads them onto a catch) — no add-on price. (2) Build the commercial layer only after M4-17 and only if pilot/sign-up data show a material share of Firm-tier jobs are non-residential-occupier contracts; sequence M4-18 → M4-19 → M4-20 with M4-21/M4-22 before marketing it to subcontractors. (3) Price it into the Firm/Contractor tier or as a flat £29–£39/month add-on under D09; never per job-month. (4) D06 professional review per contract family, no hard-coded universal deadline, explicit residential-occupier exclusion, service-method evidence, and PI/liability terms for notice errors. (5) Reminders and notices are subscription features; they never count as pursuit for the 10% withheld-payment category, and retention release is not a recovery (M4-20). (6) Stage invoices issued before lock must not vary with shadow signals (§14.3).

revised_revenue.solo: Stage payments: £0 incremental (core feature). Commercial layer: ≈£23/yr (5% adoption × £468); residential-occupier exclusion removes almost all solo work from the Act
revised_revenue.small_firm: Stage payments: £0 incremental. Commercial layer: ≈£95/yr (20% adoption × £468)
revised_revenue.firm: Stage payments: £0 incremental. Commercial layer: ≈£235–£470/yr (50% adoption × £468, up to ≈100% if folded into the Firm/Contractor tier price); the £39 per live job-month variant is rejected as a proxy for the rejected contract-value meter

verdicts.key_risk: The commercial layer is the costliest build in the plan (M4-18–22 plus professional review and liability for a late notice) for a regime that excludes the residential-occupier work most of these builders do.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts fail on the core module: CIS records, deduction statements and CIS-suffered reconciliation are penalty avoidance the builder does themselves today or pays Xero £5/month for (research report, 'UK builders already pay £25–£45'); JobGuard does no policing of HMRC or accountants, so watchdog independence is untouched; nothing is withheld. Two angles partly succeed and drive the conditions. (1) The accountant referral is, plainly, selling the builder as a lead to a third party — one of the three named trust risks. It is survivable only because a flat, disclosed £30–£50 handoff is visibly cheaper for the builder than the 15–30% refund-firm model they already resent (success_fee_benchmarks; report section on contingency fairness), and the builder initiates it. (2) A fairness trap sits in the plumbing: M4-22 already warns that 'a correctly evidenced deduction is not automatically classified as unpaid debt or a fee-eligible recovery'. If a CIS-suffered shortfall (HMRC holds 20%) ever surfaced as a withheld-payment signal or nudged the builder toward a fee-bearing recovery case, JobGuard would be earning 10% on money HMRC holds — exactly the 'exploiting an advantage' pattern Kahneman/Xia identify. Subcontractor invoices processed by the module are also §14.2 evidence, so the paid module widens the shadow-bill base; that must be said, not discovered.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Referral is flat, optional, builder-initiated, disclosed at the point of referral with the amount JobGuard receives, non-exclusive (builder may name their own accountant, and the records export is identical either way); never a percentage, never a default, no accountant sees CIS data before the builder clicks. (b) CIS deduction and CIS-suffered amounts are structurally excluded from withheld_customer_payment eligibility, recovery-case suggestions, D11 signals and shadow signals (test at the predicate level, M4-22 'Done when' extended). (c) The add-on description states that subcontractor invoices it processes are job evidence under §14.2, using the standing notice wording, not a per-document badge. (d) Subcontractor personal data (UTR, verification numbers) lives in a narrowly granted table under D12, never in audit payloads. (e) DRC VAT stays a flag until D06 review; no 'we file' or 'HMRC-recognised' claim.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£75 (unchanged; referral income only if flat and disclosed)

verdicts.key_risk: A CIS deduction being read by recovery or shadow logic as withheld customer money, producing a 10% fee on cash HMRC holds; secondarily, the referral being perceived as JobGuard selling its builders to accountants.

verdicts.reasons: The obvious refutation (charging for what Tradify bundles free on all plans) is answered by the idea itself: in tier on Builder/Firm, free on annual Solo, £9–£15 on monthly Solo, which keeps a Solo at £38–£44 under Tradify Lite plus a second user. A second refutation has more force: MTD makes categorised records compulsory for the Solo archetype (report, 'Builders' willingness to pay is anchored low' — MTD is 'a second compulsory subscription competing for the same budget'), so a toll on the bridge to a tax obligation edges toward exploiting a captive need; the annual-free route and the absence of any 'MTD-compatible' claim keep it on the fair side because the builder can leave the data in JobGuard and export it. Watchdog independence is unaffected (Xero, QuickBooks and Codat are not policed parties). The angle that nearly succeeds is withheld information: SV-7 names accounting as an approved evidence connector, so a sync the builder pays for could silently pull supplier bills from Xero into the evidence base that feeds the fee finder, and an outbound export carrying three-way-match status must not vary with signal existence (§14.3). The M5-1 rule that a Xero 'paid' label never counts as settlement evidence protects the builder from manufactured fee events and should be kept verbatim.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The paid add-on is push-out only by default (invoices, credit notes, receipts, confirmed supplier bills to the ledger); any inbound pull of bills or bank lines into JobGuard evidence is a separate, explicitly enabled toggle labelled with the §14.2 standing notice, and is never a precondition for the sync working. (b) Export payloads and the monthly reconciliation pack are byte-identical with and without shadow signals (extend Test Q to the connector). (c) A ledger 'paid' flag can never satisfy settlement for any fee category (M5-1 rule, D03). (d) Free on Solo annual and free on all tiers for a one-off full export so no builder pays to leave. (e) No 'MTD-compatible' or 'HMRC-recognised' wording; D04 destination verification for Codat/Xero/QuickBooks before any real data.

revised_revenue.solo: £72–£108 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: A builder paying for a sync that quietly widens JobGuard's shadow-bill evidence base ('I paid you to move my books and you used them to find things to charge me 10% on'), or an export whose content varies with hidden signals.

verdicts.reasons: This is the honest way to monetise prevention: a flat fee for site-visit omissions caught at quote time, which the founder accepts cannot carry a success fee. It is fully in the builder's interest, no merchant is involved, and Kreo's £25–£125 per user shows the takeoff itself is worth paying for. The refutation that succeeds is structural, not about the feature: drawings uploaded to a job are 'imported documents' and therefore §14.2 evidence. A builder without the add-on who uploads plans (or whose customer sends them through the portal) would have JobGuard hold the drawing-vs-scope gap as a shadow signal, stay silent because the paid diff was not bought, and earn 10% after lock. That is the report's 'knew on day 12, told me on day 60' scenario made worse, because the answer existed in a product feature JobGuard chose to gate, and JobGuard would earn more from builders who did not buy the warning. A reasonable builder would call that unfair (exploiting an advantage). The fix keeps 'quoting is free' literally true: omission warnings from drawings are free for everyone at quote time; the £19 buys measured, cited quantities and rate-book pricing.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The coverage diff (omission warnings such as 'the drawing shows a soil-stack move you did not mention') runs and is shown free at quote review for any job with drawings, regardless of add-on status; the paid part is measured quantities, counts and priced takeoff lines. (b) Any shadow signal whose sole or primary evidence is a drawing available before quote acceptance is treated as disclosed_before_lock (fee-ineligible), so JobGuard can never profit from a quote-stage omission it could have surfaced. (c) AGENTS §5.9 applies without exception: no invented quantities, citations to drawing regions validated against the stored file, a golden set measuring omission and unsupported additions. (d) Drawings carry the site address: D04 route and D12 apply before real files.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (unchanged; no take-up assumed)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £228 (unchanged; Kreo pricing supports £19 for takeoff alone even with the warning free)

verdicts.key_risk: A paywalled omission warning creating a path where JobGuard earns a 10% fee precisely because the builder did not pay to be told at quote time.

verdicts.reasons: Tried to refute on four fronts. Watchdog independence: the benchmark is aligned with the watchdog (it arms builders against merchants) and the idea already puts 'merchants never pay' in writing; the residual danger is that JobGuard would come to hold exactly the data merchants would pay most for, and any later merchant payment or placement would collapse the invoice watchdog. Withheld information: showing 'you paid over median' at PO pre-commit is fee-free prevention, but a price above median is not an overcharge against an agreed price, so it must never seed a supplier_overcharge case (§14.7 requires a settled cash refund against an approved case) or the builder pays £15 for the benchmark and 10% on what it found. Harm to the builder: research notes flag that merchant trade-account terms may restrict sharing negotiated prices, so contributing could put a builder in breach with their own merchant; and small builders in a sparse region would pay for empty bands for a year or more (the idea concedes year-2+). Fairness: opt-in, give-to-get, builder-only funded, aggregated with k-anonymity is how trade price surveys already work; a reasonable builder would see 'my prices help theirs, theirs help mine, merchants never see it' as fair, provided the pool is real when they are charged. Selling-builders'-data risk is present in its mildest form and must be stated on the pricing page, not the terms.
verdicts.conditions: (a) A written, tested, non-negotiable rule: no merchant, buying group, insurer or lead platform ever pays for, sees or receives any pooled figure, placement, rebate or referral; any such contract is a policy breach that disables the feature. (b) Aggregation runs under an isolated database role (as for jobguard_shadow) with catalog tests; no tenant-identifiable row leaves the tenant; k-anonymity ≥10 tenants and ≥30 observations per cell, and no single tenant above ~20% of a cell. (c) No charge until the builder's region has populated cells for the categories they actually buy; contributors on annual plans are free. (d) A benchmark finding is never a Finding of overcharge, never creates or suggests a recovery case, and is worded 'your price vs pool median' with sample size and confidence, never 'merchant X overcharges you'. (e) Onboarding copy warns that some merchant trade-account terms restrict sharing negotiated prices and lets the builder exclude specific suppliers. (f) New decision record (D14 pooling) plus CMA information-exchange and ICO anonymisation review before any real data, since M5-6 disables cross-tenant learning.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 until regional cells populate, then £36–£180

verdicts.key_risk: The pool becoming a merchant-monetisable asset (any merchant money ends the watchdog's independence) and builders breaching their own merchant confidentiality terms by contributing.

verdicts.reasons: Harder to defend than I28 because it pools selling rates, the most competitively sensitive data a builder holds, between competitors. Refutation angles: harm to the builder if a rival or homeowner could infer their rates (a FairRate-style outward leak would be fatal to word-of-mouth trust); harm to the customer relationship is indirect but real if the tool is seen as nudging every builder toward the median (a hub-and-spoke pattern regulators watch); and cold start means charging £15 for a labelled price-book comparison, not '140 confirmed rates in the South West'. No merchant is involved, so watchdog independence is intact, and there is no withheld-information path: underpricing is prevention and can never carry a fee. What keeps it: the builder opts in, contributes only accepted-quote rates, receives a direct benefit that pays for itself on one job, and JobGuard earns only the flat fee. Aggregated, historical (12-month), anonymised bands with minimum group sizes are the form competition guidance generally tolerates, but that is a legal opinion JobGuard must obtain, not assume. A builder must be able to refuse pooling and lose nothing of their own rate book.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Same pooling decision record, isolated role, k-anonymity and single-tenant share cap as I28, plus a written promise on the pricing page that rate data is never sold or shown to merchants, insurers, lead platforms, homeowners or any non-contributing party. (b) UK competition-law review of the exact cell definitions, lag and thresholds before any real data; bands only at n ≥ 20 from ≥ 10 tenants, 12-month window, no forward-looking or current-quote rates. (c) Opting out of contribution never degrades the builder's own M1-4 rate book or suggestions. (d) Until cells exist, the product is sold and labelled as 'published price-book comparison' at a lower price or free, never as a peer benchmark. (e) The benchmark never changes a quote line; it is a proposal under AGENTS §5.9 and the builder's own rate always stays selectable.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 in year 1 (or a cheaper labelled price-book tier), £180 once pool cells exist
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0 in year 1, £180 once pool cells exist
revised_revenue.firm: £0 in year 1, £180 once pool cells exist

verdicts.key_risk: Competition-law exposure and any leak or inference of a builder's selling rates to rivals or homeowners; a single outward sale would make JobGuard the channel that leaked builders' prices.

verdicts.reasons: The builder's own data leaving on the builder's instruction; no merchant, no customer, no withheld-information path provided §14.3 holds (responses byte-identical with and without shadow signals, same RLS context). Two refutations have partial force. First, fairness: charging £49 for access to your own data reads as 'pay to get out' (exploiting an advantage) unless a complete free export and the free read-only accountant seat exist regardless, so the £49 clearly buys live machine integration, not access. Second, hidden-information leakage by side channel: webhooks fired from the outbox on job events could betray shadow-table activity by timing or event count, and third-party integrations built on the API (a merchant's, say) could become a route for supplier money into JobGuard's ecosystem. Both are precisely conditionable. Demand is narrow (one in four firms) and it is not a Solo product, so the revenue estimate stands.
verdicts.conditions: (a) A free, complete export (jobs, documents, evidence packs, ledgers) and the free accountant seat exist on every tier; the API charge is for tokens, rate limits and webhooks only, and a builder can always leave with their data at no cost. (b) No webhook event type, count, ordering or latency may derive from shadow-table activity; the M5-7 conformance suite proves tokens cannot read shadow tables, reach commercial commands, or broaden finance/order/export authority. (c) Tokens are tenant-bound, scoped, rotatable, rate-limited and audited; a leaked token is a builder trust event, so the API is security-reviewed before G5. (d) JobGuard publishes no merchant-endorsed integrations and receives no payment from any integrator that supplies or invoices builders.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: 'Pay to access your own data' perception if free export is less complete than the API, and a webhook side channel leaking the existence of hidden signals before lock.

verdicts.reasons: This one the refutation wins. JobGuard's whole pricing story, per the research recommendation, is 'per business, unlimited users', chosen because per-seat pricing discourages adding the people who feed evidence (report, 'Charge for live jobs, not people'). A bookkeeper is an ordinary member of a small builder's team; charging £15 after a headline of 'unlimited users' is the drip-pricing pattern UK buyers now recognise from the DMCC enforcement mood, even if B2B is outside the law. It also taxes the acquisition channel: bookkeepers and accountants are plausibly how MTD-era sole traders find JobGuard, and Xero's free adviser access exists precisely because the adviser is a growth lever, not a revenue line. The upside is trivial (£54–£108 a year per builder) against a contradiction of the headline promise and slower adoption; it also collides with the free practice view in I61. Nothing here touches watchdog independence or withheld information, so the objection is fairness and self-interest, not integrity. The finance role and its RLS-tested permission scope are still worth building for security reasons (invoice and credit-note issue rights, D11 credit-note signals), just not as a paid seat.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a paid seat. If revisited: make the finance seat free on every tier with its own permission scope and RLS tests; charge, if at all, only external practices managing many clients under I61 practice pricing, never the individual builder.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (seat made free)

verdicts.key_risk: Contradicting 'unlimited users' and taxing the bookkeeper channel that brings MTD-era sole traders to JobGuard, for revenue too small to matter.

verdicts.reasons: On price the idea is fair and market-normal: Tradify charges 10p per SMS, ServiceM8 5p, Fergus £8 per 100, and a tiered allowance at cost plus margin is transparent. No merchant is involved. The refutation that bites is withheld information, and it is the sharpest in this batch: messages and replies routed through JobGuard are §14.2 evidence, so a builder would be paying JobGuard to carry the customer conversations that become the richest source for the post-lock fee finder ('could you also do the outside tap?' held until lock, then 10%). This stays inside the already-decided shadow-bill rule, but the paid channel adds two new pressures: JobGuard now has a margin and a fee-base incentive to move conversations in-thread, and the report's finding that disclosure does not neutralise a conflict (Cain et al.) means the onboarding sentence alone will not carry it. There is also a customer-side risk: the homeowner's late-revealed extra is a consumer transaction, and if customers come to see 'via JobGuard' messaging as an app looking for things to bill them for, the builder's relationship suffers. A reasonable builder can still see it as fair if the channel is priced like any other, nothing nudges them into it, the standing notice is on the thread, and the D13 must-surface rule for customer work requests actually fires at a threshold that feels low to a builder.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The standing §14.2 notice is shown on the message thread itself ('Messages here are part of your job record. To bill for extra work, use Log an extra. JobGuard checks your records against your final bill after you complete it'), never a per-message badge. (b) No prompt, discount, default or onboarding step nudges a builder to move a specific conversation into JobGuard; the add-on is off by default. (c) Margin capped at or below market (about Tradify's 10p) and shown on the pricing page; overage metered exactly on provider receipts and visible in-app. (d) The D13 threshold for 'clear customer request for significant work' is tested against pilot data from this channel and the pilot's 'did hiding hurt' measure (§14.17); if builders report messages they needed mid-job, lower it before G4. (e) Customer-facing wording (D12 v2, Article 14) is neutral and controlled by the builder; reminders remain infrastructure messages or go through the command boundary (AGENTS §5.3). (f) UK/EU-resident provider verified under D04; PECR consent handling for anything beyond service messages.

revised_revenue.solo: £60 (unchanged; about £40 if overage goes to cost)

verdicts.key_risk: 'I paid you to carry my messages and you used them to find things to charge me for' — the paid channel becoming the fee finder's main source, with a matching customer-side perception that JobGuard reads their messages to bill them later.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempted and mostly failed. (1) Harm to builder: none found; the CCRs 2013 off-premises cancellation notice is a real, common omission that exposes builders to cancellation up to 12 months later and to losing the right to payment for work done in the cancellation window, and a staged schedule plus a written variation clause is plainly in the builder's interest. (2) Watchdog independence: no supplier or merchant money; the only payer is the builder (and a partner solicitor who is paid by the builder for bespoke work). (3) Profiting from withheld information: the reverse. A variation clause that mirrors Log an extra and customer approval pushes more extras into builder capture (BUILD_PLAN §14.2), which shrinks JobGuard's own success-fee base. That is the strongest evidence that the idea serves the builder rather than JobGuard. (4) Customer relationship: proper terms, a cancellation notice and staged payments are what a professional builder is expected to provide; a homeowner is more, not less, likely to trust them. (5) Fairness (Xia et al.: who did the work, who bears the cost): the solicitor drafted, JobGuard integrated, the builder pays for a product they use. The one refutation that partly lands is partitioned pricing: if the watchdog flags 'your quote has no cancellation notice' on every quote and then sells the fix at £29/month, a builder will read it as the product withholding basic compliance to upsell, which is the same shape as the trust risk the brief names. That is fixable, so keep with conditions.
verdicts.conditions: (a) A plain, generic CCR cancellation-notice warning and a basic free cancellation-notice template ship inside the free quote for consumer jobs; the paid pack covers the reviewed full terms, staged schedule, variation clause and bespoke review. The watchdog never withholds a compliance warning to sell an add-on. (b) Templates are jurisdiction-profiled (England and Wales vs Scotland; consumer vs business customer) under D06 and M4-19; no universal Construction Act regime is assumed. (c) 'Solicitor-reviewed' is stated only if a named partner firm owns and periodically reviews the templates, with the review date shown; JobGuard gives no legal advice and says so. (d) Any referral or margin JobGuard earns on the £295 bespoke review is disclosed at the point of purchase. (e) The variation clause must accept written approval by any route (email, signed note) as well as the JobGuard portal, so the contract never forces the builder's customer onto JobGuard. (f) Short-form terms for jobs under a stated value so a £2k job is not buried in legal text. (g) Not an offset against, or a condition of, any success fee (D01).

revised_revenue.solo: £100–£139 (free basic cancellation notice removes some fear-driven take-up; assumes 30–40% on £29/month or per-quote £10)

verdicts.key_risk: A reasonable builder will see the pack as fair only if basic legal compliance is already free; if the watchdog nags about a missing cancellation notice and sells the fix, the pack reads as withheld protection and damages the trust the shadow bill already strains. Secondary: template liability and jurisdiction accuracy (legal review, not JobGuard's word).

verdicts.reasons: Refutation partly succeeded. (1) Harm to builder: the failure mode is charging at the moment of distress for the builder's own evidence, which they captured all job on a paid subscription. The idea's answer (free raw export always one tap away, pay only for anchoring, signature, verifier, narrative and formatting) survives the 'who did the work' test: JobGuard did produce the artefact, and £40–£149 against £350–£1,200/day for a claims consultant is a price a builder will recognise as fair. (2) Independence: no supplier money, but the £50 mediation-partner referral is third-party money for steering the builder to a provider, which is the 'selling builders as leads' risk the brief names. It creates an incentive to recommend mediation (and one partner) over settlement or other routes. As written, that part fails. (3) Profiting from withheld information: 'packs before lock never include shadow content' is required by §14.3, but ordering a dispute, ADR or small-claims pack is itself strong evidence of an active dispute, which is a D13 must-surface trigger ('an active dispute that silence would materially worsen'). Selling a builder an 'evidence-complete' bundle while a relevant signal sits in the shadow tables is exactly the betrayal scenario (Bohnet and Zeckhauser; the report's 'knew on day 12, told me on day 60'). Fixable, but only structurally. (4) Customer relationship: an ADR bundle sent identically to both parties is the ADR norm; a small-claims pack is the builder's choice; no generated threats. (5) Fairness: per-pack pricing must not read as a per-job platform fee (§5.10) and recipient-bound authority must not read as lock-in of the builder's own evidence.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Drop the mediation referral fee, or disclose it in pounds at the point of referral, offer a choice of CTSI-approved bodies, and prove (test) that the referral never changes which dispute route or body the product suggests. (b) Ordering any dispute, ADR or small-claims pack before lock is recorded as a D13 dispute event: the must-surface evaluation runs, anything surfaced is permanently fee-ineligible (§14.3), and the pack is generated only after that evaluation. (c) Free export contains every underlying file with its SHA-256 and server receive time, so a builder never needs the paid pack to obtain their evidence; the paid pack adds only anchoring, signature, verifier, manifest and narrative. (d) Recipient binding is builder-chosen and re-issuable to a new recipient (new solicitor, new insurer) at no extra charge. (e) Never 'tamper-proof' or 'court-ready'; the integrity statement says what the pack does and does not prove (§5.7/5.8). (f) D09 states in terms that pack fees are per-artefact service charges, not per-job platform fees, and never offset a success fee. (g) A dispute resolved through ADR is fee-free unless a D03-compliant withheld-payment case was already open, and if one is open the builder sees the combined cost (pack plus 10%) before ordering.

revised_revenue.solo: £40–£98 excluding any mediation referral income

verdicts.key_risk: Selling a 'complete' evidence pack pre-lock while JobGuard holds a relevant shadow signal; one such story in the trade would confirm the 'held my own money to ransom' reading and spread by word of mouth. Second: the referral fee turns a builder in a dispute into a lead.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation largely failed. (1) Harm to builder: a fixed £395/£750 for 2–5 hours of a QS or claims consultant at market day rates (£350–£1,200) is cheaper and bounded, visibly effortful (Buell and Norton), and on the builder's own evidence; a small builder in a £3k dispute cannot otherwise afford this work. (2) Independence: no supplier money; JobGuard's margin on panel work is a normal intermediary margin if disclosed. (3) Profiting from withheld information: the idea already says preparers work only from builder-visible data, but 'flags evidence gaps' is the exact point where a reviewer who could see shadow data would either leak it or, worse, stay silent while JobGuard holds the missing evidence. The same pre-lock dispute trigger as I34 applies: ordering a reviewed dispute pack is an active dispute under D13. (4) Customer relationship: factual chronology only, builder states the claimed amount, no generated threats; the builder chooses whether to escalate. (5) Fairness: the one refutation that lands is double charging where a D03 withheld-payment case is open: £395 plus 10% on a £3k recovery is an effective 23%, above the 8–15% a builder would pay a collector all-in, and the 'engagement fee plus contingency' shape is the one R&D-tax critics called excessive. The adjudication grade is also mostly inapplicable to domestic jobs (Construction Act adjudication generally excludes residential occupiers; flagged unverified in the research) so it must not be sold where the contract provides no adjudication route.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The external reviewer role has no grant on shadow tables, enforced by real-PostgreSQL role tests (SV-2 pattern), not policy; reviewers never receive break-glass access. (b) Ordering a reviewed pack before lock triggers the D13 must-surface evaluation; anything surfaced is permanently fee-ineligible. (c) Where a D03 withheld-payment case is open on the job, the builder sees the combined all-in cost (pack fee plus 10% on the expected recovery) before ordering, and the standard I34 pack is included in the case at no extra charge; only the human-reviewed grade is charged. (d) The adjudication grade is offered only where the contract actually provides for adjudication (business customer or an express clause); otherwise the product says so rather than selling it. (e) Factual assembly only: no legal advice, no conduct of litigation, 'builder to complete' on every assertion, no claims-management wording (Legal Services Act 2007; avoid CMC language). (f) Panel contracts and JobGuard's margin disclosed to the builder in the order screen.

revised_revenue.firm: £1,000–£1,600 (adjudication grade limited to contracts that provide adjudication; standard pack included where a D03 case is open)

verdicts.key_risk: A reviewer flagging 'evidence gaps' while JobGuard silently holds the missing evidence in shadow tables; must be structurally impossible pre-lock. Secondary: perceived double dip where pack fee and 10% success fee land on the same dispute.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation largely succeeded in the form proposed. (1) Independence and trust: this makes the builder's customer a paying JobGuard customer, with a homeowner account, 15-year hosted retention and share links. JobGuard would then hold paid relationships with both sides of every future payment dispute and of the withheld-payment recovery category, and would own a homeowner relationship it could later market to. That is a milder version of the two-sided conflict that makes I38 a hard reject, and it touches the brief's named risk of selling to builders' customers. (2) Harm to builder: the record is symmetric evidence; proof photos of covered work and 'uploaded by builder' certificates are as useful to a homeowner in a defect claim as to the builder in a 'you never showed me' dispute. Opt-in per job handles that only if the builder previews exactly what is sealed. (3) Fairness (who did the work): the builder did the work, paid the subscription, captured the proof; JobGuard then sells the record of that work to the builder's customer for £69 and keeps the money. A reasonable builder will ask why JobGuard is monetising their customer and their job. (4) Customer relationship: a JobGuard checkout page in the homeowner portal reads as the builder's software upselling the homeowner, and any wording error reflects on the builder. What survives: a builder-branded handover pack is a genuine professional asset (the property-logbook precedent), so a form in which the builder is the seller and JobGuard charges the builder a fixed fulfilment fee removes the two-sided conflict and passes the fairness test. Revenue is small either way (£130–£570 as proposed), so the trust cost is not worth taking to keep the higher figure.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The builder is the seller or gifter: the homeowner pays the builder (or nothing), and JobGuard charges the builder a fixed fulfilment fee on the platform statement; JobGuard takes no payment from the homeowner and holds no paying homeowner customer. If the founder insists on JobGuard as seller, then at minimum a builder revenue share and builder-set price. (b) The homeowner account exists only to view and share the record; no marketing, no other product, no data use beyond hosting, written into BUILD_PLAN §11 out-of-scope. (c) Strict subset enforced structurally: nothing from shadow tables, findings, D11 signals, supplier prices, margins, or any catch the builder dismissed or chose not to charge; the builder previews the exact contents before it is offered. (d) Never offered while a dispute or withheld-payment case is open on the job, and only after lock and final payment. (e) Certificates labelled 'uploaded by the builder, not verified by JobGuard'; multi-year retention only after D07 approval; consumer-sale rules (CRA 2015, CCRs 2013) and D12 v2 homeowner controller role resolved by legal review before launch.

revised_revenue.solo: £30 (fixed £15 fulfilment fee, 10% uptake); £130 only in the not-recommended JobGuard-as-seller form

verdicts.key_risk: Turning the builder's customers into JobGuard's paying customers creates a permanent two-sided relationship that a builder will read as JobGuard working both sides of the table; the revenue is too small to justify that reading.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation partly succeeded. What survives: the builder chooses to send their own evidence to their own insurer, pays nothing, and the pack is identical to what they can export free; that is plainly in the builder's interest and a genuine trust and marketing line ('insurers accept JobGuard packs'). What fails: the per-pack insurer fee. Insurers are not suppliers the watchdog polices, so the 'money from the policed party' refutation does not apply, but the insurer is the counterparty that decides whether the builder's claim is paid and sets their premium. Taking £75 from that party for each pack creates an incentive to shape packs for claims-handler convenience rather than the builder's case, and it is the thin end of the per-policyholder data-feed variant (I46) that the brief flags. The idea itself estimates £4–£30 a year, which is a rounding error. Trading a structural conflict of interest for negligible revenue fails the fairness test (Kahneman et al.: exploiting a position for profit is judged unfair even when small). The clean form is a free feature; a disclosed cost-recovery fee is tolerable.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Builder-initiated only; no insurer can request, pull or subscribe to packs, and no per-policyholder feed, risk score or premium-related data ever flows to an insurer (record in BUILD_PLAN out-of-scope). (b) Prefer no insurer fee; if one is retained, it is disclosed to the builder in pounds on the send screen before sending, and capped at cost recovery. (c) The pack sent is byte-identical to the builder's own I34 pack and the builder reviews it before send; nothing from shadow tables, findings or D11 signals. (d) D12 Article 14 route for the homeowner's personal data in the pack, insurer as separate controller, D07 export receipts. (e) Integrity statement only; no assertion of workmanship or liability.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (recommended free form); £4 if a disclosed fee is kept

verdicts.key_risk: Accepting insurer money per pack opens the door to insurers as a customer, and the next ask is a data feed on the builder; the builder who learns JobGuard is paid by their insurer will not believe the pack is built for them.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation succeeded on every test, and the idea is listed to be rejected. (1) Independence: JobGuard would be paid by the homeowner to audit the builder using records the builder gave it for their own protection, while simultaneously holding shadow signals of the builder's unbilled extras and earning 10% on withheld payments the same homeowner may be refusing. That is JobGuard working both sides of the same bill for money. (2) Trust: it is the single clearest way to prove the 'JobGuard is not on my side' story; in a word-of-mouth trade it would end the product. (3) Fairness: the builder did the work and paid the subscription; JobGuard sells scrutiny of that work to the counterparty. (4) Customer relationship: it invites the homeowner to dispute the final account at JobGuard's suggestion. (5) Regulatory: a serious UK GDPR purpose-limitation problem (D12) and a direct consumer sale. The portal already gives the homeowner free transparency of quote, approved variations and proof, so no legitimate need is unmet. It is trivial to build, which is exactly why it needs an explicit written 'never'.
verdicts.conditions: Record an explicit 'never build' entry in BUILD_PLAN §11 out-of-scope and in D12, covering any homeowner-paid or third-party-paid audit, score or verdict on a builder's account, quote or evidence; no exceptions for 'free' or 'partner' variants.
verdicts.key_risk: Existential trust risk: paid by the builder's customer to audit the builder, colliding head-on with the shadow bill and the withheld-payment fee; not survivable in a referral-driven trade.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation mostly failed. (1) Harm to builder: bank transfer stays free, the application fee is capped (£6–£15) and itemised, and builders on Fergus (1.6% + 20p), Tradify and Jobber already pay comparable or higher processor fees; the hosted link also protects both parties from invoice-redirection fraud because the payer uses JobGuard-verified details rather than bank details copied from an email. (2) Independence: the payer of the fee is the builder, not a supplier or merchant the watchdog polices; Stripe and GoCardless are rails, not policed parties. (3) Profiting from a withheld advantage: the one real refutation. A rail settlement bound to the invoice is what makes §14.8 attribution clean, so JobGuard gains twice when a customer pays a catch-bearing invoice by the paid rail (fee plus provable allocation). If link placement, copy, or fee level varied with the presence of a catch, that would be exploiting JobGuard's control of the invoice channel (dual entitlement) and would leak catch existence pre-lock in breach of §14.3 byte-identity. It must be structurally impossible, which is achievable. (4) Customer relationship: surcharging consumers is unlawful, so the homeowner pays nothing extra; a hosted pay link is now normal. (5) Fairness: a capped, optional, itemised service fee for a service the builder chooses passes the who-pays test; instant payout at 1.5% against Stripe's 1% is a small margin on the builder's cash flow that is fair only if never default-on and never pushed to a builder who is short of cash. Note the application-fee mechanic means the payment fee is deducted from the customer's payment before it reaches the builder, which is acceptable for the payment fee (same as Fergus) but would be a serious breach if ever used for the subscription or success fee.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Pay-link placement, copy, prominence and fee level are identical on every invoice regardless of catch lines, and bank-transfer details are always shown with equal prominence; add this to the SV-3 byte-identity tests. (b) The application fee is never waived, discounted or varied by catch presence or by JobGuard's success-fee position. (c) Only the payment-service fee is ever taken as a Connect application fee; subscription and success fees are always separately invoiced and separately authorised per statement (D05), never deducted from a customer payment or a Connect balance. (d) Instant payout is off by default, priced in pounds before the tap, never offered on fee collections, and never targeted at builders with overdue bills or low balances. (e) Rail settlement is treated as invoice-level allocation only (§14.8 rule 2 or 3), not as line-level explicit allocation unless the catch is on its own invoice; 'provider cleared' stays distinct from 'settled' across dispute windows, with chargebacks and refunds flowing into §14.9 reversals. (f) Legal opinion that Connect Standard direct charges and pay-by-bank keep JobGuard outside PSRs 2017; hosted surfaces only, no funds held (AGENTS §3); Payment Surcharges Regulations respected; new rails get their own tasks under 'Discovered later'. (g) Gross and net shown on every statement line labelled 'JobGuard payment fee', never as a percentage of the job.

revised_revenue.solo: £90–£300 rails (+£75 instant payout)

verdicts.key_risk: Any difference in how the pay link is presented on invoices carrying catches would both leak the shadow bill and look like JobGuard steering the builder's customer for its own benefit; the safeguard is structural byte-identity, not policy.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation partly succeeded. (1) Harm to builder: predictable staged cash is what small builders want and the add-on is flat and stated, but the Direct Debit Guarantee lets a homeowner reclaim a collection by indemnity claim after the work is done, which shifts the risk back to the builder at the worst moment; a deposit collected during the CCR 14-day cancellation window is refundable if the homeowner cancels, so without the I33 cancellation notice and an express request to start early the builder is exposed. Homeowners are also unused to signing a Bacs mandate to a builder, and commercial VRP may not exist in 2026, so adoption assumptions (15/40/60%) are optimistic. (2) Independence: no supplier or merchant money; GoCardless or TrueLayer is the regulated institution and settles to the builder; JobGuard holds no funds (AGENTS §3, D10). (3) Withheld information: no interaction with shadow tables as long as stage approval is the builder's proof-gated decision and no timer collects. (4) Customer relationship: a mandate that lets the builder pull money can feel coercive to a homeowner if presented as a condition of the job; Bacs advance notice and the right to cancel any single collection mitigate it, and the homeowner still approves each stage in effect. (5) Fairness: £9–£19 a month plus £1 per collection above provider cost, billed on the subscription invoice and never deducted from the customer's payment, passes the who-pays test and does not offset the success fee. Fair with safeguards, but the risk transfer to the builder needs to be said plainly.
verdicts.conditions: (a) No collection is ever submitted without a builder Decision approved against verified proof for that stage; no timer or schedule can collect on its own (§5.3, D05 bounds only JobGuard's authority). (b) The deposit template respects the CCR cancellation window: either collect after it, or record the customer's express request to start early with the I33 notice served; D06-reviewed. (c) The builder is told in plain words at add-on purchase and at each stage that a Direct Debit collection can be reclaimed by indemnity claim and that JobGuard cannot prevent it. (d) The mandate is optional for the customer; the invoice always offers free bank transfer and any I39 rail equally, and the builder cannot make the mandate a condition inside JobGuard's flow. (e) Collections are never routed through any JobGuard account; fees are on the subscription invoice only, never netted from customer money; nothing amounts to consumer credit (no instalments beyond staged payment for work done). (f) Ship only after M4-15 and M4-18, with VRP as a later option once commercially available, and adoption re-estimated from pilot data.
verdicts.key_risk: The Direct Debit indemnity and CCR cancellation rules can hand a homeowner a refund route after work is done; if JobGuard sells 'get paid on schedule' without saying so, the first reclaimed stage payment reads as JobGuard's fault.

verdicts.reasons: CIS is a statutory withholding regime (Finance Act 2004 Pt 3 Ch 3; CIS Regulations 2005). Producing verification records, deduction bases, monthly statements and CIS300 data as software the builder operates is not a regulated activity: no FCA permission exists for it, HMRC's April 2026 registration requirement for tax practitioners bites only on advisers who interact with HMRC on a client's behalf, and MLR 2017 'tax adviser' supervision (reg 11, widened in 2020 to 'material aid or assistance') attaches to firms giving assistance. So 'JobGuard does not file' and 'no human CIS advice from support' are the load-bearing boundaries, exactly as M4-22 already frames it ('does not submit a statutory return or claim a verification occurred without its evidence'). If JobGuard ever submits CIS300 or verifies via HMRC's API it needs an agent services account, HMRC software recognition and an AML supervisor: a 6–12 month, five-figure step that turns a £5–£15 add-on into a regulated business. Not worth it. DRC VAT (VATA 1994 s.55A; B2B between VAT/CIS-registered parties only, never homeowners) as a flag is consistent with D06's pilot exclusion; a wrong reverse-charge invoice shifts VAT liability, so the flag must not write invoice wording until D02/D06 v2. The flat accountant referral is lawful: tax refunds are not one of the six FCA claims-management sectors (RAO arts 89G–89M; research note §7) and HMRC's repayment-agent registration attaches to the accountant, not the referrer; the accountant's professional code (ICAEW/ACCA via IESBA s.330) requires the referral fee to be disclosed to the client. UK GDPR: subcontractor UTRs, NI and verification numbers are personal data of sole-trader subcontractors; JobGuard is processor for the builder-contractor, a role D12 v1 leaves unresolved. True cost: a CIS-competent accountant to approve the M4-22 fixtures (assumption: £2–5k one-off) plus D02 mapping review; no licence, no permission.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Records and computation only: no HMRC submission, no verification calls, no support-desk answers on gross/net status (route to the accountant partner). (2) DRC flag never generates invoice wording until D02 and D06 v2 are approved. (3) Referral fee flat, shown on screen before handoff, opt-in per referral, data passed only under a documented lawful basis. (4) D12 v2 names the processor role and D07 retention class for subcontractor data. (5) No 'CIS compliant' or 'HMRC approved' marketing claims. (6) M4-22 fixtures signed off by a named adviser before any real use. Solicitor/accountant needed for: the MLR 'tax adviser' boundary and the referral-fee wording. Timeline is dependency-driven (M4-18→M4-21 chain), not regulatory.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£60/yr (assumption: most solos are subcontractors, so only the CIS-suffered view applies; referral £0–£50 one-off)
revised_revenue.firm: £60–£240/yr (assumption: larger firms already run CIS in payroll/accounting software, so attach is lower than the £300 top)

verdicts.key_risk: Scope creep into filing or 'advice' (support staff answering CIS-status questions) makes JobGuard a tax adviser needing AML supervision and HMRC registration.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA or HMRC permission applies to pushing invoices, credits, receipts and bills into Xero/QuickBooks. Two real legal constraints. (a) MTD claims: HMRC recognition is required before saying 'MTD-compatible', 'MTD-ready' or 'recognised'; an unqualified claim risks the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 (B2B) and, for a sole trader partly acting as a consumer, DMCC Act 2024 Part 4. The idea already forgoes the claim; describe it as 'export to your MTD software'. MTD's digital-links rule (VAT Notice 700/22 §4.2.1; same principle under ITSA) means manual re-keying is not a digital link but an API push or CSV file transfer is, so the connector satisfies the builder's own record-keeping duty. (b) International transfer: Xero and QuickBooks Online host outside the UK (Xero on AWS in the US per its privacy notice; Intuit in the US), so homeowner names and addresses on invoices leave the EU/UK boundary that D04 sets. Legally that is the builder's transfer as controller to their own processor, valid under the UK–US Data Bridge or IDTA/Addendum, but D04 says 'individually verified EU/UK routes only', so D04 v2 needs an explicit 'controller-instructed export to the builder's own accounting system' carve-out with a transfer risk assessment, and Codat (UK entity) needs an Art 28 subprocessor contract. Tax-code mappings: liability for a wrong VAT/CIS/DRC code sits with the builder, but a negligence claim against JobGuard is plausible; a limitation clause in standard B2B terms must pass UCTA s.3 reasonableness, and D02 adviser-approved mappings are the substantive defence (M5-1 already requires unsupported mappings to fail explicitly). Consumer law is untouched because the invoices are already issued. Charging Solo for what Tradify bundles is a commercial, not legal, question. Cost: Xero/Intuit app-partner certification 1–3 months; Codat commercials; TRA and terms (assumption: £1–3k); D02 mapping review (assumption: £1–2k). Gated by G5.
verdicts.conditions: (1) No 'MTD-compatible/recognised' claim unless HMRC recognition is obtained (a separate product with fraud-prevention headers and HMRC testing). (2) D04 v2 carve-out for controller-instructed exports, with a documented transfer mechanism per destination. (3) Art 28 terms with Codat; direct Xero/QBO adapters treated as the builder's own processors. (4) D02-approved tax mappings; unsupported codes fail explicitly. (5) UCTA-reasonable limitation of liability for tax outcomes, reviewed by a solicitor. (6) M5-1's rule stands: an imported 'paid' label never counts as settlement evidence for the 10%.

revised_revenue.solo: £36–£108/yr (assumption: a third of Solo takes the annual-plan waiver)
revised_revenue.firm: £0/yr (in tier; the £25 Firm variant adds £0–£300 but competitors bundle it)

verdicts.key_risk: A wrong VAT/CIS/DRC mapping pushed into the builder's ledger and filed to HMRC, with JobGuard's exclusion clause failing UCTA reasonableness.

verdicts.reasons: No regulated activity: quantity surveying is not a reserved profession in the UK (RICS membership is voluntary), so measured-quantity proposals need no licence. Three legal points. (a) Copyright: drawings are graphic/architectural works (CDPA 1988 s.4); the builder normally holds an implied licence to use them for tendering and building (Blair v Osborne & Tomkins), which should extend to feeding them into a pricing tool, but the s.29A text-and-data-mining exception is non-commercial only, so JobGuard cannot rely on it for model use. Terms must have the builder warrant the rights, and D04's no-retention/no-training setting must be verified for the AI route. (b) Negligent misstatement: if a proposed quantity is wrong and the builder under-prices a fixed-price job, a Hedley Byrne-type claim is foreseeable; 'proposals only, builder confirms' plus a UCTA s.2(2)/s.3-reasonable limitation is the defence, so the product rule 'never fill a line to look complete' (AGENTS §5.9) is also the legal one. (c) Personal data: drawings carry the site address and often the homeowner's name; D12/D04 apply. One §14 consistency point: the coverage diff is safe at quote time (pre-baseline), but a drawing uploaded after switch-live that reveals unbilled work is evidence under §14.2 and cannot be shown without either a D13 must-surface event or a permanent fee-free disclosure (§14.3), so the feature must be bounded to pre-acceptance or route post-live diffs into the shadow pipeline. 'Quoting is free' must remain literally true for drawing-free quotes so the pricing page is not misleading under BPMMR 2008. Cost: copyright/liability clause by a solicitor (assumption: £1–2k); no permission; timeline is engineering (new prompt suite and golden set).
verdicts.conditions: (1) Builder warrants rights to upload drawings; no JobGuard training on uploads. (2) AI route verified under D04 for retention/training. (3) Proposals labelled and cited to drawing regions, never auto-priced; unknown quantities stay unknown. (4) Feature bounded to pre-acceptance; post-switch-live drawing diffs handled under §14.3/D13, never as a builder-visible hint. (5) Limitation clause reviewed for UCTA reasonableness. (6) Pricing page keeps 'quoting is free' unconditional.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£57/yr (assumption: a quarter of solos doing extensions take it; the original assumed none)
revised_revenue.firm: £228/yr (assumption: full take-up; legal cost is one-off)

verdicts.key_risk: A confident-looking but wrong takeoff underpins an under-priced fixed-price quote and the builder sues; standard-terms exclusions may not fully protect JobGuard.

verdicts.reasons: The binding law is the Competition Act 1998 Chapter I: information exchange between competitors through a third-party hub. Purchase-price data is less sensitive than selling prices, and the CMA's Horizontal Agreements Guidance (2023, information-exchange chapter) treats genuinely aggregated, anonymised, non-current data among many small participants as low risk; with k≥10 tenants and ≥30 observations per cell, no individual identifiable, and thousands of builders none with market power, an appreciable effect is unlikely. But a 90-day window is 'current', not 'historic', so a solicitor should confirm the cell and window rules (expect advice to widen to 6–12 months or lag the data). No buying-group issue arises because there is no collective purchasing or negotiation; if that ever changed, the joint-purchasing chapter (15% market-share thresholds) would apply. Merchant trade-account terms can restrict disclosure of negotiated prices; that binds the builder, but knowingly inducing breach is a tort against JobGuard, so terms should have the builder confirm no restriction. UK GDPR: pooling across tenants is a new purpose for which JobGuard is controller (D12 v1 only makes it controller for builder-account processing); it needs a DPIA, opt-in as the lawful basis, and the ICO's anonymisation guidance applied so cells cannot single out a tenant or a sole-trader supplier. It is also a reviewed cross-tenant exception under AGENTS §5.1 and reverses M5-6's 'cross-tenant learning disabled unless a separate privacy/commercial decision permits it', hence the D14 record. Not FCA-regulated. The trust risk the founder named is real; the design (opt-in, builder-only, no merchant money, isolated role) is its mildest form, and the written 'merchants never pay or see' rule is also the competition-law hygiene point. Cost: competition opinion plus DPIA (assumption: £3–8k), D14, an aggregation worker under a separate database role with catalog tests; revenue is year-2+ because cells need several hundred contributing tenants per region.
verdicts.conditions: (1) D14 decision record before any cross-tenant read. (2) Aggregation runs under a separate DB role with catalog tests; no tenant-identifiable row leaves the tenant. (3) Cells only at k≥10 tenants/≥30 observations, trimmed outliers, no cell that could reveal a single supplier's price to a single builder; window and lag set on counsel's advice. (4) Written, tested rule that merchants never pay for or see anything. (5) Builder confirms no trade-account confidentiality bar, or the pool uses invoice list prices only. (6) DPIA, opt-in, ICO anonymisation test. (7) Findings only: no order changes, no merchant contact.

revised_revenue.solo: Year 1 £0; year 2+ £36–£180/yr (assumption: cells populate only after several hundred tenants per region)
revised_revenue.firm: Year 1 £0; year 2+ £108–£588/yr (assumption: Firm tier at £49/month; less £3–8k one-off legal cost across the base)

verdicts.key_risk: Being characterised as an information-exchange hub if cells are too fresh or too thin; commercially, the first pound of merchant money would compromise the invoice watchdog.

verdicts.reasons: Same statute as I28 (Competition Act 1998 Chapter I), but the subject is the builders' own selling prices (labour rates), the most sensitive category for information exchange. Aggregated, anonymised, 12-month, n≥20 from ≥10 tenants, independent-hub data is the structure the CMA's Horizontal Agreements Guidance and its 2024 employer guidance on wage benchmarking (which mirrors the ≥5-contributor, ≤25%-weight, ≥3-months-old safe harbour) treat as generally acceptable, and quotes to homeowners are already semi-public, so the base risk is low. The exposure is the presentation: a 'you are below the 25th percentile' nudge delivered at scale by one platform is what regulators examine as algorithmic price alignment, so counsel should approve neutral wording ('where your rate sits'), no 'raise it' recommendations, and no forward-looking or intended prices. Seeding with a licensed price book is a licence-cost and redistribution issue: publishers commonly forbid re-publishing derived figures to third parties, may refuse, and fees are typically thousands a year (unverified; needs quotes), which may exceed £180 per tenant in year 1. UK GDPR: accepted-quote rates carry no homeowner data by design, but a sole-trader builder's rates are their personal data, so the same D14, DPIA and anonymisation conditions as I28 apply, and the FairRate precedent (homeowner-facing) shows why an outward leak would be fatal. Not FCA-regulated; no direct consumer-law issue. Cost: shares I28's opinion plus £1–2k for the selling-price analysis (assumption); price-book licence £1–5k+/yr (assumption); cold start.
verdicts.conditions: (1) D14, DPIA and isolated role as I28. (2) Only rates confirmed on accepted quotes; 12-month window; thresholds enforced in code; no single tenant above 25% of a cell. (3) Neutral, counsel-approved presentation; no price recommendations; no intended or future prices ever collected. (4) Price-book seed only under a licence that permits derived benchmark display, labelled as such. (5) Written no-outward-sale promise (merchants, insurers, lead platforms, homeowners) in the terms. (6) Solicitor review of the selling-price exchange before launch.

revised_revenue.solo: Year 1 £0 (seed-book licence may cost more than revenue); year 2+ £0–£180/yr
revised_revenue.firm: Year 1 £0; year 2+ £0–£180/yr (assumption: annual-plan contributors get it free, so paid take-up is below 100%)

verdicts.key_risk: A scaled 'you're cheap' nudge from one hub read as facilitating price coordination, and the seed-book licence being refused or costing more than year-1 revenue.

verdicts.reasons: Legally clean: a tenant-bound API on the builder's instruction is processor-on-instruction under UK GDPR Art 28, and the builder is controller for where the data goes. Two obligations bite. (a) Art 20 portability and the D07 export workflow: a sole trader's business records are largely their personal data (ICO position), and any customer must be able to leave with their data, so the paid API can never be the only route to bulk export; the free export stays and the paid API is a convenience. (b) Art 32 security: scoped tokens, rotation, rate limits, HTTPS-only signed webhooks with replay protection and minimal payloads (event and IDs, not content) are what a regulator expects; a webhook delivering content to a compromised URL is a breach JobGuard must report. The §14.3 byte-identity rule must extend to every API response: no field, count, error or timing that varies with shadow signals before lock, and no scope that reaches shadow tables or commercial commands (M5-7 conformance). No FCA, PECR, consumer or competition issue; £49 in B2B is fine.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Free bulk export retained regardless of tier. (2) Token scopes proven unable to reach shadow tables or commercial commands; write endpoints only for non-commercial fields. (3) Signed, HTTPS-only webhooks, replay protection, minimal payloads. (4) API terms make the builder responsible for onward destinations. (5) Token use audited and revocable. Cost: security review plus terms (assumption: £1–2k); no permission.

revised_revenue.solo: £0/yr
revised_revenue.firm: £147/yr expected (£588 if taken; assumption: one in four firms has someone to use it)

verdicts.key_risk: A leaked token or webhook endpoint exposing job and customer data (a JobGuard-reportable breach), or any API path that differs with shadow-signal existence.

verdicts.reasons: No permission or statute regulates selling a bookkeeper seat; the legal substance is agency and data protection. (a) Authority: a finance seat that issues customer invoices and credit notes performs commercial sends under AGENTS §5.3, so the builder must record an explicit, revocable delegation; otherwise a homeowner could contest the invoice and the builder could contest the settlement chain the 10% relies on. (b) UK GDPR: the ICO treats external accountants as independent controllers for their professional work; JobGuard grants access on the builder's instruction and should have the seat holder accept acceptable-use terms. No role can reach shadow data before lock, so §14.3 is preserved. (c) AML and MTD: the bookkeeper's own supervision and agent services account are theirs; JobGuard must not present the seat as making the builder MTD-compliant. The report's Xero counter-precedent (free adviser access drives adoption) and the MTD-driven bookkeeper channel argue for free on Solo, but that is a pricing choice, not a legal one. The conflict with I61's free practice view should be settled in one decision. Cost: near zero legally; terms wording.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Delegation record per seat for invoice and credit-note issue, revocable and audited. (2) Seat scoped by RLS and permission tests (§5.1); cannot approve success-fee statements or standing authority unless the builder explicitly grants it. (3) Seat-holder terms. (4) No MTD or compliance claims attached to the seat. (5) Decide I31 against I61 together.

revised_revenue.solo: £0/yr (recommend free for Solo to protect the bookkeeper channel; £54 if charged at 30% attach)

verdicts.key_risk: An invoice or credit note issued by a bookkeeper without recorded delegation, later disputed by the builder or homeowner, undermining both the customer debt and the fee's settlement evidence.

verdicts.reasons: The idea with the most law attached, none of it a blocker. (a) PECR reg 22: SMS and WhatsApp to individuals are 'electronic mail'; service messages (approval requests, stage sign-offs, invoice reminders) are not marketing and need no consent, but any promotional content needs prior consent or the soft opt-in. Because JobGuard transmits while the builder instigates, both are exposed to ICO enforcement, so JobGuard must control templates. (b) DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 and Sch 20 (persistent unwanted communications, with an exception for enforcing a contractual obligation) and Administration of Justice Act 1970 s.40 (harassment of debtors; applies to anyone concerned with collection) cap reminder frequency and tone. FCA debt collecting (RAO art 39F) does not apply because there is no consumer credit agreement, and must stay that way: no instalment plans without a separate decision (research note §7; D10). (c) Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013: a variation agreed by SMS for work at the homeowner's home may be an off-premises contract needing pre-contract and cancellation information; without it the cancellation period extends to 12 months and the builder may be unable to charge for the work, which shrinks the fee base. The approval template should carry the required information; solicitor to confirm. (d) UK GDPR: a homeowner replying provides data directly, so an Art 13 notice link belongs in the first message; replies become §14.2 evidence, which D12 v2 onboarding must say, and a homeowner DSAR can trigger disclosed_before_lock. (e) WhatsApp Business Platform: Meta's opt-in and template-approval rules, per-message utility/marketing pricing (which cuts the assumed 60% margin), and Meta Ireland processing need D04 verification; the SMS provider likewise. (f) Late Payment Act interest and compensation are business-debt only (report §'No rival'), so reminder templates must not claim statutory interest against homeowners. Cost: template and legal review (assumption: £2–4k); Meta business verification 1–2 weeks; provider DPA; ongoing per-message cost.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Service-only templates; no builder-editable promotional text without a consent record. (2) Frequency cap and tone rules on reminders; no statutory-interest claims to consumers. (3) Art 13 privacy link in the first message; STOP handling for anything non-essential. (4) CCR 2013 information in variation-approval templates for off-premises consumer contracts (solicitor). (5) D04 approval of the SMS/WhatsApp provider and Meta route. (6) D12 v2 wording that replies are evidence; never nudge a builder to move a specific conversation in-thread. (7) Exact, visible overage metering on provider delivery receipts.

revised_revenue.solo: £48–£60/yr (assumption: WhatsApp per-message pricing cuts margin to about 50%)

verdicts.key_risk: A reminder cadence or wording that reads as harassment of a homeowner, or a promotional message sent without consent, drawing ICO or CMA attention to JobGuard as the transmitter.

verdicts.reasons: Price is capped by the market, not by value: Xero files CIS returns for £5/month (raw notes construction_platforms_and_ai.md, Xero UK) and JobGuard would not file, so £5–£15 for records-and-handoff is above the incumbent's price for a strictly smaller job; Construction AI bundles CIS/VAT in flat suites and BuildersAI excludes it without visible harm. Most firms with subcontractors already run CIS through their accountant or accounting software (49% of no-employee businesses use accountancy software; trades-WTP note §5), so JobGuard's version is a second copy of a record the accountant owns. Build cost is large for the money: M4-22 sits at the end of M4-17→M4-18→M4-19→M4-20→M4-21, needs adviser-approved fixtures [R22], and D06 explicitly excludes CIS and DRC from the pilot, so nothing ships before M4 exit; the CIS-suffered mirror also needs contractor payment-statement ingestion that no task provides. Revenue: even at 100% attach on Builder/Firm the line is £60/year against £708–£1,428 subscriptions, a rounding error. The flat accountant referral is honest but tiny: perhaps 20% of solos are CIS-suffering subbies, one referral a year, ~£8/tenant. Gaming: none. Comparables: Xero £5 is the only paid CIS precedent found; Hammr is US payroll; Procore has no native CIS (a UK gap, but above JobGuard's segment). Top reasons it fails: priced above Xero for less; duplicates the accountant's process; arrives last in M4; DRC flagging is a compliance necessity, not a purchase trigger.
verdicts.conditions: If built at all, build M4-22 as an in-tier Builder/Firm retention feature and never above Xero's £5 as an add-on; keep 'JobGuard does not file' with no HMRC-agent or AML posture; referral only as a flat, disclosed, optional handoff (never a percentage) and only after D06 review lifts the CIS/DRC exclusion; count £0 add-on revenue in the model.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£30 (assume £5/mo cap set by Xero, 30% attach; ~£8 expected referral)

verdicts.key_risk: Spending an M4-scale build on a £5/month line accountants already own, while a wrong CIS/DRC calculation creates HMRC penalty exposure JobGuard cannot insure.

verdicts.reasons: Table stakes, not a revenue line. Tradify (all plans), ServiceM8, YourTradebase and WorkflowMax bundle Xero/QuickBooks sync free (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45 a month'; raw notes uk_trade_job_software.md, construction_platforms_and_ai.md); Powered Now gates it to its £32 Professional tier, the only precedent for charging, and at a ~£4 step, not £9–£15. A Solo at £29 + £9 sync = £38 lands above Tradify Lite £34 with sync included, so the Solo charge is the one rivals beat with a screenshot. The MTD logic is inverted: MTD ITSA makes HMRC-recognised software (Xero/QuickBooks/FreeAgent) compulsory for 860,000 sole traders from April 2026 (trades-WTP note §5), which guarantees the builder already pays £16–£38 for the ledger, not that they will pay JobGuard to feed it; the value is removed re-keying, which builders like but rarely buy separately. Build is late and expensive: M5-1 canonical export + Codat after M4-23/G5, then M5-2/M5-3 direct adapters, D02 adviser-approved tax mappings, D04 destinations (Codat/Xero/QuickBooks are not EU/UK-verified in the register), D12 (customer names on invoices leave the boundary); Codat charges per linked company (cost unverified). The M5-1 rule that an imported 'paid' label never proves settlement closes the fee-gaming route. Top reasons a paid version fails: rivals give it free; it makes tier comparison feature-based, which the report's compromise-effect advice says to avoid; it cannot exist before M5, so it earns nothing during the period the subscription must carry the business.
verdicts.conditions: Treat as retention: include in Builder and Firm; on Solo either include it or charge no more than Powered Now's ~£4 step, monthly only (free on annual). Never claim 'MTD-compatible'. Ship an export-of-record first (CSV/PDF pack an accountant can post) long before M5-1, because that captures most of the re-keying value at near-zero build cost. Keep the M5-1 'paid label is not settlement' rule. Model £0 direct revenue.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£54 (assume £9/mo monthly-only, 30% attach, annual free; expected ~£30)

verdicts.key_risk: Charging Solo for what Tradify and YourTradebase include turns JobGuard's cheapest plan into the most expensive exactly when MTD makes the builder's accountant the gatekeeper.

verdicts.reasons: The value is real and the price is under market: Kreo charges £25/£50/£125 per user for takeoff alone, Buildertrend put takeoff in Advanced ($799 last published), Handoff is $149–$899 (raw notes construction_platforms_and_ai.md), no small-builder tool found does a walk-vs-drawing gap check, and Trunk Tools sells missed-scope detection only on enterprise quotes. A missed soil-stack move or steel on a £25k extension is £500–£2,000, so £228/year pays back on one job for anyone with drawings. Refutations: (1) drawings are rare on £8k jobs, so Solo take-up is near zero; (2) the coverage diff is already an M1-4 free-quote deliverable ('unpriced captured scope, excluded items'), so the add-on must be the drawing input, not the diff, or 'quoting is free' becomes 'free unless you have drawings', breaking the founder's fixed decision and the report's reverse-trial free layer; (3) AI quantities from PDFs are the liability trap: a builder who prices off a wrong count and loses money blames JobGuard, and AGENTS §5.9 forbids invented quantities, so the honest product is a cited 'items on the drawing you did not mention' list plus proposed measurements the builder must confirm; (4) once a builder has seen three checklists they may learn the pattern and cancel, so add-on churn could be high; (5) the build is high and entirely absent from the plan (no drawing/takeoff task exists): new prompt suite, labelled drawing golden set (omission, unsupported additions, citation validity), large-PDF storage, D04 AI route and D12 (drawings carry the address). Gaming: none commercial. Top reasons it fails: accuracy on real UK drawings is unproven; year-1 revenue is zero because the golden set does not exist; Firm buyers may expect it inside £119 rather than as a £19 extra.
verdicts.conditions: Sell it as a 'Drawing check' on top of the free quote and never gate the M1-4 coverage diff; proposals only, every quantity cited to a drawing region and confirmed by the builder; price after pilot proof (a golden set of ≥100 real UK drawings with recall and false-positive rate reported separately); consider bundling into Firm and charging Builder £19–£29; model year-1 revenue as £0.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£46 (10–20% have drawings; ~10% attach × £228 ≈ £23, year 2+)
revised_revenue.firm: £0–£348 (60% attach; £19 rising to £29 after proof ≈ £140, year 2+)

verdicts.key_risk: A wrong AI quantity a builder prices from is a loss JobGuard caused, and a paywall on the gap check is a broken 'quoting is free' promise; either costs more trust than £19 buys.

verdicts.reasons: Cold start kills the year-1–2 number: cells need ≥10 tenants and ≥30 observations per SKU/region/90 days, and building materials have thousands of merchant-specific SKUs, so even several hundred contributing tenants per region populate only commodity lines (plasterboard, timber, cement); the idea's own note says year 2+, so revised revenue is £0 until then. Normalisation is harder than the plan's tenant-scoped M2-4 aliasing: cross-tenant SKU identity needs M5-4 supplier resolution (late M5) plus a new D14 pooling decision, because M5-6 disables cross-tenant learning and §11 lists cross-tenant rate learning without a reviewed policy as out of scope. Merchant trade-account terms may treat negotiated prices as confidential (unverified) and CMA information-exchange review is still needed even for purchase prices.
