The value is real but rarely acted on: Firm materials ≈ £700k/year so 3% is £21k, yet builders stay with a merchant for credit terms, delivery and the local branch, and a '12% over median' signal is confounded by delivery, quantity breaks and brand. Prolo (raised £4.2m, 185+ suppliers, revenue model undisclosed; raw notes) is attacking the same value with the merchant-side model JobGuard has ruled out: good for the value thesis, bad for a £15 flat fee competing with a free-to-builder rival. Trust: aggregated, opt-in, builder-only is the mildest form of the data risk, but the product creates standing commercial pressure to one day sell the pool to merchants, which would break the invoice watchdog; the written rule is the only defence. Comparables (report §'No rival sells…'): FairRate £0.99/audit is consumer-facing; P3 takes 50% of savings; AP recovery auditors 20–30%; none is a £15 builder-paid benchmark. Gaming is well handled (server-verified documents, trimmed outliers, M2-4 gates). Top reasons it fails: empty cells for two years; a flat £15 under-prices Firm and over-prices Solo; legal and decision overhead before any revenue; Prolo.
verdicts.conditions: Do not build before a D14 pooling decision, ICO anonymisation and CMA review, and ≥300 contributing tenants per region; when the pool exists, ship as a Firm-tier inclusion and give-to-get perk rather than a separate charge; keep the written 'merchants never pay' rule and the isolated aggregation role; meanwhile the tenant-scoped M2-1 agreed-rate pre-commit check delivers most of the prevention value for free.
verdicts.key_risk: Two years of decision, legal and aggregation work before a single populated cell, while a merchant-funded rival gives builders the same signal free.

verdicts.reasons: The weaker twin of I28. Cold start is worse: only rates confirmed on accepted quotes count (M1-4 rate_book_observation), builders' units are heterogeneous (per day, per m², per item, lump sums for composite work), and n≥20 from ≥10 tenants per trade/unit/region will take hundreds of tenants per region, so £0 for at least two years; the idea's £180 × 3 assumes 100% attach, which is indefensible. Legal risk is the higher category: selling-price exchange among local competitors is what competition guidance worries about most (the idea admits it), and '12-month regional bands of confirmed quote rates' is closer to current pricing than to historic data, so legal review could block it outright. The seed price book is an unbudgeted cost: commercial price-book licences are typically per user and often forbid embedding (unverified) and could exceed £15/month per tenant. Trust: give-to-get requires each builder to feed rates their local rivals will see; builders compete on price locally, and FairRate already shows homeowners 'local market rates' (raw notes), so the fear that JobGuard's pool leaks toward consumers is rational; the report's betrayal-aversion findings apply to exactly this information asymmetry. Value: a rate is not a margin, lower-overhead builders legitimately price lower, and builders who undercut to win work know it, so a '25th percentile' message changes few quotes. Plan: M5-6 disables cross-tenant learning and §11 excludes it without a reviewed policy, so this needs the same D14 as I28 plus competition-law sign-off. Gaming is handled (accepted-quote rates only). Comparables: no builder-facing rate benchmark exists in UK trade software; FairRate is the only demand signal and points the other way. Top reasons it fails: legal block; empty cells; builders refuse to contribute; the price-book licence eats the £15.
verdicts.conditions: Only revisit together with I28 under one D14 decision after competition-law review; if it survives, show it as a free give-to-get perk on annual plans, never a £15 charge; never seed from a licensed price book without a licence that permits embedding; never expose anything outward (merchants, insurers, lead platforms, homeowners).

revised_revenue.solo: £0 years 1–2; ~£45 year 3+ (25% attach × £180), or £0 if legal review blocks it

verdicts.key_risk: Facilitating price-information exchange between competing local builders, which a competition-law review may forbid and which builders may read as JobGuard leaking their prices.

verdicts.reasons: No buyer at £49. A 15-person, £2m firm has an office manager and a bookkeeper, not a developer; API consumers are integrators, accountancy practices and larger contractors with BI tools, so attach on Firm is closer to one in ten than one in four (expected ~£60/year), and it is £0 on Solo and Builder. No UK trade tool found charges for API access (the idea's own precedent), and read-only endpoints with no commercial writes remove most of what Zapier-style users want, which lowers willingness to pay further. £49 is 41% on top of the £119 Firm plan for a feature rivals give away, a screenshot comparison JobGuard loses. The build is medium and mandatory regardless of price: scoped tenant-bound tokens and the principal contract (AGENTS §3; M5-7 policy permissions, late in M5), webhook signing and retries on the M0-9 outbox, rate limits, and the §14.3 proof that API responses and timing are byte-identical with and without shadow signals; an API widens the surface SV-3's isolation tests must cover, and a timing leak through it would make signals permanently fee-ineligible. M5-7 conformance must prove tokens cannot broaden finance, order or export authority. Comparables: standard SaaS includes API on upper tiers; ServiceM8 and Jobber publish free developer APIs (general knowledge, not in the research). Top reasons it fails: nobody to use it; rivals free; arrives in M5; support cost of API consumers exceeds £588/year per firm.
verdicts.conditions: If built after M5-7, include the read API and webhooks free on Firm and Contractor as a channel feature (accountants, integrators), keep the free read-only accountant seat, and treat the shadow-isolation and token-scope tests as the acceptance criteria; do not list it as a paid line on the pricing page.

revised_revenue.firm: £0–£588 (10% attach × £49/mo ≈ £60 expected; £0 if included in tier)

verdicts.key_risk: A new read surface that must be proven byte-identical and timing-identical with and without shadow signals; a leak through the API is a permanent fee loss and a trust story, for ~£60/year.

verdicts.reasons: It contradicts the fixed 'unlimited users' headline: a paid finance seat is 'unlimited users*', and the report's tier advice (compare on one or two numbers, keep every tier a real offer) plus its drip-pricing warning both cut against an asterisk; B2B is outside DMCC, but the fairness perception is the same. It taxes the acquisition channel: bookkeepers and accountants are the likeliest route to Solos under MTD (49% of no-employee businesses use accountancy software; 39% of sole traders had not started MTD prep; trades-WTP note §5), Xero gives advisers free access precisely to drive adoption, and Dext prices the practice, not the client. A bookkeeper with 20 builder clients would be asking each client to pay £15/month for her login; they will share the owner login instead, which the idea admits is unpoliceable, so real attach is far below 30/60/50%. Revenue: expected ~£27 Solo, ~£72 Builder, ~£18 Firm (second seat only), trivial against £348–£1,428 subscriptions. The build is small-medium (role scope, RLS tests per AGENTS §5.1, M4-14-style metering), but D09 v2 defines a business-level subscription with no seat metering, so a seat charge needs a policy change, and the finance role itself is needed anyway for accounting export and the accountant view. It also collides with the free practice view (I61). Top reasons it fails: channel friction; login sharing; headline contradiction; no D09 basis for seat metering.
verdicts.conditions: Build the finance role (read/export of posted facts, invoice and credit-note issue, reconciliation view) and make it free on every tier; if the founder wants a seat line at all, only as a Firm-tier inclusion listed as a real feature (the tier-psychology note recommends office/admin seats as a genuine top-tier differentiator), never as a Solo/Builder charge; consider a practice-level plan for accountants with many clients instead.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£180 (15% attach × £15/mo ≈ £27; login sharing depresses it)

verdicts.key_risk: Charging the bookkeeper channel that brings Solo clients, for a seat they will bypass by sharing the owner login.

verdicts.reasons: Precedent says pennies, not bundles: Tradify SMS is 10p/message, Fergus £8 per 100, ServiceM8 5p, Payaca 4p (raw notes uk_trade_job_software.md); the £29–£49 add-ons cited (Powered Now PN Receptionist, Jobber/Joist AI receptionists) are inbound call-answering products, not messaging, so they are the wrong comparable. A Solo with 2–3 live jobs sends maybe 10–30 customer messages a month and does it free on their own WhatsApp, so a £5 bundle competes with zero. WhatsApp Business adds Meta's per-conversation charges, template approval and opt-in rules, plus a UK/EU-resident provider under D04; PECR is fine for service messages. The deeper problem is the one the idea calls a wrinkle and the report treats as the central risk: replies through JobGuard become shadow-bill evidence (§14.2), so a builder who paid £5–£20 a month to route customer chat into JobGuard and then meets a 10% fee on a catch sourced from that chat has the exact 'you profited from information you held' story the betrayal-aversion findings predict (report §'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk'). Worse, the messages JobGuard most wants sent, variation approval requests and quote acceptance links, are the ones that make catches billable and the record clean; charging per message discourages the behaviour the fee model depends on. The build is small-medium but needs a customer message page that does not exist yet (SV-7 is the nearest task), an approved provider adapter and exact overage metering on delivery receipts. Gaming: low; overage disputes if metering is not exact. Revenue at 50/70/80% attach is ~£30/£84/£190 with ~60% margin, and roughly halves if approval messages are free, as they should be.
verdicts.conditions: Price at cost-plus per message like Tradify (or a generous free allowance), no bundle tiers; include every quote/variation approval, stage sign-off and invoice reminder message free because they serve JobGuard's own evidence and fee model; state in D12 v2 onboarding that in-thread replies are job records the final check reads; never nudge a builder to move a specific conversation in-thread; the provider must pass D04; reminders stay infrastructure messages or go through the command boundary per AGENTS §5.3.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£60 (50% attach × £5/mo ≈ £30; ~£18 margin; less if approval messages are free)

verdicts.key_risk: The builder pays to route customer conversations into JobGuard, and those conversations then feed the hidden final check: the cleanest possible version of the 'you charged me for evidence against me' story.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation of the price, not the product. A £29/month add-on doubles the recommended Solo subscription (report, 'Recommendation: £29, £59 and £119') and sits at the top of what incumbents charge for add-ons (Powered Now AI receptionist £29–£39/month; raw note uk_trade_job_software, monetisation section), yet unlike a receptionist it produces no visible daily value. Builders' total software spend is anchored at £15–£40/month, construction is the least digitised sector (29% of one-person firms use software) and MTD is competing for the same budget (report, 'Builders' willingness to pay'), so 40–60% take-up of a paid add-on is not defensible. Many builders use no written contract and treat the quote as the contract; FMB member contracts (unverified) and JCT homeowner contracts are cheap one-offs. The genuinely valuable element, the CCRs 2013 off-premises cancellation notice whose omission extends the cancellation window and can leave the builder unable to charge for work done in it, is compliance hygiene any free quoting tool (Checkatrade's free tool, report 'UK builders already pay') could add, so it will not hold a standalone price. The idea also admits it shrinks JobGuard's own fee base by moving extras into fee-free builder capture. What survives: small code (templates on the M1 quote-send path; D06 must be extended for any real customer document anyway; M4-19 profiles later), zero gaming risk, top trust fit, and a credible tier differentiator supporting the compromise-effect ladder the report recommends ('Three tiers work'). Costs: solicitor drafting of the pack (assume low thousands plus annual review), PI/disclaimer arrangements, and systemic exposure if one template is wrong for every builder at once.
verdicts.conditions: Bundle the standard pack into the Builder and Firm tiers rather than selling it; offer Solo a £10 per-quote option, not a monthly add-on; take a referral share (assume 20–30%) on the partner solicitor's bespoke review rather than reselling it; ship the CCR cancellation notice as core compliance on every tier; the partner solicitor owns the templates and carries PI, and JobGuard never labels anything legal advice; D06 extended and legally reviewed before any real customer document; measure attach rate and dispute reduction in the no-charge pilot before pricing.

revised_revenue.solo: £30–£90 (assumption: 20% of quotes buy a £10 pack, 5% buy a bespoke review on which JobGuard keeps a referral share)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £100–£180 (value mostly captured as a Builder-tier upgrade; 15% buy a bespoke review, referral share only)
revised_revenue.firm: £200–£350 (largely Firm-tier upgrade value; 30% buy a bespoke review, JobGuard keeps a 20–30% referral share)

verdicts.key_risk: Builders will not pay separately for paperwork they currently skip; the pack becomes a free hygiene feature copied by free tools, leaving JobGuard with template liability and no add-on revenue.

verdicts.reasons: The idea's own numbers are small (£40–£692) and rest on guesses: there is no UK dispute-rate data for domestic builders (the idea and the report both say so), and 1–8 paid packs a year assumes most disputes escalate far enough to need a bundle. Refutation of the differentiator: in a small claim or FMB conciliation the tribunal reads dated photos, messages and invoices; nobody alleges forged photos, so the RFC-3161 anchor and standalone verifier that justify the £99–£149 price are unvalued by the buyer, and AGENTS §5.7/5.8 and BUILD_PLAN §11 forbid the 'tamper-proof' or 'court-ready' claim that would sell it. The mandatory free export, rightly kept one tap away, is the direct substitute and cannibalises the paid pack; charging £99+ at a moment of distress collides with the fairness finding that exploiting need is judged unfair (report, 'The hidden final check'). Comparable spend exists only at the top end, claims consultants at £350–£1,200/day (report table), and is uneconomic below about £3k, so the realistic paying buyer is the Firm archetype with B2B or higher-value disputes. What survives: near-zero marginal cost once M4-3 (merged) and M4-4 exist, a credible retention and tier story, and minimal gaming risk because the signed manifest states what was included. It cannot be early: M4-4 needs D07, M5-9 is an M5 task, and a paid document needs the M4-10/M4-11 command boundary.
verdicts.conditions: Standard pack included in the Builder and Firm tiers, not sold; sell only the anchored/verifier grade and ADR transmission at £49–£99 with the free export shown first; never 'court-ready' or 'tamper-proof'; do not build before M4-4 with D07 approved; measure dispute frequency in the pilot before pricing; D09 must state per-pack pricing is a document product, not a per-job platform fee (AGENTS §5.10); an ADR-resolved dispute stays fee-free unless a D03-compliant case was already open; packs generated before lock never touch shadow tables.

revised_revenue.solo: £10–£45 (assumption: 0.2–0.5 paid packs a year at £45–£99)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £40–£120 (0.5–1.5 paid packs; standard pack already in tier)
revised_revenue.firm: £100–£300 (1.5–3 paid anchored/ADR packs; mediation referrals negligible)

verdicts.key_risk: Buyers do not value the anchoring, so the only thing left to charge for is formatting of the builder's own data next to a free export, which reads as paying to get your own evidence back.

verdicts.reasons: A human review of the builder's own evidence has real value at the £10k–£50k dispute level, where £750 for a QS-checked chronology compares well with £350–£1,200/day consultants (report table). But a 50–70% purchase rate per dispute is not defensible: small builders are cash-constrained and asked for £395 up front at a distress moment; on a £3k–£5k dispute that is 8–13% of the sum with no contingency, worse than a collector's 8–15% no-win-no-fee (report table), and many will send the free I34 export instead. Delivery economics are thin at the low grade: 2–5 QS hours at £45–£100/hour cost £90–£500 against £395, before panel management, QA and PI, so roughly a 35–45% gross margin on a non-scalable human product. The £1,500+ adjudication grade mostly does not apply to domestic work because statutory adjudication generally excludes residential occupiers (raw success-fee note, unverified), leaving the B2B minority of jobs. It needs a scoped external-reviewer role, a new trust boundary for tenant and customer personal data (D12 processor terms), plus M4-3 live under G4, M4-10 and a one-off checkout, so late M4 at the earliest. Factual-assembly positioning is sound, but a QS 'summary of what was agreed' edges toward expert evidence and must stay clear of CPR Part 35 and reserved litigation drafting. Trust fit is high only if no shadow content ever reaches a preparer; a blamed loss is a word-of-mouth risk.
verdicts.conditions: Run as a panel referral with a revenue share, not a JobGuard-delivered service, until pilot dispute frequency and I34 pack demand are measured; Firm tier only at launch; preparers work from builder-visible data through a scoped, audited, time-limited role with D12 processor terms; no pre-lock shadow signal may ever inform a pack; label as factual assembly with no legal advice and no generated threats (M4-5 rules); adjudication grade for B2B jobs only.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£40 gross (assumption: 0.3 disputes a year, 20–30% buy; about £10 net after QS cost)
revised_revenue.firm: £250–£700 gross (2–3 disputes, 25–35% buy at £500–£900 blended; about £100–£280 net)

verdicts.key_risk: A low-margin human service bought rarely and at distress moments that exposes JobGuard to blame for lost disputes, for under £300 net per Firm per year.

verdicts.reasons: Uptake of 10–25% is fantasy. A homeowner who has just paid an £8k–£60k final invoice is asked for £82.80 inc VAT for a sealed copy of documents the builder can hand over free; the certificates a conveyancer actually asks for (Part P, Gas Safe, FENSA, building-control completion) are issued by the certifying bodies and already belong to the homeowner; property logbooks have not achieved consumer uptake (my understanding, not from the report) and the idea cites no market data. Buildbite already attaches proof-of-work to invoices inside a per-user price (raw note construction_platforms). Builders will not opt in on contentious jobs, since a homeowner-held sealed record of every variation is a ready-made exhibit against them, so the addressable share shrinks further. The regulatory and operational load is out of proportion to under £100 a year per builder: a direct consumer sale under CRA 2015 and CCRs 2013, consumer VAT presentation, JobGuard as controller for homeowner accounts (D12 v2), homeowner identity (I55), consumer checkout on the M4-11 adapter, M4-3 and M4-4 (D07), and a 15-year hosted-retention promise on a one-off £69 that no early-stage company should make. It also creates a direct JobGuard-to-homeowner commercial relationship, which the founder listed as a trust risk.
verdicts.conditions: None that rescue it as revenue. If a handover artefact is wanted, ship a free builder-branded handover PDF from the existing final account as a builder-retention feature, with no homeowner account, no checkout and no retention promise.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£30 (assumption: 19 jobs × 1–2% × £69, before Stripe fees and consumer support)

verdicts.key_risk: Consumer-law obligations and a 15-year retention promise taken on for a product homeowners have never shown they will buy.

verdicts.reasons: The idea concedes it is not revenue and the refutation confirms it. No UK insurer publishes a per-pack payment and none was found paying one; insurers expect policyholders to supply claim evidence free as a policy condition, so paying a third party £75 for the same evidence has no precedent (Procore and LABC Warranty, the idea's precedents, concern underwriting data and per-plot inspection, not per-pack fees). Even at the assumed £75 and 5–40% claim frequency the idea's own figures are £4–£30 a builder a year; a per-insurer delivery adapter at 2–3 weeks each (assume £5–£10k of engineering) needs hundreds of builders per insurer to pay back, and insurer partnership negotiation is a founder-time sink. Liability-claim frequency for small builders is more plausibly low single digits per business-year than 40%. The worthwhile part, a recipient-bound export the builder sends to their own insurer, is a zero-revenue feature of I34's free export (M4-3 plus M5-9 recipient binding, D12 Article 14 route). 'Insurers accept JobGuard packs' is a marketing line that requires an insurer to say so, not a revenue line.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable as revenue. Fold 'Send evidence to my insurer' into the I34 free export as a recipient-bound send; pursue insurer relationships as marketing or underwriting (I46, separately flagged), never per-pack fees.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (no insurer will pay; ceiling £5)

verdicts.key_risk: Founder time spent negotiating insurer adapters for a fee no insurer has ever paid.

verdicts.reasons: Listed to reject and it should be. Being paid by the homeowner to audit the builder, using data the builder gave JobGuard for their own protection, makes JobGuard a paid agent for both sides of one transaction. It collides head-on with the shadow bill: JobGuard would hold hidden signals of the builder's unbilled work while charging the homeowner to look for overcharges, a two-sided conflict that disclosure does not cure (report, 'The hidden final check': disclosing a conflict of interest does not neutralise it). UK GDPR purpose limitation (D12) is a serious problem because the builder's job records were collected to serve the builder. Word-of-mouth churn would follow the first builder who learns of it. Revenue could never compensate: even at 100% uptake it is £190–£330 a year per builder, and £9.99 is ten times FairRate's £0.99 audit (report, 'No rival sells a final check'). The portal already gives the homeowner free transparency on quote, approved variations and proof. Trivially buildable (M1-11 plus M4-3), which is exactly why BUILD_PLAN §11 needs an explicit exclusion.
verdicts.conditions: Never build. Add an explicit line to BUILD_PLAN §11 out-of-scope: no homeowner-paid audit or adverse use of builder-supplied job data.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (do not build; gross ceiling if built £10–£40, before churn losses)

verdicts.key_risk: Destroys the builder-side trust the whole fee model depends on, for pocket change.

verdicts.reasons: The only idea in this batch with a defensible number and a proven precedent: builders already pay Fergus 1.6% + 20p and Jobber 2.9% + 30¢ plus 1% for instant payout, and the report notes card-processing fees are the only percentage charges this category accepts (report, 'No rival sells a final check'; raw note uk_trade_job_software, monetisation section). Refutations that cut the estimate: cards are impractical for £8k–£60k invoices (limits, Stripe risk reviews and reserves on new connected accounts, chargeback exposure on services), so card volume is deposits and small invoices; consumer surcharging is unlawful so the builder eats the fee, and on a £15k stage a capped £15 fee competes with a free bank transfer, so usage on large invoices will be low unless the homeowner prefers the link (plausible, because typing bank details from an emailed invoice is the APP-fraud pattern payers are warned about; my inference, not in the report). Rails share a source with I40 and must not be summed. Gaming is low; the hazards are structural: (1) whether a Connect Standard direct charge with an application fee keeps JobGuard outside PSRs 2017 needs a legal opinion before any build, and if it fails the idea dies; (2) BUILD_PLAN §11 lists routing builders' customer funds as out of scope unless separately approved and AGENTS §1/§3 forbid extra rails before their tasks, so this needs a Discovered-later entry, its own task and a D10/D05 extension, all behind G4; (3) JobGuard benefits twice, fee plus receipt-to-line allocation that makes §14.8 rule 1 apply by construction, so any nudge toward the paid rail on invoices carrying catches is a trust breach; (4) instant payout at 1.5% is honest only off by default with the price shown before the tap. Build is medium: 4–6 weeks after the rev 2.3 M4-11 Stripe adapter, plus M4-7/M4-8 allocation, M4-15 GoCardless, M4-17 reconciliation and builder Connect KYC, a legal opinion in the low thousands, and ongoing dispute-support load.
verdicts.conditions: File the PSRs 2017 legal opinion and the §11/D10/D05 approvals first; Connect Standard direct charges only, JobGuard never holds funds; bank transfer always free and presented equally; caps as proposed (£6–£15) with the fee itemised on the platform statement; no differential prompting of the paid rail on invoices with catches, tested the way §14.3 tests isolation (builder responses identical with or without catches); instant payout opt-in per payment, never on fee collections, price shown before confirmation; 'provider cleared' kept distinct from 'settled', with refunds and chargebacks feeding §14.9 reversals; application fees refunded with refunds under a stated policy; live only after G4 and the rail-specific review.

revised_revenue.solo: £60–£150 (assumption: 10–25% of invoiced value via rails, about 9 payments mostly capped at £10, plus £20–£40 instant-payout margin)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £150–£350 (15–30% of £600k via rails, about 18 capped payments, plus £75–£150 instant payout)
revised_revenue.firm: £200–£450 (10–20% of £2m via rails, mostly capped at £15; instant payout rarely used by firms)

verdicts.key_risk: A PSRs 2017 opinion that the application-fee structure is regulated payment activity, forcing FCA authorisation and killing the idea; second, being seen to steer customers to the paid rail.

verdicts.reasons: Predictable stage cash is what small builders want, but the proposed rail and price are both wrong. Bacs Direct Debit is built for recurring known amounts, not one-off £5k–£20k stage payments to a builder: the Direct Debit Guarantee lets the homeowner reclaim any collection by indemnity long after the work (the idea admits this), providers apply per-payment limits to new merchants (my understanding, unverified), collection takes several working days after advance notice, and commercial VRP is not reliably available in 2026. A pay-by-bank link at each proof-gated stage (I39) does the same job with less risk, and builders who understand indemnity claims will refuse a mandate. On price, £9–£19/month plus £1 per collection is a 30–65% uplift on the Solo tier for scheduling that competitors include in their plans (Buildertrend and Jobber stage payments; Qted Stripe deposits, raw note construction_platforms); staged invoicing is M4-18 core functionality, and the report argues the tier ladder should rest on one simple meter, live jobs, rather than add-on sprawl ('Three tiers work'; 'Charge for live jobs, not people'). Adoption of 40–60% is therefore not defensible; 10–35% use of the mechanism is, with most of the money already counted as I39 per-collection fees. Regulatory: GoCardless and TrueLayer are the regulated institutions, but a deposit-plus-schedule design must not resemble a consumer instalment plan (credit-brokerage risk flagged in the raw success-fee benchmarks note) and Bacs advance-notice rules apply. Gaming (collecting for incomplete stages) is contained by the proof gate and cancel right. Dependencies are late M4: M4-15, M4-18, D09 metering, D05 and D06 templates.
verdicts.conditions: Do not sell as a separate monthly add-on; bundle the proof-gated stage schedule into M4-18 and the Builder/Firm tiers and earn only the per-collection rail fee under I39; pay-by-bank links per stage as the default rail, with Direct Debit limited to deposits within provider limits and only after D05/D10 record the indemnity risk and the builder is told plainly; a timer never collects without proof-gated builder approval; VRP only when commercially available and approved under D04.

revised_revenue.solo: £5–£20 (assumption: 10% adoption; incremental to I39, not additive)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £40–£90 (25% adoption; mostly per-collection fees already counted in I39)

verdicts.key_risk: Direct Debit indemnity claims on completed stage work, and builders rejecting a mandate-based rail that exposes them to it.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempted on four fronts. (1) Harm to the builder: prefunding a Stripe Issuing balance replaces the 30-day trade credit merchants extend and may forfeit trade-account pricing; a hard decline at the trade counter over a £4 delivery charge humiliates the builder in front of the yard, reads as 'JobGuard's card bounced' and damages the builder-supplier relationship, so 'prevention the builder feels' can become a grievance rather than a benefit. (2) Watchdog independence: interchange is scheme-set and paid by the merchant's acquirer with no named-merchant relationship, so the invoice watchdog is not compromised provided JobGuard never takes merchant-specific rebates or steers spend. (3) Profiting from withheld information: none. (4) Fairness (Xia, Monroe & Cox; Kahneman dual entitlement): the builder pays nothing, the merchant side bears the cost, JobGuard does visible work (exact paid fact for three-way matching, decline of a genuine overcharge), and builders already know card companies earn interchange; a reasonable builder would read 'a small card-network fee, nothing from your merchant' as fair. Residual tension: JobGuard earns on spend while promising to cut waste; at ~0.5% that is small but must be shown in pounds. Survives, but only as an opt-in tool with soft limits, and the revenue is too small to justify any nudging.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Strictly opt-in per purchase order; never the default payment path, never nudged, and PO approval must never be faster or easier when the card is chosen. (b) Plain disclosure at opt-in and on the annual value receipt: 'JobGuard receives a card-network fee of about 0.5% from the merchant's bank; you and your merchant pay nothing extra to JobGuard', with the pounds earned shown. (c) No merchant-specific arrangement of any kind: no rebates, co-marketing, preferred-merchant lists or acceptance nudges; JobGuard's take must be identical whichever merchant is used. (d) Soft limits: card limit = PO gross plus a builder-set tolerance (default e.g. 2% or £20) so trivial variances never decline; a decline above tolerance triggers an immediate builder push to approve the difference; a declined authorisation is never recorded as a watchdog Finding against the merchant. (e) The Issuing balance is the builder's own money: withdrawable at any time, never swept to pay subscription or success fees, never a condition of any feature. (f) Card spend and interchange are excluded from every watchdog metric, D11 signal and success-fee derivation. (g) Each card issuance is an exact approved Decision bound to the PO (AGENTS §5.3); no standing authority (D05). (h) Stripe is the regulated issuer and holds funds; JobGuard's programme-manager status is confirmed with FCA advice before build; D04 residency for Issuing data; behind G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £40–£80 (opt-in adoption below the original 30–40% card-spend assumption; £80 is the ceiling)

verdicts.key_risk: The trade-counter decline: if the card bounces on legitimate small variances the builder experiences 'prevention' as embarrassment and lost time in front of their supplier, blames JobGuard, and the story travels; the soft-limit and instant-override conditions are what keep this a benefit rather than a grievance.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempted. (1) Harm: escrow ties funds to third-party release and implies the builder needs policing, which is why most builders hate it; but when the builder chooses it per job to win a nervous customer it removes non-payment risk entirely (funds committed before the stage starts), which is a genuine builder interest and cheaper for them than ever needing the 10% withheld-payment path. (2) Independence and authority: the dangerous part of the idea as written is tying release to JobGuard's proof gates. That turns JobGuard's evidence rules into a payment gate over the builder, a homeowner will read 'JobGuard-verified' as workmanship approval, and a missing photo would freeze the builder's cash. This element fails the lens and must be removed: the builder raises the release request, JobGuard only attaches what the builder selects, and gates warn but never block. (3) Profiting from delay: JobGuard's share must be flat per stage or a fixed share of the provider's fee, never tied to balance, duration, interest or dispute outcome, otherwise JobGuard earns from the builder waiting. (4) Fairness: fees are visible, paid to a regulated provider, and the builder opts in per job; a builder who has lost a job to a nervous homeowner sees it as a tool, not a tax. Customer relationship improves rather than degrades when release rules are mechanical and builder-favourable. Survives only in a stripped form where JobGuard is a document courier, not an arbiter.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Offered only when the builder switches it on for a specific job; never suggested by a watchdog Finding, never in the Decision Inbox, never a default above any job-value threshold. (b) Release requests are raised by the builder as an approved command (§5.3); JobGuard's stage Decision may pre-fill but never auto-raises; proof gates may warn but never block a release request. (c) Portal language limited to 'these photos and documents existed at these times and have not changed'; no 'verified', 'approved' or 'JobGuard-checked' wording that implies workmanship. (d) JobGuard's share is a flat fee per stage or a fixed percentage of the provider's fee, disclosed to builder and homeowner in pounds; no share of interest, nothing linked to escrow balance, duration, objections or disputes. (e) Auto-release after a fixed N days absent a specific, evidenced objection under the provider's rules; JobGuard never adjudicates objections and never communicates with the homeowner about one beyond forwarding. (f) JobGuard never holds, routes or initiates funds (AGENTS §3); legal review confirms its role is not payment initiation or safeguarding under PSRs 2017/EMRs 2011; a new decision record for regulated introductions before any pilot. (g) No withheld-payment recovery case or success fee can ever arise on an escrowed stage. (h) The builder can switch the option off for future stages at any time. (i) M5, behind G4.
verdicts.key_risk: Proof-gated release making JobGuard the party the builder must satisfy to get paid; one stuck release over a missing photo, or a homeowner saying 'JobGuard didn't verify it', turns a useful option into the story that JobGuard sides with customers against builders.

verdicts.reasons: The refutation holds. (1) Harm: invoice finance costs 1.5–4% per 30 days (roughly 18–50% annualised) and loans carry 1–3% commission; JobGuard already supplies the cheaper route (M4-16 reminders and the withheld-payment case) inside the subscription, so JobGuard would earn when the builder chooses the expensive route over the free one it provides. (2) Exploiting an advantage: the cash-flow view is JobGuard's own projection; showing a shortfall and then selling a loan against it is textbook dual-entitlement unfairness and precisely the 'JobGuard sells you loans' line the founder fears; per Cain, Loewenstein & Moore, disclosing the commission does not neutralise the conflict and can license worse behaviour. (3) Independence: on the same invoice JobGuard could earn ~0.6% from finance or 10% from a recovery case, so its guidance on that invoice is conflicted whichever way it points, and internal revenue pressure to promote finance is a standing risk the idea itself names. (4) Regulatory reality: sole traders and small partnerships borrowing £25k or less are regulated credit, so the Solo archetype is largely excluded, leaving negligible revenue against a real trust cost. Variant A (builder-initiated invoice finance on business invoices, with the evidence pack lowering the lender's dispute risk) is the defensible half, but as bundled the idea fails the default-reject test.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as bundled. If Variant A alone is resubmitted it would need: limited companies and business customers only; off by default; reachable only from the invoice screen, never from the cash-flow view, Decision Inbox or a Finding; never offered while a recovery case is open or once the D03 overdue window has begun; commission disclosed in pounds before the tap; evidence pack shared only against a per-invoice consent record; lender-facing language stating JobGuard does not certify the debt; a decision record and legal review; no referrals under pilot_no_charge. Variant B (loans from the cash-flow view) should not return.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (sole traders excluded by credit-broking rules even under an A-only resubmission)

verdicts.key_risk: A builder who realises JobGuard's own cash-flow screen led them into a 2%-a-month facility while JobGuard took a commission, or that an invoice was steered toward finance instead of the free reminder path; that is the 'profited from my position' narrative in a word-of-mouth trade.

verdicts.reasons: The refutation holds. (1) Customer relationship: JobGuard would earn a lender's commission on the builder's customer, disclosed to the homeowner under CONC 4.5 as sharpened by Johnson v FirstRand; the homeowner learns the builder's software company profits from their loan, and any mis-sale, decline or s75 dispute lands on the builder's relationship and JobGuard's brand. Kanda (~700 tradesperson IARs, FCA-restricted February 2026, liquidation May 2026) is the live precedent. (2) Harm to the builder: a 0% subsidy costs the builder 8–12% of the loan; a lender satisfaction-note gate on portal sign-off gives a third party a hold over payout; the builder must become an IAR under a principal, taking on Consumer Duty obligations for JobGuard's revenue. (3) Independence: the quote watchdog exists to keep quotes honest, yet subsidy-funded 0% deals create pressure to inflate quotes that the watchdog cannot police, and give JobGuard a financial interest in larger financed quotes. (4) Fairness: the builder does the work, the homeowner bears the interest, and JobGuard takes 1–2% for an introduction; the builder gains nothing they could not get from a finance partner they choose directly, without JobGuard's cut. It sits squarely on the founder's 'selling builders' customers' trust-risk list.
verdicts.conditions: Not kept. If a founder decision ever revisits this, the only form defensible under this lens is a commission-free pointer to the builder's own chosen finance provider (no JobGuard revenue, no JobGuard branding on the credit journey, no payout linked to JobGuard sign-off, no subsidy mechanics inside the quote), which is a different idea from the one proposed.
verdicts.key_risk: A mis-sold or declined loan on a builder's customer, with JobGuard's commission disclosed to that homeowner, that ends the builder's relationship with JobGuard and becomes the 'they make money off my customers' story.

verdicts.reasons: Refutations attempted. (1) Harm: the premium is paid by the homeowner or absorbed by the builder, and scheme-member builders can already buy IBGs direct, so JobGuard's cut is fair only if the price through JobGuard is never higher than direct. (2) Independence: an insurer is not a supplier the watchdog polices, so no compromise; but insurers pay for 'documentation quality', which tempts JobGuard to feed proof, watchdog or shadow data to insurers or to shape proof capture around insurer needs, and that must be cut off structurally. (3) Withheld information: registration after lock does not interact with the shadow bill materially (the IBG line is excluded from Q), but claims-time subrogation is a live concern: an insurer holding JobGuard's proof pack could later use it against the builder, breaking the 'our evidence is yours' promise. (4) Customer relationship and fairness: the homeowner gets a real, priced, optional product protecting them from the builder's insolvency, the builder wins work with a 'guaranteed job' badge, JobGuard does visible work (registration, pack) and is paid by the insurer at the same price as direct. Under Xia et al. this is the clearest fair case in the set: visible work, cost borne by the party that benefits, no exploitation of an advantage. A reasonable builder sees it as a sales tool, not a tax.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Optional, never pre-ticked, never implied to be compulsory; price through JobGuard no higher than the provider's direct price, with premium and JobGuard's commission shown to the builder in pounds. (b) Data to the insurer limited to builder-consented, builder-visible policy inputs at registration (contract value, dates, trade, address, builder identity, and a completion proof pack the builder selects); no watchdog Findings, D11 signals, shadow signals, matching results or diary content ever leave. (c) No ongoing evidence feed; any claims-time request for evidence needs a fresh per-request builder consent or legal process; the provider contract excludes using JobGuard data to price the builder's own future premiums or to pursue the builder. (d) Proof gates, the final check and invoice issuance never depend on selling or registering cover; registration is gated on the completion pack only to prevent policies for unfinished work. (e) The IBG line is a distinct invoice kind excluded from net principal, catches and recovered principal (§14.9). (f) Badge shown only when the builder chose cover; no 'unprotected' state is ever shown. (g) IDD/RAO art 72C introducer boundary or IAR status confirmed; DMCC drip-pricing compliance (priced up front); D02 for the pass-through line; D12 for homeowner data; a new decision record for partner commissions; no commission in pilot_no_charge.
verdicts.key_risk: Insurer access to the evidence pack turning into subrogation or repricing against the builder; a builder who learns JobGuard's photos were used to deny a claim or raise their premium will conclude JobGuard's evidence works for insurers, not for them.

verdicts.reasons: Variant A refuted and survives narrowly. (1) Harm and conflict: a 'thin cover' verdict is JobGuard's own judgement, and if JobGuard earns on the referral it has an incentive to call cover thin; that conflict is neutralised only if the check is deterministic against builder-entered figures (expiry date, sum insured versus the frozen accepted value) with no JobGuard-invented 'recommended level' and no advice wording. (2) Independence: brokers are not suppliers the watchdog polices. (3) Fairness: a builder starting a £60k job on a £50k contractors' all-risks limit is genuinely helped; broker commissions are known and disclosed; nothing is gated; the builder taps through with consent. A reasonable builder sees a single dismissible reminder as service. Variant B fails the lens: it sells a builder-level data feed to an insurer (on the founder's trust-risk list), makes the builder feel surveilled, penalises a builder whose proof compliance dips with a lost discount, invites the insurer to use the feed at claims or renewal, and the discount is unproven while the metric is gameable. B is not kept.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Variant A only; Variant B is excluded and must not be built without a separate founder decision, DPIA and fairness review. (b) The check is deterministic and published: policy expiry within 30 days, builder-entered sum insured below the frozen accepted value, or no policy recorded; no recommended limits, no risk scoring, no wording that advises. (c) The card appears once per job at switch-live, is dismissible, never blocks, never repeats as a nag, and never appears in the Decision Inbox as a Finding; no feature depends on buying insurance. (d) Handoff only on an explicit tap with an audit event; data shared limited to contact details, trade, turnover band and job-mix counts; no job evidence, watchdog or shadow data under A. (e) Commission disclosed to the builder before the tap; no per-quote or renewal-steering incentive to JobGuard. (f) FCA art 72C introducer boundary or IAR status settled before any real referral; a new decision record for partner commissions; no commission in pilot_no_charge. (g) Copy audit for advice drift each release.
verdicts.key_risk: The 'thin cover' threshold drifting into a sales lever; any sign that JobGuard's check exists to generate broker referrals reads as JobGuard scaring builders into buying insurance for a commission.

verdicts.reasons: Refutations attempted. (1) Harm: the builder pays for labour they already know they need; each message is builder-approved and sent as the builder (D10), so customer-relationship risk is bounded, provided approval is per message with the facts visible rather than a batch rubber-stamp. (2) Independence: the structural conflict is that JobGuard would run ordinary chasing for a flat fee and earn 10% only if chasing fails and a case opens, so a desk could, consciously or not, let an invoice drift toward 'ignored' and nudge the builder to open a case. §14.7's rule that only cash settled after case opening counts limits this, and the safeguards below close the nudge path. (3) Withheld information: none; the desk works only from invoice facts. (4) Fairness: plain labour for money on a loss the builder already sees, priced in line with Chaser, Satago and bookkeepers; who did the work and who bears the cost are transparent. A reasonable builder sees it as fair and in their interest.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Every draft shows the exact invoice, amount, due date and recipient; one approval per message, no batch approve, no standing authority (D05); the builder is always the sender (D10). (b) The desk cannot draft, suggest, recommend or mention opening a recovery case, escalation or fees, and has no write access to the case path; the case-open command remains reachable only by the builder from the invoice screen. (c) The desk does not draft on disputed invoices, invoices with an open case, or beyond invoice facts; consumer-facing reminders reviewed for DMCC 2024/CPUT compliance. (d) Desk staff performance and pay measured on days-to-payment and builder satisfaction, never on cases opened or fee income; an internal D11-style audit signal flags any invoice the desk chased that later becomes a case. (e) Add-on entitlement recorded on subscription_terms (D09), cancellable monthly, shown separately from the 10% on the value receipt. (f) Legal sign-off that assisting a builder with their own invoices is not FCA debt collecting. (g) Behind G4 for real customers; no live use in pilot_no_charge.

revised_revenue.solo: £47 (£468 per taker)

verdicts.key_risk: The desk becoming a funnel into 10% cases: if builders perceive the chasing service they pay for goes quiet before a case is suggested, the flat fee looks like bait for the success fee.

verdicts.reasons: Refutations attempted. (1) Harm: an upsell inside a stressful dispute, stacked on the 10%; fixed small steps (letter before action, small-claims filing) are genuinely useful and cheap, but a percentage of a panel member's fees is a referral cut the builder ultimately pays. (2) Independence: JobGuard paid by the adviser it lists creates an incentive toward costly escalation over settlement, in tension with D10's factual, restrained pursuit; half-secret referral commissions are now legally hazardous (Expert Tooling v Engie) and disclosure does not cure the conflict (Cain et al.). (3) Fairness (Xia et al.): the builder bears the cost and the partner does the work, so a cut to JobGuard for a click is exploiting its position, whereas a flat builder-paid pack-preparation fee and transparent fixed-price resale at the partner's direct price pay JobGuard for work it visibly did. A reasonable builder accepts the latter and resents the former. Survives only in the flat-handoff and fixed-price forms; the 12.5% introducer fee on panel fees is rejected.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Offered only inside a recovery case the builder has already opened and after the customer has refused or ignored the builder's own reminder; never in the Decision Inbox, never model-recommended, never staff-recommended. (b) Permitted forms: fixed-price steps resold at a price no higher than the partner's direct price with JobGuard's margin stated in pounds on the screen, and a flat builder-paid handoff fee credited against the pack; no percentage introducer fee on adviser fees and no share of sums recovered. (c) The 10% success fee and shadow-bill handling never vary with whether a step was bought; the 10% is stated to exclude these costs. (d) HGCRA 1996 s.106 residential-occupier exclusion respected: no adjudication offered on domestic jobs; legal steps only through an SRA-authorised partner. (e) A consent-to-share record per handoff; only the case pack leaves. (f) Panel vetting, builder ratings, no exclusivity, and a published cap on JobGuard's margin in the terms. (g) Each offer is a commercial send audited under §5.3; a new decision record and legal review before any live partner.
verdicts.key_risk: A builder in a dispute who feels JobGuard's screen pushed a £50 filing and a £3,500 consultant on which JobGuard took a slice, then also took 10%: the 'they profit at every step' narrative.

verdicts.reasons: (1) The revenue mechanism is unproven. UK commercial-card interchange is uncapped (the IFR caps consumer cards only) so gross interchange of roughly 1–2% exists, but Stripe publishes no UK Issuing revenue share; shares are negotiated on volume, and a programme moving £2–5m a year of builder spend has no leverage. Assume 0–0.3% net until a term sheet exists; 0.5% is a hope. (2) Builders buy materials on merchant trade accounts with 30–60 day credit and rebates. A prefunded single-use card replaces that credit with the builder's own cash parked at Stripe — cash-flow negative for the most cash-strapped segment (report, 'Frame the price against lost money': £26bn owed to SMEs at any time). A 30–40% card share of materials spend is optimistic; 10–20% is more realistic and skews to small Screwfix/Toolstation tickets, not the Jewson invoices the watchdog cares about. (3) 'Declined at the till' is a liability, not a feature: a hard limit equal to PO gross declines every legitimate variance (delivery charge, substituted item, price revision, VAT rounding). The builder is embarrassed at the trade counter and merchant staff blame the app. MCC locks are coarse — 5211/5200/5251 cover B&Q personal spend as well as builders' merchants. (4) The plan already obtains the paid fact from the M4-7 bank feed and M2-4 three-way matching; the card is a duplicate rail requiring M4-15-style rail work plus programme-manager obligations (card controls, disputes, KYB flows, D04 residency for Issuing data) for pennies. (5) It does not touch the prevention problem the founder posed: interchange accrues on spend whether or not anything was prevented, and a declined overcharge earns nothing, as the idea concedes. (6) Ramp/Brex earn interchange in the US where commercial interchange is ~2.5–3% and on billions of spend; the research report contains no UK SME precedent for a platform earning material interchange at this scale.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a revenue line. If builders ever ask for PO-bound purchasing cards as a control, treat it as a subscription feature after M4 and only with a written Stripe (or equivalent) UK revenue-share term sheet, a decision record for the programme-manager role and D04 sign-off on Issuing data residency.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£30 a year (assumes £52k materials, 15% on card, 0–0.3% net share) versus a £348 subscription
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0–£120 a year (£210k materials, 20% on card, 0–0.3% net) versus £708 subscription
revised_revenue.firm: £0–£350 a year (£700k materials, 20% on card, 0–0.3% net) versus £1,428 subscription

verdicts.key_risk: Builder cash-flow harm and till declines make the watchdog feel like a nanny while yielding near-zero revenue, and JobGuard inherits programme-manager obligations for a rail the plan does not need.

verdicts.reasons: (1) The revenue mechanism does not exist at UK escrow price points. Providers charge single-digit pounds per party per transaction; none will pay JobGuard £10 per stage or 0.3% of escrowed value because that exceeds their own revenue. Any £10-a-stage line would have to be a JobGuard charge to the builder or homeowner, which is a different product with its own willingness-to-pay question. (2) Builders reject escrow for a structural reason: stage payments fund the next stage's materials and labour. Release on homeowner sign-off or after N days converts every stage into a built-in late payment — the very loss the report identifies as the robust, government-measured pain (£11bn a year). The idea's own trust note says most builders hate it. (3) Tying release to JobGuard's proof gates makes JobGuard the homeowner's policeman over the builder, the opposite of 'profit watchdog for builders' and squarely on the founder's trust-risk list. Homeowners will read 'verified' (hashes, existence, per AGENTS §5.8) as 'workmanship verified', so JobGuard gets blamed for bad work and for withheld money. (4) Regulatory: JobGuard raising release requests and configuring auto-release rules edges toward payment initiation or control of client money (PSRs 2017). AGENTS §3 forbids holding customers' funds; satisfying it only if the provider holds funds still leaves JobGuard's rules deciding when money moves, which needs a new decision record and legal review before a line of code. (5) Timing: it depends on a stage sign-off feature not in the plan (the idea's I55), M4-18 interim applications, M4-3 packs and a provider adapter — M5 at the earliest, so any revenue is years away. (6) Volume: Solo jobs average £8k, far below the £25k threshold; only Firm has meaningful large domestic jobs and roughly half of its work is likely commercial where escrow is irrelevant.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a revenue line. It could be parked as a builder-chosen sales tool with no JobGuard revenue after M4-18, and only with mechanical builder-favourable release rules, no JobGuard-controlled auto-release, and legal sign-off that JobGuard's role is not payment initiation.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£5 a year (at most one job over £25k, 5–10% uptake, and only if a provider paid anything, which none is known to)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £5–£30 a year (≈7 domestic jobs over £25k, 10% uptake, 4 stages, ≤£10 a stage, conditional on a provider paying)
revised_revenue.firm: £20–£100 a year (≈12 domestic jobs over £25k, 10% uptake, 5 stages, conditional on a provider paying)

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard becomes a payment gate over the builder; builders churn and say so in a word-of-mouth trade.

verdicts.reasons: (1) Segment mismatch. Solo and Small firm customers are mostly homeowners, so invoice finance (B2B only) barely applies; and sole traders and small partnerships borrowing £25k or less are regulated credit (CCA s.16B exemption applies only above £25k), so introducing them is credit broking under RAO art 36A. The Solo archetype is excluded unless JobGuard becomes an appointed representative, which £0–£40 a year cannot justify. (2) Construction receivables are the sector most factors exclude or restrict (applications for payment, retentions, set-off, pay-when-certified), so lender appetite for selective finance on builder invoices is thin and rates high; 5–15% financed is optimistic — 2–5% at Firm is more realistic. (3) Working-capital loan take-up of 20–30% a year is far above any plausible rate; 5–10% is generous. (4) Trust: this is the founder's named fear ('JobGuard sells you loans'), and there is a structural conflict with the withheld-payment 10% on the same invoice — JobGuard can earn a finance commission or a case fee. Forbidding the offer once a case is open does not remove the pre-case steer, and the report is explicit that disclosure does not neutralise a conflict (Cain, Loewenstein & Moore, 'The hidden final check' section). (5) Every 'Get this invoice paid early' or 'borrow against this' line is likely a financial promotion (FSMA s.21) needing an authorised approver, so the legal setup dominates a technically small build; D12 lawful basis for sharing the builder's customer data with a lender is unresolved. (6) Comparables: Chaser and Satago bundle finance, but Satago is itself a lender; the report gives no evidence that introducer commissions on SME lending are material to a platform, and the Apollo 25%-of-fees figure is the idea's own unverified cite.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected. If ever revisited: Variant A only, Firm tier, limited companies only, builder-initiated, after G4 and M4-8, with a decision record for partner commissions, an authorised-approver arrangement for promotions, and a signed lender with stated construction appetite. Never offer where a recovery case exists or could be opened on the same invoice.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (regulated credit for sole traders at £25k or under; exclude)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £20–£80 a year (limited companies only; £180k B2B invoiced, 3% financed at 0.6% ≈ £30; loans 10% take-up × £30k × 2% ≈ £60 at best)

verdicts.key_risk: Brand damage as 'the watchdog that pushes debt' for revenue below a tenth of the subscription, plus a live conflict with the withheld-payment case fee.

verdicts.reasons: (1) Regulatory cost dwarfs revenue. Direct authorisation means full permission (6–12 months) with Consumer Duty and CONC obligations and ongoing compliance overhead plausibly £50–150k a year; the faster AR route depends on a principal willing to cover a platform plus its introducing builders — exactly the model the idea says failed at Kanda in 2026 (stated by the idea, not verified in the research report), so principals will be wary. At £50–£330 per builder-year JobGuard needs several thousand paying builders merely to cover compliance. (2) A 1–2% net share for a platform sitting behind a broker and lender is generous; 0.5–1% net is more realistic. On 0% deals the builder's 8–12% subsidy funds JobGuard's commission, so the builder is paying JobGuard to sell their customer a loan. (3) Uptake of 8–10% of domestic jobs financed assumes builders who do not currently offer finance start doing so; those who already do have a broker and no reason to route through JobGuard. (4) Quote inflation to fund 0% subsidies is precisely what the quote watchdog cannot police, and it corrupts the frozen accepted value that §14.6 attribution and D11 signals rely on. (5) A mis-sold or failed loan lands on JobGuard's brand with both homeowner and builder; commission disclosure standards tightened after the 2025 motor-finance litigation. (6) The genuine product upside (builders win bigger jobs and are paid on completion) is obtainable with a plain, unpaid signpost to the builder's own broker, which needs none of this.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected for now. Revisit only with more than ~2,000 paying builders, a principal willing to cover the platform and its builders, a founder decision that lender revenue on builders' customers is acceptable, and a D11 signal on finance-linked quote inflation. Nothing before M5 and G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £50–£120 a year (19 domestic jobs, 6–8% financed, £6k loan, 0.5–1% net)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £80–£270 a year (≈17 domestic jobs, 6–8% financed, £20k loan, 0.5–1% net)
revised_revenue.firm: £80–£330 a year (≈16 domestic jobs, 6–8% financed, £25k unsecured cap, 0.5–1% net)

verdicts.key_risk: Compliance overhead and principal failure (Kanda pattern) with revenue far too small to fund it, plus quote inflation the watchdog cannot police.

verdicts.reasons: (1) This is the only idea in the set where all three parties want the thing: homeowners increasingly expect deposit protection and an insurance-backed guarantee (TrustMark requirements), builders use it to win, and the insurer or administrator pays. The commission source does not touch merchants, so the invoice watchdog's independence survives, and it does not touch the shadow bill. (2) The uptake assumptions (25–60%) are unsupported. Scheme-registered builders already sell IBGs through their scheme, and an administrator will not pay JobGuard for jobs a member would register anyway; among non-members, domestic uptake is more plausibly 10–25%, and Firm's commercial work is out of scope. (3) The money is thin: 15–20% of a premium that is 0.6–1% of job value with a £40 floor works out at £15–£400 a year, under a third of the subscription at every tier — a retention and win-rate feature, not a revenue line. (4) Regulatory: passing policy inputs (contract value, dates, address, builder identity) is more than the RAO art 72C 'introduce only' exclusion, so JobGuard needs IAR/AR status under the administrator (1–3 months) or must strip back to contact-details-only; IPT 12% applies; DMCC drip-pricing means the line must be optional and priced up front; none of D01–D13 covers partner commissions, so a new decision record is required and nothing can run in pilot_no_charge. (5) The build is small — a distinct invoice line kind excluded from net principal so it never inflates Q under §14.9, plus an M4-3 pack export — but it sits after M1-12 and M4-3, and the partnership is the long pole; the structural-warranty variant (stage-photo checklists) is a separate, larger integration. (6) The HomePro, QANW and FMB Build Assure figures are the idea's cites, not in the research report; treat them as unverified until a partner term sheet exists.
verdicts.conditions: Single-administrator pilot only. Decision record for partner commissions before any commission is received. Choose and document the IAR route or a contact-details-only introduction with legal sign-off. Never pre-ticked; never gates proof capture, the final check, the lock or invoice issue. Distinct invoice line kind excluded from Q with an automated test under §14.9. No watchdog, D11 or shadow data reaches the insurer — builder-consented, builder-visible facts only. Registration only against the completion proof pack. Measure real uptake in the pilot before building bordereau reconciliation. Not in pilot_no_charge. Position internally as win-rate and retention, with revenue capped in the model at the figures below.

revised_revenue.solo: £15–£40 a year (19 jobs, 10–25% uptake, premium ≈£64 at 0.8% of £8k, 15% commission)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £60–£150 a year (24 jobs, 10–25% uptake, premium ≈£200 at 0.8% of £25k, 15% commission)
revised_revenue.firm: £150–£400 a year (33 jobs, 10–20% domestic-only uptake, premium ≈£480 at 0.8% of £60k, 15% commission)

verdicts.key_risk: Uptake far below assumption because scheme members already have an IBG route and non-members' homeowners rarely ask, leaving a regulated partnership that earns less than it costs to administer.

verdicts.reasons: (1) Revenue is de minimis. An affiliate paying 10% capped at £100 on an annual renewal, with realistic switching through a new channel of about 10% a year, yields single digits to low tens of pounds at Solo and Small firm. Firm programmes (£5–12k contractors' all-risks and employers' liability) are broker-placed, not affiliate-link business, so the £900 top of the range is fiction. (2) The genuinely useful part — 'your public liability limit is below this job's accepted value' or 'you have staff and no employers' liability' — is a product feature that needs no commission and is cleaner without one. Adding a paid link invites advising-wording risk under FCA financial-promotion and insurance-distribution rules and a copy audit, for about £20. (3) Cover-detail fields add onboarding friction in a segment where only 29% of one-person construction businesses use any software (report, 'Builders' willingness to pay'). (4) Variant B is on the founder's trust-risk list: it sells a builder-level integrity feed to an insurer. Insurers need years of loss data before funding a 5–20% discount, and a builder who loses the discount because proof compliance slipped feels surveilled — exactly the 'JobGuard profits from information about me' reading the report warns collapses trust in a word-of-mouth trade. Per-policyholder fees of £10–£20 are nothing. (5) Comparables (Procore Risk Advisors, Buildertrend with Assurely) are enterprise or US; the Simply Business affiliate terms are the idea's own cite, not verified in the report.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a revenue line. Ship the cover check as an optional free field with a generic 'check with your broker' note once M1-7's frozen accepted value makes it cheap; never gate any feature on it; no commission link without a decision record. Drop Variant B entirely.

revised_revenue.solo: £3–£20 a year (£300 premium, 10% switch rate, 10% commission; legal-expenses add ≤£10). Variant B: £0 for years.
revised_revenue.small_firm: £15–£50 a year (£2.5k premium, 10–20% switch, capped at £100). Variant B: £0 for years.
revised_revenue.firm: £20–£120 a year (broker-placed programmes where affiliate terms rarely apply). Variant B: £0 for years.

verdicts.key_risk: Variant B turns a trust asset into a surveillance story; Variant A is compliance effort for pocket change.

verdicts.reasons: (1) The honest strength: it sells labour for a loss the builder already feels. Late payment is the robust, government-measured pain (report: £11bn a year, £26bn owed; raw notes: LSBS 2024, 51% of no-employee businesses giving credit hit late payment), and the desk lives exactly in the ordinary-late-payment zone that §14.7 says never carries a fee, so it neither cannibalises nor games the 10%. Bookkeepers at £100–£200 a month show builders buy admin labour monthly. (2) Refuting take-up: Solo builders chase by text and a £39 add-on exceeds their £29 subscription — 3–5%, not 10%. Small firms typically have an office partner or bookkeeper already chasing — 15–25%, not 35%. Firms have office staff — 15–25%, not 50%. (3) Unit economics are thin: a controller at roughly £42k loaded per 80 accounts costs about £525 per account-year. Solo at £468 loses money unless one controller carries 150+ Solo accounts; margin is 20–35% at Small firm and Firm at best. It is a headcount business with quality variance and churn when a controller leaves. Chaser (£199 a month) and Satago (£45–£200) are software, not desks, so those comparables do not prove a desk margin. (4) Homeowner customers dominate at Solo and Small firm: consumer reminders must clear CPUT/DMCC aggressive-practice tests, and the builder must remain the sender of exact text to an exact recipient (D10, M4-16). (5) JobGuard staff drafting from invoice facts must never see shadow tables (§14.3 break-glass) and need their own D12 lawful basis as processor for the builder; a desk with support-style access is the most likely accidental pre-lock disclosure route, which under §14.3 makes signals permanently fee-ineligible. (6) It sits behind G4 and needs M4-5 templates and M4-16 dunning controls, so it is not early revenue and does not capture prevention value; it deepens stickiness.
verdicts.conditions: Pilot with one part-time controller for Small firm and Firm only, after G4, M4-5 and M4-16. Replace the Solo tier with self-serve reminder templates rather than a loss-making desk. Hard grant wall between the desk role and shadow tables with break-glass audit, tested like §14.15 Test Q. Every draft approved by the builder per send (D10, AGENTS §5.3); the desk cannot open, suggest or escalate a recovery case. Cap accounts per controller and publish unit economics before hiring a second. Consumer-reminder wording reviewed under CPUT/DMCC. Add-on entitlement recorded on subscription terms (M4-13) with a D09 v3 line.

revised_revenue.solo: £15–£25 a year averaged across all Solo builders (3–5% take-up × £468); gross margin ≈0% or negative per taker
revised_revenue.small_firm: £90–£150 a year averaged (15–25% × £588); gross margin 20–35% per taker
revised_revenue.firm: £180–£300 a year averaged (15–25% × £1,188); gross margin 20–35% per taker

verdicts.key_risk: A low-margin services line that scales headcount rather than software, with a Solo tier that loses money and a staff access path that could leak the shadow bill.

verdicts.reasons: (1) The value is not the revenue. The withheld-payment 10% is a founder-fixed category, and it has no credible end-game without an escalation route: 'reminder sent, then nothing' means no settled cash and no fee. A fixed-fee ladder is what makes the 10% feel earned (report, 'The hidden final check': fairness turns on who did the work and bore the cost). (2) Refuting the revenue: case counts of 1/3/6 a year are high. Escalations beyond the builder's own reminders are more like 0.3–0.5, 1–2 and 3–5 a year, and at £2–£15 margin per Garfield-style step (£7.50 letter, £50 filing) or a £25 pack fee, Variant A yields pounds, not hundreds. Variant B is Firm-only because residential occupiers sit outside statutory adjudication (HGCRA 1996 s.106), at perhaps 0.5–1 referral a year. (3) JobGuard paid by the adviser it recommends, inside a stressful dispute, is the R&D-boutique structure builders distrust; the flat builder-paid handoff is cleaner and should be the default. (4) Legal: conducting litigation is a reserved activity, so JobGuard prepares the pack and the builder or the SRA-authorised partner files; referral fees are lawful and disclosable outside personal injury (LASPO 2012 s.56); construction payment is not a regulated claims-management sector (report legal notes). Verify the SRA disclosure rule with the partner. (5) Stacking: a builder paying JobGuard 10% plus step fees plus a £250 handoff must be compared honestly with a collector at 8–15% of fresh debt (report benchmark table; collectors also exclude court costs) or the builder will conclude JobGuard is dearer for a homeowner debt where the Late Payment Act gives no interest or compensation. (6) Build is small after recovery cases (0034) and evidence packs (#92); it needs M4-5 and partner agreements and sits behind G4 for real customers, so it is not early revenue either.
verdicts.conditions: Default to the flat builder-paid handoff or cost pass-through with zero JobGuard margin at first; measure case-to-settlement conversion in the pilot to justify the core 10% before adding any margin. Variant B for commercial and subcontract disputes only. Print every fee and JobGuard's share on the referral screen; no exclusivity; no model-driven 'escalate' prompts (AGENTS §5.9); JobGuard never varies the 10% or a shadow outcome by whether escalation was bought (D11 signal if attempted). Partner must be SRA-authorised and does the filing; JobGuard's role limited to evidence preparation under a consent-to-share record (D12). Decision record for referral arrangements before any fee is received. Show the all-in comparison with a collector's rate honestly in the case screen.

revised_revenue.solo: £5–£15 a year (0.3–0.5 escalated cases × £10–£30 margin)
revised_revenue.firm: £150–£700 a year (3–5 cases at £10–£30 plus 0.5–1 Firm-only panel referral at ≈£5k × 12.5%, or £250 flat handoffs)

verdicts.key_risk: Upsell pressure inside a dispute reads as profiteering on the builder's worst day; revenue is too small to matter, so it is justified only as the route that turns a withheld-payment case into settled cash.

verdicts.reasons: Every refutation fails. (1) The builder opts in per quote and pays for labour a named reviewer visibly does, so who-did-the-work and who-bears-the-cost line up (research report, 'The hidden final check' section: Xia/Monroe/Cox). (2) No supplier or merchant money and the reviewer sees quote plus transcript only, so the watchdog's independence is untouched. (3) It runs before the job exists, so nothing can be withheld; every adopted suggestion becomes baseline scope, which is fee-free forever under §14.2, so the service shrinks JobGuard's own contingent base rather than feeding it. (4) No customer-facing effect. The only trust seam is a suggestion the builder declines that later shows up as a shadow catch ('your QS told me, I chose not to, then you charged me'); that closes by treating reviewer output as a pre-lock disclosure.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Every reviewer suggestion is recorded as a disclosure event bound to the job, so any later signal matching it is disclosed_before_lock and permanently fee-free. (b) The external-reviewer role has no grant on evidence or shadow tables and loses access after send. (c) Reviewers declare no merchant or supplier affiliation or commission, and the 'current merchant prices' reference is never funded by suppliers. (d) Opt-in at 'Send this quote': never default-on, never send-blocking, no loss-framed nag. (e) Terms state the review is an aid; reviewer PI cover; D04 if any reviewer sits outside the UK/EU boundary. (f) The sales page states plainly that anything found at quote stage is fee-free forever.

revised_revenue.solo: £285 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: Take-up is a guess; value rests on reviewer quality and on the builder believing the review is independent of JobGuard's fee interest.

verdicts.reasons: The refutation to beat is 'your staff built my bill, then your machine found the holes and charged me' — the exact betrayal pattern the research says spreads by word of mouth (betrayal aversion, Bohnet & Zeckhauser). The idea already neutralises it with the desk_prepared permanent ineligibility, which also removes any incentive for desk staff to under-prepare. With that rule the builder pays a fixed fee for labour a person visibly did, keeps the two decisions that matter (lock and invoice issue, D06), and gets JobGuard's final check free. That passes the who-did-the-work test. Remaining seams are operational: desk staff chasing the builder's customer in JobGuard's name (relationship damage), the status of lines the desk adds, and whether the final check still runs on desk jobs.
verdicts.conditions: (a) desk_prepared is recorded on the lock and makes every signal on that job permanently fee-ineligible, including any supplier-overcharge catch the desk surfaces. (b) The final check still runs and reveals on desk-prepared jobs, fee-free, so paying for the desk never costs the builder the second check. (c) Lines the desk adds before lock are builder capture, attributed to the delegated actor in audit. (d) Desk staff hold only the ordinary builder-visible role — never jobguard_shadow or break-glass — and are organisationally separate from break-glass holders. (e) Desk staff contact the builder's customer only through builder-authorised sends in the builder's name, never in JobGuard's name and never to chase money. (f) The builder alone performs 'Complete final account' and the invoice-issue Decision. (g) D02 VAT on the service; D13 amendment text for desk_prepared.

revised_revenue.solo: £285 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: The £150 tier is near break-even, and one incident where desk staff appear to have held something back would be read as betrayal even though it is fee-free.

verdicts.reasons: Paid onboarding is ordinary (Payaca, Buildertrend precedents in the report) and the specialist does real labour, so the fee itself is fair. The refutation that lands: a builder pays £49 to have JobGuard read their WhatsApp thread and PO emails for an in-flight job, and those records — which were the builder's own capture in their old system, made before they knew the Log-an-extra rule — become fee-bearing evidence under §14.2. That is exploiting an advantage (Kahneman/Knetsch/Thaler) and goes beyond the decided rule, because the builder never had the chance to capture under JobGuard's rules. The idea's 'specialist-handled = disclosed' fix is too narrow: an automated CSV or email import of the same material carries the same unfairness. The fix is simple: nothing that predates adoption can earn a fee.
verdicts.conditions: (a) For any job adopted in-flight, every evidence item whose origin date precedes the adoption timestamp is permanently fee-ineligible (an imported_pre_adoption reason on the signal), whether specialist-handled or automated; only evidence received through JobGuard after adoption can qualify. (b) The builder's existing emailed or WhatsApp variations are imported as Log an extra records (capture), never as evidence. (c) Imported provenance is visibly marked and the attested baseline is the builder's own declaration. (d) The onboarding screen states the rule in one sentence. (e) M1-17 decision record, D12 lawful basis and Article 14 route for imported customer messages before any production import. (f) Self-serve adopt-a-job stays free and equally capable; no upsell pressure.

revised_revenue.solo: £49 year one, ~£0 after (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: A fee on an in-flight imported job is the fastest route to the 'they set me up' story; steady-state revenue is near zero so the service must be judged on conversion, not income.

verdicts.reasons: Refutations fail on the core: named support is standard and welcome, the profit review uses locked builder-visible data, and the account manager does visible work for a fixed monthly fee. Two seams survive. First, the human is who gets asked 'is there anything else on this job?'; a CSM who says 'nothing I can see' while a signal is held is later read as a lie, and the research (Cain, Loewenstein & Moore) says a disclosure line will not repair it, so the answer must be structural — no visibility at all — and honestly scripted. Second, paid priority support must never gate what a builder needs for money, locks or disputes, or the base tier looks like a hostage and the add-on like a toll on fairness.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Support and CSM memberships have no shadow grant and no break-glass; the scripted answer is 'nobody at JobGuard can see final-check candidates before you lock, and anything told to you early is fee-free'. (b) D13 attribution disputes, must-surface follow-up, lock and invoice problems, and payment or security issues are handled at the same speed on every plan; Firm Care buys a named person and the quarterly review, not access to fairness. (c) The quarterly review respects 'chose not to charge' outcomes and never quantifies unsettled savings (§14.1). (d) D09 add-on entitlement, D05 recurring authority, monthly cancellation.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (not offered; unchanged)
