verdicts.key_risk: A single CSM leak ('I'd look at the skip invoices if I were you') makes that signal fee-free and tells the trade that JobGuard staff know things they are not saying.

verdicts.reasons: The hardest refutation is 'pay us to learn how to avoid our fee': if the paid course were the only place the capture rules are properly taught, JobGuard would be selling the antidote to its own model, a toll on information it controls. Provided the free in-product onboarding and the standing diary notice (§14.2) teach the rules fully, the course is crew training that raises the builder's own billing and shrinks JobGuard's contingent base — the clearest possible signal that JobGuard is not counting on builder mistakes. Fair on every test: the trainer does the work, the fee is fixed and optional, no customer-facing effect, no supplier money.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Log an extra vs diary, proof-before-covering and the final check are taught fully in free in-product onboarding; the course is never the only place. (b) Certification is a builder-controlled profile fact, never a ranking and never a factor in fee or dispute handling. (c) No CITB grant claim until verified. (d) Partner trainers have no supplier or merchant affiliation. (e) The sales page states that the course lowers JobGuard's own fee base.

revised_revenue.solo: £10 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: Negligible revenue; the only hazard is over-selling a course to solo builders who need nothing beyond the free onboarding.

verdicts.reasons: A fixed-fee human analysis of the firm's own locked data is the honest way to sell prevention insight, and the analyst visibly does the work. Three refutations partly land and are all fixable: (1) an analyst who could see pre-lock signals would turn the report into a fee-harvesting tool — the idea already confines them to locked jobs; (2) a report that lists dismissed or fee-free catches as 'money you left behind' pressures the builder against their own goodwill decisions with customers (Simply Business: many extras are deliberate gifts) and reads as 'you are bad at billing, good thing we take 10%'; (3) analyst observations feeding D11 signals would turn a paid service into surveillance.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The analyst holds only the builder-visible role over locked jobs, with no shadow or break-glass grant, and the report states that restriction. (b) The report never quantifies unsettled savings and never re-opens dismissed or 'chose not to charge' outcomes (§14.1). (c) Recommendations aim at capture discipline that reduces future fees, and the report shows the fees JobGuard earned from the firm beside what the firm retained. (d) Analyst output is for the builder only and is not an input to D11 signals or any account action. (e) Analyst PI cover; D11 advisory-only; D02 VAT.

revised_revenue.solo: £30 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: At £295 against a £29/month subscription the Solo version looks expensive, and any over-claiming of savings breaches §14.1 and looks like a sales pitch for the 10%.

verdicts.reasons: Strongest refutation: the portal deliberately pulls the customer conversation into JobGuard, where every message is fee-bearing evidence, so JobGuard has a fee interest in the routing, and it uses the builder's own customer as the subscription meter's enforcement. Against that: (1) a hash-bound written customer approval of a builder-captured variation is the single most-wanted thing in this market and is fee-free, so the core value is entirely the builder's; (2) customer messages as evidence is the decided D13 rule, not an extension of it, and a portal that shows every request to the builder with a standing, signal-independent 'Log this as an extra' action gives the capture moment at the point of request — 'it was right there in my messages' becomes 'and the button was right there too'; (3) must-surface covers significant requests, so late-bill catches are small; (4) the meter effect is fair only if over-tier handling never touches a live customer-facing job. The relationship risk sits in the homeowner notice: if the homeowner reads that JobGuard looks for things to bill them for, the builder's customer relationship is damaged and JobGuard is seen as adversarial to both sides.
verdicts.conditions: (a) A standing, always-present 'Log an extra from this message' action on every customer message, byte-identical with or without signals (SV-2/SV-3); a customer request above the D13 threshold surfaces immediately and is fee-free. (b) The portal is the builder's channel, 'powered by JobGuard', never presented to the homeowner as JobGuard checking the builder. (c) The homeowner Article 13/14 notice (D12 v2, legally reviewed) describes record-keeping and reconciliation truthfully without adversarial framing. (d) Nothing on the homeowner side varies with signals, and no watchdog findings, D11 signals or catches are ever shown to the homeowner. (e) Over-tier handling never disables or degrades an existing job's portal, approvals or messages mid-job; only a new switch-live triggers an upgrade prompt (D09). (f) No homeowner marketing, no cross-builder data, no lead generation from portal users, ever. (g) CCRs 2013: capture the homeowner's express request to begin work with each remote approval. (h) A builder who keeps a customer off the portal is fully supported and un-penalised (§14.2).

revised_revenue.solo: £20 incremental fee (about half the idea's guess: the standing capture action converts many portal requests into fee-free captures; the portal's real return is retention and meter integrity, which is uncounted)

verdicts.key_risk: The homeowner notice wording: one honest but clumsy sentence about success fees turns the builder's tool into something the customer thinks is policing the builder, which is relationship damage builders will not forgive.

verdicts.reasons: Builder-controlled, positive, verifiable facts and a quote-hash stamp are in the builder's interest — the stamp protects them in a dispute over which version was issued. Four refutations land, each fixable but together they weaken it: (1) 'JobGuard-checked' tells a homeowner that JobGuard vouches for or polices the builder, which is untrue, DMCC/CPUT-exposed and inverts whose tool JobGuard is; (2) per-metric opt-out creates adverse selection — homeowners learn a missing metric means a bad number, so builders are pushed to show everything, a soft coercion by the platform; (3) the 'Request a quote' brief lands in Walk it as evidence, so a brief item the builder saw in the cited proposal and chose not to price could later surface as a fee-bearing catch; (4) a public JobGuard-hosted enquiry page is one policy change away from the lead marketplace named as a trust risk. Until the pilot produces locked jobs and homeowners recognise the name, it is worth little on its own.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Rename or strictly define the badge as 'records verified in JobGuard' with the definition on the page; no endorsement of workmanship; ASA/CAP review. (b) The page shows only the fixed set of metrics the builder picked, with no placeholders or hints for hidden ones. (c) Watchdog-derived facts (catches, overcharges, D11 signals, disputes, dismissed catches) are excluded by design, not by default. (d) Any brief item that appeared in the cited proposal is a disclosure for shadow purposes and permanently fee-ineligible. (e) Enquiries go only to that builder; JobGuard never routes, shares, sells or markets to enquirers and offers no cross-builder search or ranking. (f) Quote-stamp verification reveals nothing without the PDF in hand. (g) Bundle rather than charge until homeowner recognition exists.

revised_revenue.solo: £110–£120 (unchanged; likely £0 separately while bundled early on)

verdicts.key_risk: 'Checked' implying endorsement or policing: homeowners read it as JobGuard vouching for the builder, and a regulator reads it as a misleading claim.

verdicts.reasons: Clear in principle: supplying contract templates is not a reserved legal activity under the Legal Services Act 2007 s.12/Sch 2 (advice and the bespoke review sit with the SRA-regulated partner). It fixes a real builder exposure: under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 regs 29-31 and 36, a missing off-premises/distance cancellation notice extends the homeowner's cancellation right by up to 12 months and, absent an express request on a durable medium to start work, can leave work done in the cancellation period unpaid. The true cost is that one 'pack' is really four regimes needing separate variants: (1) residential jobs - CRA 2015 Part 2 (transparent, prominent terms; Sch 2 grey list on unilateral price variation, disproportionate deposits and cancellation sums) and DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 1 (the quote is the invitation to purchase and must show the total price including mandatory charges; a variation clause is fine only because extras are optional and customer-approved); (2) B2B jobs - HGCRA 1996 ss.108-113 and the Scheme (adequate payment mechanism, due and final dates, payment and pay-less notices, no pay-when-paid), because the s.106 residential-occupier exclusion removes the statutory regime only where the customer occupies or intends to occupy the dwelling; (3) interest - Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 in B2B versions only, fair contractual interest in consumer versions; (4) England and Wales, Scotland and NI profiles (contract formation, adjudication schemes, court limits) via M4-19. Referral revenue on the £295 review is constrained: SRA Code of Conduct 5.1 obliges the solicitor to disclose any referral or fee-sharing arrangement to the builder, so JobGuard earns a disclosed introducer fee, not a resale margin. JobGuard's own exposure if a template is defective is tested under UCTA 1977 s.3 (caps in its standard B2B terms must be reasonable; s.11(4) looks at insurance availability), and many tech PI policies exclude legal products, so the partner firm's PI must stand behind the templates. No FCA permission is engaged while templates stay pay-as-work-proceeds; any deferred-instalment variant raises CCA/RAO art 60F and credit-broking (art 36A) questions and needs its own decision. The £10 per-quote option sits awkwardly with the §5.10 free-quoting invariant and should be resolved in D09, not law. Cost and timeline (assumptions): £8-15k initial drafting for a two-regime, three-jurisdiction suite with CCR notices and the Sch 3 model cancellation form, £2-4k annual review, 8-12 weeks; break-even roughly 50-80 subscribing builders. Not legal advice: a solicitor must confirm the CCR express-request mechanics, the HGCRA variant and the UCTA cap.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Two contract families (residential-occupier; HGCRA/Scheme-compliant B2B) and jurisdiction profiles before real issue; unsupported combinations stay draft with an explanation. (b) CCR Sch 2 pre-contract information, the Sch 3 model cancellation form and an express-request-to-start mechanism on a durable medium embedded in the quote-send path, not optional attachments. (c) Templates licensed from and maintained by an SRA-regulated firm whose PI covers them; JobGuard states it gives no legal advice; version and review date printed on every pack. (d) Any referral fee on bespoke reviews disclosed by the firm and by JobGuard; the builder contracts with the firm directly for advice. (e) JobGuard's B2B terms cap liability at a level a solicitor judges UCTA-reasonable. (f) Prefer the monthly bundle to the per-quote charge, or have D09 expressly carve the pack out of free quoting. (g) No deferred-instalment templates without a consumer-credit decision. (h) Deposit and stage templates shared with I40 under D06.

revised_revenue.solo: £100-£140 (bespoke-review margin limited to a disclosed introducer fee)
revised_revenue.firm: £400-£500; fixed legal cost ~£8-15k plus £2-4k a year (assumption) needs ~50-80 subscribers to clear

verdicts.key_risk: A defective or mis-targeted template (residential wording on an HGCRA job, or a missing express-request mechanism) that costs many builders payment at once, with JobGuard's cap tested under UCTA s.3 and PI cover uncertain for a legal product.

verdicts.reasons: Assembling the builder's own evidence is not a reserved legal activity (LSA 2007 s.12), construction payment is outside the FCA claims-management sectors (RAO arts 89G-89M), and no funds move, so no FCA permission is engaged for the core product. Four boundaries define its true shape. (1) Conduct of litigation is reserved (LSA Sch 2 para 4): the small-claims pack may be a factual chronology and evidence set that the builder files as a litigant in person; JobGuard must not draft pleadings as legal assertions, issue or serve the claim or correspond with the court (the Ndole Assets v Designer M&E [2018] EWCA Civ 2865 line treats service as conduct of litigation). (2) Insurance: an insurer pack the builder sends to their own insurer is likely only 'assisting in the administration' of the policy, not 'administration and performance' under RAO art 39A (PERG 5.7 requires both, performance meaning e.g. negotiating settlement), provided JobGuard never notifies, negotiates or advises on the claim; that line needs written confirmation. (3) ADR: the Consumer ADR Regulations 2015 reg 19 already oblige the builder to signpost a certified ADR body when a consumer complaint is exhausted, and the DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 4 introduces ADR-provider accreditation (check commencement); sending a bundle to the homeowner or an ADR body is a builder-authorised commercial send on the command boundary, and a mediation referral fee to JobGuard must be disclosed to both parties (a misleading omission toward the consumer under DMCC Part 4 Ch 1, and Civil Mediation Council code for the mediator). (4) Evidence weight: an RFC 3161 token from a non-qualified TSA gets only the 'not denied legal effect' floor of UK eIDAS Art 41(1); the presumption of accuracy in Art 41(2) attaches only to a qualified electronic time stamp from a UK-trust-listed provider, so D04's provider choice decides what 'anchored' is worth. Marketing to builders is B2B so DMCC does not apply, but the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 do: 'court-ready' or 'tamper-proof' would be misleading (§5.7/5.8 already forbid them). Data: the bundle carries the homeowner's and third parties' personal data; the builder decides disclosure as controller (D12), DPA 2018 Sch 2 para 5 supports disclosure for legal proceedings, and minimal disclosure/redaction is the default. Free plain export is a contractual promise (UK GDPR Art 20 portability only helps sole traders as data subjects) and belongs in the subscription terms. Selling a £49/£99 small-claims pack while a D03 withheld-payment case carries 10% is lawful but must be shown as a separate charge. Cost and timeline (assumptions): £2-5k solicitor review of wording and the litigation/insurance boundaries, a qualified TSP if the presumption is wanted, 2-4 weeks. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Copy and pack cover pages state: factual assembly, integrity and existence claims only, no legal advice, not filed or served by JobGuard. (b) No drafting of particulars, defences or witness statements beyond 'builder to complete' placeholders; no correspondence with courts, ADR bodies or insurers on the builder's behalf. (c) Use a UK qualified trust-service TSA if 'anchored' is to carry the Art 41(2) presumption; otherwise say plainly that it does not. (d) Mediation and ADR referral fees disclosed to builder and homeowner before referral; ADR bundle transmission to the homeowner through an approved Decision. (e) Free export one tap from every paid pack, written into D09 terms; per-pack pricing stated as not a per-job platform fee. (f) Packs built before lock exclude shadow content by role isolation (§14.3). (g) Small-claims formats profiled by jurisdiction (England and Wales £10k, Scotland Simple Procedure £5k, NI £3k) and not offered for B2B HGCRA jobs where adjudication is the route.
verdicts.key_risk: Format or marketing drift from factual bundle into drafting pleadings, serving documents or handling an insurance claim (reserved conduct of litigation or RAO art 39A), and a timestamp claim that overstates its legal weight.

verdicts.reasons: Lawful as a fixed-fee factual review: quantity surveyors and claims consultants may advise and represent in adjudication (not court proceedings) and general legal advice is unreserved; the Damages-Based Agreements Regulations 2013 do not bite because the fee is fixed. The legal cost is liability and structure, not permissions. (1) Contracting model: if JobGuard sells the review and subcontracts the consultant (which the M4-10 service invoice implies), JobGuard owes the builder the consultant's standard of care and needs professional-services PI cover that many tech policies exclude; its cap is tested under UCTA s.3 and s.11(4). If JobGuard merely introduces and the consultant contracts directly, exposure falls but the commission should be disclosed and the builder must see who is responsible. (2) Reserved activities: the consultant must not issue or serve proceedings or act as the builder's representative in court (LSA 2007 Sch 2 para 4); adjudication-grade packs are only usable where an adjudication right exists - B2B contracts under HGCRA s.108, or residential contracts with an express clause (JCT homeowner, RICS scheme) - because s.106 removes statutory adjudication for residential occupiers; the CIC Low Value Disputes procedure is for modest claims (about £50k ceiling; verify current edition). (3) Insurance: a reviewer who deals with the builder's insurer would be assisting in the administration and performance of the policy (RAO art 39A, loss assessing) and needs FCA authorisation; forbid it in panel terms. (4) Expert evidence: a party-commissioned factual summary is not a CPR Part 35 expert report and must not be labelled one; the builder's own witness statement carries the statement of truth. (5) Data: the reviewer is either JobGuard's processor (Art 28 contract, D04 residency) or an independent controller; homeowner data disclosure rests on legitimate interests and DPA 2018 Sch 2 para 5; reviewers see only builder-visible data, and under §14.3 that must be enforced by role or the panel becomes a pre-lock disclosure route and a D13 breach. (6) Consumer side: output stays factual because a pack used to pressure a homeowner engages DMCC Act 2024 aggressive and misleading practice rules against the builder (M4-5 rules). Claims-management regulation does not cover construction payment, but avoid 'claims' wording. Cost and timeline (assumptions): panel and service terms £3-8k, PI quote, 2-3 months to contract a 3-5 person panel. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Decide and document the contracting model before launch (JobGuard-sells with matching PI, or introducer with direct consultant engagement and disclosed commission); UCTA-reasonable cap either way. (b) Panel terms prohibit conduct of litigation, court/ADR/insurer correspondence on the builder's behalf and any expert-report labelling; scope limited to factual chronology, gap flags and formatting. (c) Adjudication-grade only where an adjudication right exists; jurisdiction-profiled. (d) Scoped external-reviewer role with no read path to shadow tables, access logged; post-lock revealed signals only. (e) Art 28 or controller terms, UK/EU residency, confidentiality, PI of at least £1m per consultant (assumption). (f) Fee shown as separate from any 10% case fee; no contingency pricing without a DBA review.

revised_revenue.solo: £20-£65 gross if JobGuard sells; £15-£20 net as introducer at 25-30%

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard carrying professional-negligence liability for a subcontracted review without matching PI and an enforceable cap, or a reviewer straying into litigation conduct, insurer negotiation or pre-lock shadow data.

verdicts.reasons: Nothing prohibits it, but it turns JobGuard into a business-to-consumer trader and a controller for homeowner accounts - a large fixed legal load for a small line. (1) Consumer law: CRA 2015 Part 1 Ch 3 (digital content as described and of satisfactory quality; s.57 stops JobGuard excluding liability below the price paid) and Ch 4 (15-year hosting is a service); CCRs 2013 (Sch 2 pre-contract information; 14-day distance cancellation; immediate digital supply needs express consent and acknowledgment under reg 37; service performance in the period needs an express request under reg 36); DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 Ch 1 with CMA direct fines up to 10% of turnover - consumer headline prices must be VAT-inclusive (so '£69 + VAT' becomes £82.80 or the net drops to £57.50), any suggestion the record proves compliance or workmanship is a misleading action, and Gas Safe, FENSA and Part P marks need scheme permission with 'uploaded by builder, not verified by JobGuard' labels. The ADR Regulations 2015 reg 19 signposting duty then applies to JobGuard's own consumer disputes. (2) A 15-year hosted retention promise is a long-dated consumer obligation that survives only if JobGuard does; D07 must set the retention class and an insolvency or export fallback, and storage limitation (UK GDPR Art 5(1)(e)) needs the purpose documented. (3) Data protection: JobGuard becomes controller for the homeowner account (D12 v2) and a direct DSAR target. A shadow signal about work at the homeowner's property is plausibly the homeowner's personal data; a homeowner DSAR to JobGuard could compel disclosure that, if pre-lock, is permanent fee ineligibility under §14.3 and §14.11 and makes JobGuard's controller status for job data hard to deny product-wide. I36 does not create that exposure, but it multiplies the homeowners with a direct relationship to JobGuard. Offering the record only after lock and final payment (as proposed) is the mitigation. (4) Payment: JobGuard as merchant on its own Stripe surface raises no PSR issue; no surcharging; 14-day consumer refunds. (5) Builder side: opt-in per job protects confidential pricing; the strict-subset rule (no findings, D11 signals, supplier prices) must be enforced by the renderer, since a leak of watchdog findings into a consumer-held document is discoverable evidence against the builder. Cost and timeline (assumptions): consumer T&Cs, privacy notice and complaints process £3-6k; D12 v2 and D07 approvals; 2-3 months; then continuing B2C regulatory exposure. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) VAT-inclusive consumer pricing and DMCC-compliant copy; no 'certified' or 'compliant' wording or scheme logos without permission; certificates labelled builder-uploaded. (b) Consumer T&Cs, CCR information, reg 37 waiver, 14-day refund flow, complaints handling and ADR signposting before the first sale. (c) D07 retention class for 15 years with an export or escrow fallback stated to the consumer; D12 v2 controller analysis covering homeowner accounts and DSAR handling. (d) Available only after final-account lock, invoice and recorded final payment; renderer enforces the strict subset by construction and is tested against shadow and finding tables. (e) Builder opt-in per job, builder-branded, no other JobGuard upsell to the homeowner. (f) Legal check that offering a paid record to the builder's customer does not breach the builder's own terms or confidentiality.

revised_revenue.solo: £95-£110 (after VAT-inclusive pricing and ~5-10% refunds)

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard becomes a B2C trader and homeowner data controller: CMA direct-enforcement exposure, a 15-year service promise, and a direct homeowner DSAR route that can force pre-lock disclosure of shadow signals.

verdicts.reasons: The FCA answer is probably favourable, but for a different reason than the idea states. Delivering the builder's own evidence to the builder's insurer at the builder's request is likely no more than assisting in the administration of the policy, which does not by itself engage RAO art 39A (PERG 5.7 requires administration and performance, e.g. negotiating settlement). Being paid by the insurer to feed evidence into its claims process looks like managing claims on behalf of an insurer or expert appraisal, which art 39B excludes. So no permission is likely needed, but that needs written regulatory confirmation and flips the moment JobGuard advises the builder on the claim or negotiates. The real cost is structural: the insurer is the builder's counterparty on the claim, and a fee from the counterparty is the same conflict the founder flagged for suppliers paying JobGuard. A recipient-bound comprehensive pack can contain material the insurer uses to reduce or repudiate (poor-workmanship photos, contract gaps); the Insurance Act 2015 s.12 fraud remedies and policy conditions mean the builder must choose what to send and JobGuard must not curate for the insurer. Marketing to builders is B2B, so no DMCC, but an undisclosed insurer payment would be a misleading omission under the BPMMRs 2008 and a breach-of-trust event. Data: the insurer is a separate controller; the homeowner's data reaches it under the builder's legitimate interests with the D12 Article 14 route; D07 export receipts. Commercially, no UK insurer is known to pay per pack, insurer contracting takes 6-18 months with security due diligence, and £4-£30 a year is below the cost of one integration. If insurer revenue is wanted, the lawful route for introductions is an Introducer Appointed Representative arrangement with an authorised principal (RAO art 25 arranging; FSMA s.39), which is the flagged I46 variant, not this one. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Ship 'Send evidence to my insurer' as a free builder-initiated delivery feature; treat any insurer fee as a separate decision record with prominent disclosure to the builder before each send. (b) Written regulatory confirmation that the flow stays outside RAO art 39A; hard rule of no claim advice, notification, negotiation or curation by JobGuard. (c) Builder selects and can redact pack contents; pack states integrity and existence only; recipient-bound authority per M5-9. (d) Insurer contracts give the insurer no say over pack contents or data beyond the builder-approved set; no per-policyholder data feed (that is I46). (e) D12 Article 14 route for homeowner data reaching the insurer.
verdicts.key_risk: Being paid by the builder's claim counterparty (a supplier-pays-style conflict), plus the art 39A cliff if JobGuard ever advises on or negotiates the claim.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on legal grounds, not only trust. (1) UK GDPR Art 5(1)(b) purpose limitation: job records were obtained from the builder to run and protect the builder's job; selling an audit of the builder to the homeowner is an incompatible new purpose. If JobGuard is the builder's processor for those records, deciding that purpose itself makes JobGuard a controller in breach of Art 28(10) and its processing contract; if JobGuard is already a controller, the builder's reasonable expectations still fail the compatibility test. (2) Breach of confidence and contract: pricing, margins, supplier costs and internal findings are the builder's confidential information; deploying them against the builder for a paying third party is actionable regardless of data-protection status. (3) Consumer law: calling the read 'independent' is a misleading action under DMCC Act 2024 s.226 because JobGuard is contracted to and paid by the builder and holds a 10% interest in extras being billed; and either JobGuard withholds shadow catches from the paying consumer (a misleading omission under s.227 of material information they paid for) or discloses them (pre-lock disclosure, permanent fee ineligibility, D13 breach). There is no lawful configuration. (4) As a B2C sale it carries the full CRA/CCR/DMCC apparatus of I36, and CRA s.57 prevents excluding negligence liability to homeowners who rely on the audit below the price paid. (5) It is the FairRate model run by the party the audit targets; RICS-style conflict rules are not statutory here but a court or the ICO would apply the same reasoning. No appointed-representative or partner route cures a purpose-limitation breach. Recommend an explicit BUILD_PLAN §11 out-of-scope entry. Not legal advice, but a solicitor is unlikely to reach a different answer.
verdicts.conditions: None that make it lawful and trust-safe. Add to BUILD_PLAN §11: no homeowner-paid audit, rating or review of a builder using that builder's JobGuard records.
verdicts.key_risk: Purpose-limitation and confidence breach against the builder combined with an inherently misleading 'independent' consumer offer under the DMCC Act.

verdicts.reasons: The design is the standard lawful shape for a platform fee and stays within AGENTS §3 (hosted surfaces, no funds held), but three regulatory points set its true cost. (1) Payment Services Regulations 2017: with Stripe Connect Standard and direct charges, Stripe is the authorised PSP, the builder is the merchant, funds settle to the builder's own account and JobGuard never possesses or directs funds; the application fee is a fee Stripe deducts and remits. That keeps JobGuard outside payment services (and outside MLR 2017 as a relevant person) without even needing the commercial-agent (Sch 1 Pt 2 para 2(b)) or technical-service-provider (para 2(j)) exclusions, but a written opinion is required and pay-by-bank is the weak point: if TrueLayer or GoCardless pay-by-bank settles through a merchant account in JobGuard's name, or JobGuard initiates payment orders itself, it becomes a PISP or agent question. Each rail must be onboarded with the builder as the provider's merchant. TrueLayer is also a third rail not in AGENTS §3 and needs a Discovered-later entry and its own task. (2) Consumer Rights (Payment Surcharges) Regulations 2012 reg 6A: the homeowner must see one invoice total whichever method they use; the fee is a merchant cost on the builder, never a surcharge, and pay-by-bank cannot be shown cheaper to the consumer than card. (3) VAT: Stripe's own processing fees are exempt (VATA 1994 Sch 9 Grp 5), but a platform's application fee is very likely a standard-rated supply after Bookit/NEC, so a 0.3% fee carries 20% VAT that non-registered sole traders cannot recover - D02 tax review, and quote it gross to them. Also: Stripe Instant Payouts on Standard accounts are contracted between Stripe and the connected account, so the 0.5% margin is probably unavailable unless JobGuard runs Express or Custom accounts (more platform liability); it is not credit by JobGuard so the CCA is not engaged, but the price must be shown before the tap. Chargebacks and CCA s.75 sit with the builder and the card issuer; Stripe dispute windows mean cleared is not settled (§14.8/14.9). Data: Stripe and GoCardless are controllers for KYC and fraud; webhook payloads carry payer names and emails into the D04/D12 register. Cost and timeline (assumptions): regulatory opinion £5-15k, 4-8 weeks; VAT opinion £2-5k; Stripe Connect platform review 2-6 weeks; GoCardless partner onboarding 4-8 weeks; G4 gating applies. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Written regulatory opinion on PSR 2017 scope for each rail, with the builder as the provider's merchant of record and no settlement account in JobGuard's name; TrueLayer only after a Discovered-later entry, its own task and D04. (b) Single consumer-facing invoice total regardless of method; fee itemised only on the builder's platform statement; no method steering toward the homeowner. (c) D02 ruling on VAT treatment of the application fee; gross display to non-registered builders. (d) Instant payout only if the chosen Connect account type allows a platform margin; default off, price shown before confirmation, never on fee collections. (e) Fee caps enforced in the command boundary; provider-cleared and settled kept distinct; refunds and chargebacks feed §14.9 reversals. (f) No nudging of homeowners to paid rails and no correlation of rail prompts with jobs carrying catches (D11 signal).

revised_revenue.solo: £80-£280 rails (+£0-£75 instant payout, likely £0 on Standard accounts)

verdicts.key_risk: A pay-by-bank flow that puts JobGuard in the payment chain (PSR 2017 scope), a VAT ruling that makes the fee 20% dearer for non-registered solos, and an instant-payout margin that may not exist on Standard accounts.

verdicts.reasons: Lawful as pay-as-work-proceeds collection through a regulated institution, but the legal mechanics cut into its value. (1) Consumer credit: a deposit and stage payments due on completion of proof-gated stages are payment for services delivered, not credit; if any template lets the homeowner pay after completion in instalments, the builder becomes a creditor and JobGuard a possible credit broker (RAO art 36A) unless the art 60F(2) exemption applies (12 or fewer payments within 12 months, no interest or charges) - the research notes flag 60F as unchecked, so keep deferred variants out until a solicitor confirms. (2) Direct Debit: GoCardless is the Bacs service user and regulated institution; Bacs rules require advance notice of each amount and date (10 working days by default, GoCardless's shorter period by agreement), and the Direct Debit Guarantee lets the homeowner obtain an immediate refund from their bank for any error and cancel at any time, with indemnity claims flowing back to the builder without a fixed time limit. A disputed stage collected by DD is therefore weaker for the builder than a bank transfer, and collecting a stage the homeowner disputes invites indemnity claims plus DMCC Act 2024 aggressive-practice arguments; the proof gate and cancel right are necessary, not optional. (3) HGCRA: for B2B jobs (no s.106 residential exclusion) the schedule must provide an adequate payment mechanism, due and final dates and payment and pay-less notices (ss.109-111); a DD submitted after a valid pay-less notice would breach the contract, so the collection Decision must check notice state (M4-19) or the rail must start residential-only. (4) Consumer terms: deposit size and retention on cancellation are tested under CRA 2015 Sch 2 paras 4-6 and CMA unfair-terms guidance, and an off-premises or distance cancellation within 14 days requires refund of the deposit less a proportionate charge for expressly requested work (CCRs reg 36) - D06 templates shared with I33. (5) VRP: commercial VRP through a PISP (TrueLayer or GoCardless) is still being rolled out in phases by Open Banking Ltd and general merchant availability in 2026 is uncertain; JobGuard would not be the PISP. (6) Client money: payouts go to the builder; JobGuard holds nothing, so no PSR, MLR or client-money issue; the £1 per collection is a standard-rated software fee on the builder. Cost and timeline (assumptions): template drafting within I33's solicitor spend, GoCardless partner onboarding 4-8 weeks, late M4; no separate permission. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Pay-as-you-go schedules only; no deferred-instalment templates without a consumer-credit decision (RAO art 60F/36A). (b) Bacs-compliant advance notice for every collection; collection only after the builder's proof-gated approval; homeowner cancel and Guarantee rights stated in the mandate journey and on each notice. (c) Builder-facing warning that DD stage payments are reversible under the Guarantee; recommend bank transfer or card for the final balance. (d) Residential-occupier contracts first; B2B only once M4-19 payment and pay-less notice state gates the collection Decision. (e) D06-reviewed deposit and cancellation-refund terms; deposit sized within CRA/CMA fairness guidance. (f) VRP only when a PISP offers commercial VRP for this merchant category; consent caps set at mandate time. (g) Indemnity claims and refunds flow into §14.9 reversals as unsettled cash.
verdicts.key_risk: The Direct Debit Guarantee lets a homeowner reverse a collected stage payment without time limit, and a collection made after a B2B pay-less notice or on a disputed stage would breach the contract; the proof gate is the whole product.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation. (1) Unit economics are wrong at the bottom tier: a genuine omissions review of a priced quote against a walk-through transcript, a rate book and merchant prices is 1–1.5 h for an £8k job and 2–4 h for £20–60k; at the idea's own £45–£60/h reviewer rate the £95 tier nets JobGuard £5–£40 and the £195 tier £15–£95, not 40–55% margin, before PI cover, reviewer DPAs and ops. (2) Speed beats polish in domestic quoting: a one-working-day pause at 'Send this quote' is a real cost to a builder competing with same-day quotes from Qted/VoxTrade-style tools (research §'UK builders already pay £25–£45', voice-to-quote list). (3) A generalist panel QS does not know this builder's cost base; suggestions drift to 'add contingency/skip/scaffold', which the builder already knows, so perceived value decays after the first review. (4) A 15-staff firm at £60k average jobs usually has an estimator, cutting Firm take-up. (5) Reliance/liability: a QS-branded review invites reliance whatever the terms say; PI cover per reviewer or on JobGuard is a fixed cost the volumes below cannot carry. Revenue rework (assumptions: win rate ~40% so ~45/60/80 quotes a year; 2–4% / 6–8% / 5–8% reviewed; blended ticket £95 / £195 / £300): gross £95–£190 / £780–£975 / £1,200–£1,800 a year per customer; net to JobGuard after reviewer cost roughly £40 / £350 / £650. Against subscriptions of £348 / £708 / £1,428 (research §'Recommendation') that is a small services line, not a product. Comparables: the research report finds no trade-app precedent; freelance QS retainers from £400/month and day rates £350–£1,200 (research §'No rival sells…' table; raw success_fee_benchmarks §4) serve subcontractors on commercial contracts, not domestic builders; FairRate's £0.99 audit runs the other way. Gaming: negligible — using the review then quoting outside JobGuard costs nothing because quoting is free (§5.10). Build first: M1-3..M1-6 quote flow (exists), M2-1 rate book, a 'review requested' Decision that pauses the M1-5 send, a scoped external-reviewer membership whose only write is labelled suggestions (§5.9), plus checkout via the rewritten M4-11 (behind G4; manual invoicing before that). Data: the transcript is customer personal data leaving to a freelancer, so D04 (UK/EU reviewers) and D12 processor terms are required. Trust fit is genuinely good — findings become baseline scope, fee-free forever (§14.2) — but that is a reason it is honest, not a reason it sells.
verdicts.conditions: Do not build. Run it as a manual concierge during the pilot for quotes of £20k+ only (drop the £95 tier as uneconomic), with the review delivered as labelled suggestions by a UK-based reviewer under a DPA and PI cover, and count how often a review finds a material omission (target: >30% of reviews find something the builder accepts). Productise only if that threshold holds and Small-firm/Firm demand exceeds ~5 reviews per account per year; charge at least £195/£345 and keep reviewers out of live-job evidence.

revised_revenue.solo: £95–£190 gross (1–2 reviews/yr); ~£40 net after reviewer cost

verdicts.key_risk: Thin or negative margin at the volumes small builders will actually buy, while a reviewer network, PI cover and a send-pausing workflow are fixed costs that arrive on day one.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation. (1) It contradicts the product's own promise. JobGuard's pitch is that the final account 'assembles without re-typing' from the frozen baseline plus approved variations (M1-11/UIWIRE-9, §14.4). If that works, the desk is 30 minutes of chasing, not 3–8 hours; if it needs 3–8 hours, the product is broken and the fix is engineering, not a £150–£600 service. The idea's own cost assumption is evidence against the idea. (2) Willingness to pay: a solo builder on an £8k job with £1.5–£2.5k margin will not pay £150 to have someone assemble a five-line bill; a £2m firm already has an office admin. The honest demand is for 'chase my approvals and proof', which is admin/account-management (I52), not a per-job professional service. (3) The fee-free `desk_prepared` rule is the right ethics but produces an odd product: the desk operator holds the ordinary builder role (must, per §14.3 and AGENTS §5.14), so they prepare the account blind to shadow signals; the post-lock reveal then shows what JobGuard's own staff missed. Even fee-free, 'your desk charged me £350 and your machine then found £800 they missed' is a credibility problem the trust note underrates. (4) Labour model: a QS-trained desk with lumpy demand (a few hundred jobs a year across the early base) cannot be staffed at utilisation; margin at the £150 tier is zero at 4 hours (£140 at £35/h). (5) Cannibalisation is intended (fixed fee instead of 10%) but the 10% is itself unproven (research §'The hidden final check' and 'Conclusion': treat the fee as upside until pilot data). Revenue rework (assumptions: 19/24/33 jobs a year; 2–3% / 8% / 8% take-up; £150 / £350 / £600 tiers; desk 4 / 5–6 / 8 hours at £35/h): gross £0–£150 / ~£700 / ~£1,500; net ~£0 / ~£300 / ~£750. Comparables: no trade-app precedent (research §'No rival sells…'); outsourced QS retainers 'from £400/month' and £350–£800/day (raw success_fee_benchmarks §4) are for subcontractors on commercial contracts. Gaming: the lock records the locking member, so a desk actor cannot lock; but a builder can use the desk on every job to neutralise the fee — acceptable, as the idea says, yet it means the service is priced to be fee-neutral rather than profitable. Build first: SV-4 lock (unbuilt), a delegated-actor membership with audit attribution, a D13 v2 amendment adding `desk_prepared` as a permanent ineligibility reason, D02 VAT on the service, D06 keeping invoice issue builder-authorised — plus an ops hire before there is volume. Top failure reasons: product contradiction, low WTP at Solo/Small, utilisation risk, the post-desk reveal embarrassment, and revenue that is fee-neutral by design.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable (rejected). The one survivable kernel — chasing outstanding approvals and proof before the builder locks — belongs in a Firm-tier support offer (see I52) or in product automation, not in a per-job desk fee. Revisit only if pilot data (§14.17) show builders abandoning jobs at final review because assembly is too hard, in which case fix UIWIRE-9 first.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£150 gross (0–1 job/yr); ~£0 net

verdicts.key_risk: A paid service whose need is evidence the core product has failed, delivered by staff who must work blind to the shadow bill and are then shown up by it.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation. (1) It charges at the point of maximum churn risk. The research finds construction the least digitised sector (29% of one-person firms use software; §'Builders' willingness to pay') and says onboarding friction, not price, is the binding constraint for the smallest firms. Tradify, Fergus (free 1-hour onboarding), Powered Now and ServiceM8 — the tools in JobGuard's £29–£119 band — onboard free; the paid precedents (Payaca £1,500, Buildertrend coaching $500–$2,000, Commusoft migration fees — research §'UK builders already pay…' and raw construction_platforms notes) sit on products priced £299+/month. A £49 fee at sign-up is a conversion tax for Solo/Builder tiers. (2) JobGuard benefits more than the builder from in-flight import: every adopted job feeds the live-jobs meter and, later, the evidence base — the rational move is to subsidise import, not sell it. (3) Margin is nil: a 1–2 hour specialist call per job costs £30–£60 loaded against £49; the £750 Firm package (15 jobs, CSV migrations, two-hour setup) is 10–15 hours, so £150–£300 margin, and each CSV source (Tradify, ServiceM8, Xero) is its own adapter and support burden. (4) It cannot be sold until M1-17 has its own decision record for production import (M1-17 'Done when'), and imported customer messages/WhatsApp need the D12 v2 lawful basis and Article 14 route; that is not before G1. (5) The idea's own steady-state revenue is ~£0. Revenue rework (assumptions: 50–60% take-up; one-off): Solo ~£25 expected if charged — recommend £0; Small ~£120 one-off at ~zero margin; Firm ~£450 expected (60% of £750), ~£150–£250 margin. Gaming: negligible under v3 (no cap, so an inflated attested baseline earns nothing); imported lineage is visibly marked (M1-17). Trust: the specialist-handled-is-fee-free rule is essential (§14.2 treats imported messages as evidence); keep it. Top failure reasons: conversion drag where adoption is already the problem, free competitor onboarding, zero margin, D12/M1-17 approvals, adapter sprawl.
verdicts.conditions: Make import free for Solo and Builder tiers as an acquisition lever, with the self-serve M1-17 path as the default. Sell only a Firm package (£500–£750, up to ~15 jobs plus a two-hour setup) bundled into the first annual subscription, and only after the M1-17 production-import decision record and the D12 v2 Article 14 route are approved. Record every specialist-handled item as `disclosed_before_lock`; keep automated CSV imports as evidence and say so in one sentence on the import screen. Build one CSV adapter at a time, starting with the source the pilot cohort actually uses.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (offer free; ~£25 one-off if charged)

verdicts.key_risk: Charging the least-digitised segment at sign-up suppresses the live-job adoption the whole commercial model depends on, for revenue that rounds to zero.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation. (1) Price versus base: £99/month on a £59 Builder plan is 1.7× the software. Nothing in the research's £25–£45 band charges for support at all; Tradify's included support is rated 4.8/5 (raw uk_trade_job_software §4) and Fergus includes an onboarding hour. The comparables the idea cites are from a different tier: Chaser's £900–£2,099 add-on sits on plans for £4m–£100m-revenue firms and Buildertrend's ~£2k/year support sits on a $499–$1,099/month product (research §'No rival…' and raw notes) — support add-ons exist where the base is £300+/month. (2) Attach rate: 40% take-up of an add-on that more than doubles the bill is unsupported; typical premium-support attach in SMB SaaS is 5–15% (my assumption; no research figure). (3) Staffing: one CSM per ~60 accounts is only fundable with ~60 paying Firm Care accounts, i.e. ~100–150 Firm-tier customers at 15–40% attach; early on there will be 5–20 Firm customers and no CSM can be hired. (4) It undermines the tier ladder: the research's own tier advice is that the top tier must be a real offer, 'such as more users, office/admin seats or priority support' (raw price_level_and_tier_psychology, tier section). Selling priority support separately strips the £119 Firm tier of its best justification. (5) Relationship hazard: a named account manager is precisely who gets asked 'anything else on this job?', must be structurally unable to see shadow tables (SV-2, §14.3) and must give the onboarding-terms answer; one leak makes the signal fee-free and tells the trade JobGuard staff know things they are not saying. The quarterly 'profit review' is ~2 hours a year of analyst time on locked jobs only — thin. Revenue rework (assumptions: 5% attach at £99 on Builder, 15% at £199 on Firm): Solo £0; Small ~£60 expected per account (£1,188 per taker); Firm ~£360 expected per account (£2,388 per taker). Gaming: none material. Build: trivial (add-on entitlement in rewritten M4-13, invoice lines M4-10, a support membership with no shadow grants), but revenue is behind G4/D09 regardless; the cost is the hire. Top failure reasons: price above the product, included support elsewhere, unstaffable until scale, tier cannibalisation, the 'anything else?' conversation.
verdicts.conditions: Do not launch as a separate add-on early. Fold priority support (same-day phone line, setup help) into the Firm tier as part of what £119 buys; offer Firm Care as a paid add-on only when Firm-tier accounts exceed ~100 and a CSM can be staffed at ≥60 takers, priced £149–£199 on Firm only (not on Builder). The support role must be a distinct membership with no shadow grants and a scripted answer to 'is there anything else on this job?'; the quarterly review uses locked jobs only.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (not offered)
revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£60 expected per account (5% attach × £1,188); recommend not offered at £99
revised_revenue.firm: ~£360 expected per account (15% attach × £2,388); staffable only past ~100 Firm accounts

verdicts.key_risk: An add-on priced above the software, in a market where support is included, that cannot be staffed until the Firm base is 5–10× its early size.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation. (1) This is product onboarding rebadged. 'Walk a job, Log an extra vs diary, proof before covering, read the Inbox' is how to use JobGuard; every competitor in the £25–£45 band gives that away (Fergus free onboarding hour; Tradify/Powered Now help centres — research §'UK builders already pay…'). Charging £49 per person for the manual is a conversion tax on the behaviour JobGuard most needs (capture discipline drives retention and reduces disputes). (2) The revenue is a rounding error by the idea's own numbers (£10/£130/£460) and lower on sceptical assumptions. (3) Content cost: a self-paced course is £5–£15k of production for £49 tickets; it never pays back early. (4) CITB short-course grants require approved course content and a levy-registered employer; a half-day app course is unlikely to qualify without accreditation effort — unverified, as the idea admits. (5) A 'JobGuard capture certificate' has no market recognition; partner trainers keeping 60% is a channel built before there is demand. The trust argument is real (JobGuard selling something that lowers its own fee base) but that is a reason to give the training away loudly, not to sell it. Revenue rework (assumptions: Solo 0% pay for app training; 10% of Small firms buy one £295 remote session; 15% of Firms buy one £750 on-site half-day; trainer half-day plus travel £300–£450): Solo £0; Small ~£30; Firm ~£130 gross, ~£60 net. Gaming: none. Build: none beyond an optional certification record; cost is content and trainer time. Top failure reasons: it is onboarding, competitors give it free, trivial revenue, content cost, no certificate value.
verdicts.conditions: Not applicable (rejected as a paid product). Make capture training free in-app and in onboarding, because it lowers disputes and the shadow-bill base and is the strongest trust signal available. Keep the on-site half-day as an unadvertised, manually delivered Firm request at £750 if a firm asks — no build, no marketing.
verdicts.key_risk: Gating the behaviour JobGuard needs most (builders logging their own extras) behind a fee competitors charge nothing for.

verdicts.reasons: This is the most honest way on the list to charge a fixed fee for prevention insight, and it needs almost no code — but the demand is confined to the top of the market. Refutation. (1) Solo builders do not buy consultancy: £295 is 85% of a year's subscription for three hours of desk analysis of 19 small jobs; expect 2–3% take-up (~£8/yr). Drop the tier. (2) Year-one data is thin: a firm's first year yields 10–30 locked jobs (SV-4 is unbuilt), and the review depends on locked, builder-visible data only (§14.3 isolation; §14.1 forbidden claims), so the first sellable review is a year after the pilot. (3) The in-product VALUE-2 cards and M1-16 signals already surface quote-to-final variance and readiness/proof gaps free; the paid layer is human interpretation ('raise your plastering day rate; stop quoting extensions without a drainage survey'), and its quality varies with the analyst. (4) The idea's precedent 'larger firms already pay £2,500–£8,000 for independent QS cost reviews' is not in the research report (which gives QS day rates £350–£1,200 and claims consultants £400–£1,200/day, §'No rival…' table); treat it as unverified. (5) It is discretionary spend, easily deferred. Revenue rework (assumptions: 0% / 10% / 18% take-up; analyst £40–£60/h loaded; 6 / 12 hours): Solo £0; Small ~£75 expected per account (£750 per taker, ~55% margin); Firm ~£270 expected per account (£1,500 per taker, ~55–65% margin). Per taker the economics are good; per account it is a 10–19% uplift on Firm subscriptions. Gaming: over-claiming savings in the report is barred by §14.1 (no 'JobGuard saved you £X' before settled cash) and D11 advisory-only; the analyst must never see pre-lock shadow signals (builder role plus locked-jobs export only) and the report should state that restriction. Build first: SV-4 lock, an export of locked jobs (M4-3 packs are a source), VALUE-2 cards; minimal code, analyst time is the cost. Comparables: cost-reduction consultancies at 50% of savings (research table) show the contingent alternative is far more expensive, which supports a fixed fee. Top failure reasons: no Solo demand, thin first-year data, analyst quality/scale, overlap with free in-product views, deferrable spend.
verdicts.conditions: Offer Builder (£750) and Firm (£1,500) tiers only; drop Solo. Sell only to accounts with ≥10 locked jobs, delivered manually from a locked-jobs export by an analyst holding the builder role with no shadow access, stated in the report. Test with 3–5 pilot firms after their first year before any productisation; keep §14.1 forbidden claims out of the report; keep PI cover for the analyst.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (drop tier; ~£8 expected if offered)

verdicts.key_risk: Demand exists only where firms already have office staff and data, and it cannot be sold until a year of locked jobs exists, so it is a later, modest Firm-tier uplift rather than an early revenue line.

verdicts.reasons: Worth building for the builder's own billing and for retention; not defensible as a fee source or as the meter's enforcement. Refutation of the enforcement claim: the homeowner can only 'notice' a job that is already on JobGuard. A builder who wants to keep a job off the meter never creates it and never sends a link, so the customer never knows a portal exists. The portal makes it awkward to close a live job early to free a slot (the customer still expects stage updates), which is a partial stickiness effect, not enforcement against under-creation — the meter's main gaming vector (research §'Charge for live jobs, not people' names exactly this risk and recommends generous allowances and an upgrade prompt rather than blocking; D11 v2 keeps 'won but never switched live' as a signal, never a penalty). The honest answer on the live-jobs meter: it works because allowances are generous and the builder wants the job on the platform for approvals and proof, not because the customer polices it. Refutation of the fee revenue: a portal catch needs the customer to ask in-thread, the builder to do the work, not log it, not add it at final review, confirm post-lock, bill it late to a consumer, and the consumer to pay — and the D13 must-surface rule ('clear customer request for significant work where written agreement is needed', §14.3) fires on exactly the larger requests, making them fee-free. Late extra bills to homeowners are dispute-prone under consumer law (research §'The hidden final check', legal points). Rework (assumptions: portal used on 50% of jobs; 10% of those yield a qualifying catch that exists only because of the portal; 2% of net value; 60% billed and settled; 10% fee): Solo ~£10, Small ~£35, Firm ~£120 a year — and £0 until G4 + D13 + D12 v2 + SV-8. Willingness to use: builders want written variation approval (D06 currently only supports builder attestation in M1-6; an authenticated customer approval bound to the revision hash is the real prize, it makes every variation — builder-captured included — more collectable); homeowners largely live in WhatsApp, so thread adoption will be low while one-tap approvals and stage sign-off with photos will be used. Comparables: client portals are table stakes at TradeFlow (£36 flat), Powered Now Premium, Payaca, Houzz Pro, Buildertrend Essential (research §'UK builders…' and raw uk_trade_job_software); none charges the homeowner; none earns from it. Trust: this is the surface where JobGuard's fee interest collides hardest with the builder's relationship — a builder learning that their customer's message earned JobGuard 10% will feel it more than a supplier line; D12 v2 must disclose it, the portal must be the builder's channel ('powered by'), and the Article 13/14 notice to the homeowner must be plain. Regulatory: CCRs 2013 14-day cancellation on remotely approved variations unless the express request to begin work is captured — must be designed in. Build: medium (3–5 weeks) plus a customer principal outside tenant membership (M0-6 extension), SV-7 customer message page, and SV-2/SV-3 byte-identical responses regardless of signals; real homeowners only after G1. Gaming: builder keeping the customer off the portal is permitted and fee-free; manufactured requests earn nothing without builder confirmation and settled cash (Test E).
verdicts.conditions: Justify it on retention and collectability, not fee revenue or meter enforcement. Build the smallest slice first: authenticated variation approval (D06 method) and stage sign-off with proof photos; add messaging only after the D12 v2 lawful basis/Article 14 notice and the CCRs express-request capture are approved. Present it as the builder's channel ('powered by JobGuard'); never as JobGuard checking the builder. Must pass SV-2/SV-3 (no portal response varies with signals). Measure in the §14.17 pilot how many catches originate in portal messages before anyone cites a fee number.

revised_revenue.solo: ~£10/yr incremental fee at maturity; £0 before G4/D13
revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£35/yr incremental fee at maturity; £0 before G4/D13
revised_revenue.firm: ~£120/yr incremental fee at maturity; £0 before G4/D13

verdicts.key_risk: It is the surface where a builder most directly discovers that their customer's messages fed a JobGuard fee, and its 'meter enforcement' does nothing about jobs the builder never creates.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation. (1) A 'JobGuard-checked' badge is worth what homeowners know it means, which at launch is nothing. Checkatrade's £30–£59+/month (with real bills of £80–£500/month including leads — raw uk_trade_job_software §Checkatrade) buys a brand built by years of advertising and, above all, leads. This profile explicitly brings no leads, so the builder's ROI story is 'a page with verifiable facts I can link to' — nice, not a monthly line item. (2) Adoption of 40–50% at £9–£25/month is unsupported; standalone attach for a vanity/verification page with no lead flow is more like 10–15% (my assumption). At £9/month the payment and support cost eats most of it. (3) The public-metrics hazard is structural, not cosmetic: any published figure computed by the watchdog (variations approved before work, invoice-to-payment days) is JobGuard publicly characterising its own customer from data collected for them; the idea correctly says it drops to trust 2 if it shows catches or D11 signals, but even the 'positive' metrics create ranking pressure and DMCC 2024/CPUT exposure over what 'checked' implies (research §'The hidden final check' legal notes; 'checked' must be defined, true and not an endorsement of workmanship). (4) Locked-job denominators do not exist until SV-4 ships and the pilot produces locked jobs; before then the page is empty. (5) The genuinely valuable pieces are the cheap ones: the immutable quote hash/QR (M1-5 already stores immutable versions) and the structured quote-request brief that lands in Walk it (M1-2) — the latter directly attacks site-visit omissions, i.e. the prevention value the founder wants; but that argues for shipping them in the product, not for a paid add-on. Revenue rework (assumptions: standalone 12% / 12% / 15% attach at £9 / £15 / £25): Solo ~£13, Small ~£22, Firm ~£45 a year; bundled into the Builder tier: £0 direct, some tier-justification value. Revenue is behind G4 anyway (add-on entitlements in the rewritten M4-13, hosted checkout M4-11). Gaming: locking trivial jobs to inflate counts — mitigated by showing values and dates and counting only server-verified evidence. Comparables: Checkatrade Approved £30/Growth £59+, Which? Trusted Traders from £48, Powered Now certificates (research report and idea's own list) — all either sell leads or a recognised consumer brand, which JobGuard lacks. Top failure reasons: no homeowner recognition, no leads, rating-your-own-customer hazard, empty until locked jobs exist, price too low to matter.
verdicts.conditions: Do not sell it standalone. Ship the quote hash/QR stamp and the structured quote-request intake as ordinary product features (they are cheap and reduce omissions); defer the public profile until there are enough locked jobs to show, and until DMCC/CPUT wording for 'checked' has legal review. If a profile ships, show only builder-consented, builder-positive facts with values and dates, never anything derived from watchdog findings, D11 signals or disputes; every metric switchable off; no ranking, no leads, no marketplace. Consider it as a Builder-tier hero feature rather than a line item.

revised_revenue.solo: ~£13/yr standalone (12% × £9 × 12); £0 if bundled

verdicts.key_risk: A badge nobody recognises, sold without leads, that tempts JobGuard to publish facts about its own customers computed from watchdog data.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempted on four fronts. (1) Selling the builder's customers: the portal creates a JobGuard-held homeowner base, which is exactly the demand asset I58 would need; the only thing stopping JobGuard monetising it is a promise, and the research (Cain et al., report section 'The hidden final check') says a disclosed conflict does not neutralise it. (2) Builder-customer relationship: JobGuard-sent 'guarantee expires soon' reminders invite a snag hunt against the builder, and the proof-photo / behind-the-wall record can become the homeowner's evidence pack in a later dispute. (3) Shadow-bill leakage: a confirmed catch becomes a variation with origin=jobguard_catch (BUILD_PLAN 14.5) that goes to the customer for approval; if the portal shows that provenance or the timing story ('added after your builder said the bill was complete') the homeowner learns JobGuard found what the builder missed - the worst possible relationship outcome. (4) Hostage risk: if the builder stops paying, what happens to their customer's record and the routing promise? None of these refutes the idea because each is fixable structurally rather than by a setting, and the core - exclusive repeat and referral routing for a small flat fee - is unambiguously in the builder's interest under the Xia/Monroe/Cox test: the builder did the work, bears a small known cost, and JobGuard exploits no advantage. In a word-of-mouth trade, repeat work and referrals are the value builders rank highest (Simply Business survey cited in the report).
verdicts.conditions: (a) Exclusivity is a contractual term in the builder's subscription and the homeowner's terms, not a configuration flag: JobGuard never markets any builder, insurer, energy, solar, finance or inspection service to a portal homeowner, never uses portal homeowners as demand for I58 or any marketplace, never displays or ranks other builders to them; breach gives the builder termination plus deletion rights. (b) On builder cancellation the record stays read-only, routing goes nowhere (not to other builders), no marketing ever; the builder can export and delete the portal relationship at any time; the customer list remains the builder's (D12 v2 controller mapping). (c) The builder chooses per item which photos, certificates and documents enter the homeowner record; proof-gate photos are never auto-shared. (d) Reminders are builder-opted-in per type with builder-approved wording, framed as maintenance/renewal prompts routed to the builder, never 'check for defects before your guarantee ends'; PECR consent captured from the homeowner. (e) The portal never displays variation origin, signal IDs, lock timestamps, fee statements or anything derived from 14.3 shadow tables; a jobguard_catch variation looks identical to a builder-logged one on the customer side. (f) Portal engagement data is never a D11 input and never shared with any partner (I60-I63).

revised_revenue.solo: £95 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard's own future temptation to monetise a captive homeowner base (leads, cross-sell) - the single act that would turn the highest-trust idea into selling the builder's customers.

verdicts.reasons: Fails the lens on every test and the idea's own author recommends against it. (1) Watchdog independence: JobGuard holds every builder's variation rate, dispute rate, D11 advisory signals and shadow signals; a marketplace that calls builders 'checked' must rank or vet them, and the only data JobGuard has is the watchdog data it promised was collected for the builder. Even if contractually excluded, the builder cannot verify it, and betrayal aversion (Bohnet & Zeckhauser, report section 'The hidden final check') means suspicion alone poisons the watchdog. (2) Selling the builder's customers: the cheapest demand pool is the I57 homeowner base - one builder's customers routed to competitors. (3) Unfair under dual entitlement (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler): 2% of accepted net quote (£1,200 on a £60k job) on top of the subscription and the 10% success fee, for a job the builder quoted, won and will do; JobGuard's contribution is an introduction, and it is a third charge the builder must decode. (4) Leakage policing: the 2% needs enforcement against builders who take the homeowner off-platform (Checkatrade's known problem); the only tools are D11 signals such as 'job won but never switched live', which D11 v2 says may never trigger a charge or account action. Either JobGuard eats the leakage or it turns the watchdog on its customer. (5) Adjudication: when a marketplace-sourced job goes wrong the homeowner blames 'checked', and JobGuard - holding the builder's evidence pack - is dragged into judging between its customer and the homeowner it sourced. The research notes record Checkatrade at £80-£500/month real bills, 12-month contracts and pay-per-lead as the model builders resent most (uk_trade_job_software, lead-gen section). A free directory (I56) captures the discoverability benefit with none of this.
verdicts.conditions: None that rescue it. If ever revisited, the minimum would be: no I57 homeowners as demand, no watchdog or shadow data in matching or vetting, no leakage enforcement of any kind, no 'checked' claim beyond verified identity and insurance, and no percentage of job value - at which point it is a directory (I56), not a marketplace.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (idea's £320 not achievable without the conflicts above)

verdicts.key_risk: Structural conflict: JobGuard as both the builder's watchdog and their lead seller, ranking builders with the very data it collects to protect them.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation: (1) JobGuard would be paid by a party it recommends whose job is to find fault with the builder's work, and it earns the 15% whether the report is clean or damning - a hidden-commission position (CPUT/DMCC concern the idea itself notes) and, under Xia et al., JobGuard exploiting its position on the payment-release path. (2) The inspector receives the builder's proof photos: evidence the builder gathered for the watchdog is handed to a third party to critique. (3) Shadow-bill interaction: the inspection happens at practical completion, before lock, so the report is pre-lock evidence under 14.2 and could seed a shadow signal ('builder also fitted X, not in scope'); JobGuard would earn 15% from the inspector and then 10% on a catch the inspector surfaced, which looks like paying for information to bill the builder. (4) If the report is not clean, a tool the builder pays for now sits between them and their invoice. Why it survives: builder-enabled per job, it is genuinely in the builder's interest - an independent statement that the work matches the agreed scope is the strongest defence against 'I'm holding back the last £5k for snags', pre-empts the withheld-payment case the builder would otherwise need to open, and scope-anchored inspection stops wish-list creep. A reasonable builder who chose to switch it on would see it as fair only if JobGuard's cut is small, flat, disclosed and outcome-independent, and the inspection cannot hold their invoice hostage.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Builder-enabled per job only; JobGuard never prompts the homeowner. (b) JobGuard's referral fee is zero or a flat, disclosed amount shown to both homeowner and builder on the booking screen, never a percentage that scales with inspection price; panel membership by published criteria (RICS/RPSA), no ranking by revenue or by report outcome in either direction. (c) The builder selects which proof photos and documents the inspector receives; agreed scope and approved variations shared by default, diary and unsubmitted evidence never. (d) The inspection is advisory: it cannot gate invoice issue or the customer-approval flow; the builder can issue the final invoice regardless of the report. (e) Inspector reports are excluded as sources for shadow_commercial_signal, or any signal whose only evidence is a paid-referral inspector's report is marked ineligible; JobGuard must not earn a success fee from evidence a paying partner produced. (f) The report goes to both parties simultaneously; JobGuard neither holds it back nor interprets it.

revised_revenue.solo: £0-£50 (zero under the no-fee variant this lens prefers; £50 only with a flat disclosed fee)

verdicts.key_risk: A builder learning that the snagging inspector who held up their final payment paid JobGuard for the introduction.

verdicts.reasons: Tried to refute on: (1) undisclosed commission - the body is paid 15% per converted member and members may not know their body is remunerated; (2) the body acquiring leverage over JobGuard (demands for findings visibility or a share of success fees) - the idea already refuses this contractually; (3) the mark implying the body verified the work; (4) lock-in - 'two months free on the annual plan' commits a member to 12 months before they have experienced a final-check reveal, so the first reveal could feel like a trap endorsed by their own body; (5) partner-flow onboarding skipping the D13 / 14.11 disclosure because the body 'vouched'. None refutes it: the builder pays less than direct, bears no hidden cost, JobGuard exploits no information advantage, and trade-body member benefits are a familiar, accepted channel (FMB directory, NFB partners). Under the price-fairness framework this is a plain discount from a trusted intermediary, and the live-jobs meter suits FMB's long-domestic-job members, as the idea notes.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The offer page states that the body receives a referral payment from JobGuard (amount or basis). (b) The body receives conversion counts and payout statements only - never job data, findings, fee statements, D11 signals or per-member usage; the contract prohibits any share of, or visibility into, success fees. (c) The membership mark on customer-facing documents states membership only, never that the body checked or guarantees the work; ASA/CAP compliant wording. (d) Members keep the same trial (through first live job), monthly option and cancellation rights as direct customers; the annual discount is not the only route. (e) The D13 onboarding disclosure and the one-sentence final-check explanation appear in the partner sign-up flow unedited, before the first job. (f) One redemption per validated membership number, validated against the body's list at sign-up and annually.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation: (1) The bookkeeper introducer fee (10% of first-year fees paid to JobGuard) is JobGuard being paid by a party it recommends; the bookkeeper prices it into what the builder pays, so the builder bears the cost and JobGuard exploits its position - a kickback in a builder's eyes. Rejected as a component. (2) The referral share turns the builder's most trusted adviser into a paid recommender; ICAEW/ACCA/AAT commission rules make this disclosable and for some bodies accountable to the client - the practice's duty, but JobGuard must make it visible in the builder's terms so it is never discovered later. (3) The practice-paid pack sells a product derived from the builder's data to a third party; fair only if the builder can get the same data free (M5-1 canonical export) and the practice sees only consenting clients. (4) Adviser visibility: the adviser seat must be a 'builder-facing' role for 14.3 purposes - no shadow tables, no pre-lock response variation, no D11 signals, no fee statements without builder opt-in - otherwise the accountant learns JobGuard's suspicions before the builder does. (5) A 24-month share gives the accountant an interest in the builder staying even if unhappy; disclosed, and standard in Xero/QuickBooks partner programmes builders already know. Why it survives: the builder pays the same price, the accountant channel is how under-digitised builders (29% software use, research notes) actually choose tools, the free practice seat cuts the accountant's hours on WIP/CIS/retentions - a cost the builder bears today - and MTD ITSA makes the accountant the decision-maker. A reasonable builder sees a disclosed accountant referral as normal and in their interest.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Drop the bookkeeper introducer fee; list vetted bookkeepers free or not at all. (b) The referral share (20%, 24 months, collected revenue only) is stated in the builder's terms and on the sign-up screen whenever a practice code is used. (c) Practice view requires per-client builder consent, revocable at any time; scope limited to the published field list (WIP, unbilled approved variations, retentions, CIS, DRC flags, locked final accounts); no shadow tables, no pre-lock signal-dependent data, no D11 signals, no success-fee statements unless the builder opts in. (d) Everything in the year-end pack is obtainable by the builder free through the canonical export; the pack is a formatting convenience, never a toll. (e) Share paid only on collected subscription revenue, stops on cancellation, never on success fees. (f) WIP and 'revenue recognition' figures labelled projections from immutable records, not advice; D02 VAT labels.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation: (1) Whose side: the MC pays, the sub uses; the MC gets timestamped proof and application records it can use to reject late notices. It cuts both ways under HGCRA, but a sub reasonably reads 'the tool my MC bought' as the MC's compliance system, not their watchdog. (2) Money on both sides of a dispute: a sub's withheld_customer_payment case (14.7) is against the very MC paying JobGuard's licence. Either JobGuard pursues its paying client hard (MC churns) or the sub suspects it goes soft - and JobGuard would take 10% of money recovered from its own customer. That is a real independence compromise. (3) Shadow bill: after the sub's lock, JobGuard reveals missed variations for the sub to bill the MC; the MC is paying for a tool that finds money against it and will demand it be disabled or made visible. Disabling it degrades the sub's service because someone else pays (against the spirit of AGENTS 5.14); exposing it to the MC is disclosure to the counterparty. (4) Sole-trader subs become data subjects inside an MC-procured monitoring system (D12). Why it survives: the sub gets a real tool free on that project, keeps their own tenant, is excluded from tier counting for licensed jobs, and evidenced applications with Construction Act reminders genuinely help subs get paid - the Payapps model shows subs accept MC-bought systems when the terms are plain. Fair only if JobGuard refuses to be paid on both sides of a dispute and the MC cannot see or influence anything the sub has not submitted.
verdicts.conditions: (a) No success fee on any withheld_customer_payment case against a client that is paying JobGuard for that project; JobGuard still supports the case, fee-free, and the MC contract cannot restrict, delay or see it. (b) The MC contract acknowledges in plain terms that the final check runs for the sub, that the MC never sees shadow data, unsubmitted evidence, diary or the sub's tenant, and cannot have it switched off; an MC that will not sign that gets no licence. (c) The sub's invite screen names who pays, exactly what the MC can see (submitted applications, notices, proof attached to them, nothing else) and that the sub's fee terms are unchanged. (d) No aggregate sub-performance dashboards or scoring to the MC (the I63 objection applies); MC-to-sub communication limited to the HGCRA flows. (e) Licensed projects excluded from the sub's live-job tier count, as proposed. (f) D12 Article 13/14 route for sole-trader subs before onboarding.

revised_revenue.firm: £360 (success fees on cases against the paying MC removed; missed-variation catches still eligible)
