verdicts.reasons: Refutation: (1) OEM through a lead-gen platform (Checkatrade/MyBuilder/Rated People) puts the watchdog's evidence - variation rates, disputes, catches - inside a business whose product is ranking builders for homeowners and billing them £80-£500/month on 12-month contracts (research notes, lead-gen section). Contractual separation cannot be verified by the builder; under betrayal aversion the belief that the platform sees their disputes is enough. The partner sets the retail price, so the builder cannot see what the watchdog costs them, contrary to the report's 'the builder has to see clearly what each payment buys'. A partner-branded reveal reads as 'Checkatrade took a cut of the find', partner pressure for early hints is a standing attack on 14.3, and customer approvals (D06) inside a lead platform's wrapper expose the builder's own homeowners to that platform's demand pool. Refuted for lead-gen partners. (2) OEM through a trade-body app has no adverse interest and largely duplicates I60 - acceptable. (3) Franchise: 'consented fields' in a mandated franchise agreement are not consent; a per-showroom dashboard is per-franchisee surveillance (each showroom is one business) and franchisees already resent head-office visibility. Survives only as network-level aggregates with a minimum group size, which sharply reduces franchisor appetite. (4) Wholesale at a third of list while surrendering control of the trust-critical explanation trades trust for little revenue. Not a full reject because a trade-body OEM and a genuinely aggregate franchise licence can be fair: the franchisee gets the tool at wholesale, keeps a direct unshared fee relationship, and the franchisor learns only what a survey would tell it.
verdicts.conditions: (a) No OEM/white-label with lead-generation or review platforms; OEM only with trade bodies or partners that do not rank, sell leads about, or adjudicate builders. (b) The success fee, the reveal screen, the one-sentence final-check explanation and the D13 onboarding disclosure are delivered by JobGuard directly and unedited, and the builder is told the watchdog's price component separately from the partner's bundle. (c) Partners receive metered counts and invoices only; never job data, signals, findings, fee statements or D11 flags; no early-hint mechanism exists to be pressured for. (d) Franchise dashboard: network-level aggregates only, published field list, minimum group size (e.g. 10 franchisees) so no showroom is identifiable, opt-out per franchisee without penalty; no per-franchisee drill-down under any 'consent' in the franchise agreement. (e) No exclusivity blocking direct purchase; wholesale terms cannot make direct customers worse off. (f) Partner customers' homeowner approvals and messages never flow into the partner's own systems.

revised_revenue.solo: £468 franchise wholesale where applicable; lead-gen OEM £120 excluded; trade-body OEM not estimated

verdicts.key_risk: A builder inside a partner-branded wrapper believing the lead platform or head office can see the watchdog's findings about them.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation: (1) The inviting builder is paid (one month's credit) to recruit subs - a small kickback; subs could feel pushed onto a platform for the builder's benefit. Mitigated by its size (£29-£119 once) and by paying only on the sub's own voluntary subscription. (2) The sub's uploads become evidence in the builder's job (14.2) and can seed a shadow signal against the builder (a sub invoice showing work outside baseline) - already the D13 rule for supplier documents - but the sub should know their invoice is matched against the builder's PO and agreed prices, i.e. the sub is policed on the builder's behalf. Plain disclosure at invite resolves it; it is what a sub expects from any PO system. (3) Timestamps cut both ways in a builder-sub dispute, exactly as WhatsApp does today with less structure. (4) A 'Sub' tenant with no quoting or final account is a stripped product and invited-job data stays in the inviter's tenant on conversion - must be explicit. (5) Sub invoice data must never feed a pricing benchmark or ranking sold to anyone. None refutes it: builders already coordinate subs on WhatsApp, the invite is a convenience, the credit is a plain thank-you funded from new revenue, it never touches success fees (D09 credit only), and the sub gets free scoped access plus their own future tenant under the same fee-free capture rules. Fair under Xia et al.: nobody bears a hidden cost.
verdicts.conditions: (a) The invite states plainly what the inviter sees (the sub's own uploads and invoices on that job), what the sub sees (only their items), that the sub's invoices are matched against the builder's POs and agreed prices, and that the inviter receives a small subscription credit if the sub later subscribes. (b) Credit is a D09 subscription credit only, paid after 30 live-job days and one paid period, capped per year, with unique conversion identity; never offsets a success fee; nothing for invites that do not convert. (c) The sub's own tenant on conversion carries the same fee-free capture rules and the D13 disclosure at its first job; invited-job data remains the inviter's, stated at invite. (d) Sub-uploaded invoices and prices are used only for that builder's job checks; never aggregated into a sub/supplier pricing benchmark, ranking or lead product. (e) D12 Article 13/14 notice to sole-trader subs at invite; the sub can leave the scoped role and export their own uploads.

verdicts.reasons: No blocker, but the regulatory shape is different from 'Stripe does everything'. (1) Perimeter: issuing payment instruments and holding the funded balance are payment/e-money services (PSRs 2017 Sch 1 para 1(e); EMRs 2011). Stripe Payments UK Ltd is the FCA-authorised EMI and holds the safeguarded balance, so AGENTS §3 ('never hold customer funds') is met and JobGuard can sit inside the technical-service-provider exclusion (PSRs Sch 1 Pt 2) provided it never touches funds. However, Stripe's UK/EU Issuing programme for cards issued to connected accounts has historically required the platform to be registered as an agent or notified as a distributor of Stripe's EMI (EMRs regs 33–34). Agent registration means FCA fit-and-proper checks on JobGuard's directors and MLR 2017 obligations flowing from the principal. This must be confirmed with Stripe and a payments solicitor before build; it is a cost, not a bar. (2) Credit: a prepaid card funded by the builder's own money is not credit, so CCA 1974 and credit broking (RAO art 36A) do not arise. If Stripe ever extends a credit line on the balance, a sole-trader facility of £25k or less becomes regulated credit and the whole analysis changes; lock the product to prepaid. (3) Interchange: UK commercial cards are outside the retained Interchange Fee Regulation caps, so a revenue share is lawful; the 0.5% net figure is an unverified assumption and the share is a private Stripe term. Interchange-derived income is consideration for exempt financial services (VATA 1994 Sch 9 Grp 5), so JobGuard becomes partially exempt for VAT — almost certainly within the de minimis limit at these amounts, but an accountant should confirm. (4) Consumer Duty and PSRs protections: Solo and Small-firm builders are micro-enterprises, so Stripe owes them consumer-equivalent PSR protections and Consumer Duty, and it will contractually push oversight of card wording, complaints and disclosures down to JobGuard as a distribution-chain participant. (5) Data: Stripe processes card data globally under IDTA/SCCs; D04 approval must enumerate the Issuing route separately from the hosted-payment route already planned in M4-11/12. (6) True cost the idea understates: a decline at the till is not a legal defence — the builder still owes the contract price to a merchant that delivered to spec, and merchants running trade accounts on 30-day credit (most Firm-size spend) never see the card at all, so the card-spend share assumption is high for the Firm archetype. (7) Independence: no relationship with any merchant, so watchdog independence survives; there is no fiduciary-commission problem (Expert Tooling v Engie [2025] EWCA Civ 292 concerned an agent-broker), but the interchange share should be disclosed in amount in the builder terms so it can never be characterised as a half-secret commission.
verdicts.conditions: Written confirmation from Stripe of the UK Issuing programme structure for connected accounts and whether JobGuard must become an EMR agent or distributor; if agent registration is needed, treat it as a 1–3 month task with director fit-and-proper checks and MLR 2017 flow-downs before any live card. Prepaid only, no credit line, recorded as a product constraint. Interchange share disclosed in amount in builder terms ('a card-network fee paid by the merchant's bank; nothing from your merchant'). D04 approval extended to the Issuing data route. Card wording, complaints route and decline messaging reviewed under Stripe's Consumer Duty flow-down for micro-enterprise builders. UI states plainly that a declined authorisation stops the card payment, not the supplier's contractual claim. New decision record for partner/interchange revenue (none of D01–D13 covers it); behind G4 and the M4-11 adapter. Accountant note on partial exemption. Solicitor sign-off on the technical-service-provider position.

revised_revenue.solo: £40–£80 (card-heavy spend; assumption 30–40% of materials on card)
revised_revenue.firm: £300–£900 (most spend on 30-day trade credit, not cards; 0.5% net share unverified)

verdicts.key_risk: Stripe's UK Issuing programme turns out to require JobGuard to be an FCA-registered EMI agent, adding director vetting, AML flow-downs and Consumer Duty oversight for a revenue line worth under £1k a year per builder.

verdicts.reasons: Referral-only is lawful; proof-gated release is where the legal cost lives. (1) Perimeter: the escrow provider must hold the funds as an FCA-authorised payment institution or EMI with safeguarding (PSRs 2017/EMRs 2011) or under a solicitor's client-money regime; Transpact describes itself as FCA-authorised and TrustMark's escrow runs through a partner — verify each FCA register entry and permission scope, do not rely on marketing. JobGuard introducing homeowners to a payment service is not itself a regulated activity (there is no 'payment broking'), and payment services are not a controlled activity under the Financial Promotion Order, so no FSMA s.21 approval is needed for plain descriptive wording — verify. The risk is payment initiation: if JobGuard's 'stage-complete Decision' actually triggers or times the release (including an auto-release after N days executed on JobGuard's signal), a regulator may see JobGuard initiating payment orders (PSRs Sch 1 para 1(g)) rather than supplying information. Auto-release must be a term of the provider's own escrow agreement with both parties, executed by the provider on its own clock; JobGuard only supplies facts. (2) Consumer law: the homeowner is a consumer. The escrow agreement is subject to CRA 2015 Part 2 fairness (an auto-release-on-silence clause is exactly the kind of term the CMA scrutinises), CCRs 2013 information and cancellation duties (off-premises contracts formed in the home), and DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 unfair commercial practices. If the homeowner interacts with a JobGuard portal, JobGuard needs consumer-facing portal terms of its own; without them it has no contract and no basis to limit liability. (3) Liability for 'verified': if a homeowner releases money in reliance on a JobGuard proof pack and the work is defective, a negligent-misstatement claim (Hedley Byrne) is foreseeable; a builder whose release is delayed by a JobGuard gate has an economic-loss claim. Exclusions against the homeowner are policed by CRA s.62/s.65; against the builder by UCTA 1977 s.2–3 reasonableness. 'Verified' must be defined as hash and existence only, and the design must never let JobGuard earn more when release is delayed. (4) Construction law: HGCRA 1996 s.106 excludes contracts with a residential occupier, so no statutory payment notice/pay-less notice/adjudication regime applies to the typical domestic job and a contractual stage-escrow is free to govern. For any non-residential-occupier payer (landlord, developer, commercial), Part II applies and an auto-release that ignores a valid s.111 pay-less notice would conflict with the Act; restrict v1 to residential-occupier contracts, which D06 already contemplates by refusing to assume a universal notice regime. (5) Tax: money held by a genuine stakeholder is generally not 'received' by the builder for the VAT tax point until release (accountant to confirm); CIS is irrelevant for homeowners but would complicate escrow for commercial payers — another reason to keep v1 domestic. (6) Data: homeowner personal data and job evidence pass to the provider; needs a D12 lawful basis and Article 13/14 notice. (7) AML: the provider is the relevant person; JobGuard moves nothing. Revenue is small in every archetype, and the Solo builder rarely has a £25k domestic job.
verdicts.conditions: Provider's FCA permission and safeguarding verified on the register, not from marketing. Auto-release is the provider's contractual term executed by the provider; JobGuard supplies facts and never sends a release instruction — solicitor opinion on the PSRs payment-initiation boundary before build. Residential-occupier domestic jobs only in v1; HGCRA and CIS analysis before any commercial payer. Consumer-facing JobGuard portal terms drafted under CRA 2015/CCRs 2013/DMCC 2024, with 'verified' defined as integrity and existence only. JobGuard's fee is flat per stage or a fixed share of the provider's fee, never linked to timing or withholding; disclosed to both parties. D12 lawful basis and notice for homeowner data sent to the provider; D04 route review. New decision record for regulated introductions; M5, behind M4-18 and I55.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£40 (few £25k+ domestic jobs)
revised_revenue.firm: £100–£500 (assumes uptake 10–25% of eligible domestic jobs, £10 per stage)

verdicts.key_risk: A JobGuard-triggered or JobGuard-timed release is characterised as payment initiation or as a certification the homeowner relied on, pulling JobGuard into the PSR perimeter or into liability for workmanship it never assessed.

verdicts.reasons: Variant A is legally workable in a narrow form; Variant B is regulated credit broking for most of JobGuard's user base. (1) Invoice finance: a facility structured as a purchase of receivables is not a credit agreement, so introducing to it is not credit broking whatever the builder's legal form; but several 'invoice finance' products are loans secured on receivables, and a loan of £25,000 or less to a sole trader or partnership of three or fewer is a regulated credit agreement (the RAO art 60C(3) business exemption applies only above £25k), making the introduction credit broking under RAO art 36A. The partner's product structure must be checked, not assumed. The Business Contract Terms (Assignment of Receivables) Regulations 2018 help by neutralising most anti-assignment clauses in SME suppliers' B2B contracts — verify the exclusions. (2) Working-capital loans: introducing an individual (sole trader, small partnership) to a lender or to another broker is credit broking under art 36A(1)(a)–(d) unless the loan is over £25k and wholly for business; limited permission is unavailable because JobGuard is not the supplier of the thing financed, so direct authorisation means full permission (6–12 months, FOS membership, CONC compliance, realistic cost £20–50k plus ongoing). The IAR route under an authorised principal (1–3 months, principal-dependent) is the only fast lawful route and restricts JobGuard to effecting introductions and passing on principal-approved non-real-time promotions. Unauthorised broking is a criminal offence (FSMA s.23) and makes brokered agreements unenforceable without an FCA order (s.27), so no lender will onboard JobGuard without one of these. (3) Promotions: 'Get this invoice paid early' on a receivables-purchase product is not a controlled activity; 'borrow against this' to a sole trader is a financial promotion of providing credit and needs an authorised approver (FSMA s.21) — verify that the business-purpose exemption also carries the promotion outside the FPO for >£25k loans. (4) Commission: for regulated credit, undisclosed or large commissions engage CCA s.140A unfair relationships (Johnson v FirstRand [2025] UKSC 33) and CONC 4.5 disclosure; for unregulated B2B lending, half-secret commissions have been litigated in the energy-broker context (Expert Tooling v Engie [2025] EWCA Civ 292). Disclose the amount before the tap in every case. (5) Data: the builder's customer's invoice, payment history and evidence pack go to a lender; where the customer is a sole trader that is personal data, so D12 lawful basis (legitimate interests) and Article 14 route are needed, and the customer contract may restrict disclosure. (6) Interaction with the 10%: a sold invoice belongs to the financier, so it cannot be a withheld_customer_payment case; the idea's 'never on an invoice with an open case' rule must also run the other way (no case on a financed invoice). Ordinary late payment on a business invoice carries Late Payment of Commercial Debts Act interest and £40–£100 compensation, which the builder should see before being offered finance. (7) The founder's trust risk is real and independent of the law: a watchdog earning from a lender when the builder is short of cash.
verdicts.conditions: v1 = invoice finance only, receivables-purchase structure confirmed in writing by the partner, or borrowers limited to incorporated companies/LLPs/partnerships of four or more; no sole-trader or small-partnership loan introduction of £25k or less until JobGuard is on the FCA register as an IAR/AR of the partner. No 'borrow against this' (Variant B) until that registration exists and the principal has approved all wording. Commission amount shown before the tap; offer audited as a commercial send under AGENTS §5.3. Off by default, builder-initiated, never in the Decision Inbox or a Finding, blocked where a recovery case is open, and no case may be opened on a financed invoice. D12 lawful basis and Article 14 notice for customer data sent to the lender; D04 route review. Late Payment Act interest/compensation shown before any finance offer on a business invoice. New decision record; pilot referrals only under a decision record with no JobGuard commission. Solicitor memo on the art 36A/60C(3) perimeter and the FPO exemption scope.

revised_revenue.solo: £0–£20 (sole trader mostly excluded in v1; domestic invoices ineligible)
revised_revenue.firm: £50–£700 (assumes 5–15% of B2B invoiced value financed at 0.4–0.75%)

verdicts.key_risk: A sole-trader builder is introduced to a £15k facility before JobGuard holds IAR status: unauthorised credit broking, a criminal offence and an unenforceable agreement that the lender will refuse to fund.

verdicts.reasons: Legally viable only as an appointed representative of an authorised principal, and the market for such principals has just been damaged. (1) Perimeter: switching on 'spread the cost' on a homeowner's quote is effecting an introduction to a lender or broker and is credit broking (RAO art 36A). The consumer is a regulated borrower whatever the amount. Interest-bearing 7.9–14.9% APR loans are regulated credit agreements; even interest-free credit repayable in 12 or fewer instalments within 12 months, exempt as an agreement under art 60F(2), still counts as credit broking for the introducer, and any supplier-of-goods carve-out that helps a retailer does not extend to a platform that is not the supplier. Limited permission is unavailable for sales concluded in the customer's home, so direct authorisation means full permission (6–12 months, FOS membership, complaints handling, Consumer Duty under PRIN 2A, CONC compliance, realistic £30–80k first-year cost). The only fast route is AR/IAR under an authorised principal (1–3 months once a principal signs), and each introducing builder must also be covered as the principal's AR or IAR, which is the Kanda model of roughly 700 tradesperson IARs that the idea reports was restricted by the FCA in February 2026 and entered liquidation in May 2026 (treat that as reported, verify on the register). Unauthorised broking is a criminal offence (FSMA s.23) and brokered agreements become unenforceable without an FCA order (s.27), so no lender will pay commission without the registration. (2) Promotions: any 'from £X/month' or APR line is a financial promotion needing an authorised approver and CONC 3 content (representative APR, risk warnings). (3) Commission: CONC 4.5 requires disclosure of the existence and, on request, the amount of commission; after Johnson v FirstRand [2025] UKSC 33 an undisclosed or disproportionate commission chain risks an unfair relationship finding under CCA s.140A that lands on the lender, who will police JobGuard's disclosure. (4) Section 75 CCA: for cash prices between £100 and £30,000 the lender is jointly liable for the builder's breach, so the principal will demand tradesperson vetting, recourse and evidence about the job — this collides with the idea's own rule that no watchdog, D11 or shadow data reaches the lender, and it puts a mis-sold or badly built job on JobGuard's name. (5) Consumer law: a builder-subsidised 0% option funded by inflated quotes is a misleading price practice under DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 and CONC 3.7; 'one quote total' is the right control but JobGuard cannot police a builder who inflates every quote. (6) Data: homeowner data flows to the lender's hosted journey; D12 lawful basis and notice. (7) Uptake in construction was thin even before Kanda; the revenue range assumed 1–2% of loan value net of the broker and is not published anywhere.
verdicts.conditions: No build and no revenue assumption until a signed principal agreement exists and JobGuard (and any introducing builder) appears on the FCA register as an AR/IAR. All homeowner-facing wording approved by the principal; no monthly-cost or APR figure anywhere in JobGuard's UI before that approval. Commission disclosed to the homeowner in amount, not just existence. No builder-subsidised 0% option in v1. One quote total, finance uptake logged as a D11 signal, no per-introduction payment to the builder. Principal's s.75 recourse and vetting terms reviewed so that only builder-consented, builder-visible job facts are ever shared, never shadow or D11 data. D12 lawful basis and Article 13/14 route; D04 route review. New decision record; M5, behind G4. Solicitor confirmation of the art 36A/60F(2) position and the in-home limited-permission exclusion.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 until a principal exists; then £50–£150
revised_revenue.firm: £0 until a principal exists; then £200–£900 (unsecured caps limit larger jobs)

verdicts.key_risk: After Kanda, no authorised principal is willing to carry JobGuard and its builders as ARs on acceptable terms, leaving the only lawful path a full FCA permission that costs more than the line earns.

verdicts.reasons: The cleanest of the regulated ideas: a recognised product, a lawful cheap route and a paying insurer. (1) Perimeter: an IBG and deposit protection are contracts of insurance, so arranging (RAO art 25), assisting in administration and performance (art 39A) and advising (art 53) are regulated. JobGuard can stay outside the perimeter only if its activity is limited to providing information about the potential policyholder to the insurer or intermediary, or about the product to the policyholder, without taking further steps to conclude or perform the contract (the post-IDD art 72C exclusion). Passing consented policy inputs fits; mapping proof photos onto the insurer's stage checklist and carrying the premium as a line on the builder's invoice look like further steps (arranging or assisting performance). Either strip those back or become an IAR/AR of the authorised administrator (QANW, HIES, FMB Insurance and LABC Warranty all run intermediary or scheme structures; 1–3 months, principal-borne cost, PII sits with the principal). Whether the builder's own sale of the IBG fits the connected-contracts exclusion (art 72B) is doubtful because the premium and risk-type limits are narrow, so most schemes already register or cover their installers — confirm how the chosen partner covers the builder. (2) Tax: IPT at 12% sits on the premium; the commission base is the net premium. If the builder recharges the premium as part of its own taxable supply the pass-through may attract 20% VAT instead of being an exempt disbursement — this is a D02 question and an accountant must set the invoice mechanics (policy issued to the homeowner, builder collects as agent) before any line type is built. (3) Consumer law: no pre-ticked box (CCRs 2013 reg 40); if optional and priced at quote time it is not drip pricing under DMCC Act 2024; the 'guaranteed job' badge must not overstate cover or be presented as a trader guarantee under CRA 2015 s.30 — the policy protects against insolvency, not workmanship. (4) IDD conduct: demands-and-needs, IPID and remuneration-nature disclosure are the intermediary's duties (ICOBS 4–6); the manufacturer's fair-value assessment (PROD 4) will look at JobGuard's 10–20% in the chain — modest by market standards but the FCA's 2024 action on GAP commissions shows the direction. (5) Data: homeowner name and address to an insurer needs a D12 lawful basis and Article 13/14 notice; builder-consented facts only. (6) Registration for incomplete work is the insurer's underwriting risk; hashes prove integrity and existence, nothing more. (7) In pilot_no_charge no commission may be earned, and an IBG line must be a distinct invoice kind excluded from net principal so it never inflates Q under §14.9 — the idea already says so.
verdicts.conditions: Decide the route before build: information-only introduction under art 72C (no invoice-line handling, no stage-checklist mapping) or IAR/AR under the administrator; solicitor confirms which. Partner's coverage of the introducing builder confirmed in writing. Accountant sets the premium/IPT/VAT invoice mechanics under D02 before the invoice line type exists. Consumer copy reviewed: optional, priced up front, never pre-ticked, cover described as insolvency protection, no trader guarantee implied. Proof gates and the final check never depend on selling cover. Only builder-consented, builder-visible facts reach the insurer; no D11 or shadow data. D12 lawful basis and notice for homeowner data; D04 route review. New decision record for partner commissions; no commission in pilot_no_charge; IBG line excluded from net principal.

verdicts.reasons: Variant A is clear with copy discipline; Variant B is lawful but a data-protection and fairness project, not a feature. (1) Variant A perimeter: comparing the frozen accepted value with builder-entered PL/EL/CAR limits and stating 'no employers' liability recorded' is generic information, not advice on a particular contract (art 53 needs a specific policy); passing contact details and consented facts to a broker fits the post-IDD introducer exclusion (art 72C) provided JobGuard takes no further step. Employers' liability is compulsory (Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969, £5m), so a factual flag when staff are recorded is defensible. The moment the card compares brokers or products, or says 'you need this policy', it becomes advising or arranging and needs IAR status. Any broker marketing shown in the card is a financial promotion that the authorised broker must approve (FSMA s.21(2)(b)). Affiliate income (Simply Business 10% capped at £100 as reported) is ordinary introducer remuneration. (2) Variant B: sharing tenant-level integrity counts with an insurer is not a regulated activity, but for a sole trader business data is personal data, so it needs a lawful basis (consent tied to a discount is acceptable if genuinely optional and revocable, or legitimate interests with transparency), a DPIA under UK GDPR Art 35 because it is systematic profiling used for pricing, a data-sharing agreement naming the insurer as an independent controller, and Art 22 handling at the insurer if pricing is automated. The builder, not JobGuard, owes the duty of fair presentation under the Insurance Act 2015; if selective photography inflates a score the builder faces proportionate remedies including avoidance, so JobGuard must supply counts of server-verified evidence with no warranty of completeness, or it inherits a misrepresentation exposure to the insurer. A per-policyholder-year fee is lawful; disclose it to the builder in amount. Consumer Duty and PROD 4 fair-value duties sit with the insurer. (3) Data outside the builder's own: none should leave under A; under B the counts must contain no customer data. (4) Trust: B is on the founder's trust-risk list and should exist only on a founder decision.
verdicts.conditions: Variant A: copy audit so every card statement is factual or generic (limits, expiry, statutory EL requirement), never a product comparison or recommendation; broker-approved wording for any promotion; no feature or gate conditioned on buying cover; only contact details and consented cover facts leave; commission disclosed. Variant B held until a founder decision and: DPIA, data-sharing agreement with the insurer as separate controller, consent that is optional and revocable without losing JobGuard features, counts-only export with an express no-warranty clause, single-insurer pilot with loss data before any discount is promised, builder able to see exactly what was shared. D12 and D04 review for both. New decision record for partner commissions.

verdicts.reasons: The SRA reading the idea relies on is plausible but not safe for consumer customers with agreed payment terms; get an opinion before selling this to domestic-heavy builders. (1) Perimeter: debt collecting (RAO art 39F) is taking steps to procure payment of a debt due under a credit agreement or consumer hire agreement. An unpaid invoice for completed work with no agreed deferral is not credit, which is the SRA's building-company example. But an invoice that grants a homeowner agreed time to pay is deferred payment, and deferred payment is credit (CCA s.9; Dimond v Lovell [2002] 1 AC 384). Such terms are usually exempt as agreements under art 60F(2) (interest-free, 12 or fewer instalments within 12 months), and my understanding is that third-party collection of debts under 60F(2)-exempt agreements still falls within art 39F — the anomaly the FCA itself noted in the BNPL debate. If that is right, a JobGuard-staffed desk chasing homeowners under agreed terms is regulated debt collecting requiring full permission (6–12 months, CONC 7 compliance) unless it is done through an authorised collector. Business customers are not 'individuals' unless sole traders or small partnerships, so a B2B-only desk is outside art 39F. Two design facts help: the builder remains the sender and approves each message (D10), and the desk only drafts from invoice facts; whether a drafting-only service that never contacts the debtor is 'taking steps to procure payment' is the question for the solicitor. (2) Conduct law that applies regardless of FCA status: Administration of Justice Act 1970 s.40 (criminal harassment of debtors; false claims of authority or of criminal consequences), Protection from Harassment Act 1997 (Ferguson v British Gas [2009] EWCA Civ 46 — automated chasing letters can be harassment), DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 banned and aggressive practices for consumer debtors, and the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims where the debtor is an individual (any letter before claim must carry the information sheet and reply form — leave that step to I48's SRA partner). Late Payment of Commercial Debts Act interest and £40–£100 compensation apply only to business debtors and the templates must not claim them against homeowners. (3) Instalment offers drafted by the desk create new credit agreements between builder and homeowner; keep them interest-free and within 12 instalments so they stay 60F(2)-exempt, and never let the desk agree them without the builder. (4) Not claims management (construction payment is outside RAO arts 89G–89M) — verify. (5) VAT: standard-rated add-on; D09 entitlement; the desk must be structurally unable to open a recovery case so a reminder is never converted into a 10% case, which the idea already states. (6) Data: desk staff see homeowner personal data — role-based access, D12, no break-glass needed but audited.
verdicts.conditions: Solicitor opinion on art 39F against 60F(2)-exempt consumer terms and on whether a builder-sent, builder-approved drafting service is 'taking steps to procure payment'. Until then, v1 limited to business debtors (companies, LLPs, partnerships of four or more) or run through an FCA-authorised collector as partner. Templates reviewed against AJA 1970 s.40, PHA 1997, DMCC 2024 and the Debt PAP; no letters before claim, no legal threats, no invented deadlines, no Late Payment Act claims against consumers. Instalment plans only builder-approved, interest-free, 12 or fewer instalments. Cadence limits per debtor to avoid harassment findings. Desk role cannot open cases or touch the 10% path; D09 add-on entitlement, D05 for renewals. Role-based access and audit for staff viewing customer data.

verdicts.key_risk: Chasing homeowners under agreed payment terms is held to be regulated debt collecting, making the desk an unauthorised regulated activity for exactly the builders most likely to buy it.

verdicts.reasons: Lawful as a referral to an authorised partner; unlawful as a resale of legal steps in JobGuard's own name. (1) Legal Services Act 2007: issuing a claim and conducting proceedings are reserved legal activities (s.12) that only an authorised person or the litigant may carry on; JobGuard contracting with the builder to 'deliver' a small-claims filing and subcontracting it would risk carrying on a reserved activity itself (s.14 offence). Structure Variant A so the builder contracts directly with the SRA-regulated partner and JobGuard receives a disclosed referral fee, or charges only its own unreserved £25 pack-preparation fee. Preparing evidence and factual chronologies is not reserved; giving legal advice is not reserved either but creates negligence exposure and must be avoided in copy. (2) SRA rules: referral fees are permitted outside personal injury (LASPO 2012 s.56 ban), but the solicitor must tell the client about the fee arrangement and any financial interest (SRA Code for Firms para 5.1) and must not be bound by terms that compromise independence; the SRA Transparency Rules already require the partner to publish debt-recovery prices up to £100k. (3) Adjudication: HGCRA 1996 s.106 excludes contracts with a residential occupier, so statutory adjudication is unavailable on the typical domestic job (contractual adjudication exists only where the contract provides it, e.g. JCT homeowner forms); it is available for commercial and subcontract disputes, where claims consultants may represent parties because adjudication is not a reserved activity. Restrict Variant B to non-residential-occupier contracts and confirm the jurisdiction (England and Wales; Scotland differs). (4) Not FCA claims management (construction payment is outside RAO arts 89G–89M) and the DBA Regulations 2013 apply to legal representatives, not to JobGuard's introducer fee — verify both. JobGuard must never take a share of the recovered sum for the legal step, and the 10% must not vary with whether escalation was bought. (5) Consumer debtors: the partner's letter before action must follow the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims; DMCC 2024 and AJA 1970 s.40 govern tone; JobGuard's screen copy must stay factual (D10). (6) Data: handing the pack to a partner discloses the customer's personal data; legitimate interests and the DPA 2018 Sch 2 para 5 legal-proceedings exemption support it, with a consent-to-share record under D12. (7) Commercial customers' Late Payment Act interest and compensation belong in the pack; consumer debts get none. (8) An introducer fee from an unregulated claims consultant needs no regulatory disclosure but should be disclosed anyway to meet the builder-trust point; the flat builder-paid handoff is the cleaner default.
verdicts.conditions: Variant A as referral, not resale: builder contracts with the SRA partner directly; JobGuard's only own charge is the unreserved pack fee. Referral fee stated in pounds on the referral screen and in the partner's client-care letter (SRA para 5.1). Variant B limited to non-residential-occupier contracts in England and Wales; residential jobs routed to the small-claims path via the partner. No share of recovered sums; the 10% and the shadow bill never vary with escalation purchases. Partner letters before claim follow the Debt PAP; JobGuard copy audited against D10, AJA 1970 s.40 and DMCC 2024. Consent-to-share record and D12 lawful basis before any pack leaves. Panel vetting, no exclusivity, builder rating loop. Solicitor confirmation on LSA s.14 exposure and the claims-management perimeter.

revised_revenue.firm: £200–£1,000 (adjudication referrals only on commercial or subcontract disputes)

verdicts.key_risk: A 'fixed-price step' sold by JobGuard and fulfilled by a subcontracted solicitor is treated as JobGuard carrying on a reserved legal activity, an offence under LSA 2007 s.14, with the referral fee then unlawful too.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA permission is engaged. Reviewing a builder's quote is not credit, insurance distribution, claims management (construction is outside the six RAO arts 89G-89M sectors; research notes success_fee_benchmarks section 7) or debt collecting (RAO art 39F). Quantity surveying is not a reserved profession, so a 'panel QS' service can be sold, but any 'chartered' or 'RICS' wording must be true for every reviewer: the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 govern B2B marketing, while DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 does not apply because a builder buying for the business (including a sole trader) is a trader, not a consumer. The true legal cost is liability, not permission. A paid review for a fee creates a Hedley Byrne assumption of responsibility; under UCTA 1977 ss2(2)/3 and the s11 reasonableness test a total exclusion of negligence liability on standard written terms is at real risk of being struck down, whereas a cap linked to the fee paid and backed by professional-indemnity cover is more likely to stand (needs a solicitor's drafting). Freelance panel: JobGuard should contract as principal for the review (so it is not an employment business under the Employment Agencies Act 1973 / Conduct Regulations 2003) and structure genuine self-employment (substitution, right to refuse work) to limit limb-(b) worker claims under ERA 1996 s230(3)(b) (Uber v Aslam line); off-payroll (IR35) responsibility stays with the reviewer's own company while JobGuard is a 'small' client. Data: the transcript contains the homeowner's name and address, so each reviewer is a UK GDPR Art 28 (sub)processor under written terms with confidentiality; a reviewer outside the UK/EEA needs an IDTA/Addendum and D04 approval. VAT on the fee is standard-rated (D02). One conflict has legal teeth: if a paid reviewer misses an item that later becomes a shadow catch, JobGuard would earn 10% from its own contractor's miss; a builder could plead that fee as loss caused by the negligent review and use the pattern to attack any liability cap as unreasonable under UCTA s11. No appointed-representative or partner route is needed because nothing is regulated.
verdicts.conditions: 1) JobGuard contracts as principal with a UCTA-reasonable liability cap (for example the fee paid or a fixed multiple) and carries its own PI cover; reviewers hold their own PI. 2) Reviewer agreement = Art 28 processor terms plus NDA; UK/EEA reviewers only unless D04 approves a transfer mechanism. 3) No chartered/RICS claims unless every panel member holds them; 'aid, not a guarantee' wording in the terms and on the review output (AGENTS 5.9; BUILD_PLAN 14.1 forbidden claims). 4) D13 amendment: a shadow signal whose evidence was present in a transcript a paid reviewer saw is permanently fee-ineligible (reviewed_source), so JobGuard never earns 10% on its reviewer's miss. 5) Engagement terms reviewed by an employment solicitor for worker-status exposure. Estimated cost: PI roughly 1-3k per year, 2-5k solicitor for terms and processor pack, 4-8 weeks; not a G4 dependency (manual invoicing before G4 is acceptable).

revised_revenue.solo: £285 (unchanged per builder; year-one margin reduced by roughly £3-8k fixed PI and legal cost across the whole service, and the reviewed_source rule slightly shrinks the shadow-fee base on reviewed jobs - assumption)

verdicts.key_risk: Negligent-review liability (Hedley Byrne / UCTA reasonableness) compounded by the appearance of profiting from a reviewer's miss through the 10% fee; controlled by PI cover, a reasonable cap and a reviewed_source fee-ineligibility rule in D13.

verdicts.reasons: Unregulated as a service: assembling a final account and drafting an invoice is not an FCA activity, and asking the builder's customer to approve a variation is not RAO art 39F debt collecting because no consumer credit agreement exists (research notes success_fee_benchmarks section 7, which itself flags 'verify wording'). Three real legal costs remain. (a) Consumer law reaches JobGuard directly if desk staff communicate with homeowners: DMCC Act 2024 s216 treats a person acting in the name of or on behalf of a trader as engaging in the commercial practice, so a misleading omission or a pushy approval chase by desk staff exposes JobGuard to CMA direct enforcement, not only the builder; and CRA 2015 s51 means extras never priced can only be billed at a reasonable price, which a desk draft must not present as an agreed sum. (b) Tax: for business customers the invoice may need the VAT domestic reverse charge and CIS treatment, and D06 already forbids automating CIS, DRC and construction notices; a desk operator drafting a B2B invoice wrongly creates an HMRC exposure for the builder and a negligence claim against JobGuard. (c) HGCRA 1996: residential-occupier jobs are excluded by s106, but on B2B jobs a 'final account' sent to the client can operate as a payment application or notice under ss110A-111 with adjudication consequences; a mis-timed or mis-worded desk document can cost the builder a notified sum. Liability follows the I49 Hedley Byrne/UCTA analysis (PI, reasonable cap). Data: desk staff act on the builder's instruction, so this is processor activity under Art 28 terms in the tenant contract; separation from the jobguard_shadow role is also an Art 32 security measure. VAT on the desk fee is standard-rated. The desk_prepared permanent ineligibility reduces legal risk rather than adding it: it removes the unfair-advantage pattern a court, the CMA or a journalist would point at. Late Payment of Commercial Debts Act interest may be drafted only for business customers, never on consumer invoices. No AR or partner route applies; the constraints are scope, tax and consumer-law conduct, each needing a solicitor or tax reviewer rather than a licence.
verdicts.conditions: 1) Desk staff never contact homeowners directly; approval requests go out in the builder's name through the builder-authorised channel and the builder keeps the invoice-issue Decision (D06). 2) Scope limited to jobs inside D06's supported envelope (residential occupier or otherwise non-CIS, standard-rated, no reverse charge) until a qualified tax reviewer signs off B2B handling; a checklist blocks out-of-scope jobs. 3) Unpriced variations labelled 'reasonable price - not agreed' on drafts. 4) PI cover, UCTA-reasonable cap and Art 28 processor language in tenant terms; desk staff structurally excluded from jobguard_shadow and break-glass. 5) D13 amendment recording desk_prepared on the lock. 6) Solicitor review of service terms and of the s106/HGCRA boundary before any business-client job is accepted. Estimated 2-5k legal plus shared PI, 4-8 weeks; the ops hire is the larger cost.

verdicts.reasons: The paid onboarding is unregulated B2B services (VAT standard-rated; the builder is a trader so CRA 2015 and the CCRs 2013 are not engaged). The legal weight sits entirely in UK GDPR because the specialist reads WhatsApp threads, emails and photos containing homeowners' and suppliers' personal data. Two roles collide: importing on the builder's instruction is processor activity (Art 28), but using the same imported messages to detect fee-earning catches is JobGuard's own purpose, which makes JobGuard a controller for that purpose - the exact point D12 v2 leaves 'proposed'. As controller it needs a lawful basis (realistically legitimate interests with a written balancing assessment) and must give each homeowner an Art 14 notice within one month of obtaining the data (Art 14(3)(a)); the disproportionate-effort exemption in Art 14(5)(b) is hard to justify for a handful of named homeowners per builder. Importing whole chat histories offends data minimisation (Art 5(1)(c)) and risks incidental special-category data (Art 9). The ICO's list of processing requiring a DPIA (invisible processing combined with innovative technology or systematic monitoring) makes an Art 35 DPIA very likely required, with Art 36 prior consultation if residual risk stays high - that can add months. Homeowners may object under Art 21 to legitimate-interest processing, which would remove that job's message evidence from the shadow base. A reconstructed baseline for an in-flight job must not be shown to the homeowner as the agreed contract unless the builder confirms it (DMCC Act 2024 misleading action; CRA 2015 s50 makes trader statements binding). CSV migrations from Tradify, ServiceM8 and Xero are ordinary processor work with no extra permission, and the builder's own exports avoid competitor terms-of-service and Computer Misuse Act 1990 s1 exposure that scraping with the builder's credentials would raise. The specialist-handled fee-free rule is legally helpful because it narrows JobGuard's controller purpose to automated imports. M1-17's decision record and D12 v2 approval are hard prerequisites for message and photo imports; rate-book and customer CSV imports can start earlier under processor terms. No AR or partner route exists for data-protection duties; a DPO or data-protection solicitor is needed for the DPIA and balancing test.
verdicts.conditions: 1) Message, photo and email import gated on D12 v2 approval (lawful basis, balancing assessment, Art 14 route) and a completed DPIA; until then the paid service covers CSV rate-book and customer imports and builder-attested baselines only. 2) Imports are job-linked and date-bounded; no whole-history ingestion; a filter for special-category content. 3) Art 14 notice route defined (builder-served or via the I55 portal) with a one-month clock recorded per import. 4) Imported baselines carry provenance=imported and are labelled 'reconstructed from the builder's records' on any homeowner-facing surface. 5) M1-17 decision record signed; Art 28 terms in the tenant contract; specialist staff excluded from jobguard_shadow. 6) DPO or solicitor review of the DPIA and balancing assessment. Estimated 5-10k and 6-12 weeks for D12 v2 plus DPIA, shared with I55 and the core shadow bill, so not incremental if done once.

verdicts.reasons: Nothing regulated. Account management and a quarterly review of the firm's own numbers is business support, not FCA advice, credit, insurance or claims activity. The recurring add-on runs through the existing D09/D05 subscription mechanics on a hosted Stripe surface, so JobGuard does not become a payment institution under the Payment Services Regulations 2017 and needs only clear recurring-payment and cancellation terms. The DMCC Act 2024 subscription-contract regime (pre-contract information, reminder notices, easy exit) applies to consumers only; a builder buying for the business is a trader, though JobGuard should record a business-use declaration at sign-up to evidence that. Two small data points: per-site-lead 'capture discipline' metrics are employee-monitoring data, so they should be delivered as the builder's own data under Art 28 processor terms with the builder responsible for staff transparency (ICO monitoring-at-work guidance); a recorded phone line needs a notice under the Telecommunications (Lawful Business Practice) Regulations 2000. Conduct guardrail: account managers must never recommend customer finance products (that edges into credit broking, RAO art 36A) and must give the onboarding-terms answer to 'is there anything else on this job?' - the latter is an AGENTS 5.14 invariant rather than a legal duty, but a leak also makes that signal permanently fee-free under D13. VAT standard-rated. No AR or partner route needed; cost is a terms update and staff training.
verdicts.conditions: Housekeeping only, no gate: business-use declaration at sign-up; clear cancellation terms; Art 28 framing for staff metrics; call-recording notice; account-manager script forbidding finance recommendations and any shadow disclosure; support membership with no shadow grants (SV-2). Estimated 500-1,500 legal, 1-2 weeks.

verdicts.reasons: Training provision is unregulated in the UK; no FCA, professional or licensing permission applies and no AR route is relevant. VAT: standard-rated, because the education exemption covers eligible bodies only and JobGuard is not one. CITB grant eligibility requires CITB-approved course or Approved Training Organisation status - optional, only if grant funding is pursued, and it takes weeks to months. Three light points. (a) The certificate must not read as a trade competence, safety or Ofqual-regulated qualification: on a public profile (I56) the DMCC Act 2024 Sch 20 banned practices on approval and endorsement claims and the CAP Code apply to consumer-facing display, and the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 to B2B marketing - so name it 'JobGuard capture training' with the issuer stated and no 'certified builder' phrasing. (b) If an individual employee buys the 49 course personally, that is a B2C distance sale under the CCRs 2013 (cancellation information, express request to start digital content immediately) and CRA 2015 digital-content rights apply; selling through the tenant business avoids it. (c) Learner records make JobGuard a controller of the learner's personal data, so an Art 13 notice at enrolment is needed. Partner trainers keeping 60% need a simple licence or agency agreement and their own public-liability cover for site visits; content must not present itself as CDM 2015 health-and-safety training. Cost near zero; 1-2 weeks of wording.
verdicts.conditions: Neutral certificate naming with issuer stated; sell via the business tenant or comply with the CCRs for individual buyers; Art 13 notice for learners; partner-trainer agreement with public-liability cover; pursue CITB approval only if grants are wanted.

verdicts.key_risk: A 'certified' badge on a public profile being read by homeowners as a competence or safety qualification - a misleading-practice exposure under the DMCC Act that plain naming removes.

verdicts.reasons: Business consultancy is unregulated: not FCA advice (no investments, credit or insurance) and accountancy is not a reserved activity, so no permission and no AR route. Three legal costs. (a) Liability for negligent recommendations on rates and stages: Hedley Byrne, UCTA reasonableness for any cap, PI cover, 'aid' wording. (b) Tax: if the analyst strays into VAT, CIS or MTD advice, JobGuard becomes a 'tax adviser' by way of business under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 (a relevant person needing HMRC anti-money-laundering supervision, roughly 300 per premises per year plus an AML programme) and falls within HMRC's 2026 expectations on tax-adviser registration; cheaply avoided by excluding tax advice from scope, which a solicitor should confirm. (c) Competition law: cross-builder benchmarking such as 'your rates are 15% below other JobGuard builders in your area' risks a hub-and-spoke exchange of competitively sensitive pricing information under Competition Act 1998 Chapter I; benchmarks must be aggregated, historical, anonymised, with enough contributors that no firm can be inferred, and never forward-looking. Data: per-site-lead metrics are employee-monitoring data processed for the builder under Art 28; JobGuard should not adopt a controller purpose for them. Marketing and the report itself: BUILD_PLAN 14.1 forbidden claims plus the BPMMRs 2008 - no 'JobGuard saved you X' beyond settled figures. Locked-job-only, builder-role access is also an Art 32 security measure and keeps the analyst clear of D13. VAT standard-rated. Cost: PI shared with I49/I50, 1-3k for terms and a benchmarking policy, 2-4 weeks.
verdicts.conditions: 1) Scope excludes tax advice (VAT, CIS, MTD) with a written referral to the builder's accountant; solicitor to confirm the exclusion keeps JobGuard outside MLR 2017 reg 11. 2) Benchmarking policy: aggregated, anonymised, historical, minimum-contributor threshold; no local rate comparisons that identify competitors. 3) PI cover, UCTA-reasonable cap, 'aid' wording. 4) Analyst limited to the builder role and locked jobs; the report states that restriction. 5) Employee metrics under Art 28 terms.
