verdicts.key_risk: Sliding into tax advice (MLR 2017 supervision) or price benchmarking across builders (Competition Act 1998 information exchange); both avoidable by written scope rules.

verdicts.reasons: The portal is where UK consumer law and UK GDPR enter the product directly: the homeowner is a consumer and JobGuard gains its first direct relationship with them. (1) Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013: a variation approved remotely through the portal is plausibly a distance contract under an organised scheme; unless an exception applies (reg 6(1)(e) new-build construction; urgent repairs requested by the consumer), the homeowner has a 14-day cancellation right, the builder must give the Sch 2 information and model cancellation form on a durable medium, work may start inside the period only on the consumer's express request (reg 36), and if the information is omitted the period extends up to 12 months (reg 31) with the consumer potentially owing nothing for work done meanwhile (reg 36(6)). This is the well-known trap that has cost tradespeople whole invoices; the idea's 'capture that request' is necessary but not sufficient. (2) DMCC Act 2024 Part 4: variation prices shown to a consumer are invitations to purchase and must state the total including VAT and mandatory charges (drip-pricing ban, s230); stage sign-off must not imply waiver of CRA 2015 rights (s31/s57 make waivers non-binding, and presenting them as binding is a misleading action); because the portal operates in the builder's name, JobGuard is within s216's 'acting on behalf of a trader' and the CMA can enforce against JobGuard directly (fines up to 10% of turnover; the research report notes the first 4.2m fine). (3) CRA 2015 s50: builder statements in the thread become binding terms; s51: extras never priced can only be charged at a reasonable price, so late-revealed catches billed after the final account will be more disputable and shrink the fee base (research report, 'The hidden final check' section; research notes success_fee_psychology inferences). (4) UK GDPR: JobGuard is controller for the portal account and for its own shadow-bill purpose; it must serve an Art 13 notice at first visit that truthfully says messages may be analysed to identify unrecorded extra work the builder may bill - an adverse-interest purpose that makes the legitimate-interests balancing test contestable and gives every homeowner an Art 21 objection right that, if exercised, removes that job's message evidence from the shadow base; a DPIA is required; a homeowner DSAR (Art 15, one month) can lawfully surface a candidate signal about them before lock, which D13 then makes fee-ineligible. (5) HGCRA 1996 s106 excludes residential occupiers, so payment notices and adjudication do not apply to homeowner jobs; for any business client the Act applies and stage or final-account messages could operate as payment applications - D06 forbids automating that. (6) PECR: portal notifications are service messages, not marketing; any 'find a JobGuard builder' content to homeowners would need consent. (7) Credit and payments: no instalment or deferred-payment offers in the portal (they would engage consumer-credit lending or broking, RAO arts 36A/60B, unless within the art 60F exemption, and even then need a decision record); hosted Stripe/GoCardless in M4 keeps JobGuard outside the PSRs 2017. (8) Online Safety Act 2023: builder-homeowner messaging is user-to-user content; whether the Sch 1 internal-business-services exemption covers it is uncertain and needs a solicitor's view; if in scope the duty is a low-risk illegal-content risk assessment - cheap but mandatory. (9) E-Commerce Regulations 2002 reg 6 and DMCC trader-identity transparency: the portal must name the builder as the trader and JobGuard as operator. Evidential note: a magic-link Approve is a simple electronic signature (admissible under Electronic Communications Act 2000 s7) whose weight depends on delivery to a verified contact, timestamp, content hash and audit record. Nothing needs FCA permission or an AR route; the cost is compliance design plus legal review, and the meter-enforcement rationale creates no separate legal issue.
verdicts.conditions: 1) CCR compliance kit built into the variation-approval flow: builder identity and address, total price including VAT, Sch 2 cancellation information and model form on a durable medium, the homeowner's express request to start within 14 days captured and acknowledged, and an exceptions flag (new-build, urgent repair); solicitor-drafted, with the builder remaining the responsible trader under the terms. 2) Consumer-facing prices gross of VAT; stage sign-off worded as 'seen', never as acceptance or waiver. 3) D12 v2 approved with a controller/processor map, balancing assessment for the shadow purpose, Art 13 notice at first portal visit, Art 14 route for pre-portal data, Art 21 objection handling that marks affected signals ineligible, DSAR playbook and a DPIA (Art 36 consultation if required). 4) Residential-occupier jobs only in v1; business clients excluded until D06 is extended for HGCRA notices. 5) No instalment or deferred-payment offers; no JobGuard marketing to homeowners; portal names the builder and the operator. 6) OSA 2023 scoping opinion; illegal-content risk assessment if in scope. 7) Approval records bound to the variation hash, a verified contact, timestamp and the audit chain (D06). 8) SV-2/SV-3 byte-identical response tests extended to portal routes. Estimated legal 10-20k across the CCR kit, D12 v2 and DPIA, and the OSA opinion, 8-12 weeks in parallel with the 3-5 week build; real homeowners only after G1 and D12/D13 pilot approval.

revised_revenue.solo: £25 incremental fee
revised_revenue.firm: £350 - assumption: roughly a 30% haircut on the idea's guess for CCR cancellations, s51 reasonable-price disputes on late-billed extras and Art 21 objections removing message evidence; BUILD_PLAN 14.17 pilot data must replace this

verdicts.key_risk: The Consumer Contracts Regulations cancellation and information duties on remotely approved variations - omitted once, the builder can lose the whole variation and JobGuard's 'approved in writing' promise becomes a liability; second, the legitimate-interests basis for analysing homeowners' own messages to find work they may be billed more for is contestable and revocable homeowner by homeowner.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA permission: a builder profile with no leads, no ranking and no finance or insurance arranging is not credit broking, claims lead generation (construction is outside RAO arts 89G-89M) or insurance distribution. 'IBG offered' must stay a displayed fact; any IBG referral link or referral fee would be insurance distribution needing FCA authorisation or an appointed-representative arrangement with the IBG provider. The controlling regime is DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 plus the CAP Code: JobGuard's public page promotes another trader's services to consumers, which is a commercial practice by JobGuard under s216, so JobGuard is directly liable for a misleading action about approval or endorsement (s226) and for the Sch 20 banned practices on trust marks and approvals (paras 2 and 4) if the average consumer reads 'JobGuard-checked' as vetting of workmanship, insurance or identity. Objective claims (proof photos per job, invoice-to-payment days) need substantiation (CAP Code 3.7); immutable locked records supply it provided denominators and date ranges are shown. No ranking keeps the page clear of the DMCC ranking-transparency rules and of BPMMR 2008 comparative-advertising conditions. The quote stamp raises JobGuard's visibility as template author, so the consumer-facing quote total must include VAT and mandatory charges (drip pricing, s230) and the QR page must say only 'this is the exact document issued', never that prices were checked. UK GDPR: aggregate facts are fine; the quote-request form makes JobGuard a controller at collection (Art 13 notice) passing the brief to the builder; photos of homes and access details are personal data needing minimisation and security; PECR is not engaged if JobGuard never markets to the requester. Trade mark: register the mark at the UKIPO (170 base fee plus attorney) and licence its use with automatic revocation on churn. Accuracy (Art 5(1)(d)) and defamation risk are avoided by showing only builder-consented positive facts; publishing watchdog findings or dispute counts would turn this into a serious data-protection and fairness problem and is rightly excluded. No AR or partner route needed except for the IBG referral scenario, which should simply not be built. Cost: 1-3k consumer-law wording review, 0.7-2k trade mark, 4-6 weeks; registration itself takes 4-6 months but use may begin.
verdicts.conditions: 1) Mark name and definition reviewed by a consumer-law solicitor; adjacent plain-English statement of what was and was not checked; avoid 'approved' or 'vetted'. 2) Every metric shows denominator and date range; only server-verified locked facts; nothing derived from watchdog findings, D11 signals or disputes. 3) IBG and ADR shown as facts only; no referral links or fees without a separate decision record and FCA/AR analysis. 4) Consumer-facing quote PDF and QR page: VAT-inclusive totals, 'exact document issued' wording only. 5) Quote-request form: Art 13 notice, minimisation, no marketing use, secure handling of photos and access details. 6) UK trade mark filed; badge licence revoked on churn. 7) CAP/ASA substantiation file kept per metric.

revised_revenue.solo: £110-£120 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: 'JobGuard-checked' being read by homeowners as an endorsement of workmanship - a DMCC Act misleading-practice exposure the CMA can enforce directly against JobGuard; cured by naming, an adjacent definition and metric transparency.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on willingness to pay and on cost-to-serve. (1) Builders do not pay for their own customers' convenience: the homeowner already has the builder's number, so 'Book again' and 'Recommend' route to the same builder by default in the real world; JobGuard adds a record, not a referral. (2) Client portals are a bundled tier feature at incumbents (ServiceM8 Premium customer portal, Buildertrend Selections/warranty in Complete per the research's platform notes), never a separately priced add-on, so £8–£20/month would be compared against 'included elsewhere'. (3) The 50–60% adoption assumption is roughly three times typical SMB add-on attach; and it also needs the homeowner to activate an account after the job ends, which the plan does not model at all. (4) Cost: the plan has no consumer identity (M0-6 is tenant membership); this is a second product surface with JobGuard as UK GDPR controller for consumers, DSARs, PECR reminder consent, multi-decade retention of 'behind the wall' photos (D07 undecided), password-reset support for non-paying users, and the I55 portal it depends on is another idea, not a plan task. 8–12 weeks plus permanent support load, not 4–6 weeks. (5) Even on the idea's own numbers the ceiling is £95/£145/£240 a year, under a quarter of the subscription (£348/£708/£1,428 at the research's £29/£59/£119 tiers), for the one feature most likely to tempt JobGuard into selling homeowner attention later. The retention/lock-in effect is real but is not revenue.
verdicts.conditions: Not worth building as a paid add-on. If pilot evidence ever shows homeowners open a completion record (>40% of jobs), ship a no-login 'completion pack' link (final account, certificates, proof photos) as a bundled feature first; only consider homeowner accounts after G1, D12 v2 and a D07 retention decision, with exclusivity written into the builder terms rather than a setting.

revised_revenue.solo: £10–£15 (15% attach × £96; assumes ~30% of homeowners activate)

verdicts.key_risk: Builds a consumer-facing product with its own data-protection and support obligations to earn under £60 per builder per year, and creates the homeowner base whose monetisation the trust note itself says would be selling the builder's customers.

verdicts.reasons: Demand does not exist without the marketing spend the idea admits it ignores: Checkatrade, MyBuilder and Rated People are consumer brands whose members report real bills of £80–£500/month on 12-month contracts (research, UK trade software notes) precisely because creating homeowner demand is expensive. JobGuard has no consumer brand, so 2/3/2 marketplace-won jobs a year has no basis; the honest year-1–2 number is zero. The fee design also fails: 2% of accepted net value is £160 on an £8k job and £1,200 on a £60k job, far above lead-fee norms, so builders will take the job off-platform, and the only way to police that is to turn D11-style signals on the builder, which is the surveillance the trust research warns against. Attribution bound to acceptance (M1-6) and switch-live (M1-7) is trivially avoided by not recording acceptance in JobGuard for that job, which also removes the watchdog from the job. 'Checked' builders means JobGuard vets and disciplines its own customers under DMCC 2024 fake-review and paid-placement rules and consumer law on the claim, the conflict the trust note names. Build is a second company (consumer posting UX, profiles, matching, homeowner support, marketing), not 2–3 months; earliest M5 and after M4-10 billing. The research's own recommendation is the same: leave lead fees to Checkatrade.
verdicts.conditions: None that make it worth doing. A free directory of JobGuard users (I56) is the most that is compatible with the watchdog role, and even that must make no 'checked' or 'verified' claim about workmanship.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (no demand without a consumer marketing budget; 0–0.2 jobs/yr × £8k × 2% = £0–£32 at best)

verdicts.key_risk: Makes the builder's watchdog also their lead seller, the most resented model in the trade, and the 2% fee can only be enforced by policing off-platform leakage with the builder's own job data.

verdicts.reasons: Three refutations. (1) Market fit: £300–£600 snagging inspections are a new-build purchase product; a homeowner on an £8k refurb (inspection = 4% of the job) does their own snagging, so uptake on Solo/Small jobs is likely under 2%, and the 5/8/10% assumption is unsupported (the idea concedes the market was not looked up, and the research notes contain nothing on it). (2) The referral fee compromises the thing being sold: an 'independent' inspector who pays 15% to the builder's own software vendor is not independent to the homeowner; the research notes record Expert Tooling v Engie [2025] EWCA Civ 292 (half-secret commissions can breach fiduciary duty) and Ofgem's commission-disclosure regime, and DMCC/CPUT hidden-commission concerns apply to the homeowner disclosure. Once disclosed, the fee reads as a kickback and reduces uptake further. (3) Economics: £52.50 per inspection against panel recruitment, vetting (RICS/RPSA criteria), complaints handling and quality monitoring is a loss-making service line at £50–£175 per builder per year. Workflow conflict: 'clean report triggers the final invoice' cannot be automatic; final invoice issue requires the final-account lock (§14.4) and an exact Decision (§5.3), so the sign-off is at most an input to the builder's own lock. Dependency on the I55 portal, which is not a plan task, applies as for I57.
verdicts.conditions: Drop the panel and the referral fee. A zero-fee, builder-enabled 'share the agreed scope and proof record with an inspector the homeowner hires' export (built on M1-10 proof and the M4-3 evidence-pack assembly) captures the genuine builder-side value (a check against the agreed scope, not a wish-list) with no conflict. Any future referral fee needs homeowner-facing disclosure reviewed under DMCC/CPUT and a D12 decision on sharing job data.

revised_revenue.firm: £100–£175 (2–3 inspections/yr; before panel operating costs, which exceed this)

verdicts.key_risk: A disclosed commission from a supposedly independent inspector, paid to the builder's own tool, undermines the inspection's credibility with the homeowner and the builder alike, and the revenue never covers running a vetted panel.

verdicts.reasons: This is a customer-acquisition and trust channel, not revenue; the idea says so and the numbers confirm it (net year-1 revenue per builder is lower than direct). Refutation attempts: (1) Trade-body benefit directories are cluttered and low-conversion, and bodies typically want a listing/sponsorship fee irrespective of conversions, so year 1 can be a pure cost; the 15% and 'listing fee' figures are the idea's assumptions (the research notes contain no FMB/NFB partner terms). (2) The 'two months free' is already the research's recommended standard annual discount, so the member benefit is not really incremental; that cuts both ways: it costs JobGuard nothing extra to offer. (3) What survives: FMB members are domestic builders (the ICP), builders are anchored low and only 29% of one-person construction firms use any software (research), so a recommendation from a body they already pay is worth more than a price signal; the build is small (partner attribution table, membership-number validation, promo terms in the M4-11 Stripe subscription checkout, payout statements via M4-10), 1–2 weeks after M4-11/M4-13 and a D09 v2 with promo and annual terms; the fee share is kept out of it, which is the right line. Gaming (shared or lapsed membership numbers) is handled by validation at sign-up and annual revalidation, one redemption per number. The 'Master Builder' mark on customer documents must be governed by the body's own rules and never imply the body checked the work.
verdicts.conditions: Do it only when M4-11 and M4-13 exist and D09 v2 defines promo/annual terms. Pay the body only on collected subscription revenue (self-billed quarterly), never on success fees, and refuse any visibility of findings. Cap any listing fee at a level a realistic first cohort (say 20 conversions) pays back within 12 months, and time-box the deal to one year before renewal. Explain the live-jobs meter at sign-up (FMB members run few long jobs; fine for the meter). Record the mark's wording with the body and do not show it on evidence packs or fee statements.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 incremental; net £247 year 1 (£290 annual less 15%) then £290; i.e. ~£44 CAC per conversion plus a share of any listing fee
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0 incremental; net £502 year 1 then £590; ~£89 CAC per conversion
revised_revenue.firm: £0 incremental; net £1,012 year 1 then £1,190; ~£179 CAC per conversion

verdicts.key_risk: Trade bodies take an upfront listing/sponsorship fee and deliver a directory entry nobody reads, so the channel becomes a fixed cost with single-digit conversions; and a co-branded mark drifts into implying the body verified the builder's work.

verdicts.reasons: The strongest partnership idea in principle: the research shows construction is the least digitised sector (29% of no-employee firms use software) and MTD ITSA (April 2026, thresholds falling to £30k/£20k) is the forcing event, so the accountant often picks the tool. The refutations narrow it a lot. (1) Motivation: practices recommend tools that remove their own work (bank feeds, receipt capture: Xero, Dext), and a 20% share of £348 is £70 a year, which moves nobody; many ICAEW/ACCA practices refuse commissions outright and ask for the client discount instead. (2) The practice-paid pack has no buyers until density: a 10-client minimum means a practice needs ten JobGuard-using builders, which will not exist in years 1–2; Dext practice pricing is about £391/month for 50 clients (~£7.82/client, research), and it removes daily data entry, whereas this pack is used once a year, so a practice would rather pay a one-off per year-end than £48–£96 per client per year. (3) Relevance by archetype: Solo builders are largely cash-basis sole traders for whom a WIP/revenue-recognition schedule is irrelevant; it matters for Small and Firm accounts, and CIS/retention reconciliations need M4-20/M4-22, signed exports need M5-9, so the pack is an M5 product. (4) The bookkeeper introducer fee should be dropped: JobGuard being paid by a party it recommends is the half-secret-commission pattern the research notes flag (Engie, Ofgem disclosure). (5) What is cheap and useful now: a read-only 'adviser' principal with membership across consenting tenants (fits the M0-6 read-only role and the §5.1 single-tenant-context rule if each tenant is opened separately), plus referral attribution shared with I60, 2–4 weeks after M4-11. Gaming (enrolling clients who never use JobGuard) is controlled by paying only on collected revenue and stopping on cancellation.
verdicts.conditions: Phase 1 (after M4-11/M4-13, D09 v2): free adviser seat plus referral attribution, with an alternative of passing the share to the builder as a discount for practices that cannot take commission; the share is disclosed in the builder's terms. Phase 2 (after M4-20, M4-22, M5-1 and M5-9): the year-end pack, priced per pack per year-end rather than per client per month, and only once at least five practices each have ten or more JobGuard clients; label WIP and revenue recognition as projections from immutable records, not accounting advice; keep the free data-portability export so the pack is never a toll. Drop the bookkeeper introducer fee entirely.

revised_revenue.solo: −£70/yr for two years as referral cost (CAC), then £0; pack ≈ £0–£5 expected (cash-basis sole traders rarely need it)
revised_revenue.small_firm: −£142/yr for two years as CAC; pack ≈ £5–£10 expected until practice density exists, up to £48 at maturity
revised_revenue.firm: −£286/yr for two years as CAC; pack ≈ £10–£20 expected, up to £96 at maturity

verdicts.key_risk: Accountants are moved by their own workflow savings, not a £70 commission, and the practice-paid pack cannot be sold until JobGuard has ten-client density inside individual practices; meanwhile a WIP schedule invites reliance as accounting advice.

verdicts.reasons: A different segment and a different product, not an add-on. (1) The whole subcontract billing regime it relies on (interim applications M4-18, Construction Act notices M4-19 with reviewer sign-off, retention M4-20, CIS M4-22) is unbuilt, sits after M4-17, and each needs professional review before real use; nothing in M1/M2 serves a sub-to-main-contractor relationship. (2) The buyer is the wrong party: the sub's watchdog exists to find variations the MC has not paid, so an MC that pays JobGuard is paying to arm its subs against itself, and a sub told the MC pays wonders whose side JobGuard is on (the idea's own trust note). Payapps is bought by MCs because it processes their subs' applications at scale on an unpublished fixed annual fee (research); JobGuard would be competing with an incumbent on enterprise sales cycles with no track record. (3) Architecture: a multi-party job model where the customer is another tenant with scoped read-only visibility is new cross-tenant work that touches the §5.1 trust boundary, and AGENTS §1 forbids enterprise isolation before its task; 6–10 weeks post-M4 is optimistic. (4) The live-jobs meter exclusion for licensed projects is honest about the meter's weakness on 12-month subcontracts, but it creates the incentive for subs to want every job 'licensed'. (5) The revenue attributed to Solo/Small (£15/£120) assumes those domestic archetypes work under MCs, which the founder's framing does not; only the Firm archetype plausibly does, and then only if JobGuard wins MC accounts one by one. Gaming risk (premature case-opening for templates) is bounded by the §14.7 entry test, but the whole withheld-payment category is G4-gated anyway.
verdicts.conditions: Re-evaluate only after M4-22 is reviewed and released under M4-23, and only if pilot data show a real subcontractor population among users. If ever pursued: separate contracts stating JobGuard works for the sub on variations and applications and the MC buys evidence of submitted artifacts only; the MC never enters the sub's tenant; licensed projects excluded from the sub's tier by an explicit D09 rule; treat it as a new segment with its own decision record, not a channel.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (domestic archetype; no MC relationship)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0–£50 (only if some work is subcontracted and an MC account exists)
revised_revenue.firm: £0–£300 attributable per MC-licensed project, contingent on winning MC accounts on 6–12 month sales cycles; success fees on cases the firm opens are G4-gated and unchanged

verdicts.key_risk: Sells to the party the watchdog works against, into a Construction Act billing regime that is entirely unbuilt and needs professional review, against an established incumbent (Payapps) on enterprise sales cycles.

verdicts.reasons: Variant A (OEM to lead-gen platforms) fails on buyer motive and on trust. Checkatrade already gives members a free quoting and invoicing tool and has reportedly launched TradeMore, a free AI job-management app (research, unverified launch): the prospective licensee is building this itself and would rather build than pay £4 per live job. Wholesale at a third of list (£120/£264/£720 vs £348/£708/£1,428) cannibalises the direct channel while inheriting Checkatrade's mixed standing (12-month contracts, £80–£500/month bills). Worse, the D13 model inside a partner brand is the exact configuration the research warns about: a builder with no direct JobGuard relationship gets a JobGuard 10% statement after lock inside a Checkatrade-branded app and blames both. Partners will also press for early hints of findings to drive retention. Build needs multi-brand theming, partner SSO/provisioning (M5-7 territory), per-partner metering (M4-14, now optional), partner invoicing (M4-10), and security assurance a platform will demand (M5-12); realistically post-M5 plus a 6–12 month deal. Variant B (franchise, e.g. Dream Doors) fits the product weakly: showroom-sold kitchens and doors are short fixed-price installs where missed variations are rare, franchisees resent head-office dashboards on operational data, and the idea admits no franchisor mandatory-software terms were found. Needs the deferred organisation-hierarchy task (AGENTS §1: no enterprise isolation before its task). The network numbers (£2,000/yr plus ~£468 per franchisee) are assumptions with no precedent in the research. Gaming controls (server-side metering from switch-live/lock events, builder role cannot read shadow tables) are sound but do not fix the buyer problem.
verdicts.conditions: Not before M4-23, M5-7 and M5-12, and only with: direct channel non-exclusive; wholesale not below 50% of list; the one-sentence final-check explanation and the D12/D13 onboarding disclosure delivered by JobGuard, unedited, before the first job in the partner flow; success fee and shadow findings strictly JobGuard–builder; aggregate-only franchise dashboards with published fields and genuine consent; D04 review of partner infrastructure. Franchise variant only for networks whose jobs actually generate variations.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 for at least 24 months (no deal); if an OEM deal lands, £120/yr wholesale minus cannibalised direct revenue
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0 for 24 months; then £264 OEM or £468 franchise wholesale per franchisee, if a network signs
revised_revenue.firm: £0 for 24 months; then £720 OEM or £1,188 franchise wholesale, if a network signs

verdicts.key_risk: The natural licensees already give job tools away free and would rather build, and a partner-branded hidden final check followed by a JobGuard fee statement is the single worst trust configuration the research identifies.

verdicts.reasons: Worth doing because the feature is useful on its own; the 'channel' framing overstates the revenue. Refutations: (1) 15% twelve-month conversion of invited subs is high; invited third parties who use a tool inside someone else's job typically convert in low single digits, and many subs already run Tradify/Powered Now/ServiceM8 at £25–£45 per user (research); 5% is a defensible assumption, which cuts the numbers to roughly a third. (2) The revenue counted is new-tenant revenue attributed to the inviter, not the inviter's own spend; the inviter contributes only the referral. (3) A subtle trust point the idea does not name: a sub's invoice attached as evidence is 'supplier documents' under §14.2 and can seed a shadow signal against the inviting builder's final account; that is within the approved model, but it must be part of the D12/D13 onboarding disclosure or builders who work it out will stop inviting. What survives: sub proof photos on stage gates (M1-10) and sub invoices feeding three-way matching (M2-2) directly improve the watchdog and the evidence base, so the build pays for itself even at zero conversions; Buildbite's free-for-subs model is a real precedent (research). Build: a per-job scoped external principal needs job- and principal-scoped policies beyond tenant RLS, plus Article 13/14 notices at invite (D12), 4–6 weeks after M2-2; the inviter credit needs M4-13's explicit credit allocation (a D09 subscription credit, never offsetting a success fee). Gaming (fake sub accounts to farm credits) is contained by the 30-day live job and paid-period conditions, annual caps and unique conversion identities.
verdicts.conditions: Build the scoped 'Sub' role after M2-2 for its evidence value, with subs told exactly what the inviter can see and that invited-job records are the inviter's; tell inviting builders plainly that sub documents are evidence under the final check. Add the inviter credit only after M4-13 and D09 v2 define credit allocation; pay it only after the sub has had a live job 30 days and paid one period, capped per year. Measure conversion in the pilot before calling it a channel.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈£32 net new-tenant revenue attributed (2 invites × 5% × £348 less a £29 credit)
revised_revenue.firm: ≈£240 net (15 invites × 5% × £348 less credits); plus unquantified watchdog value from sub invoices and proof

verdicts.key_risk: Conversion of invited subs will be single-digit, so this is a feature with a referral bonus rather than a channel; and sub invoices feeding the shadow bill against the inviting builder must be disclosed plainly or builders will stop inviting.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on the watchdog-independence prong. JobGuard's flagship prevention feature is checking merchants' invoices, delivery notes and POs (report §'No rival sells a final check, an overcharge check or a success fee'). Once a merchant pays JobGuard anything — even a flat, outcome-blind connector fee — every non-flag on that merchant looks bought and every flag on a non-paying merchant looks like leverage. Merchant-blindness proven by architecture tests does not fix this: the research is explicit that disclosing a conflict does not neutralise it and can make the conflicted party behave worse (research note success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp §4, Cain/Loewenstein/Moore), and builders judge fairness by who is exploiting an advantage (Kahneman/Knetsch/Thaler dual entitlement). The energy-broker path is the precedent: supplier-paid intermediaries ended with Ofgem commission-disclosure rules and a Court of Appeal fiduciary finding on half-secret commissions (success_fee_benchmarks §2). Variant B is worse: it aggregates builders' purchase data (ingested for the watchdog under D12's job-linked-data-only basis) to negotiate on JobGuard's own account and keep a point — using builders' data as JobGuard's bargaining chip, which is the data-sale trust risk the brief names, and NMBS earns its 3.84% partly by guaranteeing supplier payment, which JobGuard can never do (AGENTS §3). Variant A's revenue (~£6/builder/yr) cannot justify any of this; Variant B's £300–£4,000 buys a permanent 'in with the merchants' story in a word-of-mouth trade.
verdicts.conditions: None. No version in which a merchant pays JobGuard money, data or preferential terms is acceptable. The only permissible cousin is builder-side and builder-paid: verifying on each invoice that the builder's own agreed trade discounts and rebates were applied (belongs in I12 / M2-1 agreed rates), with no merchant relationship at all.

revised_revenue.solo: Idea's estimate ≈£6 (A) / £300 (B); recommended £0 — rejected

verdicts.key_risk: Watchdog capture: once merchants pay JobGuard, the supplier-invoice check loses credibility with builders regardless of how the money flows are structured, and the loss spreads by word of mouth.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutation: any merchant relationship reads as 'JobGuard is in bed with Travis' and dilutes the watchdog. That perception risk is real and the idea admits it. But it survives the lens on three counts a reasonable builder would recognise. (1) Builder interest is direct and unambiguous: merchant money goes straight to the builder's own bank; JobGuard never touches it (AGENTS §3, never holds funds) and takes nothing from any merchant, so the brief's named hard risk ('suppliers/merchants paying JobGuard') is avoided by construction. (2) The FMB/TradePoint and Checkatrade/Wickes precedents mean UK builders already understand and welcome trade discounts from a membership-style body. (3) Under Xia/Monroe/Cox the admin fee is for work the builder cannot do alone (negotiating panel terms, reconciling rebate statements to POs) and costs the builder nothing they would otherwise have. Where the idea as written still fails fairness: a percentage admin fee gives JobGuard a financial interest in the builder's purchase volume at partner merchants, which is a steering incentive and therefore a conflict; and 'JobGuard negotiates' contradicts 'open panel on published terms' — negotiation creates merchant-specific commercial dependence that a merchant can later use to pressure the checks. The revenue (£54–£720 per builder at 100% uptake, lower with a flat fee) is small relative to the perception cost, so this should be late, optional and structurally boring, not a launch feature.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Merchants pay JobGuard nothing in any form: no fees, no data, no marketing spend, no 'preferred' placement; written into the panel terms with a public kill clause (a merchant that conditions membership or terms on the watchdog's behaviour is removed and the removal published). (b) Genuinely open panel on one published term sheet — JobGuard publishes terms and merchants opt in; JobGuard does not negotiate merchant-specific deals. (c) Rebate/discount paid merchant-to-builder direct, 100%; JobGuard never holds or routes it. (d) Admin fee is flat (e.g. £5/month), disclosed on the platform statement, and never a percentage of rebate or purchase volume — removes any steering incentive. (e) The product never recommends, ranks or defaults to a merchant; no purchase steering anywhere in the UI. (f) Checks stay merchant-blind against the builder's own agreed rates (M2-1); per-merchant overcharge and delivery-discrepancy scorecards are published for every merchant the builder base uses, partner or not, on the same test. (g) Data sharing with a merchant for rebate reconciliation is per-merchant builder opt-in under D12, limited to what the merchant already holds about that builder; merchants never learn what JobGuard flagged. (h) Sequence after the supplier watchdog has a public track record (M2 matching live, scorecards published, pilot fairness data under §14.17) so the first impression is 'watchdog' not 'app with merchant deals'. (i) New commercial decision record plus D11 conflict-of-interest review; competition-law check (no exclusivity, no resale-price terms); VAT on the fee (D02).

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutation: publishing a price for earlier disclosure lets a critic write 'JobGuard charges £20 a month not to withhold things from you', and it reframes the standard plan as the withholding plan. That is the strongest objection and it is about copy, not structure. On the substantive prongs the idea passes. Builder harm: none — it gives the builder a way to see every candidate as it arises, at a flat price, and cards are proposals with four builder actions and no liability (§14.3). Withheld-information profit: it reduces it — disclosure is fixed at signal creation and the §14.6 predicate gains a job-mode clause, so JobGuard cannot time anything to earn a fee. Fairness: the research says a priced choice does more than a disclosure sentence (autonomy versus Cain et al.'s finding that disclosure alone fails), flat pricing is preferred over a running meter (Lambrecht & Skiera; report §'The hidden final check…'), and a flat plan price is the only form compatible with D11 v2's 'may not reveal before lock and later charge'. Two weaknesses remain and are handled as conditions: the upgrade bridge for in-flight jobs must be free (a paid I69 peek at that moment is a toll), and the 'independent second check' rationale must visibly survive on the paid plan (the reconcile-only final check still runs and says 'nothing new'). The single-SKU 'Builder Live' placement is correctly rejected: a £70 Solo gap is 3.7× the foregone fee and reads as punitive.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Copy on both plans is written from the builder's side and pre-tested with pilot builders (§14.17 perceived fairness): the standard plan is 'a second check after you complete your bill', never 'we hold back'; Tell me now is 'told as we go', never 'we stop withholding'. (2) The post-lock final check still runs on Tell me now and the pricing page says so; the 'nothing new' screen is identical in shape to the standard reveal. (3) Upgrade bridge is free: on `effective_at`, every in-flight job gets a one-time free reveal (all current signals → `surfaced_early`, permanently fee-free, JobGuard absorbs) or is bound to live mode with existing signals disclosed; never a paid peek. (4) Downgrade: in-flight jobs keep live mode (builder-favourable), next-period effect only; no switching rule may depend on signal existence (§14.3). (5) Flat plan price only; never per card or per catch (D11 v2). (6) Must-surface cards stay mandatory-lane on every plan; the daily advisory budget can never hide a fee-eligible card (disclosure set at creation). (7) The D11 'mode changed within N days of switch-live' signal is flag-only and never shown to the builder as an accusation. (8) Solo delta re-tested: +£20 on £29 is a 69% uplift in the segment anchored at £25–£45; pilot +£10 as an alternative. (9) D09 v3 / D13 v2 / D05 / D02 / D12 v3 records before any charge; G4 and pilot_no_charge show hypothetical prices only.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on fairness and on the builder's relationship with the product at its most important moment. Switch-live is where the report says friction must be zero and where the builder commits; adding a paid tick-box there ('£19 to be told as I go on this job') is a per-transaction toll on information JobGuard will hold anyway, and it is drip-like in feel even though B2B is outside DMCC (success_fee_psychology §4). It produces the worst trust outcome of the disclosure family: a builder who did not tick on a complex job and then meets a reveal and a 10% fee will feel they were caught out by a box they missed, and two disclosure regimes inside one tenant cannot be explained in one sentence — the report's test for the hold-back framing. The idea's own honesty note concedes it is a losing trade for JobGuard on complex jobs and pointless on simple ones (net negative under 2× adverse selection), so there is no revenue case to weigh against the trust cost. The one piece worth saving is not a paid tick: a free, tenant-level rule keyed on a job attribute fixed at switch-live (e.g. always live on homeowner jobs) has real builder-and-customer merit, because late post-final-account bills to consumers are dispute-prone and can strain the builder's customer relationship (research note §4 inference on Consumer Rights Act); that belongs under I67/I70's machinery and a D13/D06 decision, not here.
verdicts.conditions: None as a paid per-job option. If anything survives: a free tenant-level disclosure rule keyed on customer type (homeowner jobs live, business jobs standard), bound immutably at switch-live, considered as a D13 v2 rule rather than a charge.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on the withheld-information prong; this is the 'held to ransom' reading made literal, as the idea itself admits. At §14.4 step 2 the builder is about to declare their complete final account and a button offers 'Show me what JobGuard found (£69)'. That is a price tag on information JobGuard already holds, presented at the moment of maximum leverage, with the price explicitly 'set near the fee JobGuard would expect on a job the builder already suspects' — i.e. JobGuard pricing its own advantage, which is the textbook dual-entitlement violation (Kahneman/Knetsch/Thaler) and the betrayal framing the report warns is fatal in a word-of-mouth trade (report §'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk'). It also destroys the only framing that survives the research — 'an independent second check after your bill, like a proofread' — because a check that can be bought before the bill is not a timing rationale that serves the builder, it is a toll with a discount. Listing the price on the pricing page from day one does not cure it: disclosure does not neutralise a conflict (Cain et al.). The net revenue (+£8 to +£223 per builder-year on the idea's own adverse-selection assumptions) is trivial against a permanent 'pay to see what they found on your job' story. The mechanic (mark every signal `surfaced_early`, reconcile-only lock) is sound and useful, but only when it is free.
verdicts.conditions: None as a paid feature. The pre-lock reveal mechanic may exist only where it costs the builder nothing: as the free in-flight bridge on an I67 upgrade, or as an unpriced goodwill/retention action initiated by JobGuard, always marking all signals permanently fee-free.

verdicts.key_risk: A priced button at the review step converts the hidden final check from 'a second check for you' into 'pay us or we take 10% later', collapsing trust in the standard plan for every builder who sees it.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutation: partial disclosure by source is hard to say in one sentence and invites 'you told me about the invoice line but kept quiet about my diary note'; and the Materials pack exposes that the standard plan sits on out-of-scope supplier lines until lock, some of which are ordering mistakes, not extras. Assessed by prong: Materials live is squarely in the builder's interest and strengthens, not compromises, the watchdog — an out-of-scope PO or invoice line is either an extra to log or a mistake to stop before payment, and the deterministic SV-3 detector is work the builder cannot easily do themselves, so a fee (or a flat price to be told sooner) passes the who-did-the-work test (Xia et al.). It does not add to JobGuard's profit from withheld information; it reduces it, with disclosure fixed at creation and a predicate clause on `signal_type`. The uncomfortable fact it surfaces is a property of the founder's fixed decision (supplier documents are evidence), not of this pack; but selling the pack without first deciding the must-surface question for probable ordering mistakes would look like monetising mistakes, so that decision is a precondition. The Customer requests pack fails the lens on value rather than harm: the customer's message is already in the builder's own inbox, D13's must-surface rule already covers significant requests, and charging £5–£15/month to be reminded about messages the builder has read looks like nickel-and-diming and multiplies disclosure regimes for £3–£31 net per builder-year; fold it into I67 or lower the D13 threshold by default. The rejected value-floor variant is rightly rejected (a low estimate hiding a big item would look like JobGuard estimating low to earn a fee).
verdicts.conditions: (1) Ship Materials live only; drop Customer requests live as a separate paid pack (include per-message request cards in I67, and set the D13 must-surface request threshold conservatively low by default). (2) Before shipping, the founder records under D13 v2 whether a deterministic 'probable ordering mistake' rule (out-of-scope supplier line with no completion evidence and quantity/spec inconsistent with the job) is must-surface on every plan; if it stays hidden, no copy on any plan may imply the standard plan checks orders against scope beyond price/quantity matching. (3) Coalescing is builder-favourable: any disclosed member discloses the whole coalesced signal; a hidden-source member can never keep a live-source extra fee-eligible (SV-3 test). (4) Same copy conditions as I67 (never 'hold back'); the pack must pass a one-sentence explanation test with pilot builders. (5) Bundle price stays below the sum of packs so I67 is always the better deal. (6) Live sources bound immutably per job at switch-live; predicate clause `signal_type NOT IN job.live_sources`; disclosure at creation; D09 v3 / D13 v2 / D12 v3 / D02 / D05; G4.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on the exploiting-an-advantage prong. The pack sells relief from the single most resented fee case (Test O: the builder's own diary note 'fitted outside tap', read by JobGuard, held, revealed, billed at 10%). The report is explicit that builders reject a fee where the extra 'was already in their head or their notes', because JobGuard did no work the builder could not do — it read the builder's own words (report §'The hidden final check…'; Xia/Monroe/Cox on who did the work). Charging £10–£20 a month to be prompted about your own notes is therefore charging to avoid being caught out by your own records: the protection-money reading, and the marketing cannot avoid advertising it ('so we never bill you for what's in your notes' tells every prospect that the standard plan does exactly that). This is different from I67, where the price substitutes for a fee on third-party evidence JobGuard genuinely assembled (supplier lines, photos, messages across a job) and the fee itself is defensible. The idea's own trust note concedes the right move may be a D13 rule change; a paid pack pre-empts that decision by putting a price on it and is unfair to every builder who does not buy it. The founder's fixed decision (unsubmitted diary and voice notes are evidence) is not re-argued here; the verdict is only that this must not be sold as a separate SKU. Any per-note prompting belongs inside I67 (Tell me now) at no separate price, and §14.17 pilot measurement should test Test O's perceived fairness directly so the D13 question is answered with data.
verdicts.conditions: None as a paid pack. If own-record prompts are wanted: include them in I67 at no separate price (same binding, predicate and coalescing rules as I70), and add Test O specifically to the §14.17 perceived-fairness measurement so the founder can decide under D13 whether own-record signals should be fee-free by rule.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutation: the fine print is where the harm sits — if exclusions read like an insurer's (judgement dismissals, documents never received, anything the builder cannot evidence), the credit damages trust more than no credit; and tying the credit to Tell me now makes the standard plan look like the plan JobGuard does not stand behind, while the standalone hidden-plan add-on (+£5–£15) is selling a warranty on a check the builder already pays for, which reads as charging twice. Against that, the substance is in the builder's interest and passes every prong: JobGuard bears the cost of its own deterministic miss, the credit never touches the success-fee book (D01), the 'JobGuard missed it so it cannot then charge to recover it' rule is exactly the fairness rule a reasonable builder expects, and verification from immutable records (evidence hashes, matching-run log) keeps disputes factual. The wrong-card £5 token is harmless but trivial and risks reading as patronising; publishing the detector error rate does more for trust. The legal shape (capped, fee-tied service-failure credit versus contract of insurance) needs review before wording ships. Expected cost is small (−£9 to −£44 per builder-year on the idea's assumptions), and its value is credibility, not revenue.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Legal review of the insurance perimeter before any wording; cap tied to fees paid in the period; called a 'service-failure credit', never insurance, guarantee or savings promise (no '4x ROI' style copy). (b) Missed-line credit applies on every paid plan as part of the base subscription; not a Tell me now differentiator and not sold as a paid add-on on the hidden plan (drop the +£5/£10/£15 variant). (c) Exclusions are a short plain-English list verifiable from immutable records; no discretionary 'judgement' denials; disputed claims reviewed by a human with a written reason, mirroring the D13 dispute route. (d) A credited miss permanently bars any success fee on the same money, and more broadly no supplier-overcharge fee (D03 category 2) ever arises on a refund the builder obtained without a prior JobGuard finding. (e) Credits are subscription-book credit notes only (M4-10), never cash and never against the success-fee book (D01/D09); VAT treatment under D02. (f) Wrong-card credit: keep only if it costs nothing to explain; otherwise replace with a published detector error rate per version. (g) Claim record needs an approved Decision; G4.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA permission is engaged as scoped: recording guarantee dates, certificates and photos and routing an enquiry to one named builder is not consumer credit, credit broking, insurance distribution, debt collection (RAO art 39F is tied to consumer-credit debts) or claims-management lead generation (RAO arts 89G–89M cover only the six CMC sectors; home improvement is not one). No appointed-representative route is needed. The exclusivity promise is a vertical, non-foreclosing commitment by JobGuard that leaves the homeowner free to go anywhere, so Chapter I CA98 is not engaged. The real constraints are data protection and e-privacy. (1) The homeowner becomes JobGuard's own account holder and data subject, so D12 v2 must be extended: JobGuard as controller for the homeowner account, the builder remaining controller of its customer list, and a written allocation (joint or independent controllers) for shared job records, photos and diary-derived content; an Article 13 notice at sign-up; and a D07 retention class that survives the builder cancelling, because the homeowner's copy cannot simply vanish when the builder leaves. (2) 'Book [Builder] again' and 'Recommend [Builder]' prompts sent by JobGuard promote a third party's services, so the PECR reg 22 soft opt-in (which only covers a seller marketing its own similar products to its own customers) does not cover JobGuard as sender; either JobGuard captures explicit consent at account creation or the messages are structured as the builder's own soft-opt-in marketing sent through JobGuard as processor, which most builders will not have set up correctly. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 raised PECR penalties to UK GDPR levels, so this is not cosmetic. (3) A refer-a-friend email that JobGuard sends to a non-user is unsolicited marketing on ICO guidance (JobGuard is the instigator); a homeowner-shared link avoids it. (4) The free homeowner account is still a consumer contract for CRA 2015 Part 2 fairness and transparency purposes; the CCRs 2013 and the CRA digital-content chapter largely fall away because nothing is paid. (5) Homeowner DSARs will now reach builder-authored notes about them; DPA 2018 Sch 2 para 16 third-party balancing applies, and D12 v2 already makes any pre-lock DSAR disclosure fee-ineligible, so the account should exist only after lock or be structurally scoped to post-lock data. The trust flip the idea warns about is also a legal flip: introducing insurance-backed guarantees, home-emergency cover or finance to this homeowner base is insurance distribution or credit broking under the RAO and would need FCA permission or an AR arrangement (6–12 months direct; weeks via a principal but at their fee), which is a further reason to hard-wire exclusivity. Cost: a data-protection solicitor to draft the homeowner terms, privacy notice, consent capture and controller allocation, roughly £3–5k, 2–4 weeks; none of it blocks the build after G1. Not legal advice; the controller allocation and PECR sender analysis need a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Extend D12 v2 to name JobGuard as controller for the homeowner account and allocate controllership of shared job records in writing; Article 13 notice and a D07 retention class for homeowner records that survive builder cancellation. Capture explicit, separately ticked consent at homeowner sign-up for re-booking and referral prompts; do not rely on soft opt-in with JobGuard as sender. Replace JobGuard-sent refer-a-friend emails with a homeowner-shared link. Make the exclusivity promise a term of the builder contract and an internal policy that bars any third-party marketing to homeowner accounts; treat any insurance, guarantee or finance introduction as a new decision needing FCA analysis. Create homeowner accounts only after final-account lock, or scope them so no pre-lock data (and no shadow signal) is reachable via the account or a DSAR through it. Consumer-fair terms reviewed under CRA 2015 Part 2 before launch.

verdicts.key_risk: A later pivot to marketing third parties to the homeowner base: it breaches the exclusivity contract, needs fresh PECR consent and, for insurance or finance products, FCA permission; day one, a JobGuard-sent refer-a-friend email is the most likely PECR breach.

verdicts.reasons: Legally survivable, strategically the worst fit, and I could not find a statutory blocker. No FCA permission: home-improvement lead generation is outside the RAO claims-management sectors and no credit, insurance or money movement is involved; no AR route needed. The true cost sits in consumer law, which since 6 April 2025 the CMA enforces directly under the DMCC Act 2024 with fines up to 10% of global turnover (the research report cites the first fine, £4.2m, against AA/BSM). Three exposures: (1) 'checked' or 'verified' is a claim about the nature of the trader that must be true, current and substantiated (DMCC s.226 misleading actions, CAP Code); a builder whose checks lapse while the label persists is a misleading action by JobGuard, so keeping the claim honest means continuously policing customers, which the idea itself flags. (2) Any influence of money on matching, whether the 2% fee, a per-shortlist fee or an implicit preference for builders who run more live jobs or generate more catches, must be disclosed to the homeowner; undisclosed paid influence over ranking is treated as misleading under the CMA's unfair-practices guidance (a solicitor should confirm the exact Schedule 20 wording that applies). (3) If reviews are shown, submitting or commissioning fake reviews and publishing reviews without reasonable and proportionate steps against fakes are Schedule 20 banned practices, which means a review-moderation process from day one. JobGuard also becomes controller for homeowner leads (a D12 extension), owes Article 13 notices, and passes lead data to builders as independent controllers; the builders' follow-up marketing is their own PECR problem but complaints land on JobGuard's brand. A public site where homeowners post jobs that builders read is plausibly a user-to-user service under the Online Safety Act 2023, which requires a written illegal-content risk assessment even for low-risk services (confirm scope with a solicitor). Anti-circumvention clauses against off-platform deals are lawful in B2B terms (Checkatrade uses them), but enforcing them with D11-style signals contradicts D11 v2's 'flag, never penalise' rule. A 2% fee triggered by acceptance and switch-live is a B2B primary obligation outside UCTA's reasonableness test. None of this is a legal bar; it is a standing consumer-law compliance function (ranking disclosure, verification currency, review moderation, OSA assessment, homeowner privacy) that has to be funded before the first lead, plus the homeowner marketing spend the idea already admits it ignores. The research report's own recommendation, a free directory (I56) with lead fees left to Checkatrade, stands on legal grounds too: it removes exposures (2) and most of (1). Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: If pursued at all: disclose to homeowners, at the point of matching, that builders pay JobGuard on won jobs and exactly what 'checked' means and when it was last verified; matching logic must be documented as independent of fee yield, live-job counts and catch rates, and never use shadow-bill data. Verification status must expire and the label must drop automatically. Review moderation and a fake-review policy before any reviews are shown. Complete an Online Safety Act illegal-content risk assessment if the posting surface is in scope. Extend D12 for JobGuard as controller of leads with Article 13 notices and independent-controller terms for builders. No D11 signal may be used to police off-platform circumvention. Fund the compliance function and marketing budget before launch; treat I56 (free directory) as the default alternative.

verdicts.reasons: Snagging inspection is unregulated; no FCA activity, no AR route. RICS and RPSA membership are private panel criteria, and using their marks in JobGuard's own marketing needs their permission. The legal issues are consumer law, money handling and data purpose. (1) A referral fee from a provider JobGuard presents to a consumer must be disclosed in existence, amount and basis; an undisclosed or half-secret commission is a misleading omission under the DMCC 2024 unfair-practices regime and, where the homeowner reasonably sees JobGuard as acting for them, risks the secret-commission fiduciary line (Expert Tooling v Engie [2025] EWCA Civ 292, cited in the research notes). (2) Calling the check 'independent' is a claim about the service that must survive three facts: the builder enabled it, JobGuard is paid by the inspector, and the inspector receives the builder's scope record. Independent of the builder is defensible; independent of JobGuard is not, and the wording must say which. (3) The homeowner's stage sign-off cannot waive CRA 2015 s.49 reasonable-care-and-skill rights or later latent-defect remedies (s.57 bars exclusion), so the portal must frame sign-off as acceptance for payment, not a release; an inspector's report is the inspector's liability under their contract with the homeowner, and JobGuard's own exclusions face CRA s.62 fairness. (4) JobGuard must not receive the homeowner's payment and pass it on: that is a payment service under the PSRs 2017 unless the commercial-agent exclusion clearly applies, and AGENTS.md already forbids holding customers' money; the homeowner pays the inspector directly and JobGuard invoices the inspector for the referral. (5) Sharing scope and proof photos with the inspector is a disclosure to an independent controller (D12) needing a named lawful basis and homeowner notice. (6) An inspection report received before lock is 'evidence' under D13 §14.2 and could support a success fee; re-using a document the homeowner paid for as JobGuard's fee evidence is a purpose-limitation and fairness point that the homeowner terms must cover, or inspector reports should be excluded from shadow eligibility. (7) Because a clean report accelerates the invoice on which JobGuard's fee base sits, panel allocation must be demonstrably uncorrelated with report outcome (round-robin or geographic, logged). VAT: the referral fee is a taxable supply by JobGuard to the inspector. Legal cost is modest: panel agreement, homeowner disclosure wording and terms, roughly £2–4k, 2–3 weeks. Not legal advice; the 'independent' wording and PSR analysis need a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Disclose the referral fee (amount and basis) to the homeowner before booking; state precisely what 'independent' means. Homeowner pays the inspector directly; JobGuard never touches the money. Stage sign-off UI and terms must state that statutory rights are unaffected. Panel allocation logged and provably outcome-blind; no ranking by clean-report rate. D12 lawful basis and notice for sharing scope and photos with the inspector; inspector as independent controller. Either exclude inspector reports from shadow-signal eligibility or state the re-use in the homeowner's terms. RICS/RPSA marks only with permission. Builder-enabled per job and never offered by JobGuard unprompted, as the idea says.

verdicts.reasons: No regulated activity: a software subscription discount plus an affiliate payment to a trade body; no FCA permission, no AR route. Four legal points, all conditions rather than bars. (1) DMCC 2024 Schedule 20 carries over the long-standing banned practice of displaying a trust mark, quality mark or equivalent without authorisation, so rendering 'Master Builder' (an FMB-registered mark) or 'NFB member' on a homeowner-facing final account or evidence pack needs a written licence from the body and must stop the moment membership lapses. The idea's annual re-validation is therefore a legal control, not just anti-gaming, and the mark must be driven by live validation, not a flag set at sign-up. (2) The mark must not imply the body verified the work; CAP Code endorsement rules (3.45–3.52) and the misleading-action risk in the builder's B2C sale both apply, and the body will insist on wording. (3) Payouts to the body require a VAT self-billing agreement under VAT Notice 700/62 with the body's VAT registration confirmed; the 15% share is an assumption the bodies have not published. (4) Membership-number validation is a data exchange with the body needing a lawful basis and a short data-sharing agreement (number in, status out, nothing else). Competition law is not engaged by a non-exclusive affinity deal, and even an exclusivity request would usually sit inside VABEO 2022 safe harbours, so refusing it is commercial. The 'two months free' promotion is B2B (sole traders buying business software are not consumers), so DMCC drip-pricing does not apply, but the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 still require the offer to be stated accurately and D09 v2 must approve promo and annual terms before any charge. Contractually refuse any success-fee share or findings visibility, which also keeps the body outside D13's disclosure routes. Cost: partner agreement, mark licence, self-billing and data-sharing agreements, roughly £3–6k, 4–8 weeks plus the body's own onboarding timeline. Not legal advice; the mark-licence terms need a solicitor's review.
verdicts.conditions: Written licence from each body for use of its mark on JobGuard-rendered documents; mark rendering tied to live membership validation with automatic removal on lapse; wording agreed with the body that the mark denotes membership, not verification of the work. VAT self-billing agreement and confirmed VAT status before the first payout. Data-sharing agreement for membership validation. D09 v2 approval of promo and annual terms before charging (G4). Contract clauses: no success-fee share, no findings visibility, one redemption per membership number.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA activity and no AR route; accountancy is not a reserved profession, so JobGuard producing schedules is lawful. Five condition clusters. (1) Professional-body rules: ICAEW Code of Ethics s.340, ACCA and AAT all require members to disclose referral fees or commissions to clients in writing (ICAEW also on retention), so the 20% share must be visible in the builder's terms and in the practice's engagement letter; JobGuard should supply the wording. (2) The bookkeeper introducer fee is money paid to JobGuard by a party it recommends: B2B, so DMCC does not apply, but the secret-commission fiduciary line (Expert Tooling v Engie 2025 was itself a B2B case) and misrepresentation law do; disclose the amount or take the idea's cleaner 'free listing, no fee' variant. (3) AML: MLR 2017 reg 11 defines an 'external accountant' as anyone providing accountancy services to others by way of business, with HMRC as default supervisor for firms outside a professional body; automated output from the builder's own data is generally not treated as accountancy services, but a practice-paid 'year-end pack' with revenue-recognition schedules and CIS reconciliations sits close enough that a solicitor must confirm JobGuard is not an accountancy service provider needing HMRC AML registration (fit-and-proper test, roughly £300 per premises plus policies and a few £k a year in compliance). (4) Tax: JobGuard must never interact with HMRC on a client's behalf, which keeps it outside the 2026 tax-adviser registration regime, and must not claim MTD ITSA compatibility unless HMRC-recognised; D06 forbids automating CIS and domestic reverse charge, so those outputs are labelled reconciliations and flags, never returns. (5) Liability: B2B disclaimers on 'projection' figures relied on for accounts are subject to UCTA s.2(2)/s.3 reasonableness and need drafting rather than a label. Data protection: the practice is an independent controller acting on the builder's revocable consent (D12 v2); the adviser role must have no route to shadow tables, otherwise a practice could become a pre-lock disclosure route and trigger D13 ineligibility. Unbilled approved variations shown to the practice are builder capture and fee-free, so the pack does not leak the shadow bill. Payouts need VAT self-billing (Notice 700/62); pay share only on collected revenue as the idea says. Cost: partner agreement, self-billing, terms and a UCTA and AML review, roughly £4–8k, 4–6 weeks. Not legal advice; the AML and tax-adviser classification needs a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Referral share and any introducer fee disclosed in amount in the builder's terms and the practice engagement letter (or drop the bookkeeper fee). Solicitor confirmation that the year-end pack is software output, not accountancy services under MLR 2017 reg 11; if in doubt, restrict the pack to raw exports the practice transforms. No HMRC interaction, no MTD-compatibility claim, no CIS or DRC 'returns' (D06). UCTA-drafted liability caps for projection figures. Adviser role structurally outside shadow tables and byte-identical responses with or without signals. VAT self-billing before the first payout; share paid only on collected revenue and stopped on cancellation. Free data-portability export preserved.

verdicts.reasons: Not FCA-regulated; no AR route. This is the one channel where UK construction statute actually applies, because sub-to-main-contractor contracts are 'construction contracts' under HGCRA 1996 s.104 and the s.106 residential-occupier exclusion does not help: s.108 adjudication, s.110A/110B payment notices, s.111 pay-less notices and the s.113 pay-when-paid ban all bite. Tooling that computes notice dates (M4-19) is lawful and unregulated, but a late or defective notice can cost a party the entire notified sum, so liability caps must pass UCTA s.3/s.11 reasonableness and the tool must present dates as derived from contract terms the parties entered, never as advice; adjudication support is not a reserved legal activity, but D10 keeps JobGuard from representing anyone. VAT and CIS are the gating cost: sub-to-MC supplies are the core domestic-reverse-charge case and CIS deductions apply, and D06 currently forbids automating CIS and DRC, so no invoice or application in this channel can be issued through JobGuard until D06 is extended and tax-reviewed. The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 applies (B2B), which helps: statutory interest and £40–£100 compensation partly offset the 10% fee on a withheld-payment case, unlike the homeowner segment where the builder bears it in full. Conflict of interest is the contractual crux: the MC pays JobGuard while JobGuard supports the sub's recovery case against that MC; both contracts need express carve-outs, data segregation (the MC's project data cannot be used against it without consent), and a good-faith clause that survives an adjudication, otherwise the MC has a confidentiality or implied-term argument. Data protection: JobGuard is likely a processor for the MC's evidenced-application data (Article 28 terms) and controller for the sub's tenant; sole-trader subs are data subjects (D12 v2); shadow data must be invisible to the MC structurally, not just contractually. Housing associations that are contracting authorities bring the Procurement Act 2023 into the sales cycle. Cost: a multi-party contract suite reviewed by a construction solicitor, roughly £8–15k over 2–3 months, plus the D06 extension and a qualified tax review. Not legal advice; the HGCRA tooling and DRC treatment need a construction and tax solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Extend and approve D06 for DRC and CIS before any subcontract invoice or application is issued through JobGuard. Notice-date tooling presented as computed from user-entered terms with UCTA-reviewed caps and no advice wording. MC licence and sub terms with express conflict carve-outs, data segregation and a clause that JobGuard acts for the sub on variations and applications and that the MC buys evidence only. Article 28 processor terms with the MC; D12 v2 analysis of dual roles. MC has no route to shadow tables or unsubmitted material. Licensed projects excluded from the sub's own live-job tier (D09 v2). No CIS returns filed by JobGuard.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA activity in either variant; no AR route. OEM: the partner controls login and support, so D13's 'no pre-lock disclosure' rule becomes partly a partner obligation; a partner support agent hinting at a finding makes the signal permanently fee-ineligible and JobGuard absorbs the loss, so the contract needs structural access limits (partner staff have no route to shadow data), audit rights and an indemnity, and the wholesale price must not assume a fee base the partner can erode. JobGuard keeps a direct success-fee contract with the builder inside a partner-branded product, so the builder must accept JobGuard's own terms and the D13 onboarding disclosure inside the partner flow before the first job; B2B, so DMCC does not apply, but the BPMMR 2008 and misrepresentation do, and an undisclosed direct fee inside someone else's product is the 'half-secret commission' pattern the courts dislike. Data protection is a mixed role, processor for the partner's account data and controller for the fee relationship, needing Article 28 terms and D12/D04 cover for the partner's infrastructure; a US-hosted partner SSO or log route breaks the EU/UK boundary and D04 must enumerate it. Continuity: builders on 12-month platform contracts must keep their tenant, exports and any open recovery cases if they leave the platform, otherwise a partner can strand data and fees; that clause will be contested. Competition: exclusivity requests are usually inside VABEO 2022 safe harbours, so refusing them is commercial, not legal. Franchise: there is no UK franchise statute; a franchisor mandating a tool is a legitimate brand and know-how control (Pronuptia line), and the aggregate dashboard is business data unless franchisees are sole traders, in which case it is personal data; 'consent' in a franchise agreement is not freely given under UK GDPR, so rely on contract or legitimate interests with transparency. Legal cost is the heaviest of the eight: £15–30k and 3–6 months for an OEM agreement, £5–10k per franchise agreement, plus a residency review of each partner. Not legal advice; the mixed controller/processor role and the direct-fee-inside-partner-product terms need a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Partner staff structurally excluded from shadow data; contractual indemnity and audit rights for partner-caused pre-lock disclosure. JobGuard's own terms and the D13 onboarding disclosure accepted by the builder inside the partner flow before the first job. Article 28 terms; D04 approval covering partner SSO, logging and support routes; D12 v2 mixed-role analysis. Tenant, export and open-case continuity clause if the builder leaves the partner. Success fee direct and never shared; the one-sentence final-check explanation unedited on partner screens. Franchise dashboard limited to published aggregate fields under contract or legitimate interests, not consent. No exclusivity that forecloses the direct channel.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA activity; a subscription credit for a referral is a lawful B2B trade incentive (CAP Code Section 8 still requires its conditions and caps to be clear), and it is not credit broking because no credit product is involved; no AR route. The legal work is e-privacy and transparency. The inviting builder supplies a sub's contact details and JobGuard sends the invitation, so for sole-trader subs (individual subscribers) PECR reg 22 is in play: an invitation JobGuard instigates that promotes JobGuard is direct marketing on ICO guidance, and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 lifted PECR penalties to UK GDPR levels. Frame the invite as a transactional job-collaboration message from the builder, keep promotional content minimal, and send no follow-up marketing without consent; limited-company subs are corporate subscribers and outside reg 22. The Article 14 UK GDPR notice at invite (D12 v2) must say what the inviter can see and, importantly, that the sub's uploaded invoices become evidence on the inviter's job and may feed JobGuard's final check; omitting that would be a transparency failure that could also be argued as unfair processing. VAT: a subscription credit is a price reduction on the inviter's taxable supply, handled by credit note under D02/D09, and because it is a credit rather than cash it is not a taxable receipt for the inviter; D09 v2 must state it never offsets a success fee. CIS between builder and sub is unaffected because JobGuard neither pays nor deducts. Scoped-role security is engineering rather than law (RLS, no shadow-table route, byte-identical responses), but a scoped sub role must not become a same-tenant cross-job leak. Fake-sub credit farming is a terms and detection matter. Cost is the lowest of the eight: PECR and Article 14 templates plus terms, roughly £1–3k, 1–2 weeks. Not legal advice; the PECR instigator analysis for the invite email should be checked by a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Invitation email drafted as a transactional collaboration message with minimal promotion, sent in the builder's name, and no further marketing to the sub without consent. Article 14 notice at invite covering inviter visibility and the evidentiary use of uploaded invoices. Credit terms and caps stated clearly (CAP Section 8); D09 v2 records that credits never offset success fees; credit accounted for by credit note under D02. Sub role scoped by job with RLS and no shadow-table grant; conversion identity unique as for fee derivations.

verdicts.reasons: Trust is definitional, not incremental: the flagship prevention feature is checking merchants' invoices (M2-4 three-way matching, M2-5 discrepancy checks), so any merchant money makes every non-flag look bought. The energy-broker trajectory in research note success_fee_benchmarks §2 (supplier-paid 0.3-2p/kWh commissions, Ofgem disclosure rules from Oct 2024, TPI authorisation ~2027-28, Expert Tooling v Engie on half-secret commissions) is exactly where supplier-paid intermediaries end up, and the report §'The hidden final check' notes disclosure does not neutralise a conflict (Cain et al.). Revenue is negligible or unattainable: Variant A at £500/month per merchant per 1,000 builders is £6 per builder-year, and a merchant will not pay a connector fee to a platform with a few hundred builders when e-invoicing networks charge suppliers only because large buyers mandate them; M5-4/M5-5 build one scoped merchant/punchout/PEPPOL adapter at a time, so connector cost per merchant dwarfs £6 a builder. Variant B needs tens of millions of routed spend before a merchant negotiates, and JobGuard cannot offer the payment guarantee or central invoicing a buying group trades on (AGENTS §3: never hold funds). The NMBS/Coupa/Tradex precedents cited are not in the research report or notes and are unverified. Gaming is unmitigable by policy (merchant pressure to soften checks; JobGuard's own incentive on paying merchants). Cost: M2-2 intake plus SV-7 connector contract, merchant agreements, rebate ledger, and D04/D12/D11 reviews, for £6-£300 a builder.

verdicts.reasons: Builders already hold trade accounts with negotiated discounts at their regular merchant, so a 'JobGuard Trade' panel must beat existing terms to be used, and a platform with hundreds of builders has no leverage to negotiate that. The POS-discount precedents cited (FMB TradePoint, Checkatrade Wickes TradePro, NMBS, Fortis) are not in the research report or notes and are unverified; they are DIY-chain trade-counter discounts, not rebates at builders' merchants, and under a POS discount there is no rebate stream to take 10% of, so the fee collapses to a flat ~£5/month. Revenue is small even on the idea's own assumptions (£54/£216/£720 per taker); with a realistic 1-3% incremental rebate over existing account terms and 20% uptake it is about £4-£11 / £14-£43 / £48-£144 weighted. A 10%-of-rebate fee makes JobGuard's income rise with the builder's spend at partner merchants, a conflict routed through the builder's statement rather than removed; and the watchdog's merchant-blindness rests on checking 'the builder's own agreed rates' (M2-1), which under a panel are rates JobGuard negotiated. Builders will not distinguish 'merchant pays builder, builder pays JobGuard' from 'JobGuard is in with Travis' (the idea concedes this). Cost: partner registry, rebate-statement import reconciled to POs, admin-fee line on M4-10, merchant scorecard, ongoing BD negotiation, a new commercial decision record plus D11 review and competition-law check, roughly 3-4 weeks after M2-4 plus BD time, for tens of pounds per builder.

None of that makes it worth building before then.
