verdicts.reasons: It is the strongest fairness lever in the set: it turns the hold-back, which the report names as the biggest pricing risk (§'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk': betrayal aversion 54% vs 37%; disclosure does not fix a conflict), into a priced choice the builder makes, and autonomy does more than a sentence in the terms (research note success_fee_psychology §4). Per-card or per-catch charges are ruled out by D11 v2 (§14.10: 'JobGuard may not reveal before lock and later charge'), so a flat plan uplift is the only compatible form; the single-SKU 'Builder Live' placement is rightly rejected (a fourth price muddles the live-jobs ladder, report §'Three tiers work'; a Firm at 15 live jobs cannot use a 10-job SKU). Refutation 1: adverse selection is structural. The builder knows their own capture discipline, so takers are the high-catch tenants and JobGuard forgoes above-central fees on exactly the tenants paying the uplift; on the idea's own high case the net is -£1,280/-£1,440/-£1,920 per taker. The partial offset is that those builders are also the ones most likely to resent a hidden-plan fee and churn or talk, so part of the foregone fee is illusory. Refutation 2: the uplifts are 69%/68%/50% on top of tier price for one feature; category feature-gates run about 30% (Tradify Lite £34 to Plus £44 for the AI bill reader, report table). Solo at £49 sits above the £25-£45 anchor, against free quoting (Checkatrade, TradeMore) and a second compulsory MTD subscription (report §'Builders' willingness to pay'). The 25/35/50% uptake assumptions are unmeasured; I expect 10-20% Solo, 20-30% Builder, 30-40% Firm until the reveal has demonstrated value. Refutation 3: the pricing page has to explain the hold-back for the toggle to make sense, which publishes a price for silence ('£20 a month not to withhold'); copy discipline reduces but cannot remove that. If uptake is high, the success-fee engine (SV-1 to SV-8, the largest remaining build) serves a minority; that is information the founder needs, not a reason to hide the option. Revenue at my assumptions is roughly neutral per builder (weighted net about +£10/+£53/+£96); its value is churn and reputation, not money. The closest precedent, Chargeflow's flat $29 Alerts beside 25% recovery (success_fee_benchmarks §6), supports flat-beside-percentage, not paid disclosure, for which no precedent exists. Build is cheap relative to what it sits on (D09 v3/D13 v2 text, `disclosure_mode` on subscription_terms and an immutable job binding at switch-live, a predicate clause in SV-1, SV-3 emitting disclosure on live jobs, one `possible_extra` card via M2-7-S, a reconcile-only SV-5 path, M4-13/M4-14 wording; about 3 PRs) but only after SV-1 to SV-5 exist and behind G4; per-tier uplifts also presuppose D09 adopts live-job tiers (M4-14 is optional). Gaming (toggle hidden before a simple job, live before a complex one) is rational selection, blunted by per-tenant scope, date-based switching and next-period downgrade; the mode clause on the §14.6 predicate stops JobGuard timing signal creation.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Pilot first: in pilot_no_charge, present both modes with hypothetical prices and measure choice share and perceived fairness (§14.17); do not fix the uplift until the foregone fee per builder-year is measured. (2) Test two uplift levels (e.g. +£10/+£20/+£30 and +£20/+£40/+£60) in the priced sign-up test the report recommends; the 50-70% relative uplift is out of category norms. (3) Bind the mode immutably at switch-live in the audit event; switching is date-based only and never conditioned on signal existence (§14.3). (4) `possible_extra` cards go through the advisory lane with disclosure set at creation; must-surface stays mandatory on every plan. (5) §14.6 gains `AND job.disclosure_mode = hidden_until_lock`. (6) Standard-plan copy is 'an independent second check after your bill', never 'we hold back'; the headline price must include the uplift once chosen. (7) D09 v3, D13 v2, D05, D02 and D12 v3 records, then G4, before any charge; a D11 advisory signal for mode changes within N days of switch-live, flag only.

A £19 charge triggered by the switch-live command is the per-job activation charge rev 2.3 removed (M4-11 replaced), relabelled; calling it a subscription-book item does not change its trigger. It adds a paid tick-box at the moment the report says must be frictionless (the switch-live commit, where even a card ask is untested; report §'Let the trial run until the first job is live'). Two disclosure regimes inside one tenant produce 'did I tick it on that job?' disputes, the betrayal framing in miniature. Gross revenue is trivial (£144/£182/£251 at 40% opt-in; £90/£114/£157 at a more realistic 25%) and net is about zero or negative. verdicts.reasons: A button reading 'Show me what JobGuard found (£69)' at the review step is the ransom reading made literal, charged at the moment of maximum leverage. Dual entitlement (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler: exploiting an information advantage is judged unfair) and betrayal aversion apply directly (research note success_fee_psychology §4), and it destroys the only framing the research says survives, 'an independent second check after your bill, like a proofread' (report §'The hidden final check'): a proofread you can buy early is not a second check, it is a hold. Revenue is small and self-limiting: on the idea's own model net is +£8/+£86/+£223. Once builders learn the button exists, peeking becomes a cheap hedge on every job with any doubt, so the fee base shrinks to jobs where the builder had no suspicion, which makes the engine's economics depend on builder ignorance. The idea's genuine merits (an honest market price for the hold-back, and an exit for in-flight jobs when a tenant upgrades) are delivered better by a free reconcile-only bridge under I67, which already prices 'cards when I build the final account' the same as 'cards as you go' because the foregone fee is identical. B2B, so largely outside DMCC drip-pricing, but it is a new paid disclosure route needing D09 v3/D13 v2 and must avoid any 'claims' language. Build is low (SV-4 trigger, SV-5 worker against a draft revision, a disclosure-event kind, an M4-10 line); cost is not the objection. No precedent exists for a paid pre-commitment reveal against a contingency default.

verdicts.reasons: The Materials pack exposes a design fault before it is a revenue line: an out-of-scope supplier or PO line is either an extra to log or an ordering mistake to stop before payment, and the standard plan hides it until lock to keep it fee-eligible. That withholds a prevention finding of the kind the founder says carries most of the product's value, and builders will assume the M2-1/M2-4 watchdog already tells them. So it is first a D13 must-surface question (should out-of-scope supplier lines be a deterministic must-surface rule?); if D13 answers yes, the pack disappears and that is the right outcome. If sold, revenue is modest: £120/£240/£480 per taker; at 20/30/40% uptake £24/£72/£192 weighted; net of the 40% catch-source foregone (about £46/£72/£119 per taker central, 1.5x for adverse selection) roughly +£10/+£40/+£121 weighted. The Customer-requests pack fails on its face: 'pay £5-£15 a month to be told your customer asked for something through JobGuard' reads as a toll, D13's must-surface rule already covers significant requests, and revenue is £60-£180 per taker (about £10/£25/£45 weighted); drop it. Partial hiding cannot be stated in one sentence and invites 'you told me about the invoice line but kept quiet about my note'; a pack menu summing to +£25/+£50/+£75 (above the full toggle) mostly exists to make I67 look like the bundle. Coalescing risk is real: one extra evidenced by a live and a hidden source must reconcile as disclosed, builder-favourably, so SV-3 coalescing must treat any disclosed member as disclosing the whole. Build is low on top of I67 (`live_sources` on subscription_terms and the job binding, a predicate clause in SV-1, reliable signal_type tagging in SV-3), still behind G4 and D09 v3/D13 v2. Feature-scoped add-ons are normal in the category (Tradify AI bill reader in Plus, Powered Now scanner in Premium; report table) but none prices disclosure timing by source.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Put out-of-scope supplier lines to D13 as a candidate must-surface rule (prevention) before pricing anything; only if D13 keeps them hidden does a pack make sense. (2) Materials pack only; drop Customer-requests. (3) Fold into I67's toggle rather than a pack menu (one price, one sentence) unless the pilot shows builders want the partial option. (4) Coalescing rule: any disclosed member discloses the whole coalesced signal. (5) SV-3 signal_type tagging must be tested reliable before any predicate depends on it. (6) Measure 'which sources produce real catches' in the pilot (§14.17) before setting a price. (7) Reject the value-floor variant as the idea does: disclosure hinging on a labelled estimate looks like estimating low to earn a fee.

verdicts.reasons: The underlying feature ('You noted this: log it as an extra?') is clearly worth doing early: it is the prevention product (Buildbite reports a self-reported 30% change-order lift from capturing changes as they happen, report §'No rival sells'), it raises builder-captured extras and invoice value, and it removes Test O in §14.15, the single most resented fee case (report §'The hidden final check': builders reject a fee where the extra 'was already in their head or their notes'). But it should be a D13 rule change, not a £10-£20/month pack. As a pack it earns roughly nothing: revenue £120/£240/£240 per taker against an own-record foregone fee of about £40/£63/£104 per builder-year on my central (35% of a small pool), so weighted net about +£32/+£71/+£54 at 40% uptake. That is not a revenue idea; it is a price on reading the builder's own notes back to them, and the pricing page must explain that the standard plan deliberately does not do so (§14.2 'no per-note prompt' rule), which publishes the withholding on the most emotionally charged case. Once the nudge exists the builder logs the extra, it becomes builder capture and is fee-free anyway, so the fee base is lost either way; the only question is whether to charge for the nudge. Gaming is nil beyond what §14.2's tie-break already handles (a post-hoc diary note already reconciles builder-favourably). Build is low once SV-7's diary and voice surfaces exist, the same plumbing as I70. No precedent exists.
verdicts.conditions: Ship the own-records nudge as a fee-free default via D13 v2 (an explicit change to §14.2's no-per-note-prompt rule), gated on pilot measurement (§14.17: 'whether anything should have surfaced earlier' and disputed attributions). If the founder insists on keeping own-record signals fee-eligible, offer only I67's whole-plan toggle, never a separate pack that prices this specific case.

revised_revenue.solo: As a pack: £120 per taker, 40% uptake gives £48 weighted, net of ~£40 foregone about +£32. As a free default: £0 direct, retention value only.
revised_revenue.small_firm: As a pack: £240 per taker, £96 weighted, net about +£71. Free default: £0 direct.
revised_revenue.firm: As a pack: £240 per taker, £96 weighted, net about +£54. Free default: £0 direct.

verdicts.key_risk: Pricing the builder's own notes turns the most defensible fairness fix into a paid ransom on the most resented case.

verdicts.reasons: It is a cost line, not revenue: the standalone add-on yields about £6/£12/£18 weighted per builder-year and the expected credit cost is £9-£44. Its claimed value is credibility for I67's uplift, but builders buy on 'does it find stuff', not on SLA fine print, and Chargeflow's '4x ROI guarantee' (research note success_fee_benchmarks §6) is a marketing guarantee on a 25% fee, not a loss-based credit. The insurance-perimeter risk is real: credit (a) pays the builder's third-party loss (the overpaid difference to a supplier) on an uncertain event, which is the shape a contract of insurance takes; opening an FCA-authorisation question for a £5-£179 credit costs more in legal review than the feature will ever earn. It is also incoherent: credit (a) covers the deterministic three-way match (M2-4), which runs on both plans and says nothing about disclosure mode, so tying it to 'Tell me now' makes no sense (the standalone variant concedes this). Ops cost is inverted: each claim needs human verification against immutable matching-run logs and evidence hashes for a £5-£179 credit, so verification exceeds the payout. The assumptions are unsupported: 0.5% overcharge/duplicate incidence has no UK small-builder data (success_fee_benchmarks §1 gaps) and the wrong-card rate is unmeasurable until SV-3's held-out set exists. Gaming is low (capped, evidenced). Build is medium (M4-10 credit notes exist by then; a claim record, an approved Decision and a verification view are new) for negative revenue. BUILD_PLAN's out-of-scope list forbids claims of guaranteed recovery, so marketing headroom is nil.
verdicts.conditions: None as specified. The cheap cousin worth revisiting post-G4: a fee-refund-shaped service credit ('if JobGuard ingested a duplicate invoice as verified evidence and M2-4 raised no finding before you paid, that month's subscription is credited'), capped at one month, never loss-based, which avoids the insurance question and needs only D09/M4-10 terms and a D01 rule that credits never touch the success-fee book. Never market it as a guarantee of savings.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct; expected cost about -£9/yr; standalone add-on £60 per taker x 10% uptake = £6.

verdicts.key_risk: A loss-based capped payout looks like a contract of insurance, a regulatory question that costs more to answer than the credit is worth.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts fail on the core case. Who did the work: the builder paid twice by mistake, JobGuard matched two settled bank payments to one invoice identity (M2-2 + M4-7/M4-8), which a small firm without AP controls does not do for itself; the builder's own effort is sending a drafted letter. Who bears the cost: the builder, out of cash they had already lost, netted at the moment it comes back (Thaler integration, report §'The hidden final check'). Nothing is withheld: the Decision fires the moment the duplicate settles, and the cash-only rule is already D03 v2 wording (BUILD_PLAN §14.7). No supplier money, no customer contact, so watchdog independence and the customer relationship are untouched. Against the recovery-audit benchmark (20-30%, research note success_fee_benchmarks §1) 10% for the classic duplicate-payment class reads as modest, and a reasonable builder would call £50 on a £500 refund found money. Two refutations survive as conditions rather than rejections: (1) a perverse incentive against prevention — if JobGuard's own intake matching held a duplicate-invoice or already-settled signal before the second payment left the builder's bank and stayed quiet, a fee on the cure is exactly 'profiting from information it withheld' and must be structurally impossible; (2) cash-steering — most merchants offer a credit, and a refund draft that pushes for cash so JobGuard can earn is the builder's money being bent to JobGuard's fee. Revenue is trivial (£9-£120), so this is a trust-building category, not a revenue line.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Prevention first, structurally: any duplicate-intake identity or 'invoice already settled' fact JobGuard held before the second payment's bank settlement time must be surfaced as a fee-free warning at once; a case where such a signal existed pre-settlement and was not surfaced is permanently fee-ineligible (same monotonic flag as `disclosed_before_lock`, D13/§14.3). (b) Builder-favourable attribution: if the builder or their bookkeeper had already requested the refund, reversed the payment, or marks 'I already knew' before the Decision, no fee; ambiguity resolves to the builder (§14.2 tie-break applied to this category). (c) Refund draft is neutral: it offers refund or account credit as equal options, states in the Decision that a credit is fee-free ('a credit on your account is fine; no fee either way unless cash is refunded'), and JobGuard never sends follow-ups asking specifically for cash. (d) The Decision cites both documents and both bank lines; invoice number alone is never the match key (M2-2 rule). (e) The fee is shown netted on the same screen and statement as the refund ('£500 refunded; JobGuard's fee £50; yours £450'), never invoiced weeks later in isolation. (f) Genuine part payments, credits and pre-Decision refunds excluded as written; reversal creates linked compensation only. (g) New D03 v3 row (a duplicate payment is not an overcharge); D01, D02, D10/D12 for the bank feed; nothing before G4; pilot shows hypothetical figures only.

revised_revenue.solo: £9 blended (unchanged; prevention-first condition makes this an upper bound)

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard earning from a duplicate its own intake matching could have prevented — the fee must never reward silence — and refund drafts that steer builders to demand cash from merchants they depend on.

verdicts.reasons: Rejected as a success-fee category; the check itself is worth keeping fee-free. The refutation that sticks is the fee base. When a sub wrongly charges 20% VAT, the builder in practice either reclaims it as input tax on their own return (wrongly, but commonly) or gets a credit note and refund from the sub. JobGuard's 'recovery' therefore mostly substitutes one route for the other: the builder gets £600 back from the sub and simultaneously loses the £600 they were about to claim from HMRC. Their felt experience is 'JobGuard charged me 10% of money I already had a route to', which fails the dual-entitlement test (exploiting a technical advantage, research note success_fee_psychology §3/§4). The genuine benefit — avoiding an HMRC disallowance and penalty later — is compliance value with an unprovable counterfactual, i.e. prevention, which the founder has already ruled fee-free. Second, the relationship cost falls on the builder: subcontractor relationships are more personal than merchant accounts, and a cash-only fee rule nudges builders to demand cash refunds (which force the sub to amend their own return) instead of accepting a credit. Third, every Decision sits one step from tax advice; a wrong rule version damages the builder's sub relationships while the builder can never earn from it. The narrow honest case (input tax actually disallowed or refused by the builder's accountant, then cash refunded after a JobGuard prompt) is unobservable without an accounting connector, and the whole category is worth £1-£150 a year. That is too little to justify carrying 'JobGuard took 10% of a VAT correction' into a word-of-mouth trade.
verdicts.conditions: None as a fee category. If revived at all, only with all of: fee restricted to cases where the accounting connector evidences the input tax was not claimed or was disallowed before the refund; a 'check with your accountant' Decision with a versioned, tax-reviewer-approved rule table (D02 owner); credit notes fee-free; the builder's own status facts never producing a fee against them. Recommended instead: ship the DRC/zero-rating check as a fee-free watchdog Finding paid for by the subscription, and record the rejection in D03 v3.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 as a fee category (check retained as a subscription feature)

verdicts.key_risk: The 'recovered' VAT is largely money the builder was about to reclaim from HMRC anyway, so the fee reads as 10% of money the builder already had access to, while straining sub relationships for £1-£150 a year.

verdicts.reasons: Survives, narrowly, because the money is the builder's own contractual entitlement that the merchant did not pay, and adding up a year of matched invoices against a threshold and a merchant's opaque rebate statement is visible work most small firms do not do (Buell & Norton effort-reciprocity, report §'The hidden final check'); AP recovery auditors treat unclaimed rebates as a standard class at 20-30% (success_fee_benchmarks §1), so 10% with the builder sending the letter is modest. Three refutations nearly kill it and become hard conditions. (1) Hold-back trap: as written, JobGuard 'computes the rebate due at period end'. If JobGuard silently knows in November that the builder is £200 short of the threshold, or that £3,750 falls due on 31 January, and says nothing until the window lapses so a Decision can earn 10%, that is profiting from withheld information about the builder's own contract — outside the D13 rule, which covers evidence about the job, not the builder's entitlements. The tracker must be visible all along, fee-free. (2) Neighbourhood to I65/I66: a platform whose income depends on merchant rebate shortfalls is one drift away from 'let us negotiate your rebate', which would end the watchdog's independence; D11 must forbid it in terms. (3) Cash steering: rebates are often paid as credit; a JobGuard draft that demands cash is the builder's relationship being spent for JobGuard's fee. With a visible tracker most builders will claim on time themselves, so the fair residual is underpayment or non-payment despite a claim — smaller but honest.
verdicts.conditions: (a) A standing, always-visible, fee-free rebate tracker for every entered term (spend to date, threshold, amount accrued, due date, amount received); no part of the calculation is held back before the payment window lapses. (b) Fee only on the shortfall between rebate due and rebate actually received after the term's own payment window, after a cited `rebate_due` Decision and a JobGuard-drafted claim; a claim the builder raised before the Decision is fee-free. (c) Credit-note or account-credit settlement fee-free, with neutral draft wording offering both routes. (d) Arithmetic on settled net spend after returns and credits; every invoice cited; where the merchant's own rebate statement disagrees, the builder is shown both and any unresolved dispute is fee-free. (e) D11 v3 statement: JobGuard never introduces, negotiates, pools, brokers or receives any merchant rebate or income, and no product surface may suggest 'better terms'. (f) Rebate terms and agreement documents are tenant-confidential: no cross-tenant aggregation, benchmarking or 'what others get' features, even anonymised, without a separate decision record. (g) Claw-back reversal creates linked compensation; D03 v3 row; D01/D02; bank feed via D10/D12; behind G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £0-£1 blended (down from £1: visible tracker means most builders claim themselves)

verdicts.key_risk: Silently tracking a builder's own rebate entitlement until the window lapses would be JobGuard profiting from withheld information outside the shadow-bill rule, and the category sits one step from merchant-negotiated terms that would poison the watchdog.

verdicts.reasons: The idea's own recommendation is right. Fairness test: the builder has just lost an entire invoice to a customer who never paid; JobGuard would then take 10% of the tax relief on that loss. The base is HMRC tax relief on a loss, not 'recovered net money' from a customer or supplier, so it falls outside every founder-decided category (§14.7) and reads as exploiting the builder's worst moment (dual entitlement; betrayal aversion, success_fee_psychology §4). The counterfactual is thin: any competent accountant claims bad-debt relief as part of ordinary fees, so 'JobGuard did work the builder could not do' fails. There is also a structural conflict: JobGuard would earn from a write-off at the same time as it earns from a withheld-payment recovery on the same invoice; even with a no-stacking rule, a platform with any income from write-offs has a whisper of interest in the builder giving up rather than recovering. 'JobGuard took 10% of my bad-debt relief' is precisely the sentence that spreads in a word-of-mouth trade. Revenue is £5-£100 a year; the trust cost is not worth it. The six-month reminder and exact-VAT calculation are useful, and belong in the subscription for free.
verdicts.conditions: None. Ship the six-month bad-debt-relief reminder with exact VAT as a fee-free watchdog Finding labelled 'check with your accountant'; record the rejection in D03 v3 so it is not revived; write the no-stacking rule with `withheld_customer_payment` into D03 regardless.
verdicts.key_risk: A fee on the tax side of a customer's non-payment kicks the builder when they are down and gives JobGuard a small interest in write-offs over recovery; word of mouth would carry it.

verdicts.reasons: Listed to reject and correctly so. Regulatory: taking a percentage of an insurance payout is claims-management activity in the FCA's 'financial services or financial product' sector (RAO arts 89G-89M; success_fee_benchmarks §7), so it is not available to JobGuard without authorisation and would place it in the same bucket as the claims firms whose fees the FCA capped at 15-30% after abuses (report §'No rival sells…' table). Fairness: a builder whose delivered materials were stolen or whose site was storm-damaged does not experience an insurer's payout as found money; it is partial restoration of a loss, and a platform slice of it reads as exploiting misfortune (dual entitlement). Who did the work: the builder kept the records and made the claim; JobGuard's contribution — an organised evidence pack — is real but is a document service, which is exactly what I37 charges for honestly. Any survival of this idea would also contaminate the 'we only earn when you're paid' quality signal the report identifies as JobGuard's best pricing asset.
verdicts.conditions: None. Record the rejection in D03 v3 with the FCA claims-management reasoning so no agent revives it; keep I37 (insurer-paid or builder-paid claim-time evidence pack) as the only form of this value.
verdicts.key_risk: Regulated claims-management activity and the claims-firm association, plus a builder who has just suffered a loss watching the platform take a slice of the insurance money.

verdicts.reasons: Every refutation lands. Independence: JobGuard's income would rise whenever a builder moves spend to a different merchant, which is indistinguishable from the outside — and eventually from the inside — from steering; even without merchant money it is the story that ends the watchdog's credibility with builders and merchants alike, and it is the structured form of I65/I66 the founder has already excluded. Attribution: the builder chose the new merchant, negotiated any account, and bears the spec, quality, delivery and credit-terms risk; a lower invoice rate on an alias-matched SKU says nothing about what JobGuard caused, and adjudicating 'same product' is quality judgement the watchdog must not make. Who bears the cost: unlike every other category there is no recovered cash to net against; the 20% share for 12 months is paid out of ordinary cash flow on the builder's own purchasing, which mental-accounting research predicts will feel like a running toll on where they shop (Prelec & Loewenstein taxi-meter effect; report §'The hidden final check'). The benchmark cited in support (P3 at 50% of savings, success_fee_benchmarks §2) is the most resented model in the set and depends on the consultancy being the client's negotiating agent, which JobGuard must never be. It could also harm the builder by nudging a switch to a worse merchant for a fee. I76 already lists switching under 'never qualifies' for these reasons.
verdicts.conditions: None. Record in D11 v3 that no JobGuard fee, credit, signal or feature ever depends on which merchant a builder uses, and that cross-merchant price comparison is at most a fee-free, builder-requested view.
verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard profiting from where the builder shops reads as steering and destroys the watchdog's independence, on an attribution the builder can always dispute.

verdicts.reasons: The cleanest fairness profile in the set: the builder asks, sees the price, approves a Decision, pays, and benefits before they commit to a customer — a coupled payment for a visible service (Prelec & Loewenstein), not a metered surprise. No supplier or merchant money, nothing withheld, no fee on the builder's labour, and the customer never sees or pays for anything. Refutations tried: (1) 'I could do this free' — true for Companies House and the Gazette, so the free layer must be free and the £19 must buy only the paid CRA/CCJ layer; at £8-£10 wholesale plus entity resolution, evidence storage and an inbox Finding, £19 is a fair service margin against Satago at £45-£200/month and TrustOnline at £6-£10 (success_fee_benchmarks §6). (2) Manufacturing anxiety — the real trust danger is not the check but the sell: risk badges on unchecked customers, nags on every quote, or copy that reads as JobGuard vetting the builder's customers would convert a fair service into fear-marketing and could push builders to refuse honest customers. (3) Data misuse — the query must never become a lead, a cross-tenant blacklist ('another JobGuard builder was stiffed by this company') or a CRA marketing footprint; those are the founder's named trust risks. (4) Third-party fairness — business customers expect credit checks, and directors' data under legitimate interests with an Art 14 route is proportionate; individuals must never be run through a business check. Note the healthy conflict direction: a good check reduces JobGuard's own withheld-payment fee base, so the incentive favours the builder. Subcontractors checking a main contractor is the highest-value case and squarely in the builder's interest.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Free data stays free and visible as such (Companies House, Gazette card, CP-1) — the £19 is charged only for the CRA/CCJ layer and the price sheet says what is free. (b) Per-run atomic Decision showing price, sources and check-policy version; failed or `outcome_unknown` runs never charged. (c) No nags, no per-quote prompts beyond one unobtrusive button, and no risk badges, colour verdicts or 'unchecked' warnings on customers who were not checked; copy is 'Findings, not a recommendation' with every line sourced and dated. (d) External sources only: no cross-tenant customer data, no JobGuard-built blacklist, no secondary use of queries; the CRA reseller contract forbids the CRA using JobGuard queries for marketing or footprints. (e) Bound to a named counterparty on a quote or job, capped per quote, rate-limited per tenant, audited; entities only — never a business check on an individual's name (route to I89/I90 under their own rules). (f) In-app view only, watermarked, no raw-report export; the finding text may go in the builder's own evidence pack. (g) D12 v3 (controller/processor split, Art 14 route, Art 14(5)(b) position), D04 provider register entries, D07 retention class for checks kept as recovery evidence, new D14 paid-data-services record, D02 VAT; separate 'data checks' statement lines never mixed with subscription or success fee; real charging behind G4; pilot absorbs costs and labels the charge hypothetical.

revised_revenue.solo: £48 gross (about £28 margin) — unchanged
revised_revenue.firm: £532 gross (about £308 margin) — unchanged; alternative to I88, not additive

verdicts.key_risk: The sell, not the service: risk badges, nags or advisory-sounding copy would turn a fair paid check into fear-marketing and read as JobGuard vetting the builder's customers; any cross-tenant or lead use of check data would breach the founder's named trust lines.

verdicts.reasons: Fair in principle: builder-paid, flat and predictable, which the flat-rate-bias research says tradespeople prefer to a running meter (research note price_level_and_tier_psychology §4; report §'The hidden final check'), and ServiceM8/Satago show allowance packaging is familiar. Refutations that partly land: (1) it adds a second meter beside the founder's fixed live-jobs meter; the report's advice is that the tier comparison should rest on one or two numbers, so a checks allowance on the tier grid muddies the plan choice and can look like drip packaging even though B2B is outside the DMCC rules; (2) unused allowances that lapse feel like waste — a builder paying £12 for three checks and using one has a small monthly reminder of a bad deal; (3) an allowance is 'free at the margin', which raises the temptation to check people who are not customers, so the I87 binding rules must not loosen; (4) a 'use your remaining checks' nudge would be the same fear-marketing risk as I87 in another form; (5) the Firm attribution (£96) is a relabelling of existing price, not new money, and must not be presented as revenue. None of these is a trust breach; they are packaging discipline. Score 3 rather than 4 because the plain per-check option (I87) delivers the same fairness with less to explain.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Presented as an optional add-on line, never as a third axis of the tier grid; the live-jobs count stays the only tier comparator on the pricing page. (b) Per-check purchase (I87) always available; nobody is forced onto a pack. (c) Add-on cancellable any month without notice; either rollover within a quarter or a clear pre-renewal utilisation statement so lapsed checks are a visible choice, not a surprise. (d) No 'use your remaining checks' nags or month-end prompts. (e) Every I87 condition applies unchanged, in particular per-run Decision ('1 of your 12 checks'), quote/job binding, per-quote caps and entity-only checks; allowance never relaxes them. (f) Firm inclusion labelled honestly in internal accounting as attribution, not new cash; overage £15 posts as statement lines, never as a block. (g) D09 v3 (inclusions, overage, notice, cancellation), D05 renewal authority, D02 VAT; charging behind G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £29 (add-on) — unchanged; alternative to I87, not additive
revised_revenue.firm: £96 attributed from the Firm price plus £0 overage — unchanged; a labelled attribution, not new cash

verdicts.key_risk: A second meter that clutters the live-jobs tier choice and a use-it-or-lose-it allowance that turns a fair service into a monthly reminder of waste or a prompt to run checks on people who are not customers.

verdicts.reasons: Net revenue is roughly zero on the idea's own arithmetic and goes slightly negative for Solo once selection is allowed for: the builders shown this screen are exactly those who just paid a fee, so the fee foregone on a switcher is the payer average (about £380 Solo, £450 Small, £625 Firm on the prior step's central catch rates), not the all-builder average the idea used. Against uplifts of £240/£480/£720 that gives about −£13 (Solo), +£4 (Small), +£13 (Firm) per builder-year before churn; one Firm in a hundred churning on the framing (−£14/builder-year) wipes it out. Against that, it is the single most quotable artefact the product can produce: the fee statement is the moment of the sting, and placing 'JobGuard first held this on 14 May' beside a 'pay £99 a month to see it sooner' button is the literal 'knew on day 12, told me on day 60' fact that the research says a terms sentence cannot neutralise (report §'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk'; research note success_fee_psychology §4 on betrayal aversion and dual entitlement, §2 on a windfall turning into a toll once the builder learns it could have come earlier). The idea also claims the hold dates are 'already required' by §14.1; they are not. §14.1's permitted claim states the lock time and that JobGuard found the item afterwards from named sources; printing the signal's first-held date is a D13 v2 transparency choice still to be made, and asserting it as settled hides a real decision. Precedent is absent; the nearest pattern ('upgrade to remove the thing we do to you') is widely disliked. Build cost is low, but the money does not justify the exposure. The symmetrical 'the other plan would have been cheaper' advice belongs in I75's periodic value receipt, where it reads as advice, not on the fee statement where it reads as pressure.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended. If revived: only after I67 exists and I75's two-way comparison has run for at least one billing period in the pilot with perceived-fairness scores no worse than the hidden arm; the plan choice visible at sign-up; the hold-date disclosure settled as an explicit D13 v2 item rather than assumed; the offer shown on the plan page and periodic receipt only, never on the fee statement; copy reviewed as a public statement; D05 plan-change Decision; G4.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈ −£13/yr net (40–60% pay a fee × 15% switch = 6–9 points × (£240 uplift − ≈£380 expected fee foregone among payers)); before any churn effect
revised_revenue.firm: ≈ +£10 to +£13/yr (12–14 points × (£720 − ≈£625)); one churned Firm per 100 shown the screen (−£14/builder-yr) cancels it

verdicts.key_risk: A screenshot of this screen becomes the trade's shorthand for 'JobGuard sat on it and then charged me to stop', collapsing trust in a word-of-mouth market for near-zero revenue.

verdicts.reasons: Cheap on top of I67 and the fairest introduction the product can give, but the revenue case is not there: the foregone trial-job fee is trivial (£12/£15/£18) and the 5-point conversion lift is a guess with no evidence behind it — the report's own trial section says reverse trials have no quantitative uplift data and that trade-specific conversion benchmarks do not exist (report §'Let the trial run until the first job is live'; research note price_level §5). It also reverses a report recommendation without new evidence: the report says to charge the fee normally on the trial job so the builder experiences the real model rather than learning the fee is negotiable (report §'Recommendation', 'The trial'). Two product-realism problems the idea does not price: (1) live mode shows raw cards before the lock-time reconciliation has removed already-in-scope, builder-captured and duplicate candidates, so the trial job exposes the engine's noise (SV-3 measures precision separately for a reason) and costs builder minutes per card; a noisy first job can lower conversion, not raise it; (2) once a builder has watched JobGuard flag things live on job 1, the silence on job 2 under the hidden plan is no longer abstract — it makes the hold-back salient exactly when the builder is deciding whether to trust it. That may push builders to Tell me now (fine if I67 is priced right, but it moves revenue from fee to uplift rather than adding to it) or make them leave. Gaming is bounded by the 90-day ceiling and card-at-switch-live, as for I10. Regulatory: every early card sets disclosed_before_lock (§14.3), so the trial job is fee-free by construction; D13 v2 needs the trial route named; pilot use needs G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval (§14.11). Also note the trial job counts against the live-jobs allowance and should be excluded from the M4-14 meter explicitly. Worth running as a pilot arm, not shipping as the default.
verdicts.conditions: Run it as one arm of I75's randomised first-job pilot, not as the launch default; keep the report's 'charge the fee normally' design in the hidden arm so both models are experienced; measure live-mode false-positive rate and builder minutes per card in the trial; the post-trial choice screen must describe the hidden model honestly including the must-surface rules; only jobs switched live after the choice take the chosen mode; trial job excluded from the concurrency meter; 90-day ceiling; D13 v2 names the trial disclosure route; no production use before G4.

revised_revenue.solo: −£12 foregone trial-job fee; conversion effect unproven, 0–5 points × £348 = £0–£17 → net −£12 to +£5 per trial starter
revised_revenue.firm: −£18 + £0–£71 → net −£18 to +£53 per trial starter; a higher Tell-me-now uptake shifts revenue from fee to uplift rather than adding to it

verdicts.key_risk: Showing the engine live on job 1 makes the hidden plan's silence on job 2 vivid, and exposes pre-reconciliation noise, so the trial can lower trust and conversion instead of raising them.

verdicts.reasons: No direct revenue, but it is the cheapest way to get the one number the whole rev 2.3 model lacks: what the hold-back actually adds to the fee base versus what builders log themselves when told. The report says the pilot must measure recovered money per job and run a priced sign-up page test before anyone is charged (report §'Recommendation'), and §14.17 already requires measuring perceived fairness and whether hiding hurt the workflow; a randomised hidden-versus-live first job is the direct instrument for both, and it stands on its own even if I67 (the paid live plan) is rejected. Refutations that stick: the pilot is 10–20 builders, so three price points across three tiers is not a test of anything — the idea concedes this, and the correction is the real priced sign-up test before G4; choices at hypothetical prices overstate willingness to pay; flat-rate bias (research note success_fee_psychology §2, Prelec & Loewenstein; Lambrecht & Skiera) predicts some builders will pick the flat live plan even when the fee would have been cheaper, which flatters uptake and should be read as a preference signal, not a price. Two corrections to the design: (1) the idea repeats I73's error that §14.1 requires printing 'JobGuard first held this on [date]' — it does not; whether hold dates appear on the value receipt is a D13 v2 decision the founder and legal must take deliberately, because the research says that fact is the most dangerous one the product can print; (2) two cards per tier turns the plan page into a six-way grid, which the report's compromise-effect evidence says weakens the comparison (report §'Three tiers work…'); present disclosure mode as one toggle per tier with one sentence. The record changes (D09 v3 disclosure_mode, D13 v2 disclosure routes and reconcile-only final check on live jobs, D11 next-version signal, D12 v3 onboarding text, D05 plan change, D01 wording) are plan-text tasks in the SV-0 pattern, cheap and correct; none is approval and an agent cannot mark them approved.
verdicts.conditions: Treat the pilot price cohorts as qualitative and run the report's priced sign-up page test before G4; make hold-date display on receipts an explicit D13 v2 decision, not an assumed requirement; collapse the choice to one toggle per tier; the comparison must always print both directions; records advance only as new proposed versions; pilot arms need G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval before any shadow processing of real data; the live arm's final check runs reconcile-only and is recorded; keep the randomised first-job arm even if I67 is dropped, because the hold-back's incremental fee base is the number the model needs.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct; determines whether a £240/yr live uplift is over- or under-priced; the useful output is the live arm's hypothetical would-have-been fee per builder-year versus what those builders logged after being told
revised_revenue.firm: £0 direct; same test against £720/yr; thin cohorts mean directional results only

verdicts.key_risk: The instrument is too small to price anything, so the founder reads directional pilot choices as a price, and the receipt's hold-date line — adopted as if already required — becomes the product's most damaging sentence.

verdicts.reasons: The measurement is clean but the attribution and the fairness story fail, and the money is smaller than claimed. The builder makes the call; JobGuard drafted a letter. Fee-fairness research says people accept a fee where the provider visibly did work they could not do and reject it where the value feels like their own (report §'The hidden final check…', Xia et al.; Kahneman's dual entitlement) — a 20% cut of the builder's own negotiation is the second story. The idea's own safety valve makes the fee voluntary: the builder-favourable 'this was a market fall' attestation stops accrual with no proof demanded, so every rational builder attests on every review and the category yields nothing; the alternative — demanding proof — is exactly the resented posture. A 20% rate on prospective savings is a second fee basis alongside '10% of settled recovered principal', breaking the one-number story the report favours (10% identical everywhere; report §'Three tiers work…') and moving JobGuard toward the P3 cost-consultancy model the benchmark note calls the most resented in its table (research note success_fee_benchmarks §2, summary table); flat-fee rivals already attack percentage models once sums grow (§6). Counterfactual is weak: merchant reps renegotiate account rates annually anyway, materials prices moved sharply in 2024–25, and Prolo is raising money to do SME merchant procurement on a flat basis (research note construction_platforms §4). Revenue haircut: half of builders sending a letter in a year is too high — most Solos buy at the counter on a cash-account rate and hold no M2-1 agreed-rate history, so the two-settled-lines entry test excludes them; use 20/35/50%, then halve for the attestation and the surcharge-offset hold. Every pound also requires the M4-7 bank feed (D10/D04/D12) to prove settlement and lands as monthly £5–£30 fee lines, the isolated-loss form the research says hurts most (success_fee_psychology §2). Build is 3–4 tasks plus D03 v3, a new D01 basis and ceiling, D05 extension, M4-13 terms and an M4-9 derivation scope beyond job — M4/M5-era work for a category that at best earns Firm a few hundred pounds. Merchant-side risk is real too: merchants will recognise a JobGuard-drafted letter, and the safest posture is the one the idea already states (no merchant relationship, ever). Deliver the letter and tracker as I77 instead.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended as a share. The letter, SKU table and 12-month savings tracker are worth building (via I77). If a share were ever revisited: 10% not 20%, same basis language as D01, only after pilot fairness data on I77's flat form, and never before M2-5, M4-7/M4-8 and G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £10–£20/yr (20% send a letter × £945 saving × 20% share × ~50% surviving attestation/offset holds ≈ £19; ≈ £10 at 10%); needs a linked bank feed
revised_revenue.firm: £250–£490/yr (50% × £9,800 × 20% × 50% ≈ £490; ≈ £245 at 10%; £1,000 per-merchant ceiling rarely binds across three merchants)

verdicts.key_risk: 'JobGuard takes a fifth of the discount I negotiated myself' spreads by word of mouth while the builder-favourable attestation quietly reduces the actual fee to near zero — the worst of both.

verdicts.reasons: Small, honest, cheap, and fully in the builder's interest: a fixed price for a letter built from their own purchase history and a tracker, with the builder keeping every pound. The refutations are about size, not shape. £49 per round is a taxi-meter charge on a £29 plan and the SKU-by-SKU purchase table is something a Builder-tier customer will reasonably expect to be included (incumbents put bill capture and purchase orders in mid/top tiers rather than per-use; research note uk_trade_job_software §5 inferences); small flat add-ons are normal in this market (Tradify's £10/month website add-on) but the idea's uptake assumptions of 30/40/50% for a £15/month Buying watch are unmeasured and high for Solos who buy at the counter. Rounds per year of 0.5/2/5 are plausible for Small and Firm, generous for Solo. The better packaging is to make the rate-review letter a tier differentiator for Builder and Firm (its value shows up as tier mix, which the report says is where premium should show) and sell Buying watch only as a Solo add-on. Build is 1–2 tasks after M2-1 and M2-4, mostly shared with the letter template and an approved send command through the outbox (§5.3); charging needs a D09 v3 add-on SKU and period_obligation extension, D05 and G4. No D01/D03 change, no success-fee basis creep, no gaming surface. Copy must say the builder negotiates and that JobGuard has no merchant relationship, otherwise a 'price review' feature reads as a buying-group tie-in.
verdicts.conditions: Pick this over I76, not both; fold the letter into Builder/Firm tiers and offer Buying watch as a Solo add-on rather than per-round charges; D09 v3 defines the SKU, VAT and period obligation; the letter is a builder-authorised send with an approved Decision; explicit 'JobGuard has no merchant relationship' statement on the feature; measure round counts and uptake in the pilot before pricing; not before M2-4; charging behind G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £10–£18/yr (0.2 rounds × £49 ≈ £10; or Buying watch at 10% uptake × £180 ≈ £18)
revised_revenue.firm: £70–£150/yr (3 rounds × £49 ≈ £147; or 40% × £180 = £72); £0 as a line if folded into the Firm tier, where it supports the £119 price instead

verdicts.key_risk: Builders expect the purchase-history letter to be part of the subscription, so a separate charge earns tens of pounds a year and mild irritation rather than revenue.

verdicts.reasons: Cleanest chain in the set and the smallest money, and the chain is weaker than it looks. The premise that the input tax would otherwise be lost is overstated: HMRC has discretion to accept alternative evidence of a supply where no valid VAT invoice exists, so a chunk of the flagged items were reclaimable anyway, and most bookkeepers already chase missing VAT invoices — Dext and Hubdoc flag them on flat plans (report §'UK builders already pay £25–£45…'). Proving the return-inclusion step requires an approved accounting connector (SV-7; M5-1 Codat or M5-2 Xero) or MTD evidence, which is M5-era, and per-invoice return inclusion is awkward to prove even then. The resulting fee lines are £2–£20 each, which the idea itself admits look petty on a statement, and they add a third fee basis ('input tax reclaimed') to D01 alongside recovered principal — more complexity in the one-number story for a few pounds. Flat-rate scheme exclusion removes a third of Solos. No product charges a success fee on input VAT for small firms (research note success_fee_benchmarks §5 gaps), and AP recovery auditors bundle VAT recovery into 20–30% contingency scopes only at enterprise scale (§1). Revenue after a 50% haircut for HMRC's alternative-evidence discretion and the bookkeeper counterfactual is £2–£3 Solo, £15–£25 Small, £50–£80 Firm — not worth D03 v3, a D01 wording change, D02 review, a new derivation scope and a connector dependency. The right move is the idea's own option B: ship the cited missing_vat_invoice Decision as a fee-free M2-5 discrepancy check and count it as subscription value on the VALUE-2 receipt, labelled as an aid to VAT records, not tax advice.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended as a fee category. Build the missing_vat_invoice Decision inside M2-5 fee-free, with tenant VAT-status facts as versioned inputs, the 'aid, not advice; JobGuard does not file' label, and the builder-favourable 'I had already asked' rule; count evidenced outcomes on the value receipt. Revisit a fee only if pilot data shows recovered input tax per builder-year above roughly £500 for Small and Firm and an approved connector exists.

revised_revenue.solo: £1–£3/yr (42% eligible × £12 × ~50% haircut for HMRC alternative-evidence discretion and the bookkeeper counterfactual)
revised_revenue.firm: £50–£80/yr (£152 × ~50%); all contingent on an approved accounting connector (SV-7 / M5-1 / M5-2) proving return inclusion

verdicts.key_risk: A £2.40 fee line on a VAT reclaim makes the whole success-fee model look petty on the statement, for revenue that does not cover the connector work needed to prove it.

verdicts.reasons: The idea's own choice of the flat form is right and the percentage variant should never be built: a cut of a tax refund is the refund-firm model the benchmark note flags as a reputational neighbour (research note success_fee_benchmarks §5; R&D contingency criticism), and the increment JobGuard genuinely causes cannot be measured honestly. The flat pack is defensible but late and small. It sits on the I25 CIS module, which in the plan is M4-22 (CIS verification, deductions and payment reconciliation, after M4-21 VAT/DRC work) with adviser-approved fixtures — so this is end-of-M4 at the earliest. Willingness to pay: Xero sells CIS as a £5/month add-on (research note construction_platforms), the accountant does the year-end reclaim, and a reconciled deduction schedule with a chase letter for missing statements is useful but modest; £59/year is plausible, uptake among CIS-eligible builders maybe half. Archetype fit is narrow: Solos are mostly domestic and outside CIS (30%), Firms at £2m are as often main contractors as subs. Revenue after uptake is £5–£10 Solo, £10–£20 Small, £20–£35 Firm per builder-year — too small to justify building early, cheap enough to add once M4-22 exists (a year-end export plus a statement-request letter is 1–2 tasks). Regulatory: the flat form needs only D09 (add-on SKU) plus the existing 'aid, not advice; no 64-8 authority; JobGuard does not file' labelling; HMRC repayment evidence via the bank feed brings D10/D12. No gaming surface on the flat form.
verdicts.conditions: Flat form only, never the percentage variant; not before M4-22 ships with adviser-approved fixtures; price as a £59/£99 year-end add-on under D09 v3 or fold into the Firm tier; every output labelled as an aid to CIS records, not tax advice, with no filing or agent role; no marketing as 'we get your tax back'; measure CIS-eligible share and uptake in the pilot before committing build time.

revised_revenue.solo: £5–£10/yr flat (30% CIS × ~50% uptake × £59 ≈ £9); percentage variant £0 — do not build

verdicts.key_risk: It cannot exist until late M4 and then earns tens of pounds a year; the only way to make it earn more is the percentage form, which imports the refund-firm stain.

verdicts.reasons: The mechanism is honest — contractor error, inspectable arithmetic, cash paid after a Decision and a correction request, mirroring the cash-only supplier_overcharge rule in §14.7 — but the revenue rests on two assumptions that do not survive contact with how CIS corrections actually happen. Contractors rarely pay a sub the over-deducted difference in cash; the normal fixes are amending the monthly CIS return and adjusting the next payment run, or the sub simply recovering it from HMRC through set-off or self-assessment. The idea's own rules hold the first for review and fold the second into I79 fee-free, so the qualifying pool is a minority of a minority: with affected invoices at 10% rather than 20% and cash corrections at 25% rather than 50%, revenue is about £3 Solo, £14 Small, £54 Firm per builder-year. Subs also will not press contractors they depend on, which the idea concedes and rightly treats as fee-free. The dependency chain is long: M4-22 CIS module, a materials split on the sub's outgoing invoices, M4-7/M4-8 settlement allocation, a correction-request send command, a derivation identity beyond job scope (M4-9 generalisation), D03 v3, D01 wording, and D12 Article 14 handling for named individuals on contractor statements. That is 1–2 tasks plus four record changes for a category that at best earns a Firm £50–£70. No precedent exists; the closest is AP recovery audit's pricing-and-tax-error class at 20–30% contingency for enterprises (research note success_fee_benchmarks §1). The check itself is real watchdog value and belongs inside M4-22 fee-free, labelled as an aid; a fee category should be reopened only if pilot data shows contractor cash corrections are common.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended as a fee category. Ship the cited cis_over_deduction Decision inside M4-22 as a fee-free check with the correction request optional and in the builder's name, 'chose not to chase' recorded as a fee-free outcome, and outcomes shown on the value receipt. Reopen only with pilot evidence of contractor cash corrections above roughly £1,000 per Firm-year, and then under D03 v3, D01, D12 and G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £2–£5/yr (£60k contractor work × 30% materials × 20% × 10% of invoices affected × 25% corrected in cash × 10% fee × 30% CIS share ≈ £2.70)
revised_revenue.firm: £40–£70/yr (same chain ≈ £54); all after M4-22 and the M4-7 bank feed

verdicts.key_risk: The qualifying event — a contractor paying the difference in cash, tied to the case — is rare in practice, so the category earns almost nothing while adding a fourth fee basis to D01/D03 and a long M4 dependency chain.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on the lens's central test. The screen pairs a fee JobGuard has just earned with 'we first held this on 14 May; pay £99 a month and you would have seen it then'. That is JobGuard profiting from a positional advantage and then selling the removal of that advantage, which is exactly what the dual-entitlement research (report §'The hidden final check', citing Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler) says a reasonable person judges unfair, and the report is explicit that a written rationale cannot neutralise it (Cain et al.). It goes beyond the decided shadow-bill rule: the founder's decision permits a fee on a catch revealed after lock; it does not permit charging to un-withhold, and offering that converts the only surviving rationale for the hold-back ('an independent second check after your own bill') into a priced silence. The symmetry defence does not cure it: telling a no-catch builder to downgrade is honest advice, but it changes nothing about what the fee-bearing builder reads on this screen. The idea also misstates §14.1: the permitted claim is anchored on the lock time and says 'JobGuard found it afterwards'; nothing in §14.1 requires printing the pre-lock hold date on the fee statement (evidence dates appear at reveal under §14.5, which is honest, but pairing that date with a price is a choice, not an obligation). By its own arithmetic it is money-neutral (≈ +£1/+£15/+£18 net a year) while producing, in its own words, the most quotable artefact JobGuard will ever make. That is the worst possible trade in a word-of-mouth trade. It also depends entirely on I67, the paid 'Tell me now' plan, which fails the same test.
verdicts.conditions: None; rejected. The only fair thing to show on a fee statement is what §14.1 already permits: the lock time, the sources, the settled amount, the fee and the retained amount, with the evidence chain. If the founder wants an exit at the moment of the sting, the exit must not be a paid tier: either a free opt-out from the hidden model (a different idea, with the commercial consequence that opted-out builders earn JobGuard no catch fees) or nothing.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected; the idea's own net estimate was ≈ +£1/yr)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0 (rejected; the idea's own net estimate was ≈ +£15/yr)
revised_revenue.firm: £0 (rejected; the idea's own net estimate was ≈ +£18/yr)

verdicts.key_risk: A screenshot of 'pay us monthly and we would have told you in May' becomes the story of JobGuard in every builders' WhatsApp group: the protection-racket reading the research predicts, attached to a real fee the builder just paid.

verdicts.reasons: The demonstration half of this idea survives refutation. On the trial job the builder sees every card as it arises, logs the work themselves through Log an extra (builder capture, fee-free under §14.2), bills it and keeps 100%. JobGuard shows its work before asking for anything, which is the operational-transparency and reciprocity effect the research supports (Buell & Norton, research note success_fee_psychology §3). The 'no fee on the trial job' is not a discretionary waiver: under D13 and §14.3, a signal shown before lock sets disclosed_before_lock and is permanently ineligible, so once cards are shown early the departure from the report's 'charge the fee on the trial job' advice is structurally required, not a commercial choice. The refutations that do land: (1) the choice screen at the trial's lock offers a paid 'Tell me now' plan against Standard, which reintroduces priced silence (see I73/I75) and turns a fair demonstration into a sales device for the withholding; (2) going quiet from job 2 can read as bait-and-switch unless the transition is stated plainly at the moment it happens; (3) cards on a real job can push a builder to chase a homeowner for work they meant as goodwill (Simply Business survey: 34% do extras unpaid, often deliberately), and false positives cost the builder minutes; (4) the 'fee that would have applied' illustration must not drift into the §14.1 forbidden claims. With those removed, a reasonable builder would see one free, fully disclosed job followed by an explicitly explained standard model as fair and in their interest.
verdicts.conditions: (1) The trial job runs in disclosed mode with every card carrying the standing notice from §14.2; cards never create a variation, invoice line or Decision on the builder's behalf; the builder logs via Log an extra. (2) Every trial-job signal sets disclosed_before_lock=true at creation (D13 v2 route 'trial_disclosed'), so fee-ineligibility is enforced by the predicate, not by a waiver. (3) The end-of-trial screen must not present a paid live plan as an alternative unless I67 has separately passed a fairness test in the pilot (see I75 conditions); absent that, it is a plain explanation of the standard model in one sentence (the report's 'independent second check after your own bill, like a proofread'), with must-surface rules stated. (4) Every card offers 'goodwill, not charging' as a first-class, final, fee-free disposition. (5) Any 'fee that would have applied' figure is a labelled illustration only; no 'JobGuard saved you £X' or 'you would have missed this' wording (§14.1 forbidden claims). (6) Onboarding says before job 1 that job 2 onward is hidden until lock; the transition is confirmed on screen at the trial lock, never silent. (7) Must-surface rules unchanged on the trial job. (8) Needs D12 v3 onboarding text and D13 v2; pilot use only after G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval (§14.11); an agent cannot mark these approved.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct; forgoes ≈ £12 (one job's central fee); speculative +£17/yr per trial starter from a 5-point conversion lift if the trial converts better; the 'higher Tell me now uptake' component is removed by the conditions
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0 direct; forgoes ≈ £15; speculative +£35/yr per trial starter; Tell me now uptake component removed
revised_revenue.firm: £0 direct; forgoes ≈ £18; speculative +£71/yr per trial starter; Tell me now uptake component removed

verdicts.key_risk: If the end-of-trial screen prices a live plan against the hidden one, the demonstration becomes the moment the builder learns that JobGuard's silence is for sale, and the fair introduction turns into the racket reading.

verdicts.reasons: Two parts of this instrument are the strongest builder-interest moves in the whole paid-disclosure lens and survive refutation: the pilot measurement (perceived fairness after lock, false-positive rate and builder minutes per card, share of 'goodwill, not charging', which sources produce real catches, plan switches with reasons, churn intent by arm) directly tests whether the hidden model is tolerable before anyone is charged, and the D13 v2 change that any pre-lock reveal route sets disclosed_before_lock at signal creation makes the builder's fee-free guarantee structural. Publishing each builder's own arithmetic on the value receipt is honest. The parts that fail: the choice screen pricing Standard against 'Tell me now', the price-variant cohorts for that tier, metric (6) ('if the would-have-been fee exceeds £240 the uplift is under-priced') and D09 v3 disclosure_mode with a price per tier all exist to discover the price of JobGuard's silence. Using a pilot to set the uplift equal to the fee the hold-back would have earned is the dual-entitlement problem written as a spreadsheet, and if that method ever became known it would confirm the 'knew on day 12' reading the research says cannot be neutralised. The idea also misreads §14.1: the permitted claim is anchored on the lock time; printing 'JobGuard first held this on [date]' on a running comparison is a design choice, defensible only if it matches what the reveal already shows (§14.5 evidence dates) and carries no price beside it. Randomising real pilot builders between arms is fine only as a consented pilot term. Kept, with its purpose reordered: first measure whether the hidden model itself reads fair, then whether a disclosed mode (offered free) changes that, and only if builders say a paid live option is fair does any pricing record follow.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Pilot arms run only after G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval, with randomisation disclosed and accepted as a pilot term; hypothetical fees only. (2) The live arm is a free disclosed mode during the pilot; no hypothetical uplift price is attached to it unless a separately consented cohort is testing that exact question. (3) Add a metric: perceived fairness of the Standard model when a paid live option is shown beside it versus when it is not; if the paid option lowers the fairness of Standard, I67, I73 and the choice screen are dropped. (4) D09 v3 gains no disclosure_mode price per tier until metric (3) passes; the D13 v2 changes (tenant_plan_live, paid_pre_lock_reveal, trial_disclosed and source-scoped routes all set disclosed_before_lock at creation; live-mode jobs run reconcile-only; must-surface rules unchanged on every plan) are adopted regardless because they only strengthen the builder guarantee. (5) The value receipt shows the other plan's arithmetic as a labelled illustration, never 'you would have kept £X'; any hold date shown must be the same evidence date shown at reveal and never appear beside a price. (6) The D11 'mode changed within N days of switch-live' signal is advisory only, never a penalty. (7) Metric (6) is reframed from 'is the uplift under-priced' to 'what did the hold-back cost builders in the hidden arm', reported to the founder as a fairness input, not a price-setting input. (8) Results are directional (10–20 builders); no charging decision rests on them alone; an agent cannot mark D01, D05, D09, D11, D12 or D13 approved.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct. Output narrowed: fairness of the hidden model, false-positive rate, source yield and the cost of the hold-back to builders; the Solo uplift price test is withdrawn unless the added fairness metric passes
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0 direct; same narrowing; the £99/£79 price test is withdrawn unless the fairness metric passes
revised_revenue.firm: £0 direct; same narrowing; the £179/£199 price test is withdrawn unless the fairness metric passes

verdicts.key_risk: The pilot design itself becomes evidence of intent: an instrument whose stated purpose is to price early disclosure at the fee JobGuard would otherwise earn proves the 'silence for money' reading if it is ever described in a deck, a terms change or a journalist's inbox.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutations: (a) who did the work: the builder makes the call and holds the merchant relationship, so a share of the saving reads as 'a cut of my own negotiation' (report §'The hidden final check': fees are accepted where the provider visibly did work the customer could not easily do, resented where the value felt like their own); at 20% for 12 months on a monthly meter this is the P3 cost-consultant model the research calls the most resented in its table, and a second, higher percentage on a JobGuard statement muddies the single '10% only when you're paid' promise that is JobGuard's identity. (b) Watchdog independence: the design is clean on merchant money (JobGuard never contacts, negotiates with or receives anything from a merchant) but creates a subtler conflict: JobGuard earns more when the evidenced prior rate is higher, so it has a reason to let a builder keep overpaying until a letter is sent rather than prompting 'you are paying above your agreed rate or band' for free. (c) Attribution: market falls, list-price cuts and the builder's own periodic haggling are indistinguishable from JobGuard's contribution; the builder-favourable attestation (no proof demanded) handles this well. (d) Customer relationship: untouched. What survives: the fee is opt-in per round at letter send with explicit terms (the same case-opening pattern as §14.7 withheld payments), the letter and evidence table are visibly JobGuard's work, the 12-month invoice-by-invoice tracking against the new rate is real work the builder cannot easily do, the £1,000 ceiling and 12-month stop bound it, the lower 10% basis on backdated cash refunds follows §14.8's 'never choose the rule that pays JobGuard most', and the builder keeps the large majority. A reasonable builder can see that as fair at JobGuard's ordinary 10%, with the flat I77 option beside it; at 20% they cannot.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Rate is 10%, JobGuard's single public rate, not 20%; the 12-month window and £1,000-per-(merchant, letter) ceiling stay. (2) At the moment the builder opens a rate review, I77's flat option is offered on the same screen so the share is a chosen basis, never the only way to get the letter. (3) Any 'you are paying above your agreed rate / band' prompt stays free and immediate and is never delayed, suppressed or gated to grow the prior-rate base; the rate-review offer appears beside such prompts, never instead of them; this is written into D11 as an integrity rule. (4) The builder can stop accrual at any time by attesting a general price cut, market fall or merchant switch, with no proof demanded; JobGuard's I28 benchmark data may never be used to contest that attestation. (5) The letter is built only from the builder's own purchase history; cross-builder benchmark bands are opt-in and the builder's data never feeds bands without consent. (6) Every monthly line is shown netted on one statement ('saved £X against your old rate; JobGuard's share £Y; you kept £Z'), with the remaining months and ceiling visible. (7) The letter and statement state that JobGuard has no arrangement with any merchant. (8) Backdated cash refunds use the ordinary 10% supplier_overcharge basis with the (tenant, invoice_line_id) uniqueness constraint; credit notes and account credits never qualify. (9) Perceived fairness is tested in the pilot with hypothetical figures; if builders resent the share, ship I77 only. (10) Needs D03 v3, D01 (category wording at 10%), D02, D05 and M4-13 terms accepted at letter send; live only behind G4.

revised_revenue.solo: ≈ £48 blended at 10% (£27–£135 for a Solo who runs one review) plus ≈ £2 from backdated cash refunds; lower where builders pick the flat I77 option
revised_revenue.small_firm: ≈ £168 blended at 10% (£192–£480 for a firm that runs a review) plus ≈ £10 from backdated cash refunds; lower where builders pick I77
revised_revenue.firm: ≈ £490 blended at 10% (£560–£1,400 for a firm that runs reviews; the £1,000 ceiling binds less at 10%) plus ≈ £30 from backdated cash refunds; lower where builders pick I77

verdicts.key_risk: The fee creates an incentive for JobGuard to let a builder keep overpaying a merchant until a chargeable letter exists; if any free overpayment prompt is ever found to have been delayed for that reason, the watchdog's independence is gone and the story is the same as the shadow-bill racket reading.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutations mostly fail. Harm to the builder: none; a fixed, visible price at the moment they choose to start a round, and they keep 100% of whatever they negotiate. Independence: no merchant money, no introducer role, the builder sends the letter in their own name. Withheld information: none; the letter is built from data the builder already has in JobGuard. Customer relationship: untouched. Fairness: a flat charge for a defined deliverable is the form the mental-accounting research says people prefer over a running meter (research note success_fee_psychology §2, Prelec & Loewenstein; Lambrecht & Skiera), and small flat add-ons are normal in this market (Tradify's £10/month Instant Website, research note uk_trade_job_software §1). Two refutations partly land and become conditions: a 'review my prices' feature can be mistaken for a merchant-funded buying-group tie-in unless the no-merchant-relationship rule is stated on the letter and pricing page; and selling packs gives JobGuard a reason to nag or to gate free overpayment prompts behind the paid round, which would be withholding for revenue. The 'what you saved' tracker must remain a labelled illustration so it does not become a counterfactual claim.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Letter and pricing page state that JobGuard has no arrangement with, and takes nothing from, any merchant. (2) Free prompts ('paying above agreed rate / band') are never gated behind the pack; the pack offer appears beside them only, rate-limited, and only where the builder's own data shows a plausible case. (3) Copy says the builder negotiates; no 'JobGuard gets you a better price'. (4) The savings tracker is labelled an illustration against the old agreed rate; no 'JobGuard saved you £X'. (5) Benchmark bands are opt-in and the builder's data never feeds them without consent. (6) The charge is an approved Decision at round start, VAT stated, refundable if no letter is produced; D09 add-on SKU (per round or monthly) defined and approved before any charge; G4 for live charging. (7) Not additive with I76: a builder who takes the flat round pays no share on that merchant's savings.

revised_revenue.solo: £25 (0.5 rounds × £49) or £54 on the £15/month add-on at 30% uptake, unchanged

verdicts.key_risk: Being mistaken for a buying group or merchant-funded scheme; the flat price is only trustworthy if the no-merchant-money rule is visible every time the feature appears.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutations: (a) 'you took 10% of my VAT reclaim' is the refund-firm shape; but unlike CIS (I80) the money here is a genuine loss without a valid VAT invoice, the sequence Decision → invoice received → return filed is provable from JobGuard's own immutable timestamps, and the routine reclaim of properly evidenced input tax is excluded, so the base is only the increment JobGuard caused. (b) Attribution: bookkeepers and accountants catch many of these; the builder-favourable 'already asked' attestation handles it, but the list of never-qualifies must also cover 'the supplier sends proper invoices on its own cycle anyway'. (c) Withholding incentive: the fee requires the Decision to precede the invoice, so JobGuard is rewarded for flagging promptly, not for sitting on it; incentives align with the builder. (d) Data reach: proving return inclusion needs an accounting connector or MTD evidence; adding a connector to the builder's tax records purely to evidence a £2 fee would be seen as intrusion for pettiness, and pettiness is the real trust cost: £5–£20 lines on a statement invite 'they charge you for your own VAT'. (e) Customer relationship and watchdog independence: untouched; nothing from suppliers or HMRC. A reasonable builder can see 10% of VAT they would otherwise have lost, spotted by a match they did not do, with a no-questions attestation, as fair; most would find it petty. Kept only with a de minimis and a preference for the fee-free form.

(2) If charged: 10% under the ordinary cumulative machinery per (tenant, VAT period), with a de minimis so any period whose fee would be under £10 is fee-free and labelled as such. (3) Never on the flat-rate scheme or partial exemption; tenant VAT status is a versioned input the builder confirms. (4) Attestation extended to 'already asked' and 'supplier would have issued it anyway'; no proof demanded; fee-free on doubt. (6) The Decision is raised as soon as the 30-day window ends, never delayed; the interval is a D11 monitored metric. (7) All output labelled 'an aid to your VAT records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file returns'. (8) Needs D03 v3, D01 base wording, D02 and D12; live only behind G4.

verdicts.reasons: Flat form survives refutation: a reconciled schedule of deductions suffered against statements and bank receipts, letters the builder sends to contractors who are legally required to issue statements, and an export for the accountant is visible work, priced in advance, optional, and JobGuard keeps nothing of the refund. No merchant or contractor money, no customer involvement, nothing withheld. It matches how the market already prices CIS (Xero's £5/month CIS returns, research note construction_platforms_and_ai §1). The refutation that lands is against the percentage variant: 'you took 10% of my tax refund' is the refund-firm story the research flags as a reputational neighbour (research note success_fee_benchmarks §5); the counterfactual (the accountant would have found the missing statement at year-end) is weak; the evidence-increment limitation is too subtle to survive word of mouth; and it requires reading the builder's bank feed for HMRC repayments to evidence a fee. The idea itself recommends the flat form; this verdict makes that binding. Residual risk on the flat form is positioning: any 'we get your tax back' wording moves JobGuard into tax-agent territory it must not occupy.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on 'who bears the cost'. A CIS deduction suffered, even one wrongly applied to materials or at 30% for a verified sub, is credited to the sub in full: sole traders claim it through self-assessment and companies set it off monthly via EPS and reclaim any excess after year end. The idea's premise that a contractor cash correction is 'cash they were not going to get' is wrong for a CIS-registered sub; the builder's loss is timing and hassle, not principal. Charging 10% of the whole corrected amount therefore takes 10% of money that was already the builder's for the benefit of getting it months earlier, an effective cost a reasonable sub would call unfair once their accountant explains it, and word of mouth would carry that explanation. Worse, the fee design misaligns JobGuard with the builder's relationship: JobGuard earns only if the sub confronts the contractor they depend on for work, and nothing if the sub lets it resolve through HMRC, so JobGuard has a reason to steer subs toward the confrontational route. That is a relationship harm created by the fee, not merely tolerated by it. The detection itself is useful and fair as a free check with inspectable arithmetic ('your contractor deducted on materials; here is the sum; it will come back through HMRC, or you can ask them to correct it'), which belongs in the I25 CIS module and the I79 flat pack. Cases where a contractor never reports or pays over the deduction are genuine losses, but those are missing-statement disputes already covered by I79's fee-free reconciliation, not this category.
verdicts.conditions: None; rejected as a fee category. Fold the cis_over_deduction detection and correction-request letter into the I25 CIS module and I79 flat pack as fee-free features, with the arithmetic shown, 'chose not to chase' respected, and the HMRC route explained alongside the contractor route.
