verdicts.reasons: The legal lens sinks this without needing the trust argument. Variant A (merchant pays a flat connector fee): JobGuard's invoice-checking is a function the builder expects to be performed impartially and in good faith, which is exactly the 'relevant function' definition in Bribery Act 2010 s.3(3)-(5); a payment from the checked party to the checker is capable of being an advantage under s.2 (receiving) if a reasonable UK person would see it as intended to induce or reward softer checks (s.5 objective test), and the merchant carries s.1/s.7 exposure. A flat, non-contingent, disclosed fee lowers the risk but does not remove it, because the test turns on the expectation of impartiality, not the fee formula. Separately, the secret and half-secret commission cases (Hurstanger v Wilson [2007] EWCA Civ 299; Wood v Commercial First [2021] EWCA Civ 471; Expert Tooling v Engie [2025] EWCA Civ 292, cited second-hand in research note success_fee_benchmarks §2) bite wherever one party owes another a duty to act in their interest or give disinterested advice, which is the watchdog's entire proposition; the remedy is rescission and disgorgement, and only the principal's fully informed consent to amount and basis cures it, not a line in standard terms. Any 'independent' or 'impartial' claim in marketing would then breach the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 (B2B misleading advertising) and CAP Code 3.1. Variant B (pooled rebates, JobGuard keeps ~1 point): JobGuard becomes a purchasing agent taking commission, so the same Bribery Act and fiduciary analysis applies, plus three more. (i) If merchants pay pooled rebates to JobGuard for onward distribution, JobGuard holds builders' money (AGENTS §3 hard rule) and is prima facie providing money remittance under the Payment Services Regulations 2017 Sch 1 para 1(f) unless the commercial-agent exclusion (Sch 1 Part 2 para 2(b)) applies, which the FCA reads narrowly (PERG 15); that means either a solicitor's perimeter opinion or authorisation as a small payment institution (6-12 months, safeguarding, MLR 2017 supervision). (ii) VAT: a merchant volume rebate is a reduction in consideration requiring merchant-to-builder credit notes (VAT Regulations 1995 regs 15C/38); a merchant-to-JobGuard 'commission' plus JobGuard-to-builder payment breaks that chain and creates Elida Gibbs-type third-party-consideration accounting. (iii) Competition Act 1998 Chapter I: joint purchasing by small builders is low-risk under the CMA Horizontal Agreements Guidance at small shares, but JobGuard already holds every builder's prices, so hub-and-spoke information-exchange risk arises, and BUILD_PLAN §11 already excludes cross-tenant rate learning. NMBS escapes these problems by being the buying-group principal that invoices and guarantees payment; JobGuard cannot be that. Cost to make A lawful: an adequate-procedures policy (s.7 defence), merchant contracts with no-influence covenants, per-builder informed-consent architecture and abandonment of any independence claim, roughly £10-20k of legal setup for about £6 per builder-year. Cost to make B lawful: PSR perimeter work or authorisation plus VAT restructuring, disproportionate and still requiring JobGuard to hold or route funds. The lawful cousin is the builder-paid pass-through in I66. Not certain legal advice; the fiduciary characterisation and PSR exclusion need a solicitor if the founder ever revisits this.
verdicts.conditions: None that make it worth doing. If A were pursued regardless: written Bribery Act adequate-procedures policy; merchant contracts forbidding any influence on checks and any outcome-linked payment; the fee amount disclosed to every builder with recorded informed consent; no 'independent' or 'impartial' marketing claims; D11 conflict-of-interest register entry; solicitor sign-off on the fiduciary analysis. B cannot be structured without either holding funds (forbidden by AGENTS §3) or Payment Services Regulations authorisation, so it is blocked as designed.

revised_revenue.solo: £0-£6 (A only, after ~£10-20k legal setup); B £0 as designed, since JobGuard cannot lawfully retain a slice without an agency-commission structure and a compliant money path

verdicts.key_risk: A merchant paying the party that checks that merchant's invoices is the Bribery Act s.2 / secret-commission fact pattern; Variant B additionally requires JobGuard to hold or remit builders' money, which is both a hard rule breach and a Payment Services Regulations 2017 perimeter problem.

verdicts.reasons: Legally the clean version of the merchant relationship. No consideration flows from merchant to JobGuard, so there is no Bribery Act s.2 receipt and no secret-commission exposure; the admin fee comes from the principal and is disclosed, which satisfies the Hurstanger/Wood line. The merchant pays the builder directly, so JobGuard never holds funds and no Payment Services Regulations 2017 or MLR 2017 question arises. Trade-body precedent (FMB at TradePoint, Checkatrade at Wickes, per the report) shows merchant-discount benefits run without FCA involvement. Five legal costs remain. (1) Credit broking: many merchant 'trade accounts' are credit; sole traders and partnerships of up to three are 'individuals' under CCA 1974 s.189, and introducing them to a lender by way of business is credit broking (RAO art 36A) unless an exclusion applies, for example the no-fee exclusion or the account being an exempt art 60F(3) running account repaid in full each period with no charge for credit. Companies (the small-firm and firm archetypes) are outside CCA entirely. Design around it: the panel covers discount or rebate on purchases however paid, and JobGuard never promotes, arranges or forwards credit-account applications; a solicitor should confirm, because FCA authorisation for credit broking would be 6-12 months and disproportionate. (2) VAT: a retrospective volume rebate is a reduction in consideration, so the merchant must issue VAT credit notes to the builder (VAT Regulations 1995 regs 15C/38) and the builder must adjust input tax; JobGuard's rebate-statement import must carry the VAT basis, and the admin fee is a standard-rated supply at 20%. (3) Competition Act 1998 Chapter I: JobGuard negotiating for many small builders is joint purchasing, low-risk under the CMA Horizontal Agreements Guidance at small combined shares, provided there is no exclusivity, minimum-share or resale-price term (Vertical Agreements Block Exemption Order 2022 hardcore list) and no cross-builder price sharing (hub-and-spoke; BUILD_PLAN §11). (4) Published per-merchant overcharge and delivery-discrepancy scorecards: Defamation Act 2013 (a merchant must show serious financial loss under s.1(2), which national merchants can) and malicious falsehood; the truth and honest-opinion defences require figures resting on human-confirmed match facts (M2-4), a published methodology and a right of reply; if the scorecards are used in marketing, BPMMR 2008 reg 4 comparative-advertising conditions apply. (5) UK GDPR: sharing a sole trader's identity with a merchant for panel verification needs a lawful basis (contract or legitimate interests) and a D12 register entry. Realistic legal cost: panel agreement template, scorecard publication review and a credit-broking memo, roughly £5-15k over 4-8 weeks, against £54-£720 per builder-year, so it needs on the order of 100 participating builders to cover its own setup. Not certain legal advice; items (1) and (4) need a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Contract term that JobGuard receives no consideration of any kind from any merchant; merchant-to-builder payment only, never collect-and-pass-through; panel excludes credit-account introductions (or a solicitor confirms an RAO art 36A exclusion); merchant VAT credit notes for rebates and 20% VAT on the admin fee (D02); no exclusivity, minimum-share or RPM terms; no cross-tenant price disclosure; scorecards published only from human-confirmed match facts with methodology and right of reply after defamation review; D12 register entry for merchant data sharing; new commercial decision record and D11 integrity review; charging behind G4.

verdicts.reasons: B2B throughout: a builder buying software for the business is a trader, not a consumer (Consumer Rights Act 2015 s.2; DMCC Act 2024 s.251), so the DMCC drip-pricing rule and CRA Part 2 unfair-terms control do not apply to JobGuard's pricing, and UCTA 1977 does not police price terms. No FCA activity: a disclosure mode is not insurance, credit or claims management. VAT: the uplift is a standard-rated supply; pro-rata upgrades and next-period downgrades follow continuous-supply tax-point rules (D02). What does apply: (a) the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 and CAP Code 3.17-3.18, so the displayed plan price must include the uplift once chosen, and because part of the audience (non-VAT-registered sole traders) cannot recover VAT, ex-VAT headlines need a prominent VAT statement, a point the report itself flags for the whole ladder; (b) the Provision of Services Regulations 2009 duty to make price and terms available before contract; (c) the deeper point: a long-term, high-trust service contract can attract an implied duty of good faith as a 'relational contract' (Yam Seng v ITC [2013] EWHC 111; Bates v Post Office [2019] EWHC 606 (QB)), and a watchdog that withholds information from its principal for its own gain is the paradigm conduct such a term tests. Express terms displace implied ones, and an informed, priced choice between disclosure modes is the strongest available evidence that the hold-back was agreed rather than imposed, so the toggle improves JobGuard's legal position on the standard plan, not only its optics. (d) Second-order consumer law favours the live mode: a builder billing a homeowner after the fact for an extra never expressly agreed faces Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 reg 40 (no additional payment without express consent), reg 36 (no charge for work in the cancellation period if cancellation information was not given) and CRA 2015 s.51 (only a reasonable price where none was agreed). 'Tell me now' lets the extra be agreed in writing at the time, which is what D13's 'significant work needing prior written agreement' rule already recognises. HGCRA 1996 s.106 excludes residential occupiers, so no statutory payment-notice or adjudication route rescues late extras on homeowner jobs. No regulatory timeline; the terms drafting sits inside the M4-13 agreement review. Marked for a solicitor: the relational-contract exposure of the standard plan and the neutral description of both modes in M4-13.
verdicts.conditions: Both modes described neutrally in terms and on the pricing page (never 'we hold back'; only 'a second check after your bill'); plan price shown with the uplift once chosen and with a prominent VAT statement; mode bound immutably at switch-live in the audit event; switching date-based only, never keyed on signal existence; D09 v3, D13 v2, D05 and D02 records; §14.6 predicate gains the mode clause; charging behind G4 with hypothetical prices only in pilot_no_charge; solicitor review of the M4-13 wording before any charge.

verdicts.reasons: Same legal footing as I67: B2B, standard-rated, no FCA activity, an explicit D05-authorised command, and a flat per-job price rather than a per-catch charge, so compatible with D11 v2's 'may not reveal before lock and later charge'. The per-job election is legally sound provided it is bound in the switch-live audit event with the price shown; that record is the evidence in any 'did I tick it?' dispute, and an unaudited or ambiguous election would be the real legal weakness. The idea's own alternative, a job attribute fixed at switch-live such as customer type, is the legally superior shape. Homeowner jobs fall outside HGCRA 1996 Part II (s.106 residential-occupier exclusion) and late-billed extras face CCR 2013 reg 40 and CRA 2015 s.51, so live disclosure on homeowner jobs reduces the builder's consumer-law exposure and improves collectability; business jobs sit under the Construction Act payment regime (ss.108-111), where a late variation claim can still be pursued through payment notices and adjudication subject to the contract's written-instruction and notice terms, so a hidden final check there is less legally fraught. The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 is B2B-only and irrelevant to this charge. BPMMR 2008 and CAP 3.17-3.18: the £19 must appear as a total price at the point of choice with the VAT position stated. Charging with the next subscription invoice or at lock is a normal payment term, not credit. No regulatory timeline; drafting sits inside M4-13. A solicitor is needed mainly for the customer-type variant, because 'homeowner' must map to the CRA/CCR 'consumer' definition (an individual acting wholly or mainly outside trade), not to a JobGuard label, and a wrong mapping would defeat the point.
verdicts.conditions: Election captured as an immutable, audited command at switch-live with the price and VAT position displayed; price charged on the subscription book (D09 v3), never on the fee book; D13 v2 and D02 records; if the customer-type selector is used, define 'homeowner' by the statutory consumer test and have a solicitor confirm the mapping; charging behind G4.

verdicts.reasons: Lawful but the most legally fragile of the disclosure ideas. B2B, standard-rated, no FCA activity, no claims-management sector engaged (RAO arts 89G-89M cover six sectors, none of which is construction payment). Three real problems. (1) UK GDPR Article 15: a sole trader is a data subject, and information about their own business activity is their personal data on ICO guidance; shadow signals derived from their notes, photos and job records are personal data that must be disclosed free of charge within one month (Art 12(5)), and §14.3 already treats a DSAR disclosure as permanent fee-ineligibility. So for unincorporated builders the paid peek competes with a free statutory route JobGuard can neither refuse nor charge for; companies are not data subjects, but their directors and staff are, so partial exposure remains for firms. Selling for £39 what the law gives free is not unlawful (compare paid versus statutory credit reports), but it is awkward and a well-advised builder will notice. (2) Relational-contract good faith (Yam Seng; Bates v Post Office): charging the principal at the moment of maximum leverage to disclose what was gathered while acting for them is the fact pattern most likely to be characterised as bad faith; only a clear, express, pre-contract term, on the pricing page from day one as proposed, displaces the implied term, and any later pop-up at lock would forfeit that protection. It is not economic duress, since there is no illegitimate pressure and the builder can simply proceed. (3) BPMMR 2008 and CAP 3.1: 'Show me what JobGuard found (£69)' implies findings exist; because §14.3 forbids any variation with signal existence the button must appear on every job, so the wording must be 'run JobGuard's check now', not 'see what we found', or an empty £69 result is a misleading price claim to a trader. Avoid 'claims' language (CMC connotation; CMCOB). No regulatory timeline; the cost is careful drafting, but the DSAR interaction means the founder should not count on this revenue from sole traders. Solicitor: express-term drafting and the Article 15 interaction.
verdicts.conditions: Price listed as a standard-plan feature from day one, never introduced at lock; button wording that does not imply findings exist; identical flow whether or not signals exist; the 'revealed state discloses all later signals' rule as a tested invariant; DSAR handling modelled in D12 v2 with the fee-ineligibility consequence; D09 v3, D13 v2, D02, D05; no 'claims' or 'recovery agent' language; do not ship before pilot fairness data (I75) and solicitor review.

verdicts.key_risk: It monetises a hold-back that a sole trader can defeat for free under UK GDPR Article 15, and it is the fact pattern most exposed to an implied good-faith challenge if the express term is anything less than prominent.

verdicts.reasons: A split verdict inside one idea. Customer requests live is legally the safest disclosure of all: surfacing every customer request at once tracks D13's 'legal or contractual duty to tell' and 'dispute that silence would worsen' rules, and lets the builder obtain the express written consent that CCR 2013 reg 40 requires before charging a homeowner an additional amount; the Article 14 route and lawful basis are unchanged (D12 v2); it is a standard-rated add-on with no FCA dimension. Materials live is where the legal lens refutes the paid add-on. A supplier line or PO item with no matching baseline or captured scope is, on the idea's own words, either an extra to log or a mistake to stop before payment. The mistake half is a prevention finding inside the advertised watchdog (PO checks against agreed prices, three-way matching). Withholding a detected likely ordering or payment error until lock so it can later become a fee-eligible 'possible extra' is hard to reconcile with the implied term of reasonable care and skill in a B2B service (Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982 s.13), with any relational good-faith duty (Bates v Post Office), and with BPMMR 2008 if the standard plan is marketed as checking supplier documents. Express scope-limiting terms could carve it out, but a clause limiting the watchdog's duty to warn is a limitation clause subject to the UCTA 1977 s.3 reasonableness test, and it hands any builder who paid a wrong invoice a ready claim ('you knew and said nothing'). The right structure is a D13 must-surface rule: any deterministic supplier-line or PO-line-not-in-scope detection surfaces immediately on every plan, fee-ineligible like the safety rule, and only residual 'possible extra' inferences from other sources stay hidden. That removes most of the Materials pack's revenue and makes the rejected value-floor variant moot. The coalescing rule (any disclosed member discloses the whole coalesced signal) is legally required, not merely consistent: a fee on a partly disclosed signal would breach D11 v2's 'may not reveal before lock and later charge' and should be a tested invariant. No regulatory timeline; the cost is a D13 amendment and a UCTA-aware terms review by a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: Move deterministic supplier/PO out-of-scope detection into a D13 must-surface rule on every plan (fee-ineligible) rather than selling it; keep only Customer requests live plus any residual materials-sourced inference as paid add-ons; coalescing across sources must reconcile as disclosed whenever any member is disclosed, with a test; SV-3 must tag signal_type reliably; D09 v3, D13 v2, D12 v3, D02, D05; solicitor review of any term that limits the watchdog's duty to warn under UCTA s.3.

verdicts.reasons: B2B, standard-rated, no FCA activity. Four legal points. (1) For a sole trader, diary and voice notes and photos are their personal data and so are the signals derived from them; UK GDPR Article 15 gives free access within a month, and §14.3 makes a DSAR disclosure fee-ineligible, so the hidden own-records mode for unincorporated builders is only as hidden as their unawareness of Article 15, and a paid pack sold against a free statutory right carries the same awkwardness as I69. (2) The own-records fee case is the weakest under the plan's own North-star test and the most exposed to contra proferentem: §14.2's distinction between a 'Log an extra' record (capture, fee-free) and a diary note (evidence, fee-eligible) is a form distinction inside JobGuard's standard terms; ambiguity in standard B2B terms is construed against the drafter, and a builder's contemporaneous note is strong evidence the work was 'in their head', which is exactly where the report says builders reject fees. A court applying a relational good-faith term would find 'your own note, used against you for 10%' the hardest fact pattern to defend. (3) Voice notes raise no interception issue (the builder records their own notes); third parties captured on site make the builder the controller and JobGuard the processor, with D04 residency for transcription. (4) Copyright and licence in notes and photos are covered by ordinary terms. Net: the pack is lawful, but the legal lens strengthens the idea's own alternative, which is to make own-record signals fee-free by D13 rule. That removes the most litigable fee case, aligns the fee with 'found from third-party sources', and gives up the smallest share of catches. If the paid pack ships first as price discovery, it must be an express term and the DSAR interaction must be modelled. No regulatory timeline; cost is a terms review. Solicitor: the capture/evidence definition and the good-faith exposure of the own-records fee.
verdicts.conditions: Express term describing the pack and the default; DSAR handling modelled with the fee-ineligibility consequence; the capture-versus-evidence definition drafted so that a diary note's status is unambiguous (contra proferentem); coalescing rule from I70 applied; D13 v2 exception to the no-per-note-prompt rule, D09 v3, D12 v3, D02, D05; treat the pack as a price-discovery step and revisit making own-record signals fee-free by D13 rule after pilot fairness data.

verdicts.key_risk: The fee it prices, a builder's own contemporaneous note used to earn 10%, is the one a court, ombudsman or trade press would find least defensible, so pricing it may be less wise than removing it.

verdicts.reasons: The FCA insurance perimeter is the real question, and it is a perimeter rather than a permission: effecting a contract of insurance without authorisation breaches the FSMA 2000 s.19 general prohibition, is a criminal offence (s.23) and makes the contract unenforceable against the builder (s.26); there is no appointed-representative route for carrying insurance risk yourself. The test (Prudential v IRC (1904), applied in PERG 6): the provider undertakes to pay money or a benefit on an uncertain event adverse to the recipient, for consideration. The FCA's discriminating factors (PERG 6.6-6.7) point away from insurance where the obligation arises only from the provider's own failure to perform the contracted service, since a warranty of one's own performance is an incident of the underlying contract rather than risk transfer, and towards insurance where the benefit is proportionate to a third-party loss, separately priced and optional. Credit (b), £5 per verified wrong card, is plainly a service credit. Credit (a) as drafted is mixed: the trigger is JobGuard's own matcher failing on evidence it held (own performance), but the benefit is the builder's overpayment to a supplier (third-party loss, proportionate). It stays on the safe side if drafted as a liquidated remedy for breach of a defined check, capped at fees paid for the period, with proof of the service failure required; that is then a limitation-of-remedy clause which must pass the UCTA 1977 s.3 reasonableness test as the sole remedy (B2B SLA caps at fees paid are routinely upheld, but a solicitor should draft it). The standalone variant on the hidden plan (+£5/£10/£15 for credit (a) alone) is the version that fails: a separate, optional, priced promise to pay on an uncertain event is the classic insurance shape, and PERG 6.7 treats separate pricing and optionality as insurance indicators. Reject that variant; if the founder wants sold reassurance, it has to be an insurer's product with JobGuard as an authorised or appointed-representative intermediary under the IDD (RAO arts 21/25/39A), disproportionate at £6-£18 per builder-year. Tax follows the characterisation: if any variant were insurance, IPT at 12% would apply and the supply would be VAT-exempt (VATA 1994 Sch 9 Group 2), harming JobGuard's input-tax recovery, another reason to keep it a service credit. As a service credit, the credit note reduces consideration for the subscription: VAT Regulations 1995 regs 15C/38 credit note within 14 days referencing the original invoice (D02); do not alternatively treat it as damages outside the scope of VAT, pick one. Marketing: CAP Code 3.53-3.57 guarantee rules; never 'insurance', 'cover', 'protection' or 'guaranteed savings' (BUILD_PLAN §11 forbids guaranteed-recovery claims). D01/D09: credits never touch the success-fee book and are not an offset against fees, consistent with 'subscription never offsets fees' because the credit is applied only against the subscription. Chargeflow's '4x ROI guarantee' is a US precedent and carries no UK weight. Cost: a solicitor's PERG 6 perimeter memo and clause drafting, roughly £3-8k over 2-4 weeks, before any wording ships; no FCA application. Not certain legal advice; the perimeter memo is the gate.
verdicts.conditions: Drop the standalone paid add-on variant (insurance-shaped); draft credit (a) as a capped liquidated remedy for JobGuard's failure to perform a defined check, cap tied to fees paid, breach proven from immutable matching-run logs and evidence hashes; sole-remedy clause reviewed against UCTA s.3; PERG 6 perimeter memo from a solicitor before wording ships; VAT credit-note mechanics per regs 15C/38 in D02; D01 rule that credits never touch the fee book; no 'insurance', 'cover', 'protection' or 'guarantee of savings' language (CAP 3.53-3.57); claim record with an approved Decision; charging and crediting behind G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct; expected cost ≈ -£9/yr; standalone add-on £0 (rejected as insurance-shaped)

verdicts.key_risk: Drifting across the FSMA insurance perimeter, which is a criminal offence and voids the promise, most likely through the separately priced standalone variant or loss-based wording that pays the supplier overpayment rather than remedying JobGuard's own failure.

verdicts.reasons: Would builders pay? Yes, nobody objects to 10% of cash they paid twice, and the chain is the cleanest in the set. The problem is that almost no cash reaches the chain. (1) Base rate: the idea's 0.3% of spend has no small-builder support; the only benchmark is PRGX's '$1M per $1B' (0.1%) across ALL recovery classes in large AP shops (research note success_fee_benchmarks §1; §6 of success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp records no UK data on supplier errors for small builders). (2) Payment pattern: Solos mostly pay at the counter or by card per pro-forma, where duplicates are rare; account customers (Small/Firm) pay monthly statements, not invoices, so the 'two settled payments against one invoice identity' detector in M2-2/M4-8 misses the real failure mode (statement paid twice), which needs a statement-level reconciliation nobody has planned. (3) Counterfactual: a merchant statement shows the credit balance next month, so the builder or merchant catches most duplicates unaided; the fee then lands on money that was coming back anyway, which the report's fairness finding ('who did the work') says is the resented case. (4) Cash: trade accounts settle overpayments as credit; D03 v2 excludes credits, so most events are fee-free by design. Rework (assumptions: materials 35% of turnover = £52k/£210k/£700k; duplicates 0.3%; bank feed linked under D10 consent 40/50/60%; invoice ingested via M2-2 60/70/80%; JobGuard first to spot 50%; cash rather than credit 30%; fee 10%) gives about £1/£3/£15 per builder-year versus the idea's £9/£36/£120. Build-first: M2-2 identity, M4-7 bank feed, M4-8 allocation, a refund-request send command, a D03 v3 row and a new Decision type; nothing ships before live M4-8 and G4. Cost: one task plus legal/accounting review of a new category, for single-digit pounds. Comparables: AP recovery auditors earn 20-30% but sell to mid/large AP departments and nothing to micro construction firms (success_fee_benchmarks §1 gaps). Gaming risk is nil. Top failure reasons: no cash reaches the chain; the detector models the wrong payment pattern for account customers; a fee on money the statement would have returned anyway feels petty.
verdicts.conditions: Build duplicate-payment detection as a fee-free watchdog Decision (the prevention form, before the second payment leaves, is where the value is). Add the category to D03 only as a one-line clarification of the existing supplier_overcharge row when D03 is next revised, not as a separate row needing its own review, and only after pilot bank-feed data shows any cash refund at all. Never let the Decision copy steer builders to demand cash instead of credit. Do not extend M4-8 to statement-level reconciliation for this fee; do it only if it earns its place as a feature.

revised_revenue.solo: ~£1/yr (assumes £52k supplier spend, 0.3% duplicates, 40% bank-linked, 60% invoices captured, 50% JobGuard-first, 30% cash refunds; counter/card payers rarely duplicate)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£15/yr (£700k spend, 60% bank-linked, 80% captured, 50% JobGuard-first, 30% cash); idea's £120 requires 50% cash refunds and 100% feed/capture coverage

verdicts.key_risk: Trade accounts settle duplicates by credit and the merchant statement reveals them anyway, so the fee-eligible cash pool is close to zero and the detector needs statement-level matching the plan does not contain.

verdicts.reasons: Would builders pay 10% of a VAT refund? The sum is small, the sub made the error and the builder's accountant is the person they expect to catch it, so the reaction is 'why is my app taking a cut of a tax correction', which invites exactly the tax-advice framing the idea has to disclaim. Refutation of the number: (1) timing kills it: the check runs at M2-3 invoice confirmation, before payment, so most cases are prevention and fee-free under the founder's rule; the idea's 50% 'paid before correction' is far too high for a system that checks at intake (30% at most). (2) Subs on live jobs invoice monthly, so a wrongly charged VAT amount is netted off the next payment, which is a credit against future supply and fee-free under D03 v2; cash refunds are the exception (25%). (3) DRC has run since 2021; error rates among VAT-registered subs are falling and a 5% wrong-invoice rate is a guess with no source (research finds no UK supplier-error data, success_fee_psychology_and_trades_wtp §6). (4) Half of what remains is caught by the bookkeeper at the quarterly return. Rework (sub spend 10/20/25% of turnover; VAT-registered subs 30/50/60%; 3% wrongly charged; VAT 20%; 30% paid first; 25% cash; 50% JobGuard-first; Solo x60% VAT-registered): £0/£1/£7 per builder-year versus the idea's £1/£30/£150. Build-first: M2-3 VAT extraction, versioned tenant/job VAT and CIS facts, a rate-rule table reviewed by a qualified tax reviewer (D02 owner), M4-7/M4-8 cash matching, and the DRC support matrix lives in M4-21 which depends on M4-20, near the end of M4. Cost: 1-2 tasks plus a tax reviewer's sign-off of a versioned rule table, plus D03 v3 and D02 amendments, for single-digit pounds. Comparables: Construction AI and Site Samurai list CIS/VAT handling as flat features (construction_platforms_and_ai §1/§2); no success-fee precedent. Gaming: none by builders; JobGuard's exposure is a wrong rule version raising false Decisions that sour sub relationships. Top failure reasons: prevention captures nearly all the value; netting-off replaces cash refunds; tax-adjacent fee is a trust liability out of proportion to £1-£7.
verdicts.conditions: Reconsider only if pilot data shows VAT-registered builders being refunded DRC errors in cash after paying, at a rate that would clear £50/yr per Firm; even then fold it into the supplier_overcharge row by wording, not a new category. Ship the DRC/zero-rating rule check itself as a fee-free aid inside M4-21 with 'check with your accountant' wording and a tax-reviewed, versioned rule table.

revised_revenue.solo: £0/yr (60% VAT-registered, few VAT-registered subs, intake check prevents rather than recovers)
revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£1/yr (£60k VAT-registered sub spend, 3% wrongly charged, 30% paid first, 25% cash, 50% JobGuard-first)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£7/yr (£300k VAT-registered sub spend, same chain); idea's £150 needs 5% error rate, 50% paid-first and 50% cash

verdicts.key_risk: The check catches the error at invoice confirmation, so the value is prevention (fee-free by founder rule) and what slips through is netted off the sub's next invoice rather than refunded in cash.

verdicts.reasons: Would builders pay? A Firm with a written retro-rebate term might accept 10% of a rebate the merchant failed to pay, but the pool is tiny and the feature only works with disciplined full invoice capture. Refutation: (1) Prevalence: written retro-rebate terms are a £1m+-with-one-merchant phenomenon; at £2m turnover with materials spread over several merchants, 50% (not 70%) is generous for Firms and 5%/25% for Solo/Small is optimistic; verbal 'settlement discount' arrangements are commoner and do not qualify (no document). (2) Coverage: the rebate-due arithmetic needs every invoice from that merchant in JobGuard, net of returns and credits; partial forwarding through the M2-2 alias produces an understated spend figure and a wrong or missing Decision, and the merchant's own statement is the authoritative spend record, which JobGuard does not ingest. (3) Cash: merchants settle rebates as account credit almost by default (20% cash, not 50%), which D03 v2 makes fee-free. (4) Counterfactual: a Firm with a rebate term has a bookkeeper who knows the period end. Rework (term share 5/25/50%; covered spend £20k/£100k/£300k; 2% rebate; 20% unpaid; 20% cash; 60% JobGuard-first; 10% fee): about £0/£1/£7 per builder-year; even the idea's own assumptions only reach £88 for Firms. Build-first: M2-1 rate-book rebate-term revisions with agreement-document evidence, M2-4 matched settled spend net of credits, a period-end Graphile job, a claim-letter send command, M4-7/M4-8 cash matching, a D03 v3 row and a D11 statement; two tasks and a legal review for pounds. Comparables: AP recovery auditors treat unclaimed rebates as a class at 20-30% but sell to large AP departments (success_fee_benchmarks §1); enterprise rebate software is flat-subscription; nothing exists for small builders. Trust: the idea correctly flags proximity to I65/I66; even reading merchant terms and drafting claims against merchants puts JobGuard in the merchant's line of sight, which the report says is the watchdog's one unaffordable conflict (report §'The hidden final check'). Gaming: low. Top failure reasons: pool near zero; requires complete capture the product cannot guarantee; credit settlement is the merchant norm.
verdicts.conditions: Do not add a D03 row. If Firm-tier pilots ask for rebate tracking, consider it as a fee-free Firm-tier feature (rate-book rebate term + period-end reminder with arithmetic) after M2-4, with a D11 line that JobGuard never negotiates, pools or receives merchant terms. Revisit a fee only if pilot Firms show cash rebate recoveries above £100/yr each.

revised_revenue.solo: ~£0/yr (5% hold a written term; £20k covered spend; cash 20%)
revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£1/yr (25% hold a term; £100k covered spend at 2%; 20% unpaid; 20% cash; 60% JobGuard-first)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£7/yr (50% hold a term; £300k covered spend; same chain); idea's £88 needs 70% term share, £500k covered and 50% cash

verdicts.key_risk: Merchants settle rebates by account credit and the Decision depends on complete invoice capture JobGuard cannot verify, so the fee-eligible cash is a rounding error against a two-task build and a merchant-facing claim letter.

verdicts.reasons: The idea already recommends fee-free; the commercial case confirms it. Would builders pay? No: a fee on the tax side of a debt the customer never paid is the 'exploiting an advantage' case in the report's fairness section (Kahneman/Xia findings, report §'The hidden final check'), and any accountant claims bad-debt relief as routine, so the counterfactual is close to nil. Refutation of the number: (1) Scheme: cash accounting is available below £1.35m turnover and common for small builders, and flat-rate traders get no relief either, so Solo and Small firm pools are essentially £0, not £5/£30. (2) Firm (£2m, accrual): write-offs 0.75% of turnover = £15k gross, VAT £2,500; the share not already handled by the accountant is 15% (not 40%) = £375; evidence must come from an accounting connector (M5-1/M5-2, a milestone away) and the invoice must not be under a withheld-payment case, which is exactly where a written-off invoice tends to be, 50% = £188; fee £19. (3) Reversals: whenever the customer later pays, relief is repayable and the fee compensates negatively, so lifetime revenue trends toward zero. Build-first: M1 invoices, M4-7 receipt matching, a write-off command with audit, a six-month clock, SV-7 accounting-connector evidence, D03 v3 row, D01 base change (fee on tax relief), D02 review, plus a D03 stacking rule with withheld-payment cases. Cost: cheap in code, expensive in trust and in reviewer time. Comparables: none charge for this; accountants include it (success_fee_benchmarks §5 gaps note no VAT-reclaim contingency data). Gaming: none meaningful. Top failure reasons: word-of-mouth damage ('JobGuard took 10% of my bad-debt relief'), cash-accounting traders excluded, connector dependency, reversal churn.
verdicts.conditions: Record in D03 v3 that tax reliefs are never a fee base. Optionally keep a fee-free 'bad-debt relief may be available, check with your accountant' aid after the write-off command exists, subject to D02 review and only for accrual-scheme tenants.

revised_revenue.solo: £0/yr (cash accounting or flat rate: no output VAT paid, no relief)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£19/yr gross before reversals (£15k write-offs, £2,500 VAT, 15% not already claimed by the accountant, 50% connector-evidenced and not under a withheld-payment case); net trends lower as later payments repay relief

verdicts.key_risk: A visible fee on tax relief from an unpaid customer reads as profiting from the builder's loss, in a trade that runs on word of mouth, for under £20 a year from the only archetype that can claim it.

verdicts.reasons: Correctly listed to reject. Taking a percentage of an insurance payout is 'financial services or financial product' claims-management activity under RAO arts 89G-89M unless JobGuard is authorised (success_fee_benchmarks §7), and it would place JobGuard in the CMC bucket whose fees the FCA capped at 15-30% and whose reputation the report says to avoid (report §'No rival sells' table; §'The hidden final check' legal notes). Commercially the numbers are also weak: 5-15% annual probability of a claimable loss, average claims of £1,000-£5,000 and a 10% fee give £5/£25/£75, from a builder who has just been robbed or flooded and whose excess may exceed the claim, so the fee is both small and maximally resented. Authorisation would cost more than the category could ever earn. Gaming: not applicable. Build: none. The value is real but sits in the evidence pack (M4-3 packs already assemble GRNs, photos, diary and supplier invoices), which the builder can hand to their insurer for free.
verdicts.conditions: Record the rejection in D03 v3 with the regulatory reason so no later agent revives it. Keep insurer-ready evidence-pack export as a fee-free feature of M4-3 packs; obtain a one-line legal note that exporting a pack for the builder's own claim is not claims management.

revised_revenue.solo: £0/yr (not offered; would be ~£5 if offered)

verdicts.key_risk: Regulated claims-management activity without FCA authorisation, plus the reputational association with capped-fee claims firms, for a handful of pounds.

verdicts.reasons: Correctly recommended for rejection. Would builders pay a share of lower prices at a new merchant for 12 months? No: it is a running meter on where they shop, the form of charge the report says people dislike most (Prelec & Loewenstein, report §'The hidden final check'), and it contradicts the fixed 10% (the idea proposes a 20% share). Attribution is the weakest in the set: builders switch merchants for credit terms, delivery, branch proximity and relationships; a lower unit price at merchant B proves nothing about JobGuard; SKU alias matching across merchants surfaces spec and quality differences the watchdog cannot adjudicate, so every statement invites a dispute. The watchdog conflict is decisive: a platform that earns when builders move merchants is, to merchants and builders alike, a steering platform, which is the conflict the founder has already ruled out (I65/I66) and which the energy-broker precedent shows ends in regulation and litigation once discovered (success_fee_benchmarks §2). D11 should say fees never depend on which merchant the builder uses. The comparable, P3 at 50% of savings for 12-60 months (report table), is the client's negotiating agent, a role JobGuard must not take. Build cost would be the I76 machinery plus cross-merchant alias matching for revenue that would evaporate in disputes. Gaming: high on the JobGuard side (spec mismatches counted as savings) and unsolvable. Top failure reasons: unprovable attribution, watchdog conflict, a 12-month meter on shopping behaviour.
verdicts.conditions: Record in D11 v2 that no fee may depend on which merchant a builder uses or on savings measured against a prior rate. Nothing to build.

revised_revenue.solo: £0/yr (not offered)
revised_revenue.firm: £0/yr (not offered); the idea's £54/£192/£560 would not survive spec disputes and churn

verdicts.key_risk: Earning from merchant switches is indistinguishable from steering, and the counterfactual cannot be shown from JobGuard's own records.

verdicts.reasons: This is the only idea in the set that captures prevention value honestly: the builder pays a known price before committing, no counterfactual is needed, no merchant money, nothing withheld. Would builders pay? Plausibly for business customers on £25k-£60k jobs, because late payment is the one robustly measured pain (£11bn/yr, ~14,000 closures, report §'Frame the price'; success_fee_psychology §6) and £19 against a £25k exposure is trivial. Refutations: (1) Solos mostly serve homeowners; business-customer share of 10% and a 25% attach leave about one check a year, so I87 is a Firm/Small-firm product and the Solo case rests on the individual checks (I89/I90, out of scope here). (2) Attach rates of 50-60% assume builders check every business quote; repeat main-contractor customers are not re-checked and many builders will not 'insult' a prospect, so 25-35% on new business customers is defensible. (3) Firm's 50% business share is high for a £2m domestic/light-commercial builder; 40% used. (4) DIY substitutes: Companies House is free and CCJ searches are cheap, so the paid value is the CRA score, CCJ detail and the assembled card; the price ceiling is real. (5) Margin: wholesale £5-£15, Creditsafe/Registry Trust prices, 'Satago bundles credit reports' and 'Chaser offers Creditsafe' are not in the supplied research (success_fee_benchmarks §6 only records Satago and Chaser flat tiers), so treat them as unverified; CRA reseller contracts commonly carry minimum commitments (assumption), which at 1-15 checks per builder-year need hundreds of tenants to clear. (6) Legal: D12 v3 (controller split, Art 14 route for officers/PSCs), D07 retention class versus CRA report-retention caps, a new D14 for paid data services, D02 VAT, G4 for charging; in pilot_no_charge JobGuard absorbs the cost. Rework (quotes 47/60/95; business share 10/25/40%; attach on new business customers 25/30/35%; £19 ex VAT; wholesale £9 assumed): gross £23/£86/£253, margin £11/£45/£133 per builder-year. Comparables: no UK trade app reviewed sells a customer check (report §'No rival sells'); FairRate sells per-audit at £0.99 to consumers (construction_platforms_and_ai §4), which anchors per-use pricing low; trade apps sell add-ons at £10-£39/month and SMS per message (uk_trade_job_software §5), so per-use charges are familiar. Gaming: bind checks to a quote/job and named counterparty, cap per quote, rate-limit per tenant; in-app view only, no export of the raw CRA report. Top failure reasons: attach rate below 20% in pilot, CRA contract minimums exceeding early volume, retention conflict forcing storage of derived findings only, and any copy that reads as JobGuard vetting customers.
verdicts.conditions: Ship CP-1 (Companies House + Gazette entity resolution and the 'Findings, not a recommendation' card) free in M2 as a watchdog feature, bound to a quote/job, and measure attach on business quotes and later withheld-payment cases (§14.17 metric). Sign a CRA contract (CP-2) only once pilot attach on new business customers is at or above ~25% and firms say they would pay; confirm wholesale price and any minimum commitment first. Price-test £19 vs £29 ex VAT; never bundle into the subscription or the success fee; statement lines only. D12 v3, D07 retention class, D14 and D02 approved and G4 open before any charge; pilot_no_charge labels the charge hypothetical. No colour verdicts, no 'do not proceed', no export of the raw report, watermark in-app.

revised_revenue.solo: ~£23 gross / ~£11 margin per year (47 quotes, 10% business, 25% attach on new business customers, £19 ex VAT, £9 wholesale assumed)
revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£86 gross / ~£45 margin per year (60 quotes, 25% business, 30% attach)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£253 gross / ~£133 margin per year (95 quotes, 40% business, 35% attach); £0 in pilot_no_charge

verdicts.key_risk: Attach rate is unmeasured and DIY substitutes are free or cheap, so the paid CRA layer may not clear a reseller minimum commitment; ship the free layer first and let pilot data decide.

verdicts.reasons: The packaging fails on its own numbers. (1) Solo/Builder add-ons: a £12/month pack of 3 checks is 36 checks a year sold to a Solo who runs about one business check a year (I87 rework); a £35/month pack of 12 is 144 a year for a Small firm running 5-8 including property checks. The idea's 20%/35% attach rates are not defensible for a monthly charge on a rare event; 5%/10% is generous, giving £7/£42 per builder-year, and every unused allowance is the 'paying for unused subscriptions' resentment the research records (success_fee_psychology §5). Pay-per-check (I87) is the right vehicle for these archetypes. (2) Firm inclusion: 30 checks/month included, £8/month of the £119 attributed = £96/yr; the idea's own expected Firm usage of ~45 checks/yr at £7-£10 wholesale costs £315-£450, so the inclusion is loss-making on its attribution and still under water against the whole £240/yr Firm-vs-£99 delta; 'priced assuming 40-60% utilisation' applies to the add-ons, not to a Firm inclusion whose cost is set by usage, not by allowance. (3) It is a second meter: the founder fixed live jobs as the meter, the report says the tier comparison should rest on one or two numbers, not a feature grid (report §'Three tiers work'), and allowance counters, overage at £15 and no-rollover are exactly the running-meter complexity to keep out of a builder's pricing page. (4) Build-first: M4-13 terms, M4-14 metering (optional per rev 2.3 and late M4), M4-10 overage lines, D09 v3 inclusions/overage/notice terms, D05, D02, G4, plus the I87 adapters; a late-M4 build for a low-value packaging choice. Comparables: ServiceM8 sells workload allowances (report §'UK builders already pay') but its allowance is the primary meter, not a bolt-on; Satago's fixed tiers are credit-control software, not per-check bundles (success_fee_benchmarks §6). Gaming: minor (allowance per tenant, checks bound to quotes). Top failure reasons: wrong vehicle for rare purchases, negative margin on the Firm inclusion as sized, second meter against the founder's decision.
verdicts.conditions: Drop the Solo/Builder add-on packs; sell checks per use (I87). If a Firm-tier differentiator is wanted after I87 pilot data, include a small number (about 2 per month, no rollover, overage at the I87 price) so expected wholesale cost stays inside the £119-vs-£99 delta, and present it as a Firm perk in the tier list, not a metered allowance. Revisit only after I87 utilisation is measured and a CRA wholesale price is contracted.

revised_revenue.solo: ~£7/yr (5% attach x £144; 36-check allowance against ~1 check of need)
revised_revenue.firm: £0 incremental (attribution of existing £119); net about -£260 to -£350/yr at expected 45 checks x £8-£10 wholesale as posed; roughly -£100 to -£200 with a 2/month inclusion

verdicts.key_risk: A monthly allowance for a rare purchase either goes unused (resentment, no attach) or, on Firm, costs more in wholesale reports than the price attributed to it, while adding a second meter the founder did not choose.

verdicts.reasons: Legally the cleanest fee category in the set. Recovering a mistaken duplicate payment from a trade supplier is a restitutionary claim (mistaken payment, Limitation Act 1980 s.5/s.32) owed to the builder as a business; it is not 'debt collecting' under RAO art 39F (which attaches only to consumer credit/hire agreements — research note success_fee_benchmarks §7), not one of the six claims-management sectors (RAO arts 89G–89M), not credit broking and not insurance distribution. JobGuard neither takes assignment nor collects in its own name: the builder sends the letter (D10) and the refund lands in the builder's bank, so no client money, no AML 'relevant person' status and no Payment Services angle beyond the bank feed. Drafting a factual refund-request letter is not a reserved legal activity under the Legal Services Act 2007 (only conduct of litigation and rights of audience are), and the DBA fee caps (SI 2013/609) bind legal representatives in proceedings, not a software platform, so the 10% needs no cap on legal grounds. Consumer law (Consumer Rights Act 2015, DMCC Act 2024 drip-pricing) does not apply: JobGuard-to-builder and builder-to-supplier are both trader-to-trader; the only B2B marketing constraint is the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008, satisfied by the plan's own permitted/forbidden claim rules (§14.1). The Late Payment Act does not apply either (a mistaken payment is not 'contract price'), so no statutory interest sits in the fee base. The bank-feed dependency carries the one genuine perimeter question, but it belongs to D10, not this idea: account data must reach JobGuard only through TrueLayer as the authorised AISP (FCA PERG 15 'data received from an AISP' position) or via an agent arrangement — solicitor to confirm; already a D10 condition. Two tax details need an accountant, not a solicitor: the duplicate cash contains no VAT in substance (no second supply), so the D02 'ex-VAT' base should treat the whole refunded duplicate as principal; and a duplicate payment to a CIS subcontractor is refunded net of the CIS deduction, with the HMRC portion recovered through the CIS300 correction, which is not a supplier cash refund and must never enter Q.
verdicts.conditions: (1) D03 v3 adds a distinct `duplicate_supplier_payment_recovered` row (a duplicate is not an 'overcharge'), with 'cash refund only; account credit and credit notes never qualify; refunds made before the Decision never qualify'. (2) D02 wording: fee base = the duplicate cash actually refunded, treated as VAT-free principal; accountant sign-off. (3) First version limited to non-CIS suppliers (merchants); CIS subcontractors need a separate rule so the HMRC-side correction is never counted. (4) Refund letters stay factual and non-litigious (no letter-before-claim language) per D10. (5) Bank-feed perimeter (PERG 15 / TrueLayer AISP route) confirmed in the D10 legal review before M4-7 activation — a dependency, not a new obligation. (6) UK GDPR: sole-trader suppliers are data subjects; the M2-2 D12 Article 14 route already covers them. (7) Builder-facing copy states plainly that an account credit is acceptable and fee-free. Timeline/cost: no new permission; one D03 row plus accountant review of the VAT/CIS base (assume under £1k and days, not months).

revised_revenue.solo: £8 (unchanged £9 less CIS-subcontractor cases excluded from v1)
revised_revenue.firm: £110 (from £120; CIS cases excluded); zero before M4-7 bank feed and D10 approval

verdicts.key_risk: Not legal but evidential: mis-pairing two legitimate invoices sharing a number from one merchant and asking a supplier for money that is not owed — the Decision must cite both documents and both bank settlements, and the builder must confirm before any letter goes. Residual legal risk is the TrueLayer perimeter (PERG 15), which is D10's problem and a solicitor question.

verdicts.reasons: Not blocked, but the compliance cost is out of proportion to £1/£30/£150 a year. The refund chain itself is lawful and unregulated by the FCA (B2B, no consumer credit, no claims-management sector). The problems are elsewhere. First, the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 reg 11(d) define a 'tax adviser' as anyone who by way of business provides 'material aid, or assistance or advice, in connection with the tax affairs of other persons' — widened in 2020 precisely to catch non-advisory 'assistance'. A product that computes a specific VAT error on a specific invoice and prompts a credit request is arguably material aid on the builder's tax affairs even when labelled 'check with your accountant'. If a solicitor agrees, JobGuard becomes an MLR 'relevant person' supervised by HMRC as an accountancy service provider: registration (assume £300 per premises per year plus fit-and-proper fees), an MLRO, a written risk assessment, and customer due diligence on every builder tenant — a business-wide onboarding cost triggered by a category worth tens of pounds. Second, liability: the DRC is only deterministic when JobGuard also holds whether the builder gave the sub a written end-user/intermediary notification (VAT Notice 735); if the rule says 'no VAT' and it is wrong, the sub is exposed to HMRC for output tax and the builder to an input-tax denial; 'aid not advice' wording narrows but does not remove a Hedley Byrne assumption of responsibility, and any B2B liability cap is subject to UCTA 1977 s.2–3 reasonableness — professional indemnity cover priced for tax-rule outputs is needed. Third, the fee base is itself VAT: if the builder had already (wrongly) reclaimed the input tax on the sub's invoice, the cash refund is not the builder's money and must be repaid to HMRC via error correction, so Q must exclude any amount the builder reclaimed — JobGuard cannot see that without the accounting connector, so it needs connector evidence or a builder-favourable attestation. Fourth, D06 expressly defers DRC and non-standard VAT categories for the pilot; raising DRC Decisions on inbound invoices needs a D06 rescoping (outbound only) or a D06 v2. Fifth, zero and reduced rating rules for subcontractor supplies are not uniform (subs can zero-rate on new dwellings under VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 5 but not on charity/RRP buildings; 5% conversions under Sch 7A; energy-saving materials relief timing changes in 2027), so the rule table must be signed off by the D02 qualified tax reviewer and kept narrow. Nothing here is a hard bar; all of it is cost. The better legal shape is to ship the check fee-free under the subscription (no fee, no fee-driven incentive to push a sub into a wrong credit) and only add the fee row if pilot data shows real cash refunds.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Solicitor opinion on MLR 2017 reg 11(d): whether an automated, labelled VAT-rate check is 'material aid… in connection with tax affairs'; if yes, register with HMRC for AML supervision and implement CDD before any real Decision — or redesign the output as a generic rate-rule reference without invoice-specific arithmetic. (2) D06 v2 (or explicit rescoping to outbound invoices) before any DRC check on inbound sub invoices. (3) Versioned DRC/zero-rate rule table limited to clear cases (DRC on CIS-scope standard/reduced-rated services between VAT- and CIS-registered parties with the end-user notification fact held; new-build dwelling zero-rating only), signed off by the D02 qualified tax reviewer; every Decision carries 'confirm with your accountant' and cites the rule version. (4) D03 v3 wording: fee only on VAT cash refunds from the supplier, net of any input tax the builder reclaimed from HMRC on that invoice, evidenced by the accounting connector or builder attestation resolved in the builder's favour; amounts recovered from HMRC never qualify; prevention never qualifies. (5) D02: fee base is the refunded tax amount treated as principal; JobGuard's own fee is standard-rated. (6) Professional indemnity insurance covering tax-rule outputs and a UCTA-reasonable limitation clause reviewed by a solicitor. (7) D12: sole-trader subs as data subjects; Article 14 route already needed for M2-3. Timeline/cost assumption: tax reviewer £2k–£5k, solicitor £1k–£3k, plus AML registration and CDD programme (2–3 months) if reg 11(d) applies.

verdicts.key_risk: Being pulled into HMRC AML supervision as a 'tax adviser' (MLR 2017 reg 11(d)) for a category worth tens of pounds, imposing customer due diligence on every tenant; secondarily, a wrong rule version pushing a sub into an incorrect VAT credit with liability landing on JobGuard.

verdicts.reasons: Unregulated and lawful in substance: an unpaid rebate is a contractual debt under a B2B supply agreement between the builder and the merchant; enforcing it is neither FCA debt collecting (art 39F) nor claims management, and JobGuard is not a party. The legal costs are contractual and data-related rather than regulatory. (a) Confidentiality: merchant rebate agreements commonly carry confidentiality clauses; the builder uploading the agreement to JobGuard is disclosure to a service provider, usually permitted under a 'professional advisers/service providers under equivalent confidentiality' carve-out but sometimes not — JobGuard's terms must have the builder confirm they are entitled to share it and must treat the document as confidential (never aggregated, benchmarked or surfaced to other tenants). Cross-tenant aggregation of merchant terms would also raise Competition Act 1998 Chapter I concerns about circulating competitively sensitive pricing, so it must be structurally excluded — this is the same D11 'no merchant income, no negotiation, no pooling' line, and the Bribery Act 2010 s.1/s.2 make any merchant payment to JobGuard for steering a plain no. (b) VAT: a retrospective rebate is a reduction in consideration; the merchant should issue a credit note with a VAT adjustment (VAT Regulations 1995 reg 38 as amended in 2019, which requires the supplier to refund the customer before adjusting output tax), and the builder must reduce input tax accordingly. The fee base must therefore be the rebate net of VAT (consistent with D01 'ex-VAT'), and JobGuard must never present the gross as 'recovered'. (c) The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 does not help: a rebate owed by supplier to purchaser is not 'contract price' and is unlikely to be a qualifying debt, so no statutory interest enters Q. (d) Claim windows: many rebate terms lapse if unclaimed within a period; the Decision must fire inside the window or the 'recovery' is a claim the builder has already lost. (e) UK GDPR is minimal (merchants are companies; account-manager names are incidental). Nothing needs a new permission; the conditions are contract terms, a D02 base rule and structural D11 separation.
verdicts.conditions: (1) D11 v3 text: JobGuard never arranges, negotiates, pools, benchmarks or receives rebates; rebate terms are tenant-confidential and never aggregated or compared across tenants (competition and confidentiality). (2) Terms of service: builder warrants they may share the merchant agreement; JobGuard holds it as confidential evidence. (3) D02/D03 v3: `unpaid_agreed_rebate_recovered` row; Q = cash rebate net of VAT after any credit note; account credits and credit notes never qualify; rebate periods with no Decision before the merchant's claim deadline never qualify. (4) Decision cites every settled invoice in the spend base net of returns and credits. (5) Claim letters factual, builder-sent (D10). (6) Bank-feed perimeter as for I81 (D10). Solicitor items: confidentiality carve-out wording and the D11 competition statement (assume £500–£1.5k); accountant: reg 38 credit-note treatment of the base.

verdicts.key_risk: Drift: the moment JobGuard holds many builders' merchant terms, the temptation to benchmark or 'negotiate better rebates' turns a clean contractual claim into a confidentiality breach, a Chapter I information-sharing question and the merchant-conflict the founder has ruled out; must be prevented by policy and by structure, not by intention.

verdicts.reasons: Rejected as a success-fee category; the underlying reminder is fine as a fee-free subscription feature. Three legal reasons. First, the fee base is a tax relief from HMRC computed by JobGuard against VATA 1994 s.36 and VAT Regulations 1995 regs 165–172 (supply made, VAT accounted and paid, consideration written off in a refunds-for-bad-debts account, six months from the later of due date and supply, claim within four years and six months, repayment on later receipt). Computing a specific reclaimable amount for a specific trader is the clearest possible case of 'material aid… in connection with the tax affairs of other persons' under MLR 2017 reg 11(d); unlike I82 there is no 'supplier made the error' framing — this is the builder's own return. That would make JobGuard an HMRC-supervised accountancy service provider with CDD obligations on every tenant, a business-wide cost triggered by £5–£100 of fee. Second, the rules are not uniform: cash-accounting traders get no relief, Flat Rate Scheme traders have their own treatment, and partial payments and later receipts (including through the withheld-payment case, which must not stack) all change the figure; a JobGuard 'write-off' command is not the accounting write-off the regulations require unless it reaches the ledger, so the counterfactual cannot even be evidenced without the connector. Third, the counterfactual is any competent accountant doing routine work, so the fee is a charge on money the builder would have got anyway — exactly the 'took a cut of money I'd have had anyway' base the research identifies as the perception risk (success_fee_benchmarks §6), on the tax side of a customer who never paid. There is also a real-time policy risk: HMRC's tax-advice-market reforms (registration for advisers who interact with HMRC from 2026, and consultation interest in contingent fees on tax claims) are moving against percentage fees on reliefs. Recommend recording the rejection in D03 v3 alongside I85 so no later agent revives it.
verdicts.conditions: None for the fee. If the reminder is built fee-free: label it an aid, not advice; cite the rule version; require the accounting-connector evidence of the write-off before showing an exact figure; state that cash-accounting and Flat Rate Scheme traders may be treated differently; never stack with an open withheld-payment case; solicitor to confirm that a fee-free, generic reminder stays outside MLR reg 11(d).

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (fee rejected; feature value absorbed into the subscription)

verdicts.key_risk: Becoming an MLR 'tax adviser' with customer due diligence on every tenant, plus the word-of-mouth damage of 'JobGuard took 10% of my bad-debt relief' — for a counterfactual an ordinary accountant already covers.

verdicts.reasons: Rejected on two independent regulatory grounds, agreeing with the idea's own recommendation. First and most directly: helping a policyholder make and pursue an insurance claim for reward is 'assisting in the administration and performance of a contract of insurance' (RAO art 39A), a regulated insurance-distribution activity; the art 39B exclusions cover loss adjusting and expert appraisal for the insurer, not loss assessing for the policyholder. FCA PERG 5.7 draws the line between merely providing information or forms (unregulated) and assisting a policyholder to notify, evidence and negotiate a claim for a fee (regulated). A 'this loss looks claimable' Decision, a drafted claim and a 10% fee on the payout sits on the regulated side. Second: claims on insurance contracts fall within the 'financial services or financial product' claims-management sector (RAO arts 89G–89M), so the CMC regime and its CMCOB fee caps (15–30% by band, report benchmark table) would also bite. Either route means FCA authorisation or appointed-representative status under an authorised principal (assume 3–6 months, principal fees, and ongoing conduct rules), for a category worth £5–£75 a year and one that reads as a claims firm taking a slice from a builder who has just been robbed. The founder's fixed decision that JobGuard is not a regulated firm before G4 makes this a blocker. The safe form is I37: a factual evidence pack the builder submits themselves, with no fee tied to the claim and no negotiation, which should stay within the PERG 5.7 'providing information' exclusion — solicitor to confirm that boundary when I37 is built.
verdicts.conditions: None; record the rejection in D03 v3 and note that I37 must remain a factual, fee-free evidence pack with no claim advice, no insurer negotiation and no fee contingent on a payout.

verdicts.key_risk: Carrying on regulated insurance-distribution (RAO art 39A) and claims-management activity without authorisation — a criminal offence under FSMA s.23 — for a trivial fee.

verdicts.reasons: Not regulated by the FCA (B2B, no consumer credit, no claims sector), so the refutation is contractual and structural rather than a permission. (a) Contractual certainty: a fee on 'savings' measured by JobGuard's own cross-merchant alias matching gives JobGuard a discretion over the fee base; under English law such a discretion is enforceable only if exercised rationally and in good faith (the Braganza duty), and a builder disputing a spec mismatch has a live contractual defence every time. Cost-reduction consultancies survive this with signed baselines and client-agreed equivalence (success_fee_benchmarks §2); JobGuard cannot adjudicate quality without becoming the adjudicator the watchdog must not be. (b) Misleading B2B claims: presenting 'you saved £X' on a fee statement when the counterfactual is a different product from a different merchant risks the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 and cuts across the plan's forbidden-claims list (§14.1). (c) Founder decision: prevented or avoided spend earns nothing; a lower price at a new merchant is avoided spend by another name, not settled recovered cash, so it fails the §14.6 north-star test (no immutable proof of money that came back). (d) Conflict: a platform paid when builders switch merchant is one merchant relationship away from Bribery Act 2010 exposure and the D11 conflict the founder has excluded even in structured form. Nothing here requires a solicitor to reject; D11 should record that fees never depend on which merchant the builder uses.
verdicts.conditions: None; record in D11 v3 that no fee may depend on the builder's choice of merchant, and keep 'switching' in I76's never-qualifies list.

verdicts.key_risk: A fee base JobGuard itself controls through alias matching — unenforceable in practice, disputed in every case, and a standing invitation to merchant conflict.

verdicts.reasons: Lawful and unregulated for company counterparties, with real but ordinary conditions. FCA: 'providing credit references' (RAO art 89B, CCA 1974 s.145(8)) is regulated only for information about the financial standing of individuals, and for CCA purposes 'individual' includes sole traders, partnerships of two or three persons and unincorporated bodies (CCA s.189). Company and LLP reports are outside the perimeter, as the idea says; the design must therefore enforce 'companies and LLPs only' structurally (Companies House match required, no CRA product or Registry Trust search on an unincorporated business or on any director personally), otherwise JobGuard risks furnishing regulated credit references. No credit broking, no debt collecting and no claims management arise. Consumer law does not apply (the report is bought by a trader about a trader; the customer never sees it), and the Equality Act 2010 s.29 is satisfied by findings-only, no-verdict presentation. UK GDPR is the main compliance load: directors and PSCs are data subjects; Companies House and Gazette data are public-register data reusable under their open licences, lawful under legitimate interests (Art 6(1)(f)) with a documented balancing test; the builder as controller instructing the check cannot practically give an Article 14 notice, so JobGuard must supply it through the quote email and portal (Art 14(3)(b)) with a recorded Art 14(5)(b) position for non-contact directors, and D12 v2 does not yet cover this — a D12 v3 is required. Confirm the analysis against the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amendments to legitimate interests and subject access. There is no Article 22 issue because no decision is automated. Commercially the CRA reseller contract is the true cost: wholesale company reports usually come with permitted-use limits (credit-risk assessment only), in-app display, no onward supply, retention caps that conflict with D07 evidence retention, and annual minimum commitments (assume £3k–£15k) that exceed Solo/Small revenue until the tenant base is large; the free CP-1 version (Companies House plus Gazette) has none of these and can ship first. The £19 charge is a new platform charge needing D14, D02 VAT at 20%, statement mechanics under D09, and real charging behind G4; in pilot_no_charge JobGuard absorbs the cost and labels it hypothetical.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Structural scope: companies and LLPs only; no reports, CCJ searches or CRA calls on sole traders, partnerships or named directors; unincorporated customers route to I89/I90 with their own analysis. (2) Solicitor confirmation that combining Companies House, Gazette, a CRA company report and a Registry Trust company search does not make JobGuard a credit reference agency for art 89B purposes. (3) D12 v3: builder as controller, JobGuard as processor for the check and controller for its own audit/retention; legitimate-interests assessment on file; Article 14 notice in the quote email and portal; DSAR route for directors; DUAA 2025 check. (4) CRA reseller agreement: in-app view only, watermarked, no export of the raw report, retention class agreed with D07 so recovery-evidence retention does not breach the contract. (5) D14 'paid data services' decision plus D02 VAT and D09 statement lines; charging only behind G4; pilot absorbs cost. (6) Anti-misuse: every check bound to a quote or job and named counterparty, per-quote cap, per-tenant rate limit, purpose stated in terms, every run audited. (7) Copy: findings and sources only, no traffic-light verdict, never 'do not proceed'. Timeline/cost assumption: solicitor and LIA £2k–£4k; CRA contract 4–8 weeks; CP-1 free-data version has no legal cost beyond D12 v3.

verdicts.key_risk: Scope creep into individuals — a sole-trader 'business customer' or a director-level search turns an unregulated company check into regulated credit-reference provision (RAO art 89B); secondarily, a CRA contract whose retention cap conflicts with keeping the check as recovery evidence.

verdicts.reasons: Legally the same activity as I87 (and inherits every I87 condition); the packaging adds only subscription-contract questions, which are light because the counterparty is a trader. The DMCC Act 2024 subscription-contract rules (Part 4 Chapter 2) and its drip-pricing provisions apply to consumer contracts only; a builder — including a sole trader — subscribing for business purposes is not a 'consumer' (DMCC s.253, acting wholly or mainly outside trade), so pre-contract information, reminder notices and cooling-off duties do not apply, though the CMA's approach is a sensible template for the terms. B2B marketing must still not mislead under the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008: 'from £29' is fine because the checks add-on is optional; the overage price, the non-rollover rule and the 'included in Firm' attribution must be stated in the terms and on the pricing page. UCTA 1977 does not police price terms, so allowance forfeiture and £15 overage are enforceable as written; the Consumer Rights Act does not apply. VAT: a bundle of platform access and included checks is a single standard-rated supply (D02). Standing authority for recurring collection is a D05 matter (bounded renewal terms), and tier inclusions, overage, price-change notice and cancellation are D09 v3 items; real charging sits behind G4. Competition law is not engaged (no market power, optional add-on, no tying of a dominant product). The one hidden cost is the CRA contract: an allowance implies committed volume, and some CRAs price per report even inside 'unlimited' partner packages, so the reseller agreement must permit the pack model and the Firm inclusion before the price is printed.
verdicts.conditions: (1) All I87 conditions (companies/LLPs only, D12 v3, CRA reseller terms, D14, G4). (2) D09 v3 items: allowance per tier, overage rate, non-rollover, included-in-Firm attribution, price-change notice and cancellation; D05 bounded renewal authority; D02 VAT on the bundle. (3) Terms and pricing page state overage and non-rollover plainly (BPMMR 2008); keep the per-check option alongside so nobody is forced onto a pack. (4) CRA reseller agreement must permit allowance/pack pricing and the Firm inclusion; confirm retention and per-report cost before publishing prices. (5) Allowance is per tenant and every check is bound to a quote or job in that tenant. (6) Solicitor confirmation that sole-trader tenants are not 'consumers' for DMCC subscription rules (expected no, but it is the terms' foundation). Timeline/cost: no new permission; D09 v3 drafting inside the existing M4-13 legal review.

revised_revenue.solo: £29 (unchanged; alternative to I87, not additive)
revised_revenue.firm: £96 attributed from the Firm price, £0 overage at expected volume; margin depends on the CRA contract permitting pack pricing

verdicts.key_risk: A CRA reseller contract that charges per report regardless of the pack turns the allowance into negative margin at full utilisation; legally, the only exposure is misdescribing overage or inclusions in B2B marketing.

verdicts.reasons: JobGuard-to-builder is trader-to-trader, so the consumer regimes in the brief do not bite: the DMCC Act 2024 Part 4 unfair-practice and drip-pricing rules, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 cooling-off all protect consumers, and a builder buying software for the business acts for purposes relating to trade (research note success_fee_psychology §4; report §'The hidden final check'). No FCA permission is engaged: a plan uplift is a service price, not credit, insurance or claims management. UCTA 1977 s.3 controls only exclusion and 'substantially different performance' clauses in written standard terms, not the price of a plan. What does bite: (1) the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008 reg 3 and, if the screen is ever reused in marketing, CAP Code 3.1/3.3 — 'you would have seen it on 14 May and billed it yourself with no fee' is half record (signal created_at, the §14.1 permitted claim) and half counterfactual about builder behaviour, the mirror of the §14.1 forbidden 'you would have forgotten this'; (2) contract law — a long-running platform relationship with a discretionary hold-back is the kind of contract into which courts have implied a duty of good faith (Yam Seng [2013] EWHC 111 (QB); Bates v Post Office (No 3) [2019] EWHC 606 (QB)); the implied duty yields to clear express terms, so the danger is not the offer itself but a screen that contradicts how onboarding and D13 describe the hold-back ('an independent second check') by pricing it as something the builder pays to switch off. That screen would be the first exhibit in any Misrepresentation Act 1967 s.2(1) or good-faith claim, and in any press story. True cost: no permission, no regulatory timeline; a solicitor review of the statement copy and the plan-change clause inside the M4-13 terms work (roughly £1–3k, 2–4 weeks). Not legal advice; the good-faith and misrepresentation points need a solicitor's view.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Reword to plan facts, not builder counterfactuals: 'JobGuard first held this on 14 May. On Tell me now, cards are shown as they arise and JobGuard's own finds never carry a success fee.' Drop 'billed it yourself with no fee'. (b) The plan choice must have been shown at sign-up (I75) and the same two dates must print on every statement whether or not the offer appears, so the offer is information already owed, not a lever. (c) Symmetrical downgrade advice (I75) ships in the same release. (d) The plan-change Decision under D05 needs a defined effective date, pro-rating and 'only jobs switched live after the change take the new mode' in the D09 v3 terms; no introductory discount (report §'Where premium should show'). (e) Ex-VAT prices carry a prominent '+VAT at 20%' (CAP Code 3.18) because sub-threshold and flat-rate sole traders cannot recover it. (f) Solicitor confirms the express terms describe the hold-back and the paid alternative consistently so no implied-good-faith or misrepresentation argument opens. (g) Never reuse the screen in marketing without BPMMR/CAP substantiation.
