verdicts.key_risk: The screen is a permanent, quotable record that JobGuard prices its own silence; if its wording or the onboarding terms describe the hold-back as being for the builder's benefit, it becomes the central exhibit in a misrepresentation or implied-good-faith claim and in the word-of-mouth 'knew on day 12' story (research note success_fee_psychology §4).

verdicts.reasons: No regulated activity: a free first live job with a stored card is a trader-to-trader trial; the DMCC Act 2024 subscription-contract and unfair-practice rules and the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 are consumer-only, and a builder is a trader. Storing a card at switch-live without charging is an ordinary hosted Stripe set-up under D05 bounded authority; no FCA permission, no AML (no funds move). Showing signals live removes, for the trial job, the parts of the model that carry legal exposure: no hold-back to characterise under an implied good-faith duty (Bates v Post Office (No 3) [2019] EWHC 606 (QB)), no DSAR race (§14.3/§14.11), and the builder can agree extras with the homeowner before the work — exactly what the Consumer Rights Act 2015 s.51 'reasonable price' problem and the DMCC drip-pricing exposure on the builder's own B2C bill argue for (report §'The hidden final check'; research note success_fee_psychology §4). The recorded choice at the end of the trial is also the strongest legal defence the standard plan can have: an informed, evidenced election between a transparent and a delayed-disclosure mode at displayed prices converts the hold-back from a unilateral design into an express term, which is what displaces an implied duty. Data protection is unchanged in kind — the same analysis of job records under D12/D13, only the disclosure timing differs — so the Article 14 route for homeowner messages must still exist before real pilot data. The departure from the report's 'charge the fee on the trial job' (§'Recommendation') is commercial, not legal. True cost: none regulatory; trial-terms drafting inside M4-13 and the D13 v2 tenant_plan_live route; pilot use needs G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval (§14.11). Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Trial terms state plainly that the card is stored not charged, what triggers the first subscription charge, the 90-day ceiling, and that the trial job carries no success fee; 'free' claims must satisfy BPMMR 2008 reg 3 / CAP Code 3.23. (b) The end-of-trial choice screen is a consent record: store it immutably with copy version and prices shown; it is the evidence in any later 'you knew' dispute. (c) Mode binding at switch-live in D09 v3; only jobs switched live after the choice take the chosen mode. (d) Must-surface rules unchanged on the trial job. (e) In pilot_no_charge no card is taken and prices are hypothetical (AGENTS §5.10). (f) Ex-VAT prices carry a prominent VAT statement. (g) Solicitor checks the trial-to-paid transition wording once, inside the M4-13 review.

verdicts.key_risk: The legal benefit only materialises if the choice screen is honest and preserved; a trial described as 'free' while a card is captured, or a choice screen whose wording later diverges from the D09/D13 terms, hands a builder the misrepresentation argument the trial was meant to close.

verdicts.reasons: This is the instrument that makes the delayed-disclosure model legally defensible, so the lens supports it. English law implies a good-faith duty only into 'relational' contracts and only where the express terms leave room (Yam Seng [2013] EWHC 111 (QB); Bates v Post Office (No 3) [2019] EWHC 606 (QB)); an express, priced, recorded choice between 'Tell me now' and 'Standard' with one-sentence descriptions is the clearest way to make the hold-back an agreed term rather than an undisclosed design. Publishing the other plan's arithmetic each period also answers the BPMMR 2008 reg 3 and Misrepresentation Act 1967 risk of a one-sided value story. The paid-reveal tier is not insurance distribution (no indemnity of an uncertain loss; it is a tiered service price) and no FCA permission is engaged; a solicitor should confirm that in one line. Three real legal costs. (1) Copy: the live-plan line 'on Standard your fee on items you had missed at lock would have been £Z' is a counterfactual about the builder, the mirror of the §14.1 forbidden claims, and must be recast as a conditional fact. (2) VAT display: CAP Code 3.18 requires a prominent VAT statement on ex-VAT prices when some buyers (sub-threshold or flat-rate sole traders) cannot recover it (report §'£29 beats £30'). (3) The pilot arms: randomising real pilot tenants between hidden and live modes and showing different hypothetical prices to cohorts is lawful in B2B (no consumer regime; unilateral pricing raises no Competition Act 1998 issue), but the pilot agreement and privacy notice must disclose the randomisation and the measurement purpose (UK GDPR Art 13 purpose transparency for sole-trader builders), the hidden arm needs G1 plus D12/D13 pilot approval before any shadow processing of real data (§14.11), and hypothetical prices must be framed so no contract at that price forms (AGENTS §5.10: pilot jobs can never be billed retroactively). The D09 v3 / D13 v2 / D11 / D12 v3 / D05 / D01 record changes are internal governance; none needs a regulator; a solicitor should review D09 v3 and D13 v2 wording together with the M4-13 terms (roughly £3–6k, 4–6 weeks). An agent cannot mark any of them approved. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Recast counterfactual copy as conditional fact: 'cards first shown to you by JobGuard that you then logged: £N; on Standard, any of these still missing when you completed your account would have carried a 10% fee.' (b) Prominent VAT statement beside every ex-VAT price. (c) Pilot agreement discloses randomisation and hypothetical prices, that nothing is charged and no price term is created; privacy notice names pilot measurement as a purpose. (d) G1 + D12 + D13 pilot approval before the hidden arm touches real data; Article 14 route for homeowner messages in place. (e) Store each builder's plan choice, copy version and prices as an immutable consent record. (f) Must-surface rules identical on both plans in the terms as well as the code. (g) Solicitor review of D09 v3 and D13 v2 wording for consistency with the 'independent second check' description in onboarding, plus a one-line confirmation that the paid-reveal tier is not a contract of insurance. (h) Treat cohort results as directional only; repeat with the priced sign-up page test before G4 (report §'Recommendation').

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct (instrument only; it sets what I67–I71 may charge)

verdicts.key_risk: The running comparison necessarily prints 'JobGuard first held this on [date]' on every standard-plan statement; if D13 v2 or onboarding ever describe the hold-back as for the builder's benefit while the plan page prices it as an option, the contradiction is documented monthly and becomes the basis for a misrepresentation or implied-good-faith claim and for churn.

verdicts.reasons: No regulator is engaged. The builder sends a letter in its own name to a business supplier: not consumer credit, credit broking, insurance distribution, debt collecting under a consumer credit agreement (RAO art 39F) or claims management (RAO arts 89G–89M) (research note success_fee_benchmarks §7). No money passes through JobGuard, so no AML. The merchant relationship is B2B, so the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and DMCC Act 2024 do not apply; the Late Payment Act and the Construction Act are irrelevant. JobGuard is not a buying group: it aggregates no purchasing and negotiates nothing, so Competition Act 1998 Chapter I is not engaged by the letter itself; the only competition exposure is the opt-in I28 benchmark band, which is an exchange of purchase-price information among competing builders and must be aggregated, anonymised and historic under the CMA's horizontal-agreements guidance (an I28 point inherited here). The DBA Regulations 2013 50% cap applies only to legal representatives' damages-based agreements, so a 20% share with a £1,000 ceiling is unregulated in B2B; UCTA 1977 s.3 does not control price terms. So the lens cannot refute I76 on external law; its true cost is internal and contractual. (1) It conflicts with AGENTS §5.6 (a positive fee needs 'available unallocated settled value') and with D03 v2's express exclusion of 'invoice reductions' and prevented spend (§14.7: 'prevention stays terminal and fee-free'): a lower invoiced rate is an invoice reduction and there is no landing of cash to allocate. Under AGENTS §1 a conflict is a blocker for the affected behaviour, so I76 needs a signed AGENTS §5.6 amendment plus D03 v3/D01 vNext defining a savings-measured category before any code, not just a new D03 row. (2) The fee base is a counterfactual (prior_rate − invoiced_rate) that will be disputed on market-price grounds; the builder-favourable attestation is the right contractual answer but must be an express term accepted at letter send (M4-13), with the 12-month, 90-day and ceiling limits, or the fee clause is unenforceable for uncertainty. (3) BPMMR 2008 reg 3 accuracy for 'Saved £X against your old rate' and any marketing; the letter must say the builder negotiated. (4) Negligent-misstatement exposure if unit normalisation in the letter is wrong (limit under UCTA-reasonable standard terms); some merchant trade-account terms contain pricing-confidentiality clauses — a builder using its own data with its own merchant is fine, but a letter citing a JobGuard benchmark could put the builder in breach (again I28). (5) The backdated cash-refund limb is the cleanest part legally (settled cash from the supplier) but it is a negotiated retrospective rebate, not an 'overcharge', so D03's supplier_overcharge wording must be extended and the cross-basis uniqueness rule stated in the terms. Timeline/cost: no permission; an AGENTS/D03/D01 amendment cycle plus solicitor drafting of the rate-review terms (roughly £2–4k, 4–8 weeks), plus a competition-law check if I28 bands are included (£2–5k). Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Signed decision record amending AGENTS §5.6 and D03 (v3) to define a savings-measured category and lift the 'invoice reductions never qualify' exclusion for this category only; D01 vNext for the rate and £1,000 ceiling; D02 for net-of-VAT measurement; D05 for collection authority. Until then the fee path stays disabled and synthetic. (b) Rate-review terms accepted at letter send as an express contract term: measurement formula, 12-month window, 90-day anchor, ceiling, builder-favourable general-price-cut attestation, offset-line hold rule, reversal rule, lower-basis rule for backdated refunds, and 'JobGuard receives nothing from any merchant'. (c) Pilot at 10%, not 20%, unless the §14.17 fairness measure supports 20% (report §'The hidden final check' on who-did-the-work fairness). (d) I28 bands only after a competition-law review (aggregated, anonymised, historic) and builder opt-in; the letter must not cite other builders' prices individually. (e) Letter copy states the builder negotiates and JobGuard has no merchant relationship; standard limitation of liability for figures. (f) Extend D03 supplier_overcharge wording to 'settled cash refund or retrospective rebate'; account credits and credit notes excluded; one derivation identity per (tenant, invoice_line_id) across both bases. (g) Live only behind G4.

verdicts.key_risk: It is a fee on money not spent, which AGENTS §5.6 and D03 v2 currently forbid; shipping it without a signed amendment breaks the build's own invariant, and shipping it with one puts a disputed counterfactual (did the market fall?) at the centre of JobGuard's fee book for the first time.

verdicts.reasons: A flat charge for a drafted letter and a 12-month tracker is an ordinary trader-to-trader software add-on: no FCA permission (not credit, insurance, debt collecting or claims management), no AML (no funds move), no success fee so no D01/D03 change, and D09 v3 only needs an add-on SKU with amount, unit (per round or monthly) and VAT (standard-rated). Consumer law does not apply to either the JobGuard–builder or the builder–merchant relationship. UCTA 1977 s.3 does not touch a fixed price; there is no cooling-off for traders, so a builder who abandons a round after paying gets a refund only if the terms say so. JobGuard is not a buying group or purchasing agent — it negotiates nothing and takes nothing from merchants — so Competition Act 1998 Chapter I and agency law are not engaged by the product; the sole competition exposure is the opt-in I28 band (aggregated, anonymised, historic purchase-price data — an I28 review point). The remaining legal points are accuracy and independence: the 'what you saved' tracker is an illustration and must be labelled so (BPMMR 2008 reg 3; CAP Code 3.1/3.3 if marketed; CAP 3.18 VAT statement on the £49/£15 prices); an express 'JobGuard receives no payment, commission or benefit from any merchant' term keeps the product outside the hidden-intermediary pattern that drew Ofgem's commission-disclosure rules onto energy brokers (research note success_fee_benchmarks §2) and away from any secret-commission argument. Negligent-misstatement exposure for figures in the letter is ordinary SaaS liability, limited under reasonable standard terms. Tradify's £10/month add-on (research note uk_trade_job_software) shows flat add-ons are normal in this market. No timeline or cost beyond folding one SKU clause into the M4-13 terms review (under £1k). Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: Labelled illustration, express no-merchant-benefit term, prominent VAT statement, 'the builder negotiates' copy, and an I28 competition review before benchmark bands appear in the letter; otherwise clear.

revised_revenue.solo: £25 (0.5 rounds × £49) or £54 on the £15/month add-on at 30% uptake (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: Naming or copy ('Buying watch', 'review my prices') drifting into what looks like a buying group or merchant tie-in; the legal safety rests on JobGuard visibly taking nothing from merchants and doing no negotiating.

verdicts.reasons: Tax law does not stop it. Input-tax evidence is governed by the VAT Regulations 1995: reg 29 (a VAT invoice, or alternative evidence at HMRC's discretion under reg 29(2)), reg 16 less-detailed invoices up to £250, and the flat-rate scheme in Part VIIA (no input tax except capital goods of £2,000 or more incl. VAT). Applying those as deterministic checks labelled 'an aid to your VAT records' is not a regulated activity: tax advice is not FCA- or statutorily-licensed in the UK and tax is not a claims-management sector (RAO arts 89G–89M). JobGuard files nothing and holds no 64-8, so HMRC's 2026 registration requirement for advisers who interact with HMRC does not bite. Two things do. (1) Money Laundering Regulations 2017 reg 11(d), widened from 10 January 2020: a 'tax adviser' is anyone who by way of business provides 'material aid, or assistance or advice, in connection with the tax affairs of other persons'. A passive tool is generally treated as outside this; a service that raises tax-specific Decisions, drafts the chase letter and charges a fee measured on input tax reclaimed looks more like material aid. If HMRC would treat it so, JobGuard needs HMRC AML supervision (registration in the region of £300 per premises a year plus fit-and-proper fees — verify current figures — and a customer-due-diligence programme on every builder). That fixed cost alone exceeds the Solo revenue line. It needs an AML specialist's view before build; the same question attaches to I79/I80 and, dormant, to the existing I25/I26 modules. The partner route that avoids it is to keep JobGuard a tool: hand the flag and evidence to the builder's accountant (already AML-supervised) and take no fee measured on the tax outcome. (2) The counterfactual is weaker than stated: HMRC may accept alternative evidence (reg 29(2)) and input tax can be claimed in any return within four years (reg 29(1A)), so 'VAT they would otherwise have paid to HMRC' overstates the loss; BPMMR 2008 reg 3 accuracy applies to statement wording. Internally, a reclaim netted in a VAT return is not 'available unallocated settled value' (AGENTS §5.6), so D03 v3, D01 (base = input tax reclaimed) and D02 changes plus an AGENTS §5.6 clarification are required; D04/D12 cover the accounting connector. Timeline: AML assessment 2–4 weeks (£1–3k); if registration is needed, 2–3 months and ongoing compliance. Not legal advice; the MLR characterisation needs a specialist.
verdicts.conditions: (a) AML/MLR 2017 reg 11(d) assessment by a specialist before any tax-aid feature charges a fee; if 'tax adviser' applies, either register for HMRC supervision or restructure to the tool-plus-accountant route. (b) Default to the fee-free goodwill form in pilot and count it as subscription value (the idea's own alternative); enable the 10% only after the AML position is settled and D03 v3/D01/D02 plus an AGENTS §5.6 clarification are signed. (c) Never charge flat-rate or partially exempt tenants; tenant VAT-status facts versioned and builder-attested. (d) Statement wording: 'input tax reclaimed after JobGuard's flag', never 'VAT you would have lost'; 'aid to your VAT records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file' on every output. (e) Return-inclusion evidence only from an approved connector (D04/D12); builder attestation never qualifies in production. (f) Builder-favourable 'I had already asked' attestation as an express term.

revised_revenue.solo: £5 gross at 10%; £0 or negative net once any AML registration cost is spread — run fee-free
revised_revenue.small_firm: £43 gross at 10%; only worth charging if the AML position needs no registration

verdicts.key_risk: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 'tax adviser' definition (material aid in connection with others' tax affairs) could pull JobGuard into HMRC AML supervision for a category worth £5–£150 a year per builder; the fee form is what makes it look like a tax service rather than a tool.

verdicts.reasons: Flat pack: legally an information product built from the builder's own records under the CIS regime (FA 2004 ss.57–77; Income Tax (Construction Industry Scheme) Regulations 2005, including reg 4 payment-and-deduction statements and reg 56 company set-off). Not FCA-regulated, not claims management, no filing, no 64-8 agent authority, so HMRC's adviser-registration requirement does not apply; VAT standard-rated on the £59/£99; no consumer law (trader buyer). The same MLR 2017 reg 11(d) 'tax adviser' question as I78 arises — a reconciled year-end schedule with gaps chased is closer to bookkeeping than a passive tool — and needs the same specialist view; Xero's £5/month CIS add-on (research note construction_platforms_and_ai) shows the market treats software CIS features as tools, which is the position to preserve: the builder or their accountant files. Percentage variant: refuted on the law, not on taste. A subcontractor's entitlement to credit for deductions does not depend on holding the contractor's statement — HMRC accepts a claim on the sub's own payment records where the contractor fails to provide one and can pursue the contractor — so the 'evidence increment JobGuard caused' is not an entitlement increment, and a fee on it is a fee on the builder's own tax with no defensible counterfactual (BPMMR 2008 reg 3 accuracy; the §14.1 forbidden 'you would have lost this' shape). It also sits next to the repayment-agent regime: HMRC voided assignments of income-tax repayments in 2023 and requires repayment agents to register; JobGuard stays outside only because the repayment goes to the builder's bank and JobGuard merely observes it (D10 bank feed), but a percentage of an HMRC repayment is exactly the product profile the research warns carries the R&D-boutique stain (research note success_fee_benchmarks §5). Repayment observation via TrueLayer needs D10/D12; payroll-connector set-off evidence needs D04/D12; contractor names and UTRs on statements are third-party personal data (D12 Article 14). Cost: AML assessment shared with I78; a D09 add-on SKU; no regulator otherwise. Not legal advice.
verdicts.conditions: (a) Flat pack only; drop the percentage variant (no D03/D01 change). (b) AML/MLR 2017 assessment before launch; keep JobGuard a tool: builder or accountant files, no HMRC interaction, no repayment ever routed via JobGuard. (c) Every output carries 'aid to your CIS records, not tax advice; JobGuard does not file, hold 64-8 authority or claim on your behalf'; marketing never says 'we get your tax back'. (d) Statement-request letter sent by the builder in its own name. (e) D10/D12 for bank-feed repayment observation; D12 Article 14 route for contractor personal data. (f) D09 v3 add-on SKU with VAT.

revised_revenue.solo: £18 flat (£59 × 30% in CIS); percentage variant £0 (refuted)

verdicts.key_risk: Being characterised as a tax adviser under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 or as a repayment agent; both are avoided only while JobGuard files nothing, receives no repayment and charges a flat price rather than a share of HMRC's money.

verdicts.reasons: The category rests on a mistaken view of what an over-deduction costs the builder. Under FA 2004 s.61 the contractor deducts from the labour element only (materials excluded) at 20% for a verified sub or 30% otherwise, but under s.62 and the CIS Regulations 2005 (reg 56 for companies; Self Assessment for sole traders) every sum actually deducted and shown on the payment-and-deduction statement is credited to the subcontractor as tax paid. An over-deduction is therefore not lost money; it is money routed through HMRC with a delay (monthly set-off for companies, up to about 21 months via Self Assessment for a sole trader). The correct remedy is for the contractor to amend its CIS300 return and issue a corrected statement, after which the sub's HMRC credit falls and any cash top-up makes the sub whole. A contractor who pays the difference in cash without amending leaves the sub with both the cash and the full HMRC credit — a double recovery the sub must correct in its own return — and leaves the contractor out of pocket. The idea's qualifying test ('contractor paid the difference in CASH after the Decision, matched on the bank feed') counts exactly that cash, so the fee would fall either on a cash-flow acceleration or on a double recovery; a fee on the second is JobGuard profiting from a tax error it helped create, which no D03 row, D01 base or D12 route can cure, and the §14.1 'you would not have got this' shape is untrue. No regulator forbids it (not FCA, not claims management, no AML) and D12 could handle contractor personal data, but the counterfactual fails on the statute. The detection itself is valuable and should stay: a Decision that prompts the builder to get the contractor to correct the deduction before the CIS300 is filed (by the 19th of the following month) saves real cash-flow and is ordinary fee-free watchdog value under the subscription, consistent with the founder's rule that prevented spend earns nothing. The MLR 2017 tax-adviser question from I78/I79 applies to the check too and is easier to answer if no fee is measured on a tax outcome. Not legal advice; a CIS specialist should confirm the set-off mechanics before the watchdog copy is written.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as a success-fee category. Keep the cis_over_deduction check as a fee-free watchdog Decision with copy that tells the builder the deduction is credited by HMRC and that the contractor should amend its CIS return and statement; never present a cash payment from the contractor as a recovery unless a corrected statement is held; no D03 v3 row, no D01 change.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (fee category rejected); watchdog value only, counted under the subscription

verdicts.key_risk: Paying a 10% fee on a contractor's cash top-up that is duplicated by the subcontractor's HMRC credit would make JobGuard the beneficiary of a double recovery the builder later has to unwind in its tax return.

verdicts.reasons: Refuted on four grounds. (1) It damages the builder's relationship with exactly the customers a small firm depends on. A minimum of three contributing tenants is no anonymity in a local trade: a property manager or small developer that has used three JobGuard builders in two years knows who they are, and a line saying it 'pays 41 days late, 2 disputed' will be traced back to the builders who invoiced it. The builder never asked to be party to rating their own customers. (2) 'Disputed' is a smear of the third party: a dispute recorded by the builder may have been the builder's own defective work, yet it becomes a negative fact about the customer; the correction route the idea proposes means JobGuard adjudicating between non-users and its own tenants. (3) It is the named trust risk, 'builders' data reused across tenants', for almost no benefit. Below several hundred business-invoicing tenants the line reads 'Not enough JobGuard data' for years, so the builder pays the trust cost (their invoice facts leaving the tenant, a required change to their own customer contracts under D12 v3) and receives nothing. Where the line does reach threshold (housing associations, main contractors, large property managers) Creditsafe/Experian trade-payment data already covers the company far better and can be licensed into I87 without any builder's data leaving its tenant; where CRAs are thin (micro-companies with two or three trade suppliers) is exactly where deanonymisation bites. The usable zone is already served; the unserved zone is harmful. (4) Fairness: the £5/month add-on for non-contributors contradicts the stated symmetry and lets a builder buy access to data other builders did the work to create (Xia/Monroe/Cox: who did the work). A subtler point: JobGuard earns 10% on withheld-payment cases (BUILD_PLAN §14.7), so a JobGuard-authored 'slow payer' line is the fee-earning party characterising the counterparty; a reasonable builder or customer could read it as priming for cases. The one point in the idea's favour is that helping a builder avoid a bad customer is prevention, on which JobGuard earns nothing, so its incentive is not obviously self-serving; that does not outweigh the structural deanonymisation. Revenue of £0–£42 a year is not worth a single word-of-mouth story that 'JobGuard shares your invoice data'.
verdicts.conditions: Not to be built. Meet the underlying need by licensing CRA payment-performance data into the I87 'Check this customer' card, which gives the builder the benefit with no cross-tenant reuse. Revisit only if all of the following hold, and even then treat 'never' as the default: JobGuard has several hundred business-invoicing tenants; threshold raised to at least 5 contributing tenants and 10 invoices with no tenant supplying more than 40% of counted invoices; the 'disputed' count removed (or limited to disputes resolved against the customer with recorded outcome); a separate, revocable opt-in per tenant in plain words ('your invoice dates for company customers will be pooled with other builders'), never bundled into general terms; no £5 non-contributor add-on (strict give-to-get only); a staffed correction route for named companies; a decision record with legal review covering defamation wording and the personal-data status of micro-companies; the cross-tenant read model built as a reviewed AGENTS §5.1 exception with its own role and RLS-exemption tests; and the withheld-payment case flow never references the network line.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected; idea's estimate £0)

verdicts.key_risk: A rated company deanonymises the three local builders who contributed, one of them loses a repeat commercial customer, and the story that 'JobGuard shares your invoice data with other builders' spreads through the trade, for revenue of under £50 a year per tenant.

verdicts.reasons: Attempted refutations and why they fail with safeguards. (1) Independence: insurer money does not touch the supplier-invoice watchdog and does not use the builder's customers as leads, so it avoids the two named conflicts, provided no data flows to the partner (see conditions). (2) Profit from withheld information: none; the trigger uses exposure the builder can already see on I95. (3) Fairness: the builder pays JobGuard nothing, the line is disclosed on its face, the referral is a familiar pattern (accountants and trade bodies refer insurance), and it appears only when the builder has real exposure. A reasonable builder would see a free, disclosed pointer to cover against a customer going bust as in their interest, especially since the alternative JobGuard offers, a recovery case, costs them 10% (§14.7) while a claim costs JobGuard's commission relationship nothing further; JobGuard pointing at the route where it earns less is evidence of good faith, if it actually does so. (4) The refutation that survives partially: JobGuard would sit between two paid routes for the same non-payment (insurer claim, on which it has a commission relationship; recovery case, on which it earns 10%), and the report's own finding is that disclosure does not neutralise a conflict and can worsen adviser behaviour (Cain, Loewenstein & Moore, cited in §'The hidden final check, not the 10%, is the pricing risk'). That is why the conditions bind behaviour, not just wording. (5) Suitability harm: trade credit insurance is usually whole-turnover with minimum premiums and typically excludes disputed debts, which in construction is the common form of non-payment. A builder nudged into a £2k–£5k policy that does not cover their disputed £20k will blame JobGuard even though JobGuard 'did not advise'. The line must describe the product factually and must never be shown with the builder's exposure figure beside it as a prompt. (6) Regulatory: taking commission plus supplying exposure figures likely puts JobGuard outside the RAO art. 72C information-only exclusion; the idea already says so. Fair to the builder only if JobGuard is properly positioned (IAR/AR under the partner or a counsel-confirmed exclusion) before any live line. Economics are poor (£15–£94 a year against a regulatory route) but that is a founder call, not a trust objection.
verdicts.conditions: (a) No live line until counsel confirms the regulatory route in a signed decision record: introducer-appointed-representative or appointed-representative status under the one partner, or a confirmed exclusion; commission is never taken under an assumed exclusion. (b) Off by default; per-tenant, revocable opt-in labelled 'Show insurance introductions'. (c) Zero data to the partner beyond the consented introduction (business name, contact, consent timestamp). Exposure figures, customer names and invoice data never leave JobGuard; the builder gives the broker their own figures. Partner and flows entered in D04 and D12 v3. (d) No premium loading: contractual term that the builder pays no more than the partner's direct price and JobGuard's share comes out of the broker's commission; the basis of JobGuard's remuneration disclosed in the tenant's terms and fee statement, not only 'may be paid'. (e) One partner, fixed and reviewed copy, no ranking, no performance-based placement; the line describes the product as cover against customer insolvency or protracted default and never states or implies that disputed invoices are covered; the builder's exposure figure is never displayed alongside the line. (f) When a policy is recorded on a job and a payment is withheld, the case-opening screen shows the insurer route first (notification deadline, claim conditions) alongside the JobGuard recovery case, with both costs stated; a recovery case cannot be opened on a debt already notified to the insurer without explicit acknowledgement; JobGuard never delays or suppresses the insurer route to protect its 10%. (g) 'Insured builders open fewer cases' is recorded as a conflict indicator, never a target; partner commission is reported separately and never used to tune the threshold or the copy. (h) The partner may not market to the builder beyond the single introduction. (i) Withdraw the line if the partner's product materially excludes the tenant's dominant non-payment mode or complaints exceed a set threshold. (j) All of this behind a G4-equivalent gate with its own decision record, as for I43/I46.

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard becomes the party choosing between an insurer claim (partner relationship) and its own 10% recovery case for the same unpaid invoice; if a builder ever finds the case route promoted over a claim they could have made, or buys cover on JobGuard's prompt that does not cover their disputed debt, the 'independent watchdog' claim is gone, and doing this under an assumed FCA exclusion adds unauthorised-distribution exposure.

verdicts.reasons: Demand is weaker than the attach rates assume. The trigger is 'quote at £5k+', but a Solo builder wins roughly 45% of quotes (19 jobs from 42 quotes at the stated £150k/£8k), so a £12 check at quote-send costs ~£26 per won job before the builder knows they have the work; the rational trigger is acceptance, which cuts the volume by half. Most domestic work below ~£20k is won by recommendation, where the builder already knows the household. The free self-verification path is shown first by design, which cannibalises the paid path further. Reworked at acceptance on won jobs (Solo 19 jobs x 60% at £5k+ x 20% attach; Small 24 x 80% x 30%; Firm ~20 homeowner jobs x 90% x 40%; named-person add-on on half), the gross is about £40 / £100 / £120 a year and the margin about £15 / £37 / £45, i.e. 4-7% of a £348 / £708 / £1,428 subscription (report §'Recommendation', prices unapproved). Against that sits a 3-week build (HMLR Business e-services OC1 ordering, a semi-structured title-register parser with a golden set under M0-12, a Registry Trust adapter, IIR lookup), a recorded Art 6(1)(f) balancing test and Article 14 notice under D12 v3, and a 'D14' charging record that does not yet exist in docs/decisions. At £15-£45 margin per builder JobGuard needs on the order of a thousand paying builders to recover the build, and nothing can be charged before G4, so this is a late-M4 feature earning pocket money. The one genuinely valuable output is the name-mismatch finding (quote addressed to someone other than the registered proprietor), which is protective and rare; the CCJ search on a named homeowner (Part B) is the weak half: low true-positive rate, a builder can already run TrustOnline for £6, and it is the part most likely to be reported as 'JobGuard credit-checks homeowners' in a trade forum or a DSAR response (report §'The hidden final check' on fairness and betrayal). Comparable: tenant referencing at £15-£30 is consented and mandatory for the tenant; here the homeowner has a choice and the builder fears losing the job.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Ship Part A (title register) only, as a pass-through at the HMLR fee inside a tier checks allowance (I88) rather than a £12 SKU; the customer self-verify path stays first. (2) Defer Part B (CCJ/insolvency on a named individual) until pilot data show builders ask for it unprompted on jobs above ~£20k; if built, findings only, search terms shown, never 'identity confirmed'. (3) Trigger at acceptance or switch-live, not at quote-send, and bind each order to a quote/job address with a per-job cap. (4) Create the checks-charging decision record (the 'D14' the ideas assume) and extend D12 to v3 before any real order; Article 14 notice in the first customer communication. (5) Treat revenue as retention/tier value, not a line item; measure name-mismatch rate and self-verify share in the no-charge pilot.

revised_revenue.solo: £40 gross / ~£15 margin a year (2-3 title checks, 1 named-person add-on); ~4% of a £348 subscription
revised_revenue.small_firm: £100 gross / ~£37 margin a year (6 title checks, 3 add-ons)
revised_revenue.firm: £120 gross / ~£45 margin a year (7 title checks, 3-4 add-ons); Firm homeowner mix is smaller than the idea's 48 quotes implies

verdicts.key_risk: Trust and optics: a homeowner learning through a DSAR or a dispute that their builder ran a CCJ search through JobGuard, combined with margins too small to justify the build and legal work; the title-register mismatch finding is the only part with defensible value.

verdicts.reasons: The customer-facing ask kills the demand. A builder who has just won a £15k kitchen must ask the homeowner to consent to a credit search before starting; the idea's own key metric is 'drop-off in acceptance after a verify request'. Builders sell on trust and word of mouth, and the free alternative (deposit plus stage schedule, I40) is standard and costs nothing, so the request rate will be far below the assumed 40-50% and consent below 50%: unlike tenant referencing, where the tenant has no choice, the homeowner can simply pick the builder who did not ask. Reworked at 25-30% request and 30% consent on the same £10k+ quote counts, completed searches are about 0.9 / 2.0 / 3.0 a year, or £14 / £30 / £45 per builder. Platform economics are negative: at £3 wholesale and an assumed £10k CRA minimum, break-even is ~800 completed searches a year, which at these rates needs 400+ active builders, all of whom must pass the CRA's end-user vetting (assumption: CRAs vet each end user for a quotation-search product and may not accept a non-credit trade purpose at all; tenant referencing is an established permitted purpose, 'building work' is not). It also changes what JobGuard is: the first product surface that touches a consumer credit file, with CCA s.157-160 dispute routing, ICO credit-referencing guidance, a new D12 category and legal review before build, all for an M4-era item behind G4 and a CRA contract that takes months. The report finds no UK trade-software precedent and warns that fee/fairness objections come from 'who bears the cost' (Xia, Monroe & Cox 2004); here the homeowner bears an intrusion for the builder's comfort. The protective value it targets (paying party identity, ability to pay a large bill) is mostly delivered by I89 Part A, the portal declaration and I40, without a credit file.
verdicts.conditions: Not recommended even with conditions. If revisited after the pilot, only as: threshold £25k+, builder opt-in per job, consent captured in the customer's authenticated portal session, CRA contract with no data-contribution obligation, legal review completed, and a measured acceptance-drop-off test on synthetic-then-real jobs before charging.
