revised_revenue.small_firm: £30 a year (2 completed searches); negative contribution at pilot scale
revised_revenue.firm: £45 a year (3 completed searches); positive only above ~400 active builders platform-wide

verdicts.key_risk: Lost jobs for the builder and a fixed CRA cost JobGuard cannot cover at pilot scale, plus becoming a consumer-credit-file handler with the regulatory and reputational load that brings.

verdicts.reasons: The prevention value is real and the trust fit is the best in the set (no third party pays, no personal data beyond an address, source-linked facts), but the £5 per-address meter is the wrong commercial shape and the revenue is trivial. The research says people prefer flat charges to a running meter (Prelec & Loewenstein 1998; Lambrecht & Skiera 2006, report §'The hidden final check'), and every £5 charge under AGENTS §5.3 needs its own approved Decision, statement line and VAT line, so the metering machinery costs more than the £5 earns. Attach rates of 40-50% are high: small domestic jobs (bathrooms, boilers, decorating) never need a listed-building or Article 4 check and builders know their patch; a defensible attach is 20-35% of domestic quotes on external/structural work, giving £42 / £68 / £84 a year as a meter, or £0 direct as a tier feature. Coverage is the honesty problem the idea half-acknowledges: NHLE covers England only (Cadw and HES are separate sources), planning.data.gov.uk conservation-area and Article 4 coverage is partial, and council planning history needs a paid aggregator; the card will say 'not checked' often, which undermines a paid check but is acceptable for an included one. The build is also a little heavier than 2 weeks: UPRN resolution needs address matching, and OS Open UPRN carries no addresses, so either OS Places (commercial licence, not free outside PSGA) or a paid geocoder is required (assumption). Comparable: conveyancing searches sell to solicitors at tens of pounds because a transaction depends on them; no trade app reviewed offers this (report §'No rival sells a final check'), which makes it a differentiator for the £59 Builder tier rather than a SKU.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Include it in Builder and Firm tiers (and the first-job trial) rather than metering; no Decision/charge per address. (2) Build in M2 as part of the M2-6 site-readiness factual adapters, with 'not checked' as the default where a dataset is absent, dataset publication dates on the card, and application references without applicant names. (3) Reviewed fixed wording for the listed-building offence statement (D06-style), with a 'facts, not advice' label and source links. (4) D04 register entries for any aggregator and geocoder; budget for OS Places or equivalent. (5) Measure constraint-hit rate and later readiness blocks for missing consent in the pilot; only consider pricing above the allowance if hit rates justify it after G4.

revised_revenue.solo: £42 a year if metered at £5 (20% of 42 domestic quotes); £0 direct as a tier feature
revised_revenue.small_firm: £68 a year if metered (30% of 45); £0 direct as a tier feature
revised_revenue.firm: £84 a year if metered (35% of 48); £0 direct as a tier feature; value shows as tier conversion and retention, not revenue

verdicts.key_risk: Coverage gaps make a paid check look unreliable ('not checked' on most cards), and per-address metering adds Decision, statement and VAT overhead that exceeds the £5; as an included tier feature both risks disappear.

verdicts.reasons: This is the strongest paid check in the set because it answers the question that determines whether a builder gets paid at all: the legal entity that owes the money. For Firms doing subcontract work for main contractors, a payer with overdue accounts, recent CCJs or a Gazette notice is the single most useful pre-contract fact, and the Late Payment Act interest and compensation only apply to business debtors (research note success_fee_benchmarks §3), so knowing the payer is a business entity also improves any later D03 case. The frequency assumptions hold: Solo 2, Small 6, Firm 15 off-quote payers a year is plausible for the stated mix. Attach should be trimmed (25 / 35 / 50%) because builders believe they already know their regular main contractors and Companies House is free, giving £15 / £61 / £218 gross a year at £29, with ~60% margin. That is negligible for Solo and Small but ~15% of a £1,428 Firm subscription, which is defensible as a Firm-tier line. Refutations that stand: the free parts (Companies House filings, charges, officers, The Gazette, Payment Practices data) can be self-served, so the £29 buys assembly, the CCJ line (which needs a CRA or Registry Trust commercial feed with contract minimums, assumption) and the bundled 90-day watch; the Payment Practices line appears only for payers above the £36m turnover threshold, so rarely for a small builder's clients; and the paid data dependency (I87's CRA reseller contract) is a fixed cost that only pays back at scale. Comparable: Satago and Chaser bundle debtor risk insights into £45-£899 flat subscriptions rather than selling per check (success_fee_benchmarks §6), which argues for including the free-source version in the Firm tier and charging only for the CRA-backed report. Note the job spine has no payer field today (only a free-text counterparty on recovery_case), so the 'who will pay' capture is a data-model change worth making early regardless of the paid check.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Add the tenant-qualified paying_party reference to the job spine (M0-7) and the contract-pack hook (I33) early and free; that is the structural value and is needed for D03 cases anyway. (2) Ship the free-source payer card (Companies House, Gazette, Payment Practices) inside the Firm tier, not metered; price the £29 check only once a CRA/Registry Trust feed with CCJ data exists, and only if the reseller contract minimum is covered by projected Firm volume. (3) Card states plainly that naming a payer creates no contract; bind checks to a quote or job and rate-limit. (4) D12 v3 covers officer/PSC data under legitimate interests with the Article 14 notice in the contract pack as well as the quote; D04 entries; the 'D14' checks-charging record must be created; charging behind G4. (5) Measure share of jobs with a distinct payer and later withheld-payment outcomes by payer type in the pilot.

revised_revenue.solo: £15 a year (2 off-quote payers x 25% x £29); ~£9 margin; treat as £0
revised_revenue.firm: £218 a year (15 x 50% x £29); ~£130 margin; roughly 15% of a £1,428 Firm subscription, the only archetype where it is a real line

verdicts.key_risk: The paid data feed (CRA/Registry Trust reseller minimum) is a fixed cost that Solo and Small volumes cannot cover, so the check is only viable as a Firm-tier product; without it, the free-source version is a feature, not revenue.

verdicts.reasons: Volume kills it as a product: 0.3 / 1.5 / 4 block jobs a year at 30-50% attach is £4 / £23 / £78 gross, and even those assumptions are generous for a Solo builder. Half of the £39 is a questionnaire the builder completes themselves with documents they obtained from the managing agent; JobGuard then applies a fixed statutory text (the s.20 £250 per-leaseholder cap) that anyone doing block work already knows and that the managing agent, not the builder, is responsible for. The reserve-fund line is unreliable: many RMC/RTM companies file micro-entity or dormant accounts with no legible reserve-fund figure (assumption from typical filings), so the card will often say 'not shown'. The statutory text also needs maintenance: the consultation thresholds have been under review in the leasehold-reform programme (assumption; treat the £250 figure as a versioned fixture with a review date), and a D06-style legal wording review costs more than the feature earns for years. Reworked at lower attach (Solo 0, Small 1.5 x 30%, Firm 4 x 40%) the revenue is £0 / £18 / £62. The underlying insight is sound but it is a payer-type-specific question set, not a product: when I92's 'who will pay' answer is an RMC, RTM company, freeholder or managing agent, ask the s.20 questions and read the accounts there, at no extra charge.
verdicts.conditions: Do not build as a standalone £39 check. Salvage inside I92: when payer type is RMC/RTM/freeholder/managing agent, add the dated s.20 document-upload questionnaire and the reviewed statutory text as a payer-type module, included in the Firm tier; leaseholder counts only, never names; hashes and receive times stored without asserting authenticity (AGENTS §5.8).

revised_revenue.solo: £0 a year (0-1 block job every three years)
revised_revenue.small_firm: £18 a year (1.5 block jobs x 30% x £39); not worth a separate SKU
revised_revenue.firm: £62 a year (4 x 40% x £39); ~£50 margin, below the cost of maintaining the legal text

verdicts.key_risk: A niche, self-completed check whose fixed legal wording needs review and upkeep, sold to a handful of Firm jobs a year; the value lives in I92's payer-type logic, not in a £39 product.

verdicts.reasons: The monitoring is useful; the £3 per counterparty per month meter is not. Revenue is £6 / £32 / £139 a year on the idea's own numbers, and lower once I92 (which already bundles a 90-day watch in its £29) is taken into account, because a builder will not pay twice for the same watch: reworked at Solo 1.9 x 2 months x 30%, Small 6 x 3 x 40%, Firm 16.5 x 4 x 50% it is £3 / £22 / £99. A pro-rata per-entity meter that starts at switch-live and stops at final payment needs a Decision per monitored entity, proration logic, statement lines and VAT handling under AGENTS §5.3-5.5, which is far more engineering than the revenue, and the research is explicit that customers dislike taxi-meter charges (report §'The hidden final check'). The core feeds are free (Companies House streaming API, The Gazette), so the marginal data cost is near zero until a CRA monitoring product is added at £0.50-£1 per entity-month with contract minimums. The honest packaging is the one Satago and Creditsafe/Experian use: monitoring included in the plan (success_fee_benchmarks §6), here as a Firm-tier feature that only fires for business counterparties. Excluding homeowners is right and the D03 entry test is untouched, but the trust point stands: an inbox event followed by an 'open a withheld-payment case' action will read as JobGuard fishing for a 10% case unless that action is hidden until the D03 test is independently met. Build cost (Graphile scheduled/streaming worker, idempotent source-event IDs, M2-7 advisory lane) is reasonable at ~2 weeks after I87, and the events themselves (winding-up petition, strike-off, new charge) are exactly what a subcontractor needs to hear mid-job.
verdicts.conditions: (1) No per-entity meter; include monitoring for business counterparties in the Firm tier (optionally Builder), running on free Companies House and Gazette feeds; add CRA monitoring only when a contract exists and Firm volume covers its minimum. (2) Bound to jobs with an accepted quote from switch-live to final payment recorded, auto-stop on close; unique source-event IDs (AGENTS §5.4). (3) Findings in the M2-7 advisory lane only, factual wording with source and date; the 'open a case' action appears only when the D03 entry test is already met. (4) D12 v3 names monitoring as a purpose with a balancing test and stop point; D07 retention for event records; D04 entries. (5) Domestic title re-check stays a pass-through option, not a meter.

revised_revenue.solo: £3 a year if metered; £0 as a tier feature
revised_revenue.small_firm: £22 a year if metered; £0 as a tier feature
revised_revenue.firm: £99 a year if metered (16.5 business jobs x 4 months x 50% x £3), overlapping I92's bundled watch; £0 direct as a Firm-tier inclusion

verdicts.key_risk: A metered SKU whose billing machinery costs more than it earns and that overlaps I92's bundled watch; as an included Firm-tier feature on free feeds the risk drops to the optics of nudging builders toward 10% cases.

verdicts.reasons: As framed, the reach is tiny: the curve only appears when a CRA suggested credit limit exists, i.e. on business customers who were checked under I87 (about 2 / 6 / 16 jobs a year, times attach), so a Solo builder almost never sees it, and the £24 'attributed' revenue is, as the idea admits, a label rather than a number. CRA reseller terms commonly restrict on-screen display of derived figures such as suggested limits to the licensed end user (assumption; must be confirmed before design), which could remove the comparison half of the feature entirely. The chart is also close enough to advice that wording needs review. What survives refutation is the pure function itself: peak unpaid exposure over time from the deposit and stage schedule (cumulative work done minus cumulative payments due) is a prevention finding valuable on every job, including the homeowner jobs that make up most of Solo and Small work ('under these terms you are £12,400 out of pocket at week 6'). That version has no CRA dependency, no display-rights problem, exact Money arithmetic in packages/core with property tests, about a week of work after I40, and it directly supports the deposit/stage-schedule and escrow actions (I40, I42). No trade app reviewed shows exposure against a schedule (success_fee_benchmarks §6 notes credit-control tools show limits against balances only), so it is a credible Builder-tier differentiator and a retention feature, not revenue.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Build the exposure curve as a schedule-only feature first, available on every quote with a stage schedule or payment terms; add the CRA-limit comparison only if the reseller contract permits display and I87 exists. (2) Descriptive copy only: two facts side by side, the limit attributed to the named CRA with retrieval date, no 'reduce exposure' recommendation; legal wording review of the card. (3) Include in Builder and Firm tiers; do not claim attributed revenue in planning figures. (4) Depends on I40 (stage schedule model); ship after it, not before.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct; no attributed figure is defensible; value is tier differentiation on homeowner jobs once the CRA dependency is removed
revised_revenue.firm: £0 direct; retention/upsell justification only; the CRA comparison fires on ~8 checked business jobs a year at best

verdicts.key_risk: Built as specified it depends on a CRA figure the reseller contract may forbid displaying and reaches almost no Solo or Small builders; built as a schedule-only exposure curve it is cheap and broadly useful but earns nothing directly.

verdicts.reasons: This is a design rule, not a revenue idea, and it is correct as a design rule: evidence already in the job (checks, portal declarations, acceptance record, approved stage terms) should pre-fill the M4-1 case workbench, the M4-5 pursuit templates and the M4-3 evidence pack, and debt collectors and solicitors do require debtor identity and terms evidence before instruction (success_fee_benchmarks §3, §7). The revenue estimate does not survive scrutiny. The D03 v2 withheld-payment entry test (§14.7: overdue beyond the threshold, customer refused/disputed/ignored the builder's own reminder, builder explicitly opens and approves fee terms, only cash settled after opening counts) makes cases rarer than 1 / 2 / 4 a year; 0.5 / 1 / 2 is a more defensible guess. The 10-point settlement uplift is concentrated in business debtors, where the wrong legal entity really does derail pursuit; for homeowners identity is rarely the obstacle (the debtor lives at the site), the dispute is about scope or quality, and the Late Payment Act gives no interest or compensation to offset the fee (§3). The uplift also only applies where a check was bought (25-50% attach). Reworked (cases x value x uplift 5-12 points x 10% fee x attach): Solo ~£1, Small ~£14, Firm ~£145 of incremental success fee, which the report says to treat as upside until pilot data exist (report §'Recommendation'). Cost is about a week of integration once M4-1/2/3/5 exist and no new providers, so it is worth doing, but the optics condition the idea itself names is load-bearing: the moment checks are marketed as 'so JobGuard can chase for you', a builder will feel the check was upsold to feed the fee, which is the betrayal pattern the report warns collapses trust in a word-of-mouth trade.
verdicts.conditions: (1) Never make a check a precondition of the fee, never change the 10%, never market checks as feeding recovery; keep the raw export free (I34). (2) D12 v3 must name pursuit as a purpose for officer/proprietor data and the Article 14 notice must mention it. (3) Exclude the CRA report itself from packs and templates (reseller terms commonly prohibit litigation/collection use, assumption); include JobGuard's finding text and public-register copies only. (4) D03 v2 entry test unchanged; contradictory evidence (declaration vs title) shown side by side with dates, JobGuard asserts neither. (5) Regulated-activity legal sign-off per research note §7 before any real pursuit; measure settlement rate and days-to-settle with and without a pre-contract check in the pilot (§14.17).

revised_revenue.solo: ~£1 a year incremental success fee (0.5 cases x £2,000 x 5-point uplift x 10% x 25% attach); effectively £0
revised_revenue.small_firm: ~£14 a year incremental success fee (1 case x £5,000 x 8 points x 10% x 35% attach)
revised_revenue.firm: ~£145 a year incremental success fee (2 cases x £12,000 x 12 points x 10% x 50% attach); upside only, not plan revenue

verdicts.key_risk: Optics: if checks are ever framed as feeding JobGuard's recovery fee, builders will read the check as an upsell that serves JobGuard, the exact betrayal pattern the fairness research says travels by word of mouth; the money is too small to justify taking that risk.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) Part B is a judgments search on a private individual who is not JobGuard's customer and did not ask for it. A homeowner who learns of it (via the Article 14 notice in the quote, or a later DSAR) may feel judged, which is the builder's relationship to lose, not JobGuard's; common-name false positives could lead a builder to mistreat a good customer. (b) Charging a margin on public registers can look like charging for what the builder could do on gov.uk. (c) Builders may use a CCJ finding to demand unreasonable deposits. What survives: the builder pays, chooses per quote, and gets the finding at once (nothing is withheld, so the shadow-bill trust problem does not arise); the data is public register data, not a credit file; the proprietor/quote name mismatch and leasehold-restriction findings protect both sides (work instructed by a non-owner is a classic non-payment and dispute pattern); the free customer self-verification path is shown first, which gives the homeowner agency; and the price is a confirmed HMLR £7 pass-through plus a small disclosed service margin, which price-fairness research treats as passing on a cost rather than exploiting an advantage (report, 'The hidden final check' section citing Kahneman/Knetsch/Thaler and Xia/Monroe/Cox). No supplier money, no fee linkage, no withheld information. Part A alone would be a clean keep; Part B is fair only with the safeguards below.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Part A (property) and Part B (named-person) are separate Decisions; Part B is never default-on, never bundled into an allowance, and is offered only after the free portal self-verification (I55) has been shown first. 2. Part B runs only if the quote the customer actually received carried the versioned Article 14 notice naming public-register checks; the builder chooses whether that clause is in their quote terms, and no check runs against a quote sent before it. 3. Card copy is findings-only: 'an entry matching the searched name and address', the search terms used, the register's own address match, source and date; no score, risk rating, or deposit recommendation; no wording implying a CCJ means the customer will not pay. 4. Bound to the quote's site address; one check per part per quote; no re-runs on the same address without a new quote; per-tenant rate limit. 5. Statement line shows the cost split ('HMLR fee £7 + JobGuard £5'); JobGuard takes no referral or volume payment from any register or data provider that is not passed through and disclosed. 6. The finding never feeds any fee derivation, D03 entry test or D11 signal on its own. 7. D07 retention class: named-person results deleted at job close or a fixed short period; official copies retained under HMLR re-use terms only; nothing aggregated or resold. 8. Legitimate-interests balancing test recorded in D12 v3 before any real data; HMLR Business e-services and Registry Trust terms confirmed for this stated purpose.

revised_revenue.solo: £113 gross (about £44 margin): Part A unchanged at £90; Part B take-up assumed 30% of Part A checks rather than 50% once it is opt-in per quote and pre-noticed in the quote terms
revised_revenue.small_firm: £189 gross (about £74 margin): Part A £151 unchanged; Part B £38 on the reduced 30% take-up
revised_revenue.firm: £259 gross (about £102 margin): Part A £207 unchanged; Part B £52 on the reduced 30% take-up

verdicts.key_risk: The named-person CCJ search (Part B) being seen by homeowners as intrusive, so the builder loses the customer's goodwill and JobGuard becomes 'the app that runs checks on your customers'; plus a false-positive name match causing a builder to treat a good customer badly.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation succeeds on four counts. (1) Customer relationship: asking a homeowner to submit to a credit search to have building work done is a request no rival trade tool makes and one the homeowner is likely to resent; the idea's own key risk metric is drop-off in acceptance, and that loss is borne entirely by the builder while JobGuard's £15 is earned only on completed searches, so JobGuard's incentive and the builder's are misaligned at the exact moment of asking. (2) Category shift: this is the first place JobGuard touches a consumer credit file, which changes what JobGuard is and creates a homeowner-facing data relationship JobGuard cannot fully control; a single mishandled dispute or breach becomes a word-of-mouth story about builders' customers being credit-checked, in a trade that runs on referrals (research note success_fee_psychology §4 on betrayal aversion and reputational spread). (3) Weak builder benefit: a CRA affordability band is built for lending, not for a one-off £10k+ project often funded from savings, remortgage or family; the protective value (identity, address, authority to instruct) is available without a credit file through I89 Part A, the portal declaration and a deposit/stage schedule (I40) or escrow (I42), which protect the builder better and offend nobody. (4) Fixed-cost incentive: the assumed £10k CRA minimum needs roughly 800 completed searches a year to break even, which creates pressure on JobGuard to prompt builders to request verification, precisely the nudge that would cost builders jobs. Regulatory weight (CRA vetting, CCA s.157-160 routing, ICO credit-referencing guidance, Equality Act optics) is heavy for a feature whose value can be obtained elsewhere. A reasonable UK builder would see this as a way to lose a kitchen, not win one.
verdicts.conditions: None; rejected. If the founder wants to revisit after the pilot, the only defensible route is evidence that builders lose money on verified-identity failures that deposit and stage terms do not prevent, and even then: customer-initiated only, never a JobGuard prompt to the builder, threshold well above £10k, and legal sign-off before any CRA contract.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (rejected; idea's own estimate was £38)

verdicts.key_risk: Customers declining or walking away after a 'Verify me' request, with the lost job and the 'they credit-check homeowners' reputation borne by the builder while JobGuard carries a fixed CRA cost that pushes it to promote the feature.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) Harm to the builder from false reassurance: national datasets are incomplete, so a card that reads 'none found' could lead a builder to execute works on a listed building without consent, an offence for the person who does the work; this is the one real way the feature could hurt a builder, and it is a wording and coverage problem, not a structural one. (b) Charging £5 per address for Open Government Licence data could be read as charging for what is free on gov.uk, and per-use micro-charges trigger the taxi-meter aversion the research notes describe (Prelec & Loewenstein; Lambrecht & Skiera); the fair answer is that JobGuard does the resolution and aggregation work, but the trust-optimal packaging is inclusion in the subscription. (c) Advice risk: the listed-building offence line is a statutory fact but could be taken as JobGuard's legal view. What survives is the strongest trust fit in the set: pure prevention, builder-paid or included, nothing withheld (a consent constraint is surfaced at quote time, which is when the builder needs it), no third party pays JobGuard, no customer personal data beyond an address, and a direct feed into site readiness. A reasonable builder sees this as the app doing homework they would otherwise skip.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Coverage honesty: every line distinguishes 'no entry found in [dataset] published [date]' from 'not checked (this council/dataset not available)'; the card never says 'no constraints' or 'clear'. 2. Statutory wording (listed-building consent, Article 4, s.20-style facts) is a reviewed, versioned fixed text with a 'facts, not advice' label and a source link per line. 3. Data minimisation: planning history shows application references, descriptions, decisions and conditions, never applicant names. 4. Preferred packaging is inclusion in Builder and above (or the I88 allowance) rather than a £5 per-use charge; if sold per address, the statement shows the cost basis and no charge applies when every dataset returns 'not checked'. 5. The feed into site readiness (M2-6) is a Finding the builder can act on or dismiss, never a hard block. 6. Any aggregator used is paid by JobGuard at a flat fee, never pays JobGuard, never receives builder or customer identifiers beyond the address, and is registered under D04. 7. Dataset publication dates shown; a re-check offered before start on site if the quote is older than a set age.

revised_revenue.solo: £84 if sold per address as estimated; £0 direct if included in the Builder tier (preferred packaging), where it becomes an attributed tier feature
revised_revenue.small_firm: £101 if sold per address; £0 direct if included in the tier (preferred)
revised_revenue.firm: £120 if sold per address; £0 direct if included in the tier (preferred)

verdicts.key_risk: False reassurance from incomplete open datasets leading a builder to carry out works without listed-building or conservation-area consent, a criminal exposure the builder bears after JobGuard collected £5.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) Fee adjacency: the idea itself says the payer identity is the single most useful fact for a later D03 withheld-payment case, so JobGuard is selling a check whose downstream use includes JobGuard's own 10%; if the check were ever a condition of the fee, or marketed as 'so we can chase for you', a builder would rightly see the prevention product as bait for the recovery product. (b) CRA reseller relationships commonly expect data contribution; if JobGuard ever fed 'this main contractor paid our builder late' into a CRA, that would be selling builders' customer data by the back door and a named trust risk. (c) Misidentification: a check run on the wrong company with a similar name could push a builder into a bad commercial decision. (d) Innuendo: lines such as 'parent registered in Jersey' are factual but can read as JobGuard's opinion. What survives is strong: the builder pays to learn about the entity that controls their cash flow; contracting with the wrong party is the biggest single cause of unrecoverable construction debt; Late Payment Act rights only exist against business debtors (research note success_fee_benchmarks §3), so knowing the payer is worth money to the builder regardless of JobGuard; the finding is surfaced immediately; open government data plus a disclosed wholesale report; no supplier or merchant money. A reasonable builder sees this as the app making them contract properly.
verdicts.conditions: 1. The builder confirms the exact legal entity (company number, registered name) before the check runs; the card shows the match basis. 2. Findings-only card: source and date per line, no JobGuard risk rating, no characterisation beyond the register's own words; 'does not create a contract' stated with the contract-pack action. 3. No data contribution or reciprocity with any CRA or data provider, ever: JobGuard never sends builder-customer payment behaviour, invoice status or job data to a third party; written into D04 and D12 v3. 4. Statement shows the wholesale cost and JobGuard's service charge; no undisclosed volume rebates or referral fees from data providers. 5. The check is never a precondition for a D03 case, never changes the 10% or its terms, and the 'open a case' action is hidden unless the D03 entry test is independently met; no copy anywhere links buying a check to JobGuard's pursuit. 6. Article 14 notice to the payer routed through the contract pack or order acknowledgement, documented in D12 v3 before real data; officers' personal data under a recorded legitimate-interests balancing test. 7. The included 90-day watch produces Findings only, stops at job close, and inherits I94's conditions. 8. The CRA report itself is not reused in pursuit unless the licence permits; only JobGuard's finding text and public copies go into an evidence pack (per I96).

revised_revenue.solo: £17 (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: The payer check being seen as, or becoming, a feeder for JobGuard's own 10% withheld-payment cases rather than prevention, and any CRA data-reciprocity that would amount to selling builders' customer data.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) The s.20 arithmetic ('38 x £250 = £9,500 recoverable against a £48,000 quote') is easy to misread as JobGuard saying the builder can only recover £9,500; in fact the cap limits the landlord's recovery from leaseholders, not the builder's contractual claim against the RMC, so a careless card could make a builder refuse good work or misquote the law to an agent. (b) Fairness of a £39 price where the builder fills in the questionnaire themselves and the wholesale report is about £8: 'who did the work' cuts partly against JobGuard, though the accounts read, the structured check and the reviewed statutory text are real work. (c) Filed RMC accounts are often filleted and may not show a reserve fund; an extraction that reports '£0' where the figure is simply absent would mislead. (d) Forged notices cannot be verified. What survives: this is builder-paid prevention of a specific, well-known way block work goes unpaid; asking a managing agent for its consultation notices is normal practice and makes the builder look professional rather than suspicious; nothing is withheld; leaseholder names are never collected; no third party pays JobGuard. A reasonable builder doing a £48k roof for an RMC would see £39 as cheap insurance, provided the card does not pose as a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Reviewed, versioned statutory text that states plainly that the s.20 limit constrains the landlord's recovery from leaseholders, not the builder's contract, and that the concern is the payer's ability to fund the works; no figure is presented as what the builder can recover. 2. Accounts extraction uses 'not shown in filed accounts' rather than a zero; filing date and accounts type shown. 3. Leaseholder count only, from the agent or title data; no leaseholder names or addresses collected or stored. 4. Questionnaire answers are builder-entered, never AI pre-filled; uploaded notices stored with receive time and hash and the card states JobGuard does not verify authenticity (AGENTS §5.8). 5. Statement shows the cost split (company report at wholesale plus JobGuard's service charge). 6. Never a precondition for a D03 case and no nudge to open one; the actions are contract-side (deposit and stage schedule, applications for payment). 7. Company data conditions inherited from I92 (entity confirmation, no data reciprocity, Article 14 route).

revised_revenue.solo: £4 (unchanged, about zero)

verdicts.key_risk: Builders reading the £250-cap arithmetic as JobGuard's legal opinion on what they can recover, then refusing good work or misquoting the law to managing agents, with JobGuard blamed either way.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) The serious one: Companies House streaming and the Gazette are free, so JobGuard's platform may receive a winding-up petition or strike-off notice about a counterparty on a live job whether or not the builder paid £3 a month. If JobGuard holds that event behind the paywall, a builder who later learns of it has the exact 'you knew and stayed silent' grievance the research says destroys trust (research note success_fee_psychology §4), and it would be silence for money rather than the decided shadow-bill rule. That is a refutation of the design as priced, not of monitoring. (b) Funnel risk: monitoring events that end in 'Open a withheld-payment case' can look like JobGuard cultivating its own 10% cases. (c) Alarm risk: a petition can be dismissed; a stark Finding could make a builder down tools wrongly. (d) Meter interaction: watching until 'final payment recorded' could keep a job counting as live on the founder's live-jobs meter after the work is done. What survives: monitoring a business payer during a job is squarely in the builder's interest, is what Satago and Creditsafe sell to credit controllers (success_fee_benchmarks §6), surfaces events immediately, excludes homeowners on purpose, and produces Findings only. It is fair once the free-source layer is not paywalled and the £3 buys only the paid CRA and Registry Trust monitoring.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Any event JobGuard actually receives from a free source (Companies House streaming, the Gazette) about a counterparty on a live job is surfaced to that builder whether or not they bought the watch; the £3 covers only paid CRA/Registry Trust monitoring, and JobGuard never holds a received risk event behind a paywall (stated in D12 v3 and the terms). 2. Business customers and named payers only; homeowners never monitored; the domestic title re-check stays builder-initiated at pass-through plus £2. 3. Findings are factual with source, date and the register's own status wording; no JobGuard risk score; 'a petition may be dismissed' style context where the source itself notes it. 4. The 'open a withheld-payment case' action appears only when the D03 entry test is independently met, sits below builder-side actions, carries no fee language in the Finding, and per-case fee approval (§14.7) remains mandatory. 5. Monitoring needs an accepted quote, stops automatically at job close, and a job awaiting final payment must not be forced to count toward the live-jobs meter solely because it is being watched (D09 v2 to define). 6. No CRA data contribution or reciprocity; wholesale cost disclosed on the statement. 7. D12 v3 names monitoring as a purpose with a balancing test, a defined stop point and the Article 14 route; D07 retention for event records; D04 entries for each provider. 8. Unique source-event identities and idempotent processing (AGENTS §5.4).

revised_revenue.solo: £4 (down from £6): the free-source layer moves into the subscription, so the paid watch covers only CRA/Registry Trust monitoring; attach assumed about two-thirds of the original

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard being seen to hold a counterparty risk event it already received behind a £3 paywall, or to run monitoring as a funnel for its own 10% withheld-payment cases.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) Advice by chart: showing peak exposure above a CRA suggested limit implies 'tighten your terms' however neutral the copy; if the builder then demands a bigger deposit and loses the job, JobGuard is blamed. (b) Gating a protective insight: the Solo builder paid for the check that produced the limit, and their own schedule produced the exposure; withholding the derived view to sell an upgrade is a mild instance of the 'JobGuard withholds what you paid for' pattern this lens targets. (c) CRA licences sometimes restrict on-screen display of suggested limits. (d) Stale limits could drive decisions. What survives: no charge, no third-party money, nothing withheld about the job, a pure function over the builder's own stage schedule and a dated third-party figure, and the builder sees the effect of their own edits, which is the kind of visible, effortful work the report says builders reward (Buell & Norton). Tier differentiation by tooling is normal; it is fair provided the bare facts are not gated.
verdicts.conditions: 1. When both a stage schedule and a CRA limit exist, the peak-exposure figure and the limit are shown as two plain facts on every tier, including Solo; only the interactive curve and live-editing view are Builder-and-above. 2. Copy is descriptive: no 'reduce', 'risky' or 'recommended' language; the limit is attributed to the named CRA with retrieval date and a re-check offer; wording reviewed. 3. Confirm in the CRA reseller contract that suggested limits may be displayed and compared on screen before build. 4. Pure function in packages/core on Money pence with property tests, half-even where rounding is needed; no network or vendor dependency. 5. The curve never feeds any fee derivation, D03 entry test or D11 signal.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: The chart reading as JobGuard's recommendation to tighten terms, with a lost job blamed on JobGuard, or Solo builders feeling a protective fact derived from data they paid for is held back to force an upgrade.

verdicts.reasons: Refutation attempts. (a) Double-dip optics: the builder paid for a check under I87/I89/I92/I93 and JobGuard then uses that same record to make its own 10% cases settle more often; if any copy ever says 'run a check so your case is stronger', the prevention products look like bait for the recovery fee, which is exactly the vendor-profits-from-your-loss framing the research warns spreads by word of mouth (report, 'The hidden final check' section). (b) Licence risk: CRA reports typically cannot be reused in debt collection, so the pack must not contain them. (c) Purpose creep: reusing officer and proprietor personal data for pursuit is a new purpose needing its own notice. (d) Regulated-activity boundary: helping a builder collect its own invoice appears outside FCA debt collecting on the sources found (success_fee_benchmarks §7), but that is a legal sign-off, not an inference. What survives: there is no new charge; the fee arises only from a case the builder explicitly opens after refusal or dispute, with per-case fee approval, and only on cash settled after opening; the builder keeps 90% of money they were not going to get; addressing the right legal entity first time is unambiguously in the builder's interest; contradictory evidence is shown with dates and JobGuard asserts neither. A reasonable builder would see pre-filled, correct debtor identity as the app doing its job, provided the check was never sold on that basis.
verdicts.conditions: 1. No check is ever a precondition for a case, the fee or the fee rate; the D03 v2 entry test and per-case fee approval before any pursuit remain unchanged. 2. Checks are marketed and prompted as prevention only; no screen, email or pricing page links buying a check to a stronger JobGuard case or to the 10%. 3. The evidence pack section includes JobGuard's finding text, the builder's declarations, the acceptance record and public-register copies; the CRA report itself is excluded unless the licence permits litigation or collection use. 4. The raw export of the builder's own evidence stays free (I34) so a builder can pursue outside JobGuard without paying the fee. 5. D12 v3 names the pursuit purpose and the Article 14 notice mentions it before any real data; D07 retention applies. 6. Workbench pre-fill is a proposal the builder confirms; JobGuard never asserts debtor identity, and contradictory evidence (declaration says owner, title says otherwise) is shown side by side with dates. 7. Legal sign-off on the regulated-activity position before any live case uses this section.

revised_revenue.solo: £20 incremental success fee (unchanged; highly uncertain, uplift is a guess to measure in the pilot)

verdicts.key_risk: Builders perceiving the checks as an upsell that feeds JobGuard's own 10%, so that prevention products look designed around JobGuard's recovery revenue rather than the builder's protection.

verdicts.reasons: (1) It earns nothing by design. The honest version is free-with-contribution; the £5 cash add-on is a fallback almost nobody chooses. Even the idea's own figures (£0/£12/£42 a year) are noise against a £29–£119/month subscription (report §'Recommendation'). Reworked cash revenue is £0–£6 a year per tenant. (2) The network cannot reach threshold at any scale JobGuard will plausibly have. The line needs ≥3 opted-in tenants to have invoiced the SAME company inside 24 months. Most small-builder customers are homeowners (research note success_fee_benchmarks §3), so business customers are a minority, and they are local: a landlord, a developer, a shop, a main contractor. Assume 3,000 tenants, 30% with business customers, ~5 distinct business customers each over 24 months: ~4,500 (tenant, company) pairs spread over tens of thousands of UK companies that buy small building work. Almost no company hits three contributors except national buyers, and those already publish payment performance under the Reporting on Payment Practices regime and are covered by Creditsafe/Experian. So the line says 'Not enough JobGuard data' nearly always, which trains builders to ignore the card. (3) The fact source is unreliable. Under M1-12 'Record customer payment' is a manual, builder-attested receipt whose provenance 'cannot become qualifying recovery proof'. Builders enter receipts late or not at all, so 'paid 41 days after due date' mostly measures data-entry lag, not the customer. Bank-verified dates arrive only with M4-7 (TrueLayer), and only for linked tenants. 'Disputed yes/no' is one-sided. Publishing that as a counterparty signal is an accuracy liability. (4) The anonymity is weak where it matters. With k=3 in a local market, a company shown as '2 disputed' can guess which of its three builders contributed; the builder's biggest commercial customer is exactly the one they will not risk. That fear suppresses opt-in, and give-to-get dies without density. (5) It is a named trust risk (builders' data reused across tenants) and a deliberate exception to AGENTS §5.1 tenant isolation, needing a separate read model, role, RLS-exemption tests, a D09/terms change, D12 v3 wording, a correction route for named companies and legal wording review. Realistic cost: 3–5 engineering weeks plus legal and ongoing support for corrections, for a line that is rarely populated. (6) Even where it works it is prevention: steering a builder away from a slow payer earns no fee (D03 v2 §14.7) and reduces withheld-payment cases, so it cannot be justified as a fee feeder either. (7) Precedent is thin: Creditsafe/Experian trade-payment programmes are not in the research notes and run on ledger feeds from thousands of contributors, not a few hundred manual receipts; Chaser/Satago (note §6) sell credit control at £45–£899/month without such a network.
verdicts.conditions: Do not build now and do not create the cross-tenant read model or isolation exception for it. Reopen only if all of these hold: ≥5,000 active tenants with bank-feed-verified receipt dates (post M4-7) rather than manual receipts; D12 v3 and D09 terms approved with an explicit data-reuse clause and a correction route for named companies; contributor threshold raised to ≥5 tenants and ≥10 invoices with tenants outside the company's own locality, so a customer cannot identify contributors; companies already covered by Payment Practices Reporting excluded from the value claim (JobGuard must add something); legal review of the wording; pilot evidence that the line changed at least one builder's pre-contract decision. Never attach a cash price to it: if it exists at all it is a give-to-get retention feature, not revenue.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 (assumption: at most one business customer a year; will not pay £5/month for a line that almost always reads 'Not enough JobGuard data')
revised_revenue.small_firm: £0–£2 a year cash (assumption: 30% have ≥3 business customers; 10% of those choose the £5 add-on over free contribution: 0.3 × 0.1 × £60 ≈ £1.80). In-kind contribution is not revenue.
revised_revenue.firm: £0–£6 a year cash (assumption: 60% have business customers; 15% pay cash: 0.6 × 0.15 × £60 ≈ £5.40). Ex VAT, unvalidated; assumes the line reaches threshold, which at <5,000 tenants it rarely will.

verdicts.key_risk: The three-contributor threshold is never met for the local business customers small builders actually invoice, so the card is a permanent 'Not enough data' while JobGuard has already paid for a tenant-isolation exception, a terms change, legal review and a named trust exposure; and where it is met, weak k=3 anonymity lets a company work out which builder reported it, which stops builders opting in.

verdicts.reasons: (1) The product does not cover the risk JobGuard's users actually face. Trade credit insurance pays on buyer insolvency and protracted default; it excludes disputed debts. Construction non-payment is overwhelmingly a dispute (defects, variations, pay-less notices, 'ordinary late payment'), which is why D03 v2 §14.7 builds the withheld-payment category around refusal/dispute. Construction also carries the highest UK sector insolvency rate, so insurers load, limit or withdraw cover on construction buyers and set minimum premiums a £600k firm will not pay. Whole-turnover underwriting is the norm; per-invoice SME cover has had a patchy history. (2) Take-up assumptions are an order of magnitude too high. UK SME penetration of trade credit insurance is low single digits at best, and a neutral one-line link with no advice converts at a fraction of that. Reworked: Solo £0; Small firm £0–£1; Firm £1–£14 a year, first year only, with introducer share more realistically 2.5–7.5% of premium (a slice of the 12.5–25% broker commission the idea cites), not 7.5% flat. (3) Regulation costs more than it can ever earn. Taking commission and passing exposure figures takes the activity beyond the RAO art. 72C incidental-information exclusion, so JobGuard needs FCA authorisation or IAR/AR status under a principal broker, ICOBS remuneration disclosure, a new D-record, a G4-equivalent gate, PI cover and ongoing compliance monitoring. That is thousands of pounds a year of fixed cost and founder attention against single-digit pounds per tenant across a small eligible population. The idea itself concedes 'the regulatory route is the dependency, not the code'. (4) It cannibalises the only 10% category that fits B2B customers. An insured builder claims from the insurer (and the insurer subrogates) instead of opening a withheld-payment case; JobGuard earns a one-off introducer fee and forgoes the recurring fee base. The idea admits this conflict. (5) Trust is worse than the idea's rating of 3. Sending the insurer the builder's named business customers and how much they owe is the 'builders' customers as leads' pattern with the builder's consent bolted on. The report's trust section says disclosure does not neutralise a conflict (Cain, Loewenstein & Moore 2005), and the UK energy-broker precedent (research note success_fee_benchmarks §2: Ofgem commission-disclosure rules, Expert Tooling v Engie on half-secret commissions) shows remunerated introductions are a live legal-risk area. (6) Precedent is overstated: the research notes describe Satago as credit control plus invoice finance and Chaser as credit control plus collections (§6); neither is shown earning insurance commission. Comparable pure-introduction revenue for a niche B2B SaaS is not in the research at all. (7) Dependencies: I95 exposure figures do not exist in the plan; M4-1 recovery cases and M4-7 bank data would be needed for credible exposure; D12/D04 entries for the partner; the whole thing sits behind G4 anyway.
verdicts.conditions: Do not build. If it is ever reopened it must be after G4, with counsel confirming the route (IAR under a principal broker or a confirmed exclusion), a signed single-partner agreement that actually writes construction SME cover including protracted default at premiums the Firm archetype will pay, a separate explicit consent per introduction before any exposure figure or customer name leaves JobGuard, fixed reviewed copy with the commission stated in pounds, and a pilot measurement of whether insured builders stop opening withheld-payment cases. If the trust position requires it, rebate the commission to the builder and treat the line as a service, not revenue. A no-commission, no-data educational link needs none of this and earns nothing, which is the honest floor.

revised_revenue.small_firm: £0–£1 a year (assumption: 20–30% have ≥£250k business invoicing; 10% click; 2–5% of clickers bind; £2,500 premium; introducer share 4–7.5% of premium; first year only, renewals not assumed)
revised_revenue.firm: £1–£14 a year (assumption: 50–60% eligible; 10% click; 5–10% bind, or at best 5% take-up among eligible; £6,000 premium with construction loading; introducer share 4–7.5%). Ex VAT, unvalidated; the generous end assumes a partner willing to write construction SME risk.

verdicts.key_risk: JobGuard takes on FCA authorisation or IAR compliance and a customer-data-sharing conflict for a product that excludes disputed debts (the main way construction customers withhold payment), converts at a fraction of a percent, and, where it does convert, removes the builder from the withheld-payment fee base that was the point of serving B2B customers.

verdicts.reasons: Tried to refute on four grounds; none is a hard blocker, but each narrows the design and the legal spend dwarfs the cash. (1) FCA / consumer credit. 'Providing credit references' (RAO art. 89B) is a regulated activity when the information concerns the financial standing of individuals or 'relevant recipients of credit'; that term (CCA 1974 s.189, RAO art. 60L) covers partnerships of two or three persons and unincorporated bodies, so excluding sole traders is not enough. Restricted to bodies corporate only (Ltd, PLC, LLP), the line sits outside art. 89B and outside the DPA 2018 s.13 credit-reference-agency duties: no FCA permission, appointed-representative or partner route is needed. A solicitor must confirm that reading and the exclusion list before any real data. (2) UK GDPR. A company's payment record is not personal data, but ICO guidance treats information about a one-director company as capable of 'relating to' that director, and, the larger problem, the contributors' data is personal data where the contributing builder is a sole trader. A customer company knows who invoices it; with a floor of three contributors and a displayed count of seven invoices it can usually work out who reported it. That fails the ICO anonymisation 'motivated intruder' test, turns the line into the builder's personal data, and exposes the builder to retaliation. A DPIA (Art. 35) is required because this is systematic evaluation of counterparties; the threshold and bucketing must change. (3) Competition Act 1998 Chapter I. Builders are competitors pooling information about a shared customer. Asnef-Equifax (CJEU C-238/05) holds that credit-information registers are not restrictive by object where contributors cannot be identified, access is non-discriminatory and the market is not concentrated; the design meets this if contributor identity is never derivable, access terms are the same for everyone (a paid non-contributor route is permitted) and no price or rate data is mixed in, so I29 must stay a separate pool. There is no buying-group or boycott mechanic, so collective-refusal risk is low. (4) Defamation Act 2013. A trading company must show serious financial loss (s.1(2)) and truth (s.2) defends accurate aggregates, but the realistic error path is a mis-recorded 'disputed' flag or a wrong due date: on a business construction contract a valid pay-less notice under HGCRA 1996 s.111 lawfully changes the sum due, so 'paid 41 days after the due date' can be false unless the data model captures notices. Reviewed factual wording and a correction route with a response time keep this low. Also: contributing tenants may breach confidentiality clauses common in bespoke main-contractor subcontracts; JobGuard's terms must warn and allocate that risk, and any exclusion of liability for the line's accuracy is subject to the UCTA 1977 s.3 reasonableness test because these are standard B2B terms. Not engaged: Consumer Rights Act 2015 and DMCC Act 2024 (no consumer recipient), Late Payment Act 1998 (no debt is pursued), CIS, VAT, MTD, AML (no money moves). True cost: DPIA plus data, competition and defamation counsel roughly £8k to £15k and six to ten weeks, against at most £42 a year per firm. The value is network stickiness, not cash, and the threshold is unreachable until several hundred business-invoicing tenants exist, so the legal spend should be deferred until then. Nothing here is certain legal advice; the art. 89B reading, the anonymisation design and the customer-contract confidentiality point need a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Subject scope: bodies corporate only (Ltd, PLC, LLP); exclude all partnerships, unincorporated associations, sole traders and individuals so the line stays outside RAO art. 89B; solicitor to confirm before real data. 2. Anonymisation: raise the floor (suggested at least five contributing tenants and ten invoices), bucket days-late into bands, suppress the disputed count below its own floor, and document a DPIA with a motivated-intruder test that assumes the customer knows its own suppliers. 3. Contributor opt-in with plain warnings: re-identification risk, possible confidentiality clauses in their customer contracts, a warranty that they may share, and withdrawal that stops future contributions; historic rows follow the D07 window (24 months assumed). 4. Terms: tenant terms (D09) grant the reuse licence; D12 v3 records the processing, with an Article 14 route only where a director is identifiable; a one-line notice in the builder's customer terms template. 5. Accuracy rules: due date taken from the invoice terms; 'disputed' includes HGCRA payment and pay-less notices; a correction route for the named company with a stated response time; wording reviewed for defamation ('recorded from invoices raised by participating JobGuard builders', never 'slow payer'). 6. Competition: no contributor identity ever derivable, identical access terms for all tenants, no price or rate data in this pool, and a short counsel note referencing Asnef-Equifax. 7. Use limits: advisory display only; never an input to fee entitlement, D11 signals or any automated account action; no export, resale or third-party access to the pool. 8. Engineering: separate read model and role with RLS-exemption tests (AGENTS §5.1), off by default. 9. Timing: do not build or spend on legal review until business-invoicing tenant count makes the floor reachable.
