verdicts.key_risk: Contributor re-identification: a named customer company can infer which sole-trader builders reported it, converting 'not personal data' into the builder's personal data, inviting retaliation and confidentiality-clause claims against the builder, with scope creep into RAO art. 89B if partnerships or director-level inference slip in.

verdicts.reasons: The legal route is real but non-trivial, the economics are thin, and the product conflicts with JobGuard's own withheld-payment fee. (1) FCA insurance distribution. Contracts of insurance are specified investments (RAO art. 75); introducing a builder to a broker with a view to cover is 'arranging' (art. 25(2)), and a per-policy commission makes it 'by way of business'. The art. 72C 'provision of information on an incidental basis' exclusion (PERG 5.6) applies only where JobGuard's business does not otherwise consist of regulated activities (true), the information is incidental, and JobGuard takes no additional step to assist conclusion of the contract; passing exposure figures to the partner is an additional step, and commission weakens reliance on the exclusion. Getting this wrong breaches the general prohibition (FSMA s.19, offence under s.23), the card's line is a financial promotion (s.21, offence under s.25) unless approved by an authorised person or generic under FPO art. 17 (a named-partner link defeats the generic exemption), and s.27 makes policies sold through an unauthorised introducer unenforceable against the customer, so a competent broker will insist on a compliant route anyway. Cleanest route: Introducer Appointed Representative of the broker (FSMA s.39), scope limited to effecting introductions and distributing approved promotions; no FCA fee, the principal registers JobGuard and approves the copy, typically one to three months once a principal is found (after PS22/11 principals are choosier about small ARs). Alternative: a counsel opinion on art. 72C (about £3k to £8k, four weeks) with zero data passed and fixed copy. A solicitor must pick the route; do not assume the exclusion. (2) Conduct rules. Trade credit is a 'large risk' (Solvency II art. 13(27): classes 14 and 15 where the policyholder acts professionally), so much of ICOBS and the Consumer Duty falls away for the partner; ICOBS 4.3 remuneration disclosure remains the broker's. Separately, half-secret commission case law (Expert Tooling v Engie [2025] EWCA Civ 292, noted in the research notes) means JobGuard should disclose the existence and basis of its commission before the click, not merely 'may be paid'. (3) Art. 39A 'assisting in the administration and performance' of a contract of insurance. Recording the policy as evidence and generic reminders to the builder are fine; notifying the insurer, preparing a claim, or agreeing a payment plan to satisfy policy conditions is claims handling and needs permission. (4) Fee conflict with D03 v2 withheld_customer_payment. An insurer payout or a subrogated recovery is not the customer's cash settled after case opening and must be declared non-qualifying, otherwise JobGuard earns commission on the policy and 10% on its proceeds. Credit insurers typically exclude disputed debts until adjudicated and often exclude contract works and retentions, so cover rarely pays on the disputes that become recovery cases; the take-up and premium assumptions look two to three times too high. (5) UK GDPR, D12, D04. Exposure figures include sole-trader customers' personal data; do not transmit them, let the builder self-serve on the partner's site, which also helps the 72C 'no additional step' analysis. (6) Consumer credit. If the same partner offers invoice finance, introducing a sole-trader builder to it is credit broking (RAO art. 36A); confine the link to trade credit insurance and treat finance introductions as a separate decision. (7) VAT. Introducer commission is exempt (VATA 1994 Sch. 9 Group 2 item 4) only where JobGuard genuinely brings the parties together; a bare click-through is likely standard-rated under HMRC Notice 701/36, a small partial-exemption admin point. Not engaged: Consumer Rights Act 2015, DMCC Act 2024, HGCRA 1996, Late Payment Act 1998, CIS, MTD, AML. True cost: one to three months, a partner agreement, a new decision record and a G4-equivalent gate, for £0 to about £60 a year per firm. This is analysis, not legal advice; the regulated-activity route, the promotion approval and the large-risk classification need a solicitor.
verdicts.conditions: 1. Regulated route settled before any live line: Introducer Appointed Representative status with the partner (FSMA s.39) or a written counsel opinion that art. 72C applies; the partner approves the promotion copy under s.21. 2. No data passed: JobGuard shows the fixed line and link only; the builder enters exposure figures on the partner's site; no exposure export, no quote handling, no comparison, no ranking. 3. Commission disclosed on the line itself, stating that JobGuard is paid by the partner and the basis (share of premium), before the click. 4. D03 v2 amended so that insurer payouts, subrogated recoveries and any sum received under a credit policy are never qualifying cash for withheld_customer_payment; the recovery workbench records the policy so the fee guard can exclude them. 5. Policy evidence handling stays on the builder's side: reminders to the builder only; JobGuard never notifies the insurer, prepares claims or manages payment plans (RAO art. 39A). 6. Partner scope confined to trade credit insurance; any invoice-finance or factoring introduction needs its own decision because of credit broking (art. 36A) for sole-trader builders. 7. D12 v3 and D04 entries for the partner even though no data is sent (the click-through and referral tracking are still a provider relationship); consent record for the introduction. 8. One partner, fixed neutral copy, threshold-triggered only, off by default; a new decision record and a G4-equivalent gate before any live introduction. 9. VAT treatment of commission confirmed with the accountant.

revised_revenue.small_firm: £0–£8/yr (take-up 3–5%, introducer share 3–5% of premium, disputes often excluded from cover)

verdicts.key_risk: Carrying on insurance distribution and issuing a financial promotion without authorisation or an appointed-representative arrangement (FSMA ss.19, 21, 23, 25, 27), compounded by a structural conflict where JobGuard could earn both partner commission and a 10% fee on insured recoveries unless D03 expressly excludes insurer proceeds.

verdicts.reasons: Part A (title register) is legally clean. The register is open under the Land Registration Act 2002 s.66; anyone may obtain an official copy, and conveyancing search platforms already resell OC1s at the HMLR fee plus a margin, so the intermediary model is established practice, not novel. Proprietor names are personal data: UK GDPR Art 6(1)(f) with a recorded legitimate-interests assessment, a right-to-object route (Art 21), and an Article 14 notice through the quote email/portal. The Art 14(5)(b) 'disproportionate effort' exemption is unlikely to be available because JobGuard already communicates with the customer, so the notice must actually be served. Part B is where the idea's regulatory paragraph is incomplete. It is right that no CRA consumer file is touched, so CRA permissible-purpose rules and CCA s.157 are not engaged. It misses that JobGuard itself, by collecting CCJ (Registry Trust) and Individual Insolvency Register data about a named individual for the purpose of supplying it to the builder for a fee, may be carrying on the regulated activity of 'providing credit references' (FSMA 2000 Regulated Activities Order art 89B; Consumer Credit Act 1974 s.145(8) definition of a credit reference agency: a business furnishing information relevant to the financial standing of individuals, collected for that purpose). That activity needs full FCA authorisation, not limited permission; on my reading the appointed-representative regime does not extend to it, and the art 89C onward exclusions cover firms already authorised for other credit activities and legal professionals, not a software intermediary. Whether a single pass-through of public-register results is 'collected for the purpose of furnishing' is genuinely unsettled (tenant-referencing firms take divergent positions) and needs a solicitor. If it bites, the cost (6–12 months, application and periodic fees, Financial Ombudsman and Consumer Duty exposure because the homeowner is a retail customer, CCA s.159 correction duties, complaints handling) dwarfs £38–£86 per builder per year, so Part B is economically dead in that scenario. Registry Trust: one-off public searches are for the searcher's own use; a commercial reseller needs a Registry Trust data licence with purpose terms (weeks; £6–£10 per search plausible; minimum volumes possible). The Insolvency Service register permits individual look-ups but has no API and restricts bulk re-use; check current terms. The Register of Judgments' statutory purpose (Register of Judgments, Orders and Fines Regulations 2005) expressly contemplates creditworthiness checks, which helps the LIA. Consumer law: no exposure because the homeowner pays nothing, but JobGuard must never auto-add a 'check fee' to the customer-facing quote; if a builder recharges it, DMCC Act 2024 drip-pricing rules require it in the headline consumer price. Equality Act 2010 does not bite on a findings-only card. VAT: the HMLR fee is outside the scope of VAT, but the bundled £12 service is a VATable supply (D02).
verdicts.conditions: 1) Build Part A now behind D12 v3 (LIA, Art 14 notice text naming ownership checks above a value, Art 21 objection handling), D07 retention class for official copies, D04 entry for HMLR, and an HMLR Business e-services/Business Gateway agreement. 2) Do not build Part B until a solicitor opines on RAO art 89B / CCA s.145(8) for a pass-through single search; if caught, either drop Part B, or restructure so Registry Trust (as licensor) furnishes directly and JobGuard stores only what the builder or customer uploads, or obtain FCA authorisation (only sensible if other ideas also need it). 3) Registry Trust commercial data licence and Insolvency Service re-use terms before any Part B search. 4) Card wording fixed as 'an entry matching the searched name and address', with search terms shown; no identity assertion. 5) Never place check charges on customer-facing documents. 6) Charging behind D14/D02 and G4; pilot absorbs. Solicitor needed for item 2 (estimate £2k–£6k, 2–4 weeks; assumption).

revised_revenue.solo: Part A £90 gross (£37 margin); Part B £0 until the art 89B opinion clears it, then up to £38 gross (£8–£15 margin)
revised_revenue.small_firm: Part A £151 gross (£63 margin); Part B £0 until cleared, then up to £63 gross (£13–£25 margin)
revised_revenue.firm: Part A £207 gross (£86 margin); Part B £0 until cleared, then up to £86 gross (£17–£34 margin)

verdicts.key_risk: Part B turns JobGuard into a 'credit reference agency' (RAO art 89B) requiring full FCA authorisation, with a compliance cost far above the £10-per-check revenue; Part A carries only ordinary UK GDPR transparency conditions.

verdicts.reasons: Three independent refutations, each sufficient on its own. (1) The data product almost certainly does not exist for a non-lender. The 'CRA affordability indicator' is derived from shared credit-account data governed by the SCOR Principles of Reciprocity. The idea's claim that reciprocity 'does not apply to a soft search' is wrong: reciprocity governs who may access shared data and for what purpose, not whether the search leaves a footprint. A builder is neither a contributor nor a lender, so the CRAs will supply only identity verification and public-record data (CCJs, insolvency, electoral roll), which duplicates I89 Part B at a £10k annual minimum. Quotation searches are a lender product. (2) Regulated activity. JobGuard running the search and furnishing a financial-standing card about an individual to a builder is the paradigm of 'providing credit references' (RAO art 89B; CCA 1974 s.145(8)). Full FCA authorisation would be needed; the appointed-representative route does not on my reading cover art 89B; Consumer Duty would apply because homeowners are retail customers; Financial Ombudsman jurisdiction, SMCR, periodic fees and a compliance function follow. Realistic cost: 6–12 months and low tens of thousands a year all-in (assumption) against £38–£126 per builder per year. That is a blocker in economic terms, not merely a condition. (3) Consent validity. UK GDPR Art 7(4): consent sought as the price of getting a quote accepted risks not being 'freely given'; the ICO expects a non-consent basis where there is a power imbalance or conditionality, and CRA-approved wording does not cure Art 7(4). The idea's CCA ss.157–160 line is also inaccurate: the s.157 disclosure duty falls on creditors and negotiators (not applicable), while s.159 correction duties fall on any credit reference agency, which would include JobGuard if it is one. Secondary points: the builder using the band to decline a job risks indirect discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 (JobGuard's exposure is reputational); the portal copy is a trader-to-consumer communication so it must not imply verification is legally required (DMCC Act 2024 unfair commercial practices). A lawful and cheaper structure exists but is a different idea: the customer obtains their own statutory credit report or uses a consumer-permissioned share (tenant-passport-style products) and uploads it as customer-provided evidence, so JobGuard collects and furnishes nothing. That redesign should be logged separately, not treated as this idea with conditions.
verdicts.conditions: Rejected as designed. If revisited: redesign as customer-provided evidence only (the consumer shares a report they obtained themselves), with no JobGuard-run CRA search and no JobGuard-authored financial-standing card; obtain a solicitor's opinion on RAO art 89B before any build; confirm with a CRA in writing which data a non-lender end-user population can lawfully receive; document a non-consent lawful basis or a genuinely optional consent flow that survives Art 7(4).
verdicts.key_risk: Full FCA authorisation for providing credit references, Consumer Duty and Ombudsman exposure, for a product the CRAs are unlikely to supply to non-lenders at all.

verdicts.reasons: No FCA permission, no consumer credit, no consumer-law exposure: the builder pays £5 B2B and no money moves. Address-level constraint data is not personal data in itself; planning application records carry applicant and agent names, so show reference, description and decision only (UK GDPR Art 5(1)(c) minimisation) and treat any cached raw response as personal data under legitimate interests. Stating that works to a listed building need consent and that carrying out unauthorised works is an offence for the person who executes them (Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990 ss.7 and 9, strict liability) is general legal information, not a reserved legal activity under the Legal Services Act 2007, so no solicitor regulation issue, but the wording needs a D06-style review and a facts-not-advice label. The real legal costs are two. First, data licences: planning.data.gov.uk and Environment Agency flood data are Open Government Licence; Historic England NHLE re-use terms must be checked, and any dataset containing Ordnance Survey-derived geometry (NHLE polygons, many council layers) carries OS redistribution restrictions, so use point or reference data or a licensed OS route; scraping council planning portals can breach their terms, so use a licensed aggregator; OS Places API is paid with its own terms. Second, negligent misstatement (Hedley Byrne): a builder who relies on 'no constraints' and does unauthorised works to a listed building bears a criminal exposure and may look to JobGuard. Mitigate with 'not checked' rather than 'none found', dataset publication dates, an explicit statement that the NHLE omits locally listed and curtilage-listed structures and that many Article 4 directions are not yet in the national dataset, and a liability cap in JobGuard's B2B terms that satisfies UCTA 1977 s.2(2)/s.3 reasonableness (death and personal injury can never be excluded). If a builder recharges the £5 to a homeowner it must sit in the headline price (DMCC Act 2024 drip pricing), so JobGuard must not auto-add it to customer-facing quotes. No AML, competition, HGCRA, CIS or MTD angle.
verdicts.conditions: Ordinary hygiene, none blocking: a written licence audit per dataset (OGL vs Historic England terms vs OS-derived geometry vs aggregator contract) recorded in the D04 register; reviewed fixed wording for the statutory facts with a version and review date; coverage statements per source; a UCTA-compliant liability cap and 'facts, not advice' label in the builder terms; data minimisation on planning records; never surface the charge on customer documents. Solicitor only for the wording and terms review.

revised_revenue.solo: £84 gross, margin near gross (aggregator ≤£100/month platform-wide, OS Places pennies per lookup)

verdicts.key_risk: False negatives from incomplete datasets leading a builder into a strict-liability listed-building offence and a negligent-misstatement claim against JobGuard.

verdicts.reasons: Company data from Companies House, The Gazette and the Payment Practices and Performance Regulations 2017 reports is public; officer and PSC names are personal data processed under legitimate interests with the Article 14 notice carried in the contract pack or order acknowledgement, as the idea already proposes. CRA business reports on limited companies and LLPs raise no 'providing credit references' issue because bodies corporate are not 'individuals'. The gap: RAO art 89B also covers 'relevant recipients of credit' (sole traders, small partnerships, unincorporated bodies), so a payer who is an individual landlord or a sole-trader main contractor cannot be given a CRA financial-standing report without the I89 Part B question being answered; restrict CRA data to incorporated payers and give individual payers the title and self-declaration route only. Construction Act: contracts with main contractors, landlords, managing agents, housing associations and insurers' networks are not with a residential occupier, so the Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 ss.104–117 (as amended 2009) applies: payment and pay-less notices, statutory adjudication, no pay-when-paid; the linked 'applications for payment' and contract-pack actions must stay inside D06's deferral (no automated notices) and the card must not imply compliance. CIS: when the payer is a contractor, 20% or 30% deductions on the labour element and the VAT domestic reverse charge change what cash the builder receives; a lawful CIS deduction is not a withheld payment, so the check should state the fact and D03/I96 must exclude it from case value. Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 interest and fixed compensation apply only against business debtors, correctly stated. No AML (no funds move), no insurance distribution (JobGuard arranges nothing with the insurer). CRA reseller terms govern on-screen display and redistribution to the builder. The 90-day watch inherits I94's conditions (defined stop, LI balancing, D05 bounded recurring charge). Naming a payer creates no liability, correctly stated. Legal Services Act: templates and 'name the payer' prompts are general information, not reserved activities.
verdicts.conditions: CRA financial-standing data only for incorporated payers until the art 89B opinion (I89) exists; a paying_party field with an Article 14 notice route in the contract pack and order acknowledgement; D12 v3 category and LIA; CRA reseller agreement covering end-user display; a factual CIS/reverse-charge line where the payer is a contractor, with D06 forbidding automated notices; the watch component subject to I94's conditions; D14/D02 for the £29, G4 for real charging. Solicitor: only to confirm the incorporated-only carve-out and Construction Act wording in the card.

revised_revenue.solo: about £14 gross (roughly 20% of distinct-payer jobs are individual landlords excluded from CRA data)

verdicts.key_risk: Sole-trader and individual-landlord payers pulling the check into credit-referencing territory, and CIS deductions being misread downstream as withheld payments.

verdicts.reasons: RMC, RTM and corporate freeholder data is company data, so no art 89B or consumer-credit issue; an individual freeholder would need the I89 Part B treatment, so exclude. The statutory statements are accurate on my knowledge: Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.20 and s.20ZA; Service Charges (Consultation Requirements) (England) Regulations 2003 reg 6 (£250 per leaseholder for qualifying works, £100 for qualifying long-term agreements); First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) dispensation. Three conditions follow. Jurisdiction: England only at first, because Wales has its own 2004 Regulations and Scotland has no s.20 regime at all; the card must refuse rather than guess outside England, consistent with D06's jurisdiction limits. Currency: the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 gives powers to reshape the service-charge regime and the government consulted in 2025 on raising the s.20 thresholds, so the fixed text must carry a version and review date and be re-checked before each release. Data minimisation: s.20 notices supplied by managing agents may include the leaseholder mailing list; request the notice template and proof of service without recipient names, or redact on intake, and say plainly that JobGuard does not authenticate uploads (AGENTS §5.8). Legal Services Act 2007: presenting a statutory fact is not a reserved activity, but negligent-misstatement exposure and UCTA reasonableness apply to the builder terms as in I91. Filed accounts of micro-entity RMCs often omit reserve-fund detail; show 'not disclosed in filed accounts' rather than a zero. The builder's contract with an RMC or agent is a Construction Act contract (not a residential occupier), so statutory adjudication and payment-notice rules apply; D06 defers any automation. Charge £39 B2B, VAT applies.
verdicts.conditions: England-only jurisdiction guard with Wales added only after its Regulations are reviewed; reviewed statutory text as a versioned fixture with a review date tied to LFRA 2024 secondary legislation; exclude individual freeholders from any financial-standing data; intake rules that strip or refuse leaseholder personal data from uploaded notices; explicit 'not authenticated' and 'facts, not advice' labels; UCTA-compliant liability cap; D12 v3, D14/D02, G4. Solicitor: statutory wording review.

revised_revenue.solo: £4 gross (unchanged; England only)
revised_revenue.firm: £78 gross (unchanged; England only, minor loss if Welsh or Scottish blocks appear)

verdicts.key_risk: Stale or wrong-jurisdiction statutory thresholds presented as fact, and leaseholder personal data arriving inside uploaded notices.

verdicts.reasons: Companies House streaming API and The Gazette are public sources with usage terms but no personal-data barrier beyond the officers' names. Ongoing monitoring is, however, a different UK GDPR posture from a one-off check: the ICO treats continuous tracking of named people as more intrusive, so it needs a legitimate-interests assessment with a defined stop (job closed or final payment recorded), scope limited to public registers and business-bureau data, D12 v3 naming monitoring as a purpose, and an Article 14 notice served at the first check that says monitoring may follow; document a DPIA even though Art 35 'systematic monitoring' is unlikely at this scale. CRA monitoring for new CCJs and score changes must be restricted to incorporated entities: monitoring a sole-trader or partnership customer is furnishing financial-standing information about an individual (RAO art 89B, see I89) and the consumer bureau's permissible-purpose rules apply; Registry Trust monitoring of individuals is the same. The homeowner exclusion is right; a one-off HMLR title re-check before a large stage invoice is covered by the first notice if it mentions re-checks. Charging: a per-entity, pro-rata, variable monthly charge is a standing recurring debit, so D05's bounded standing authorisation must cover it (amount bounds, notices, revocation) and D09 must classify it as metered usage, not subscription; the 'Watch' button is the approving Decision. FCA debt collecting (art 39F) is untouched because the case action appears only when the D03 entry test is independently met and the builder collects its own invoice debt. Provider duplicate and out-of-order events are handled by unique source-event identity (AGENTS §5.4). Revenue is small against these conditions.
verdicts.conditions: Incorporated counterparties only for CRA and Registry Trust monitoring; LIA and a recorded DPIA with a defined stop; D12 v3 monitoring purpose and Art 14 wording at first check; D07 retention class for event records; D04 entries for streaming and monitoring providers; D05 bounded recurring authorisation and D09 metered classification for the £3/month; case action gated by D03; D14/D02, G4. Solicitor: confirm the sole-trader exclusion and the standing-charge authorisation wording.

revised_revenue.solo: about £4 gross (incorporated-only haircut ~30%)

verdicts.key_risk: Monitoring unincorporated customers becomes credit referencing, and the recurring per-entity charge needs standing-authority approval that the revenue does not justify on its own.

verdicts.reasons: A pure calculation on the builder's own schedule set beside a third-party figure attributed to its source. No FCA regulated activity is engaged: not advising on investments (RAO art 53), not credit broking (art 36A), and not 'providing credit references' where the counterparty is a company; for a sole-trader counterparty the limit display inherits I87/I92's incorporated-only condition. The real legal cost is contractual: CRA reseller agreements often restrict on-screen display of suggested limits and derived figures and any redistribution, so the right to show the limit must be confirmed in the reseller contract. Negligent misstatement: the curve is arithmetic on the builder's data, the limit carries source and retrieval date, and the B2B terms should cap liability within UCTA 1977 reasonableness. It is not financial advice while the copy stays descriptive; wording review only. Consumer angle: deposits and stage payments from homeowners are payments in advance, not credit; only post-completion instalments would be a credit agreement (RAO art 60F exemptions), and this feature creates none. For business payers under CIS and the VAT domestic reverse charge the exposure arithmetic should use expected net cash, and D06 defers CIS automation, so label the figure as gross of deductions. No data-protection issue beyond I87's.
verdicts.conditions: Confirm limit-display and derived-figure rights in the CRA reseller contract before shipping; incorporated-only inheritance from I87/I92; descriptive-only card copy reviewed; source and date on the limit with a re-check offer; UCTA-compliant liability cap; a 'gross of any CIS deduction' label where the payer is a contractor. No solicitor beyond the terms and wording review.

revised_revenue.solo: £0 direct (unchanged)

verdicts.key_risk: CRA contract terms forbidding display of the limit, and copy drifting from comparison into recommendation.

verdicts.reasons: Purpose limitation (UK GDPR Art 5(1)(b)): reusing pre-contract check data to pursue the same counterparty on the same contract is likely a compatible purpose under the Art 6(4) test (link, context, foreseeability, safeguards), but D12 v3 must name pursuit as a purpose and the Article 14 notice must mention it. CRA reseller terms commonly prohibit using a report in litigation or debt collection or disclosing it to third parties, so the pack may carry JobGuard's own finding text and official public-register copies (HMLR official copies and Registry Trust certificates are admissible), never the CRA report itself; that lowers the evidential uplift somewhat. FCA: 'debt collecting' (RAO art 39F) covers debts under credit agreements and consumer hire, not trade invoices, and the builder collects its own debt (D10), consistent with the research note §7; construction payment is not a regulated claims-management sector; JobGuard's 10% is not a damages-based agreement because s.58AA Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 applies to advocacy, litigation and claims-management services. All three still require solicitor sign-off, not agent inference. One wrinkle: if a builder's terms allow post-completion instalments, the debt sits under a (probably exempt, art 60F) credit agreement and the debt-collecting provisions must be checked for exempt agreements; keep instalment terms out of scope until opined on. Civil procedure: where the debtor is an individual or sole trader the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims applies (Letter of Claim with information sheet, reply form, statement of account, 30 days), so M4-5 templates must comply; s.40 Administration of Justice Act 1970 and the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 constrain tone; DMCC Act 2024 unfair-practice rules apply to the builder's conduct toward a consumer. Consumer Rights Act 2015 s.51 (reasonable price where none agreed) makes unpriced extras more contestable, which the research note already flags. Lawful CIS deductions and reverse-charge VAT are not withheld payments and must be excluded from case value. Retention: check records and declarations should be kept for the Limitation Act 1980 six-year period after final payment under a D07 class. Portal declarations bound to an authenticated customer session are valid evidence (Electronic Communications Act 2000 s.7).
verdicts.conditions: D12 v3 names pursuit as a purpose with matching Art 14 wording; pack excludes the CRA report and includes only JobGuard findings and public-register copies, per the reseller contract; D03 v2 entry test unchanged and CIS/reverse-charge amounts excluded from case value; M4-5 templates conform to the Pre-Action Protocol for Debt Claims and s.40 AJA 1970 for individual debtors; instalment payment terms excluded from scope pending a solicitor's view on exempt credit agreements; solicitor sign-off on the art 39F, claims-management and DBA positions before G4; D07 retention aligned to the six-year limitation period; checks never marketed as a fee precondition.

revised_revenue.solo: £15–£20 incremental success fee (guess; haircut because the CRA report cannot enter the pack)

verdicts.key_risk: Purpose creep and CRA contract breach if reports are reused for pursuit, plus the unresolved regulated-activity sign-off that D03/D10 already require.

weaknesses: TEN-SECOND TEST: the headline passes ("£29 a month, 3 jobs on the go, extra jobs £20 a month, small jobs free, first job free") but the ladder's own 'counting in one breath' paragraph is nine clauses, and the full rule set a builder is bound by is about fifteen rules carrying about twenty numbers (four prices, four allowances, £20, four ceilings, £2,000, £4,000, fair-use 10, 90-day combined-value window, 90-day trial cap, day-31 import grace, 45-day prompt, 60-day dormancy, next-day pause, 3-in-12 subscription pause, £50k/£150k reserved bands). The research report (§'Three tiers work because people pick the middle') says the comparison must rest on one or two numbers; this ladder claims 'one number per tier' while shipping a meter whose mechanics only stay invisible if the builder never crosses a line — and by design all three archetypes sit at or over their plan's limit (Solo 2–3 live on 3 places, Small firm 5–6 on 6, Firm 15 on 12), so the average customer meets the meter several months a year. That is the running-meter experience the ladder itself cites Prelec & Loewenstein / Lambrecht & Skiera against (raw note price_level_and_tier_psychology §4).

'LIVE' DOES NOT MEAN WHAT A BUILDER MEANS. The meter runs from the `switch_live` command (BUILD_PLAN §3.1, M1-7) to the final-account lock (§14.4). A builder's 'job on' runs from 'we started on site' to 'we've sent the final bill'. The front gap matters most: JobGuard's prevention story (PO price checks, readiness warnings, deposit invoicing) needs the job live BEFORE site start, and small builders routinely win work 2–8 weeks ahead of starting. So the meter charges the won-not-started period, or the builder learns that accepted-but-not-live is free and delays switch-live — forfeiting exactly the prevention value the product is built around. The meter is aligned against the product. The ladder's dormancy rule cannot help because raising POs is metered activity.

JOB IDENTITY IS QUOTE-BASED, THE BUILDER'S IS ADDRESS-BASED. 'Separate accepted quotes are separate jobs' means the common 'while you're here, price the bathroom too' second quote at the same address for the same customer takes a second place. The builder sees one job ('the Elm Road job') and reads '3 of 3 places used' while thinking they have two jobs on. Nothing in the ladder merges same-customer-same-site jobs in the builder's favour; its only same-customer-same-site rule (the sub-£2,000 combined-value test) works AGAINST the builder.

THE HERO PLAN LOOKS MEAN NEXT TO BOTH COMPARATORS. Builder at £69 for 6 jobs sits beside ServiceM8 Growing at £59 for 150 jobs/month (raw note uk_trade_job_software, ServiceM8 table) and the research ladder's £59 for 10 live jobs (report §'Recommendation'). A builder will not parse jobs-per-month versus jobs-at-once in ten seconds; the ten-second read is '150 jobs for £59 vs 6 jobs for £69', and the Solo read is '50 jobs for £25 vs 3 jobs for £29'. ServiceM8's 15p extra job beside JobGuard's '£20 per extra job' has the same optics problem if 'per month' is ever dropped. The ladder's rejection of 10 places for Builder is a revenue argument (per-place £6.90; 'the small firm never grows into Firm'), not an acceptance argument, and it puts the hero plan — the one meant to sell most — at the weakest comparative position on the page.

RULES THAT FIRE AT THE WRONG MOMENT. (a) The £4,000 trip is 'shown on the variation-approval screen': the builder is approving a customer extra and is told JobGuard's price just went up. That attaches a JobGuard billing event to the one action AGENTS §5.14 says must carry no friction (fee-free capture; 'never degrade the builder's own billing'), and it invites the inference 'logging extras costs me money'. (b) The £20 line at switch-live ('This job takes an extra place') attaches the charge to a specific job in the builder's head, contradicting the ladder's own principle that places are tenant-level, 'never attached to a job'. (c) The combined-value rule ('sub-£2,000 jobs for the same customer and site within 90 days are tested on their combined value') punishes repeat business — a £900 gutter job in March makes May's £1,500 fence job for the same customer count — and the ladder is internally inconsistent about whether it is a counting rule (counting_rules list) or a D11 advisory signal (gaming list). Petty-feeling rules are what get talked about on site (report §'The hidden final check', Kahneman/Knetsch/Thaler on exploiting an advantage).

FIVE BUILDER-FACING CONCEPTS TO STOP A JOB COUNTING. Explicit PauseJob (next-day effect), activity-resume, a 45-day prompt, 60-day auto-pause, and a 'more than three resumes' D11 signal — plus CloseJob-with-reason and lock. A builder who is waiting six weeks for windows or planning (under the 60-day threshold) pays unless they know to press Pause; a subcontractor whose B2B final account is agreed after the defects period sees the job flicker between counting and dormant for a year if they wait to lock. The ladder does not say whether the watchdog keeps running on a paused job, so 'pause' reads as 'protection off'. Vocabulary compounds it: 'places', 'place-days', 'lock', 'accepted-but-not-live' and the job-list copy 'next place £20/month (or free until [date])' are engineering words a builder has to translate.

THE CEILING IS A PAYMENT GATE AT SWITCH-LIVE. 'At the ceiling the next switch-live presents a one-tap upgrade Decision … or the builder leaves the job accepted-but-not-live' is a block on going live, on site, with a won job — the friction the research report §'Charge for live jobs, not people' says to avoid ('suggest an upgrade, never block'). The ladder's mitigation is real (at the ceiling the upgrade costs £0–£10 more than what the builder already pays) but only if the screen says so; as written the builder experiences 'pay £179 a month or this job can't go on'.

THE BILL ITSELF IS A METER. 'Every bill lists each job that counted, its place-days and the rule applied' is honest, but a bill with a per-job days line is the running meter on paper. It is only needed on periods with overage; the ladder makes it universal.

THE PER-USER COMPARISON ASSUMES SUBSTITUTION. 'Lands under the per-user comparator at every point' treats JobGuard as replacing Tradify/Powered Now. JobGuard does no scheduling, staff tracking or reactive invoicing, so for most builders it is a second (or, with MTD-driven accounting software, third) subscription (report §'Builders' willingness to pay'; raw note success_fee_psychology §5: 'a subscription materially above about £40–£50/month would need a clearly separate value story'). This is a willingness-to-pay caveat, not a meter flaw, but the ladder's comparator claim overstates its position.

LESSER: identity checks for 'one trial per business' name the UTR; asking a sole trader for tax identifiers at sign-up is more friction (and more sensitive data under D12) than a first-job trial is worth — company number or VAT number where they exist, phone and payment method otherwise. Subscription pause says 'zero live jobs for a whole period' without saying whether dormant jobs block it. Annual prepay plus monthly overage in arrears is two billing cadences on one account.
fixes: USE BUILDER WORDS EVERYWHERE, RECORD THEM IN D09 v3 AS POLICY TEXT. 'Live jobs' / 'jobs on the go', never 'places'; 'Finished on site', never 'pause'; 'Send final bill' as the visible action that also creates the lock; job list reads '2 of 3 live jobs — next job included' or '— next job +£20 a month'. Bills are a flat line when within included jobs; only overage periods list the jobs that went over and their days. D09 v3 should carry the ten-second sentence as the policy's builder-facing text and M4-14 replay fixtures should prove that sentence reproduces the effective-price table, so the plain rule and the metering rule are one artifact. Never print 'per extra job' without 'a month'.

LET THE METER FOLLOW SITE WORK, NOT THE COMMANDS. Start counting at the earlier of the first site evidence on the job (proof/progress photo, delivery note, diary entry, or the first scope item entering `in_progress` in the existing §3.1 scope-stage machine) or day 31 after switch-live — one rule shared with the import grace. POs and supplier invoices do not start the clock (that is pre-start prevention work JobGuard wants) but do count as activity for dormancy. Stop counting at the earliest of lock, close, dormancy, or a builder-declared 'Finished on site' (the renamed PauseJob, prompted automatically when every scope item is `complete` or when the builder opens the final-account builder); any later site evidence resumes counting from that day (the ladder's existing rule) so it cannot be gamed. This aligns both ends with 'we started / we finished', removes the incentive to delay switch-live, and needs no new state machine.

ONE DORMANCY RULE, NO PROMPTS, NO EXPLICIT PAUSE BEYOND 'FINISHED ON SITE'. 'A job with nothing happening on it for 30 days stops counting until something does.' Drop the 45-day prompt and the builder-visible resume mechanics; keep 'more than three resumes' as an internal D11 signal only. State plainly that watchdog checks, must-surface rules and shadow signals run identically on a job that is not counting.

SAME CUSTOMER + SAME SITE + OVERLAPPING LIVE PERIODS = ONE LIVE JOB FOR COUNTING, regardless of how many accepted quotes. Deterministic from data the job already binds (accepting party, site address, live interval), builder-favourable, mirrors 'the Elm Road job'. The merge-different-customers risk is already structural (one accepting party per job) so nothing is opened. Delete the sub-£2,000 combined-value COUNTING rule; keep it, if at all, as a D11 advisory signal (that also resolves the ladder's internal inconsistency about which it is).

TEST THE SMALL-JOB ALLOWANCE ONCE, AT SWITCH-LIVE, AND NEVER ON THE VARIATION SCREEN. Greater of accepted and quoted net at switch-live; fair-use 10 at once stays. Drop the £4,000 trip entirely (a sub-£2,000 job that grows past £4,000 through approved extras is rare and the exposure is £20/month, bounded by fair use and a D11 signal). If the founder insists on keeping the trip, it may appear only on the job list and the next bill, never on Log an extra, pricing or approval screens, so AGENTS §5.14's fee-free capture stays friction-free.

RE-SIZE ALLOWANCES SO THE AVERAGE CUSTOMER SITS INSIDE THE PLAN AND THE HERO PLAN SURVIVES THE SIDE-BY-SIDE: Solo £29 / 4 live jobs, Builder £69 / 8, Firm £179 / 14, Contractor £349 / 28; ceilings unchanged at 2 / 5 / 8 / 16; £20 overage unchanged. Checks: Solo 4+2=6 < 8 and £29+£40 = £69 = Builder; Builder 8+5=13 < 14 and £69+£100 = £169 < £179; Firm 14+8=22 < 28 and £179+£160 = £339 < £349; Contractor 28+16=44 then custom. Effective price stays monotone (1–4 → £29; 5 → £49; 6 → £69; 7 → Builder £69; 9 → £89; 13 → £169; 14 → Firm £179; 15 → £199; 22 → £339; 23 → Contractor £349). D05 bounds unchanged (£69 / £169 / £339 / £669). Per included job £7.25 / £8.63 / £12.79 / £12.46, still rising with tier. Honest cost, labelled: the Firm archetype (15 live, ~14.25 countable) lands at about £184–£199 a month instead of £224–£239, roughly £400–£600 a year less per firm; firm revenue then rests on the Firm/Contractor workflow features (option 6) and the reserved weighting, which is where the ladder already says it belongs. Solo 4 costs almost nothing (the ladder's own 4-job Solo month is the only revenue lost) and buys the most word-of-mouth protection.

NEVER GATE A SWITCH-LIVE. At the ceiling, the job goes live on overage as one grace job for that period and the upgrade Decision is shown on the same screen as the cheaper choice ('You're already paying £69 — move to Builder for the same price and get 8 jobs'); the D05 bound becomes plan + (ceiling+1) × £20 for at most one period, and the two-period prompt stays. If the founder prefers to keep the hard ceiling, the Decision screen must lead with the fact that the upgrade costs £0–£10 more than the current bill and default the tap to 'upgrade', so the block reads as a gift, not a gate.

PUT THE UNIT DIFFERENCE ON THE PRICING PAGE IN BUILDER WORDS, ONCE: 'We count jobs you're working on right now, not jobs you've ever created. Most sole traders have 2–4 on the go; most small firms 5–8.' Show ServiceM8-style comparisons only with the unit stated, and state that JobGuard sits alongside a job-management or accounting app rather than replacing it, so the £29 is sold as the second subscription it usually is (this also argues for keeping Solo at £29 in the planned £29-vs-£39 test).

TRIAL AND IDENTITY: keep 'your first job is free until you send its final bill (up to 3 months); we take a card when you switch it live' as the entire trial sentence. Identify a business by company number or VAT number where they exist, otherwise phone and payment method; do not collect UTRs for a trial. Define subscription pause as 'no counting jobs for the whole month' so dormant jobs do not block it. On annual plans show overage as one monthly line, 'extra jobs this month', never a second invoice stream.

SEQUENCE FOR D09 v3: record the ten-second sentence, the four prices and allowances above, £20 overage by the day, the ceilings and D05 bounds, small-job £2,000 tested once at switch-live with fair-use 10, same-customer-same-site merge, site-activity start and 'Finished on site' end, 30-day dormancy, first-job trial, day-31 import grace, annual at two months free, subscription pause as a pilot experiment, and the reserved weighting switched off. Move the £4,000 trip, the combined-value test and the resume-count to D11 v3 as advisory signals. Everything else in the ladder (job-days, server timestamps, audit-chain events, replay fixtures, no offset, no per-job fee, G4 gating, no-charge pilot) stands unchanged.
result.summary: Refuted on acceptance and simplicity, not on the meter. Jobs live at once is still the right subscription meter, and the ladder's economics (job-days, £20 overage, ceilings that make the upgrade always the cheaper tap, post-lock never counting, retention never re-entering, no offset against the 10%) are sound and fair for long jobs. But as specified it fails the ten-second test on its own terms: the 'one number per tier' claim hides roughly fifteen rules and twenty numbers, all three archetypes sit at or over their plan's limit so the average customer meets the meter regularly, and the hero plan (6 jobs for £69) reads worse than both ServiceM8 (£59 for 150 jobs/month) and the research ladder (£59 for 10 live) in a side-by-side a builder will not decode. More seriously, 'live' as metered (switch-live to lock) does not match a builder's 'on site' and charges the won-not-started period in which JobGuard's prevention value (PO checks, readiness, deposits) is delivered, so the meter is aligned against the product; quote-based job identity makes the common second quote at the same address a second place while the builder sees one job; and three rules fire at trust-sensitive moments (the £4,000 trip on the variation-approval screen, the combined-value rule punishing repeat customers, the ceiling gate at switch-live). The fixes keep jobs as the meter: builder vocabulary recorded as policy text in D09 v3; count from first site activity (or day 31) to 'Finished on site' / lock / 30-day dormancy with activity resuming; merge same-customer-same-site overlapping jobs into one live job; test the small-job allowance once at switch-live and drop the trip; re-size to Solo 4 / Builder 8 / Firm 14 / Contractor 28 with ceilings and D05 bounds unchanged (monotone, checked), accepting about £400–£600 a year less on the Firm archetype and leaving firm revenue to the workflow features and the reserved weighting; never gate a switch-live; and state the unit difference and the 'alongside, not instead of' position plainly on the page. Everything here is analysis against a proposed D09; nothing is approval, and every archetype figure remains an assumption until the pilot measures it (§14.17).

weaknesses: OVERAGE CEILING IS ONLY CHECKED AT SWITCH-LIVE, SO IT CAN BE BYPASSED AND ITS OVER-CEILING BEHAVIOUR IS UNDEFINED. The ladder says 'tier fit is checked once, at switch-live, on the instantaneous place count', but places are also added by resume-from-pause, resume-from-dormancy, reopen-after-close, the £4,000 allowance trip and import maturation on day 31, none of which is a switch-live. Worked exploits: (a) on Solo (3 places, ceiling 2) switch 11 jobs live one at a time, pausing each straight after activation so the instantaneous count never exceeds 5, then resume them all; (b) import 15 in-flight jobs on Solo, all of which start counting on day 31 (over(D)=12 against a ceiling of 2). In both cases JobGuard must either bill beyond the D05 bound of £69 (a breach of the bounded standing authority in M4-13/AGENTS §5.3) or cap at the bound, which makes every place beyond the ceiling free and inverts the upgrade incentive. The ladder never says which. This is the direct answer to 'is the overage rule exploitable': yes, through every place-adding event that is not a switch-live.

EXPLICIT PauseJob WITH NO MINIMUM DURATION TURNS THE CONCURRENCY METER INTO AN ACTIVITY-DAYS METER. Pause stops counting from the next calendar day and any metered activity resumes the job for that day only. A job captured weekly (site lead uploads Monday, office pauses Monday evening) costs 1/7 of a place; a firm running 15 extensions with weekly capture can sit on Builder at £169 or lower instead of Firm + 3 at £239, and CloseJob('abandoned') + audited reopen is the same rotation under another label. The only stated mitigation, 'more than three resumes in a quarter is a D11 advisory signal, never a penalty', is toothless by D11's own design (no signal may change a price or take an account action) and would fire on legitimate use anyway, so it is telemetry, not a mitigation. Job-days were chosen so that 'a genuinely idle job costs nothing and an active one pays', but pause redefines 'active' as 'captured today', which the founder did not choose.

EARLY LOCK IS A DOUBLE WIN FOR THE BUILDER AND THE LADDER'S 'STRUCTURAL' DEFENCE IS ACTUALLY A BONUS. Lock is not a job state (§3.1 has no locked state; the job stays live until invoiced) and the ladder says nothing counts after lock. §14.4 explicitly permits 'later final-account revisions ... for corrections' and requires only that a lock exists before the final invoice, not that the invoice derives from the locked revision. Nothing in §14 or the ladder stops builder-logged extras, POs, supplier documents, progress photos or diary notes after lock, and no rule switches the watchdog off on a locked job. So: switch live, lock on day 1 with the baseline as the 'complete final account', run the whole job on a locked-live job with PO price checks, three-way matching, readiness and proof gates still running, then invoice from a post-lock revision. Cost to the builder: about one job-day and a false declaration with no consequence. Bonus to the builder: every shadow signal is 'received after lock' and permanently fee-ineligible (§14.6), which is what a fee-averse builder wants. The ladder's claim that 'it is the builder's own final check, not the place, that leaks' has the incentive backwards, and the two D11 signals it relies on (material evidence after lock, lock with low proof of completion) are advisory only. This is the single biggest hole because it dodges the subscription and the success fee at once while keeping all the prevention value.

IMPORT GRACE IS PER IMPORT, NOT PER ONBOARDING, SO EVERY JOB CAN BE A 30-DAY-FREE IMPORT. M1-17 is a first-class builder-attested path with no limit on frequency. A tenant can quote elsewhere (or quote in JobGuard and never record acceptance) and adopt each new job as lifecyclePoint: live: a solo's 48-day job becomes 63% free, a small firm's 83-day job 36% free; closing a job and re-importing it as a new job_id resets the clock. Worse, 'lifecyclePoint: invoiced never counts' combined with no live-state guard on metered commands (a pattern search of the variation, purchase-order, proof, supplier-document and final-account handlers found none today) makes an invoiced import a permanently free live job that can still receive POs, photos and variations. The ladder's only comfort ('harmless to the meter') assumes imports are rare onboarding events; nothing enforces that.

METERED ACTIVITY IS NOT GATED ON THE LIVE STATE, SO ACCEPTED-BUT-NOT-LIVE (THE LADDER'S OWN SANCTIONED PARKING LOT AT THE CEILING) CONSUMES THE WATCHDOG FOR FREE. The ladder's core answer to 'keep jobs off JobGuard' is that the builder forgoes PO price checks, proof gates and the final account on the off-platform job. That is only true if those commands require live, and neither §3.1 nor the current API enforces it: the state machine constrains transitions, not which commands a job in accepted may receive. Until that gate exists, a builder at the ceiling can leave jobs 'accepted-but-not-live', keep uploading, ordering and logging extras on them, and only switch live for the lock and invoice. The mitigation fails not because the idea is wrong but because it is asserted rather than built.

THE SMALL-JOB ALLOWANCE TRIPS ONLY ON APPROVED VARIATIONS AND ITS FAIR-USE CAP IS FLAT ACROSS TIERS. Quote £1,900, run £5,000 of extras as priced-but-never-approved variations or add them as lines at final review (both are fee-free capture and neither is an 'approved variation'), and the job never takes a place; this also rewards exactly the weak customer-approval discipline JobGuard exists to fix. Separately, 10 free small jobs sit on top of Solo's 3 paid places (13 concurrent jobs for £29) while Firm gets the same 10 on top of 12, so the allowance is disproportionately generous where the incentive to game is largest, and it invites a '£1,999 quote' culture from maintenance outfits. The combined-value rule ('same customer party and site within 90 days') needs identities the model does not have: the customer party is a free-text builder-attested name and there is no site-address field, so the rule is unenforceable as specified.

'ONE CUSTOMER PARTY + ONE SITE + ONE ACCEPTED QUOTE' IS A TERMS RULE, NOT A STRUCTURE, AND THE RULES CONFLICT. There is no site on the job and the customer is a string, so 'different sites for the same customer are separate jobs' cannot be checked, and it contradicts 'one accepted quote = one job' when a single quote legitimately covers several properties (quoting is free and unconstrained, so any split would have to happen at switch-live, which the ladder does not specify). The ladder also concedes that a subcontractor working for a main contractor runs a whole development as one job. That is not gaming, it is adverse selection: the highest-value, highest-cost-to-serve users (many POs, many suppliers, retention, notices) legitimately pay Solo or Builder, the reserved weighting is switched off, and the Firm/Contractor features that are supposed to pull them up do not exist yet (M4+). The size-disparity section names this honestly for the 15-job firm but not for the 3-development subcontractor, who is the more likely Contractor-tier buyer.

THE D11 ADVISORY-SIGNAL BACKSTOP IS USED AS A MITIGATION IN AT LEAST SEVEN VECTORS (pause rotation, early lock, close-without-lock, multi-tenant split, trial duplicates, under-attested imports, phase merging) BUT BY D11'S OWN RULE A SIGNAL MAY NEVER CHANGE A PRICE OR TAKE AN ACCOUNT ACTION. Every vector whose only defence is a D11 signal is therefore an accepted residual, not a mitigated risk, and the ladder should say so instead of listing signals under 'mitigation'. The trial-identity check is a specific example: sole traders have no company number, most are below the VAT threshold, and a UTR cannot be validated by a third party (and collecting it at sign-up is a D12 question), so 'one trial per business identity' rests on phone number and card, both cheap to change.

SMALLER SPECIFICATION GAPS THAT WOULD SURFACE AS TRUST INCIDENTS RATHER THAN GAMING: an inbound customer message through JobGuard resumes a paused job and charges the builder a day they did not choose; the D05 bound is stated 'per period' but annual plans bill overage monthly, so the bound must be restated per month; the effective-price table is monotone (checked: 11 jobs £169 on Builder, 12 jobs £179 on Firm; Solo+2=£69=Builder, Builder+5=£169<£179, Firm+8=£339<£349), but the ceiling-bypass in weakness 1 means the table is not what a tenant can actually be charged.
fixes: Enforce the ceiling at every place-adding command, not only switch-live: ResumeJob, ReopenJob, the £4,000 allowance trip and import maturation each run the same instantaneous fit check and raise the same one-tap upgrade Decision when the tenant is at places + ceiling. Define the over-ceiling state explicitly in D09 v3: over-ceiling job-days are metered, shown on the bill and charged only up to the D05 bound; while over the ceiling no further switch-live, resume, reopen or import maturation can commit without the upgrade Decision. For bulk imports, present the plan-fit Decision at import time with a deferred effective date (day 31) so the migrating firm chooses its plan before anything counts.

Give pause a tail: the first 7 consecutive paused days still count; day 8 onward is free (a pause shorter than 8 days therefore costs nothing extra to model and is billed as if it never happened). Weekly rotation then pays in full, a genuine three-week materials delay pays 7/21, and a winter shutdown pays a week. Apply the same tail to CloseJob-then-reopen. Keep the D11 resume-count signal but stop listing it as a mitigation.

Make the lock the end of site work for the meter and for the command boundary. Split post-lock events into two classes in D09 v3 and §14.4: post-lock flow (catch confirmation, catch-driven and correction revisions that reference the lock, invoice issue, receipts, allocation, retention release, snagging photos tagged as snag) never counts; post-lock site work (builder-logged variation, PO created or changed, delivery note or supplier invoice, progress photo, diary or voice note) is rejected with 'this job's final account is complete; start a linked job for new work', or, if the founder prefers not to block, re-counts that day and raises the linked-job prompt. Either keeps the trust rule (the reveal day never costs) while closing the exploit.

Make the lock a real completion declaration: it requires every scope stage to be complete or explicitly dispositioned (not done, removed, deferred to a linked job, each with a reason and recorded in the lock hash). This turns the advisory 'lock with low proof of completion' signal into a gate and improves the honesty of the final account for the customer as well.

Require the final customer invoice to derive from the locked revision plus revisions that reference the lock through a catch or a correction with a reason; an arbitrary later revision cannot be invoiced. This is the same rule §14.4 intends and it removes the day-1-lock route to invoicing a different account.

Scope the import grace to onboarding: only imports committed within the tenant's onboarding window (for example the first 60 days after the tenant's first import or first paid period) count from day 31; later imports count from day 1. An import whose customer party and site match an existing quoted or accepted job in the tenant is linked to it and gets no grace. Imports at lifecyclePoint: invoiced accept only receipts, allocations and credit notes; any site-work command on an invoiced import is rejected or converts it to live, counting from that day.

Gate every metered command type on the live state: PO create/revise/place, supplier-document intake, proof and progress upload, variation log/price/approve, diary and voice notes, and customer messages after acceptance are rejected on draft, quoting, accepted and lost jobs with 'switch this job live to use the watchdog'. This makes the ladder's central off-platform argument true instead of asserted, and it also gives M4-14 a clean event stream to replay.

Tighten the small-job allowance without touching fee-free capture: trip the place on the greater of (baseline + variations in any priced or approved state) and any pre-lock final-account revision net exceeding £4,000; scale fair use to the tier (free small jobs at once = the tier's places: 3/6/12/24); and add a structured customer party and site address to the job at switch-live (needed anyway for §14.6 attribution, the combined-value rule and D12 transparency). Show on the pricing page: 'jobs under £2k don't count, up to as many as your plan's places'.

Decide the multi-site quote rule at switch-live rather than in terms: a quote whose scope sections carry different site addresses activates as N linked jobs (one per site) sharing the customer party and acceptance record, or the builder attests it is one site. State the subcontractor case plainly in D09 v3: a whole development for one main contractor is one job, and Contractor-tier revenue from that segment depends on the Firm/Contractor workflow features shipping, so record it as a known under-capture until M4-18/M4-20 exist rather than as a mitigated vector.

Relabel every vector whose only defence is a D11 signal as 'accepted residual, telemetry only' in the ladder and in D11 v3, and reserve the word 'mitigation' for deterministic rules that change what is counted or what can commit. For the trial, drop UTR from the identity rule (unverifiable, sensitive), key the one-trial rule on payment method plus phone plus company number where one exists, and accept that the residual exposure is one place for at most 90 days.

Close the small gaps: an inbound customer message resumes a paused job for evidence purposes but does not count that day unless the builder also acts; state the D05 bound per calendar month for annual plans; and add the ceiling-bypass, pause-rotation, early-lock, invoiced-import and accepted-not-live scenarios to the M4-14 replay fixtures so the effective-price table is provably what a tenant can be charged.
result.summary: The meter itself (jobs live at once, job-days, £20 overage with ceilings that never exceed the next plan, post-lock never counts, dormancy, a small-job allowance) survives; the arithmetic checks out and the effective-price table is monotone. What does not survive is the boundary definition of 'live'. Four material flaws, each a concrete exploit rather than a hypothetical: (1) the overage ceiling is checked only at switch-live, so resume, reopen, import maturation and the allowance trip can push a Solo tenant to 11 or 15 counted jobs with no upgrade Decision, forcing JobGuard either to breach the D05 bound or to make places beyond the ceiling free; (2) PauseJob with no minimum duration converts concurrency into activity-days, so a weekly-captured job costs one seventh and the only defence is a D11 signal that by rule can do nothing; (3) early lock is a double win because lock is not a state, site-work commands and the whole prevention suite keep running on a locked-live job, the invoice may derive from any later revision, and every post-lock signal becomes fee-ineligible, so the ladder's 'structural' defence rewards the fee-averse builder; (4) import grace is per import, not per onboarding, and invoiced imports plus accepted-but-not-live jobs can receive metered activity because nothing gates those commands on live today. Two further weaknesses are adverse selection rather than gaming: the customer party is free text and there is no site field, so the 'one party, one site, one quote' rule and the combined-value rule are unenforceable as written, and the highest-cost-to-serve users (subcontractors running a development as one job) legitimately pay Solo until Firm features exist. The fixes keep jobs as the meter: fit checks on every place-adding command with a defined over-ceiling state, a 7-day pause tail, lock as the end of site work with a completion gate and invoice derivation from the lock, onboarding-scoped import grace, live-state gating of metered commands, an allowance trip on priced variations with tier-scaled fair use, structured party and site identity at switch-live, and honest relabelling of D11-only defences as accepted residuals.

weaknesses: Lower tier plus overage weakly dominates every next tier by construction. The ceiling rule 'plan + ceiling x £20 never exceeds the next plan' means Solo+overage costs no more than Builder at every count up to 5, Builder+overage no more than Firm up to 11, and Firm+overage no more than Contractor up to 20. At the small-firm archetype (5.5 live, 15% under £2k = 4.67 countable) the rational bill is Solo £62.40 on job-days, not Builder £69; at exactly 5 jobs the two are equal, so nothing ever makes the 'hero' plan the cheaper choice. The ladder's small-firm revenue (£69 -> £828/yr) assumes the builder buys Builder out of flat-rate bias while JobGuard's own transparency rule prints 'next place £20/month' on the job list. Structurally this is Option 1 (a running meter with a rising floor), which the ladder rejected, wearing three tier labels; the compromise-effect argument (research report §'Three tiers work because people pick the middle') has no bite when the middle option is never strictly cheaper for anyone.

The 15-job firm is under-monetised more than the meter requires. The ladder kept the founder's price points but gave Firm and Contractor 20% more capacity (10->12, 20->24 places) at the same price, and a flat £20 overage. Result: £224-£239/month, 0.13-0.14% of turnover against 0.23% for the solo (regressive by ~40%), £110-£125 under the founder's £349, and 55-65% of the 10-seat Tradify comparator (£370-£440, report §'Why £119 rather than £99'). About a third of the gap is recoverable inside a pure jobs meter (see fixes) and was left on the table because the ladder only varied allowances, never Firm's price or overage. The stated reason for 12 over the founder's 10 ('a £50 step at 11->12') only requires Firm >= 11, not 12; Contractor at 24 has no monotonicity justification at all (Firm 12 + ceiling 8 = 20 already makes 20 places smooth), so 4 Contractor places are given away for nothing.

The 20-job firm's ceiling is a design artefact, not a willingness-to-pay fact. The ladder says a jobs meter 'will not go past about £349-£669 ... do not try'. A 20-user firm pays Tradify Plus up to £880/month today (report §'Why £119 rather than £99') for a narrower tool, and construction-volume pricing (Procore, Buildertrend 2026, raw note construction_platforms_and_ai §Enterprise) sits at 0.1-0.2% of volume with a ~£3,500/yr floor. JobGuard's 20-job firm pays £339-£349 (0.16% of ~£2.7m). The cap comes from Contractor = 24 places at £349 with £20 overage, not from evidence about what such a firm will pay.

The two-consecutive-period upgrade prompt can never fire on Builder or Firm. Max overage is ceiling x £20 = £100 on Builder against a £110 step-up, and £160 on Firm against £170; only Solo reaches equality (£40 = £40) and only at its ceiling. The ladder credits this rule (borrowed from Design B) with pulling firms up a tier; as specified it is dead code on the two tiers that matter for revenue.

The value-of-live-work meter would have earned materially more from firms, and the ladder's levers for closing that gap do not exist at launch. Calibrated so the solo pays £29, a live-value meter yields Small ~£199 and Firm ~£1,305 a month; calibrated to the 10-15 seat comparator (£600 for the firm), it yields Small ~£92 and Firm £600, i.e. 1.3x and 2.5x the ladder. The ladder is honest that a jobs meter cannot fully close this without becoming a turnover meter, but its two named closers are Option 6 features (M4-18 interim applications, notices, retention, multi-approver: all post-G4 and unbuilt, so Contractor at launch is '24 places + multi-entity' and no 15-job firm buys it) and the reserved weighting (switched off, with no pre-committed switch-on trigger). That contradicts the research report's own conclusion that 'the subscription has to pay its own way, and the success fee should be treated as upside until pilot data exist' (§Conclusion): the ladder's firm economics lean on the fee and on features that do not exist.

Trial mechanics are under-specified in a way that changes solo revenue by 15-40%. The trial is defined as a place exclusion ('excluded until it locks or 90 days'), but Solo is a flat £29 plan: excluding one job from a count of 1-2 changes nothing unless the plan fee itself is waived while the only live job is the trial job. Either the trial is empty for the archetype it targets (the solo), or it is a plan waiver and Solo year-one revenue is ~£200-£290 (2-3 trial months, up to 3 £0 pause months, annual 'two months free'), not £348. The 1,000-builder illustration (£735k, £61 ARPA) applies none of trial, pause, annual or the firm's allowance; on year-one terms it is nearer £575k-£620k.

The per-user comparator is overstated in the ladder's favour. '£480-£660 for 15 seats' assumes every labourer holds a Tradify seat; the raw note price_level_and_tier_psychology §4 says most small builders have 1-3 office users and per-seat pricing discourages adding site staff, so a 15-staff firm more plausibly buys 4-10 seats (£150-£440). The ladder also never states whether JobGuard replaces Tradify or sits beside it; if it is an add-on, £239 on top of a £300-£440 seat bill is at the ceiling of what a firm adds, and the 'under the comparator at every point' claim reverses. Adjacent inaccuracy: 'per-place price rises mildly with tier' is false at Contractor (£14.54 < Firm £14.92), and lever 2 of the disparity fix quotes only three of the four tiers to hide it.

The solo is not over-priced on level (£29 matches YourTradebase, Qted Solo and Powered Now £28 and sits under Tradify Lite £34; the report recommends the same £29), but the overage premium bites hardest at the bottom: £20 is 2.1x Solo's included place price (1.7x Builder, 1.3x Firm). A solo running 4-5 mid-size live jobs pays £49-£69 against £34 on Tradify with unlimited jobs; the £2k allowance covers repairs, not a busy solo doing £3-8k jobs. The research's warning that a jobs meter makes builders keep jobs off the platform (§'Charge for live jobs, not people') applies most to exactly this pocket. Solo's residual risks are conversion, not price: £34.80 gross for a sub-threshold sole trader, the MTD accounting subscription competing for the same budget, and the untested card-at-switch-live (report §'Let the trial run').
fixes: Make the hero plan the rational choice for the hero archetype: cut Solo's ceiling from 2 to 1 (bound £49). Then 4 countable jobs cost £49 on Solo and the 5th is a one-tap move to Builder £69 (a £20 step, the same as any overage step, so no cliff). The small-firm archetype (4.67 countable) lands on Builder at £69 as the ladder already assumes, and a busy solo's maximum automatic bill falls from £69 to £49, which also answers the over-pricing pocket.

Recover the recoverable third of the firm gap inside the jobs meter: tier-scale the overage (Solo/Builder £20, Firm £25, Contractor £30) with Firm's ceiling at 6 so the D05 bound stays under the next plan (£179 + 6 x £25 = £329 < £349). The 15-job firm moves from £224-£239 to £235-£254 (0.14-0.15% of turnover) and the upgrade tap becomes strictly cheaper before the ceiling instead of merely equal at it. Alternative with the same effect if a single overage number is preferred: Firm £199 for 12 places with ceiling 7 (bound £339), giving £244 at 14.25 countable.

Restore the founder's allowance shape where monotonicity does not need the extra places: Firm 11 places (the minimum for a smooth Builder 6+5 -> Firm handover; the ladder's '£50 step' only proves >= 11) and Contractor 20 places (Firm 12+8 = 20 is already smooth). Per-place then reads £9.67 / £11.50 / £16.27 / £17.45, which makes the 'per-place rises with tier' statement true at every tier and adds £20/month at the archetype firm.

Give the largest target firm a real rung instead of a declared ceiling: Contractor £399 for 20 places with £30 overage and ceiling 16 (bound £879, in line with the 20-seat Tradify comparator), or a fifth rung 'Contractor Plus' at 40 places for £699 with 'priced on request' only above 60. Keep it a capacity price; the honest positioning line is 'still under what 20 seats cost you today'.

Replace the dead two-period prompt with one that can fire: prompt an upgrade when overage job-days in two consecutive periods equal or exceed (ceiling - 1) x days_in_period, i.e. the builder is living within one job of the ceiling, and show the exact saving. If no such rule is wanted, delete the claim rather than keep a rule that cannot trigger on Builder or Firm.

Specify the trial as a plan waiver and restate revenue on year-one terms: 'no subscription period line is raised while the tenant's only live job is the trial job; the trial job never occupies a place; the card is taken at that switch-live'. Then publish two archetype tables, steady-state and year-one (trial, subscription pause, annual discount, allowance applied), and rebuild the 1,000-builder illustration on year-one ARPA (~£48-£52, not £61).

Fix the comparator and the positioning assumption before any price conversation: state seats actually purchased per archetype (assume 1 / 3 / 6-10) rather than headcount, and record whether JobGuard is sold as a Tradify replacement or an add-on; compute headroom on the stated basis. Add both questions to the 10-20 structured price conversations the report asks for.

Pre-commit the reserved weighting's switch-on test in D09 v3 so the reserve is a rule, not a hope: for example 'switch on by D09 v3.1 if pilot data (§14.17) show Firm-tier subscription revenue below 50% of the seats-purchased comparator for the 12+ job cohort, or measured cost-to-serve per place on jobs over £50k above 2x the Solo median'. Record the same for Contractor features: until M4-18 and notices ship, the pricing page must not describe Contractor as anything but places.

Correct the two factual slips in the ladder text so D09 v3 does not inherit them: the per-place claim at Contractor, and the '£50 step at 11->12' justification (true only for Firm < 11). Keep the honest disparity paragraph, but add the sentence the analysis omits: 'as specified, every tier is weakly dominated by the tier below plus overage throughout that tier's ceiling range, so the ladder is a piecewise-linear meter; the fixes above are what make the middle plan a real choice.'
result.summary: Refuted on revenue adequacy, with the meter itself intact. Jobs live at once is still the right subscription meter (the research supports it and the founder fixed it), and the solo is not over-priced on level: £29 equals YourTradebase, Qted and Powered Now and sits under Tradify Lite, and the residual solo risks are conversion (VAT-inclusive display, MTD budget competition, card at switch-live), not price. The material flaws are elsewhere. First, the ceiling rule 'plan + overage never exceeds the next plan' makes every lower tier plus overage weakly dominate the next tier throughout its range, so the hero plan is never strictly cheaper for anyone; at the small-firm archetype's 4.67 countable jobs the rational bill is Solo £62.40, not the Builder £69 the ladder books, and the structure is the running meter the ladder rejected as Option 1, wearing tier labels. Second, the 15-job firm is under-monetised more than a jobs meter requires: the ladder gave Firm and Contractor 20% more capacity at the founder's prices with a flat £20 overage, landing at £224-£239 (0.13-0.14% of turnover against the solo's 0.23%, £110-£125 under the founder's £349, and 55-65% of the 10-seat Tradify comparator), while the two closers it names, Firm/Contractor features and the reserved weighting, are unbuilt or switched off at launch, which contradicts the research report's rule that the subscription must pay its own way. A live-value meter would have earned roughly 1.3x from the small firm and 2.5-5x from the firm; a jobs meter cannot close all of that without becoming turnover pricing, but it can recover about a third (tier-scaled overage £25/£30, Firm £199 or 11 places, Contractor 20 places or a £399/£699 rung for the 20-seat-equivalent firm whose current £880 Tradify bill shows the £349-£669 'ceiling' is a design artefact). Smaller defects: the two-period upgrade prompt cannot fire on Builder or Firm (max overage £100/£160 against step-ups of £110/£170); the trial is specified as a place exclusion that does nothing for a flat Solo plan unless the plan fee is waived, and the 1,000-builder £735k illustration ignores trial, pause, annual and allowance (year-one is nearer £575-620k); the per-user comparator counts every labourer as a seat and never says whether JobGuard replaces or sits beside Tradify; and the 'per-place rises with tier' claim is false at Contractor. Every fix listed keeps jobs as the unit, keeps the D05 bound at or under the next plan, and touches nothing in the 10% fee, the no-offset rule or the shadow bill. Archetype figures are the ladder's own assumptions and remain unmeasured until the §14.17 pilot.

Report written to `/Users/benharwood/Claude/Projects/my-new-project/reports/JobGuard monetisation and jobs pricing.md`.

**Summary (under 250 words)**

The jobs meter works. Charging by jobs live at once is the right subscription meter: builders already accept it (ServiceM8), adding site staff costs nothing, and it spreads twelve-fold from sole trader to large firm while landing under per-seat tools at every size. All three refutations kept the meter and attacked its edges; the report adopts their fixes. Recommended ladder: Solo £29 (4 jobs), Builder £69 (7), Firm £179 (13), Contractor £349 (20); extra jobs £20/£20/£25/£30 a month up to a cap never dearer than the next plan; counting starts at first site activity (or day 31), stops at final bill, "Finished on site" or a month of quiet; jobs under £2,000 free; first job free.
